Method: Construct AVTrace: 34,114 training examples; dev 3,500; test 7,000; tasks include onset/span grounding, synchronization verification, next-step prediction, cross-modal localization, chain parsing, event-conditioned comprehension; evaluate five open omni models with reference-blind normalization and deterministic scoring; perturbations to study sensitivities; temporal post-training evaluation.

Result: All five models score below the majority-baseline (0.556) on synchronization verification; low scores on chain parsing and event-grounding/comprehension; Qwen3-Omni-30B shows task-dependent sensitivity to modality removal and changes in visual input processing; temporal post-training improves Gemma4-E4B-it on several benchmarks; on three external image benchmarks, metrics change modestly with some degradations, while teacher-forcing perplexity decreases.

Conclusion: Semantic reference-text overlap should not be treated as a proxy for temporal localization; AVTrace reveals task-specific weaknesses and provides a testbed for temporal post-training.

Abstract: Omni models can describe video content, but can they locate events in time, preserve event order, and judge audio-visual synchronization? We introduce AVTrace (Audio-Visual Temporal Reasoning Assessment and Capability Evaluation), a silver-standard diagnostic suite spanning onset and span grounding, synchronization, next-step prediction, cross-modal localization, chain parsing, and event-conditioned comprehension. It contains 34,114 training examples and category-balanced development and test splits of 3,500 and 7,000 examples. We evaluate five open omni models under their respective input configurations using reference-blind response normalization followed by deterministic scoring. All five off-the-shelf systems score below the test split's majority-label baseline of 0.556 on synchronization verification, and obtain low scores on chain parsing and event-conditioned grounding and comprehension. Development-set perturbations reveal task-dependent sensitivity in Qwen3-Omni-30B to modality removal and changes in visual input processing, without isolating their underlying causes. Parameter-efficient temporal post-training improves Gemma4-E4B-it on several benchmark metrics. On three external image benchmarks, task metrics change modestly, including some degradations, while teacher-forcing perplexity decreases. Together, these findings show that semantic reference-text overlap should not be treated as a proxy for temporal localization, and that AVTrace can identify task-specific weaknesses while providing a testbed for temporal post-training.

</details>


### [50] [GRF-Recon: Global Ray-Field Optimization for Long-Sequence Feed-forward Reconstruction](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20012)
*Enpeng Li,Yunzhou Zhang,Zhiyao Zhang,Dexuan Lyu,Chenyu Wang,Chiyuan Cui,Cheng Cheng*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: A unified feed-forward 3D reconstruction framework for long monocular sequences, combining coarse-to-fine trajectory alignment, LoRA-informed monocular cues, sparse hybrid ray-field optimization, and joint ray-error trajectory stitching to achieve scalable, globally consistent 3D reconstructions with competitive SLAM-level accuracy.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To overcome GPU memory bottlenecks, degraded local geometry, and long-term drift in large-scale monocular reconstruction; existing chunk-based methods offer limited global consistency across extended trajectories.

Method: Coarse-to-fine trajectory alignment augmented by lightweight geometric priors; LoRA adaptation distills monocular cues into the feed-forward backbone to improve depth on fine structures; hybrid-weight sparse ray-field optimization leverages high-frequency geometric features to guide local point-cloud refinement and enforce cross-frame ray constraints; joint ray-error optimization during trajectory stitching to reduce drift; scalable architecture designed to outperform chunk-based methods.

Result: Extensive experiments show competitive trajectory accuracy compared with representative SLAM systems and globally consistent 3D reconstructions in large-scale scenarios; improved depth accuracy on fine structures while preserving inference efficiency.

Conclusion: The proposed framework delivers stable, scalable, and globally consistent feed-forward 3D reconstruction for long monocular sequences, achieving strong cross-frame coupling and effective drift mitigation beyond existing chunk-based approaches.

Abstract: Feed-forward 3D reconstruction provides an efficient paradigm for scene modeling from image sequences. Scaling these models to large monocular scenarios are constrained by excessive GPU memory footprint, degraded local geometry, and long-term trajectory drift. Existing chunk-based optimization strategies provide limited geometric constraints and fail to maintain global consistency over extended trajectories. We present a unified framework for stable and scalable feed-forward 3D reconstruction from long monocular sequences. Our approach builds on coarse-to-fine trajectory alignment augmented by lightweight geometric prior injection. Distilling monocular geometric cues into the feed-forward backbone via LoRA adaptation improves depth accuracy on fine structures while preserving inference efficiency. We introduce a hybrid-weight sparse ray-field optimization that leverages high-frequency geometric features to guide local point-cloud refinement and enforce consistent inter-frame ray constraints. Unlike prior chunk-based methods, this establishes strong cross-frame geometric coupling while maintaining scalability. Finally, an efficient trajectory stitching strategy with joint ray-error optimization explicitly reduces accumulated drift. Extensive experiments show that our approach achieves competitive trajectory accuracy compared with representative SLAM systems, while maintaining globally consistent 3D reconstruction in large-scale scenarios.

</details>


### [51] [Astronex-World 1.0: Real-Time Interactive World Model Foundation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20034)
*Xin Zhou,Cong Miao*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: A 5B video-world-model foundation (Astronex-World 1.0) enabling text/image-to-video prediction with text events, bidirectional and causal models, block-causal attention, and action-conditioned control; real-time streaming and strong benchmarks against larger models.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Develop a scalable, controllable video world-model capable of embodied AI tasks (vision-language-grounded video prediction with action conditioning and post-training interfaces for driving/embodied intelligence).

Method: Five-stage training on the Wan2.2-TI2V-5B prior, with PRoPE camera embedding, a 64-d action stream injected per Transformer layer, and two model variants (bidirectional full-context and block-causal causal) using cross-block KV caching; five-stage distillation/restoration/distribution matching, converting backbone to block-causal generation, and creating a few-step student; 832x480 video at 24 fps; training on two NVIDIA L20 48 GB GPUs; real-time streaming on a single GPU.

Result: Achieves 832x480@24fps; WBench Navi 73.5 and WBench Full 70.0; outperforms some larger 13.6B–14B models (LongCat-Video, Helios) and is near the 22B LTX-2.3; surpasses YUME 1.5; demonstrates post-training interfaces for embodied intelligence and autonomous driving.

Conclusion: The 5B Astronex-World 1.0 delivers competitive, efficient controllable video-world modeling with strong benchmarks, real-time capabilities, and practical post-training interfaces for embodied AI applications.

Abstract: We present Astronex-World 1.0, an open controllable video world-model foundation. Given a text prompt (text-to-video) or an initial observation (image-to-video), the model predicts future visual states under frame-aligned camera trajectories, continuous actions, and an embodiment identifier, and accepts text events inserted at a specified position of a rollout. The family provides a bidirectional model for full-context generation and a causal model with block-causal attention and cross-block KV caching for persistent generation, both built on the Wan2.2-TI2V-5B prior. PRoPE injects camera intrinsics and extrinsics, while a 64-dimensional action stream modulates every Transformer layer. A five-stage training path develops bidirectional camera and action control, converts the backbone to block-causal generation, distills a few-step student, restores mixed-domain dynamics, and applies asymmetric DMD/DMD2 distribution matching. The causal model generates 832x480 video at 24 fps. All five training stages run on two NVIDIA L20 48 GB GPUs, and the causal model streams in real time on one. It scores 73.5 on WBench Navi and 70.0 on WBench Full. On Full, this 5B model is above the 13.6B LongCat-Video and the 14B Helios, within one point of the 22B LTX-2.3, and above YUME 1.5, which is post-trained from the same 5B prior on NVIDIA A100 GPUs. The reserved action input and output interfaces allow post-training for embodied intelligence and autonomous driving.

</details>


### [52] [A Free Lunch? Adapting PP-OCRv6 for Historical Text Recognition](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20064)
*Benjamin Kiessling*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: Lightweight, recurrence-free recognizers (PP-OCRv6) for historical HTR show limited gains from scratch but improve with heterogeneous pretraining; fine-tuned PP-OCRv6 can outperform a large VLM (Medusa) tailored for Latin-script historical HTR.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Evaluate whether compact, language-model-free recognizers can match or surpass larger vision-language models on historical handwriting recognition across cross-domain pretraining, domain adaptation, corpus-level fine-tuning, and few-shot adaptation.

Method: Adapt PP-OCRv6 for historical line recognition; compare against a conventional CRNN across generalized pretraining, domain-specific training, corpus-level fine-tuning, and manuscript-specific few-shot adaptation on multilingual Latin- and Arabic-script manuscripts; benchmark against Qwen3.5-based Medusa.

Result: PP-OCRv6 does not consistently outperform CRNN when trained from scratch; heterogeneous pretraining markedly improves generalization; fine-tuned PP-OCRv6 can outperform Medusa in targeted tasks.

Conclusion: Appropriate pretraining strategies enable lightweight, recurrence-free recognizers to reach competitive performance for historical HTR, and can surpass large VLMs after fine-tuning, highlighting practical advantages in terms of cost and data requirements.

Abstract: Despite impressive reported scores, large vision-language models have seen limited practical uptake in historical automatic text recognition because of their computational cost, dependence on large-scale pretraining, and hallucination. Historical ATR therefore continues to rely largely on compact CRNN line recognizers, which are visually grounded and trainable on modest data. Lightweight recurrence-free recognizers promise the accuracy of larger models with the practical advantages of CRNNs, yet have not been comprehensively evaluated on historical writing. We adapt PP-OCRv6, a recent compact text recognizer without strong language modeling, for historical line recognition and compare it with a conventional CRNN across generalized pretraining, domain-specific training, corpus-level fine-tuning, and manuscript-specific few-shot adaptation on multilingual Latin- and Arabic-script material. While PP-OCRv6 does not consistently outperform the baseline when trained from scratch, heterogeneous pretraining produces markedly better generalization. Comparisons with the Qwen3.5-based Medusa recognizer further show that fine-tuned PP-OCRv6 can outperform a large VLM tailored towards historical Latin-script HTR.

</details>


### [53] [PointEvent: Rethinking Event-based Tiny Object Detection via Serialized Motion Evidence Accumulation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20066)
*Zongze Wu,Baofeng Jia,Weiqi Yan,Jingyuan Zhang,Yu Zang,Xiaoyu Chen,Jing Han*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: Serialized motion evidence accumulation for event cameras via complementary serializations of the event stream (locality-preserving spatiotemporal paths and chronology-preserving temporal paths), implemented in a lightweight PointEvent state-space framework that alternates serialized scans to consolidate motion signals beyond local neighborhoods. Achieves state-of-the-art results with fewer parameters and faster inference; code available.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Distant UAV targets produce sparse, fragmented events that are easily overwhelmed by clutter and ego-motion; existing dense representations or local sparse spatiotemporal models are inefficient or fail to capture motion continuity across asynchronous events. A method that enforces motion continuity via directed, serialized propagation can better consolidate evidence with less computation.

Method: Organize the same event stream into two complementary serializations: (1) locality-preserving spatiotemporal paths and (2) chronology-preserving temporal paths. Alternate serialized scans across these orders within a lightweight event-wise state-space framework (PointEvent). Progressive consolidation of fragmented motion evidence beyond fixed local neighborhoods. A high-resolution event branch captures fine-grained responses; compact context modulation reduces interference.

Result: Experimental results show state-of-the-art performance with the fewest parameters and fastest measured inference among the compared methods on the tested task (tiny UAV detection). Code available at the provided GitHub link.

Conclusion: Serialized, complementary serializations enable robust motion evidence propagation for distant, sparse event data. The PointEvent framework provides an efficient, real-time capable approach that balances high-resolution responses with compact contextual processing to suppress clutter and ego-motion effects.

Abstract: Event cameras offer high temporal resolution and motion sensitivity for tiny UAV detection, yet distant targets generate sparse and fragmented events that are easily overwhelmed by clutter and ego-motion. Existing methods mainly rely on dense event representations or local sparse spatiotemporal modeling, resulting in redundant computation or fragmented modeling of motion continuity across distant asynchronous events. To address this limitation, we introduce serialized motion evidence accumulation, which treats motion continuity as an ordered evidence propagation process. Specifically, the same event stream is organized into locality-preserving spatiotemporal paths and chronology-preserving temporal paths through the latent complementary serializations. Based on this principle, we propose PointEvent, a lightweight event-wise state-space framework that alternates serialized scans across the complementary orders, progressively consolidating fragmented motion evidence beyond fixed local neighborhoods. A high-resolution event branch preserves fine-grained target responses, while compact context modulation suppresses interference. Experiments demonstrate that PointEvent achieves SOTA with the fewest parameters and fastest measured inference among the compared methods. Code: https://github.com/wzz-z/PointEvent

</details>


### [54] [G^2RA-NET: Graph-based Cross-Slice Relation Modeling with Attention Gating for Medical Image Segmentation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20088)
*Shengye Wang,Zonglin Wu,Liang Fan,Yule Xue,Haozhe Zhao*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: G^2RA-Net uses graph-based cross-slice relationship modeling and cross-slice attention gating to improve segmentation of anisotropic medical volumes, outperforming baselines on brain MRI and abdominal CT with better boundary quality.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Anisotropic volumes pose challenges for cross-slice context; existing methods struggle to model inter-slice dependencies efficiently, affecting segmentation consistency and accuracy.

Method: Graph-Based Slice Relationship Modeling (GSRM) models each slice as a graph node and propagates semantic context via graph message passing; Cross-Slice Attention Gate (CSAG) selects relevant neighboring context and modulates features with attention to emphasize target anatomy.

Result: On brain MRI and abdominal CT datasets, G^2RA-Net achieves superior segmentation accuracy and boundary quality compared with representative methods; ablation studies validate each design component.

Conclusion: The proposed framework effectively integrates graph-based cross-slice modeling with attention gating to enhance segmentation in anisotropic volumes; demonstrates improved accuracy and boundary delineation, with ablations supporting the contributions.

Abstract: Medical image segmentation supports quantitative clinical analysis and computer-aided diagnosis. Recent methods for medical image segmentation have improved both local feature representation and volumetric context modeling. However, existing methods still strug- gle to efficiently model cross-slice relations in anisotropic volumet- ric images, limiting segmentation consistency and accuracy. This pa- per proposes G^2RA-Net, a medical image segmentation framework that combines graph-based cross-slice relation modeling with atten- tion gating. Graph-Based Slice Relationship Modeling (GSRM) cap- tures anatomical dependencies across consecutive slices by repre- senting each slice as a graph node and propagating semantic con- text through graph message passing. The Cross-Slice Attention Gate (CSAG) then selects relevant neighboring context and emphasizes target anatomical regions through attention-guided feature modula- tion. Experiments on brain MRI and abdominal CT datasets demon- strate that G^2RA-Net outperforms representative methods in seg- mentation accuracy and boundary quality. Ablation studies further validate the proposed design.

</details>


### [55] [A Smaller Transformer in Your Transformer](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20100)
*Dhananjay Tomar,Marius Aasan,Andreas Kleppe,Adín Ramírez Rivera*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: Introduces Transformer-Within-Transformer (TWT): a post-hoc block fusion that aggregates contiguous redundant Transformer layers into a single learned surrogate layer, reducing parameters and compute while preserving accuracy on natural images and histopathology tasks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Vision Transformers exhibit depthwise redundant computation; existing redundancy-exploitation methods either fail to reduce compute or degrade expressivity; a unified framework is needed to separate geometric computation from surrogate interventions and enable effective, post-hoc compression.

Method: Formalize a unified view of block redundancy and apply post-hoc fusion by aggregating contiguous redundant layers into a single learned surrogate layer (Transformer-Within-Transformer, TWT). This decouples geometry from surrogate interventions and reduces depth without sacrificing expressivity.

Result: Parameter count and inference compute are reduced; models with half the depth remain competitive on natural images; in histopathology settings, TWT matches or improves the original baseline.

Conclusion: TWT demonstrates effective redundancy exploitation in vision transformers via post-hoc surrogate fusion, preserving expressivity while lowering compute and parameter costs; the approach is broadly applicable across domains.

Abstract: Recent findings indicate that Vision Transformers settle into locally similar computational phases, implying a level of depthwise computational redundancy. However, existing methods to exploit this redundancy either fail to reduce inference compute or severely degrade model expressivity. In this work, we formalise a unified view of block redundancy that decouples the geometry from specific surrogate interventions. We then introduce Transformer-Within-Transformer (TWT), a post-hoc method that fuses contiguous groups of redundant layers into a single learned surrogate layer. TWT reduces parameter count and inference compute while remaining competitive with original models using half the depth on natural images, and in several downstream histopathology settings, TWT matches or even improves on the original baseline.

</details>


### [56] [AnyviewMeter: Adapting Robotic Reward Models with Camera Geometry and Multi-View Attention](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20106)
*Yuang Tu,Runjia Tan,Yujie Yan,Jinghan Hu,Chen Lv*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: AnyviewMeter adapts robotic reward models to local camera geometry to improve task-progress estimation across single- and multi-view observations, yielding substantial reductions in prediction error compared with RGB fine-tuning or simple view-averaging.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Reward models based on visuals vary with viewpoint and occlusion; adapting them to the observed geometry is necessary for accurate task assessment.

Method: Geometry-conditioned adaptation using low-rank fine-tuning, token-aligned Plucker rays to encode camera geometry into visual features and attention queries/keys, and synchronous block attention to fuse synchronized multi-view evidence in a pretrained Robometer backbone.

Result: Single-view: ~21% MAE reduction when FOV changes on PickCube. Multi-view: 41–69% reduction vs averaging single-view RGB predictions; temporal ordering improved in ~88% of task-camera groups. Real-task evaluation: ~21% MAE reduction vs averaged RGB fine-tuning.

Conclusion: Camera geometry and joint visual evidence are effective components for task-specific robotic reward adaptation, enabling better, geometry-aware reward estimation across views.

Abstract: Robotic reward models evaluate task execution from visual observations, but their predictions can change with camera viewpoint and occlusion even when the underlying task state is unchanged. Adapting a pretrained reward model to a local task therefore requires accounting for how that task is observed. We introduce AnyviewMeter, a geometry-conditioned adaptation framework for robotic reward models that represent task progress as a scalar reward signal. It combines low-rank fine-tuning with token-aligned Plucker rays and synchronous block attention: ray conditioning incorporates camera geometry into visual features and attention queries and keys, while block attention fuses synchronized views inside the pretrained decoder. The framework supports both single-view reward prediction and joint multi-view evaluation through parameter-efficient adaptation of a pretrained Robometer model. On PickCube, single-view adaptation improves progress prediction in every camera group and reduces mean absolute error under a changed field of view by approximately 21% relative to RGB fine-tuning. Across simulated manipulation tasks, joint multi-view prediction reduces progress error by 41-69% compared with averaging single-view RGB predictions and improves temporal ordering in approximately 88% of task-camera groups. On real tasks with fixed and wrist-mounted cameras, mean absolute error decreases by approximately 21% relative to averaged RGB fine-tuning. These results support camera geometry and joint visual evidence as useful components of task-specific robotic reward adaptation.

</details>


### [57] [Cross-Modal Attention Acts as a Frequency Filter: Why Verbose Prompts Improve Robustness in Vision-Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20139)
*Farooq Ahmad Wani,Maria Sofia Bucarelli,Mujtaba Hussain Mirza,Oleksandr Pryymak,Aryo Pradipta Gema,Iacopo Masi,Pasquale Minervini,Fabrizio Silvestri*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: Question phrasing in vision-language models acts as a cross-modal spectral filter on image patches. Verbose prompts broaden the filter, boosting robustness to some corruptions; fine-grained questions concentrate the filter, increasing fragility under corruption. Across Qwen3-VL and LLaVA-OneVision on GQA and CLEVR, paraphrasing with verbose prompts reduced drift variance by 70–81% for 8B models; padding the prompt also yields accuracy gains under corruption.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To understand how question-conditioned cross-modal attention affects robustness of VLMs to image corruption and to identify practical prompt-engineering strategies.

Method: Empirical study comparing verbose vs. semantically complex questions across two VLMs (Qwen3-VL, LLaVA-OneVision) and two datasets (GQA, CLEVR), analyzing drift under image corruption. Introduces a spectral-filter view of cross-modal attention over image patches. Tests pad-the-prompt as a practical intervention and validates across 8B model scales.

Result: Verbose paraphrasing reduces drift variance by 70–81% on 8B models; cross-modal attention behaves as a spectral filter that interacts with image corruption depending on the alignment of frequencies; and padding prompts yields measurable gains in accuracy under corruption.

Conclusion: Question-conditioned cross-modal attention acts as a spectral filter over image patches. Prompt design (verbose paraphrase; prompt padding) is an effective, practical approach to improve robustness of VLMs to image corruption across models and datasets.

Abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) are fragile under image corruption. We find that the wording of the question affects VLMs in two opposite ways. Verbose questions make VLMs substantially more robust---e.g., rephrasing "Is there a cat?" into "Please look carefully and answer: is there a cat?". Conversely, VLMs become more fragile under corruption when the question is semantically complex or finer-grained, e.g., "what colour is the cup left of the chair?" instead of "is there a cup?". Both effects stem from question-conditioned cross-modal attention, which induces a spectral filter over image patches: verbose questions broaden its frequency support, while fine-grained questions concentrate it onto fewer visual scales. The model's answer drifts most when this filter and the corruption sit on the same spatial frequencies. We test the filter view on Qwen3-VL and LLaVA-OneVision across GQA and CLEVR; verbose paraphrasing reduces drift variance by 70--81% on the 8B models. The practical recipe---pad the prompt---further yields measurable gains in accuracy, even under image corruption.

</details>


### [58] [Bridging Modalities on the Cortex: Surface-based MRI to PET Translation with a Diffusion Bridge](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20147)
*Yitong Li,Alexandra Samoylova,Fabian Bongratz,Timo Grimmer,Dennis M. Hedderich,Igor Yakushev,Christian Wachinger*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: A surface-based diffusion bridge framework (DB-SUiT) translates MRI to PET on the cortical surface using a spherical U-shaped vision Transformer to preserve cortical topology, achieving higher-fidelity cross-modal synthesis and improved dementia classification with strong generalization.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: FDG-PET is a sensitive dementia biomarker but limited by cost, radiation, and accessibility. Cross-modal MRI synthesis is promising but existing volumetric methods ignore folded cortical geometry where disease patterns reside.

Method: DB-SUiT operates on the cortical manifold and uses a conditional spherical U-shaped vision Transformer. It employs spherical convolutional encoders for multi-scale surface feature extraction, bottleneck Transformers to capture long-range spatial dependencies, and integrates demographic and subcortical conditions to refine MRI-to-PET synthesis.

Result: DB-SUiT achieves high-fidelity MRI-to-PET surface synthesis that substantially outperforms baselines. In automated dementia classification, synthesized PET surfaces improve accuracy by 14.2% over MRI and 11.3% over PET volumes, nearing real PET performance. In a blinded reader study, synthetic PET achieved 85.5% diagnostic accuracy (MRI 75.8%, real PET 95.2%). Demonstrates cross-cohort and cross-pathology generalization without retraining on an external cohort.

Conclusion: A surface-based diffusion bridge framework on the cortical manifold with a conditional spherical U-shaped transformer yields superior cross-modal PET synthesis from MRI, improving diagnostic performance and generalization while reducing reliance on costly PET imaging.

Abstract: Cortical hypometabolism measured by Fluorodeoxyglucose Positron Emission Tomography (FDG-PET) is a highly sensitive biomarker for dementia diagnosis. However, high costs, radiation exposure, and limited accessibility constrain its clinical utility. While cross-modal synthesis from Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) offers a promising alternative, existing volumetric generation methods do not explicitly account for the highly folded cortical geometry, where disease-related patterns predominantly reside. To address this, we introduce a novel surface-based diffusion bridge framework DB-SUiT for MRI-to-PET translation that operates natively on the cortical manifold. A conditional Spherical U-shaped vision Transformer (SUiT) is specifically designed to model the intricate cross-modal relationships while preserving surface topology. It combines spherical convolutional encoders for multi-scale surface feature extraction with bottleneck Transformers to capture long-range spatial dependencies, while incorporating demographic and subcortical conditions to refine the synthesis. Evaluated on two datasets, including subjects with different dementia types, DB-SUiT demonstrates high-fidelity synthesis that substantially outperforms other baselines. In automated dementia classification, synthesized PET surfaces improve performance over MRI by 14.2% and PET volumes by 11.3%, approaching the performance of real PET surfaces. In a blinded reader study, synthetic PET achieved 85.5% diagnostic accuracy, compared with 75.8% for MRI and 95.2% for real PET. This further demonstrates cross-cohort and cross-pathology generalization, as the model was evaluated without retraining on an external cohort that included a dementia subtype not represented during training. Our code is available at https://github.com/ai-med/DB-SUiT.

</details>


### [59] [Task-Oriented Semantic Feature Transmission for Multi-Task Satellite Remote Sensing over Low-SNR Channels](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20150)
*Shuoyuan Sun,Hongyu Wang,Mugen Peng,Wenjia Xu*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: A task-oriented JSCC framework transmits semantic features instead of reconstructed images, improving classification/detection under AWGN with CAM and feature restorer.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Pixel-level reconstruction metrics misalign with downstream remote-sensing tasks; low-SNR channels exacerbate reconstruction quality gaps, creating inefficiency for bandwidth-limited satellite links. A task-centric approach aims to preserve task-relevant information directly.

Method: Freeze a multitask-pretrained backbone to extract semantic features. Add a lightweight channel adaptation module (CAM) to compress feature dimensionality; include a feature restorer to recover task-relevant structure after channel corruption. Jointly optimize CAM and downstream task heads under task and feature-level supervision with random-SNR training in an AWGN setting.

Result: Experiments on scene classification and object detection show consistent gains over reconstruction-oriented JSCC baselines across SNRs, with the largest improvements in the low-SNR regime.

Conclusion: Task-oriented transmission of semantic features via CAM and a restorer, with a frozen backbone, yields robust performance and bandwidth efficiency for satellite sensing, outperforming reconstruction-based JSCC especially at low SNR.

Abstract: Conventional satellite remote sensing transmission follows a reconstruct-then-infer paradigm that optimizes pixel-level fidelity, creating an objective mismatch with downstream tasks such as classification and detection, especially at low SNR. This paper investigates a task-oriented framework that bypasses image reconstruction and directly transmits semantic features extracted by a multitask-pretrained backbone. A lightweight channel adaptation module (CAM) compresses feature dimensionality for bandwidth reduction, and a feature restorer recovers task-relevant structure after channel corruption. With the backbone frozen, the CAM and task-specific downstream heads are jointly optimized with task and feature-level supervision under random-SNR training. Under the adopted AWGN setting, experiments on scene classification and object detection show consistent gains over reconstruction-oriented JSCC baselines across different SNR conditions, with the largest improvements in the low-SNR regime.

</details>


### [60] [Ischemic Stroke Segmentation and Net Water Uptake Quantification on Multicenter Non-Contrast CT Using Supervised Target-Domain Adaptation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20151)
*Linus Britt,Maximilian Nielsen,Susan Klapproth,Andre Kemmling,Michael H. Lev,Gabriel Broocks,Rene Werner,Thilo Sentker*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: Domain-aware deep learning enables NCCT-based ischemic lesion segmentation and NWU quantification with cross-domain adaptation; external testing shows variable segmentation performance across cohorts, but NWU estimates are promising for clinical use.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Enable automated, reliable NWU biomarker extraction from NCCT without MRI/CT perfusion, by automating ischemic lesion segmentation and addressing multicenter domain shifts.

Method: nnU-Net-based segmentation trained on NCCT from two datasets; targeted domain adaptation via fine-tuning on small Boston (n=11) and ISLES (n=75) subsets; evaluated on held-out cases; NWU computed from automated segmentations and compared to expert references.

Result: Lesions ≥30 mL: Dice 0.68 (Boston), 0.56 (ISLES). All lesions: 0.54 (Boston), 0.20 (ISLES; compared to post-treatment infarct). Automated NWU MAE: 1.37 percentage points (Boston). Conclusion: Target-domain adaptation enables NCCT-only infarct segmentation across heterogeneous cohorts, with performance varying by domain; supports low-error NWU quantification from baseline NCCT.

Conclusion: Domain-aware adaptation can facilitate NCCT-based infarct segmentation and NWU quantification across multicenter datasets, but small-lesion performance and cross-domain variability warrant further prospective validation.

Abstract: Objectives: Quantitative assessment of infarct hypodensity on non-contrast computed tomography (NCCT), including net water uptake (NWU), requires manual or semi-manual lesion delineation, often guided by CT perfusion or diffusion-weighted MRI, limiting clinical applicability. Automated segmentation on NCCT could enable efficient biomarker extraction such as NWU but remains challenging across heterogeneous multicenter data. This study aimed to develop and externally test a domain-aware deep learning framework for ischemic stroke segmentation on NCCT and assess its suitability for NWU quantification.
  Materials & Methods: In this retrospective multicenter study of 801 patients from four datasets, an nnU-Net-based model was trained on NCCT scans from the University Medical Center Hamburg-Eppendorf and the Acute Ischemic Stroke Dataset. To adapt to new domains, the model was fine-tuned on target-domain subsets from Boston (n=11) and ISLES (n=75), with evaluation on held-out cases not used for fine-tuning. Automated segmentations and NWU values were compared with expert references.
  Results: For lesions $\geq$ 30 mL, median Dice was 0.68 (Boston) and 0.56 (ISLES). Including smaller lesions, which predominated in ISLES, median Dice was 0.54 (interquartile range [IQR] 0.30-0.70) for acute lesion segmentation (Boston dataset) and 0.20 (IQR 0.03-0.41) for NCCT lesion segmentations when compared to post-treatment infarct (primary target of the ISLES challenge). Automated NWU mean absolute error was 1.37 percentage points (SD 1.61, Boston).
  Conclusion: Target-domain adaptation supported NCCT-only infarct segmentation across heterogeneous external cohorts, although performance varied across domains. The approach enabled low-error NWU quantification from baseline NCCT without advanced imaging, supporting further prospective clinical evaluation.

</details>


### [61] [Needles in a Raystack: Ultra-Sparse LiDAR Occupancy Detection for Bat Tracks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20160)
*Nico Klar,Pankaj Rana,Nizam Gifary,Jakob Traub,Aamir Ahmad*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: A lightweight 3D U-Net on sensor-centered LiDAR raystacks improves occupancy detection of sparse bat flight paths over a reconstruction-based autoencoder baseline, enabling coherent trajectory recovery and downstream biodiversity-aware turbine management.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Nocturnal bat monitoring with LiDAR yields ultra-sparse 3D data; standard loss functions bias models toward background, hindering recovery of real flight trajectories. A robust occupancy-detection approach is needed to enable validation-scale studies and integration with biodiversity-aware management.

Method: Propose voxel-wise occupancy detection using a lightweight 3D U-Net that preserves temporal resolution, employs skip connections for spatial detail, and optimizes a combined weighted binary cross-entropy and Dice loss to address severe class imbalance. Represent data as sensor-centric LiDAR raystacks. Compare against a reconstruction-based 3D convolutional autoencoder baseline and validate on real bat LiDAR recordings cross-checked with acoustic monitoring.

Result: The 3D U-Net recovers sparse foreground occupancy and produces coherent occupancy patterns along bat flight trajectories, whereas the autoencoder baseline fails to recover foreground. The approach provides a practical basis for validation-scale experiments, subsequent clustering of flight tracks, and future integration of bat activity information into turbine-curtailment strategies.

Conclusion: A practical, scalable method for tracking bat activity from sparse nighttime LiDAR data, enabling downstream ecological analyses and management actions that account for biodiversity.

Abstract: Monitoring flying animals is important for understanding and protecting biodiversity, but nocturnal species such as bats are difficult to observe in the field. Using LiDAR, bat movements at night result in ultra-sparse 3D spatio-temporal data in which standard reconstruction losses tend to predict only background and miss real flight paths. We study this problem as voxel-wise occupancy detection in sensor-centric LiDAR raystacks. A lightweight 3D U-Net is proposed that preserves temporal resolution, uses skip connections for spatial detail, and combines weighted binary cross-entropy with Dice loss to handle the strong class imbalance.
  In real LiDAR recordings of bats over open fields, cross-checked with acoustic monitoring, a reconstruction-based 3D convolutional autoencoder baseline fails to recover foreground trajectories. In contrast, the proposed U-Net recovers sparse foreground occupancy in diagnostic experiments and produces coherent occupancy patterns along bat flight trajectories, providing a practical basis for validation-scale experiments, later clustering of flight tracks, and future integration of bat activity information into biodiversity-aware turbine curtailment strategies.

</details>


### [62] [MTF-Net: Multi-Modal Temporal Feature Fusion Network for Pedestrian Intention Prediction](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20178)
*Md Mahfuzur Rahman,Pengzhan Zhou,A. F. M. Abdun Noor,Md Imam Ahasan,Md Mustafizur Rahman,Fang Qu*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: MTF-Net uses multi-modal temporal fusion with GLU-based gating to predict pedestrian crossing intentions, outperforming transformer/graph baselines on PIE/JAAD while running in real time.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Accurately predicting pedestrian intentions is crucial for safe autonomous driving. Prior work either models temporal dependencies within a single modality or fuses modalities only at coarse semantic levels, limiting early and robust anticipation.

Method: MTF-Net integrates four modalities—bounding-box dynamics, human pose keypoints, local context, and scene-level semantics—within a recurrent fusion framework enhanced by gated linear units (GLUs). It employs three temporal encoding branches and an attention-guided fusion head for cross-modal interaction and temporal aggregation.

Result: On PIE and JAAD benchmarks, MTG-Net (MTF-Net) achieves up to 0.95 AUC on PIE and 0.94 AUC on JAAD, surpassing recent transformer- and graph-based models while maintaining real-time performance.

Conclusion:  principled multi-modal temporal fusion with GLU-based cross-modal gates yields reliable pedestrian intention prediction without relying on excessively complex architectures.

Abstract: Accurately predicting pedestrian intentions is crucial for ensuring safe and proactive interaction between autonomous vehicles and pedestrians. However, existing approaches often depend on architectures that either model temporal dependencies within individual modalities or fuse modalities only at coarse semantic levels. To address these limitations, we propose MTF-Net, a novel Multi-Modal Temporal Feature Fusion Network that jointly models kinematic, appearance, and contextual cues for pedestrian intention prediction. MTF-Net integrates four complementary modalities-bounding-box dynamics, human pose keypoints, local context, and scene-level semantics within a recurrent fusion framework enhanced by gated linear units (GLUs). These GLU-based modules adaptively regulate cross-modal information flow, enabling interpretable and efficient feature interaction across temporal scales. Through three dedicated temporal encoding branches and an attention-guided fusion head, the proposed model robustly anticipates pedestrian crossing intentions several frames before they occur. Extensive evaluations on the PIE and JAAD benchmarks demonstrate that MTF-Net surpasses recent transformer- and graph-based models, achieving up to 0.95 AUC on PIE and 0.94 AUC on JAAD, while maintaining real-time performance. The results highlight that reliable pedestrian intention prediction arises from principled multi-modal fusion rather than excessive architectural complexity.

</details>


### [63] [MoSSGate: Memory-Modulated State-Space Gating for Skin Lesion Segmentation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20181)
*Anum Awan,Mahnoor Buriro,Muhammad Younas Khan,Md Imam Ahasan*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: MoSSGate is a plug-and-play U-Net module combining boundary-aware gating, an external memory modulator, and 2D state-space modeling to enable efficient, boundary-preserving global context. It reports state-of-the-art results on ISIC 2017/2018 with lower FLOPs.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Convolutional and transformer-based models often struggle to jointly capture long-range spatial dependencies and fine lesion boundaries within limited compute, leading to over-segmentation, fragmented predictions, or missed thin peripheral structures.

Method: A plug-and-play module for U-Net with (i) boundary-aware spatial gating to restrict long-range propagation to informative regions, (ii) an external memory modulator for sample-adaptive dynamic control, and (iii) parallel 2D state-space modeling for efficient global context aggregation with linear complexity.

Result: On ISIC 2017 and ISIC 2018, MoSSGate achieves 86.3% and 85.9% mIoU, and 92.6% and 90.6% Dice, respectively, while requiring substantially fewer FLOPs than most competing CNN-based methods, indicating a favorable accuracy-efficiency trade-off.

Conclusion: The design enables adaptive, context-aware information propagation while preserving sharp and accurate lesion boundaries, demonstrating state-of-the-art performance with improved efficiency for high-resolution medical image segmentation.

Abstract: Accurate skin lesion segmentation is crucial for reliable computer-aided dermatological diagnosis, yet existing convolutional and transformer-based models often struggle to jointly capture long-range spatial dependencies and fine boundary details under limited computational budgets. This trade-off between global context modeling and boundary-aware localization frequently leads to over-segmentation, fragmented predictions, or missing thin peripheral structures. To address this challenge, we propose MoSSGate, a plug-and-play module for U-Net that integrates (i) boundary-aware spatial gating to restrict long-range propagation to informative regions, (ii) an external memory modulator that provides sample-adaptive dynamic control, and (iii) parallel 2D state-space modeling for efficient global context aggregation with linear complexity. The proposed design enables adaptive, context-aware information propagation while preserving sharp and accurate lesion boundaries. Extensive experiments on the ISIC 2017 and ISIC 2018 benchmarks demonstrate state-of-the-art accuracy with strong efficiency, achieving 86.3% and 85.9% mIoU and 92.6% and 90.6% Dice, respectively, while requiring substantially fewer FLOPs than most competing CNN-based methods. These results highlight a favorable accuracy efficiency trade-off for high-resolution medical image segmentation.

</details>


### [64] [A Two-Stage Multi-Scale Attention-Based Network for Weakly Supervised Cataract Fundus Image Enhancement](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20222)
*Xiaoyong Fang,Yue Wang,Xiangyu Li,Wanshu Fan,Dongsheng Zhou*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: Proposes TSMSA-Net, a two-stage multi-scale attention network for weakly supervised cataract fundus image enhancement that uses domain transformation to synthesize paired real-like cataract images, achieving superior enhancement on Kaggle and ODIR-5K, without paired data, and improving downstream vessel segmentation and classification.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Cataract-caused vision loss and difficulty in fundus image analysis stem from limited paired cataract retinal data and loss of fine retinal details during enhancement. A weakly supervised approach with synthesized pairs and attention-based multi-stage processing aims to recover details while limiting artifacts.

Method: Two-stage architecture (TSMSA-Net) with a domain transformation step to synthesize real-like cataract images for weak supervision, followed by a multi-scale attention-based enhancement stage to learn rich, detail-preserving features and suppress artifacts.

Result: On Kaggle and ODIR-5K datasets, TSMSA-Net outperforms current state-of-the-art cataract fundus image enhancement methods, even without paired images, and shows generalization potential; enhancement also improves vessel segmentation and classification performance in cataract images.

Conclusion: A weakly supervised, two-stage, multi-scale attention framework effectively enhances cataract fundus images using synthesized paired data, with strong qualitative and downstream benefits and cross-dataset generalization.

Abstract: Cataract is a major cause of vision loss and hinders further diagnosis. However, cataract fundus image enhancement often grapples with challenges such as limited paired cataract retinal images and insufficient recovery of fine details in the retinal images. To mitigate these challenges, we in this paper propose a two-stage multi-scale attention-based network (TSMSA-Net) for weakly supervised cataract fundus image enhancement. Our TSMSA-Net leverages the domain transformation to synthesis paired real-like cataract images, solving the problem of difficult acquisition of paired images. To further extract detailed information from fundus images and reduce the generation of artifacts during the enhancement process, we propose a multi-scale attention-based stage to learn more useful features for cataract image enhancement. Experimental results on Kaggle and ODIR-5K demonstrate that our TSMSA-Net outperforms current state-of-the-art cataract fundus images enhancement even without paired images and exhibits certain generalization ability. Experimental results on Kaggle and ODIR-5K datasets indicate that our TSMSA-Net outperforms the current state-of-the-art methods for cataract fundus image enhancement, even in the absence of paired images. Additionally, it demonstrates a certain level of generalization capability. The enhancement also can improve the performance of vessel segmentation and classification in cataract images.

</details>


### [65] [Scene-Q: Confidence-Aware Coarse-to-Fine Querying of 3D Scenes with Selective VLM Reasoning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20235)
*Juno Kim,Yesol Park,Hye-Jung Yoon,Byoung-Tak Zhang*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: Scene-Q: a confidence-aware, coarse-to-fine open-vocabulary 3D querying framework that uses temperature-normalized high-confidence fast retrieval and selective reasoning VLM on low-confidence cases to substantially improve 3D instance segmentation and NL 3D instance retrieval with efficient compute.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Cosine-similarity retrieval with contrastive image-text encoders is brittle when labels are near-synonymous or multiple similar instances appear; indoor 3D groundings require consistent multi-view understanding and efficient, scalable querying.

Method: Normalize encoder scores with temperature scaling; a two-path retrieval: fast path for high-confidence; for low-confidence, rerank top-K candidates using multi-view images and instance bounding boxes, leveraging a reasoning VLM for contextual disambiguation.

Result: Reported improvements on ScanNet200 for open-vocabulary 3D instance segmentation and on real-world reconstructions for NL 3D instance retrieval; largest gains on spatial/relational queries; many queries still served by fast path.

Conclusion: Scene-Q demonstrates that confidence-aware coarse-to-fine querying can balance efficiency and accuracy in open-vocabulary 3D grounding, enabling robust, scalable grounding in indoor robotic perception.

Abstract: Indoor mobile robots require open-vocabulary scene understanding that grounds natural-language queries in a consistent 3D map. Many existing systems ultimately rely on cosine-similarity retrieval with contrastive image--text encoders, which is efficient but brittle when labels are near-synonymous or multiple similar instances appear. We present Scene-Q, a confidence-aware coarse-to-fine querying framework that normalizes encoder scores with temperature scaling and selectively invokes a reasoning VLM only for low-confidence cases. High-confidence queries are answered by fast retrieval, while ambiguous ones are reranked over a small top-K candidate set using the original multi-view images and instance bounding boxes, enabling context-aware disambiguation at low cost. Scene-Q improves open-vocabulary 3D instance segmentation on ScanNet200 and natural-language 3D instance retrieval on real-world reconstructions, with the largest gains on spatial and relational queries while keeping a substantial fraction of queries on the fast path.

</details>


### [66] [SAGE-Yoga: Multi-Cue Learning for Yoga Pose Classification and Joint-Level Correction](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20245)
*Hung Le Chi,Khanh Minh Huynh,Long Nghia Tran Pham,Tan Phuc Huynh,Trong-Thuan Nguyen,Minh-Triet Tran*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: Proposes SAGE-Yoga, a unified coarse-to-fine framework for yoga pose classification and joint-level correction from a single RGB image, combining visual ensemble and selective geometric verification with medoid reference and joint-angle distributions; achieves state-of-the-art results on Yoga-82.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Address limitations of existing pose-analysis methods that rely on a single visual prediction, struggle with visually similar poses, and separate classification from correction; aim for accurate, interpretable, and actionable feedback.

Method: Bagging-based ensemble of complementary visual backbones to generate a ranked set of candidate pose classes; margin-based gating to preserve confident predictions and invoke geometric verification only for ambiguous cases; retrieve a medoid reference pose for the final class and compare observed joint angles against class-specific distributions to identify misaligned joints; translate deviations into corrective feedback.

Result: On Yoga-82, visual ensemble achieves 89.0% Top-1 accuracy; the full framework attains 90.7% Top-1 accuracy and 90.1% Macro-F1.

Conclusion: Combining complementary visual evidence with selective geometric verification yields improved fine-grained pose classification and enables interpretable, joint-level correction.

Abstract: Automated yoga analysis requires both accurate pose classification and interpretable feedback on pose execution. However, existing methods often rely on a single visual prediction, struggle to distinguish visually similar poses, and treat pose classification and correction as separate tasks. To address these limitations, we propose SAGE-Yoga, a unified coarse-to-fine framework for yoga pose classification and joint-level correction from a single RGB image. Inspired by how yoga instructors assess posture using multiple complementary cues, SAGE-Yoga first employs a bagging-based ensemble of complementary visual backbones to generate a ranked set of candidate pose classes. Additionally, a margin-based gating mechanism preserves confident visual predictions while invoking geometric verification only for ambiguous cases. Moreover, once the final pose class is determined, SAGE-Yoga retrieves a medoid reference pose and compares the observed joint angles with class-specific distributions to identify misaligned joints. Finally, these deviations are translated into actionable corrective feedback. Empirically, experiments on the Yoga-82 dataset show that the visual ensemble achieves 89.0% Top-1 accuracy, while the complete framework improves performance to 90.7% Top-1 accuracy and 90.1% Macro-F1. These results demonstrate that combining complementary visual evidence with selective geometric verification improves fine-grained pose classification while enabling interpretable, joint-level correction.

</details>


### [67] [Distance to Class Prototypes: Active Learning for Object Detection](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20248)
*Licheng Zhang,Zheng Gong*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: Proposes a single-pass, signal-rich active learning criterion for object detection that uses a supervised contrastive term to shape per-object embeddings. Scores unlabeled detections by distance to the region for the predicted category, weighted by confidence, avoiding ensembles or repeated inferences. Demonstrates improved data efficiency over posterior-based selection on PASCAL VOC and MS-COCO with modest parameter overhead.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Active learning for object detection is limited by annotation cost. Posterior-based signals are cheap but poorly calibrated; ensemble/disagreement signals improve selection but require heavy extra inference. A single-pass, richer signal is needed to reduce labeling cost without increasing inference burden.

Method: Train a detector with an added supervised contrastive loss that structures a per-object embedding space where distances reflect class membership. Unlabeled detections are scored by how far their embeddings lie from the region associated with the predicted category, weighted by confidence. This yields a scoring signal without ensembles, auxiliary predictors, or repeated inference. The approach increases parameters by 2.89M (≈8.3%) over a bare detector and is evaluated on a single-stage detector.

Result: On PASCAL VOC and MS-COCO, the method consistently beats the posterior-based selection in every active-learning round, achieving up to 1.08% mAP50 improvement with small run-to-run variance (0.02–0.18%). It remains competitive with ensemble and Monte Carlo dropout criteria that require 3–50 additional forward passes per unlabeled image.

Conclusion: A cost-effective, single-pass active learning signal for object detectors that improves data efficiency beyond posterior-based scoring while avoiding ensembles or repeated inferences, with modest model size overhead and compatibility with single-stage detectors.

Abstract: Deploying a deep object detector in a new setting is limited less by architecture than by the cost of annotating data from that setting. Active learning lowers the cost by choosing which images to label, and the choice is only as good as the signal used to score an unlabeled image. That signal is usually the class posterior, which is cheap but poorly calibrated, or the disagreement across several models or several stochastic passes, which is better but multiplies inference over a pool far larger than the labeled set. We propose a signal richer than the posterior yet still read from one forward pass of one network. A supervised contrastive term added to the training objective shapes a per-object embedding space in which distance encodes class membership, and an unlabeled detection is scored by how far it lies from the region occupied by its predicted category, weighted by its confidence. The criterion needs no ensemble, no auxiliary predictor and no repeated inference, and its entire cost is 2.89M parameters, an increase of 8.3% over a bare detector. On PASCAL VOC and MS-COCO it beats the posterior of the same detector in every round in which a selection is made, by up to 1.08% mAP50 against run to run deviations of 0.02% to 0.18%, and it stays competitive with ensemble and Monte Carlo dropout criteria costing three to fifty forward passes per unlabeled image. Experiments use the single-stage detector under which the compared criteria report their results, so that the selection decision is isolated from the strength of the detector.

</details>


### [68] [Generative Verification: Rethinking the Uncertainty Signal for Active Learning of Object Detection](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20262)
*Licheng Zhang,Zheng Gong*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: Introduces a generative verification framework for active object detection using an independent diffusion-based verifier that re-derives labels from predicted box crops; yields a robust acquisition signal and about 1 mAP50 gain per active-labeling round on MS-COCO.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To decouple verification from the detector, avoiding hand-tuned, combined classification/localization terms and failure modes that arise when the same model is both detector and evaluator; enabling a scalar, self-contained acquisition signal based on verification disagreement.

Method: Train a conditional diffusion model as a verifier whose target is a label representation (not an image). The verifier ingests crops inside predicted boxes and outputs a label distribution; repeated generations yield a distribution whose concentration reflects label certainty. The detector and verifier are independent; the acquisition signal is the disagreement between detector output and verifier. The approach avoids using detector confidence and leverages a distributional, stochastic reverse process.

Result: On PASCAL VOC and MS-COCO, the verifier-based signal outperforms output-uncertainty, feature-geometry, perturbation, and ensemble criteria, achieving about 1 mAP50 point per labeling round on MS-COCO, with the largest gains in early rounds where confidently wrong detections are common.

Conclusion: Decoupling verification from detection yields robust, self-derived acquisition signals that naturally capture labeling uncertainty without hand-tuned terms, improving active object detection efficiency and accuracy, particularly for early rounds with common detector errors.

Abstract: Nearly every acquisition function for active object detection shares one arrangement, in that the model being improved is also the model being interrogated. We depart from it. In generative verification an independent generative model re-derives the label of a detection from the pixels inside its predicted box, and the disagreement between the two becomes the acquisition signal. Two properties follow from the arrangement itself rather than from any tuning. A displaced box, a box on background and a correct box carrying the wrong label all yield a crop that fails verification, so the failure modes arrive already combined in one scalar and the hand-weighted classification and localization terms of existing criteria are no longer needed. And because the verifier never observes the detector confidence, confidently wrong detections score highest, although a self-derived signal reads them as uninteresting and they are the costliest to leave unlabeled. We build the verifier as a conditional diffusion model whose diffusion target is a label representation rather than an image. Its reverse process is stochastic, so repeated generations return a distribution whose concentration reports how firmly the evidence determines the label, where a classifier returns a single point estimate. On PASCAL VOC and MS-COCO the signal outperforms output-uncertainty, feature-geometry, perturbation and ensemble criteria, gaining about one mAP50 point per round on MS-COCO, with its largest margins in the early rounds where confident detector errors are most common.

</details>


### [69] [AI or Real: Detecting Partially Altered Videos Under Resource-Constrained Environments](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20263)
*Tamoghna Chakraborty,Md Nurul Absur,Sourya Saha,Saptarshi Debroy*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: A compact, edge-friendly full-frame detector for partially manipulated AI-generated video using teacher-student distillation (DINOv2-Base → MobileNetV3-Small) achieving 0.766 AUC and 3.65 ms / 16-frame clip, narrowing 58% of the teacher gap on a 55k-sample splice test set.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Edge deployment of video forgery detectors is hampered by the large size of state-of-the-art models and the need for real-time inference without face detection. The work targets practical, resource-constrained settings and addresses failure modes specific to partial manipulation, such as false positives on scene cuts and calibration issues.

Method: Distill DINOv2-Base teacher into a frozen MobileNetV3-Small student using (i) temperature-annealed soft-label transfer, (ii) attention-diversity regularization, (iii) frame-level supervision, and (iv) a residual feature adapter to condition ImageNet features for artifact detection. It also mitigates two failure modes with (a) within-video temporal hard negatives and (b) calibration-aware sampling.

Result: Evaluation on 55,393-sample spliced test set with fake-frame ratios 6.2%–31.2% yields a student AUC of 0.766, closing 58% of the gap to the DINOv2-Base teacher. Inference runs at 3.65 ms per 16-frame clip on an RTX A4000, with a 150.4 MB checkpoint suitable for edge budgets.

Conclusion: The proposed distillation pipeline yields a practical, edge-capable detector for partially manipulated video that approaches teacher performance while meeting memory and latency constraints, enabling deployment without face-detection preprocessing.

Abstract: The proliferation of generative video models has shifted the practical detection threat from fully fabricated clips to partially manipulated footages. Although modern detectors achieve strong accuracy using foundation backbones of 400M+ parameters, their resource footprint precludes edge deployment. In this paper, we present a lightweight full-frame detector for partially manipulated AI-generated video, designed for deployment on edge hardware without face-detection preprocessing. The system distills a DINOv2-Base teacher into a frozen MobileNetV3-Small student through a pipeline that combines temperature-annealed soft-label transfer, attention-diversity regularization, frame-level supervision, and a residual feature adapter that conditions ImageNet features for artifact detection. We additionally target two failure modes specific to the partial-manipulation regime: false positives on legitimate scene cuts, addressed through within-video temporal hard negatives; and threshold-level miscalibration on the dominant pure-real class, addressed through calibration-aware sampling. Evaluation on a 55,393-sample spliced test set across fake-frame ratios from 6.2% to 31.2% demonstrates the student model closing 58% of the gap to the DINOv2-Base teacher (AUC 0.766) while running at 3.65 ms per 16-frame clip on RTX A4000 with a 150.4 MB checkpoint compatible with edge-device memory and latency budgets.

</details>


### [70] [CleanVideo: Adaptive Concept Erasure for Text-to-Video Diffusion Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20267)
*Junchi Liao,Hongji Li,Wenrui Zhou,Lijie Hu*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: CleanVideo introduces a tri-modal gated, low-dimensional subspace intervention for selective concept erasure in video diffusion models, jointly leveraging spatiotemporal features, timestep signals, and text to decide where/when/if to intervene, achieving faithful, temporally coherent erasure and outperforming baselines, including against concept-recovery attacks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Extending concept erasure from images to video is nontrivial due to gradually emerging targets across frames and varying denoising steps, which cause fixed interventions to miss targets or distort content.

Method: A selective erasure framework that uses low-dimensional subspace interventions guided by a tri-modal gate over spatial-temporal features, timesteps, and textual semantics to decide intervention locations and times, steering erased content toward well-defined surrogate concepts when possible while preserving non-target regions.

Result: Empirical evaluation on three video diffusion models shows CleanVideo erases target concepts effectively, preserves visual fidelity and temporal coherence, and outperforms baselines on frame- and video-level metrics, with resilience to concept-recovery attacks when the protected pipeline remains.

Conclusion: CleanVideo enables robust, controllable concept erasure in video generation by combining adaptive gating with surrogate concept alignment to minimize artifacts and maintain content integrity.

Abstract: Concept erasure aims to selectively eliminate undesired visual semantics from pre-trained generative models without compromising their general utility. Extending concept erasure from images to video is nontrivial. Target concepts emerge gradually and vary across frames and denoising steps. As a result, fixed interventions may miss the target or introduce blurring, jitter, and content distortion. We propose CleanVideo, a selective erasure framework that performs low-dimensional subspace intervention controlled by a tri-modal gating mechanism. By jointly processing spatiotemporal visual features, timestep signals, and textual semantics, CleanVideo determines where, when, and whether to intervene, steering erased content toward natural surrogate concepts when such surrogates can be clearly defined while preserving non-target content. Experiments on three video diffusion models show that CleanVideo effectively erases target concepts while maintaining visual fidelity and temporal coherence, outperforming existing baselines under frame-level and video-level evaluations and under concept-recovery attacks when the protected pipeline remains intact.

</details>


### [71] [Queries Knew More Than We Thought: Uncovering Latent Knowledge in Segmentation Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20283)
*Ignacio M. De la Jara,Cristian Rodriguez-Opazo,Damith Ranasinghe*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: Hidden potential in frozen DETR-like segmenters can be unlocked by a lightweight offline selector (HYDRA) that uses cached outputs, yielding substantial gains without additional queries or retraining.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Address the output-selection bottleneck in frozen DETR-family models where good masks are present among query-conditioned candidates but not exposed due to the selection rule.

Method: Train HYDRA on cached, frozen outputs to score candidates against a baseline; at inference, emit only if a calibrated margin indicates a clearly better candidate; calibration on held-out data; training on training-split caches; evaluation includes ablations with LoRA and TinyDETR to connect to query specialization.

Result: Up to +7.41 mIoU points on ADE20k and COCO for Mask2Former, MaskDINO, OneFormer; +9.4 class-macro prompt-IoU points on SAM 3 across eight domains; calibration preserves useful predictions; LoRA controls show weight adaptation doesn't solve bottleneck; TinyDETR supports link to bipartite matching.

Conclusion: Frozen segmenters should be evaluated on both exposed predictions and suppressed but potentially useful candidates; narrow selection bottlenecks can be mitigated with cache-based selectors like HYDRA, revealing latent headroom without extra computation.

Abstract: Modern segmenters often fail after the expensive computation has already been done: a useful mask is present among the model's query-conditioned candidates, but the deployed selection rule does not expose it. We study this output-selection bottleneck in frozen DETR-family models. A ground-truth-only oracle first shows substantial hidden headroom in already-computed mask proposals. This raises a simple question: How can we better use the masks a segmenter has already computed but does not expose? We then ask whether that headroom can be recovered without adding queries, generating new masks, rerunning the backbone, or updating weights. HYDRA is a small selector trained only on cached frozen outputs. At inference time, it scores the cached candidates against an explicit keep-baseline option and acts only when a held-out calibrated margin indicates the selected candidate is sufficiently better. Trained on training-split caches and calibrated on held-out data, HYDRA improves Mask2Former, MaskDINO, and OneFormer by up to +7.41 dataset mIoU points on ADE20k and COCO, and improves SAM 3 by +9.4 class-macro prompt-IoU points on average across eight domains while preserving useful predictions through calibration. Paired LoRA controls show that lightweight weight adaptation does not remove the bottleneck: exposed predictions are often flat or worse, while routing over the adapted candidates still recovers accuracy. Finally, we connect the effect to query specialization under bipartite matching and verify it in a controlled TinyDETR study. These results show that frozen segmenters should be evaluated not only by the masks they expose, but also by the useful candidates they suppress.

</details>


### [72] [TinyCNN: A 193K-Parameter Network for On-Device Plant Disease Detection, with a Cross-Dataset Robustness Diagnosis](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20290)
*Ngoc-Bao Ho-Lam,Thai-Anh Nguyen*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: TinyCNN delivers on-device, energy-efficient plant-disease classification with depthwise separable convs; achieves near-state accuracy with ~193k parameters and strong compression via knowledge distillation; robustness to real-world conditions is limited by background cues (shortcut learning).


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Enable accurate, on-device crop-disease detection in resource-poor regions to support SDG2 while minimizing energy/memory footprint.

Method: Design TinyCNN with depthwise separable convolutions (~193k parameters, 110.05M MACs for 224x224); train on PlantVillage (38 classes); perform vanilla knowledge distillation with alpha in {0.3,0.5,0.7} and T in {2,4}; ablation selects alpha=0.3, T=4; evaluate on PlantVillage; conduct cross-dataset evaluation to PlantDoc; use Grad-CAM to analyze attention and shortcut learning.

Result: PlantVillage test accuracy 98.88% and macro-F1 98.03%; model is ~58x smaller than ResNet18 and ~11.8x smaller than MobileNetV2 teacher; distilled TinyCNN achieves 98.81% accuracy; cross-dataset evaluation reveals robustness gap due to background-driven, off-leaf cues explained by Grad-CAM.

Conclusion: TinyCNN is a viable, energy-efficient building block for sustainable agricultural intelligence; real-world impact limited by field robustness and distribution shift caused by background-induced shortcut learning; future work should address robust generalization to real-world conditions.

Abstract: Detecting crop disease early is central to sustainable agriculture and food security under United Nations Sustainable Development Goal 2 (Zero Hunger), and is especially urgent in resource-constrained regions where expert diagnosis is scarce but low-cost mobile devices are widespread. This paper presents TinyCNN, a lightweight convolutional neural network for on-device plant disease classification. TinyCNN uses depthwise separable convolution blocks and contains only 193,190 trainable parameters with 110.05M MACs for a 224x224 input image. On the 38-class PlantVillage benchmark, TinyCNN achieves 98.88% test accuracy and 98.03% macro-F1 while being approximately 58x smaller than ResNet18 and 11.8x smaller than a MobileNetV2 teacher, directly reducing the energy, memory, and cost footprint of inference in line with Green AI principles. The paper further analyzes vanilla knowledge distillation as a sustainable model-compression strategy; an ablation over alpha in {0.3, 0.5, 0.7} and T in {2, 4} selects alpha=0.3, T=4, producing a distilled TinyCNN with 98.81% test accuracy. Finally, cross-dataset evaluation from PlantVillage to PlantDoc reveals a substantial robustness gap under real-world conditions, which a Grad-CAM analysis attributes to off-leaf, background-driven attention consistent with shortcut learning. TinyCNN is thus an energy-efficient, deployable building block for sustainable agricultural intelligence, while field robustness remains the key barrier to durable real-world impact.

</details>


### [73] [Not All Layers Are Equal: Dynamic Layer Routing for Reliable CLIP OOD Detection](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20299)
*Ignacio M. De la Jara,Cristian Rodriguez-Opazo,Damith Ranasinghe*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: Learnable router to select final-layer-anchored expert over CLIP layers for OOD detection, outperforming prompt-learning methods with efficient routing.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Shift from crafting layer fusion methods to learning which layers to trust for each input, using weak OOD supervision to train a lightweight router.

Method: Train a sparse router that selects a final-layer-anchored expert from CLIP's layer depth, using a weak OOD supervision context; aims for high efficiency (≈2 minutes, <1 GB).

Result: On three benchmarks, e.g., ImageNet-1K, Voyager achieves average FPR@95 of 18.86, outperforming the strongest comparable prompt-learning method by 8.8 points; gains persist across multiple supervision sources.

Conclusion: Learnable routing via a lightweight router is effective and practical for OOD detection; the router’s learning, not the supervision source, is the key driver of gains; Voyager offers fast, scalable OOD detection.

Abstract: Information aggregation across model layers are revealed to improve OOD detection. In contrast to crafting a method for layer-wise information aggregation in recent work, we investigate if layer selection is a learnable problem. In other words, we transpose the question from how to fuse layers to one asking which layers to trust for an input. Using a generalizable, weak, out of distribution context crafting approach for supervision, shown to be more effective than state of the art methods' mechanisms, we formulate learning a lightweight router to select a sparse, final-layer-anchored expert over CLIP's layer depth for OOD detection.
  Across three diverse benchmarks we demonstrate our learnable routing method dubbed Voyager improves OOD detection. On ImageNet-1K, Voyager achieves an average FPR@95 of 18.86, outperforming the strongest, comparable, prompt-learning method by 8.8 points. These gains persist across multiple supervision sources, including those used by existing state-of-the-art prompt-learning methods, demonstrating that, whilst our weak OOD supervision context is highly effective, the key advantage is realized from the learnable router component rather than the supervision source. Significantly, Voyager is highly practical; router learning takes approximately two minutes using less than 1 GB of memory, making it approximately 20x more efficient than current prompt-learning approaches.
  Anonymized Code: https://anonymous.4open.science/r/Voyager/

</details>


### [74] [AgriScope: Pixel-Grounded Multimodal Understanding for Agricultural Images](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20325)
*Abderrahmene Boudiaf,Mohamad Alanssari,Irfan Hussain,Sajid Javed*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: AgriScope+: a unified pixel-grounded multimodal framework for agricultural image understanding enabling image-, region-, and pixel-level tasks, supported by AgriGround—an ~500k-image, 11M-sample dataset for dense grounding and instruction-tuning.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current Multimodal LLMs in agriculture are text-only and lack pixel-level grounding, limiting precise diagnosis, crop management, and phenotyping under real-world conditions.

Method: AgriScope combines biological-semantic encoding, dense spatial representations, and pixel decoding to support grounded captioning, referring expression segmentation, and multi-turn multimodal interaction. AgriGround is built via a multi-stage automatic annotation pipeline (caption generation, phrase grounding, segmentation, instruction synthesis) to provide densely grounded supervision.

Result: Extensive experiments demonstrate effectiveness of pixel-grounded multimodal understanding across multiple agricultural vision-language tasks; establishes a new benchmark; dataset and code to be released publicly.

Conclusion: The work advances agricultural vision-language understanding by tightly integrating semantic and spatial grounding, enabling scalable training and evaluation and enabling more precise agricultural insights and decision support.

Abstract: Agricultural image understanding requires fine-grained recognition of plant diseases, pests, crop structures, and botanical species under complex real-world conditions. Despite recent advances in Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs), existing models remain limited to text-only outputs and lack pixel-level visual grounding capabilities. In this work, we introduce AgriScope, a unified pixel-grounded multimodal framework for agricultural image understanding. AgriScope jointly supports image-level, region-level, and pixel-level understanding within a unified framework, enabling tasks such as grounded caption generation, referring expression segmentation, and multi-turn multimodal interaction for agricultural imagery. AgriScope integrates biologically specialized semantic representations with dense spatial grounding through biological-semantic encoding, dense spatial representations, and pixel decoding. To support large-scale grounded learning, we introduce AgriGround, a large-scale pixel-grounded agricultural multimodal instruction-tuning dataset containing over 500K images and 11M instruction-following samples spanning plant disease analysis, crop and weed identification, insect pest recognition, and fine-grained botanical understanding.
