AgriGround is constructed through a multi-stage automatic annotation pipeline that integrates multimodal caption generation, phrase-level grounding, segmentation mask generation, and task-oriented instruction synthesis to produce densely grounded supervision. Extensive experiments across multiple agricultural vision-language tasks demonstrate the effectiveness of AgriScope in pixel-grounded multimodal understanding, establishing a strong benchmark for agricultural vision-language learning and visual grounding. The dataset and code will be made publicly available at (https://github.com/boudiafA/AgriScope)

</details>


### [75] [FreqDINO++: A Frequency-Guided Multi-Task Routing Vision Foundation Model for Universal Ultrasound Analysis](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20340)
*Qing Xu,Yixuan Zhang,Yue Li,Xiangjian He,Qian Zhang,Mainul Haque,Rong Qu,Wenting Duan,Jieyun Bai,Zhen Chen*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: FreqDINO++ is a frequency-guided, multi-task vision foundation model for ultrasound analysis that uses a Multi-task Routing Adapter (MR-Adapter) for parameter-efficient task-common and task-specific integration, a Frequency-aware Feature Enhancer (F^2-Enhancer) to capture multi-scale frequency characteristics, and a Task-aligned Collaborative Decoder (TC-Decoder) to enable dense and global prediction synergy. It achieves state-of-the-art results across 27 ultrasound tasks and generalizes to unseen data, with code released.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Ultrasound analysis faces a large domain gap relative to natural images, limiting the effectiveness of existing vision foundation models. There is a need for a parameter-efficient, universal framework that can jointly handle multiple ultrasound tasks by exploiting commonalities and frequency information.

Method: Introduce MR-Adapter to enable task-common and task-specific parameter-efficient knowledge integration; design F^2-Enhancer to exploit multi-scale frequency features in ultrasound images; develop TC-Decoder to promote collaboration between dense and global predictions via global-local token interactions.

Result: Comprehensive experiments on large-scale multi-task ultrasound benchmarks and external single-task benchmarks show FreqDINO++ consistently outperforms strong baselines and recent foundation models across 27 clinical tasks, with good generalization to unseen data.

Conclusion: FreqDINO++ offers a unified, efficient solution for universal ultrasound analysis by combining task-aware routing, frequency-aware enhancement, and collaborative decoding; the work demonstrates strong cross-task performance and generalization, with code available at the authors’ repository.

Abstract: Ultrasound image analysis plays a crucial role in cancer screening and prenatal diagnosis, yet comprehensive assessment requires jointly addressing tasks such as lesion segmentation and benign-malignant classification. While recent vision foundation models have shown remarkable universal representations, unlocking their potential for ultrasound is bottlenecked by the considerable domain gap from natural images. Existing methods typically fine-tune heavy vision encoders for isolated tasks, incurring substantial computational overhead while overlooking the underlying commonalities across heterogeneous tasks. In this work, we propose FreqDINO++, a frequency-guided multi-task routing vision foundation model for universal ultrasound analysis. We first introduce a Multi-task Routing Adapter (MR-Adapter) to support parameter-efficient integration of task-common and task-specific knowledge, a Frequency-aware Feature Enhancer (F$^2$-Enhancer) is then designed to capture the rich multi-scale frequency characteristics of ultrasound images, and a Task-aligned Collaborative Decoder (TC-Decoder) is devised to promote collaboration between dense and global prediction tasks through global-local token interaction. Extensive experiments on large-scale multi-task and external single-task ultrasound benchmarks demonstrate that FreqDINO++ consistently outperforms strong baselines and recent foundation models across 27 diverse clinical task scenarios, while also showing promising generalization to unseen data. The code is at https://github.com/MingLang-FD/FreqDINO-Plus.

</details>


### [76] [Fast Cross-Strength Multi-Contrast Brain MRI Translation using Latent Bridge Matching](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20341)
*Siddharth Srivastava,Till Bretschneider*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: A unified conditional latent bridge model for field-to-field MRI synthesis that handles modality- and field-strength translations with a single inference step, achieving competitive results across three tasks in MRIxFields2026.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: MRI acquisitions vary across field strengths, causing noise, resolution, homogeneity, and contrast differences that hinder cross-study comparability. Existing solutions often rely on task-specific architectures; a single, controllable model is desirable for multi-task synthesis with efficient inference.

Method: A single model based on conditional latent bridge matching within the MRIxFields2026 framework. It enables controllable field-to-field synthesis across modalities and field strengths, requiring only a single inference step. It can produce all modality/field-strength combinations for 30 axial slices and perform cross-modality-strength translation for a full volume on a single GPU.

Result: The model achieves highly competitive results on all three MRIxFields2026 tasks. It enables fast generation: 30 axial slices in under 90 seconds for all modality/field-strength combinations, and cross-modality-strength translation for a full volume in under 70 seconds, on an NVIDIA A5000 GPU. The work includes extensive ablations of its components and provides code (link cited).

Conclusion: A single model without task-specific architectures can match or exceed task-specific baselines across multiple MRI synthesis tasks, enabling efficient, standardized multi-field translations and practical deployment.

Abstract: Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) acquired at different field strengths exhibits pronounced variation in noise, resolution, homogeneity, and contrast, which limits comparability across acquisition settings and complicates downstream analysis. We address this with a unified conditional model for controllable field-to-field synthesis, built on the framework of conditional latent bridge matching. Our single model achieves highly competitive results across the validation phase for all three tasks of the MRIxFields2026 challenge without task-specific architectures or training. We achieve fast generation with only a single inference step, producing all modality and field-strength combinations for $30$ axial slices in under $90$ seconds, as well as cross-modality-strength translation for a full volume in under $70$ seconds, on a single NVIDIA A5000 GPU. We further provide extensive ablations regarding different components of our solution. Code: https://gitlab.com/siddharthsrivastava/mrixfields-2026

</details>


### [77] [EliGSiR: Continual RGB-D Mapping with Gaussian Splatting under Bounded Compute](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20348)
*Björn Ellensohn,Elmar Rueckert,Christian Rauch*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: EliGSiR is a continual Gaussian mapper that uses evidence-guided, load-adaptive updates and image replay to maintain and improve 3D reconstructions under streaming observations.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To address continual RGB-D mapping where new observations arrive online while previously reconstructed regions must be preserved, under limited optimization budgets.

Method: Propose EliGSiR with three core mechanisms: (1) Map-Guided View Scheduling to filter redundant views and reassess retained views based on current map state; (2) Load-Adaptive Fidelity to adjust supervision resolution to the mapping load rather than a fixed schedule; (3) Targeted Geometry Growth to separate depth supervision from Gaussian creation, adding geometric capacity where repeated RGB-D observations indicate missing or misplaced structures; plus Image Replay as a component implied in the name.

Result: Empirical evaluation on Replica, TUM RGB-D, ScanNet++, and real RGB-D sequences. On TUM fr3/long_office_household, PSNR reaches 21.52 dB (vs 19.42 dB for SplaTAM). In tracked-pose tests, EliGSiR with live ORB-SLAM3 achieves 23.02 dB in 155.5 s vs CaRtGS achieving 20.10 dB in 230.9 s with its native tracker. Additional results show improved utilization of the mapping budget and reconstruction quality throughout acquisition.

Conclusion: EliGSiR demonstrates how adaptive view management, fidelity control, and geometry growth enable higher-quality continual 3D Gaussian mapping under streaming observations, with efficient use of computation and memory across diverse datasets and live-tracking scenarios.

Abstract: Conventional 3D Gaussian Splatting assumes a closed set of observations and long optimization schedules. Continual RGB-D mapping in contrast poses the problem that new observations arrive online, while previously reconstructed regions must be preserved. We present EliGSiR (Evidence-guided Load-adaptive Incremental Gaussian Splatting with Image Replay), a continual Gaussian mapper that controls how the available optimization budget is used as the reconstruction evolves. Map-Guided View Scheduling filters redundant incoming views and reconsiders retained views according to the current state of the map. Load-Adaptive Fidelity adjusts supervision resolution to the current mapping load instead of following a fixed resolution schedule. Targeted Geometry Growth separates depth supervision from Gaussian creation and adds geometric capacity only where repeated RGB-D observations indicate missing or misplaced structure. Together, these mechanisms adapt which views are optimized, how much image detail is used, and where the representation grows while mapping remains active. We evaluate EliGSiR on Replica, TUM RGB-D, ScanNet++, and real RGB-D sensor sequences, considering both the final reconstruction and the map available throughout acquisition. On TUM RGB-D fr3/long_office_household, EliGSiR reaches 21.52 dB with the same ground-truth mapping poses used by the controlled baselines, compared with 19.42 dB for SplaTAM. In the tracked-pose comparison, EliGSiR with live ORB-SLAM3 poses reaches 23.02 dB in 155.5 s, compared with 20.10 dB in 230.9 s for CaRtGS using its native tracker. We further evaluate reconstruction throughout acquisition and show how EliGSiR adaptive view scheduling, supervision fidelity, and geometry growth improve the use of the available mapping budget.

</details>


### [78] [MM-Future: Multi-Mode Joint World-Action Modeling for Autonomous Driving](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20377)
*Shuai Liu,Hechangle Gong,Hao Jiang,Runlin He,Junxiang Zhan,Kai Huang,Sheng Yang,Shaoqing Ren*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: MM-Future is a multi-modal world-action model for autonomous driving that generates multiple paired scene-action hypotheses and jointly models their evolution with a diffusion Transformer; it compresses video into planning-oriented MM-Tokens and uses a future-conditioned scorer to rank trajectories; achieves strong multi-modal metrics on NAVSIM/HUGSIM in both closed-loop and zero-shot settings.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Address the coupling between decision-making and scene evolution under multi-mode uncertainty by enabling multi-modal planning and robust trajectory generation.

Method: Generate multiple world-action hypothesis pairs initialized from a structured action prior and an independent future scene source; co-evolve each pair with a modality-aware diffusion Transformer; compress multi-view video into planning-oriented MM-Tokens; apply a future-conditioned proposal scorer to rank trajectories based on history context and their predicted futures.

Result: On NAVSIM navtest, MM-Future achieves 94.0 PDMS and 91.5 EPDMS; in zero-shot closed-loop evaluation on HUGSIM it attains 32.3 HD-Score; ablations show improvements over single-mode and action-only variants.

Conclusion: The work demonstrates that multi-mode joint world-action modeling with planning-oriented MM-Tokens and a future-aware scorer yields consistent gains, validating the benefit of coupling world evolution with action planning for autonomous driving.

Abstract: Autonomous driving involves coupled decision-making and scene evolution under multi-mode uncertainty. To capture this coupling and uncertainty, we introduce MM-Future, a world-action model that generates multiple paired scene-action hypotheses and models bidirectional interaction within each pair. Each hypothesis is initialized from a structured action prior and an independent future scene source, which are then co-evolved through a modality-aware diffusion Transformer. To support efficient multi-mode rollout, MM-Future compresses multi-view video into planning-oriented representations, dubbed MM-Tokens. Finally, a future-conditioned proposal scorer ranks trajectory candidates by shared history context and their paired predicted future. On NAVSIM navtest, MM-Future achieves 94.0 PDMS and 91.5 EPDMS, while attaining a 32.3 HD-Score in zero-shot closed-loop evaluation on HUGSIM. Ablations show consistent improvements over both single-mode and action-only variants, validating the benefit of multi-mode joint world-action modeling.

</details>


### [79] [Compact Vision Models for Iris Presentation Attack Detection under Presentation Attack Instrument Shift and Environmental Degradation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20386)
*Athanasios Angelakis,Marta Gomez-Barrero*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: Three ultra-compact iris PAD models (~0.26M params) trained from scratch are benchmarked on the LivDet-Iris 2017 Notre Dame subset under PAI-driven domain shift and environmental degradation. Using a single validation threshold transferred to all test partitions, known→unknown attacks show large performance drops (APCER and D-EER). ZACH-ViT yields best unknown-attack APCER and D-EER; Compact-TransMIL yields best BPCER; overall, results indicate deployment readiness under unknown PAIs is not achieved despite relative model advantages.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Evaluate whether very small, scratch-trained CV models can robustly detect presentation attacks in iris recognition under unseen PAIs and environmental variation, without external pretraining or data augmentation.

Method: Compared three compact scratch-trained CV models (~0.26M params) on Notre Dame subset of LivDet-Iris 2017. No external pretraining or data augmentation. Training over five seeds. A single validation-selected threshold is applied unchanged to known-attack, unknown-attack, corrupted, and pooled test partitions. Metrics: APCER, BPCER, D-EER across partitions.

Result: From known to unknown attacks, APCER increases by 17.11–30.47 percentage points; D-EER increases by 7.38–12.73 points. At the validation threshold, ZACH-ViT achieves the lowest unknown-attack APCER (47.69±4.84%) and D-EER (38.87±0.93%), while Compact-TransMIL achieves the lowest unknown-attack BPCER. ZACH-ViT also yields the lowest unknown-attack BPCER at an APCER limit of 10% (81.29±1.95%). However, the absolute errors are high, implying the compact models’ advantage does not translate to deployment readiness under unknown PAIs.

Conclusion: Compact scratch-trained models exhibit limited generalization to unseen PAIs and degraded performance under domain shift; despite some strengths (ZACH-ViT on APCER/D-EER, Compact-TransMIL on BPCER), none approach deployment readiness for unknown attacks. Improved generalization, possibly via data augmentation, pretraining, or more diverse PAI data, is needed.

Abstract: Iris presentation attack detection (PAD) is security-critical when a subsystem that appears reliable during development encounters presentation attack instruments (PAIs) or acquisition conditions absent from validation data. We benchmark three compact scratch-trained computer-vision models, each with at most approximately 0.26 million trainable parameters, on the Notre Dame subset of LivDet-Iris 2017 under PAI-driven domain shift and environmental degradation. All models are trained without external pretraining or data augmentation and evaluated over five seeds. A validation-selected threshold is transferred unchanged to the known-attack, unknown-attack, corrupted, and pooled test partitions. From known to unknown attack presentations, Attack Presentation Classification Error Rate (APCER) increases by 17.11-30.47 percentage points and Detection Equal Error Rate (D-EER) increases by 7.38-12.73 percentage points. At the validation-selected threshold, ZACH-ViT obtains the lowest unknown-attack APCER (47.69 +/- 4.84%) and D-EER (38.87 +/- 0.93%), while Compact-TransMIL obtains the lowest Bona Fide Presentation Classification Error Rate (BPCER). ZACH-ViT also gives the lowest unknown-attack BPCER at an APCER limit of 10% (81.29 +/- 1.95%). The high absolute errors show that the comparative advantage of the best compact model does not constitute deployment readiness under unknown PAIs.

</details>


### [80] [TouchSight: Bare-Handed Tactile Prediction from Egocentric Video via Generative Visual Augmentation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20414)
*Danyan Zhou,Jinxuan Lu,Jiawei Lin,Tianxing Chen,Chuqiao Lyu,Wenbo Ding*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: TouchSight uses monocular egocentric vision to predict dense hand contact forces, leveraging glove data and a generative re-rendering (TwinTouch-20H) to bridge appearance gaps; achieves dense tactile signal recovery without tactile instrumentation during capture and shows strong generalization and scaling with glove supervision.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Dense tactile sensing is essential for dexterous manipulation but current data collection requires invasive tactile instrumentation; a scalable approach is needed to recover tactile information from vision.

Method: Combine 500 hours of pressure-glove data with hand-object interaction data; TwinTouch-20H provides 20 hours of paired visuals where generative models re-render gloved views as bare-hand observations in new contexts while preserving tactile labels; TouchSight predicts dense force from both actual glove videos and generated bare-hand videos.

Result: Outperforms prior contact prediction methods on OakInk2; qualitatively generalizes to natural bare-hand egocentric videos from unseen datasets; improvements scale with glove supervision; demonstrates dense tactile signal recovery from vision alone.

Conclusion: Dense tactile signals can be recovered via egocentric vision without real-time tactile instrumentation, enabling dense contact-force prediction from monocular video and synthetic paired data.

Abstract: Tactile signals provide direct contact and force measurements that are essential for understanding physical interactions and enabling dexterous robotic manipulation. However, tactile sensing requires direct measurement at contact interfaces, making large-scale data collection reliant on intrusive, costly, and restrictive instrumentation. We present TouchSight, a monocular egocentric vision framework for dense full-hand contact force prediction that leverages 500 hours of pressure-glove recordings and extensive hand-object interaction (HOI) data. To address the appearance gap between gloved training data and bare-hand real-world scenarios, we construct TwinTouch-20H: 20 hours of paired visual data in which generative video models re-render gloved recordings as bare-hand observations against new backgrounds while preserving the original measured tactile labels. TouchSight predicts dense force from both gloved and generated bare-hand videos, outperforms prior contact prediction methods on OakInk2, qualitatively generalizes to natural bare-hand egocentric videos from unseen datasets, and improves consistently as glove supervision scales. These results demonstrate that dense tactile signals can be recovered from egocentric vision alone, without tactile instrumentation at capture time.

</details>


### [81] [WeVisDoc: From Coverage to Capability for Robust End-to-End Document Parsing](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20423)
*Hao Yu,Kang Liu,Linnan Zhao,Jiabo Zhan,Chong Sun,Chen Li,Jing Lyu*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: WeVisDoc is a two-stage data-centric framework for robust end-to-end document parsing. Stage I broadens semantic, structural, and appearance coverage via heterogeneous data and structure-preserving degradation; Stage II uses a held-out probe to measure residual errors within fixed visual-structural clusters, guiding targeted data construction and reallocation of the target-token budget.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Training corpora for document parsers are biased toward clean digital pages; simply expanding data coverage does not necessarily address the parser's remaining weaknesses.

Method: Stage I Augment data with heterogeneous content and implement structure-preserving degradation to widen coverage. Stage II Use a held-out probe to quantify residual errors within predefined visual–structural clusters; diagnostics guide targeted data construction and reallocation of the target-token budget.

Result: WeVisDoc-4B achieves an Overall score of 95.38 on OmniDocBench v1.6 and a mean Overall score of 75.54 across the three PureDocBench tracks, ranking first among end-to-end parsers in all four settings. Stage II yields improvements over Stage I for 2B and 4B models, with larger gains on degraded tracks, including a 4.03-point gain for the 4B model on the Real Degraded track.

Conclusion: A two-stage, data-centric approach yields state-of-the-art robustness for end-to-end document parsing across diverse layouts and degradation conditions; Stage II diagnostics effectively identify residual weaknesses to guide targeted data construction and budget reallocation.

Abstract: Document parsing converts document images into structured content and requires reliable performance across diverse layouts and acquisition conditions. Yet training corpora are biased toward common document types and clean digital pages, while expanding coverage alone does not specify how to address a parser's remaining weaknesses. We present WeVisDoc, a two-stage data-centric framework for robust end-to-end document parsing. Stage I broadens semantic, structural, and appearance coverage through heterogeneous data and structure-preserving degradation synthesis. Stage II uses a held-out probe to measure the Stage I parser's residual errors within fixed visual-structural clusters. These diagnostics guide targeted data construction and reallocation of the target-token budget. WeVisDoc-4B achieves an Overall score of 95.38 on OmniDocBench v1.6 and a mean Overall score of 75.54 across the three PureDocBench tracks, ranking first among the compared end-to-end parsers in all four settings. Compared with Stage I, Stage II improves Overall scores for the 2B and 4B models on both benchmarks, with larger gains on the degraded PureDocBench tracks, including a 4.03-point gain for the 4B model on the Real Degraded track.

</details>


### [82] [When Do Language-Grounded Explanations Help? A Graph-Bottleneck for Farm Monitoring Interpretable Sheep Facial Pain](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20427)
*Alam Noor,Miguel Guti'errez Gait'an*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: Attention-based SPFES model yields explanations that poorly align with pain predictions; adding a concept bottleneck using SPFES concepts improves interpretability but requires supervision; pooled explanation metrics can be misleading; a cross-validated benchmark of seven methods is provided.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Assess trust and interpretability in automated sheep pain assessment by evaluating whether explanations justify SPFES-based pain scores and by testing a concept bottleneck approach.

Method: Baseline: region-wise attention over text embeddings of SPFES descriptors; assess if explanations align with predictions; ablate descriptors; then introduce a concept bottleneck classifier that reads SPFES concept scores, supervised by per-region state annotations (image-level pipelines discarded). Compare prediction performance and explainability metrics (e.g., Cohen's kappa), assess concept accuracy, and analyze effects of supervision vs. architectural changes. Also report on cross-validated benchmark across seven methods on the dataset.

Result: Ablating a descriptor changes the logit by about 1e-4; the most-attended cue agrees with the predicted pain level in only 32.6% of regions. After implementing a concept bottleneck that uses SPFES concept scores, minority pain-indicating states are recovered at 3.5–8.3× their base rates, and ear/eye severity orderings emerge without severity supervision. Removing supervision leaves Cohen’s kappa unchanged but concept accuracy falls to 0.109, showing architectural necessity does not imply semantic validity. Pooled concept accuracy is misleading under clinical imbalance. The authors also provide a cross-validated, protocol-matched benchmark of seven methods on the dataset.

Conclusion: Architectural choices strongly impact semantic validity of explanations. A concept bottleneck with supervision yields more semantically meaningful concepts, improving interpretability, while relying solely on attention or appearance bypass is unreliable. Evaluation should consider per-concept metrics and balanced benchmarks rather than pooled concept accuracy.

Abstract: Automated pain recognition from facial expression could make continuous welfare assessment practical in sheep, but adoption depends on trust: a stockperson cannot act on a score that arrives without justification. We ground a model in the Sheep Pain Facial Expression Scale (SPFES) by letting each detected facial region attend over text embeddings of the clinical descriptors and then test whether the resulting explanations mean anything. They do not. Ablating an entire descriptor changes the predicted logit by about $10^{-4}$, and the most-attended cue agrees with the predicted pain level in only $32.6\%$ of regions, although the attention maps, the learned gate, and the generated text all proposed otherwise. We therefore remove the appearance bypass with a concept bottleneck whose classifier reads only SPFES concept scores, supervised by per-region state annotations that image-level pipelines discard. This costs $0.05$--$0.10$ in Cohen's $κ$ but yields concepts that are demonstrably learned: minority pain-indicating states are recovered at $3.5$--$8.3\times$ their base rates, and the ear and eye severity orderings emerge without severity supervision. Removing the supervision alone leaves $κ$ unchanged while concept accuracy falls to $0.109$, showing that architectural necessity does not imply semantic validity. We also show that pooled concept accuracy is misleading under clinical imbalance and provide a cross-validated, protocol-matched benchmark of seven methods on this dataset.

</details>


### [83] [Cross-Architecture Foundation-Model Distillation for Edge Flood Segmentation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20441)
*Fabian Schmalstieg,Karsten Mueller,Wojciech Samek*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: Distill a 300M-parameter geospatial foundation-model into a 0.7M edge-friendly student for flood segmentation, using unlabeled Sentinel-2 data to scale training beyond manual annotations; achieves competitive or matching performance with a compact INT8 deployment on Jetson Xavier NX, and suggests foundation-model supervision amplifies limited annotation budgets at edge scale.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Enable deployable, high-performance flood-segmentation on memory-constrained edge devices by leveraging foundation-model supervision and unlabeled data to expand the effective training set without increasing manual labeling effort.

Method: Student–teacher distillation from a large Prithvi-EO-2.0 teacher (300M) to a compact EfficientViT-B0 student (0.7M), with additional unlabeled Sentinel-2 imagery used to augment the training set; experiments at 252 scenes (budget-matched) and 2,500 scenes (scaling); activation replacement and quantization-aware training; comparison to a fixed MNDWI threshold baseline; geometry-matched control to assess label-source effects.

Result: With 252 scenes, student training competes with direct training and improves STURM-Flood performance; scaling to 2,500 scenes narrows the student–teacher gap (student 0.787 IoU on Sen1Floods11 vs teacher 0.822; matches teacher on STURM-Flood; below teacher on WorldFloods-v2). After optimization, the 1.5 MB INT8 TensorRT model runs at 5.57 ms per 512×512 image on Jetson Xavier NX with ~14 MB RAM. A fixed MNDWI threshold remains competitive on external benchmarks, indicating generalization tests rather than model superiority.

Conclusion: Foundation-model supervision can transform a fixed, small manual-annotation budget into a much larger effective training set, yielding a compact, deployable edge model without sacrificing competitive performance.

Abstract: Geospatial foundation models can provide strong flood-segmentation performance, but their size limits deployment on memory-constrained edge hardware. We distill a 300-million-parameter Prithvi-EO-2.0 teacher, fine-tuned on the 252 manually labeled Sen1Floods11 training scenes, into a 0.7-million-parameter EfficientViT-B0 student. The teacher supervises additional unlabeled Sentinel-2 imagery, allowing the student training set to grow without new manual annotations. At the matched budget of 252 scenes, teacher-supervised training is competitive with direct training and improves STURM-Flood performance across tested configurations; a geometry-matched control shows that label source alone does not explain the difference. Scaling the teacher-supervised pool to 2,500 scenes narrows the remaining student--teacher gap: the float student reaches 0.787 water intersection over union on the Sen1Floods11 test split against 0.822 for the teacher, matches the teacher on STURM-Flood under our evaluation protocol, and remains below it on WorldFloods-v2. After activation replacement and quantization-aware training, the student runs as a 1.5-megabyte 8-bit integer (INT8) TensorRT engine on a Jetson Xavier NX at 5.57 milliseconds of graphics processing unit (GPU) compute per 512-by-512 image, with approximately 14 megabytes of runtime device memory. A fixed modified normalized difference water index (MNDWI) threshold is competitive with both models on the two clean external benchmarks, so we interpret those benchmarks as generalization tests rather than as evidence of learned-model superiority over a spectral rule. The results support the conclusion: foundation-model supervision can amplify a fixed manual annotation budget into a substantially larger training set and yield a compact, deployable edge model.

</details>


### [84] [SenseFuse: Label-Free Fusion of Image and Shape Encoders for Open-Vocabulary 3D Instance Segmentation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20475)
*Euiseok Han,Tri Ton,Hwanhee Kim,Seungyeon Ryu,Chang D. Yoo*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: SenseFuse is a label-free fusion framework that adaptively fuses 2D image and 3D shape encoders for open-vocabulary 3D instance segmentation, improving mask labeling without labels in milliseconds. It yields substantial gains across ScanNet200, Replica, and ScanNet++, approaching oracle-level improvements; most settings see increased instance AP.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Open-vocabulary 3D segmentation is underexplored beyond image-based cues and current methods rely on image-distilled labeling, leaving potential complementary information in 3D shape cues underutilized. The paper aims to leverage complementary failure patterns of 2D and 3D encoders to improve labeling accuracy in a label-free manner.

Method: SenseFuse introduces an adaptive scene-level fusion weight that balances 2D and 3D encoders during the mask-labeling stage. The weight is chosen to maximize a label-free sensitivity measure estimated from unlabeled proposals in a few milliseconds for each scene. The approach relies on observed disjoint failure patterns between 2D and 3D encoders (3D errors differ from 2D errors, whereas two 2D encoders often produce identical mistakes) to achieve complementary labeling improvements without requiring labeled data.

Result: Across ScanNet200, Replica, and ScanNet++, SenseFuse improves labeling accuracy in every evaluated setting, recovering 67-100% (median 93%) of the gain achievable with an oracle fusion weight, and increases instance AP in 21 of 22 reported settings. Code is provided at the project link.

Conclusion: Adaptive, label-free fusion of 2D and 3D encoders at the mask-labeling stage yields robust open-vocabulary 3D instance segmentation improvements, leveraging complementary error patterns and enabling fast, per-scene fusion weight selection without labeled data.

Abstract: Open-vocabulary scene understanding is fundamental for robotics, laying the groundwork for spatial reasoning and object manipulation. While closed-vocabulary 3D instance segmentation heavily leverages 3D shape information, state-of-the-art open-vocabulary methods remain predominantly restricted to 2D image features or image-distilled representations during mask labeling. In this paper, we propose SenseFuse, a label-free fusion method that balances 2D image and 3D shape encoders for robust open-vocabulary 3D instance segmentation, refining only the mask-labeling stage of existing pipelines. We reveal that 2D image and 3D shape encoders exhibit largely disjoint failure patterns and rarely share identical wrong labels, whereas two 2D image encoders frequently repeat the same errors. This distinct behavior makes the 2D and 3D pair inherently complementary. We introduce an adaptive mechanism that selects a scene-level fusion weight to maximize a label-free sensitivity measure, estimated directly from a single scene's unlabeled proposals in milliseconds. SenseFuse improves labeling accuracy in every evaluated setting across ScanNet200, Replica, and ScanNet++, recovering 67-100% (median 93%) of the gain achievable with an oracle weight, and it raises instance AP in 21 of 22 reported settings. Code is available at https://github.com/hanes1207/SenseFuse.

</details>


### [85] [Grounded Product Understanding in Livestream Videos](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20508)
*Xinyu Zhang,Junjie Chen,Jiawei Ge,Qianlong Li,Libin Ma,Baokun Pan,Yahui Luo*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: A new large-scale benchmark (GPUB) for grounded product understanding in e-commerce livestreams, with 3,000 videos and 31K products, enabling joint product identification and moment localization (GPrU) plus product retrieval and local- ization; a strong baseline (UniPro) improves performance but tasks remain challenging.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current benchmarks evaluate product retrieval or temporal localization in isolation, neglecting the crucial link between product identity and its supporting moments in livestreams. This hampers downstream tasks like clipping for product information gathering.

Method: GPUB setup: 3,000 livestream instances with quality-controlled multi-moment temporal annotations and a catalog of over 31K fashion products; defines three tasks: Grounded Product Understanding (GPrU), Product Retrieval, and Product Moment Localization; uses Pair mAP@.3 and Joint R@1@.3 as evaluation metrics. UniPro: a unified model that derives product-aligned and temporally structured representations from a shared multimodal encoding.

Result: Baseline best for GPrU: 10.13% Pair mAP@.3. UniPro improves to 21.53% Pair mAP@.3 and 37.23% Joint R@1@.3 on GPrU.

Conclusion: GPUB provides a challenging, multi-task benchmark bridging product identity and temporal evidence in livestreams. UniPro demonstrates that joint, temporally structured representations substantially close the gap, signaling potential directions for future models that fuse product catalogs with moment-level cues.

Abstract: E-commerce livestreams have emerged as an important channel for presenting products to online consumers, containing multiple products whose information is scattered in different moments. This poses significant challenges for downstream product understanding applications, such as product-centric livestream clipping, where models need to identify the product and its relevant segments for information gathering. However, existing benchmarks for general product understanding typically evaluate product retrieval and temporal localization in isolation, leaving the critical correspondence between product identity and temporal evidence largely unassessed. To address this limitation, we introduce GPUB, a large-scale benchmark comprising 3,000 livestream instances with quality-controlled multi-moment temporal annotations and a catalog of over 31K fashion products. GPUB supports three evaluation tasks: the main task Grounded Product Understanding (GPrU) requires jointly identifying the target product and localizing its supporting moments from a livestream video and a candidate product set; Product Retrieval and Product Moment Localization serve as two complementary subtasks. Evaluation of existing multimodal models shows that GPrU remains highly challenging, with the best-performing baseline achieving only 10.13% Pair mAP@.3. To narrow the performance gap, we further develop UniPro, a unified product understanding model that derives product-aligned and temporally structured representations from shared multimodal encoding, improving Pair mAP@.3 to 21.53% while achieving 37.23% Joint R@1@.3 on GPrU.

</details>


### [86] [Automated Goldsmith's Mark Retrieval in Silverware](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20509)
*Atmik Tiwari,Vincent Christlein,Mark Fichtner,Freya Gohlke,Birgit Schübel,Theresa Witting,Heike Zech,Mathias Zinnen*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: Self-supervised DINOv2 ViT-S/14 with learned cropping and metric-learning fine-tuning achieves strong retrieval performance for goldsmith marks; learned cropping approaches manual cropping without ground-truth at inference; broad evaluation across backbones; dataset and code released.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Art historians rely on labor-intensive comparison of marks; automated, localization-aware retrieval can expedite dating/identification and standardize evaluation; assess impact of pretraining, localization, and cropping strategies.

Method: AI-assisted retrieval pipeline with mark localization and metric-learning fine-tuning across three backbones: ImageNet ResNet-50, supervised ViT-S/16, self-supervised DINOv2 ViT-S/14. Evaluate cropping strategies: none, ground-truth, learned detection-based; metrics: mAP and Top-1; release dataset, code, and web interface.

Result: Best config: DINOv2 ViT-S/14 with manual crop and metric-learning: mAP 62.63%, Top-1 73.74%. Self-supervised pretraining and mark localization are primary drivers; learned cropping recovers most of manual crop gains without ground-truth at inference.

Conclusion: The pipeline demonstrates viable AI-assisted retrieval for art-historical marks; enables reproducibility, reduces manual effort, and provides resources for the digital humanities community.

Abstract: For art historians, goldsmith marks play a critical role in the identification and dating of artifacts. In practice, experts must manually compare a query mark against hundreds of documented examples, a process that is both tedious and highly dependent on specialist knowledge. To address this, we present an AI-assisted retrieval pipeline that combines mark localization with metric-learning fine-tuning across three backbone architectures: an ImageNet-pretrained ResNet-50, a supervised ViT-S/16, and a self-supervised DINOv2 ViT-S/14. We conduct a systematic evaluation of cropping strategies, where we measure the impact of no cropping, manual ground-truth cropping, and learned detection-based cropping, and assess their interaction with each backbone. Our strongest configuration, DINOv2 ViT-S/14 with manual crop and metric-learning fine-tuning, achieves an mAP of 62.63% and a Top-1 accuracy of 73.74%. Our experiments show that self-supervised pretraining and mark localization are the two most impactful factors, with learned cropping recovering the majority of the gain from manual cropping without requiring ground-truth annotations at inference time. To enable reproducibility and adoption in the digital humanities, we release our manually annotated dataset and codebase, and deploy the system via a public web interface.

</details>


### [87] [A Dual-Stream Regulated Reconstruction and Segmentation Network with Hierarchical Artifact-Prior Modeling for Ultra-Low-Field Pediatric Neuroimaging](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20562)
*Bahram Jafrasteh,Leo Milecki,Qingyu Zhao*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: Unified, multi-task pipeline for quality assessment, enhancement, and subcortical segmentation in ultra-low-field pediatric MRI (0.064 T). Uses a two-stream 3D U-Net that reconstructs an enhanced uLF volume and fuses it with the original for segmentation, an auxiliary outside-brain class, an artifact graph predicting seven artifact ratings from residuals and segmentation features, and atlas-based label propagation via diffeomorphic registration. Validated across three tasks within a single inference pipeline.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Ultra-low-field pediatric MRI suffers from very low SNR, weak anatomical boundaries, and frequent artifacts, hindering automated quality assessment, enhancement, and segmentation. Dense annotations are scarce. A unified, data-efficient approach that addresses all three tasks in one pipeline is needed, particularly for challenge settings like LISA 2026.

Method: A two-stream 3D U-Net framework: (1) Reconstruction stream enhances the uLF volume; (2) Segmentation stream uses the original and enhanced images to perform subcortical segmentation. An auxiliary class for brain tissue outside target structures is introduced to stabilize boundaries, derived from whole-brain masks. A head module conditioned on an artifact graph predicts seven artifact ratings from reconstruction residuals and frozen segmentation features. Due to limited dense annotations, diffeomorphic registration from atlas to target enables label propagation and regularizes anatomical reconstruction, enabling joint training and evaluation of all three tasks in one inference pipeline.

Result: Validation results are reported for all three tasks, indicating the framework can operate in a single pipeline and achieve joint quality assessment, enhancement, and segmentation in ultra-low-field pediatric MRI, with improved boundary handling and plausible artifact rating predictions.

Conclusion: The work presents a cohesive, data-efficient approach for simultaneous quality assessment, enhancement, and segmentation in challenging ultra-low-field pediatric MRI. The combination of atlas-based label propagation, a two-stream architecture, boundary-aware auxiliary supervision, and an artifact-aware head supports robust performance in low-SNR, scarce-annotation regimes and is well-suited for challenge settings and potential generalization to similar imaging modalities.

Abstract: Automated quality assessment, enhancement, and segmentation of multiple structures in $0.064\,\mathrm{T}$ ultra-low-field pediatric MRI are limited by a low signal-to-noise ratio, weak anatomical boundaries, and frequent artifacts. We present a unified framework for the LISA 2026 Challenge that performs all three tasks together within one inference pipeline. A network with two coupled streams, built on a 3D U-Net, first reconstructs an enhanced uLF volume and then combines the original and enhanced images for subcortical segmentation. To improve boundary stability, we add an auxiliary class covering brain tissue outside the target structures, derived from whole brain masks. A head conditioned on an artifact graph predicts the seven artifact ratings from reconstruction residuals and frozen segmentation features. We address the scarcity of dense annotations using diffeomorphic registration from atlas to target for label propagation and to regularize anatomical reconstruction. We report validation results across all three tasks.

</details>


### [88] [DocAttriBench: Benchmarking Answer Grounding in Document Visual Question Answering](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20574)
*Luca De Grandis,Silvia Cappelletti,William Raccagni,Marcella Cornia,Lorenzo Baraldi,Rita Cucchiara*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: Proposes DocAttriBench (DAB), a large-scale dataset for element-level grounding in Document VQA, built via MAPPET, a mask-based perplexity attribution method; evaluates grounding and answer quality; larger models improve answer accuracy but often fail at precise element localization.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Grounding answers to specific layout elements is essential for trustworthy Document VQA. Existing datasets lack high-quality grounding labels or are costly to annotate; scalable, automatic grounding is needed.

Method: Create DAB by applying MAPPET to existing Document VQA datasets. MAPPET masks candidate layout elements (text blocks, tables, images) and uses the change in perplexity to attribute the answer to the most informative element. Produces 237k documents and 296k QA pairs with element-level grounding. Benchmark grounding-capable multimodal LLMs on DAB across answer accuracy, attribution accuracy, and overall answer quality.

Result: DAB offers a scalable, ground-truth-rich benchmark for evaluating grounded Document VQA. Larger models show higher answer accuracy but often fail to localize supporting elements; code and dataset released.

Conclusion: DAB enables grounded, verifiable, and trustworthy Document VQA development and evaluation; a valuable community resource for grounding and attribution research in document understanding.

Abstract: Answer grounding in document visual question answering remains an open challenge: most benchmarks lack grounding annotations or provide limited-quality labels, while constructing grounded datasets still requires costly manual effort. We introduce DocAttriBench (DAB), a large-scale benchmark for fine-grained, element-level source attribution in Document VQA, grounding answers to specific layout elements such as text blocks, tables, and images. To build DAB, we propose a Mask-based Perplexity-Derived Attribution method (MAPPET) that combines document layout and language modeling to identify the most informative element for each answer. MAPPET measures the increase in perplexity after masking candidate elements and attributes the answer to the element contributing most to model confidence. Applying MAPPET to multiple existing Document VQA datasets yields DAB, with 237k documents and 296k question-answer pairs with element-level grounding. We benchmark grounding-capable multimodal LLMs on DAB, evaluating answer accuracy, attribution accuracy, and overall answer quality. Results show that while larger models generally achieve higher answer accuracy, even the strongest models often fail to localize the supporting elements. DAB provides a scalable benchmark for developing grounded, verifiable, and trustworthy Document VQA models. Dataset and code are available at https://aimagelab.github.io/DocAttriBench/.

</details>


### [89] [RawSLAM: Online HDR Gaussian SLAM from Linear Radiance](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20589)
*Marina Orozco González,Luis Merino*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: First online Gaussian SLAM on single-exposure 16-bit HDR imagery (RAW16); improves robustness to extreme lighting vs 8-bit LDR and offline HDR pipelines; introduces HDR Gaussian Splatting with log-color features, Reinhard photometric objective, and gradient weighting; generalizes to other SLAM systems; accompanies the RawSLAM dataset.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Address robustness gaps in dense visual SLAM under extreme lighting by leveraging 16-bit linear HDR data in an online framework, overcoming limitations of 8-bit LDR and offline HDR pipelines.

Method: An architecture-agnostic HDR Gaussian Splatting module with an MLP-free logarithmic parameterization of Gaussian color features; a Reinhard range-compressed photometric objective; and structure-guided spatial gradient weighting, enabling online tracking and mapping directly on single-exposure 16-bit linear HDR imagery.

Result: Outperforms a direct HDR adaptation of MonoGS in trajectory and reconstruction accuracy; same formulation works on 8-bit inputs, roughly halving MonoGS baseline error; transfers to SplaTAM, Gaussian SLAM, and DROID-W, eliminating tracking failures on challenging illumination sequences.

Conclusion: Proposes a practical, online HDR SLAM framework that operates on RAW HDR imagery, improves robustness to lighting, and offers transferability across SLAM systems; introduces RawSLAM dataset to enable research in 16-bit HDR SLAM.

Abstract: Current dense visual SLAM systems rely almost exclusively on 8-bit tonemapped Low Dynamic Range (LDR) inputs, limiting their robustness in extreme lighting where shadows and highlights trigger tracking drift and mapping collapse. Conversely, existing raw and High Dynamic Range (HDR) reconstruction pipelines operate strictly offline. They depend on Structure-from-Motion preprocessing and are not suited for large inter-frame motion. We present, to the best of our knowledge, the first online Gaussian SLAM framework that tracks and maps directly on single-exposure 16-bit linear HDR imagery. Our method rests on three core components: an architecture-agnostic HDR Gaussian Splatting module featuring an MLP-free logarithmic parameterization of Gaussian color features; a Reinhard range-compressed photometric objective; and structure-guided spatial gradient weighting. Combined, these components allow our approach to outperform a direct HDR adaptation of MonoGS in both trajectory and reconstruction accuracy, while rendering natively in linear scene radiance for post-rendering processing. The same formulation runs unchanged on standard 8-bit inputs, roughly halving the MonoGS baseline error. Furthermore, our HDR Gaussian module transfers seamlessly to SplaTAM, Gaussian SLAM, and DROID-W, eliminating all tracking failures these systems suffer on challenging illumination sequences. To enable this research, we introduce RawSLAM: a dataset of 10 real-world indoor sequences featuring 16-bit RAW imagery, aligned depth, IMU measurements, and external OptiTrack poses. Code and dataset will be made publicly available soon.

</details>


### [90] [PhGS: Post-Hoc Pruning and Refinement of Single-View Feed-Forward 3D Gaussian Reconstructions](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20623)
*Rinto Yagawa,Han Cheng,Dieter Schmalstieg,Hideo Saito,Shohei Mori*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: Backbone-agnostic post-hoc pruning and recurrent refinement for single-view 3D Gaussian Splatting to reduce memory while preserving novel-view quality.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Single-view 3DGS uses a fixed, potentially redundant number of Gaussians per ray, leading to memory inefficiency. Existing compaction methods rely on multi-view cues and retraining; there is a need for lightweight, model-agnostic, inference-time compression without changing the base network.

Method: Apply post-hoc, importance-score-based pruning to the generated Gaussians from a frozen base feed-forward model, followed by a lightweight trainable recurrent refinement module that iteratively updates surviving primitives to restore image quality and fidelity.

Result: Demonstrates seamless integration with existing baselines, preserves novel-view rendering fidelity, achieves substantial memory reduction, and supports flexible inference-time keep ratios.

Conclusion: The proposed backbone-agnostic compaction pipeline provides an effective, non-retraining compression solution for single-view 3DGS, enabling memory-efficient deployment while maintaining rendering quality across views.

Abstract: Recent single-view feed-forward 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) generation predicts a fixed number of Gaussians per camera ray, introducing severe spatial redundancy. Most existing compaction strategies target multi-view setups to exploit cross-view consistency and are incompatible with single-image models. Instead of retraining the base feed-forward network to directly output compact representations, our insight is to keep the base models frozen and apply post-hoc pruning and recurrent refinement to the generated Gaussians. Consequently, we propose a backbone-agnostic compaction pipeline for single-view feed-forward 3DGS that couples an importance-score-based pruning mechanism with a trainable, lightweight recurrent refinement module, which iteratively updates the surviving primitives to restore image quality. Our results demonstrate seamless integration with existing baselines while preserving novel-view rendering fidelity and achieving high memory reduction. Furthermore, our method supports flexible inference-time keep ratios for application needs.

</details>


### [91] [Refinement Is Inherently Editable: Training-Free Prompt-to-Prompt Image Editing with Generative Refinement Network](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20633)
*Yulong Chen,Ziqian Zhang,Haoyu Zhang,Ao He,Senmao Li,Kai Wang*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: RefineEdit is a training-free prompt-to-prompt editor using a Generative Refinement Network to couple edit localization with content generation via binary image codes. It uses two editing branches and adaptive bit-level controls to refine edits while preserving the rest, achieving state-of-the-art background preservation and CLIP-based quality on PIE-Bench across nine categories.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Text-guided image editing must apply requested changes while preserving unrelated content. Diffusion-based editors suffer from imprecise spatial controls; causal autoregressive editors face fixed decoding orders that limit revisiting earlier decisions. A training-free, flexible framework is desired to improve locality and revisionability without relying on external masks or attention control.

Method: A training-free framework built on a Generative Refinement Network that evolves the image by refining a global set of binary image codes. An editing branch is initialized from an intermediate source state and reuses the emerging layout. The system compares probabilities from two branches on the same source-sampled bits, using their signed differences to identify editable positions and bits. Editable bits follow an editing refinement path; remaining bits copy the evolving source. Adaptive spatial freezing limits mask expansion; finite bit locking keeps recently selected bits editable. No additional training, external masks, or attention control is required; operates across nine PIE-Bench editing categories.

Result: RefineEdit achieves the best background preservation across PSNR, LPIPS, MSE, and SSIM, and records the highest whole-image and edited-region CLIP scores among evaluated methods on PIE-Bench.

Conclusion: RefineEdit provides a training-free, robust prompt-to-prompt editing framework that improves locality and revisionability without external supervision, demonstrating strong quantitative performance across diverse editing categories. Future work could explore robustness across prompts, scaling of bit-level refinement, and broader generalization beyond PIE-Bench.

Abstract: Text-guided image editing must introduce the requested changes while preserving unrelated source content. Diffusion-based editors rely on spatial controls whose inaccuracies can leave edits incomplete or alter unrelated regions. Causal autoregressive editors face a further constraint: their fixed decoding order limits revision of earlier decisions. We introduce RefineEdit, a training-free prompt-to-prompt image editing framework built on a Generative Refinement Network. Our key idea is to couple edit localization with content generation through the global refinement of binary image codes, allowing editing evidence to be reassessed as the image evolves. RefineEdit initializes an editing branch from an intermediate source state, reusing the emerging layout. We compare the probabilities assigned by the two branches to the same source-sampled bits, using their signed differences to select editable positions and bits. Selected bits follow editing refinement, while the remaining bits copy the evolving source state. To stabilize editing across refinement steps, adaptive spatial freezing limits unnecessary mask expansion, while finite bit locking keeps recently selected bits editable. The framework requires no additional training, external masks, or attention control. Across nine editing categories of PIE-Bench, RefineEdit achieves the best background-preservation scores in PSNR, LPIPS, MSE and SSIM, together with the highest whole-image and edited-region CLIP scores among the evaluated methods.

</details>


### [92] [PROVIA: Procedure State Tracking for Online Mistake Detection in Egocentric Videos](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20638)
*Di Wen,Kailun Yang,Jimmy Weissert,Luc Maria Scherrer,Cedric Zöllner,Ruiping Liu,Yufan Chen,Jiale Wei,Junwei Zheng,Kunyu Peng*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: PROVIA is a real-time online mistake-detection framework for egocentric video that maintains a factual state and an accepted-progress state, uses Bayesian state merging to model automaton states, and applies a sequential test to emit alarms. It improves mistake recall under tight false-alarm budgets across multiple datasets with real-time performance; code is released.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: First-mistake protocols used by online methods cut recordings at the first mistake, ignoring how mistakes alter subsequent work. There is a need to detect and reason about mistakes and recoveries within complete trials, under controlled false-alarm budgets.

Method: PROVIA maintains two concurrent records: a factual state (learned summary of steps performed, including mistakes) and an accepted-progress state (posterior over the correct execution). Transitions occur only in the correct-status branch; mistake/correction branches keep the source state. A Bayesian state-merging automaton is learned from correct demonstrations. A sequential test converts per-frame mistake probability into alarms using a single filter and an optimization rule.

Result: PROVIA ranks mistakes better than evaluated baselines on CaptainCook4D, IndustReal, HoloAssist and IMPACT-ego. At a validation budget of 0.1 false alarms per minute, recalls are 0.154 vs 0.128 on CaptainCook4D and 0.034 vs 0.015 on HoloAssist, leading at every budget. The pipeline runs at 58-70 fps.

Conclusion: PROVIA provides accurate and real-time detection of mistakes and their recoveries in egocentric tasks, outperforming baselines under constrained false-alarm budgets, with real-time performance and publicly available source code.

Abstract: An assistant watching egocentric video should notice a mistake from past frames alone, before the next step begins, and keep working once the person recovers. A mistake changes the state of the work, so every later step has to be read against what was done rather than against the plan. The first-mistake protocol that current online methods report on cuts each recording at its first mistake, so a fixed-time rule that never looks at the video is right on every case. We evaluate on complete trials, where mistakes and recoveries arise naturally, under a validation false-alarm budget and against controls that use timing alone. PROVIA keeps two records apart: a factual state, a learned summary of the steps each actor performed, mistakes included, and the accepted progress, an exact posterior over the state of an automaton induced from correct demonstrations by Bayesian state merging and over the execution status of each actor. Procedure-state transitions occur only in the correct-status branch; the mistake and correction branches retain the source state. A sequential test turns the per-frame mistake probability into alarms. With one filter and one optimization rule, PROVIA ranks mistakes best among the evaluated controlled baselines on CaptainCook4D, IndustReal, HoloAssist and IMPACT-ego. At a validation budget of 0.1 false alarms per minute it recalls .154 against .128 on CaptainCook4D and .034 against .015 on HoloAssist, where it leads at every budget. The pipeline runs at 58-70 frames per second. The source code is available at https://github.com/Kratos-Wen/PROVIA.

</details>


### [93] [Earth Surface Immune System for Rapid Monitoring of Unknown Anomalies](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20662)
*Jingtao Li,Qian Zhu,Xinyu Wang,Deren Li,Liangpei Zhang,Yanfei Zhong*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: ESIA integrates innate (category-agnostic) localization and adaptive (open-vocabulary) recognition for Earth-surface anomalies using immune-inspired mechanisms, achieving strong localization and recognition on a global dataset with fast test-time adaptation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Earth-surface anomalies driven by climate change and human activity are increasingly diverse and data are sparse/uncertain; existing methods focus on predefined categories or localization only, lacking a bridge to actionable, open-world insights.

Method: Two-stage immune-inspired framework: (1) innate stage—non-specific time-series anomaly detection yielding binary localization maps at 14.51 km^2/s without assuming category; (2) adaptive stage—negative selection to filter text prompts, then match surviving prompts with localized patches via a multimodal foundation model for open-vocabulary recognition of unknown attributes (category, affected area, damage severity); a test-time mutation mechanism tunes minimal embeddings per scene using a single reference image pair, achieving ~3.26 s per scene.

Result: Validated on a global-scale dataset covering 19,801.60 km^2 across six anomaly categories, comparing against 22 models; localization F1 surpasses strongest baseline by 37%; recognition F1 exceeds 80%; demonstrated on degraded farmland in the Dnipro Delta after Kakhovka Dam collapse and burn severity from 2025 Palisades Fire in Los Angeles.

Conclusion: ESIA offers unprecedented flexibility for unknown anomalies, enabling real-time disaster response and broad-scale environmental surveillance.

Abstract: Earth surface anomalies, driven by escalating climate change, and expanding human activities, are increasing in both frequency and diversity, yet their limited historical data and unpredictability make them fundamentally different from conventional remote sensing targets. Existing methods address specific anomaly categories or stop at localization, leaving a gap between detection and actionable information. Here we present ESIA, an Earth Surface Immune System whose architecture is constrained by three principles from the biological immune system, refined over millions of years against equally diverse and uncertain threats. A non-specific innate immune stage treats anomalies as unobserved changes in time-series satellite imagery, generating binary localization maps at 14.51 km2/s without assuming any anomaly category, surpassing the strongest general baseline by 37% in F1. A specific adaptive immune stage applies negative selection to filter text prompts and matches surviving prompts with localized image patches through a multi-modal foundation model, enabling open-vocabulary recognition of unknown anomaly attributes including category, affected area, and damage severity, with recognition F1 exceeding 80%. A mutation mechanism tunes minimal embeddings at test time, adapting to each scene in 3.26s using a single reference image pair. We validate ESIA on a global-scale dataset covering 19,801.60 km2 across six anomaly categories, comparing against 22 models, and further apply it to quantify degraded farmland in the Dnipro Delta following the Kakhovka Dam collapse and assess burn severity from 2025 Palisades Fire in Los Angeles. This unprecedented flexibility in handling unknown anomalies opens new avenues for real-time disaster response and environmental surveillance.

</details>


### [94] [FunArt: Decoding Functional Structure and Articulation from Generative 3D Latents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20673)
*Dennis Rotondi,Abdelrhman Werby,Kai O. Arras*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: Single-shot articulation-aware 3D scene understanding from a static RGB-D scan: reconstruct objects, convert to TRELLIS O-Voxel, and use a frozen VAE prior with a lightweight decoder to jointly segment movable parts, functional elements, and estimate articulation parameters; achieves state-of-the-art on Articulate3D.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Robots must identify articulated objects and their kinematics in human environments. Prior work often relies on interactions to recover kinematics or treats articulation and functional elements separately from static scans, leaving a gap for integrated, interaction-ready perception from a single observation.

Method: 1) Reconstruct object instances from posed RGB-D in a single static configuration. 2) Fuse geometry and convert to O-Voxel representation of TRELLIS.2. 3) Use its frozen, sparse-compression VAE as a structural prior. 4) Employ a lightweight query-based decoder that fuses compact object-level latents with dense, surface-aligned features to jointly segment movable parts and functional interactive elements and estimate motion type, axis, origin, and range. 5) Train/evaluate on Articulate3D, including end-to-end with/without ground-truth object input.

Result: Achieves state-of-the-art across movable-part segmentation, articulation estimation, and functional-element segmentation on Articulate3D. In the end-to-end setting, improvements over the strongest baselines: 1.5 AP50 for movable parts, 2.8 AP50 for joint origin-and-axis constraints, and 6.7 AP50 for functional elements. Works with or without GT object input.

Conclusion: Generative 3D latents encode actionable structural cues that can initialize robotic perception and planning before physical interaction.

Abstract: To operate effectively in human environments, robots must identify articulated objects, segment their movable and interactive parts, and estimate their kinematic models. Existing articulated scene representations typically recover kinematics from observed interactions, while methods operating on static scans often decouple articulation from functional interactive elements. We present FunArt, a framework that constructs articulation-aware functional 3D scene graphs from posed RGB-D observations captured in a single static configuration. FunArt reconstructs object instances, converts their fused geometry directly into the O-Voxel representation of TRELLIS.2, and exploits its frozen, sparse-compression VAE as a structural prior. A lightweight query-based decoder combines compact object-level latents with dense, surface-aligned features to jointly segment movable parts and functional interactive elements while estimating motion type, axis, origin, and range. On the Articulate3D dataset, FunArt achieves state-of-the-art performance across movable-part segmentation, articulation estimation, and functional-element segmentation, both with and without ground-truth object input. In the end-to-end setting, it outperforms the strongest baselines by 1.5 AP_{50} points for movable parts, 2.8 AP_{50} points under joint origin-and-axis constraints, and 6.7 AP_{50} points for functional elements. These results demonstrate that generative 3D latents encode actionable structural cues that can initialize robotic perception and planning before physical interaction.

</details>


### [95] [Should This Case Be Adapted? Prediction Fragmentation Controls Test-Time Adaptation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20700)
*Lili Wang,Jing Li,Xiaowen Sun,Xiangyu Hu,Zhuangzhuang Gu,Jian Liu,Srihari Nelakuditi,Yan Tong*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: Episodic test-time adaptation of a frozen segmenter can cause per-case harm; introducing harmful accepted area (HA) quantifies this risk. A prediction-fragmentation signal between the original and adapted masks forecasts HA without labels or extra gradients. A case-level router using this signal substantially reduces HA across multiple benchmarks and architectures with minimal overhead, generalizing across domains, while sometimes trading a bit of accuracy for less harm.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Fixed-horizon adaptation blends cohort-level budget decisions with per-case adaptation, masking when adaptation should not occur. This leads to measurable harm in medical segmentation (e.g., cross-vendor cardiac MRI). There is a need for a low-latency, label-free predictor of potential harm and a routing mechanism that reduces harm without requiring per-case labels or backpropagation.

Method: Episodic test-time adaptation resets the segmenter to source weights M0 for each case and adapts for a fixed number of gradient steps. Harm is quantified by Harmful Accepted Area (HA) — the fraction of edited area that degrades clinically. Prediction fragmentation (the disagreement geometry between M0 and Mk) is proposed as a label-free predictor of HA. A case-level router uses this signal with thresholds calibrated on a labeled split (no labels or gradients used at decision time) and is deployed across architectures (nnU-Net, SegFormer) and domains (Cityscapes → ACDC, cross-vendor cardiac MRI, prostate). The router is designed once and only its thresholds / per-bucket actions are recalibrated per domain. Baselines include fixed-horizon adaptation and held-out tuning, with comparisons on multiple benchmarks.

Result: Prediction fragmentation correlates with HA (Spearman ρ ≈ 0.50–0.60) at ~1/4 the gradient-norm latency, enabling a per-case router that reduces HA significantly. On a cardiac MRI benchmark, HA dropped from 0.228 to 0.139 with routing; on the cardiac-design benchmark, HA dropped from 0.129 to 0.013 with matched Dice and 1.10 deployed updates, reducing the observed harm from 58.7% to 20.0%. In cases like prostate where some retained cases are not net-helped, the router still reduces HA at the cost of some accuracy. Thresholds are fixed from a labeled split; no labels or gradients are used at decision time. The approach transfers across architectures and domains (nnU-Net → SegFormer; Cityscapes → ACDC).

Conclusion: A fragmentation-based, case-level router provides substantial, label-free, low-latency harm reduction during test-time adaptation, generalizing across architectures and domains. It yields a practical template for deploying adaptive medical segmentation with explicit tradeoffs: reduced harm with latent accuracy loss in some cases. The method hinges on a simple, prior-free predictor (prediction fragmentation) and a one-time threshold calibration per domain.

Abstract: Episodic test-time adaptation resets a frozen segmenter to source weights $M_0$ on each case and adapts for a fixed step count. A fixed horizon conflates a cohort-level question, how far to adapt, with an irreducibly per-case one, whether this case should be adapted at all. Cohort means hide that decision: on cross-vendor cardiac MRI the mean $Δ$Dice from adaptation is statistically indistinguishable from zero while 58.7% of cases are individually made worse. We quantify this harm as harmful accepted area (HA), the harmful fraction of the edited area a controller deploys. Held-out tuning gives a stronger baseline than a fixed horizon, but the budget it selects transfers on neither of the two main medical benchmarks, and no global budget can condition on the case. We show that prediction fragmentation---the disagreement geometry between $M_0$ and the adapted mask $M_k$---predicts HA with no labels or extra backward passes at decision time, comparably on three benchmarks (Spearman $ρ$ 0.50--0.60), at a quarter of gradient-norm's latency. A case-level router built on it cuts HA from 0.228 to 0.139 on a benchmark that took no part in its design, with the design frozen and only cut-points recalibrated there. On the cardiac benchmark the design was selected on, the router cuts HA from 0.129 to 0.013 at matched Dice and 1.10 deployed updates, against the retrospective-best budget found post hoc on evaluation labels, and reduces that 58.7% to 20.0%, an upper bound we quantify. Where the retained cases are not net-helped (as on prostate), the router still cuts HA but concedes accuracy, a boundary we report. Thresholds are fit once on a labeled split disjoint from evaluation; decisions use no labels or gradients. The template ports across architecture and domain (nnU-Net$\to$SegFormer, Cityscapes$\to$ACDC) with coordinate, thresholds and per-bucket actions instantiated per domain.

</details>


### [96] [FlowSGS: Improving Flow Matching Priors for Inverse Imaging with Stochastic Interpolants](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20769)
*Tianao Li,Xinhui Qian,Emma Alexander*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: A flow-based inverse solver FlowSGS uses Split Gibbs Sampling to separate likelihood and prior steps, enabling efficient posterior sampling via Langevin dynamics for the likelihood and SI-based reverse-time SDE for the flow-prior, achieving state-of-the-art results including nonlinear Fourier phase retrieval.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To overcome limitations of existing flow-based inverse solvers that assume linear forward models or rely on approximations in posterior sampling, and to improve efficiency when integrating pretrained flow priors in plug-and-play frameworks.

Method: Split Gibbs Sampling decomposes the posterior into a likelihood step (sampled via Langevin dynamics) and a prior step (implemented with Stochastic Interpolants using the reverse-time SDE of a pretrained flow model). A novel timestep correction enhances efficiency. The flow prior provides straight probability paths, reducing network evaluations relative to plug-and-play diffusion solvers.

Result: Demonstrates state-of-the-art performance across a range of inverse problems and, for the first time, shows a flow-based solution for a nonlinear inverse problem (Fourier phase retrieval).

Conclusion: FlowSGS broadens flow-based priors to nonlinear inverse problems with improved sampling efficiency and links to existing PnP methods, offering a practical and scalable framework for posterior inference.

Abstract: Flow matching has emerged as the state-of-the-art generative model and has been used for plug-and-play (PnP) priors to solve inverse problems in computational imaging. However, existing flow-based inverse solvers assume linear forward models and/or make simplifying approximations in posterior sampling. To circumvent these problems, we introduce FlowSGS, a flow-based posterior sampling method using Split Gibbs Sampling (SGS) to decompose the posterior into a likelihood step and a prior step. Specifically, we sample from the likelihood step using Langevin dynamics and leverage the Stochastic Interpolants (SI) framework to integrate a pretrained flow model into the prior step. We provide a form for the prior step that uses SI's reverse-time SDE, and show connections to previous PnP methods. Moreover, with the aid of the flow prior's straight probability paths and a novel timestep correction technique for the reverse-time SDE, FlowSGS requires fewer network evaluations in its prior step than plug-and-play diffusion samplers. Our experiments show state-of-the-art performance on a range of inverse problems. For the first time, we provide an experiment on a nonlinear inverse problem (Fourier phase retrieval) for flow-based inverse solvers.

</details>


### [97] [ERCPMP-Gx: Endoscopic Image and Video Dataset for Morphological, Histopathological, and Genomic Characterization of Colorectal Polyposis](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20815)
*Zahra Ghaffari,Massih Bahar,Mojgan Forootan,Ali Darvishi,Hamidreza Bolhasani*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: ERCPMP-Gx is a public, AI-ready, patient-level dataset linking endoscopic images, histopathology, and germline data for hereditary colorectal polyposis syndromes, enabling AI-based recognition and classification.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To address the lack of integrated, patient-level datasets that connect polyposis phenotype, histopathology, and germline findings, enabling AI development for identification, classification, and surveillance of hereditary polyposis syndromes.

Method: Data were collected primarily with the Olympus EVIS X1 system using WLE, NBI, M-NBI, and near-focus modes, yielding 160 images and accompanying video clips. About 80% of cases are clinically/genetically confirmed hereditary polyposis syndromes (FAP, PJS, JPS, GNS), with 20% Non-PG. Each record includes AI-ready, patient-level annotations linked to standardized endoscopic annotations, histopathology, and germline findings. Public release via Mendeley; updates via DataBioX.

Result: Created an AI-ready, patient-level CT-like resource for colorectal polyposis research, including multi-modal endoscopic data linked to histopathology and germline data, with a framework for annotations and differential diagnosis; publicly accessible for AI development and benchmarking.

Conclusion: ERCPMP-Gx constitutes a valuable, publicly available resource that can accelerate AI research in recognizing and classifying hereditary polyposis polyps, supporting personalized surveillance and familial management; ongoing updates and expansion are anticipated to enrich phenotypic and genotypic coverage.

Abstract: Hereditary polyposis syndromes can be precursor lesions to colorectal cancer and are associated with a broad spectrum of extracolonic tumors. Early identification and accurate classification of these syndromes are essential for timely diagnosis, individualized patient management, and targeted surveillance strategies for affected families. However, public endoscopic datasets are largely organized around the individual sporadic polyp, and none links the polyposis phenotype to histopathology and germline findings at the patient level. Here, we present ERCPMP-Gx, an endoscopic, histopathological, and genomic dataset developed to support the application of artificial intelligence (AI) in the recognition, characterization, and classification of colorectal polyposis. Most procedures were performed using the Olympus EVIS X1 system with white-light endoscopy (WLE), narrow-band imaging (NBI), magnifying NBI (M-NBI), and NBI with near focus modes, yielding 160 images and accompanying video clips. Approximately eighty percent of cases represent clinically and/or genetically confirmed hereditary polyposis syndromes (PG), including familial adenomatous polyposis (FAP), Peutz-Jeghers syndrome (PJS), juvenile polyposis syndrome (JPS), and ganglioneuroma syndrome (GNS), while the remaining twenty percent comprise non-hereditary polyps and polyp-mimicking lesions with overlapping morphological features (Non-PG), included to support differential classification.
