Each released record is linked, where available, to standardized endoscopic annotations, representative histopathology, and clinically reported germline findings, forming an AI-ready, patient-level annotation framework. The dataset is publicly accessible at Mendeley (https://doi.org/10.17632/nzyfc544bx.2). For the latest updates and further information, readers are referred to the DataBioX website: https://databiox.com.

</details>


### [98] [Paint-Anything: Unified Any-Color Control for Image Generation and Editing](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20816)
*Ji Xie,Dewei Zhou,Xinyu Huang,Zhennan Chen,Xun Wang*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: Paint-Anything enables any-24-bit hex color control for image generation/editing via a shared hex-prompt interface trained with object-level color supervision; introduces the Paint-500K dataset with perceptual color labeling and editing-pair synthesis plus pure-color anchors; introduces ACBench benchmark; achieves substantial gains on color-fidelity metrics.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Professional design requires precise, object-level color control across generation and editing. Existing methods rely on specialized color representations or procedures; large language models can map hex values to color semantics, enabling a unified, text-based interface for color specification.

Method: Train a model with a shared hex-prompt interface using object grounding, perceptual color labeling, and editing-pair synthesis to learn color-aware generation/editing. To mitigate color-label noise from shadows in real images, introduce pure-color anchors whose pixels exactly match their hex values; anchors are used only at high-noise timesteps, while low-noise training uses natural images. Build Paint-500K dataset via the described pipeline. Propose Any Color Benchmark (ACBench) with ACBench-T2I and ACBench-Edit to assess object-level hex color fidelity. Evaluate on FLUX.2-4B with ablative studies.

Result: Quantitatively, Paint-Anything improves ACBench-T2I by 85.3% and ACBench-Edit by 28.3% over the base model; achieves the highest average CompColor score among compared methods; ablations corroborate essential components of the training recipe.

Conclusion: A hex-prompt interface enables reliable any-color control for both generation and editing; the combination of object-grounded supervision, shadow-robust anchors, and a large, perceptually labeled dataset yields substantial color-fidelity gains, validated by a new benchmark (ACBench).

Abstract: Professional design requires any-color control: the ability to specify an object's target color with any 24-bit hex value for image generation and editing. Prior work has explored color generation, editing, and colorization, but often relies on dedicated color representations or specialized inference procedures. Advances in large language models offer a simpler starting point: even compact models can associate hex values with color semantics. We present Paint-Anything, which learns a shared hex-prompt interface for generation and editing through object-level color supervision. We develop a data pipeline that constructs Paint-500K from real images through object grounding, perceptual color labeling, and editing-pair synthesis. Since shadows make real-image labels only approximate colors, we complement this supervision with pure-color anchors whose pixels exactly match their paired hex values. These anchors are used only at high-noise timesteps, leaving low-noise training to natural images. We further introduce Any Color Benchmark (ACBench), comprising ACBench-T2I and ACBench-Edit, to measure object-level hex color fidelity across both tasks. On FLUX.2-4B, Paint-Anything improves ACBench-T2I and ACBench-Edit scores by 85.3% and 28.3%, respectively, relative to the base model, with ablations supporting the training recipe. It also achieves the highest average CompColor score among the compared methods.

</details>


### [99] [FAMOS: Feed-Forward 3D Articulation Modeling from Sparse Observations](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20817)
*Kevin Qu,Tao Sun,Massimiliano Viola,Liyuan Zhu,Zhizhuo Zhou,Sayan Deb Sarkar,Konrad Schindler,Iro Armeni*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: FAMOS is a feed-forward model that estimates movable-part segmentation and joint parameters from sparse, unordered partial point clouds by jointly reasoning over multiple views using a Multi-state Articulation Transformer and a novel articulation-span supervision, trained with a procedural data generator; it achieves consistent improvements over baselines on PartNet-Mobility, ACD, and ArtiCraft-10K.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Modeling articulated objects from sparse monocular views is challenging due to partial geometry and motion evidence in each observation and reliance on category-level shape priors. The work aims to leverage multiple observations, handle variable input counts, and improve joint parameter estimation without heavy optimization.

Method: Introduce FAMOS: a feed-forward model that takes a sparse, unordered set of partial point clouds and predicts movable-part segmentation and joint parameters. It jointly reasons over observations with a Multi-state Articulation Transformer that alternates between state-wise and global attention, includes an observed articulation span objective to supervise motion range, and uses a procedural data generator to synthesize diverse training data.

Result: Empirical evaluation on PartNet-Mobility, ACD, and ArtiCraft-10K shows consistent improvements over both feed-forward baselines and optimization-based methods.

Conclusion: The approach enables robust articulation understanding from sparse, unordered views, scales with data augmentation via synthetic generation, and demonstrates strong cross-dataset performance improvements along with effective integration of multi-view cues.

Abstract: Modeling articulated objects from sparse monocular views is challenging because each observation reveals only partial geometry and motion evidence. Most feed-forward methods infer articulation from a single observation and therefore rely heavily on learned category-level shape priors. We present FAMOS, a feed-forward model that predicts movable-part segmentation and joint parameters from a sparse, unordered set of partial point clouds. Our model jointly reasons over multiple observations and naturally supports a variable number of inputs, including a single view. To aggregate articulation cues across observations, we introduce a Multi-state Articulation Transformer with alternating state-wise and global attention. We further propose an observed articulation span objective that supervises the motion range each part exhibits across the input observations, encouraging the model to leverage the full observation set. To overcome the limited scale and diversity of existing datasets, we introduce a procedural data generator that synthesizes self-annotated assets during training. Experiments on PartNet-Mobility, ACD, and ArtiCraft-10K demonstrate consistent improvements over both feed-forward and optimization-based baselines. Project page: https://kevinqu7.github.io/famos

</details>


### [100] [SplashSplat: Reconstructing Splashing Liquids from Real-World Multi-View Videos](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20818)
*Peiyu Liu,Dingxi Zhang,Federico Tombari,Marc Pollefeys,Christina Tsalicoglou,Daniel Barath*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: SplashSplat introduces a synchronized 7-camera 4K/60fps dataset of real splashes and a reconstruction method that uses per-frame liquid SDFs, velocity from level-set transport, Lagrangian particles, and differentiable rendering with Gaussian splats—striking a balance between data-driven constraints and physical structure.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: There is no existing synchronized multi-view dataset of splashing liquids, and reconstructing such fast, textureless phenomena is challenging; a dataset plus a physics-informed representation is needed to advance reconstruction, motion capture, and rendering of splashes.

Method: 1) Build SplashSplat: per-frame liquid SDFs fused from refined per-view masks; 2) Compute coarse velocity via level-set transport between consecutive SDFs; 3) Advect Lagrangian carriers along the flow, correct with new observations, reseed where coverage is lost; 4) Decode local Gaussians for differentiable rendering; 5) Create SplashSplat dataset with synchronized multi-view 4K/60fps captures and manual masks; fixed evaluation splits.

Result: SplineSplat achieves superior performance vs. state-of-the-art dynamic Gaussian splatting on real and synthetic data, with more physically plausible motion and lower training cost; enables temporal interpolation and style transfer without re-optimization.

Conclusion: A physics-informed, observation-constrained representation (SDFs + flow + particles + local Gaussians) effectively reconstructs splashing liquids, supports novel tasks like interpolation and style transfer, and provides a valuable real dataset to drive future work.

Abstract: A splash lives for a fraction of a second: sheets tear into ligaments and droplets, appearance is view-dependent and nearly textureless, and little persists long enough to track. Reconstruction research has consequently focused on smoke, synthetic liquids, or gently deforming surfaces. To our knowledge, no synchronized multi-view dataset of splashing liquids exists. We therefore introduce a benchmark of 20 real scenes, from coherent streams to violent splashes, captured by seven synchronized, calibrated 4K cameras at 60 fps, with manually refined per-view liquid and container masks and fixed evaluation splits. We further present SplashSplat, built on a single principle: impose physical structure only where the observations can constrain it. Per-frame liquid SDFs fused from the masks provide the geometry, level-set transport between consecutive SDFs yields a coarse velocity field, and Lagrangian carriers advected along this flow, corrected against each new observation and reseeded where coverage is lost, decode local Gaussians for differentiable rendering. SplashSplat outperforms state-of-the-art dynamic Gaussian splatting methods on our real captures and on a synthetic benchmark, with physically more plausible motion and a lower training cost. The same representation supports temporal interpolation and style transfer without re-optimization.

</details>


### [101] [Can 4D Foundation Models Remember?](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20819)
*Guangzhao He,Hadar Averbuch-Elor,Wei-Chiu Ma*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: PersistBench introduces a dataset and metric suite to evaluate object-centric visual memory in 4D foundation models using omniscient 360° videos, revealing models’ memory decays after objects leave the field of view.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing benchmarks rely on pixel-level metrics and lack ground truth for occluded objects; there is a need to assess how well models remember seen objects over time to advance 4D foundation models.

Method: Construct PersistBench with 360° videos as ground truth; define three evaluation aspects: object permanence, motion continuity, appearance preservation; develop metrics; evaluate diverse models across categories.

Result: Current models exhibit only short-term consistency; memory degrades significantly when objects leave FOV; reveals a gap between perception and robust visual memory.

Conclusion: PersistBench provides a resource and impetus for improving long-term object-centric memory in 4D models; dataset and code are publicly available for future research.

Abstract: Perceiving and remembering the visual world is fundamental to navigating and interacting with our environment. Current 4D foundation models, such as camera-controllable video models or 4D reconstruction models, can perceive and reconstruct dynamic environments, but how well they remember what they have perceived remains an open question. Existing benchmarks largely rely on pixel-level metrics and lack ground truth for objects once they leave the field of view, making them unable to evaluate visual memory in an object-centric manner against references. To fill this gap, we introduce PersistBench, a dataset and metric suite that leverages 360° videos as omniscient ground truth and proposes three evaluation aspects: object permanence, motion continuity, and appearance preservation. Evaluating various models across diverse categories reveals that current models can only maintain short-term consistency that degrades significantly once objects leave the field of view. Our findings highlight the gap between current model capabilities and robust visual memory ("seeing is not remembering"), providing guidance for future development of 4D foundation models. Dataset and code are available on the project page: https://guangzhaohe.com/persistbench.

</details>


<div id='cs.LG'></div>

# cs.LG [[Back]](#toc)

### [102] [Generative Query Suggestion via Intent Coverage and Query-Level Credit Assignment](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.19209)
*Xinpeng Liu,Lu Ma,Jiayi Qiao,Mengyu Zhou,Linglong Li,Xiaofeng Bian,Haonan Chen,Xiaoxi Jiang,Guanjun Jiang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Introduces an Intent-Driven Query Suggestion framework with dual-stage optimization to maximize per-query usefulness and slate-wide intent coverage; achieves CTR, query quality, and intent coverage gains in production-scale tests.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To generate slates of follow-up queries that are both individually useful and collectively diverse across intents, addressing limitations of methods that optimize only local query quality or generic diversity.

Method: Two-stage approach: (1) intent-aware diversity modeling to produce intent-aligned supervised fine-tuning data and optimize an Intent-Aware Diversity Reward for broad intent coverage; (2) query-level credit assignment that allocates quality signals to specific query tokens while sharing a slate-level diversity signal across the slate.

Result: Large-scale experiments on production data with online A/B testing and offline evaluation showing improvements in click-through rate, query quality, and intent coverage.

Conclusion: The framework effectively balances intent coverage and per-query quality in generated query slates and is suitable for deployment in real-world systems; further work may address optimization complexity, richer intent taxonomies, and broader evaluation across domains.

Abstract: Generative query suggestion aims to enhance user engagement by anticipating user intents and recommending relevant follow-up queries. A central challenge is to generate slates whose individual queries are useful while the slate covers distinct intents. We propose an Intent-Driven Query Suggestion Framework with dual-stage optimization. First, intent-aware diversity modeling constructs intent-aligned supervised fine-tuning (SFT) data and uses an Intent-Aware Diversity Reward to optimize intent coverage. Second, query-level credit assignment routes individual quality signals to the corresponding query tokens while sharing a slate-level diversity signal across the slate. Experiments on a large-scale production dataset, including online A/B testing and offline evaluation, show improvements in click-through rate, query quality, and intent coverage.

</details>


### [103] [Layer-wise Curriculum Learning for Efficient LLM Compression](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.19213)
*Donggeon Lee,Dooyeon Na,Seungmin Oh,Jongbin Ryu*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Layer-wise curriculum learning for efficient LLM compression, enabling segmented knowledge transfer that speeds convergence and reduces memory/compute, achieving strong results across models under fixed training budgets.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Tackle the high computational cost and memory footprint of compressing large language models, improve stability of teacher–student transfer, and address inter-layer misalignment during compression.

Method: Partition the model into layer-based segments and apply curriculum learning from easier to harder optimization tasks; perform knowledge transfer from teacher to student within segments; provide a theoretical analysis of cumulative error to explain faster convergence; introduce a feature caching method with multi-threading to mitigate cross-layer misalignment and maximize GPU utilization.

Result: Achieves state-of-the-art compression performance, reduces GPU memory usage and training hours by more than 50% on BERT and GPT-2, and outperforms pruning methods on LLaMA-family and Qwen under the same training hours with lower GPU memory footprint.

Conclusion: Layer-wise curriculum learning accelerates convergence and stabilizes knowledge transfer in LLM compression, yielding efficient, scalable improvements across architectures and datasets.

Abstract: In this paper, we introduce layer-wise curriculum learning for efficient LLM compression. The proposed method facilitates the knowledge transfer from the teacher model to the student model, utilizing a curriculum learning approach that begins with easier optimization tasks and progressively tackles harder ones. In order to adopt the layer-wise learning in LLM compression, we partition the whole model into multiple segments consisting of layers, thereby enabling more computationally efficient knowledge transfer for LLMs. Based on our theoretical analysis of cumulative error phenomenon, layer-wise curriculum learning accelerates convergence while stabilizing the knowledge transfer process. In addition, we present a feature caching method with a multi-threading strategy to efficiently address feature misalignment across layers, maximizing GPU utilization. Consequently, our method exhibits advanced model compression performance, as well as high computational efficiency in terms of minimized memory usage and short training hours. Experiments on multiple datasets show that the proposed method achieves state-of-the-art performance while reducing GPU memory usage and training hours by more than 50\% on BERT and GPT-2. Moreover, it outperforms the other pruning methods on LLaMA-family and Qwen models under the same training hours, with a lower GPU memory footprint.

</details>


### [104] [Block Parallelism For Efficient Distributed Long-Context Diffusion Language Model Training](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.19242)
*Tarun Suresh,Pranshu Chaturvedi,Hangoo Kang,Parth Shroff,Ishan S. Khare,Hermann Kumbong,Azalia Mirhoseini*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: CSBP: a scalable, memory-efficient training framework for block diffusion language models that uses block parallelism and context-sharded block parallelism to scale BDLMs to very long contexts (256K-1M) with substantial throughput gains and preserved training semantics.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: BDLMs enable long-context dependencies but are bottlenecked by distributed attention communication and activation memory with conventional context parallelism. Scaling BDLMs to hundreds of thousands of tokens requires reducing cross-block communication and duplicative data.

Method: Introduce block parallelism (BP): assign each corrupted-block computation to a separate rank. Extend to context-sharded BP (CSBP) by sharding the shared clean sequence across ranks to scale to long contexts. CSBP keeps corrupted K/V and gradients local, avoids replicated clean prefixes, and preserves BDLM training semantics. Implemented and evaluated on 16 H200s (256K context) and 8 H100s; benchmarks include supervised fine-tuning and conversion of autoregressive models to BDLMs, plus DFlash2 and DiffusionGemma SFT benchmarks.

Result: CSBP yields 1.18-1.45x throughput improvement over baselines for supervised fine-tuning and 1.27-1.33x for converting autoregressive models to BDLMs at 256K context; peak HBM is matched or reduced; full-model speedup reaches 1.61x at 512K. On 8x H100s, DFlash2 speculative-decoder training speeds up 2.48x at 512K and 7.59x at 1M. In DiffusionGemma 26B-A4B SFT runs, CSBP achieves higher pass rates across checkpoints on SWE-bench Verified and Terminal-Bench Lite.

Conclusion: CSBP provides a scalable solution for long-context BDLM training by decoupling corrupted-block computations and leveraging shared-sequence sharding, achieving meaningful throughput gains while preserving BDLM training semantics and reducing memory pressure; code is released for reproducibility.

Abstract: Block diffusion language models (BDLMs) combine autoregressive dependencies across blocks with parallel denoising within blocks, but long-context training is constrained by distributed attention communication and activation memory. Conventional context parallelism (CP) shards the combined clean-plus-corrupted sequence by position, communicating shared clean K/V together with block-specific corrupted K/V and their gradients. We observe that the BDLM objective separates over target blocks. We introduce block parallelism (BP), a new distributed parallelism dimension that assigns each corrupted-block computation to one rank. To scale BP to long contexts, we introduce context-sharded block parallelism (CSBP), which also shards the shared clean sequence across those ranks. CSBP keeps corrupted K/V and gradients local, avoids replicated clean prefixes, and preserves BDLM training semantics. On 16 H200 GPUs at 256K context, CSBP improves throughput over the best baseline by 1.18-1.45x for supervised fine-tuning and 1.27-1.33x for conversion of autoregressive models to BDLMs, while matching or reducing peak HBM. Full-model speedup reaches 1.61x at 512K. On eight H100 GPUs, CSBP accelerates DFlash2 speculative-decoder training by 2.48x at 512K and 7.59x at 1M. In matched 12-hour DiffusionGemma 26B-A4B SFT runs, CSBP achieves higher pass rates at every trained checkpoint on SWE-bench Verified and Terminal-Bench Lite. Code: https://github.com/ScalingIntelligence/Turbo-dLLM

</details>


### [105] [Randomized SVD Approximations for Spectral Co-Clustering of Word-Document Matrices](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.19243)
*Fateme Mazdarani,Carlos Toxtli*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Two randomized approximations for normalized spectral co-clustering of bipartite text data reduce runtime vs full SVD; random projection is more reliable overall, while sampling-based method favors dense matrices; method choice should align with data sparsity.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Spectral co-clustering relies on SVD, which is costly for high-dimensional word-document matrices; efficient randomized alternatives are sought to scale to large text corpora.

Method: 1) randomized SVD via random projection; 2) partial SVD with element-wise random sampling; both designed for bipartite text data where the numbers of document and word clusters may differ.

Result: Both approaches reduce runtime relative to full-SVD baseline; performance depends on matrix sparsity; random projection is the more robust approximation across tested settings; sampling-based method is most beneficial for denser matrices and provides limited gains on already sparse data.

Conclusion: Rand. approximations for spectral co-clustering should be chosen according to data structure; consider sparsity in the data; use random projection for general reliability and efficiency; use sampling-based method when matrices are dense to maximize speedups.

Abstract: Spectral co-clustering is a useful tool for discovering latent structure in word-document matrices, but its reliance on singular value decomposition (SVD) can make standard formulations expensive on high-dimensional data. This paper presents two randomized approximations for normalized spectral co-clustering of bipartite text data when the numbers of document and word clusters may differ. The first method uses randomized SVD through random projection, while the second combines partial SVD with element-wise random sampling. Across real-world and synthetic datasets, both methods reduce runtime relative to the full-SVD baseline, but their behavior depends on matrix sparsity. The random projection method is the more reliable approximation across the tested settings, whereas the sampling-based method is most useful on denser matrices and provides limited benefit on already sparse text data. These results show that randomized approximations for spectral co-clustering should be selected according to the underlying structure of the data.

</details>


### [106] [Radio-Frequency Convolutional Neural Networks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.19279)
*Zhihui Gao,Shi-Yuan Ma,Yiran Chen,Dirk Englund,Tingjun Chen*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: RF-CNNs repurpose radio-frequency mixers to perform CNN inference in the frequency domain, enabling ultra-low-energy edge AI using existing wireless hardware.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Edge devices are limited by size, weight, power and cost (SWaP-C), and lack sufficient compute for modern neural networks. Leveraging existing wireless hardware can enable efficient on-device AI without additional accelerators.

Method: Multi-channel convolutions are mapped onto frequency tones so a passive mixer executes the convolution in the frequency domain. Weights can arrive over the air, and the same analog hardware is shared with communication, allowing inference in a single pass with minimal energy. The study demonstrates CNNs up to 26.4M parameters (9 layers) across tasks such as wireless-signal and image classification and controllable image generation.

Result: RF-CNN achieves near full-precision performance on the tested networks and tasks, with edge energy per multiply-accumulate of about 0.72 femtojoules, two orders of magnitude lower than a digital accelerator would require, and generalizes across signal and image data.

Conclusion: Deployed wireless infrastructure can enable efficient, state-of-the-art AI inference on billions of connected devices without adding extra edge hardware; RF-CNNs offer a promising path to low-energy, scalable edge AI by reusing existing radio hardware.

Abstract: Running artificial intelligence (AI) models directly on edge devices such as smartphones, wearables, and drones offers low latency, pervasive scalability, and data privacy, but these devices rarely carry the computing capability that modern neural networks demand. Edge accelerators have been developed in response, yet each adds computing hardware to devices already constrained in size, weight, power, and cost (SWaP-C). An alternative lies in what these devices already carry: the frequency mixer in every wireless radio multiplies signals in time, natively performing convolution in the frequency domain. Here we introduce radio-frequency convolutional neural networks (RF-CNNs), which repurpose existing communication hardware for CNN inference. Multi-channel convolutions are mapped onto frequency tones for a passive mixer to execute in a single pass. We experimentally demonstrate that RF-CNN runs deep CNNs up to 26.4 million parameters and nine layers from classification of wireless signals and images to controllable image generation, close to full-precision performance. Because the weights arrive over the air and the analog hardware is shared with communication, the edge device spends energy only on data preparation and readout-down to 0.72 femtojoules per multiply-accumulate, two orders of magnitude less than it would cost on an added digital processor. These results suggest that deployed wireless infrastructure can bring efficient, state-of-the-art AI inference to the billions of devices it already connects.

</details>


### [107] [Learning-Induced Dynamical Transition in Recurrent Neural Networks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.19288)
*Varun Vaidya*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A non-equilibrium DMFT framework shows how slow, feedback-driven learning reshapes recurrent networks from chaotic to stable dynamics via a bifurcation in the DMFT solution, uncovering a critical feedback strength and a learning-rate–dependent critical time; the theory predicts training trajectories and agrees with simulations.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To understand how learning reshapes RNN dynamics—from initial chaos to stable, task-dependent behavior—by developing a predictive, dynamical-field-theoretic description of learning-induced transitions.

Method: Formulate a non-equilibrium dynamical mean-field theory for recurrent networks undergoing slow, feedback-driven learning; derive the two-time correlation function, track the evolution of an effective feedback strength, and identify a bifurcation in the DMFT solution; determine a critical feedback strength and a learning-rate–dependent critical time; validate with numerical simulations.

Result: The theory yields the time evolution of network output during training, specifies the critical feedback strength and the associated critical time, and shows quantitative agreement with numerical simulations.

Conclusion: Learning progressively deforms the dynamical landscape through the grown feedback structure, driving a chaotic-to-stable transition in RNNs. The non-equilibrium DMFT framework provides a predictive, tractable description of learning-induced dynamical transitions.

Abstract: Learning in recurrent neural networks can fundamentally reshape their underlying dynamics, transforming initially chaotic activity into stable task-dependent behavior. We develop a non-equilibrium dynamical mean-field theory(DMFT) to describe this transition during learning. We show that a slow feedback-driven learning process generates an evolving effective feedback strength that drives the network through a transition from chaotic to stable dynamics defined by a bifurcation of the DMFT solution. By deriving the two-time correlation function throughout learning, we identify a critical feedback strength and a corresponding learning rate dependent critical time separating these regimes. The transition arises from the progressive deformation of an effective dynamical landscape by the growing learned feedback structure. Starting from the untrained state, the theory predicts the time evolution of the network output during training and shows quantitative agreement with numerical simulations.

</details>


### [108] [Personalized Federated Hierarchical Gaussian Processes for Privacy-Preserving Modeling of Heterogeneous Distributed Systems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.19337)
*Xianjian Xie,Hao Yan*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Proposes Personalized Federated Hierarchical Gaussian Processes (pFedHGP) for probabilistic regression/classification across heterogeneous clients. Latent functions decompose into a shared global component, a client-specific deviation sharing the global kernel, and a flexible local residual. Uses sparse inducing-variable approximations and federated variational inference to keep data local while the server aggregates low-dimensional statistics for the shared part, yielding full predictive distributions with uncertainty. Demonstrates strong results in fault classification with limited labeled data and federated air-quality zoning, and links to multi-output GPs via an Instantaneous Linear Mixing Model.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Enable privacy-preserving probabilistic regression/classification on federated, heterogeneous (non-IID) client data with uncertainty quantification, without centralizing raw data.

Method: Hierarchical GP with three components: (i) a shared global component; (ii) a client-specific deviation that preserves the global kernel structure; (iii) a flexible local residual. Employ sparse inducing-variable approximations and federated variational inference. Server synchronizes only low-dimensional statistics for the shared component; full predictive distributions are available. An Instantaneous Linear Mixing Model viewpoint links the hierarchy to multi-output GPs for correlated sensors.

Result: Application studies show perfect fault classification in press tonnage monitoring using 13.77% of labeled cycles and recovery of geographic zones in federated air-quality modeling without centralizing station-level time series. The approach preserves data locality and provides uncertainty-aware predictions.

Conclusion: pFedHGP offers a scalable, privacy-preserving probabilistic modeling framework for federated data with heterogeneity, achieving strong task performance and enabling principled uncertainty quantification. The hierarchical decomposition supports sharing kernel structure while allowing client-specific and local residuals, with connections to multi-output GP formulations via instantaneous linear mixing.

Abstract: We present Personalized Federated Hierarchical Gaussian Processes (pFedHGP) for probabilistic regression and classification when data are distributed across heterogeneous clients. Each client's latent function decomposes into (i) a shared global component, (ii) a client-specific deviation that shares the global kernel structure, and (iii) a flexible local residual. Sparse inducing-variable approximations and federated variational inference keep raw data local while the server synchronizes only low-dimensional statistics for the shared component. Full predictive distributions support uncertainty-aware decisions. In application studies, pFedHGP attains perfect fault classification in press tonnage monitoring using 13.77% of labeled cycles and recovers geographic zones in federated air-quality modeling without centralizing station-level time series. An Instantaneous Linear Mixing Model viewpoint links the hierarchy to multi-output Gaussian processes for correlated sensors.

</details>


### [109] [How to Guide Your Language Flow](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.19356)
*Rohit Dilip,Tianrong Chen,Yuyang Wang,David Van Valen,Joshua Susskind,Miguel Angel Bautista*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Introduces probe guidance, a signal derived from frozen internal states of a diffusion model to steer flow matching without extra inference passes; achieves state-of-the-art unconditional generation on diffusion LMs and improves QA benchmarks for a 1.7B model; analyzes autoguidance by showing the weak model must originate from a low-entropy training region.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Improve diffusion-language-model performance efficiently and illuminate the autoguidance mechanism by studying how weak and strong models align dynamically using internal-state probes.

Method: Constructs a guidance signal from frozen internal states (probes) of an existing diffusion model, enabling a guidance mechanism similar to autoguidance but without an extra forward pass at inference time. Applied to continuous diffusion language models, with probes used to compare strong and weak models and to study autoguidance.

Result: Achieves new state-of-the-art results for unconditional generation on continuous diffusion LMs; a 1.7B diffusion LM shows consistent gains on multiple-choice QA benchmarks; probes reveal that, for autoguidance, the weak model must come from a low-entropy region of training.

Conclusion: Probe guidance provides a practical means to enhance diffusion language models and offers insight into the autoguidance mechanism, potentially clarifying why autoguidance works and reducing inference costs.

Abstract: We introduce a new method to guide flow matching models. Our approach, which we call probe guidance, uses the frozen internal states of an existing diffusion model to construct a guidance signal. This works using a similar principle as autoguidance, but eliminates the need for an additional forward pass at inference time and provides a reliable path to ensure that the weak and strong model share similar dynamics. We apply and benchmark this method on continuous diffusion language models, where probe guidance sets a new state-of-the-art performance on unconditional generation. When applied to a 1.7B diffusion language model, probe guidance consistently improves on multiple choice question answering benchmarks. Using our probes, we study the traditional autoguidance setting where the strong model is a weak checkpoint, and find that the weak model must come from a low-entropy region of training. These findings both provide a practical way to improve diffusion language models and shed light on the actual mechanism behind autoguidance, which is currently poorly understood.

</details>


### [110] [Smart Insole Human Activity Recognition for Continuous Monitoring in Elderly Care](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.19359)
*Edwin Rios,Antony Garcia,Fengpei Yuan,Xinming Huang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Wireless insole with 16 plantar pressure sensors + 6D IMU accurately classifies sit/stand/walk/unstable-walk in unseen users; Histogram-Based Gradient Boosting (HGB) outperforms a 1D-CNN (not significantly; p=0.0625); bilateral sensing gives best macro-F1; solid cross-validation to support generalization.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Falls risk in older adults often accompanies changes in mobility; unobtrusive activity recognition using plantar-pressure and inertial data can enable monitoring and fall prevention.

Method: 15 healthy adults; data at 80 Hz; 16 pressure sensing locations + tri-axial accelerometer and gyroscope. Data segmented into overlapping windows. Stratified 10-fold cross-validation (window-level). Participant-independent 5-fold Stratified Group CV to ensure all windows from a participant are in one fold. Compare Histogram-Based Gradient Boosting (HGB) vs a compact 1D-CNN; primary metric macro-F1.

Result: HGB macro-F1: left 0.954, right 0.959, bilateral 0.980. 1D-CNN did not significantly outperform HGB (p=0.0625).

Conclusion: Low-profile footwear sensing with pressure and IMU can infer activity states for participants unseen during training, supporting potential for activity monitoring and fall prevention in elderly care.

Abstract: Falls in older adults are often preceded by changes in mobility, balance, and postural transitions. This paper presents a wireless smart insole platform and machine-learning workflow for recognizing sitting, standing, walking, and unstable walking from plantar-pressure and inertial signals. Each insole integrates 16 active pressure-sensing locations and a six-dimensional IMU stream consisting of tri-axial acceleration and angular velocity. Data were collected from 15 healthy adults at 80~Hz and segmented into overlapping windows. Window length and candidate model families were first screened with stratified 10-fold cross-validation; the primary performance estimate was then obtained with participant-independent 5-fold Stratified Group cross-validation, ensuring that all windows from a participant remained in a single fold. Under this protocol, Histogram-Based Gradient Boosting (HGB) achieved macro-F1 scores of 0.954 and 0.959 for the left and right feet, respectively, and 0.980 with bilateral sensing. A compact 1D-CNN evaluated with the same participant-independent folds did not significantly outperform HGB ($p=0.0625$). The results show that low-profile footwear sensing can infer activity state from pressure and IMU measurements for participants unseen during training, establishing a basis for activity monitoring and fall prevention in elderly care.

</details>


### [111] [Stiefel Attention: When the Geometry of Transformer Projection Matrices Dominates Optimizer Choice---and When It Does Not](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.19363)
*Rubén Darío Guerrero*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Constrain attention projections to the Stiefel manifold and optimize with a Riemannian Adam variant; prove steepest-descent, well-conditioning, and exact O(d)-equivariance; weight decay has zero Riemannian gradient; empirical gains on modular arithmetic grokking and CIFAR-10; ablations isolate scale-free step as the driver; gauge-removal not motivating.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Improve stability and geometry of attention by enforcing a manifold constraint and principled Riemannian optimization, addressing gradient scale, conditioning, and symmetry to yield better optimization and robustness.

Method: Reparameterize query/key projections W_Q, W_K on St(d,r); use a Riemannian Adam with one scalar second moment per frame, a trust-region step cap, and polar retraction; prove update is steepest descent in the embedded metric; show weight decay has identically zero Riemannian gradient on St(d,r).

Result: Four propositions establish steepest-descent property, conditioning, and exact O(d)-equivariance, numerically certified in float64. Empirical gains: modular arithmetic grokking reaches ~97.0% validation by epoch 20,000 vs baseline 61.1%; CIFAR-10 patches show +8.98 pp over 12 paired starts. The fixed-step Riemannian update is 24–40x smaller per step than an identically shaped AdamW, with frames remaining near initialization; freezing gives only 0.28 pp cost. Ablations attribute gains to scale-free step, not projector or equivariance; a negative result shows gauge removal cannot motivate the method since a direction with invariant loss carries no gradient."

Conclusion: The mechanism—scale-free, fixed-step Riemannian update on St(d,r)—robustly preserves attention geometry and yields practical performance gains, while traditional motivations like gauge removal fail to justify the method; the gains arise from scale-free dynamics rather than particular projectors or equivariance.

Abstract: The query and key projections $\WQ,\WK$ in attention are almost always trained by Euclidean optimizers with no constraint on their geometry. We constrain them to the Stiefel manifold and optimize them there with a Riemannian Adam that carries one scalar second moment per frame, caps its step by a trust region, and retracts polarly. Four propositions prove this update is steepest descent in the embedded metric, independent of gradient scale, well conditioned, and exactly $\mathrm{O}(d)$-equivariant, each certified numerically in \texttt{float64}. A fifth supplies the mechanism: weight decay has \emph{identically zero} Riemannian gradient on $\St(d,r)$, since $W = W I_r$ lies in the normal space, so the learned attention geometry survives the collapse cycles that decay drives through the rest of the model. On modular arithmetic grokking, a single run holds $97.0\%$ validation accuracy at epoch 20\,000 against the baseline's $61.1\%$---an unstable endpoint we report as evidence for the mechanism rather than as an effect size. On CIFAR-10 patches the same rule gains $\mathbf{+8.98}$\,pp over 12 paired starts ($t{=}60.6$, $12/12$), and the gap widens with data rather than eroding. The step rule earns this: a fixed-step Riemannian update is degree one in the gradient, so it moves $24$--$40\times$ less per step than an identically shaped AdamW matrix---its frames barely leave their initialization, and freezing them outright costs only $0.28$\,pp. An ablation credits the whole gain to making the step scale free, and nothing measurable to the projector or to equivariance. A negative result sharpens the account: gauge removal cannot motivate the method, because a direction along which the loss is invariant carries no gradient at all.

</details>


### [112] [Machine-Learning Assessment of the Predictive Value of Inflammatory Biomarkers for Cognitive Impairment in an Older Hispanic Adult Cohort](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.19374)
*Antony Garcia,Gabrielle Britton,Alcibiades Villarreal,Diana Oviedo,Giselle Rangel,Xinming Huang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A small clinical tabular study shows that an interpretable leakage-safe Naive Bayes classifier identifies CCL1 (I-309) as a robust incremental predictor of cognitive impairment in PARI-HD data, with significant AUC gains and strong cross-partition consistency, though external validation is needed.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Demonstrate that interpretable ML approaches can yield clinically useful predictive signals on small, high-stakes tabular datasets, where deep learning is impractical and traditional significance testing may overstate utility.

Method: Leakage-safe threshold-likelihood Bernoulli/Categorical Naive Bayes (BNB/CNB) trained within repeated stratified 10-fold CV (30 repeats). Continuous predictors discretized to supervised chi-square-derived states; income modeled via a categorical likelihood. All steps data-dependent and cross-validated to prevent leakage.

Result: Baseline ROC-AUC 0.630±0.017. I-309 (CCL1) incremental feature increased AUC by 0.110; DeLong p<0.05 in 100% of repeats. Primary fixed-partition DeLong p=0.0018; across 200 random partitions median p=0.0011. Among 18 markers, I-309 BH-adjusted q=0.032 on frozen partition; 85% of random partitions satisfied q<0.05; no other marker showed reliable value.

Conclusion: I-309/CCL1 is an interpretable, candidate predictive feature for tabular prediction of cognitive impairment in this cohort, with robust evidence across partitions; external validation is needed.

Abstract: Small clinical tabular datasets require interpretable machine learning because deep learning is often impractical and ensemble models can be difficult to inspect. A key pitfall is that statistical significance does not necessarily imply predictive utility. Using data from the Panama Aging Research Initiative--Health Disparities (PARI-HD) cohort (n=165), we implemented a leakage-safe threshold-likelihood Bernoulli/Categorical Naive Bayes (BNB/CNB) classifier. Within every training fold, each continuous predictor was reduced to a supervised chi-square-derived state, while income entered the model through a categorical likelihood. All data-dependent steps were performed within repeated stratified 10-fold cross-validation with 30 repeats. The demographic baseline achieved a ROC-AUC of 0.630 +/- 0.017. I-309 (CCL1) was the dominant incremental feature, increasing AUC by 0.110, with paired DeLong tests yielding p<0.05 in 100% of repeats. In the pre-specified primary analysis, I-309 produced a fixed-partition DeLong p=0.0018, with robustness assessed across 200 random partitions, where the median p-value was 0.0011. Within the exploratory family of 18 candidate markers, I-309 achieved a Benjamini-Hochberg-adjusted q=0.032 on the frozen partition and satisfied q<0.05 in 85% of random partitions, whereas no other marker demonstrated reliable incremental predictive value. Because the fitted model is an inspectable table of thresholds and class-conditional probabilities, these results identify I-309/CCL1 as an interpretable candidate feature for tabular prediction of cognitive impairment, pending external validation.

</details>


### [113] [FCx: An algorithm for finding Feasible Counterfactual Explanations](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.19383)
*Kleopatra Markou,Vana Kalogeraki,Dimitrios Gunopulos*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Feasible Counterfactual Explanations (FCx) propose an efficient framework to generate CFs that are realistic, low-cost, and feasible by integrating hard domain constraints and soft constraints inferred via causal models into a modified VAE with a multi-factor loss; validated on four public datasets against state-of-the-art.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing CF explanations often produce feasible-looking changes that are not practically feasible or violate future changes, such as altering sensitive attributes. There is a need to enforce feasibility explicitly (hard constraints) or through data-driven soft constraints to improve actionability and safety.

Method: FCx uses a modified Variational Autoencoder trained with a multi-factor loss, incorporating hard feasibility constraints specified by domain knowledge and soft feasibility constraints inferred via causal inference from data. The cost is a combination of proximity (absolute value changes) and sparsity (number of features changed), while realism is ensured by LOF-based density checks to keep CFs in dense regions.

Result: Extensive experiments on four public datasets show FCx matches state-of-the-art performance across multiple metrics while guaranteeing feasibility.

Conclusion: Feasibility-aware counterfactuals can be generated efficiently without sacrificing realism or high cost, enabling more trustworthy and actionable explanations in real-world deployments.

Abstract: Counterfactual (CF) explanations identify changes that alter an input's classification. While existing methods produce realistic and low-cost CFs, they often fail to ensure feasibility, by suggesting non-constructive modifications or incompatible with future changes (e.g., changing an individual's race to secure a job offer). We introduce a refinement of CF explanations that explicitly enforces feasibility. Our approach is the first to efficiently generate CFs that are realistic, low-cost and feasible. We accommodate both hard feasible constraints, specified by domain knowledge users, and soft feasible constraints, inferred automatically via causal inference from the dataset. Our method, Feasible Counterfactual Explanations (FCx), is based on a modified Variational Autoencoder (VAE) optimized with a multi-factor loss function. We measure the cost of a change based on the absolute change in values (proximity) as well as the number of features changed (sparsity) while realism is measured based on the LOF for density estimation, guaranteeing that CFs reside in densely populated regions. Extensive experiments on four public datasets show that our approach matches state-of-the-art performance across multiple metrics while guaranteeing feasibility.

</details>


### [114] [Improving Offline Goal-Conditioned Reinforcement Learning via Selective Reward Stimulation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.19414)
*Jing Zhang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: RSIQL is a reward-stimulation technique for offline goal-conditioned RL that injects progress-promoting intermediate rewards using an auxiliary value function, enabling a non-hierarchical policy that competes with hierarchical methods.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Offline goal-conditioned RL struggles with sparse rewards and long-horizon credit assignment. Goal achievement can be temporally distant from early decisions, and offline value estimation introduces bias; better reward propagation is needed.

Method: Reward Stimulation Implicit Q-Learning (RSIQL) is a non-hierarchical method that annotates offline trajectories with auxiliary reward signals at intermediate states identified by a goal-conditioned value function, providing earlier supervisory signals without learning a separate subgoal policy.

Result: Empirical evaluation on D4RL goal-reaching benchmarks and OGBench shows RSIQL improves over goal-conditioned IQL on average and is competitive with hierarchical offline goal-conditioned methods, while maintaining a simple flat policy.

Conclusion: Reward stimulation via intermediate progress states can mitigate delayed credit assignment and estimation errors in offline goal-conditioned RL, offering competitive performance without the complexity of hierarchical architectures.

Abstract: Goal-conditioned reinforcement learning aims to learn policies that reach specified goals, but remains challenging in offline settings with sparse rewards and long-horizon dependencies. In such settings, goal-completion information can be temporally distant from the early decisions that enable success, while offline value estimation introduces additional error. We study this issue from a reward-propagation perspective and show, in a stylized delayed-goal setting, how goal-directed value separation can become small relative to local estimation error. Motivated by this analysis, we propose Reward Stimulation Implicit Q-Learning (RSIQL), a simple non-hierarchical method that introduces additional reward signals at progress-making intermediate states in offline trajectories. RSIQL uses an auxiliary goal-conditioned value function to identify intermediate states estimated to make progress toward the goal and applies reward stimulation to provide less-delayed training supervision. Unlike hierarchical methods, RSIQL does not learn a separate high-level subgoal policy. Experiments on D4RL goal-reaching benchmarks and OGBench show that RSIQL improves over goal-conditioned IQL on average and achieves performance competitive with hierarchical offline goal-conditioned methods, while retaining a simple flat policy structure.

</details>


### [115] [Bayesian Optimization with Rich Auxiliary Information via LLMs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.19437)
*Tejus Gupta,Efe Mert Karagözlü,Rohit Sonker,Barnabás Póczos,Jeff Schnieder*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Three methods using LLMs to incorporate rich auxiliary information into Bayesian Optimization; across hyperparameter optimization benchmarks and a real-world nuclear fusion task, outperforming standard BO and existing LLM-based optimization methods.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Real-world optimization problems provide more information than objective function values (training curves, expert notes/images, prior knowledge). Leveraging this data via LLMs can guide search more efficiently.

Method: Developed three methods to integrate auxiliary information into BO using LLMs. Methods utilize LLMs to process heterogeneous auxiliary data and influence the BO surrogate or acquisition process. (No specifics in abstract.)

Result: Consistent outperformance of standard BO and existing LLM-based optimization approaches on HPO benchmarks and a nuclear fusion optimization task.

Conclusion: LLMs are effective at leveraging rich auxiliary information to enhance BO; potential for broader adoption in settings where auxiliary data is available.

Abstract: Bayesian Optimization (BO) is widely used for optimizing expensive black-box functions, yet many real-world optimization problems contain substantially richer information than function evaluations alone. Examples include training curves in hyperparameter optimization, expert notes and images in scientific experimentation, and prior knowledge about where optima may lie. We show that large language models (LLMs) can effectively leverage such rich auxiliary information to guide optimization. Motivated by these findings, we develop three methods for incorporating auxiliary information into BO using LLMs. Across hyperparameter optimization benchmarks and a real-world nuclear fusion optimization task, our methods consistently outperform both standard BO and existing LLM-based optimization approaches. Our results demonstrate the effectiveness of LLMs for leveraging rich auxiliary information in BO.

</details>


### [116] [Sharpness-Aware Minimization (SAM) Improves Classification Accuracy of Bacterial Raman Spectral Data Enabling Portable Diagnostics](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.19453)
*Kaitlin Zareno,Jarett Dewbury,Siamak K. Sorooshyari,Hossein Mobahi,Loza F. Tadesse*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: SAM enhances generalization in Raman spectroscopy-based bacterial classification, yielding accuracy gains over Adam and potentially reducing preprocessing needs.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Antimicrobial resistance poses a high mortality burden globally; Raman spectroscopy offers rapid, portable diagnostics, but existing AI pipelines struggle to generalize across diverse patient data and rely on non-trivial preprocessing. This work proposes Sharpness-Aware Minimization (SAM) to improve generalization across varied hyperparameters.

Method: Train bacterial isolate classification models on Raman spectral data using Sharpness-Aware Minimization (SAM) and compare performance to the traditional Adam optimizer across multiple data splits and hyperparameter configurations.

Result: SAM achieved up to a 10.5 percentage point improvement in accuracy on a single split, and an average accuracy increase of 2.7 percentage points across all splits compared with Adam.

Conclusion: SAM demonstrates the potential to advance AI-powered Raman spectroscopy for clinical pathogen detection by improving generalization across diverse datasets and reducing dependence on extensive preprocessing.

Abstract: Antimicrobial resistance is expected to claim 10 million lives per year by 2050, and resource-limited regions are most affected. Raman spectroscopy is a novel pathogen diagnostic approach promising rapid and portable antibiotic resistance testing within a few hours, compared to days when using gold standard methods. However, current algorithms for Raman spectra analysis 1) are unable to generalize well on limited datasets across diverse patient populations and 2) require increased complexity due to the necessity of non-trivial pre-processing steps, such as feature extraction, which are essential to mitigate the low-quality nature of Raman spectral data. In this work, we address these limitations using Sharpness-Aware Minimization (SAM) to enhance model generalization across a diverse array of hyperparameters in clinical bacterial isolate classification tasks. We demonstrate that SAM achieves accuracy improvements of up to 10.5% on a single split, and an increase in average accuracy of 2.7% across all splits in spectral classification tasks over the traditional optimizer, Adam. These results display the capability of SAM to advance the clinical application of AI-powered Raman spectroscopy tools.

</details>


### [117] [Enhanced Agriculture-informed Neural Network by Domain Knowledge](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.19466)
*Ci Lin,Futong Li,Rose Chong-Wu,Tet Yeap,Iluju Kiringa*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Hybrid KAINN framework combines neural networks with soil physics to improve N2O emission predictions, outperforming data-driven and original AINN models across CNN/LSTM/Transformer architectures.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: N2O emissions arise from complex soil-climate-biogeochemical interactions and data are limited; integrating domain knowledge can improve predictive accuracy, interpretability, and generalization.

Method: Extend Agriculture-informed Neural Network (AINN) by embedding domain knowledge on fertilizer diffusion, soil respiration, and water-filled porosity into a neural-mechanistic architecture (KAINN). Evaluate with CNN, LSTM, and Transformer architectures across multiple seasons and input configurations; compare against purely data-driven models and the original AINN; analyze learned interfaces for physical consistency and uncertainty.

Result: KAINN achieves lower RMSE/MAE and higher R^2 than purely data-driven models and the original AINN; results consistent across architectures and input configurations; learned interfaces exhibit smoother, more physically plausible parameter trajectories with reduced uncertainty.

Conclusion: Incorporating environmental knowledge into neural networks enhances reliability, interpretability, and generalization for agricultural N2O-emission predictions; KAINN demonstrates the value of hybrid physics-informed neural networks in this domain.

Abstract: Accurate prediction of nitrous oxide (N2O) emissions from agriculture is important for assessing environmental impacts and supporting sustainable farming. However, prediction remains difficult because N2O emissions result from complex interactions among soil properties, climate, biochemical processes, and management practices, while high-quality observations are limited. Deep learning models can capture nonlinear relationships but often lack physical interpretability and may generalize poorly across environmental conditions. We propose the Knowledge-enhanced Agriculture-informed Neural Network (KAINN), a hybrid neural-mechanistic framework that extends the Agriculture-informed Neural Network by incorporating domain knowledge about fertilizer diffusion, soil respiration, and water-filled porosity. We evaluate KAINN using CNN, LSTM, and Transformer architectures across multiple growing seasons and input-feature configurations. The results show that KAINN generally provides lower root mean square error and mean absolute error and higher R-squared values than purely data-driven models and the original AINN. Analysis of the learned interfaces also shows smoother and more physically consistent parameter trajectories with reduced uncertainty. These findings demonstrate that incorporating environmental knowledge into neural networks can improve the reliability, interpretability, and generalization of agricultural N2O-emission predictions.

</details>


### [118] [Search at the Cost of Sampling: Nearly-Instant Latent Space Bayesian Optimization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.19476)
*Donney Fan,Colin Doumont,Aleksandra Kalisz,Paul Duckworth,Jacob R. Gardner,Henry Moss,Geoff Pleiss*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A scalable Bayesian optimization approach for de novo generative pipelines using a linear model on a spherical latent space, achieving ~100x speedups with competitive performance on molecular and image generation tasks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: BO is conceptually well-suited for guided exploration in de novo design but becomes a bottleneck due to sequential querying, especially when virtual screening is inexpensive. A spherical latent space concentrates high-dimensional latents, enabling linear surrogates to be effective and fast.

Method: Constrain a linear surrogate to a spherical domain and derive nearly closed-form solutions for both surrogate modelling and acquisition by exploiting spherical symmetry; builds on recent justification for linear surrogates and targets accelerations in BO for generative design tasks.

Result: Attains at least 100x speedup over state-of-the-art baselines with matching or improved performance on molecular and image generation benchmarks.

Conclusion: BO can be a practical drop-in for de novo pipelines where prior methods were too slow, enabling scalable, efficient optimization in generative design.

Abstract: Generative models are increasingly central to many de novo discovery pipelines, in which designs are generated at scale and filtered through virtual screens to determine a set of candidates to experimentally validate. While Bayesian optimization (BO) is a natural fit for this setting, as it uses past evaluations to guide future proposals, the computational overhead required for its sequential decision-making becomes a bottleneck when virtual screens are relatively cheap. We make BO practical in this regime by exploiting the unique combination of a linear model constrained to a spherical domain where high-dimensional latents concentrate. We build off recent work justifying the use of linear surrogates, while deriving nearly closed-form solutions to the surrogate modelling and acquisition problems that exploit spherical symmetry. The result is at least a 100x speedup over state-of-the art baselines, with matching or improved performance across molecular and image generation benchmarks. Altogether, our method makes BO a practical drop-in for de novo pipelines where it was previously too slow to consider.

</details>


### [119] [Sample Count Is Not Enough: Candidate-Generation Strategy Shapes the Energy and Performance of LLM Test-Time Scaling](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.19499)
*Mobina Kashaniyan,Ali Jannesari*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Candidate generation budget N alone does not capture test-time cost in multi-candidate LLM reasoning; generation schedule (how many calls, batch sizes) critically affects latency and energy. Fewer, larger batched calls are often more efficient than many small serial calls when memory permits. Reports should include candidate count, accuracy, generation schedule, and GPU-level systems metrics.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To disentangle the effect of candidate count from execution strategy in test-time scaling for LLM reasoning and to quantify the GPU-level system costs of different generation schedules.

Method: Empirical study using Phi-3-mini and Qwen2.5-1.5B on 500 GSM8K prompts. Compare N across 1..8; fix N=8 and evaluate generation schedules 1x8, 2x4, 4x2, 8x1. Measure latency (P95), throughput, GPU-hours, and gross GPU-device energy on A100 GPUs; replicate across three nodes and additional short-output SciQ/V100 experiments.

Result: Increasing N from 1 to 8 improves accuracy by 8.4pp (Phi-3-mini) and 18.4pp (Qwen2.5-1.5B). However, the same total candidate count yields vastly different system costs across schedules: eight serial calls cost ~4.64–4.86x more energy and ~5.77–6.12x higher P95 latency than one batched 8-candidate call on A100. Similar patterns hold across nodes and datasets. When memory allows, fewer calls with larger batches are more efficient.

Conclusion: Candidate count alone is insufficient to describe test-time cost. Generation schedule and GPU-level metrics are essential. Evaluations should report candidate count, accuracy, generation schedule, and GPU-level system metrics.

Abstract: Test-time scaling can improve large language model reasoning by generating and combining multiple candidate responses. In sampling-based methods, the inference budget is often described by the number of generated candidates, N. However, N tells us how many candidates are generated, not how they are executed. The same candidate budget can be produced in one batched generation call or split across several sequential calls with smaller batch sizes. We first study the effect of increasing N on reasoning accuracy using Phi-3-mini and Qwen2.5-1.5B on 500 GSM8K prompts. As expected, increasing N from 1 to 8 improves accuracy by 8.4 percentage points for Phi-3-mini and 18.4 points for Qwen2.5-1.5B. However, accuracy alone does not show the systems cost of using a larger candidate budget. We therefore fix N = 8 and compare four generation schedules: 1x8, 2x4, 4x2, and 8x1, where axb denotes a generation calls with b candidates per call. We measure latency, throughput, GPU-hours, and gross GPU-device energy while keeping the total candidate count fixed. On A100 GPUs, eight serial calls use 4.64-4.86x as much gross GPU-device energy and have 5.77-6.12x the P95 latency of one batched call with eight candidates. The same pattern appears across three independently scheduled A100 nodes per model and in short-output SciQ/V100 experiments. These results show that candidate count alone is not enough to describe the systems cost of multi-candidate test-time scaling. When candidates are independent and memory allows it, fewer generation calls with larger batch sizes are more efficient. Evaluations should therefore report not only candidate count and accuracy, but also generation schedule and GPU-level systems metrics.

</details>


### [120] [LSTM-UT and Recurrent-Depth Transformers on Cellular Automata](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.19521)
*Aras Kavuncu*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: BUT generalizes to unseen recurrent depths better than CoTFormer but eventually fails at very high depths; CoTFormer benefits less from extended caching and can be misled by its state-cache interaction; LSTM-UT with bounded gated memory outperforms both on depth extrapolation and delayed recall.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To understand how different recurrent-like architectures with varying memory and attention caching handle persistent information across computation steps, and how these choices affect extrapolation to deeper recurrent steps and retrieval tasks.

Method: Empirical evaluation across two tasks: Rule 30 cellular automata to test depth extrapolation and a delayed-recall task. Models compared: Block Universal Transformer (BUT), CoTFormer, and a new LSTM Universal Transformer (LSTM-UT). Investigations include ablation-like state and cache interventions to analyze failure modes.

Result: BUT extrapolates to unseen depths more reliably than CoTFormer on Rule 30, though accuracy degrades at very large depths. CoTFormer failures arise from interactions between current state and retained cache; correcting the current state can temporarily restore accuracy but history retention can undermine corrections. In delayed-recall, BUT outperforms CoTFormer despite lacking direct access to past states; CoTFormer struggles to reliably select requested cached representations. LSTM-UT improves both depth extrapolation and delayed recall relative to the baselines.

Conclusion: Bounded gated memory provides a robust inductive bias for repeated computation and later retrieval in these tasks. LSTM-UT demonstrates that explicitly gating and bounding memory yields systematic gains over both a purely stateful-but-bounded BUT and a cache-heavy CoTFormer.

Abstract: Recurrent-depth Transformers apply shared computation repeatedly, but differ in how they retain information across steps. We compare a Block Universal Transformer (BUT), which carries only its current hidden state; CoTFormer, which also retains an expanding attention cache; and a new LSTM Universal Transformer (LSTM-UT) with bounded gated memory. On Rule 30 cellular automata, BUT extrapolates to unseen recurrent depths more reliably than CoTFormer, although its accuracy eventually degrades. State and cache interventions show that CoTFormer's failure depends on their interaction: correcting the current state can temporarily restore accuracy, while retained history can undermine that correction. In a delayed-recall task, BUT also outperforms CoTFormer despite lacking direct access to past states; CoTFormer does not reliably select the requested cached representation. LSTM-UT improves both depth extrapolation and delayed recall over these baselines. The results support bounded gated memory as an effective inductive bias for repeated computation and later retrieval in these tasks.

</details>


### [121] [Compressed Active Subspaces for Scalable Bayesian Inference](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.19539)
*Thomas Flynn,Sanket Jantre,Byung-Jun Yoon,Kibaek Kim*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: CAS provides a scalable way to construct active subspaces by compressing the parameter space with a structured isometric embedding, enabling Bayesian uncertainty quantification for large models while reducing memory requirements.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Standard active subspace methods require storing many full-gradients, which is infeasible for large models; this work seeks scalable uncertainty quantification by reducing dimensionality before subspace construction.

Method: Introduce Compressed Active Subspaces (CAS) that first map parameters to a compressed space via a structured isometric embedding, then build the active subspace in this reduced space and perform Bayesian inference on the compressed parameters.

Result: CAS substantially reduces memory usage for active subspace construction, enabling Bayesian inference for large models (e.g., neural networks) while preserving predictive performance and yielding robust uncertainty estimates.

Conclusion: CAS enables scalable active subspace-based uncertainty quantification for large models where standard active subspace methods are impractical.

Abstract: Active subspace methods provide a framework for quantifying predictive uncertainty in high-dimensional models by identifying and performing inference along parameter directions that have the greatest influence on the model output. However, the construction of active subspaces requires storing many full-dimensional model gradients, which becomes prohibitive as model size increases. We address this limitation by proposing Compressed Active Subspaces (CAS), a scalable approach that first maps the model parameters to a compressed space using a structured isometric embedding and then constructs the active subspace within this reduced parameterization. Our approach substantially reduces the memory required for active subspace construction and enables Bayesian inference for large models where standard active subspace methods become impractical. We demonstrate the scalability of CAS on neural networks of increasing size while maintaining predictive performance and robust uncertainty estimates.

</details>


### [122] [FedFIbOS: Fisher Importance based Optimal Submodelling for Heterogeneous Federated Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.19559)
*Yasmeen Afzal,Jeremiah D. Deng,Haibo Zhang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Fisher Importance-based Optimal Submodelling (FedFIbOS) for heterogeneous federated learning uses Fisher information as a principled criterion for submodel selection, improving convergence and accuracy under non-IID settings by replacing magnitude-based heuristics with Fisher-based top-k masking; it is efficiently estimable and yields ~10% accuracy gains on CIFAR-10/100 and AGNews.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current submodel selection in heterogeneous FL relies on magnitude-based heuristics with no theoretical convergence justification. Heterogeneity and partial participation introduce estimation effects in Fisher scores, creating a mismatch between selected submodels and convergence guarantees.

Method: Derive a Fisher-weighted quadratic masking surrogate for submodel selection. Show that under a Fisher-dominant ranking condition, the raw Fisher top-k rule matches the surrogate’s solution. Preserve the convergence structure of the masked Federated optimization bound. Estimate Fisher scores from the empirical diagonal Fisher information via squared gradients, enabling stable, adaptive parameter selection without extra optimization.

Result: Empirical evaluation on CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and AGNews under pathological and Dirichlet non-IID settings shows FedFIbOS achieves about 10% higher accuracy than the state of the art, with larger gains under stronger heterogeneity.

Conclusion: FedFIbOS provides a theoretically grounded, efficient submodel selection criterion based on Fisher information that aligns with the convergence behavior of masked federated optimization, yielding robust gains under non-IID client heterogeneity.

Abstract: Heterogeneous federated learning requires clients with diverse computational capacities to collaboratively train a global model, where each client trains a capacity-constrained submodel. Existing methods select submodel parameters using heuristic importance measures---most prominently parameter magnitude---without theoretical justification for why these measures support convergence. We identify a fundamental gap: existing parameter selection criteria lack theoretical grounding in the convergence framework, partial client participation introduces additional estimation effects in the Fisher scores. We propose \textbf{FedFIbOS}: Fisher Importance-based Optimal Submodelling for heterogeneous federated learning, using Fisher Information in a principled criterion derived from minimizing submodel masking error. %We formally establish when magnitude selection is equivalent to Fisher selection fail under non-IID heterogeneous federated learning. We theoretically formulate submodel selection through a Fisher-weighted quadratic masking surrogate and show that the raw Fisher top-$k$ rule implemented by FedFIbOS solves this surrogate under a Fisher-dominant ranking condition. The resulting method retains the convergence structure of the underlying masked federated optimization bound. Fisher scores are efficiently estimated from empirical diagonal Fisher information using squared gradients, enabling stable and adaptive parameter selection without additional optimization overhead. Experiments on CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and AGNews under pathological and Dirichlet non-IID settings show FedFIbOS achieves ${\approx}10\%$ higher accuracy than the state of the art, with improvements becoming more pronounced under stronger heterogeneity.

</details>


### [123] [The Complexity Kink: A Prompt-Side Structural Complexity Index for Code-Generation Reliability](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.19616)
*Michael Hernandez,Tian Zhao*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Introduces a six-dimension pre-generation prompt-side structural-complexity index; analyzes 5,000 Python prompts, 21 models, 105k generations; finds nonuniversal pass-rate breakpoints; high inter-rater reliability; shows complex relation between prompt complexity and output success; suggests a pre-generation measurement framework and bounded observational analysis without causal claims.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Understand how prompt design complexity affects generation success and to separate prompt-side factors from correctness.

Method: Six-dimension, pre-generation complexity index evaluated across 5,000 prompts in six bands; single-rater rubric; four LLM raters rescore prompts; 21 models per prompt, totaling 105,000 generations; analyses include unadjusted mean-pooled pass rates, task-type fixed effects, frame controls, model-specific fits; 365-prompt audit extension; Lizard complexity as an input dimension for zero-pass cases; cross-language and paraphrase rescoring tested; overidentification tests applied; 2SLS attempted with restrictions; composite index treated as a measurement framework rather than causal variable.

Result: Inter-rater reliability ICC = 0.872 on 4,998 prompts with all four ratings; pass-rate breakpoint around composite 13.75 in unadjusted analysis (79.9% at/below, 87.6% above); task-type fixed effects shift breakpoint to 10.75 and reduce regime gap from 7.6 to 2.1 points; construction-frame control yields breakpoint 8.50 with raw gap -3.5; model-specific fits include 16 upward and 5 downward changes; audit-extension aligns with original model estimates at higher bins but adds few prompts; 28.5% of zero-pass generations with computable Lizard complexity pair prompt composite >8 with output complexity ≤10; paraphrase/cross-language rescoring preserves score ordering; overidentification tests reject joint restrictions on the six dimensions, hence no causal interpretation of 2SLS estimates; the work provides a pre-generation measurement framework and a bounded observational analysis of reliability regimes.

Conclusion: Proposes a pre-generation measurement framework and bounded observational analysis of reliability regimes; emphasizes regime-dependent effects and nonuniversal cutoffs; cautions against inferring causality from 2SLS results; the composite six-dimension index functions as a reliability-monitoring tool for prompt design rather than a deterministic predictor.

Abstract: Complexity measured from generated code is failure-dependent: a difficult prompt can yield a short failing program and be assigned low output complexity. We introduce a six-dimension prompt-side structural-complexity index scored before generation and kept separate from correctness. We select 5,000 Python prompts across six bands of a preliminary single-rater rubric. Four out-of-panel LLM raters rescore the locked prompts, giving 19,997 score rows; composite inter-rater reliability is ICC = 0.872 on the 4,998 prompts with all four ratings. We evaluate 21 models per prompt, yielding 105,000 generations. In the unadjusted mean-pooled analysis, pass rate has a nonmonotone breakpoint at composite 13.75, with 79.9% at or below and 87.6% above. This is not a universal failure cutoff. Task-type fixed effects shift the breakpoint to 10.75 and cut the regime gap from 7.6 to 2.1 points. A construction-frame control shifts it to 8.50 with a raw gap of -3.5 points, and neither frame alone reproduces the pooled +7.6-point change. Model-specific fits include 16 upward and five downward changes. A 365-prompt audit-clean extension matches the original five-model estimates at bins 15 and 16 but adds only 14 prompts above bin 16.
