Among zero-pass generations with computable Lizard complexity, 28.5% pair a prompt composite above 8 with output complexity at most 10. Human agreement is moderate and rater-dependent on a disagreement-enriched calibration set; paraphrase and cross-language rescoring preserve score ordering. Overidentification tests reject the joint restrictions on the six dimensions, so we treat the composite as an index and make no causal interpretation of the 2SLS estimates. The contribution is a pre-generation measurement framework and a bounded observational analysis of reliability regimes.

</details>


### [124] [A Policy Profile for Croissant: Refusal as a Property of the Dataset](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.19640)
*Alexander Chernov*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Defines an additive evaluation semantics for Croissant by introducing a formal, five-operator decision profile and gate; demonstrates alignment with native descriptors and ODRL usageInfo across 552 cases, with low overhead and clear separation of evaluation from the carrier.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To fill the gap in Croissant where evaluation semantics were previously underspecified, enabling verifiable, auditable, and auditable enforcement of data-use and operation-admittance policies.

Method: Introduce a closed set of five operators with a full decision procedure; build a gate that decides from the descriptor alone and records checks; evaluate using two corpora and three gated nf-core pipelines; create a grammar-derived corpus to ensure breadth; compare decisions against native descriptors and ODRL in usageInfo; separate evidence records for corpora.

Result: Demonstrates that: (a) profile decisions match the gate’s native descriptor record; (b) stripping the added layer yields a valid Croissant document; (c) the time cost is 11.7 μs for profile-based decision versus 119 μs for direct decision; a grammar-generated corpus covers all operator/refusal/conformance cases; 552 complete decision records agree across native descriptor, profile terms, and ODRL-like usage policy; caller-bound and data-bound policies occupy non-overlapping state spaces.

Conclusion: The core contribution is the evaluation semantics for Croissant, not the carrier format itself; the additive profile enables verifiable, auditable policy decisions with clear separation of concerns, and non-overlapping policy spaces provide predictable interoperability.

Abstract: Croissant is the de facto machine-readable descriptor for ML datasets: JSON-LD over schema.org. Since version 1.1 it also carries data use conditions, recommending DUO and ODRL for them. What no version specifies is how any of them is evaluated: no decision procedure, no bound on evaluation cost, no outcome for a condition an implementation cannot evaluate, no record of what was checked, and nothing on composition with caller-side authority. We supply that half. An additive profile lets a dataset declare the operations it admits and the conditions under which it admits them, over a closed set of five operators whose decision procedure is given in full, so a gate decides from the descriptor alone and records what it checked. Two corpora evaluate it and their evidence is kept apart. Three descriptors that gated a real nf-core pipeline give the deployment result: decisions from a profile document match the gate's native descriptor record for record, stripping the layer leaves a valid Croissant document, and the added cost is 11.7 $μ$s against a 119 $μ$s decision. A corpus generated from the profile's grammar gives the breadth, covering every operator, refusal class and conformance clause. Across its valid cases, 552 complete decision records agree three ways -- native descriptor, profile terms, and the same policy as ODRL in usageInfo. The carrier is therefore not the contribution; the evaluation semantics is. Finally, caller-bound and data-bound policies range over non-overlapping state spaces, so neither permit set contains the other.

</details>


### [125] [CoRe: Coherence and Relational Alignment for Multivariate Time Series Forecasting](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.19670)
*Xiaoyu Lin,Huiran Duan,Yining Liu,Zhixiang Wu,Chu Lin,Lin Lu*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: CoRe proposes a model-agnostic, loss-based objective for direct multivariate forecasting that preserves trajectory structure without adding trainable parameters. It replaces pointwise losses with two output-space constraints: (1) a frequency coherence loss aligning predicted and target spectra, and (2) a low-rank relational graph loss matching pairwise differences in a PCA-derived subspace of the target. This loss can be plugged into any forecasting backbone and improves performance across datasets and hyperparameters.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Direct forecasting often optimizes pointwise errors (e.g., MSE) which stabilizes training but can erode temporal coherence within variables and relational structure across variables. A training objective that explicitly preserves structural properties of the future trajectory could yield better forecasts without modifying model architecture.

Method: Introduce CoRe, a loss-based, model-agnostic objective with no trainable parameters. It imposes two constraints in the output space: (i) frequency coherence loss to align predicted and target spectral content, and (ii) a low-rank relational graph loss enforcing consistency of pairwise differences in a target-derived PCA subspace. The total loss replaces standard pointwise supervision and can be applied to existing forecasting backbones by changing only the loss function.

Result: Empirical evaluation on standard multivariate forecasting benchmarks shows that CoRe consistently improves strong baselines, competes favorably with recent forecasting objectives, and remains effective across different backbones, datasets, and hyperparameter settings, indicating robustness and general applicability.

Conclusion: CoRe provides a lightweight, plug-in objective that enforces structural properties of the future trajectory without adding parameters. By ensuring spectral coherence and relational consistency, it enhances direct multivariate forecasting across diverse settings.

Abstract: Direct forecasting has become a standard paradigm for multivariate time-series forecasting because it predicts the full future horizon in a single pass. However, its training objective is often still decomposed into pointwise errors such as MSE. Such objectives provide stable supervision, but they do not explicitly preserve the structure of the future trajectory: temporal coherence within each variable and relational consistency across variables can both be weakened. We propose CoRe, a model-agnostic learning objective for direct multivariate forecasting. CoRe replaces pointwise supervision with two output-space constraints: a frequency coherence loss that aligns predicted and target spectra, and a low-rank relational graph loss that matches sampled pairwise differences in a target-derived PCA subspace. The resulting objective introduces no trainable parameters and can be applied to existing forecasting backbones by changing only the loss. Experiments on standard benchmarks show that CoRe improves strong baselines, compares favorably with recent forecasting objectives, and remains effective across different backbones, datasets, and hyperparameter settings overall consistently.

</details>


### [126] [Conservation Buys Stability and Factoring Buys Counterfactuals in Physical World Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.19674)
*Yufeng Wang,Parivesh Priye,Lu Wei,Haibin Ling*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Different failure modes in learned simulators need distinct structural remedies: long-horizon stability comes from symplectic energy evolution, while counterfactual generalization under parameter interventions comes from explicit factorized coupling; these effects are separable and generalize beyond simple systems.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Understand why learned physical simulators fail under long rollouts and under interventions, and how to achieve both stability and counterfactual generalization.

Method: Systematic comparison of architectures: (1) energy-evolving with a symplectic integrator; (2) equal-capacity predictors; (3) energy-regularized predictor; (4) tuned neural ODE. Also compare explicit linear factorization of physical coupling vs unrestricted parameterization. Use matched-control double-dissociation experiments, test on three-body dynamics and state inference from pixels.

Result: Symplectic-energy models preserve geometry and keep rollouts bounded for up to ~100x training horizon; other predictors diverge. Explicitly factorized coupling enables counterfactual transfer to unseen coupling signs; unrestricted parameterization remains locked to training law. The two mechanisms are separable: removing stability structure preserves counterfactual transfer; removing factorized coupling destroys counterfactual transfer without eliminating stability. Findings persist beyond three-body systems and when states are inferred from pixels.

Conclusion: Long-horizon stability and changed-law generalization are due to distinct structural commitments and can be imposed independently to improve physical world models.

Abstract: A learned simulator can reproduce its training conditions accurately yet fail in two distinct ways once those conditions change. Over long rollouts, small errors accumulate until the trajectory drifts away from physically plausible behavior; under an intervention on a physical parameter, the model may continue to follow the law seen during training rather than the intervened one. We show that these two failures require different structural remedies. Evolving a learned energy with a symplectic integrator preserves the geometry of the conservative dynamics and keeps rollouts bounded and physically meaningful for up to $100\times$ the training horizon, while equal-capacity predictors, an energy-regularized predictor, and a tuned neural ODE diverge. By contrast, encoding the physical coupling through an explicit linear factorization enables the model to follow a never-seen sign of that coupling, whereas an unrestricted parameterization remains locked to the training law. Crucially, the two mechanisms are separable: removing the structure responsible for long-horizon stability leaves counterfactual transfer intact, while removing the factorized coupling destroys counterfactual transfer without eliminating stability. This double dissociation, established with matched controls that remove or replace one structural component at a time, persists beyond the headline three-body system and remains visible when the physical state must be inferred from pixels rather than provided directly. The result is a concrete design principle for physical world models: long-horizon stability and changed-law generalization arise from distinct structural commitments, and each can be imposed deliberately without requiring the other.

</details>


### [127] [Opinion Dynamics-based Coalition Formation for Federated Learning in Heterogeneous IoT Systems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.19695)
*Mohammed El Hanjri,Anas Abouaomar,Hamidou Tembine,Abdellatif Kobbane*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: HK-based weight-space coalitions in federated learning for IoT time-series improve local and global performance, achieving stable coalitions within 10 inner iterations without extra overhead and lowering MAE significantly while attaining high global accuracy (83–85%).


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Statistical heterogeneity across IoT devices (e.g., smart-metered households) causes FedAvg to poorly capture client-specific patterns. Forming coalitions directly in the local-weight space and aggregating at the coalition level aims to better reflect heterogeneity and improve forecasting accuracy.

Method: Model coalition formation as a Hegselmann-Krause bounded-confidence opinion-dynamics process on local weights. Develop Euclidean-distance and cosine-similarity confidence criteria variants. Apply to short-term water-consumption forecasting with local LSTM models. Evaluate against FedAvg, Per-FedAvg, FedProx, and FedAvg with coalition formation.

Result: Coalitions converge to stable, endogenous structures within at most ten inner iterations. No additional client-side computation or communication compared to FedAvg. MAE reductions: up to 54% vs FedAvg, 39% vs FedProx, 24% vs Per-FedAvg. Global accuracy achieved: 83–85%.

Conclusion: HK-based, weight-space coalition formation is an effective, low-overhead enhancement for FL on heterogeneous IoT time-series data, yielding notable accuracy gains and stable client groupings without increasing communication or computation.

Abstract: Federated learning (FL) enables privacy-preserving, on-device training across heterogeneous Internet-of-Things (IoT) deployments such as smart-city water-metering networks, where each smart meter observes a household-specific consumption time series. Under such statistical heterogeneity, the standard Federated Averaging (FedAvg) aggregation averages dissimilar local models into a single global model that may fail to capture client-specific patterns. We address this by forming client coalitions directly in the local-weight space and aggregating at the coalition level. Extending a prior weight-driven coalition-formation scheme, we model coalition formation as a Hegselmann-Krause (HK) bounded-confidence opinion-dynamics process acting on the local weights, and develop variants of the HK interaction based on Euclidean-distance and cosine-similarity confidence criteria. The framework is applied to short-term water-consumption forecasting with local Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) models and evaluated against FedAvg, Per-FedAvg, FedProx, and FedAvg with Euclidean-distance or cosine-similarity coalition formation. Experiments on a real smart-metering dataset of water consumption show that the proposed HK-based coalition formation produces stable, endogenous coalition structures within at most ten inner iterations, incurs no additional client-side computation or communication compared to FedAvg, and reduces the average MAE by up to 54% relative to FedAvg, 39% relative to FedProx, and 24% relative to Per-FedAvg, while achieving the highest global accuracy (83-85%).

</details>


### [128] [Odds-Ratio Thompson Sampling: A Specification and Design Guide for Contrast-Based Multi-Armed Bandits](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.19709)
*Sulgi Kim*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: OR-TS updates on a per-batch basis by carrying the joint posterior over log-odds contrasts and re-estimating the shared level in each batch (marginalizing it), with two controls: memory decay and allocation aggressiveness. It outperforms absolute-rate memory in nonstationary batched settings across extensive synthetic and real evaluations, but fails when the contrasts themselves move.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To overcome the stale memory problem of batched bandits that carry each arm’s absolute reward rate across updates; when the shared level drifts, this memory degrades comparisons and allocation decisions. OR-TS avoids this by re-fitting the level anew each batch and conditioning on log-odds contrasts.

Method: A Bayesian bandit agent that uses an odds-ratio (log-odds) contrast model. Each batch updates a joint posterior over contrasts and the current level; the level is marginalized out, so the batch-specific fit does not carry stale level memory. Two hyperparameters control (i) decay of past evidence and (ii) aggressiveness of belief-to-allocation. Evaluations compare OR-TS against absolute-rate memory across 86 public A/B series (level varies ~25x more than contrast). Synthetic moving-level environments quantify regret and allocation; a policy simulation built from 71 real experiments tests performance with small, hard-to-resolve contrasts.

Result: Moving level costs absolute-rate memory fivefold in regret and can push the best arm to receive less than 50% of traffic in 7/20 runs, while OR-TS avoids this in the reported runs. In 71 real experiments with tiny contrasts, expected-click differences stay within 0.1% for 58 cases, yet contrast memory still ends up on the better arm more than twice as often. The approach fails when the contrasts themselves move, and this limitation is explicitly reported.

Conclusion: OR-TS provides robust performance under nonstationary level conditions by separating level estimation from arm-contrast memory and allowing decay/aggressiveness hyperparameters. It improves over absolute-rate memory in many batched settings, but its efficacy degrades when the contrast signals themselves are nonstationary. The method is well-supported by large empirical evaluations but has a clear limitation in fast-moving contrast regimes.

Abstract: Batched multi-armed bandits update on a service's own schedule, and the usual implementation carries each arm's absolute reward rate from one update to the next. When the shared level moves between batches, that memory goes stale even though the comparisons between arms may not have. Odds-Ratio Thompson Sampling (OR-TS) instead carries the joint posterior over log-odds contrasts and fits the common level afresh in every batch, marginalizing it out. This paper specifies that update, places it inside a Bayesian bandit agent with two controls, decay for how much past evidence survives an update and aggressiveness for how sharply belief becomes allocation, and evaluates it against absolute-rate memory. Across 86 public A/B series the level varies about twenty-five times more than the contrast. In prespecified synthetic environments a moving level costs absolute-rate memory five times the regret and leaves the best arm below a majority of traffic in 7 of 20 runs, against none for OR-TS. In a policy simulation built from 71 real experiments, where the contrasts are too small to resolve, expected-click differences stay within 0.1% for 58 of them, yet contrast memory still ends on the better arm more than twice as often. Where the contrasts themselves move, the bet fails, and that case is reported too.

</details>


### [129] [Learn Your Own Thoughts: Abstract Token Curriculum](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.19717)
*Khashayar Gatmiry,Avrajit Ghosh,Parsa Mirtaheri,Jason D. Lee,Nika Haghtalab,Emmanuel Abbe,Peter Bartlett*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: ATC is a curriculum-based framework that elicits continuous intermediate representations (abstract thoughts) without explicit thinking-token supervision, progressively increasing task complexity to guide internal representations; with theoretical and empirical evidence showing advantages over prior methods, including parity tasks and graph/arithmetic benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Overcome reliance on explicit CoT supervision and manual scratchpad design; enable models to develop internal, continuous reasoning representations without labeled thinking tokens.

Method: Introduce Abstract Token Curriculum (ATC) that uses a sequence of problem distributions to gradually raise complexity; train model to produce continuous abstract representations; no direct supervision on thinking tokens; theoretical analysis for parity with single-layer softmax; empirical evaluation on graph reachability and arithmetic tasks.

Result: Theoretical result: ATC causes attention to focus on the CoT tokens that yield the easiest path to next-token prediction in parity tasks with single-layer softmax attention. Experimental results showing effectiveness on graph reachability and arithmetic learning.

Conclusion: ATC provides a principled route to training continuous 'thoughts' without explicit supervision, offering advantages over prior CoT-based methods and expanding capabilities in reasoning tasks.

Abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have achieved remarkable reasoning capabilities by utilizing chain-of-thought (CoT) as a scratchpad for intermediate stages of thinking. However, CoT techniques require explicit supervision on thinking tokens, which requires rich, task-specific data. In this work, we propose Abstract Token Curriculum (ATC), a novel curriculum learning framework that elicits effective continuous intermediate representations without direct supervision or manual scratchpad design. ATC gradually increases problem complexity through a sequence of distributions, training the model to develop internal abstract ``thoughts'' in the continuous representation space. This paper provides both theoretical and experimental evidence for the benefits of ATC and its advantages over previous methods for training continuous thoughts. Theoretically, we show that for learning parity functions with single-layer softmax attention using ATC, attention naturally focuses on the CoT tokens in the context that provide the ``easiest path'' to predicting the next token. Experimentally, we show ATC's effectiveness on graph reachability and arithmetic learning tasks.

</details>


### [130] [Alliance Beats Isolation: Unifying Heterogeneous Allied Datasets Improves Classifier Performance](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.19748)
*Girish Keshav Palshikar*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Merge feature-spaces of allied heterogeneous datasets into a unified representation via matrix completion, enabling cross-dataset knowledge transfer; empirically improves classifiers trained on the unified representation over those trained on individual datasets across multiple pairs.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Address learning across multiple labelled datasets that share labels but have disjoint underlying objects and heterogeneous features. The goal is to enable transfer of classification knowledge by constructing a common feature space.

Method: For a pair of allied heterogeneous datasets, merge their feature spaces into a single representation. Apply a matrix completion step to fill gaps and create a unified dataset. Train classifiers on this unified representation and compare to classifiers trained on each dataset separately to assess transfer gains.

Result: Experiments on several allied dataset pairs show that classifiers trained on the unified representation outperform those trained on the constituent datasets across multiple classifiers and pairs.

Conclusion: Unifying allied heterogeneous datasets with feature-space merging and matrix completion provides an easy, effective way to enhance classifier performance and enable cross-dataset knowledge transfer.

Abstract: In many application domains, such as student dropout, insurance fraud, loan approval, and machine failures, several labelled public datasets are available where (i) data is about the same type of objects but the set of actual underlying objects are disjoint; and (ii) the class labels are same; and (iii) the feature spaces of the datasets are largely distinct (heterogeneous), with a few shared features. We call such datasets as allied. A single classifier cannot be trained on both datasets together, and one classifier trained on one dataset cannot be tested on the other. In this paper, we propose a method to merge the feature-spaces into a single feature-space for a pair of given allied heterogeneous datasets. We then use a matrix completion method to create a unified dataset based on the merged feature-space. The hypothesis is that the merged representation facilitates the transfer of classification knowledge from one dataset to another. We conduct experiments on several pairs of allied, heterogeneous datasets and several classifiers to demonstrate that any classifier trained on the unified representation always outperforms classifiers separately trained on the constituent allied datasets on several pairs of allied datasets. This work provides an easy way to substantially improve classifier performance by unifying and using multiple allied datasets together.

</details>


### [131] [OceanMoE: Structured Conditional Sparse Computation for Long-Horizon Multivariate Ocean Forecasting](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.19768)
*Yishun Zhu,Jian Wang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: OceanMoE introduces a structured conditional sparse Mixture-of-Experts framework for multivariate ocean forecasting that balances shared context with target- and location-specific specialization. It uses content-conditioned routing to select a variable- and location-dependent subset of experts, with adaptive active experts based on router confidence. A geographic bias is encoded via spherical-harmonic bases in the decoder, and shared residual/seasonal paths provide global context. Evaluated on long-horizon ORAS5 forecasts, OceanMoE improves aggregate error and maintains lower geometric-mean normalized RMSE across many rollout months; expert allocation varies by target and location.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Forecasting multiple ocean variables jointly benefits from shared physical context but must accommodate heterogeneous statistics and dynamics across variables and spatial locations. Fully shared models can miss local nuances; fully independent models discard cross-variable information. A principled framework is needed to retain shared ocean context while enabling target- and location-specific computation.

Method: A structured conditional sparse Mixture-of-Experts (MoE): at each spatial location, target-specific local representations are built by fusing cross-variable information; content-conditioned routing selects active experts, with the number of active experts adapting to router confidence. The decoder adds a geographic bias via learnable parameters informed by spherical-harmonic spatial bases. Shared residual and seasonal pathways provide global cross-variable and monthly context. Training likely involves autoregressive long-horizon forecasting (ORAS5) with MoE routing.

Result: OceanMoE lowers aggregate forecasting error compared to baselines in long-horizon ORAS5 forecasting and maintains a lower geometric-mean normalized RMSE over many rollout months. Routing analyses show that expert allocation depends on prediction targets and spatial locations, indicating meaningful specialization. Overall, the approach supports structured conditional computation to balance shared ocean context with adaptive specialization.

Conclusion: Structured conditional computation via OceanMoE effectively balances shared and specialized representations for multivariate ocean forecasting, with adaptive routing and geography-aware decoding improving long-horizon predictive accuracy and yielding interpretable, target-location dependent expert usage.

Abstract: Multivariate ocean forecasting must exploit shared evolution in a coupled ocean system while adapting to the heterogeneous statistical and dynamical characteristics of different prediction variables and locations. Fully shared models may lack the flexibility to handle this heterogeneity, whereas fully independent models discard the common ocean context shared across variables. The key question is how to retain shared context in a unified model while allowing computation to specialize according to the prediction target and local state. We propose OceanMoE, a structured conditional sparse Mixture-of-Experts framework that combines sharing and specialization for multivariate ocean forecasting. OceanMoE fuses cross-variable information to construct target-specific local representations and uses them to perform content-conditioned sparse routing at each spatial location, with the number of active experts adapted to router confidence. In the decoder, routing is augmented with a learned geographic bias parameterized by spherical-harmonic spatial bases, while shared residual and seasonal pathways provide common cross-variable and month-dependent context. Experiments on long-horizon autoregressive ORAS5 forecasting show that OceanMoE lowers aggregate forecasting error in both evaluated settings and maintains lower geometric-mean normalized RMSE than the corresponding baselines over most later rollout months. Routing analyses further show that expert allocation varies with prediction targets and spatial locations. These results support structured conditional computation as a modeling strategy for balancing shared ocean context with adaptive specialization.

</details>


### [132] [PhyRestore: Physics-Structured Latent-Factor Restoration](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.19776)
*Ahmed Shafee,Chayan Lahiri*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: PhyRestore is a physics-structured latent-factor restoration method that recovers temporal soil-loss changes by restoring corrupted input factors within the RUSLE framework, evaluated against ML baselines in a watershed setting.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Estimating temporal soil-loss change is difficult when input factors are noisy or corrupted, and many locations show little change, making robust recovery essential.

Method: PhyRestore restores corrupted physical factors (e.g., rainfall erosivity, cover management) using the known physical relationship of RUSLE to reconstruct temporal change, vs. comparing degraded RUSLE estimates with ML models (RF, XGBoost, MLP, CNN) in a bitemporal, raster, watershed-scale setting under isolated and joint corruption.

Result: Factor restoration improves high-magnitude recovery when corrupted factors remain identifiable; the advantage diminishes under joint corruption, sparse positive extremes, and factor values outside the training support.

Conclusion: A physics-informed restoration approach can enhance recovery of large soil-loss changes under certain corruption regimes, but performance degrades when multiple factors are corrupted simultaneously or fall outside the training distribution.

Abstract: Estimating temporal soil-loss change is challenging when physically meaningful input factors are noisy or corrupted, particularly because substantial changes are rare relative to the large number of locations exhibiting little change. We study this problem through the Revised Universal Soil Loss Equation (RUSLE) and introduce PhyRestore, a physics-structured latent-factor restoration framework. Rather than directly predicting soil-loss change or correcting a degraded physical estimate, PhyRestore restores corrupted physical factors and reconstructs temporal change through the known physical relationship. We evaluate PhyRestore in a watershed-scale bitemporal raster setting under isolated and simultaneous corruption of rainfall erosivity and cover management, comparing it with the degraded RUSLE estimate and Direct RF, XGBoost, MLP, and CNN models. Factor restoration improves high-magnitude recovery when the corrupted factors remain identifiable, but its advantage weakens under joint corruption, sparse positive extremes, and factor values outside the training support.

</details>


### [133] [Learning-Based Reconstruction of Optical Properties in Bilayered Media from Single-distance Time-Resolved Reflectance Measurements](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.19786)
*Caterina Amendola,Giulia Maffeis,Lorenzo Buffoni,Lorenzo Chicchi,Francesco Coghi,Duccio Fanelli,Raffaele Marino,Fabrizio Martelli,Riccardo Paoli,Lorenzo Pattelli,Lorenzo Spinelli*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: An ML-based framework reconstructs optical properties (absorption and scattering) in bilayered media from DTOF measurements, using Monte Carlo forward data; it achieves faster, more accurate reconstructions than diffusion-based solvers and can infer the number of layers without prior information; future work includes multi-distance joint reconstruction.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Address inaccuracies of diffusion-based inverse solvers in multilayer, heterogeneous media, especially superficial absorption and deep-layer scattering, by leveraging data-driven models trained on high-fidelity Monte Carlo forward simulations.

Method: Generate a large synthetic DTOF dataset with exact Monte Carlo simulations for bilayer geometries at multiple source-detector distances; train a machine learning pipeline to map DTOF to optical properties; benchmark against model-based diffusion-reconstruction methods; discuss the ability to infer layer count and dimensionality.

Result: ML framework offers significant reconstruction speed-up and higher accuracy than model-based solvers; can estimate the parameter-space dimensionality without a priori layer information; potential for improved accuracy by joint multi-distance DTOF training.

Conclusion: ML-based reconstruction is a promising alternative for bilayered media; expect further gains with multi-distance joint training and extension to multiple DTOF curves per medium.

Abstract: The inverse problem of reconstructing optical properties, specifically absorption and scattering coefficients, in layered biological media from time-domain reflectance measurements remains a significant challenge for traditional analytical models. Inverse solvers based on the diffusion equation often struggle with structural heterogeneity, frequently yielding poor accuracy for superficial absorption and deep-layers scattering. In this work, we propose a machine learning framework as an alternative approach to reconstruct the optical properties of a bilayered medium, benchmarking its efficiency and accuracy against model-based algorithms. To overcome the intrinsic approximations of diffusion theory and inverse reconstruction, we generated a robust synthetic dataset of forward DTOF using exact Monte Carlo simulations at multiple source-detector distances. A machine learning pipeline was then trained on this dataset and validated against state-of-the-art model-based reconstruction methods. Besides the significant reconstruction speed-up, the machine learning approach achieves higher accuracy than model-based inverse solvers, further providing an estimate of the parameter space dimensionality without requiring any a priori information about the number of layers in the investigated geometry. Further enhancements in the reconstruction accuracy can be expected in future extensions of this work, by training the pipeline over multiple DTOF curves from the same medium, in a joint multi-distance reconstruction approach.

</details>


### [134] [DeliveryGym: An RL Environment for Long-Horizon Embodied Agent Planning with Adaptive Curriculum](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.19801)
*Haoqiang Kang,Yiming Zhang,Yiyang Guo,Chuying Li,Jianzhi Shen,Tianruo Rose Xu,Xiaokang Ye,Lianhui Qin*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: DeliveryGym is a 3D executable RL environment for continuous courier shifts that preserves trajectory-level costs and enables learning from complete shifts; it uses adaptive training shifts and multimodal tool interaction; results show large income gains on a fixed test suite and with curriculum adaptation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: There is a need for environments that preserve dependencies across entire trajectories so RL agents can learn planning under resource constraints (time, energy, money) rather than optimizing isolated tasks.

Method: Introduce DeliveryGym, a 3D environment for continuous courier shifts that combines multimodal tool interaction with persistent world dynamics and computes trajectory rewards from simulator events. It includes adaptive training shifts (curriculum) based on policy weaknesses and evaluates across six models and 13 city maps.

Result: On a fixed test suite, RL improves Qwen3-VL-4B's net income by 54.3%. Adapting training shifts improves test income by 16.5% over uniform sampling at the same rollout budget.

Conclusion: DeliveryGym provides an executable setting to study how agents learn to coordinate deliveries and preserve resources for later orders within an episode, enabling learning from complete shifts and benefiting from adaptive curricula.

Abstract: Executable environments enable LLM agents to learn from the consequences of their actions. For embodied agents, those consequences extend beyond whether the current task succeeds: completing a delivery can consume the time, energy, or money needed for later work. Learning to plan therefore requires environments that preserve these dependencies and turn them into feedback across a complete trajectory. We introduce DeliveryGym, a 3D environment for evaluating and training agents on continuous courier shifts. It couples multimodal tool interaction with persistent world dynamics and computes trajectory rewards from simulator events, making the costs of an agent's decisions available for reinforcement learning (RL). The environment also adapts future training shifts to the policy's observed weaknesses while keeping evaluation fixed. Across six models and 13 city maps, evaluation exposes a gap between reliably executing assigned deliveries and choosing and sequencing work over a shift. On the fixed test suite, RL improves Qwen3-VL-4B's net income by 54.3%, showing that learning from complete shifts improves performance under these coupled constraints. Adapting the training environment improves test income by 16.5% over uniform sampling at the same rollout budget, indicating that which situations an agent practices also matters. DeliveryGym provides an executable setting for studying how agents learn to coordinate deliveries and preserve resources for later orders within an episode.

</details>


### [135] [Beyond Flattened Tokens: Structure-Preserving EEG Decoding with Reusable TriDim Blocks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.19842)
*Shiyue Su,Song Wang,Zekai Zhan,Junjie Zeng,Ziling Lu,Zongsheng Li,Xinyuan Ye,Zhiyuan Ma,Xinke Shen,Quanying Liu*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: TriDim introduces a three-axis EEG block that preserves channel (spatial), short-term temporal (within-patch), and long-term temporal (across patches) structures, enabling cross-axis coordination. It achieves state-of-the-art cross-subject performance and improves other models when replacing Transformer blocks, with fewer parameters.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Preserve distinct EEG information dimensions (spatial, short-term temporal, long-range temporal) rather than collapsing to a single token sequence; existing architectures struggle to coordinate interactions across these axes.

Method: Propose TriDim block with explicit channel, patch-sample, and patch axes. Apply axis-wise feed-forward transformations and cross-axis attention. Stack TriDim blocks with a multi-level tri-axis readout to build TriDimEEG as a standalone EEG decoder. Evaluate under strict cross-subject settings across eight datasets (clinical diagnosis, sleep staging, motor imagery, emotion recognition) and test substituting TriDim blocks into three EEG foundation models.

Result: TriDimEEG achieves the best overall performance among 15 models with a 4.3% relative improvement in average accuracy over the second-best. Replacing Transformer blocks with TriDim in three EEG foundation models yields an average 7.4% improvement in downstream accuracy while reducing parameter counts by 17.0% to 47.3%.

Conclusion: TriDim is a reusable, effective EEG building block; TriDimEEG is a strong standalone decoder. Code and pretrained parameters are available at the provided GitHub link.

Abstract: Effective EEG decoding requires representations that preserve organization among channels, local waveform dynamics, and long-range temporal context. Existing EEG architectures often capture these structures using separate specialized modules or collapse them into a single token sequence, making it difficult to maintain their distinct roles and coordinate their interactions throughout the backbone. We propose TriDim, a reusable block that preserves the representation shape and keeps three EEG axes explicit: channel, sample position within each patch, and patch position across the recording. These axes correspond to spatial, short-term temporal, and long-term temporal information, respectively. Each TriDim block applies feed-forward transformations along individual axes and cross-axis attention to coordinate information exchange among them. By stacking TriDim blocks with a multi-level tri-axis readout, we construct TriDimEEG, a standalone EEG decoder. Under strict cross-subject evaluation on eight datasets spanning clinical diagnosis, sleep staging, motor imagery, and emotion recognition, TriDimEEG achieves the best overall performance among fifteen evaluated models, with a 4.3% relative improvement in average accuracy over the second-best model. Replacing Transformer blocks in three EEG foundation models with TriDim blocks yields an average relative improvement of 7.4% in downstream accuracy while reducing parameter counts by 17.0% to 47.3%. These results establish TriDim as an effective and reusable building block and TriDimEEG as a strong standalone EEG decoder. Code and parameters of TriDimEEG are available at https://github.com/ncclab-sustech/TriDim_model.

</details>


### [136] [Expected Hypervolume Maximization for Multiobjective Optimization under Uncertainties](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.19858)
*Victor Trappler*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Bayesian hypervolume optimization for multiobjective problems under uncertainty using GP surrogates and gradient-based stochastic optimization with active learning.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Uncertainties in objectives motivate a Bayesian approach; hypervolume is a principled performance metric for multiobjective optimization; a differentiable surrogate enables gradient-based optimization.

Method: Formulate optimization as maximizing the expected hypervolume with respect to a finite set of input points; use gradients in a stochastic optimization framework; account for dominated points; employ Gaussian Processes as differentiable surrogates when the objective code is non-differentiable; introduce acquisition-function–driven active learning to build suitable surrogates for the MO problem; compare strategies on simple analytical problems.

Result: Demonstrates feasibility of gradient-based optimization of expected hypervolume using GP surrogates; presents several active-learning acquisitions for surrogate construction; performs comparative evaluation on simple analytical problems to assess performance.

Conclusion: Bayesian decision formulation with expected hypervolume is viable for MO optimization under uncertainty; GP surrogates enable differentiable optimization in the absence of differentiable code; acquisition strategies can improve surrogate quality and optimization performance; further work needed on scalable computation and broader benchmarks.

Abstract: The problem of multiobjective optimization under uncertainties is often approached by taking the expectation of each objective. In this work, we propose instead to formulate this as a Bayesian decision problem and to rely on the expected value of the hypervolume, which is to be maximized with respect to a finite set of input points. We show that this can be performed using methods based on gradients in a stochastic optimization framework, provided that care is taken with respect to dominated points. Moreover, in the absence of readily available differentiable code, we propose to use Gaussian Processes as differentiable surrogate models, in order to perform the optimization. An additional contribution in this work are some active learning strategies, through acquisition functions which helps construct a surrogate model well-designed for the multiobjective optimization problem at stake. These strategies are compared on simple analytical problems to assess their performances.

</details>


### [137] [Pretrained Medical Representations for the Practical Screening of Drug Repositioning Candidates](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.19865)
*Yuhei Fujioka,Daitaro Misawa,Shingo Fukuma*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Unified pre-training for medical code sequences that captures hierarchical code structure and cross-references to enable hypothesis discovery and prioritization in observational data.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Despite advances in representation learning from electronic health records (EHR) and claims data, translating these models to scientific hypothesis discovery is hindered by the hierarchical nature of medical codes and the interactions between diagnoses and treatments. Existing BERT-based models often fail to capture these structures, limiting hypothesis generation.

Method: A unified pre-training framework integrating hierarchical sub-token aggregation, partial masking, and cross-reference mechanisms. Additionally, a Task-Adaptive Representation Approach is proposed for hypothesis prioritization to mitigate over-encoding of historical prescription information. An exploratory workflow is developed for hypothesis generation (in silico drug repositioning case study for Alzheimer's) and prioritization based on observational associations.

Result: The model outperforms baselines on both pre-training objectives and downstream clinical event prediction tasks, including dementia onset and hospitalization. In silico drug repositioning for Alzheimer's disease rediscovered known promising drugs in a data-driven manner without external literature. The Task-Adaptive Representation Approach enables robust prioritization of generated hypotheses by controlling the influence of historical prescriptions. This establishes a practical screening workflow for hypothesis generation and prioritization from observational data.

Conclusion: Domain-informed representation learning coupled with task-adaptive representation control can enable a practical hypothesis discovery workflow. The framework is intended for exploratory screening and hypothesis generation rather than causal inference, providing candidates for subsequent rigorous causal analysis.

Abstract: Representation learning from medical code sequences in electronic health records and medical claims data has been successful in various clinical applications, such as those regarding disease prediction. However, significant challenges remain in extending this approach to the discovery of scientific hypotheses. One reason is that many existing BERT-based models fail to adequately capture the hierarchical structure of medical codes and the complex interactions between diagnoses and treatments. To address these limitations, we propose a new unified pre-training framework that explicitly integrates hierarchical sub-token aggregation, partial masking, and cross-reference mechanisms. The proposed model consistently outperformed existing methods on both pre-training objectives and downstream clinical event prediction tasks, including the onset of dementia and hospitalization. We also conducted an in silico drug repositioning case study targeting Alzheimer's disease. In the hypothesis generation step, our approach successfully rediscovered known promising drugs in a data-driven manner without relying on such external knowledge sources as the literature. Subsequently, in the hypothesis prioritization step, we introduced a Task-Adaptive Representation Approach to alleviate the over-encoding of historical prescription information within diagnostic vectors, enabling the robust prioritization of generated hypotheses. This study establishes an exploratory screening workflow for hypothesis generation and prioritization based on observational associations. Importantly, this framework is not intended to provide causal evidence, but rather to identify promising candidates for subsequent rigorous causal inference. Overall, this study demonstrates that domain-informed representation learning combined with task-adaptive representation control can enable a practical hypothesis discovery workflow.

</details>


### [138] [AURA: Adaptive Uncertainty-Routed Analysis for Email Threat Detection](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.19873)
*Omran Berjawi,Walid fahs,Rida Khatoun*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: AURA is a two-layer multimodal email threat detector that combines a URL-uncertainty estimator with a fine-tuned transformer for semantic analysis, achieving strong in-distribution and cross-domain generalization against phishing and spam across multiple datasets.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Improve robustness of email threat detection against evolving adversaries, including LLM-generated content, by generalizing across diverse and shifting attack scenarios while reducing unnecessary computational cost.

Method: A two-layer cascade: (1) URL classifier estimates prediction uncertainty and (2) only uncertain cases are passed to a fine-tuned transformer encoder for semantic analysis. Trained on eight heterogeneous corpora and evaluated on two held-out real-world corpora (NazPhish-Eval, GuenterTrap-Eval) over a decade of campaigns.

Result: Macro F1 in-distribution: 0.9858. On NazPhish-Eval: 0.9502; on GuenterTrap-Eval: 0.9436, indicating strong generalization under distribution shift.

Conclusion: AURA demonstrates high detection performance and robust cross-domain generalization by routing only uncertain messages to deep semantic analysis, offering an efficient and scalable approach for real-world email threat detection.

Abstract: Email spam and phishing attacks remain a critical security threat. Adversaries increasingly exploit large language models to craft contextually convincing malicious messages, and existing spam detection systems often struggle to keep pace. Generalization across diverse and evolving attack scenarios is limited, which reduces effectiveness once these systems are deployed in practice. This paper introduces Adaptive Uncertainty-Routed Analysis (AURA), a multimodal email threat detection system that analyzes both the content of an email and its embedded URLs. AURA is built around two layers: the first quantifies prediction uncertainty from a URL classifier, and only ambiguous messages are escalated to a fine-tuned transformer encoder for semantic analysis. The system is evaluated on eight heterogeneous training corpora together with two held-out real-world corpora spanning a decade of adversarial campaigns. AURA reaches a macro F1-score of 0.9858 in-distribution, and on NazPhish-Eval and GuenterTrap-Eval it maintains 0.9502 and 0.9436, respectively, which is evidence of robust generalization under genuine distribution shift.

</details>


### [139] [Uni-LaDiR: Latent Diffusion Unifies Multimodal Reasoning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.19878)
*Haoqiang Kang,Yizhe Zhang,Nikki Lijing Kuang,Yian Ma,Lianhui Qin*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Uni-LaDiR introduces a unified latent diffusion reasoning framework for multimodal reasoning by mapping modality-specific reasoning steps into a shared latent token space, using diffusion to predict the next thought block, and enabling inference without teacher observations, achieving notable gains on VLM and VLA benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Multimodal reasoning is hampered when models combine modality-specific tokens in a single sequence; bridging cross-modal representational gaps is challenging. A shared latent space for reasoning steps can improve coherence, transfer, and predictability across modalities.

Method: A unified encoder maps teacher reasoning steps from different modalities into shared thought tokens; diffusion models predict the next block of thought tokens from the input and preceding blocks; joint training with shared weights encourages tokens to be both task-relevant and predictable; inference generates tokens without teacher observations.

Result: Achieves relative gains over strongest baselines of 7.3% on visual reasoning tasks and 6.1% on robot manipulation tasks across eleven vision-language model benchmarks and two vision-language-action suites.

Conclusion: Unified latent diffusion reasoning via Uni-LaDiR effectively aligns cross-modal reasoning tokens, enabling improved multimodal reasoning and strong cross-domain generalization across diverse benchmarks.

Abstract: Multimodal reasoning requires models to draw on information from multiple modalities throughout the reasoning process. Yet existing methods often concatenate modality-specific thought tokens in a single sequence, leaving the model to bridge representational differences as it reasons across modalities. We introduce Uni-LaDiR (Unified Latent Diffusion Reasoner), a framework that brings these thoughts into a shared latent space for reasoning. A unified encoder maps teacher reasoning steps from different modalities into shared thought tokens, trained to preserve the information needed for later reasoning steps and the final answer or action. Because the same context can support multiple valid next steps, we use diffusion to predict the next block of thought tokens from the input and preceding blocks. Jointly training the encoder and diffusion reasoner with shared model weights encourages thought tokens to be both useful for the task and predictable from the available context. At inference, the model generates these tokens without teacher observations. Across eleven vision-language model (VLM) benchmarks and two vision-language-action (VLA) suites, Uni-LaDiR achieves relative gains over the strongest evaluated baselines of 7.3% on visual reasoning tasks and 6.1% on robot manipulation tasks.

</details>


### [140] [Online Adaptive Kernel Mixing for Gaussian Process Decision Making](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.19891)
*Kavin Aravindan,Mani Tej Sriram,Gautam Dasarathy,Tejas Bodas*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A hedging-based framework (HACK GPs) to adaptively select kernels for Gaussian Processes in Bayesian optimization, level set estimation, and Bayesian active learning. Treats each kernel as an expert and updates weights online via AdaHedge. Two variants: Mixture of Gaussians and categorical sampling. Provides theoretical guarantees that the best kernel dominates under a loss-gap condition and that the acquisition function aligns with the best expert. Empirically robust across tasks against standard kernels and simple ensembles.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Kernel misspecification leads to suboptimal GP performance in sequential decision problems. An adaptive kernel selection method can improve robustness and performance without committing to a single kernel.

Method: Cast kernel selection as online learning with expert advice. Each candidate kernel is an expert; AdaHedge updates a weight distribution over kernels based on a predictive loss proxy for fit and task alignment. Two variants: (i) Mixture of Gaussians (MoG) and (ii) categorical sampling. Theoretical guarantees show weight concentrates on the best kernel under a loss-gap condition; the resulting acquisition function is close to that of that best expert.

Result: The approach yields general guarantees and empirically robust performance across BO, LSE, and BAL, outperforming standard kernels (e.g., Squared Exponential, Matern-5/2) and simple ensembles.

Conclusion: Adaptive kernel hedging (HACK GPs) improves GP-based decision making under kernel misspecification, with theoretical guarantees and strong empirical performance across multiple sequential tasks.

Abstract: Gaussian Processes (GPs) are widely used as surrogates for black-box functions in sequential decision-making problems such as Bayesian optimization (BO), level set estimation (LSE), and Bayesian active learning (BAL). GP performance critically depends on kernels, and standard kernels can lead to suboptimal decisions under misspecification. To address this, we introduce HACK GPs (Hedge Adaptive Cumulative Kernels), a method that views kernel selection as an online learning with expert advice problem. HACK treats each candidate kernel as a GP "expert" and updates a distribution over experts online using AdaHedge, based on a loss received as a proxy for their ability to fit the function and align with the task objective. We provide two variants of HACK: (i) Mixture of Gaussians (MoG) and (ii) categorical sampling. We establish general guarantees showing that, under a loss-gap condition, the weight concentrates on the best kernel and the resulting acquisition function is close to that of the best expert. Empirically, we observe robust performance across BO, LSE, and BAL compared to standard kernels such as Squared Exponential and Matern-5/2, as well as simple ensemble baselines.

</details>


### [141] [REARL: A Closed-loop Autonomous Driving Simulation Enhancement Framework with Real Traffic Data and Large Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.19903)
*Xiaojun Bi,Jun Jiang,Yiwen Sun,Quanyi Ou,Ke Cheng,Mingjie Bi,Yexin Li*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: REARL introduces a closed-loop simulation enhancement that uses clustering of real traffic data and an LLM to adjust initial simulation configuration and real-time decisions, with a sliding-window detector to trigger updates; it refines simulation realism by aligning speed and spacing distributions and by referencing real-vehicle actions.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Accurate traffic simulation is essential for autonomous driving, but static rules and data playback fail to capture dynamic real-world traffic evolution; a method that continually aligns simulated traffic with real data is needed.

Method: Real traffic data are clustered; cluster centers serve as representative scenarios for LLM guidance. A timed sliding-window detector monitors discrepancies in speed distribution and mean spacing. If thresholds are exceeded, the LLM adjusts vehicle decision-making; otherwise controllers remain. The LLM also selects a matching real vehicle from a snapshot and modulates simulated vehicles based on real actions.

Result: In HighD highway experiments, REARL reduces speed distribution Hellinger distance to 0.3067 and mean-spacing MAPE to 0.8371, achieving THW of 22.8575 and lane-change rate of 0.0708, outperforming the CRITICAL baseline and a PPO-based learning baseline.

Conclusion: A closed-loop, data-grounded integration of LLMs with traffic simulators can better track real-world traffic distributions over time, improving realism and potentially driving policy improvements, but questions of generalization, safety, and efficiency remain.

Abstract: Accurate simulation is crucial for autonomous driving development, yet capturing real-world traffic complexity remains challenging. Existing simulators that rely on predefined rules or static data playback struggle with dynamic traffic. CRITICAL uses real traffic data and a large language model (LLM) to adjust the initial simulation configuration, but the simulated distribution still diverges from real traffic as the rollout evolves. We propose REARL, a closed-loop simulation enhancement framework that integrates real traffic data with LLMs. Real traffic data are clustered, and each cluster center is used as a representative scenario that provides typical real-world traffic patterns for the LLM. A timed sliding-window detector then monitors discrepancies in vehicle speed distribution and mean spacing between pairs of vehicles. If a metric exceeds a threshold, the LLM adjusts vehicle decision-making; otherwise the existing controller is kept. The LLM also selects a matching real vehicle from a traffic snapshot and modulates the simulated vehicle with reference to that real action. In a controlled HighD highway setting, compared with the CRITICAL baseline and a PPO-based learning baseline, REARL reduces the Hellinger distance for speed distributions to 0.3067 and the MAPE for mean spacing to 0.8371, while achieving a time headway (THW) of 22.8575 and a lane change rate of 0.0708.

</details>


### [142] [Digital Twins for Opinion Dynamics: A Generative LLM Framework for Social Networks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.19913)
*Omran Berjawi,Giuseppe Fenza,Rida Khatoun,Sherali Zeadally*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A digital-twin framework clones real Twitter networks to simulate opinion dynamics using Mistral-7B, validated on COVID-19 and 2020 US election data, achieving substantial predictive gains and insights from ablation studies.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Address limitations of simplified opinion-dynamics models and unvalidated LLM-based simulations by grounding an LLM-based update in empirically observed network structure and agent attributes, enabling realistic, verifiable dynamics.

Method: Clone real-world Twitter networks; assign agent attributes (persona, emotions, centrality, stubbornness, influence); use Mistral-7B to update opinions based on memory and social exposure; validate on two datasets (COVID-19 discourse and US Election 2020) using MAE, structural alignment (Delta_r), and polarization dynamics (Delta_Var); conduct ablation studies.

Result: Framework reproduces opinion trajectories; reduces MAE by >50% relative to strongest classical baseline (MAE 0.150 for COVID-19 and 0.121 for US Election 2020); improved Delta_r (0.120, 0.180) and Delta_Var (0.106, 0.115); ablations show agent attributes, memory, and social exposure all contribute, with attributes being most critical.

Conclusion: Grounding Mistral-7B in empirically cloned interaction networks yields a realistic, validated simulation framework capable of reproducing complex social dynamics and polarization.

Abstract: The study of opinion dynamics in social networks is one of the key challenges in computational social science with direct relevance to understanding political polarization, misinformation, and health responses. Current approaches focus on simplified mathematical models that ignore linguistic and contextual factors related to belief updates or use Large Language Model (LLM)-based simulations that have not been validated against real data. We present a framework based on the concept of a digital twin to simulate opinion dynamics in social networks. The approach fills the gap by cloning a real-world Twitter network, assigns a set of attributes for agents (such as persona, emotions, centrality, stubbornness, and influence), and employs Mistral-7B to perform opinion update based on memory and social exposure. To evaluate the proposed approach, we validate it against two real Twitter datasets (COVID-19 discourse and U.S elections 2020). The results show that the capability of the proposed framework reproduces opinion trajectories and reduces individual prediction error by more than 50% compared to the best-performing classical baseline (Mistral-7B achieves Mean Absolute Error (MAE) = 0.150 and 0.121 on the COVID-19 and US Election 2020 datasets, respectively). We observe similar improvements in structural alignment (Delta_r = 0.120 and 0.180) and polarization dynamics (Delta_Var = 0.106 and 0.115) on the two datasets, respectively. Additionally, the ablation studies confirm that agent attributes, memory, and social exposure all contribute to the framework's predictive fidelity in reproducing opinion trajectories, with agent attributes being the most critical contributor. Overall, our results demonstrate that grounding Mistral-7B within empirically cloned interaction networks produces a realistic simulation framework capable of reproducing complex social dynamics.

</details>


### [143] [Amortizing Physics-Informed Neural Solvers via Graph Hypernetworks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.19915)
*Cheng Jing,Abhishek Verma,Kallol Bera,Yixuan He,Kookjin Lee*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Graph-based coefficient conditioning for amortizing physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) across related PDEs using an operator graph and a graph hypernetwork to initialize meta-trained PINNs; compares coefficient vectors, term‑set, and graph conditioning; graph conditioning improves adaptation, especially in coupled PDEs, though performance is problem-dependent.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Enable reusable, solver-like performance across related PDEs by making equation structure explicit and learnable, reducing reliance on labeled data for adaptation.

Method: Construct an operator graph with nodes for fields, derivatives, terms, residuals; retain coefficients as term attributes. Use a graph hypernetwork to generate diagonal codes to initialize a meta-trained factorized PINN for each target equation. Train using governing equations and prescribed conditions without solution labels. Compare coefficient-vector, DeepSets-based term-set, and graph conditioning under fixed adaptation budget across scalar convection-diffusion-reaction, two-field Fisher-KPP, and capacitively coupled plasma models.

Result: Term-based descriptors improve high-reaction accuracy in scalar CDR problems; in two-field Fisher-KPP, after 3,000 adaptation steps on unseen two-way coupling, the graph-conditioned model achieves mean final error 35.7% lower than term-set and 67.7% lower than coefficient-vector. In a fixed-structure capacitively coupled plasma model, the coefficient-vector method performs best.

Conclusion: Explicit equation relationships via operator graphs can enhance adapter performance for physics-based solvers, particularly in coupled systems, suggesting a productive direction beyond pure coefficient conditioning.

Abstract: Amortizing physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) across related PDEs requires describing each equation to a reusable solver. Coefficient vectors encode numerical parameters in predefined slots, leaving operator and cross-field assignments implicit. We make these relationships explicit in an operator graph, with nodes for fields, derivatives, terms, and residuals and coefficients retained as term attributes. A graph hypernetwork generates diagonal codes that initialize a meta-trained factorized PINN for each target equation. Meta-training and target-specific adaptation use governing equations and prescribed conditions without solution labels. We compare coefficient-vector, DeepSets-based term-set, and graph conditioning by solution accuracy within a fixed adaptation budget. In scalar convection-diffusion-reaction problems, both term-based descriptors improve high-reaction accuracy, with similar performance. In two-field Fisher-KPP, meta-training sees uncoupled and one-way systems; after 3,000 adaptation steps on unseen two-way coupling, the graph's mean final error is 35.7% below the term set and 67.7% below the coefficient vector. In a fixed-structure capacitively coupled plasma model, the coefficient vector performs best. These results support extending coefficient conditioning with explicit equation relationships for physics-based solver adaptation.

</details>


### [144] [One Intervention per Component is Enough: Towards Identifiability in Linear Stochastic Dynamics from Steady State](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.19955)
*Saber Salehkaleybar*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Identifiability and parameter recovery for multivariate Ornstein-Uhlenbeck processes from steady-state observational and interventional data using one intervention per strongly connected component (SCC), with a topological recursive algorithm and a regularized LS estimator; validated on simulated data.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Enable learning OU dynamics from snapshot data when time-series is unavailable, a common scenario in large perturbation studies (e.g., gene perturbations), by combining interventional and observational data.

Method: Theoretical identifiability: one intervention per SCC suffices to recover all OU parameters generically up to a global scaling factor, assuming the SCC condensation graph is connected with a single root and spectral nondegeneracy. A recursive algorithm orders SCCs topologically, isolates each component’s marginal dynamics, and solves a linear system from steady-state moment equations using upstream parameter estimates. A regularized least-squares estimator jointly minimizes residuals of steady-state mean and covariance equations across observational and interventional data.

Result: Identifiability up to a global scale under the stated conditions; a practical algorithmic procedure with proofs of concept; experimental validation on simulated data demonstrates recovery of OU parameters.

Conclusion: Contributes a framework to recover high-dimensional OU process parameters from non-time-series data by blending observational and interventional data, via a structured identifiability result, a topological recursive learning algorithm, and a regularized LS estimation approach. Limitations include scale ambiguity, reliance on SCC structure and spectral assumptions, and finite-sample considerations.

Abstract: We study the problem of recovering the parameters of a multivariate Ornstein-Uhlenbeck (OU) process from steady-state observational and interventional data. In many applications, such as large-scale gene perturbation experiments, only stationary "snapshot" measurements are available, making standard stochastic differential equation estimation methods that rely on time-series trajectories inapplicable. We first establish an identifiability result: one intervention per strongly connected component (SCC) of the drift graph suffices to recover all OU process parameters generically up to a global scaling factor. This holds provided that the SCC condensation graph is connected with a single root and certain spectral nondegeneracy assumptions hold. We propose a recursive learning algorithm that orders SCCs topologically and, for each component, isolates its marginal dynamics and solves a linear system derived from the steady-state moment equations, leveraging parameters recovered for upstream components. Building on this theoretical foundation, we propose a regularized least-squares estimator that jointly minimizes residuals of the steady-state mean and covariance equations across observational and interventional data. Experimental results validate our theoretical findings in recovering parameters of the underlying OU process.

</details>


### [145] [Graph-Based Stochastic Power-UCT: Monte-Carlo Graph Search with Power Mean Estimation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.19956)
*Tung Tran,Viet Bao Mai,Hoang Ta,Tuan Dam*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Graph-Based Stochastic-Power-UCT (GS-Power-UCT) shares states at the same planning depth in stochastic MDPs to reuse samples across different trajectories while maintaining depth-specific value estimates; with full-state variants and adaptive horizon, it achieves convergence to finite-horizon and infinite-horizon values; improved sample efficiency empirically.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Tree MCTS duplicates states across trajectories in stochastic MDPs, wasting samples; cycles and general stochastic MDPs require effective sample reuse and depth-aware evaluation.

Method: Introduce GS-Power-UCT that groups nodes by planning depth but keeps separate value estimates for each depth; prove root convergence to finite-horizon value at rate O(n^-1/2); develop GS-Power-UCT-F (one node per physical state) and GS-Power-UCT-F+ (adaptive horizon) to balance sample reuse and bias; analyze convergence to V*(s0) as cross-depth gap vanishes.

Result: The root estimate converges at rate O(n^-1/2); GS-Power-UCT-F and F+ have trade-offs with horizon mixing; F+ converges to optimal infinite-horizon discounted value when depth gaps collapse; experiments show improved sample efficiency vs tree-based and graph-based baselines on stochastic planning benchmarks.

Conclusion: Graph-based sharing in GS-Power-UCT yields better sample efficiency while preserving convergence guarantees; adaptive horizon can achieve optimal infinite-horizon value; practical relevance shown in benchmarks.

Abstract: Tree-based Monte-Carlo Tree Search (MCTS) duplicates the same state when it is reached through different trajectories, which can waste simulations in stochastic MDPs. We introduce Graph-Based Stochastic-Power-UCT (GS-Power-UCT), which shares states reached at the same planning depth while keeping separate values for states reached at different depths. This design applies to general stochastic MDPs, including problems with cycles. We prove that for a fixed planning horizon, the root estimate converges to the finite-horizon value at rate $O(n^{-1/2})$, matching tree-based Stochastic-Power-UCT while reusing samples across shared states. We also study two full-state variants: GS-Power-UCT-F, which stores one node per physical state to increase sample sharing but may mix values from different remaining horizons, and GS-Power-UCT-F$^+$, which uses an adaptive horizon to control this bias. The latter converges to $V^{\star}(s_0)$, the optimal infinite-horizon discounted value at the root state $s_0$, when the remaining cross-depth gap vanishes. Experiments on stochastic planning benchmarks show improved sample efficiency over tree-based and graph-based baselines.

</details>


### [146] [CellRFT: Reinforcement Fine-Tuning for Single-Cell Perturbation Modeling](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.19970)
*Jie Yan,Li Liu,Hanze Guo,Jiaxin Hu,Houxin He,Xiaoning Qi,Haoran Wang,Cong Li,Zhong-Yuan Zhang,Yong Wang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: CellRFT is a reinforcement learning–based fine-tuning framework that aligns training with biological evaluation criteria for perturbation predictions, using policy-gradient and hierarchical rewards to integrate multiple biological signals.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: There is a mismatch between surrogate optimization objectives and non-differentiable, biology-grounded evaluation metrics in single-cell perturbation modeling, hindering real predictive value.

Method: Policy-gradient reinforcement learning that optimizes non-differentiable biological evaluations; hierarchical reward aggregation to combine multiple biological rewards; adaptable to various pretrained models; code to be released.

Result: Improves perturbation prediction across pretrained models; reveals that optimizing a single biological criterion can have mixed effects on others; supplementary rewards can improve additional criteria; demonstrates how metrics shape model behavior and offers insight for evaluation design.

Conclusion: CellRFT provides direct biological-criteria-guided training, enhancing predictive performance and enabling analysis of metric interactions; supports broader evaluation-driven model development; code will be released.

Abstract: Predicting cellular responses to perturbations supports the study of gene function, disease mechanisms, and therapeutic strategies. Despite advances in single-cell perturbation modeling, existing models typically optimize surrogate losses that do not directly reflect the biological criteria used for evaluation, so better data fitting need not yield better biological predictions. To address this mismatch, we introduce \textbf{CellRFT}, a reinforcement fine-tuning framework that uses biological evaluation as direct training feedback. CellRFT uses policy-gradient optimization to learn from non-differentiable evaluations of generated cell populations and integrates multiple biological rewards through hierarchical reward aggregation. Comprehensive experiments demonstrate CellRFT's applicability across different pretrained models and effectiveness in improving perturbation prediction, reveal that optimizing one biological criterion can help or hinder others, and show that complementary rewards can improve criteria beyond those directly optimized, offering a way to probe how biological metrics shape model behavior, with the potential to inform evaluation design. Code will be made available.

</details>


### [147] [Past, Future, All at Once: Mitigating Stability-Plasticity Dilemma via Post-hoc JANUS Rectification](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.19985)
*Zhilong Zheng,Letian Tao,Yang Guan,Yujie Yang,Wei Xiong,Kehua Sheng,Bo Zhang,Jingliang Duan,Keqiang Li,Shengbo Eben Li*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: JANUS projects fine-tuning updates into the Jacobian null space to enforce parameter-space orthogonality, preserving historical performance while learning new tasks; a post-hoc, tuning-agnostic framework with adaptive rectification and efficiency optimizations.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Catastrophic forgetting during fine-tuning of foundation models; existing parameter-efficient approaches rely on restrictive subspace orthogonality and may not fully preserve prior knowledge. A post-hoc, tuning-agnostic method targeting first-order preservation is desirable.

Method: Post-hoc weight rectification that projects updates into the Jacobian Null Space (JANUS); Multi-step Adaptive Rectification using JANUS shifts to verify a valid trust region and adjust step sizes; ghost projection, ghost orientation comparison, and sequence-level SVD compression for efficiency; designed to be compatible with various fine-tuning methods.

Result: Empirical results show mitigation of forgetting while preserving adaptation to new tasks; improved stability-plasticity balance; reported gains in both historical knowledge retention and downstream performance with efficiency gains in time and space.

Conclusion: JANUS provides a general, tuning-agnostic framework for maintaining historical performance via parameter-space orthogonality (first-order preservation) while enabling effective fine-tuning; its techniques aim to be broadly compatible and computationally efficient.

Abstract: Fine-tuning foundation models on new tasks inevitably suffer from catastrophic forgetting. While existing works attempt to mitigate this on the basis of parameter-efficient fine-tuning methods, they adopted an overly restrictive Subspace Orthogonality condition. In this paper, we introduce a purely post-hoc and tuning-agnostic weight rectification framework that achieves Parameter Space Orthogonality, which is the necessary and sufficient condition for preserving historical performance to the first order. By projecting parameter updates into the JAcobian NUll Space (JANUS), our method significantly recovers compromised historical knowledge without interfering with the underlying fine-tuning process. To overcome the local validity of the Jacobian approximation, we further propose a Multi-step Adaptive Rectification mechanism that utilizes the JANUS shift to dynamically verify the valid trust region and adjust step sizes. Coupled with our proposed ghost projection, ghost orientation comparison, and sequence-level singular value decomposition compression techniques, JANUS also achieves great temporal and spatial efficiency. Experiments demonstrate that JANUS seamlessly integrates with various fine-tuning methods, significantly mitigating the stability-plasticity dilemma by recovering historical knowledge while preserving downstream task adaptation.

</details>


### [148] [EPIG-Tree: Compute-Optimal Branching for Gradient-Efficient Reinforcement Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20004)
*Nikita Khomich,Leopold Hermansson,Ido Hakimi*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: EPIG-Tree proposes a principled compute-allocation for policy-gradient rollouts by branching where it most reduces gradient uncertainty per compute, yielding two laws and improved gradient estimation across RL benchmarks and LLM settings.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current GRPO collapses trajectories into a single reward; this is compute-inefficient for credit assignment given multiple decision points and environmental randomness. A variance-based, tree-structured rollout can allocate compute where it most reduces gradient uncertainty.
