Method: Derive from law-of-total-variance. Two allocation laws: (1) new branches reduce decision uncertainty; (2) repeated suffix rollouts reduce continuation uncertainty. Introduce EPIG-Tree score that uses occupancy- and score-weighted value uncertainty. Branch placement follows n_e ∝ w_e ||∇_θ log π(a_e|h_e)|| σ_e / √c_e, using rollouts already computed. Applied to cloned-state control and LLM gradient calibration; evaluated across diverse tasks.

Result: EPIG reduces gradient MSE in cloned-state control, wins in all nine dense continuous-control environments and recovers reference gradient direction. Improves frozen-LLM gradient calibration vs entropy branching. In online single-turn math, tree-local credit beats flat GRPO; in online multi-turn Wordle, EPIG attains the highest final win rate (0.850), surpassing flat GRPO (0.790) and entropy branching as training proceeds.

Conclusion: Tree-based, variance-guided rollout branching yields more efficient gradient estimation and policy optimization. The allocation laws justify branching where it most reduces gradient uncertainty per compute, with empirical gains across control tasks and language-model settings. It demonstrates that targeted branching, not just broader uncertainty, drives performance and scalability.

Abstract: Reward-based reinforcement learning for language models, exemplified by Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO), collapses an entire stochastic trajectory into a single scalar reward. This is clean and scalable, but it explores and allocates reward inefficiently: a trajectory may contain many causal decisions, recovery attempts, and environment-randomness events, yet every token or action inherits one trajectory-level advantage. We study tree-based rollout construction as a compute-allocation problem for policy-gradient estimation. Our central claim is that branches should be placed not where the policy is merely uncertain, but where an additional branch most reduces uncertainty about the policy gradient per unit of compute. From a law-of-total-variance decomposition of the local policy-gradient random variable, we derive two allocation laws: new branches reduce decision uncertainty, while repeated suffix rollouts reduce continuation uncertainty. The resulting EPIG-Tree score allocates branches using the already computed rollouts. It estimates occupancy- and score-weighted value uncertainty, along with a suffix law $n_e \propto w_e \|\nabla_θ\log π(a_e|h_e)\| σ_e / \sqrt{c_e}$. Empirically, EPIG reduces gradient MSE in cloned-state control, winning in all nine dense continuous-control environments of a 13-environment sweep and recovering the reference gradient direction near-perfectly, and it improves frozen-LLM gradient calibration relative to entropy branching. In online single-turn math, tree-local credit beats flat GRPO, while branch placement is secondary to token-level credit assignment. In online multi-turn Wordle, EPIG attains the highest final win rate (0.850), overtaking flat GRPO, which saturates early at 0.790, and entropy branching as training proceeds, confirming that the gradient-estimation advantage transfers to a stateful, large-action setting.

</details>


### [149] [Dynamic Generalized Gromov-Wasserstein Optimal Transport](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20008)
*Junda Ying,Zhiwei Zeng,Peijie Zhou,Lei Zhang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: TP-DATE introduces Travelling Pair Dynamical Alignment and Trajectory Estimation, a simulation-free dynamic extension of Gromov-Wasserstein OT for reconstructing tissue trajectories in spatial transcriptomics, using static/dynamic Quadratic-form OT and travelling-pair flow matching to improve structure preservation and 3D trajectory reconstruction.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Static GW-OT captures structure-aware alignment but lacks a general dynamic formulation for reconstructing continuous trajectories in spatial transcriptomics; a dynamic framework is needed to preserve tissue structure while matching expression patterns.

Method: Propose TP-DATE as a dynamic GW-OT framework; formulate a broad class of static and dynamic Quadratic-form OT via path actions and prove static–dynamic equivalence; develop travelling-pair flow matching to allow interacting conditional paths and marginalize their interactions into a single vector field.

Result: On synthetic and real spatial transcriptomics data, TP-DATE better preserves spatial structure and improves continuous 3D dynamics reconstruction.

Conclusion: TP-DATE provides a unified dynamic OT framework that extends GW-OT to dynamic trajectory reconstruction, enabling more accurate tissue dynamics modeling and improved structure-aware analysis in spatial transcriptomics.

Abstract: Gromov--Wasserstein optimal transport (GW-OT) extends classical optimal transport by introducing structure-aware transport cost. This is particularly relevant for spatial transcriptomics, where dynamical reconstruction should preserve tissue structure in addition to matching expression patterns. While static formulations have been widely used for such structure-aware alignment, a general dynamic formulation for reconstructing continuous trajectories is still missing. We introduce Travelling Pair Dynamical Alignment and Trajectory Estimation (TP-DATE), a theoretical and computational framework to generalize GW-OT dynamically in a simulation-free manner. We formulate a broad class of static and dynamic Quadratic-form OT (QOT) through path actions and prove the static dynamic equivalence. We further develop travelling-pair flow matching, which allows interacting conditional paths and marginalizes their interactions into a single vector field. On synthetic and real spatial transcriptomics data, TP-DATE better preserves spatial structure and improves continuous 3D dynamics reconstruction.

</details>


### [150] [Correct Now, Insufficient Later: Auditing Update Sufficiency in Context Compression](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20045)
*Guangzhe Zhang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A paired-history audit reveals that an AI memory can give the correct current answer while discarding details needed for later updates; the paper develops a structured diagnostic methodology and reports a pilot with multiple mechanisms, memory conditions, and model backends, showing several failure modes and limited effectiveness of a proposed repair.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To diagnose and quantify how memory updates affect correctness across time, and to separate retained-state adequacy, response delivery, and answer-schema conformity in order to identify robust failure modes and guide repair strategies.

Method: A pilot study using paired-history pairs (24 pairs) across six synthetic memory mechanisms, 12 memory conditions, two repeats, and two model backends. It employs: (i) a deterministic frontier selector for strict reveal accuracy; (ii) a structured writer for memory composition; (iii) a four-outcome joint contrast with finite-sample identification intervals; (iv) a record-level audit to decompose performance into retained-state adequacy, response delivery, and answer-schema compliance; (v) systematic perturbations (tombstone removal, identifier renaming); (vi) a label-equivariant repair attempt; and (vii) separate offline tests and retrospectives, with no independent held-out validation claimed.

Result: Key results include: frontier reveal accuracy of 96/96 on DeepSeek and 82/96 on GLM; structured writer achieving 62 successes with one unresolved and 56/96; finite-sample identification intervals [0.521,0.542] and [0.292,0.313]; record-level audit finding 26 semantically wrong but well-formed structured memories and 25 such cases; GLM frontier failures hid correct values in incorrect wrappers; tombstone removal caused 16/16 exact replay failures; identifier renaming reduced late-reference adequacy from 8/8 to 94/320; label-equivariant repair preserved only 2/8 late-reference answers; overall, results suggest scoped evaluation and reproducible failure analysis rather than general superiority of the repaired method.

Conclusion: The study validates a scoped evaluation methodology for diagnosing memory-update failures and demonstrates specific failure modes and repair limitations. It emphasizes the need for more extensive, natural-task validation and independent held-out testing to generalize findings.

Abstract: A memory can answer a current query correctly while discarding distinctions required by a later update. We investigate this failure with a paired-history audit: two histories have the same current answer, receive a shared future update, and require different subsequent answers. A pilot evaluates 24 history pairs across six synthetic mechanisms, 12 memory conditions, two repeats, and two model backends. A deterministic frontier selector obtains strict reveal accuracy of 96/96 on DeepSeek and 82/96 on GLM; a structured writer obtains 62 successes with one unresolved outcome and 56/96. The configured four-outcome joint contrast has finite-sample identification intervals of [0.521, 0.542] and [0.292, 0.313], not confidence intervals. A record-level audit distinguishes retained-state adequacy, response delivery, and answer-schema compliance without changing those original scores. It finds 26 and 25 well-formed but semantically wrong structured reveal memories, while all 14 GLM frontier reveal failures contain correct values in the wrong wrapper. Tombstone removal produces 16/16 exact replay failures in the targeted mechanism. Identifier renaming then exposes a separate flaw: original frontier late-reference adequacy falls from 8/8 to 94/320 transformed instances. We provide and test a label-equivariant repair, but it preserves only 2/8 original late-reference answers: eliminating a naming shortcut does not solve unknown future relevance. These results support a scoped evaluation methodology and reproducible failure analysis, not general superiority of the repaired algorithm. Paid pilot evidence, retrospective diagnostics, and new offline tests are reported separately; no independent held-out or natural-task validation is claimed.

</details>


### [151] [Evaluating Explanation Methods by the Predictors They Induce](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20058)
*Jacob Selbæk,Hugo L. Hammer*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Proposes a fidelity-based test for explanations: convert an explanation into a predictor by summing feature effects and check if it can reproduce a model's predictions on unseen data, without fitting. Applies to PDP, ALE, SHAP, LIME; shows additive PDP is optimal under feature independence, but fails with dependence; empirical results show SHAP or PDP depending on feature dependence; paradoxical findings where some metrics favor damaged explanations.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current explanation quality criteria are hard to compare across methods. A direct, falsifiable test is needed to judge whether an explanation truly approximates how a model uses its features.

Method: Transform each explanation into an additive predictor by aggregating per-feature effects. No parameter fitting is performed. Evaluate the predictor's ability to reproduce the model's predictions on held-out data. Apply to PDP, ALE, SHAP, and LIME. Provide theoretical results about summing PDP under feature independence and empirical results across 13 real datasets, 9 synthetic designs, 4 model families.

Result: The evaluation reveals that method rankings depend on feature dependence: with independent features SHAP is slightly worse than PDP, but on dependent real data SHAP performs best. Several widely used quality metrics can even prefer damaged explanations to intact ones.

Conclusion: Explanation quality is context-dependent, governed by feature dependence. The proposed test helps compare explanations in a model-agnostic way, but effectiveness varies with data structure; caution is needed when selecting explanation methods and evaluating them.

Abstract: Explanations of machine learning models are usually judged by criteria that are hard to compare. We propose a simpler test: if an explanation really describes how a model uses its features, it should be possible to rebuild the model's predictions from it. We turn each explanation into a predictor by reading each feature's effect and adding them up, and measure how well that predictor reproduces the model on unseen data. Nothing is fitted, so the score reflects the explanation itself. The test applies to any explanation that can be written as a function of the features; we demonstrate it on partial dependence plots (PDP), accumulated local effects (ALE), SHAP and LIME. We prove that summing partial dependence curves gives the best possible additive summary of a model when its features are independent, and that this fails when they are dependent. Across 13 real datasets and 9 synthetic designs and four model families, which method scores best depends entirely on feature dependence: where features are independent SHAP is slightly worse than PDP, exactly as the theory predicts; on dependent real data SHAP leads. Some widely used quality metrics even prefer a damaged explanation to an intact one.

</details>


### [152] [MATCH: Model-Aware Tool Learning with Curriculum Scheduling and Hierarchically Gated Rewards](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20082)
*Shihao Liu,Hao Yin,Lijun Liu,Zhengzong Chen,Yuanyuan Zhao,Fei Huang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: MATCH is a closed-loop tool-learning framework for LLMs that jointly learns tool use with model-aware curriculum scheduling and hierarchically gated rewards, addressing misaligned curricula and credit leakage in RL tool-learning. It achieves state-of-the-art results on API-Bank and BFCL V3 and generalizes across multiple backbones.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current RL-based tool-learning suffers from fixed-threshold curricula that fail to track the policy's evolving capability, and additive rewards that miscredit when tool predictions are wrong. There is a need for a framework that aligns sample difficulty with the policy and provides granular credit at tool-name, argument key, and value levels.

Method: MATCH introduces Model-Aware Curriculum Learning (MACL), which co-evolves reward-derived sample difficulty with the policy and selects samples near the current capability boundary together with a top-k pool of harder cases each epoch. It also proposes Hierarchical Tool-call Gated Reward (HTGR), which scores tool name, argument key, and argument value as a gated chain and grants credit at each level only when prerequisites hold. The HTGR rewards drive both GRPO updates and MACL's difficulty refresh, creating a closed loop between policy optimization and sample scheduling.

Result: Empirical results show MATCH achieving 72.19% overall accuracy on API-Bank and 62.87% on BFCL V3, outperforming supervised and RL-based baselines. Additional backbone experiments indicate consistent improvements across four backbones from two model families.

Conclusion: The proposed MATCH framework effectively closes the loop between policy optimization and sample scheduling, enabling robust, model-aware tool learning that generalizes across backbones and improves tool-use performance over existing baselines.

Abstract: Tool learning enables large language models (LLMs) to use external tools for tasks beyond parametric knowledge. Reinforcement learning can optimize tool-call behavior from feedback, but current methods still face two problems: fixed-threshold curricula can become misaligned with the policy's evolving capability boundary, and additive rewards can leak argument-level credit when the predicted tool is wrong. To address these problems, we propose MATCH, a closed-loop framework for model-aware tool learning with curriculum scheduling and hierarchically gated rewards. Model-Aware Curriculum Learning (MACL) maintains reward-derived sample difficulty that co-evolves with the policy, and each epoch selects samples near the current capability boundary together with a top-k pool of harder cases. Hierarchical Tool-call Gated Reward (HTGR) scores tool name, argument key, and argument value as a gated chain, granting credit at each level only when prerequisites hold. The same HTGR rewards drive both GRPO updates and MACL's difficulty refresh, closing the loop between policy optimization and sample scheduling. On API-Bank and BFCL V3, MATCH reaches 72.19% and 62.87% overall accuracy, outperforming the main supervised and RL-based baselines. Backbone experiments further show consistent improvements across four backbones from two model families.

</details>


### [153] [SETTer: Sparse-Encoder Transformer for Long-term Multivariate Time Series Forecasting](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20086)
*Abraham Ezema,Chijioke Eze,Ferdinanda Ponci,Antonello Monti*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: SETTer is a transformer-based model for long-term multivariate time series forecasting that uses decoupled self-attention and hybrid masking to capture short- and long-term temporal and channel patterns, with explainable structures; a single-layer transformer suffices and it outperforms SOTA in 88% of tested scenarios.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Long-term multivariate forecasting faces high dimensionality and complex dependencies; vanilla transformers struggle with oversmoothing, limited capacity, and opacity; need architectures that capture temporal/channel patterns and provide interpretability.

Method: Proposes SETTer with decoupled self-attention and hybrid masking; integrates simple explainable structures; demonstrates that a single-layer transformer can model long-range dependencies effectively in varying data complexities.

Result: Extensive experiments on real-world benchmarks show SETTer outperforms state-of-the-art models in 88% of scenarios.

Conclusion: SETTer achieves strong long-term dependency modeling with a compact architecture and built-in interpretability, offering robust performance across diverse datasets.

Abstract: Long-term multivariate time series plays a significant role in many application areas such as power systems, trading, etc. However, their accurate prediction is quite difficult for conventional forecasting methods as they often exhibit high dimensionality and complex relationships. Recent works show that transformer-based approaches are quite effective for long-term forecasting thanks to their attention mechanism. However, in the presence of complex high-dimensional inputs, they show evidence of oversmoothing, limited capacity, and opacity. To this end, this paper introduces SETTer, a transformer-based model that addresses these challenges by incorporating novel techniques for decoupled self-attention and hybrid masking. The proposed techniques enable SETTer to effectively capture the dominant short- and long-term patterns across the temporal and channel dimensions. In addition, we enrich the model layers with simple explainable structures that indicate the discriminative pattern of SETTer. We show that with a single-layer transformer architecture, SETTer can effectively model long-term dependencies in the presence of varying data complexities. Extensive experiments on real-word benchmark datasets for long-term multivariate time series forecasting demonstrate that SETTer outperforms state-of-the-art models in 88% of the scenarios.

</details>


### [154] [CARE-VI: Conservative Adaptive Reliability Estimation for Value Improvement in Off-Policy Actor-Critic Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20098)
*Xiang Zou,Shengzhu Shi,Junqi Gao,Zhichang Guo*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: CARE-VI is an evidence-regulated TD target construction framework for off-policy actor-critic learning, combining Conservative Adaptive Ranking and Screening (CARS), Selector-Evaluator Value Assessment (SEVA), and Dynamic Adaptive Risk-aware Enhancement (DARE). It bounds boundary errors and overestimation, recovers to fixed policy, and improves performance across SAC/TD3/TD7 on MuJoCo.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Temporal-difference targets in off-policy actor-critic RL are fragile due to noisy action rankings, bias from reused scores, and fixed enhancement weights. Robust, adaptive, and risk-aware target construction is needed to improve reliability without compromising interfaces.

Method: CARS preserves an ordered candidate prefix within a budget and narrows when the boundary gap exceeds a scaled uncertainty radius. SEVA uses selector critics to order candidates and a separate evaluator critic to review and cap the value at the selector reference. DARE adjusts each residual correction based on candidate reliability, the gap between selector and evaluator, and a finite-stage factor. Together, CARE-VI maintains standard critic regression and actor update interfaces.

Result: Theoretical bounds on CARS boundary error, SEVA overestimation, and DARE residual deviation; fixed-policy recovery after finite perturbation. Empirically, across SAC, TD3, TD7 on four MuJoCo tasks, CARE-VI achieves the highest mean return in all twelve settings; ablations and diagnostics corroborate component roles.

Conclusion: CARE-VI offers improved target reliability while preserving algorithm interfaces, enabling stable learning with evidence-regulated TD targets; demonstrated robustness and superior performance on standard benchmarks.

Abstract: Reliable temporal-difference targets are central to off-policy actor-critic learning. Direct value improvement refines the next-state target with alternative actions, but the reliability of this refinement depends on how candidate actions are ranked, reviewed, and weighted. Noisy rankings may force premature candidate commitment, reusing selection scores may bias target valuation, and fixed enhancement weights may amplify weak evidence. To address these risks, we develop Conservative Adaptive Ranking and Screening (CARS), which retains an ordered candidate prefix within a preset budget and narrows it only when the observed boundary gap exceeds a disagreement-scaled uncertainty radius. Selector-Evaluator Value Assessment (SEVA) uses selector critics to order candidates and a separately parameterized evaluator critic to review the selected value, then caps the reviewed value at the selector reference. Dynamic Adaptive Risk-aware Enhancement (DARE) then regulates each residual correction using candidate reliability, the gap between selector and evaluator signals, and a finite stage factor. Together, CARS, SEVA, and DARE form CARE-VI, an evidence-regulated target construction framework that preserves the backbone interfaces for critic regression and actor updates. The analysis bounds the CARS boundary error, the SEVA selected-value overestimation, and the one-sided deviation of the DARE residual displacement from its population counterpart, and establishes fixed-policy recovery after the finite-stage perturbation ends. Experiments with SAC, TD3, and TD7 on four MuJoCo tasks show that CARE-VI achieves the highest mean return in all twelve settings. Grouped ablations and scalar diagnostics support the roles of the three components in improving target reliability.

</details>


### [155] [QoS-Aware Federated Learning for Multimodal In-Cabin Interaction in Smart Vehicles](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20123)
*Baran Can Gül,Mert Nakıp,Nasser Jazdi,Michael Weyrich*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: FedQoS is an asynchronous, event-triggered Federated Learning framework for autonomous/connected vehicles that decouples local computation from global communication using two gating phases. It aims to handle heterogeneous QoS constraints in vehicular networks while preserving safety and efficiency.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Standard FL with synchronous rounds fails under heterogeneous and time-varying QoS constraints in rich multimodal vehicular environments, risking safety, energy depletion, and inefficiency. There is a need for an FL scheme that adapts to network/resource variability.

Method: FedQoS introduces a two-phase gating mechanism: (1) a resource-aware training gate that starts local learning only when sensing buffers and energy reserves meet safety thresholds, and (2) a QoS-aware transmission gate that uploads updates based on an efficiency score balancing model novelty, latency, and energy. Locally, clients optimize a staleness-aware proximal objective that modulates the global anchor strength with update age.

Result: Empirical evaluation on multimodal vehicular datasets shows FedQoS achieves competitive personalized accuracy with only mild accuracy loss compared to FedAvg, while substantially reducing QoS violations, cutting communication overhead by 76.7% and lowering latency cost by 26.0%.

Conclusion: FedQoS provides a practical, asynchronous FL framework for real-world vehicular deployments, delivering strong accuracy-efficiency trade-offs by dynamically gating computation and communication to respect QoS constraints.

Abstract: Modern smart vehicles leverage multimodal sensors, ranging from high-bandwidth vision systems to low-rate physiological monitors, to provide personalized in-cabin services. However, integrating high-fidelity multimodal fusion with collaborative training is often hindered by the heterogeneous and time-varying Quality of Service (QoS) constraints of vehicular networks. Standard Federated Learning (FL) approaches enforce rigid synchronous rounds that fail to account for these resource asymmetries, leading to safety-critical timing violations and energy exhaustion. In this paper, we propose FedQoS, a novel asynchronous, event-triggered FL framework that decouples local computation from global communication via a two-phase gating mechanism. First, we introduce a resource-aware training gate that initializes local learning only when sensing buffers and energy reserves meet safety thresholds, preventing ML tasks from compromising core vehicle mobility. Second, a QoS-aware transmission policy gates uplink updates based on an efficiency score that balances model novelty against instantaneous latency and energy costs. Locally, clients optimize an objective featuring a staleness-aware proximal term that dynamically adjusts the global anchor strength based on update age. Extensive experiments on multimodal vehicular datasets demonstrate that FedQoS achieves competitive personalized accuracy with only marginal performance loss compared to FedAvg, while substantially reducing QoS violations, cutting communication overhead by 76.7\%, and lowering latency cost by 26.0\%, demonstrating a highly favorable accuracy and efficiency balance for real-world vehicular deployments.

</details>


### [156] [Local Sparsity Enables Unsupervised LLM Safety Detection](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20129)
*Xin Chen,Gil Kur,Alexander Shevchenko,Andreas Krause*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Locally masked SAE-based anomaly detection in concept space under LRH enables deployment-time LLM safety with minimal calibration data and computation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Supervised safety methods rely on unsafe data and struggle to cover emerging harms; high-dimensional LLM activations raise feasibility concerns for anomaly detection. The LRH with local sparsity offers a promising, data-efficient path to detect out-of-distribution (OOD) inputs for safety.

Method: Recover a concept space via a sparse autoencoder (SAE) under the linear representation hypothesis (LRH); leverage local sparsity (nearby points share a small active support) to design a locally masked SAE-based anomaly detector; provide theoretical justification; validate across architectures and safety/capability datasets; use 1% OOD data for calibration to improve performance.

Result: Empirical validation on multiple architectures/datasets shows the framework detects safety-relevant anomalies effectively; with 1% OOD calibration data, performance approaches near-optimal, and only 1–2% of SAE neurons are needed for computation.

Conclusion: Locally sparse SAE-based anomaly detection under LRH is a viable, efficient deployment-time safety strategy for LLMs, capable of extracting meaningful safety signals with limited calibration data and modest computational cost.

Abstract: Deployment-time safety methods for large language models (LLMs) are predominantly supervised and assume access to unsafe training data. Nevertheless, new attacks and harm categories regularly arise, not captured by models trained in such a supervised fashion. An alternative approach is to view this problem through the lens of anomaly detection, namely, to rely solely on modeling safe data and flagging out-of-distribution inputs. However, LLM activations lie in a high-dimensional space, raising concerns about whether anomaly detection is statistically feasible. We show that, under the linear representation hypothesis (LRH), there may indeed be hope. In the LRH concept space, which is typically recovered via a sparse autoencoder (SAE), nearby points share a small common active support. Using this local sparsity insight, we propose a framework for locally masked SAE-based anomaly detection, supported by theoretical justifications. We validate it on various architectures and datasets, including both capability-testing datasets and safety-specific datasets. Finally, when we allow algorithms to use 1% out-of-distribution data for calibration, locally sparse methods achieve near-optimal performance, demonstrating their ability to capture meaningful safety information while using only 1-2% of SAE neurons for computation.

</details>


### [157] [Fast-varying Natural Frequencies and Damping Ratio Identification for Linear Time-Varying System](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20138)
*Melisa Bozaci,Alice Cicirello*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Physics-informed ML framework combining LSTM and EKF for fast-varying LTV system identification, validated on wind-turbine FEM data; robust to damping mis-spec and capable of damping and frequency estimation with improved methods over SSI.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Identify time-varying modal parameters (natural frequencies and damping) of LTV systems under changing operating conditions, where conventional methods struggle due to rapid changes and limited physics-data integration.

Method: Integrate a long short-term memory (LSTM) network with an Extended Kalman Filter (EKF). Use displacement/velocity data, physics-based frequency-time dependency models, and domain knowledge of modal damping. Train models on EKF-estimated data and on physics-based data. Validate on synthetic FEM data of a 2-blade offshore wind turbine under realistic environmental/operating conditions. Extend to damping ratio identification via grid search; compare with covariance-driven stochastic subspace identification (SSI).

Result: Accurate identification of the FA-1 mode natural frequency with RMSE up to 0.0012 Hz. EKF-estimate-trained models are sensitive to damping values, whereas physics-based-data-trained models show robustness to damping mismatches. Damping identification via grid search yields good approximations, outperforming SSI in certain aspects.

Conclusion: A physics-enhanced ML approach that fuses data-driven and physics-based models can reliably identify fast-varying modal parameters in LTV systems, with robustness to damping uncertainty and improved damping estimation via grid search over EKF-driven estimates.

Abstract: This work proposes a physics-enhanced machine learning approach for the system identification of Linear Time-Varying (LTV) systems under time-varying operating conditions in terms of fast-varying natural frequencies and damping ratios by combining a long short-term memory network with an Extended Kalman Filter (EKF). The proposed approach uses vibration data (displacement and velocity measurements), domain knowledge of modal damping ratios, and a physics-based model that can yield an approximate natural frequencies time-dependency model. The approach is validated using synthetic data generated from a finite element model of a 2-blade offshore wind turbine under realistic environmental and operating conditions. This system displays fast time-varying frequencies due to operating conditions, whose identification is particularly challenging because of the wind and wave loading. The robustness of the proposed approach is assessed under assumed incorrect system information (e.g. damping ratio). The proposed approach is evaluated across different environmental and operating conditions to show its applicability to different operating regimes. The results show the approach can accurately identify the selected fast-varying natural frequency, 1st Fore-Aft (FA-1) mode, with a maximum root mean square error of 0.0012 Hz. The results demonstrate that the model trained on EKF estimates depends on accurate damping values, whereas the model trained on physics-based data exhibits robustness to incorrect damping assumptions. The approach is extended to damping ratio identification for the selected mode by estimating the root mean square error between models trained on EKF estimates and physics-based data. The results show that the approach can yield a good approximation of the FA-1 mode damping ratio using grid search, offering an improvement over covariance-driven stochastic subspace identification.

</details>


### [158] [QUALS: Corpus Equilibrium for Universal Forecasting via Pattern Quantization and Learnability Synchronization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20156)
*Yujie Li,Zezhi Shao,Chengqing Yu,Yisong Fu,Weijie Zhu,Yifan Du,Jilin Hu,Bin Yang,Yongjun Xu,Fei Wang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR:  QUALS is a data-centric framework for time-series pre-training that improves data efficiency by quantizing patterns and synchronizing learnability across heterogeneous motifs, yielding superior zero-shot forecasting with less data.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current work on foundation models for time series emphasizes architectural innovations but neglects data diversity and sampling strategies, leading to inefficient use of training data and suboptimal performance.

Method: Pattern quantization: vector quantization and uniform binning to extract and encode heterogeneous patterns from mixed corpora. Learnability synchronization: calibrates sampling weights for different patterns to bridge optimization gaps between simple and complex motifs, enhancing training efficiency.

Result: Extensive benchmarks show that pre-training on QUALS achieves superior zero-shot performance while using a substantially reduced training budget.

Conclusion: QUALS demonstrates a data-centric path to improve the efficiency of time-series foundation-model pre-training, enabling superior zero-shot capabilities with much less data and highlighting the importance of pattern-aware sampling and representation learning.

Abstract: Ubiquitous time series data across diverse domains enables critical applications in areas such as transportation systems and power grids. Recently, training foundation models on massive datasets to achieve accurate zero-shot forecasting has emerged as a major research focus. However, current studies predominantly prioritize architectural innovations while insufficiently addressing data diversity, often relying on simple data sampling strategies that fail to manage complex data distributions effectively, leading to inefficient use of training data and suboptimal performance. To address this, we propose QUALS, a large-scale time series corpus equilibrium framework. QUALS significantly enhances data efficiency, i.e., enabling existing models to achieve superior performance using only a small fraction of the original training data. Specifically, QUALS operates through two core mechanisms. First, a pattern quantization framework systematically decodes heterogeneous patterns from mixed corpora via vector quantization and uniform binning. Second, a learnability synchronization framework calibrates sampling weights for heterogeneous patterns, bridging the optimization gap between simple and complex motifs to maximize overall training efficiency. Extensive benchmarks demonstrate that pre-training on QUALS consistently achieves superior zero-shot performance, even under substantially reduced training budgets.

</details>


### [159] [A Noise Optimum in Rehearsal-Free Continual Learning: Isolation, Mechanism, and Scope](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20162)
*Gunner Levi Howe*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Inverted-U retention with stochastic noise in continual learning; optimum arises from coherent restoring toward consolidated weights, not random directions; coupling the anchor gain to the noise variance (sigma^2) captures most of the optimum; optimum requires shared task structure and degrades with more tasks; the claims are based on simulations across common benchmarks, with a BrainScaleS-2 example reported separately; exponent and precise governing quantity remain open.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Understand what drives the nonmonotonic effect of injected noise on memory retention in continual learning, and map the conditions under which this optimum occurs, using simulations.

Method: Simulated continual-learning experiments across Split-MNIST, Fashion-MNIST, and Yin-Yang. Compare a magnitude-matched ladder to isolate directionality effects; implement a one-line rule coupling anchor gain to sigma^2; perform a forced Ornstein-Uhlenbeck analysis to derive the rising flank; analyze barrier-conditioning via the Doob h-transform; test permuted MNIST and rotated-vs-permuted controls to localize the role of task structure; reference a separate single-seed BrainScaleS-2 demonstration.

Result: The retention curve shows an inverted-U as noise variance increases. Optimum retention requires coherent shifting toward consolidated weights; random-direction noise with identical magnitude yields no optimum and can harm if directed wrong. Most of the optimum is recovered when the anchor gain is coupled to noise variance (sigma^2), a simple rule not captured by fixed Ornstein-Uhlenbeck adaptation or MESU. A forced OU calculation explains the rising flank and predicts optimal noise grows with per-task interference g; a Doob-h transform barrier bounds forgetting when coupling is too weak. The optimum exists only with shared task structure (absent on permuted MNIST) and is attenuated as the number of tasks increases; a compact-group identity rules out rotation-based explanations. A BrainScaleS-2 single-seed demonstration cited separately supports the originating rule; no hardware claims here.

Conclusion: The nonmonotonic retention effect stems from coherent consolidation dynamics under stochastic perturbation, and a simple coupling between anchor gain and noise variance captures the majority of the optimum within a simulation-based regime. The boundary conditions depend on task structure; precise governing quantity and exact exponent remain open questions, inviting further theoretical refinement and hardware-validated testing.

Abstract: Injecting stochastic noise into a consolidation rule can improve a network's retention of earlier tasks up to an optimal level, then degrade it -- an inverted-U in retention vs. noise. This paper isolates what produces that optimum and maps where it holds, entirely in simulation. (1) Phenomenon: the retention inverted-U appears on several related-task continual-learning benchmarks (Split-MNIST, FashionMNIST, continual Yin-Yang). (2) Isolation: a magnitude-matched ladder shows the effect requires coherent restoring toward the consolidated weights -- a random-direction force of identical magnitude produces no optimum, and a coherent force toward the wrong target actively hurts. (3) Active ingredient: most of the optimum is recovered by coupling the anchor gain to the injected-noise variance sigma^2 -- a one-line rule that neither Ornstein-Uhlenbeck Adaptation (fixed gain) nor MESU (posterior-variance gain) implements. A forced Ornstein-Uhlenbeck calculation derives the rising flank and predicts that the optimal noise rises with per-task interference g -- confirmed out-of-sample in direction against pre-existing measurements (the exponent is unresolved at our grid). The barrier-conditioning of the originating Doob h-transform is a low-sigma safety net that bounds forgetting where the coupled gain is too weak. (4) Scope: the optimum requires shared task structure -- it is absent on permuted-MNIST, and a controlled rotated-vs-permuted comparison localizes the boundary to task structure; the precise governing quantity is left open. (5) Length: at matched severity the advantage persists but attenuates with task count, and we show no rotation family can attribute the trend (a compact-group identity). A single-seed BrainScaleS-2 demonstration of the originating rule is reported separately (Howe, arXiv:2607.06924); this paper makes no hardware claim.

</details>


### [160] [Small Enough to Know Everything: The Fully-Enumerable Transformer as an Instrument for the Science of Delayed Generalization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20166)
*Yoshiyuki Ootani*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Tiny fully-enumerable transformers enable exact measurement of generalization ceilings and enable controlled manipulation of a single structural variable across scale; some task-side laws persist across 4,000x scale, while weight-decay relationships change with scale.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To investigate whether task-side generalization laws observed in small-scale grokking hold across large parameter regimes, using a fully-enumerable experimental regime as a scientific instrument for precise, repeatable study.

Method: Train very small transformers on fully-enumerable tasks. For each task, measure exact generalization ceilings, perform task surgeries that alter one variable while fixing others, observe every weight, and collect survival-time statistics across many seeds. Conduct a preregistered conservation study across scales (12K, 1M, 50M parameters) with identical protocols (360 runs plus 44-run control). Test three laws: recoverability-ceiling law, role-conflict delay law, weight-decay response law. Use Holm corrections, Spearman rho, and permutation p-values to assess conservation.

Result: The ceiling law and delay law are conserved across scales (0/144 Holm-corrected ceiling violations; Spearman rho ≥ 0.75 at all scales, permutation p < 1e-4). The weight-decay law deforms with scale, steepening as models get larger. Controls show the 50M role-conflict deficit persists despite learning-rate adjustment and budget increase. One deforming law would have failed the preregistered test if criteria frozen differently.

Conclusion: Fully-enumerable transformers offer a model-organism platform for studying the task-side laws of delayed generalization. Larger models largely obey the observed laws, and deviations are themselves lawful and measurable, providing precise insights into how generalization and grokking scale with parameter count.

Abstract: Tiny transformers trained on fully-enumerable tasks occupy an unusual position in the study of grokking: every input can be evaluated, every generalization ceiling can be computed exactly, and hundreds of seeds cost minutes. We argue this regime is a scientific instrument with four capabilities that approximate settings cannot offer: (a) exact, falsifiable generalization ceilings; (b) task surgery that manipulates one structural variable while provably fixing all others; (c) direct observation of every weight; and (d) survival-time statistics over many seeds that recast "does not grok" as a censored observation. The obvious objection is that laws characterized at 10^4 parameters may not mean anything beyond them. We answer it with a preregistered conservation study: three task-side laws established at 12K parameters -- a recoverability-ceiling law, a role-conflict delay law, and a weight-decay response law -- are re-measured under an identical from-scratch protocol at 12K, 1M, and 50M parameters (a 4,000x span; 360 runs plus a 44-run control arm). The ceiling law and the delay law are conserved (0/144 Holm-corrected ceiling violations; Spearman rho >= 0.75 at every scale, permutation p < 1e-4), while the weight-decay law deforms systematically, steepening with scale. Preregistered controls show the 50M role-conflict deficit survives learning-rate adjustment and a tripled budget. Conservation was tested against criteria frozen before data collection, and one law's deformation shows the test could have failed. These results license the fully-enumerable transformer as a model organism for the task-side laws of delayed generalization: what it measures exactly, larger models largely obey -- and where they deviate, the deviation is itself lawful and measurable.

</details>


### [161] [Support Thresholds, Not Algorithms, Limit Rare-Association Recovery in Co-Purchase Networks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20171)
*Xiao Han,Zhen Zhang,Xin Zhao,Jiechun Lei,Moxuan Zheng,Youting Wang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Network-based edge filtration (noise-corrected and disparity filter) outperforms Apriori in recovering rare high-lift co-purchase associations while providing complementary edge sets; top-K lift filtering yields highest average lift; both NC and top-K show stronger persistence of edges in held-out data, indicating robust statistical significance and discovery of rare patterns.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Apriori thresholding trades off between capturing frequent associations and generating excessive rules. The study evaluates five filtration methods to balance lift, significance, and discovery of rare high-lift associations in co-purchase networks using large retail datasets.

Method: Comparative evaluation of five filtration methods for co-purchase edges on two grocery datasets (Instacart: 3.2M baskets; Dunnhumby: 208k baskets): (1) Apriori, (2) Apriori + lift post-filtering, (3) top-K ranking by lift, (4) Noise-Corrected (NC) network filter, (5) Disparity Filter (DF). Metrics include average lift, capture of rare high-lift associations, overlap between methods, and rolling-origin holdout to assess edge recurrence and statistical significance in held-out networks.

Result: Top-K lift filtration achieves maximum average lift. NC achieves comparable lift with a single significance parameter (α). Both NC and top-K uncover substantially more rare high-lift associations (80-100% vs 22-28% for Apriori). NC and top-K edges have 18-29% non-overlap; NC prioritizes statistically validated pairs, while top-K favors rare high-lift but potentially statistically weak edges. Rolling-origin evaluation shows top-K edges recur more often across splits, while NC edges are about 12 percentage points more likely to remain statistically significant in the held-out network.

Conclusion: Network-based filtration (NC and DF) and top-K lift filtration offer stronger discovery of rare high-lift co-purchase relations than standard Apriori, with NC providing more statistically robust edges over time and top-K capturing high-lift but rarer signals. The methods yield complementary edge sets, suggesting a potential benefit from combining them for more comprehensive market-basket insights.

Abstract: The support threshold of the Apriori algorithm involves a trade-off in conducting market basket analysis: the associations that occur frequently are noted with high threshold; however, the low ones lead to generating the large amount of rules. The paper compares five methods for co-purchase edge filtration on two grocery datasets: i.e., Instacart (3.2 million baskets) and Dunnhumby (208 thousand baskets), including Apriori, Apriori + lift post-filtering, top-$K$ ranking based on lift, and two methods based on networks, noise-corrected (NC) and disparity filter (DF). The top-$K$ method ensures the maximum average lift, while the NC achieves similar lift level by means of a single value of the significance parameter ($α$). These two methods recover substantially more rare high-lift associations than Apriori (80-100% against 22-28%). NC and top-$K$ select meaningfully different edges (18-29% non-overlapping): NC retains statistically validated pairs, while top-$K$ retains rare pairs with high lift but low statistical significance. A rolling-origin holdout evaluation shows that top-$K$ edges recur at higher rates at every split, but NC edges are ~12 pp more likely to remain statistically significant in the held-out network.

</details>


### [162] [Robust Federated Q-Learning with Almost No Communication](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20174)
*Sreejeet Maity,Aritra Mitra*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Robust Fed-Q achieves exact asymptotic convergence and near-optimal finite-time learning rates in a federated RL setting with adversarial agents, using median-of-means robust aggregation and a hybrid model-based/model-free Q-learning approach, with constant communication rounds.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Investigate the potential and limits of collaborative sample-complexity speedups in federated reinforcement learning when a fraction of agents can be Byzantine/adversarial, and establish robustness and communication-efficiency guarantees.

Method: Introduce Robust Fed-Q, a federated Q-learning algorithm that blends model-based and model-free RL components and employs median-of-means robust aggregation to withstand adversarial clients. Provide high-probability convergence guarantees and finite-time rates, with only O~(1) communication rounds.

Result: Proves that, despite corruption, Robust Fed-Q achieves exact convergence to the optimal value function in the infinite-sample limit and attains near-optimal finite-time rates benefiting from collaboration. Requires only polylogarithmic (O~(1)) communication rounds per guarantee.

Conclusion: Robust federated RL with efficient communication is theoretically achievable: the proposed algorithm attains exact asymptotic optimality and favorable finite-sample performance under adversarial settings, thanks to robust aggregation and a hybrid learning strategy.

Abstract: We consider a federated reinforcement learning setting involving $M$ agents, all of whom interact with a common Markov Decision Process (MDP). The agents exchange information via a central server to learn the optimal value function. Our goal is to understand to what extent one can hope for collaborative sample-complexity speedups in such a setting, when a small fraction of the agents are adversarial and can act arbitrarily. To that end, we propose Robust Fed-Q}, a federated Q-learning algorithm that blends ideas from both model-based and model-free RL, along with the median-of-means device from robust statistics. We prove that despite corruption, with high-probability, Robust Fed-Q (i) guarantees exact convergence to the optimal value function in the limit of infinite samples, and (ii) enjoys near-optimal finite-time rates that benefit from collaboration. In addition, our approach requires just $\tilde{O}(1)$ rounds of communication to achieve each of the above guarantees, a feature of independent interest in FL where communication is the major bottleneck.

</details>


### [163] [When Does Retrieval Help Time-Series Forecasting?](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20193)
*Mert Onur Cakiroglu,Elham Buxton,Mehmet Dalkilic,Hasan Kurban*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Retrieval plug-ins’ gains come from the evaluation regime defined by the relation between lookback S and dominant period L, not the plug-ins themselves; a regime map and simple baselines reveal when benefits occur; two interpretable statistics predict benefit with high accuracy; no new plug-in is proposed—focus on regime-aware evaluation protocol.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current evaluation protocols fix the S–L relation, obscuring when retrieval plug-ins actually help. The paper argues the observed gains are regime-dependent and often achievable by simple baselines when S and L align, urging regime-aware evaluation.

Method: Empirical stratification by S and L; synthetic sweeps over horizon, period, and window; paired phase-controlled controls; zero-shot pretraining comparisons; cross-dataset leave-one-out evaluation; development of two interpretable predictors (trend test and staleness rate); comparison across multiple datasets (ETTm1, ECL, etc.); release of regime map and code.

Result: Found that at S=12 a simple last-period repeat baseline beats six backbones on four of seven benchmarks (8–44% MSE) and rivals the strongest plug-in on ETTm1 while matching it on ECL; performance worsens on datasets lacking a concentrated shared period; benefit tracks period correlation (+0.71) rather than horizon; phase-aligned controls erase much of the effect; zero-shot models underperform by 22–50%; exact lookup aligns with graph diffusion; two predictors achieve 0.76 accuracy in sign prediction under leave-one-dataset-out; overall, no new plug-in is introduced, the regime map and screening statistics are the contributions.

Conclusion: The core contribution is a regime-aware evaluation framework (regime map, protocol, and two screening metrics) to identify when retrieval plug-ins are beneficial. The practical implication is to screen deployments using regime diagnostics rather than relying on any specific plug-in technology.

Abstract: Retrieval plug-ins supply a deep forecaster with information its lookback window cannot carry. Published evaluations report consistent gains, and each credits its own mechanism. We show that the benefit belongs instead to the operating point: the relation between window length $S$ and dominant seasonal period $L$, an axis the standard protocol never varies. Stratifying the evaluation by that relation exposes the regime. At $S{=}12$, a simple control that repeats the last observed period beats the six standard backbones, in aggregate, on four of seven benchmarks by $8\%$ to $44\%$ of MSE. It beats the strongest plug-in we run on ETTm1 and matches it on ECL. It is worse by up to $25\%$ on the three datasets whose training-split spectra lack a concentrated, shared period. A controlled synthetic sweep of horizon, period, and window shows the benefit boundary tracks the period (correlation $+0.71$), not the horizon ($-0.23$). A paired control with no phase to recover nearly erases the effect, consistent with phase starvation. Zero-shot pretraining does not escape it: a foundation model trails trained backbones by $22\%$ to $50\%$ on the periodic benchmarks. Within our instrument, exact lookup matches graph diffusion: the payoff is consulting the record, not the machinery on top. Two interpretable statistics, a trend test and a staleness rate, predict the sign of the per-cell benefit at $0.76$ accuracy under leave-one-dataset-out evaluation, a suggestive margin over the $0.69$ majority rule, where a 22-feature stack manages $0.57$. We propose no new plug-in. The contribution is the regime map, the protocol that reveals it, and two statistics that screen it before deployment. Code: https://github.com/KurbanIntelligenceLab/retrieval-regime.

</details>


### [164] [SoftTri: Smooth Triangular Membership Functions for Adaptive Fuzzy Inference Systems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20194)
*Babak Sarani,Rahman Ardakanian,Ali Mousavi*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A differentiable triangular membership function (SoftTri) using a smooth soft-hinge (Swish-inspired) enables gradient-based learning in fuzzy networks while preserving interpretability; it improves optimization stability and accuracy and competes with Gaussian MFs under the same structure.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Classical triangular MFs are nondifferentiable at knot points, hindering gradient-based optimization in adaptive neuro-fuzzy models. A smooth, differentiable alternative could enable efficient backpropagation without sacrificing interpretability.

Method: Introduce SoftTri: a differentiable triangular MF parameterized by (a,b,c) with a finite sharpness beta>0, built via a smooth soft-hinge mechanism that yields C^∞ smoothness in input and parameters. Derive closed-form analytical gradients for backpropagation. Embed SoftTri in a Takagi–Sugeno fuzzy neural network with grid-partitioned rules and train on one- and two-dimensional nonlinear benchmarks plus Airfoil Self-Noise regression.

Result: SoftTri achieves improved optimization stability and higher approximation accuracy than classical triangular MFs, while matching or surpassing Gaussian MFs under the same rule structures and training settings. It maintains the interpretability of triangular MFs and provides fully differentiable learning.

Conclusion: SoftTri offers a favorable compromise between interpretability and differentiable optimization in neuro-fuzzy systems, enabling stable gradient-based training without sacrificing the geometric locality of triangular membership functions.

Abstract: Triangular membership functions (MFs) are widely used in fuzzy systems because of their interpretability, low parameterization complexity, and strong locality properties. However, their inherent nondifferentiability at knot points limits the effectiveness of gradient-based optimization in adaptive neuro-fuzzy architectures, often necessitating subgradient approximations or heuristic smoothing techniques. In this paper, we propose \emph{SoftTri}, a differentiable triangular membership function constructed using a smooth soft-hinge mechanism inspired by Swish-type activations. The proposed formulation preserves the geometric structure and localized behavior of classical triangular MFs while providing $C^\infty$ smoothness with respect to both the input variable and the membership parameters $(a,b,c)$ for any finite sharpness parameter $β>0$. Closed-form analytical gradients are derived to enable efficient and fully differentiable backpropagation-based learning. SoftTri is integrated into a Takagi--Sugeno fuzzy neural network with grid-partitioned rules and evaluated on multiple one-dimensional and two-dimensional nonlinear approximation benchmarks as well as a real-world regression task using the Airfoil Self-Noise dataset. Experimental results demonstrate that SoftTri consistently improves optimization stability and approximation accuracy compared with classical triangular membership functions, while achieving performance comparable to or better than Gaussian MFs under identical rule structures and training settings. The proposed approach provides an effective compromise between interpretability and differentiable optimization in modern neuro-fuzzy learning systems.

</details>


### [165] [Evaluating Financial Sentiment in the Age of AI](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20198)
*Arslan Bisharat,Oudom Hean*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: General-purpose LLMs match finance-specific models for sentiment classification, but stronger economic validity is limited; sentiment captures economic performance more than short-run price moves; large earnings surprises drive signals, moderate surprises do not.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Evaluate whether general-purpose LLMs can improve financial sentiment measurement over finance-specific methods by assessing linguistic and economic validity.

Method: Compare twelve sentiment models (dictionary-based, finance-specific transformers, open-source LLMs) on linguistic validity (classification accuracy) and economic validity (association with earnings surprises and next-day returns) across announcements with varying surprise magnitudes.

Result: General-purpose LLMs provide classification performance on par with finance-specific transformers without fine-tuning; higher accuracy does not imply stronger economic relationships; some models' sentiment measures correlate with earnings surprises, but none with next-day returns; strongest performance for large surprises, weaker for moderate ones.

Conclusion: Financial sentiment conveys information about firms' economic performance but has limited explanatory power for short-run market reactions.

Abstract: Financial sentiment measures are widely used in empirical finance, but it remains unclear whether general-purpose large language models (LLMs) improve on existing finance-specific methods. This paper evaluates twelve sentiment models, including dictionary-based methods, finance-specific transformers, and open-source LLMs, using two criteria: linguistic validity and economic validity. We find that general-purpose LLMs achieve classification performance comparable to finance-specific transformer models without task-specific fine-tuning. However, higher classification accuracy does not translate into stronger economic relationships. Several models produce sentiment measures that are significantly associated with earnings surprises, but none is significantly associated with next-day stock returns. Model performance is strongest for announcements with large earnings beats or misses and substantially weaker for announcements with more moderate earnings surprises. These findings suggest that financial sentiment captures information about firms' economic performance but has limited ability to explain short-run market reactions

</details>


### [166] [Towards a Unified Modality-Agnostic Multimodal Framework for Cognitive Workload Assessment](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20199)
*Stefanos Gkikas,Christian Arzate Cruz,Calvin Joseph,Giorgos Giannakakis,Raul Fernandez Rojas*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A unified hierarchical Transformer architecture processes heterogeneous biosignals (ECG, EDA, RESP, SpO2, EEG) for cognitive workload assessment. In a pilot, EEG dominates as a single modality; five-modality fusion yields best averages; adding modalities doesn't always help; architecture achieves ~50% model-size reduction vs late fusion with faster inference.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Address limited evidence on multi-modal fusion of heterogeneous biosignals for cognitive workload; develop modality-agnostic, scalable model to handle diverse inputs and evaluate exhaustive modality combinations.

Method: Unified Transformer-based architecture that is modality-agnostic and hierarchical; evaluate all 31 combinations of five modalities under leave-one-subject-out validation across three tasks (IQ, MATH, GAME); compare to late-fusion baselines; measure accuracy/average scores; report model size and inference time.

Result: EEG is strongest single modality across tasks; no consistent improvement with adding more modalities; full five modalities yields the highest Average scores (73.02% IQ; 68.08% averaged over IQ,MATH,GAME,ALL); ~50% reduction in model size vs late-fusion; lower inference time.

Conclusion: Modality-agnostic hierarchical Transformer can effectively fuse heterogeneous biosignals; EEG remains most informative; careful modality selection matters; multi-modality fusion yields diminishing returns; the proposed approach offers efficient, scalable cognitive workload assessment suitable for adaptive human-machine systems.

Abstract: Cognitive workload reflects the mental effort required during task performance and is central to the design of adaptive human-machine systems. The use of biosignals to measure cognitive workload has been extensively researched and documented; however, studies examining the effects of combining heterogeneous biosignal modalities for this purpose remain limited. To provide insight into this area, we developed a unified, modality-agnostic, hierarchical Transformer-based architecture to process heterogeneous biosignal modalities within a single model. We use this framework in a pilot study evaluating all $31$ possible combinations of five modalities: Electrocardiogram (ECG), Electrodermal Activity (EDA), Respiration (RESP), Peripheral Oxygen Saturation (SpO$_2$), and Electroencephalogram (EEG), under leave-one-subject-out validation across three cognitively distinct tasks: abstract reasoning (IQ), arithmetic problem solving (MATH), and a game task (GAME). In this pilot setting, the results suggest that: (i) EEG is the strongest single modality, ranking highest in IQ, GAME, and the pooled ALL setting, where samples from all three tasks are combined; (ii) adding more modalities does not consistently improve performance; (iii) the full five-modality combination achieves the highest \textit{Average} score of $73.02%$ on IQ and $68.08%$ when the \textit{Average} scores are averaged over the four evaluation settings: IQ, MATH, GAME, and ALL; and (iv) the proposed method reduces model size by approximately $50%$ compared with late-fusion alternatives while maintaining a lower inference time.

</details>


### [167] [Scene-Conditioned Relation Routing for urban cellular activity forecasting](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20209)
*Qingzhong Li,Jingye Lin,Hui Ma,Yajun Zhang,Xinjun Pei,Ming Yan,Fei Xing*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A scene-conditioned, adaptive framework SCRR-Net for multi-signal urban spatiotemporal forecasting, jointly modeling SMS, network traffic, and call activity with context-driven routing.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing methods often treat temporal modeling, spatial relation learning, and multi-signal prediction separately and rely on fixed graphs or static multi-task schemes, limiting adaptability to dynamic urban environments.

Method: SCRR-Net uses a scene-conditioned spatial relation routing framework: a context encoder to capture urban context, a spatial graph expert routing module to select spatial dependencies, a temporal Transformer encoder for temporal dynamics, and a task knowledge routing module for cross-task knowledge transfer; routing decisions are conditioned on context and are interpretable.

Result: On Milano and Trento datasets, SCRR-Net consistently outperforms baselines in forecasting SMS usage, mobile network traffic, and call activity, and yields interpretable routing behavior.

Conclusion: Scene-conditioned routing enables adaptive, interpretable joint modeling of heterogeneous urban signals, improving predictive accuracy across tasks and offering insights into spatial dependency patterns under different urban contexts.

Abstract: Urban cellular activity forecasting requires jointly modeling heterogeneous spatiotemporal signals, including SMS usage, mobile network traffic, and call activity. Existing methods often separate temporal modeling, spatial relation learning, and multi-signal prediction, relying on fixed graph structures or static multi-task learning schemes, which limits their adaptability to changing urban scenes. We propose SCRR-Net, a scene-conditioned spatial relation routing framework in which urban contextual information jointly controls spatial dependency selection and cross-task knowledge transfer. SCRR-Net includes a context encoder, a spatial graph expert routing module, a temporal Transformer encoder, and a task knowledge routing module. Experiments on the Milano and Trento datasets demonstrate that SCRR-Net consistently outperforms competing methods on SMS, network traffic, and call activity forecasting, while providing interpretable routing behaviors.

</details>


### [168] [Subdomain-aware representation compression for pretrained image embeddings](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20213)
*Poowanut Niamluang,Jittat Fakcharoenphol*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Using dimensionality reduction (PCA, LDA) for subdomain representation compression in image domains; shows space/computation efficiency and accuracy gains, plus transfer learning with compressed representations.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To reduce storage and compute requirements for subdomain representations on edge devices while potentially improving accuracy by extracting salient subdomain features.

Method: Apply PCA and LDA to subdomain representations in image datasets; evaluate space, compute efficiency, and accuracy against full embeddings; conduct transfer learning experiments using compressed representations.

Result: Compressed representations reduce space and compute requirements and can improve accuracy over direct full-embedding approaches; evidence suggests subdomain features are effectively captured by dimensionality reduction; transfer learning with these representations is feasible and beneficial.

Conclusion: Dimensionality reduction can effectively compress subdomain representations, yielding efficiency gains and potentially improved accuracy, with viable transfer learning performance on compressed subdomains.

Abstract: Dimensionality reduction is a well-known technique for improving space efficiency, typically applied uniformly across an entire dataset. This paper investigates the possibilities of using dimensionality reduction techniques for subdomain representation compression. We explore standard techniques such as Principal Component Analysis (PCA) and Linear discriminant analysis (LDA) in image domains. The results not only demonstrate the expected improvements in space and computation complexity crucial for edge-device ML applications but also show improvements in accuracy over direct full-embedding procedure. One possible explanation is that dimensionality reduction effectively extracts subdomain features. We also performed experiments to demonstrate transfer learning capabilities using the compressed representations.

</details>


### [169] [Explaining spatial information flow in short-term traffic forecasting models using a gated graph attention network](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20217)
*Yue Li,Shujuan Chen,Ying Jin*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Gated GAT with per-sensor, per-time-step neighbor-vs-self gating provides graded ablations to explain spatial information flow in traffic forecasting. On ST-MetaNet with two GAT layers, two layers are largely redundant; gating offers modest accuracy gains and interpretable dynamics of spatial coupling.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: GATs are standard for modeling spatial dependence in traffic forecasting, but attention weights lack ground-truth comparability, hindering explanation and identification of necessary components. A gate that quantifies neighbor contribution enables explainability and controlled ablation.

Method: Introduce a learnable gate at every sensor and time step to fractionally replace the sensor's updated state with neighbor information in GAT layers. Apply this gated GAT to ST-MetaNet (an encoder–decoder with a GAT between two recurrent layers). Train on one calendar year of loop detector data (498 sensors) from England's strategic road network. Regularize the gate to induce graded reduction of neighbor info. Analyze gating behavior, temporal patterns, and perform ablation by removing GAT layers (single vs. both) and by inspecting encoder vs. decoder gating order.

Result: Mild regularization slightly improves forecasting accuracy; stronger regularization reduces accuracy as neighbor information is withdrawn too much. Gates allocate more neighbor influence to heavily loaded sensors and follow daily/weekly cycles. The encoder gate closes before the decoder gate; ablation shows that removing either GAT layer alone does not hurt and can match or exceed keeping both, while removing both degrades substantially. Thus the two GAT layers are largely redundant in this setup, with gated GAT providing a modest accuracy gain and interpretable insights into spatial information flow.

Conclusion: Gated GAT offers explainability about where and when spatial information flows and reveals which layers are required in this architecture. The approach yields modest performance gains and a diagnostic tool to assess architectural necessity of graph attention components in traffic forecasting.

Abstract: Short-term traffic forecasting supports real-time monitoring and control of road networks, and graph attention networks (GAT) are the standard means of representing spatial dependence in these models. GAT layers are widely described as capturing the influence of neighbouring locations, but this is seldom verified, because the attention weights offered in support cannot be compared against any measured quantity. That leaves two questions open, how the model should be explained and which of its components are necessary. We address this by adding a gate to the GAT layer which learns, at every sensor and every time step, what share of a sensor's updated state is drawn from its neighbours rather than from itself. Regularising the gate withdraws neighbour information progressively and thereby provides a graded form of ablation. We apply the gated GAT to ST-MetaNet, whose encoder and decoder each place one GAT layer between two recurrent layers, and train it on one calendar year of records from 498 loop detectors on the strategic road network of England. The gate assigns a larger share of neighbour information to sensors carrying heavier traffic and follows the daily and weekly cycle of travel, consistent with adjacent locations being more strongly coupled when busy. Mild regularisation improves accuracy slightly, and accuracy declines at higher strengths as the penalty withdraws information the model needs. The encoder gate closes before the decoder gate, but direct ablation qualifies that ordering. Removing either GAT layer alone leaves accuracy at least as good as keeping both, whereas removing both degrades it substantially, so the two layers are largely redundant rather than either being indispensable. The gated GAT therefore yields a modest accuracy gain, an explanation of where and when spatial information flows, and evidence on which layers the architecture requires.

</details>


### [170] [Is It Still Worth Training a Classical Model in the Era of LLMs? A Crossover Benchmark on Tabular Data](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20218)
*Kaihua Ding*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Training a classical model beats a small frozen LLM for labeling tabular rows much of the time with only a small labeled data budget; the crossover occurs at a median around 6% of the training set, implying few hundred labels for typical business tables; prompts for LLMs do not replicate training curves and exhibit variability across implementations.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To determine whether, for labeled-data-limited business prediction tasks, it is more effective to use a frozen LLM with prompt-based labeling or to collect labeled data and train a traditional model, and to quantify the data efficiency (N*) of the crossover.

Method: Empirical meta-analysis combining 126 independent evaluations of small GPT models across eight prompting configurations and 18 tabular datasets, with authoritative power-law learning curves for six classical model families to estimate the labeled-data crossover N*.

Result: Trained classical models outperform frozen LLMs using no more labeled data than is already available in 86% of cases; they win with the smallest labeled subset in 40%; median crossover occurs at about 6% of the training data; few-shot prompts do not follow power-law learning; cross-run variability (coefficient of variation) ~0.148; LLMs rely on recognizable feature-name semantics, suggesting the crossover may be conservative.

Conclusion: For typical business tables, collect a few hundred labels and train a gradient-boosted model rather than relying on prompting a frozen LLM for labeling.

Abstract: Large language models can label a tabular row from a plain-English description with no training - a capability now shipping in mainstream spreadsheet tools such as Microsoft Copilot in Excel and Anthropic's Claude for Excel - raising a practical question for the many business prediction problems where labels are expensive: should you prompt a frozen LLM, or collect data and train a model - and if so, how much data? We quantify the answer with the labeled-data crossover N*, the training-set size at which a trained classical model's learning curve overtakes a frozen LLM's training-free (and therefore flat) error. Aggregating 126 independent student evaluations of small GPT models under eight prompting configurations across 18 tabular datasets, paired with authoritative power-law learning curves for six classical model families, we find that training wins fast: even given an oracle choice of its best prompt configuration, a trained classical model beats the small frozen LLM using no more labeled data than is already on hand in 86% of cases, and wins by the smallest labeled subset we evaluate in 40%, with the observed crossover at a median of ~6% of the training set. In-context few-shot examples do not behave like training - error versus shot count does not follow a power law - and the same protocol re-run by independent implementers varies with a coefficient of variation of 0.148. A controlled probe indicates the LLM depends on recognizable feature-name semantics, which plausibly makes our crossover a conservative estimate (we do not claim memorization). For a typical business table, the evidence is clear: collect a few hundred labels and train a gradient-boosted model.

</details>


### [171] [Accuracy Is Not Enough: A Cross-Architecture Audit of Demographic Bias in Deep Knowledge Tracing](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20249)
*Dang Quang Minh,Nguyen Dung Son,Nguyen Huu Loi,Truong Viet Vu,Nguyen Thai Anh*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Cross-architecture audit of deep knowledge tracing (DKT, DKVMN, SAKT, AKT) reveals context-dependent demographic bias; AKT has highest accuracy but largest socio-economic bias; standard debiasing (reweighting, adversarial) largely fails to reduce ABROCA while preserving accuracy.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Extend fairness auditing from Bayesian KTM to modern deep knowledge tracing architectures using demographic metadata and robust bias metrics (ABROCA) with bootstrap CIs and permutation tests to address stability critiques.

Method: Train four DKT architectures (DKT, DKVMN, SAKT, AKT) under standard, reweighting, and adversarial debiasing on two public datasets with demographic data (Eedi, OULAD). Evaluate using ABROCA, per-group AUC, student-level bootstrap CIs, and permutation tests; conduct ablation of Rasch embeddings.

Result: Bias is real and context-dependent: socio-economic ABROCA significant on Eedi for all architectures; gender bias significant on OULAD for 3/4 architectures after multiplicity correction; AKT achieves highest accuracy but strongest ABROCA. Ablating Rasch embeddings removes both accuracy gains and excess bias. Standard debiasing methods (reweighting, adversarial) leave ABROCA unchanged while preserving accuracy.

Conclusion: Deep fairness issues in knowledge tracing are architecture- and context-dependent. High-accuracy architectures can amplify bias through specific embeddings (Rasch components). Simple mitigation strategies may be ineffective; robust, architecture-aware fairness interventions and more diverse evaluations are needed.

Abstract: Deep knowledge tracing (DKT) models implicitly decide which students an adaptive system believes have mastered a skill, yet almost all evidence on their demographic fairness comes from Bayesian knowledge tracing; the deep models that power modern systems have received no comparable cross-architecture audit.
