We close this gap: four architectures (DKT, DKVMN, SAKT, AKT) trained under three regimes (standard, reweighting, adversarial) on two public datasets with demographic metadata, Eedi (15.9M interactions) and OULAD (167k after preprocessing), evaluated with ABROCA, student-level bootstrap confidence intervals, and permutation tests addressing recent critiques of fairness-metric instability. Three findings emerge. (i) Bias is real but context-dependent: every architecture shows a significant socioeconomic ABROCA on Eedi (0.018-0.023, $p<0.005$), with per-group AUC lower for economically disadvantaged students, while gender bias is significant on OULAD for three of four architectures after multiplicity correction yet negligible on Eedi. (ii) The most accurate architecture is the most biased: AKT gains about 4 AUC points from item-level Rasch embeddings and shows the largest socioeconomic ABROCA, exceeding every other architecture under a paired bootstrap ($p\leq0.002$); ablating only the Rasch embeddings removes the accuracy gain and the excess bias together. (iii) Standard mitigation is unreliable: reweighting and adversarial debiasing leave ABROCA essentially unchanged in every configuration that preserves accuracy, even though the adversary is pinned at chance at full reversal strength and a weak-strength positive control rules out a dead probe.

</details>


### [172] [How Far Can Sub-3B Open Language Models Go in Zero-Shot Essay Scoring on an 8 GB Consumer GPU?](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20250)
*Nguyen Dung Son,Dang Quang Minh,Nguyen Huu Loi,Truong Viet Vu,Nguyen Thai Anh*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Sub-3B open models can perform rubric-decomposed essay scoring locally, but lag behind human inter-rater ceilings; best macro QWK ~0.388 vs human ~0.769, so suitable mainly for formative, supervised feedback.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Privacy-preserving, on-device automated essay scoring for settings like public schools where sending student work to third-party APIs is unacceptable; evaluate the feasibility of sub-3B open models running locally with rigorous statistics and realistic deployment constraints.

Method: Systematic evaluation of four instruction-tuned models from two families (Qwen2.5 at 0.5B/1.5B/3B, SmolLM2 at 1.7B) on all eight ASAP-AES prompts using a single 8 GB GPU, with bootstrap confidence intervals, Holm-corrected paired tests, and deployment-realistic design variants. Compare rubric-decomposed vs holistic prompting, mean vs min-max aggregation, and normalization strategies (Multi-Trait Specialization).

Result: Three findings: (i) Rubric-decomposed prompting beats holistic prompting for all models under batch min-max aggregation; under mean aggregation two unrelated families converge within 0.01 at ~1.5–1.7B. (ii) Trait-score mapping into prompt range is sensitive to grader calibration; one model narrows outputs (2–4/10) with naive mean, but min-max normalization with Multi-Trait Specialization fixes it (macro QWK 0.204→0.388) and remains stable with 30 held-out essays. (iii) Signed error tends to decrease with essay length in 11 of 12 configurations; normalization reduces this slope for well-calibrated models. Best local configuration yields macro QWK 0.388, still far below human inter-rater ceiling 0.769 and a length-only baseline 0.523; conclusion: sub-3B locally run models are suitable for formative, human-supervised feedback, not high-stakes scoring.

Conclusion: On-device, privacy-preserving essay scoring with sub-3B models is feasible for formative use with careful prompting and calibration, but current performance remains below human agreement; further calibration and normalization strategies are essential to close the gap.

Abstract: Zero-shot essay scoring with large language models is usually demonstrated with proprietary API models, yet the settings where automated scoring is most needed, such as public schools grading thousands of essays under strict privacy rules, are often those where sending student writing to a third-party API is unacceptable. We ask how much capability survives when the model must be a sub-3B open model running fully locally in FP16, with a controlled study of four instruction-tuned models from two families (Qwen2.5 at 0.5B/1.5B/3B, SmolLM2 at 1.7B) on all eight ASAP-AES prompts on a single 8 GB consumer GPU, with bootstrap confidence intervals, Holm-corrected paired tests, and deployment-realistic variants of the key design choices. Three findings emerge. (i) Rubric-decomposed prompting beats holistic prompting for every model under batch min-max aggregation (though Qwen2.5-3B drops significantly on one prompt), and under mean aggregation two unrelated families land within 0.01 at the 1.5-1.7B scale. (ii) Mapping trait scores into the prompt range is fragile to grader calibration: one model compresses traits into a narrow low band (2-4 on 0-10) and naive mean aggregation collapses, while the min-max normalization of Multi-Trait Specialization repairs it (macro QWK 0.204 to 0.388) and stays within 0.03 when its statistics are frozen on 30 held-out essays. (iii) Signed error falls with essay length in eleven of twelve configurations, opposite to the verbosity bias reported for large LLM judges; normalized rubric decomposition largely flattens this slope for well-calibrated models. We anchor results honestly: the best local configuration (0.388) remains far below both the human inter-rater ceiling (0.769) and a length-only baseline (0.523), so we position sub-3B local models strictly for formative, human-supervised feedback.

</details>


### [173] [Improving Online Reinforcement Learning via Bidirectional Behavior Prior Distillation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20268)
*Gong Gao,Xiao Lai,Jiaji Shen,Ning Jia,Xianhui Liu,Weidong Zhao*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: B2PD uses action-value priors and a conditional VAE to generate a high-value behavior support set, which is distilled into online RL to improve sample efficiency and stabilize learning by mitigating critic errors, with bidirectional knowledge flow.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Online RL suffers from poor sample efficiency and unstable learning due to critic estimation errors amplified by greedy updates; offline behavior priors are limited by dataset quality and lack expert trajectories.

Method: Introduce Bidirectional Behavior Prior Distillation (B2PD) that leverages action-value priors to train a CVAE to produce high-value behavioral trajectories and priors, which are distilled into the agent to constrain and shape online policy updates with a bidirectional knowledge flow.

Result: Empirical results on state- and pixel-based tasks show substantially improved sample efficiency and stable policy optimization compared to baselines.

Conclusion: Enforcing high-quality behavioral support during online learning effectively mitigates critic-induced error amplification, enabling structured behavior priors to guide policy updates in a principled and sample-efficient manner.

Abstract: Online reinforcement learning (RL) algorithms frequently exhibit poor sample efficiency and unstable learning dynamics, stemming from systematic critic estimation errors that are exacerbated by greedy policy updates. Existing behavior-prior reinforcement learning methods attempt to alleviate this issue by relying on offline pre-training to learn behavior models from fixed datasets and using policy priors to constrain online policy updates. However, the limited quality of offline datasets often hinders the ability to provide high-value policies that can effectively guide policy updates. The absence of expert trajectories significantly impairs online policy learning, leading to low sample efficiency and suboptimal performance. To address these challenges, we depart from conventional behavior prior approaches and propose a Bidirectional Behavior Prior Distillation (B2PD) algorithm. B2PD leverages action-value priors to guide a conditional variational autoencoder (CVAE) in generating a high-value behavior support set. The resulting expert behavior priors are further distilled into the agent, effectively reducing inefficient exploration and enabling stable policy optimization, while establishing a bidirectional knowledge flow mechanism. Empirical evaluations on both state- and pixel-based tasks verify that B2PD substantially improves sample efficiency while maintaining stable policy optimization. More broadly, this work shows that enforcing high-quality behavioral support during online learning effectively mitigates critic-induced error amplification, enabling structured behavior priors to guide policy updates in a principled and sample-efficient manner.

</details>


### [174] [Placement Is Free, Composition Is Not: The Latin Square as a Provably-Balanced Construction for Heterogeneous Sequence-Mixer Stacks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20269)
*Taebong Kim,Youngsik Hong,Minsik Kim,Sunyoung Choi,Jaewon Jang,Minseo Kim*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A heterogeneous mix of seven sequence-mixing mechanisms arranged in a Latin square across a 49-layer model shows that depth-wise heterogeneity, not exact placement, drives performance. Permutation effects are small; contiguous clustering and homogeneous stacks hurt. Findings hold at larger scales; authors release resources.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To causally disentangle the effects of mechanism choice vs placement in stacked sequence mixers and test whether distributing diverse mixing mechanisms across depth improves performance versus reusing a single mechanism per layer.

Method: Construct Aether-7B-5Attn, a 6.59B-parameter mixture-of-experts model with 49 layers containing seven sequence-mixing mechanisms arranged in a 7×7 Latin square. Build a parameter-matched 4×4 Latin square proxy over 16 layers (~700.9M params) with eight seeds per arm. Evaluate across arrangements: balanced Latin square vs rearranged cycles vs contiguous depth bands vs homogeneous stack. Scale to 1.514B parameters to test robustness. Report per-mechanism cost, English and Korean evaluations, and conduct a causal-safety audit. Release model weights, training recipes, code, logs, and architecture source code.

Result: Rearranging into a balanced periodic cycle changes validation loss by only 0.16%, indicating placement has little effect. Clustering mechanisms into contiguous depth bands incurs 0.59% penalty, while using a homogeneous stack incurs 1.68% penalty. At 2.16× larger scale (1.514B params), the homogeneous-stack penalty grows to 2.63% and removing the SSM-family mechanism yields a 3.20% degradation. Per-mechanism cost profiles and English/Korean evaluations are reported; a causal-safety audit is performed. Resources are released.

Conclusion: Performance is driven primarily by heterogeneous composition distributed across depth rather than by any specific permutation of mechanisms. A diversified, evenly exposed mechanism mix across layers yields better performance than particular placements or homogeneous stacks; results persist at larger scale.

Abstract: Since GPT, most Transformers have repeated the same attention mechanism at every layer. Yet this design is largely a convention rather than a tested conclusion. When multiple sequence mixers are combined in one stack, improvements may arise from mechanism choice, placement, or both, making causal attribution difficult. We introduce Aether-7B-5Attn, a 6.59B-parameter mixture-of-experts model ($\approx$2.98B active) whose 49 layers contain seven sequence-mixing mechanisms arranged as a $7\times7$ Latin square. Because each mechanism appears exactly once in every row and column, the design guarantees balanced exposure across depth while eliminating placement confounds. To evaluate this principle, we build a parameter-matched proxy with four mechanisms arranged as a $4\times4$ Latin square over sixteen layers, matched to 700.9M parameters and trained with eight seeds per arm. The results reveal a clear dissociation. Rearranging a distributed heterogeneous stack into a balanced periodic cycle changes validation loss by only 0.16\%, indicating that exact placement has little effect. In contrast, clustering the same mechanisms into contiguous depth bands incurs a 0.59\% penalty, while replacing the heterogeneous stack with a homogeneous one incurs a 1.68\% penalty. These results indicate that performance depends primarily on heterogeneous composition distributed across depth rather than on any particular permutation. We confirm this finding at 2.16$\times$ larger scale (1.514B parameters), where the homogeneous-stack penalty increases to 2.63\% and removing the SSM-family mechanism produces a 3.20\% degradation. We further report per-mechanism cost profiles, English and Korean evaluations, and a causal-safety audit of all 49 layers. We release model weights, training recipes, training code, logs, and architecture source code.

</details>


### [175] [Labeled Incidence Structures for Native Transformer Modeling of Text, Knowledge Graphs, and Hypergraphs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20278)
*Mahesh Godavarti*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A uniform, endpoint-based representation (LIS) for text, graphs, and hypergraphs enables a single transformer to process heterogeneous data without flattening. It encodes each endpoint as (content, role, relation) and uses slot and instance operators to obtain addresses, enabling a role- and relation-aware attention via relative transport.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To preserve structural information across diverse data types and avoid flattening into token sequences, while enabling a single Transformer to operate uniformly.

Method: Define labeled incidence structures (LIS) with endpoints (x_d, s, e). Build the address A(s,e)=R_s R_e from slot and instance operators. Analyze conditions for unique path-independent addresses. Introduce relative transport P_{j->i}=A_i^{-1}A_j. Compare additive encodings to joint s-e interactions. Examine persistent knowledge repositories and compute operators from content to avoid storage-order sensitivity; derive a capacity bound independent of repository size M under fixed architecture and Lipschitz assumptions.

Result: Characterizes when LIS yields unique, path-independent addresses; shows relative transport provides a natural, role- and relation-aware inductive bias for attention; proves additive encodings cannot capture joint s-e interactions in a controlled example; demonstrates that content-derived relation–instance operators mitigate storage-order sensitivity and yield a capacity bound independent of M under specified assumptions.

Conclusion: LIS offers a principled, architecture-agnostic framework for representing heterogeneous data for a unified Transformer, preserving structural roles and enabling biases through operators; highlights the insufficiency of additive position+relation encodings and addresses issues of storage order in persistent repositories.

Abstract: Text, knowledge graphs, and hypergraphs all have elements that play distinct roles within relation instances, structure that is lost when data is flattened into token sequences. We introduce labeled incidence structures (LIS), a uniform representation that encodes each endpoint as $(x_d, s, e)$: content $x_d$, a role or slot $s$, and the relation instance $e$ in which that role appears. Because every data type maps to the same $(x_d, s, e)$ representation without flattening, a single standard transformer can process them all natively, structural differences are carried entirely by the operators, not the architecture.
  LIS assigns a structural address to each endpoint by composing a slot operator and an instance operator, $A(s,e) = R_s R_e$. We characterize when this factorization gives every token a unique, path-independent address. When it does, the natural operator comparing endpoint $j$ to endpoint $i$ is the relative transport $P_{j\to i} = A_i^{-1} A_j$, which gives attention a role- and relation-aware inductive bias without imposing an arbitrary sequence order.
  Additive encodings of the form "position term plus relation term" can miss information that depends jointly on $s$ and $e$. We prove this in a controlled example family: when the journey operator is approximated by the sum of a position-only term and a relation-only term, the approximation cannot capture how position and relation combine, only their separate effects.
  We also analyze persistent knowledge repositories. Identifiers tied to storage locations make models sensitive to storage order, while freely learned identifiers can become harder to control as the repository size $M$ grows relative to the sample size $n$. Computing relation-instance operators from content avoids this storage-order issue and yields a capacity bound independent of $M$, under fixed architectural and Lipschitz assumptions.

</details>


### [176] [Personalising a Cross-User Surface Electromyography Encoder Under a Small Calibration Budget](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20296)
*Jethro Odeyemi,W. J. Zhang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Full fine-tuning of a cross-user encoder yields the highest accuracy across calibration budgets for a myoelectric interface; a gradient-free prototypical rule can recover 52–78% of its benefit without optimization or per-user weight copies, enabling on-donning personalization. The idea that a good representation suffices without retraining is not supported; the relative performance to per-user clinics varies by database.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Determine how to best utilize a fixed set of calibration repetitions to personalize a cross-user encoder for a myoelectric interface, balancing accuracy against calibration cost and deployment practicality.

Method: Evaluate four strategies using the same labeled calibration repetitions on a held-out subject across three databases: prototypical adaptation, linear probes, scaled fine-tuning, and full fine-tuning. Tests span budgets up to the maximum allowed (five repetitions on DB1, four on DB2/DB5) across 77 subjects.

Result: Full fine-tuning consistently provided the highest accuracy at all budgets with no exceptions across subject subsets. A gradient-free prototypical rule achieved 52–78% of its benefit without an optimizer or per-user weight copies. The expectation that representing features alone suffice (only retraining a classifier) is contradicted by these results. Relative performance to a per-user clinic-trained classifier varies by database.

Conclusion: Careful calibration strategy selection matters: full fine-tuning offers the best accuracy but higher complexity/cost; low-cost prototypical adaptation affords meaningful gains without optimization, enabling wear-at-donning personalization. The advantage of a cross-user representation vs per-user classifier is database-dependent.

Abstract: A myoelectric interface needs calibration from the user before it will function. Earlier work has treated calibration as a quantity, but has not asked the question of what a device should do with the calibration repetitions once they have been collected. This paper views personalizing the cross-user encoder as a design decision with a cost. Four alternative approaches to using exactly the same labeled repetitions were tested from a single cross-user encoder per held-out subject. Prototypical adaptation, linear probes, scaled fine-tuning and full fine-tuning were tested at every budget up to the maximum each database allows, five repetitions on DB1 and four on DB2 and DB5. Comparing four ways to spend a small calibration budget across 77 subjects, full fine-tuning is the most accurate at every budget, consistently enough that there is no exception among subsets of subjects. The result which impacts how one might make an engineering decision however is that a gradient free prototypical rule recovers 52 to 78 per cent of its benefit with no optimiser and no per-user copy of the weights, which makes personalisation something a worn device can do at donning time. The widespread intuition that a good representation only needs a fresh classifier is incorrect here. How well each method may perform relative to a per-user classifier that would be fitted by a clinic will depend on the specific database.

</details>


### [177] [Intact-to-Amputee Transfer in Surface-EMG Gesture Decoding: Training Source and Calibration Budget](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20297)
*Jethro Odeyemi,W. J. Zhang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Zero-shot cross-population transfer from an intact-limb trained, montage-agnostic encoder to amputees fails; but with labeled data and larger, diverse source pools, cross-user transfer improves beyond per-user pipelines; training on more intact subjects helps transfer more than training on amputees alone; the proposed account on EMG separability holds only after multiple repetitions and diverse amputee data.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Assess cross-user generalization of EMG-based recognisers for transradial prostheses, specifically whether an encoder trained on intact-limb data can transfer to amputees, and identify data requirements (labels, source diversity) for robust performance.

Method: Train a montage-agnostic cross-user encoder on intact-limb EMG data. Test on eleven transradial amputees with a protocol matched to intact-limb training. Attempt zero-shot transfer, then 3 labeled repetitions, compare to per-user classifier. Expand source pool by training on forty intact subjects and assess transfer to new amputees. Evaluate with macro-F1 across repetitions and cohorts; pre-register the prediction, compare amputee-only vs mixed (intact+amputee) source pools.

Result: Zero-shot transfer fails. With three labeled repetitions, macro-F1 improves to 0.190 over a typical per-user classifier baseline. With three repetitions, the encoder achieves 0.779 macro-F1 versus 0.589 for the per-user pipeline. Training on forty intact subjects yields better transfers to a new amputee than training on ten amputees; combining both sources yields the best transfer. The proposed amputee-EMG separability account holds only after some repetitions and with a richer amputee source pool. At a single repetition, or when the source is matched to intact-limb data, the approach fails.

Conclusion: Cross-user transfer from intact-limb trained encoders to amputees is limited and data-dependent. Achieving robust cross-user performance requires labeled data from the new user and diverse source data, with gains realized when incorporating both intact and amputee sources and a sufficient number of repetitions. The boundary conditions suggest the proposed separability account is not universally applicable and depends on data richness and repetitions.

Abstract: A recogniser trained on one person rarely transfers to the next, and useful performance usually demands a fresh round of labelled calibration from the end user. A systematic review of 1077 studies quantifies where the evidence is thin: amputees appear in about one in six. Here a montage-agnostic cross-user encoder is carried to eleven transradial amputees on a protocol matched to its intact-limb training data. Zero-shot cross-population transfer fails outright: the encoder requires labeled data from the new user before it begins decoding, and it then exceeds the per-user classifier a clinic would fit by 0.190 macro F1 at three repetitions and for every subject in the cohort. Given three labelled repetitions it reaches 0.779 macro-F1 against 0.589 for the per-user pipeline. Training on forty intact subjects produces better transfers to a new amputee than training on ten other amputees, and combining the two produces better transfers than either individually. The prediction pre-registered for this study, which extends the encoder's baseline-strength account with the premise that amputee EMG is less separable, holds true only after a few repetitions become available and after enriching the source pool with additional amputees. At a single repetition, and at every budget under a source matched to the intact-limb comparison, it fails. Thus, it locates the boundary of the proposed account.

</details>


### [178] [A Learning Algorithm for Threshold Boolean Networks with Prescribed Fixed Points](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20298)
*Gonzalo A. Ruz*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Differentiable learning for threshold Boolean networks with fixed-point constraints achieves high-quality network reconstruction with minimal spurious attractors on FOS-GRN, outperforming standard classifiers.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To enforce desired dynamic properties (fixed points) in inferred gene networks while reducing spurious attractors, all within a sparse, binary-amenable framework.

Method: A custom differentiable loss that (i) enforces fixed-point preservation, (ii) penalizes spurious attractors, (iii) encourages binary outputs, and (iv) imposes L1 sparsity. Evaluated on the Arabidopsis thaliana FOS-GRN model; compared to Perceptron and Logistic Regression; includes a sparsity-regularization study with λ up to 0.01.

Result: The method achieved perfect reconstruction in 5 of 30 independent runs, recovering on average 8.53 ± 0.90 correct fixed points with no spurious attractors. Baselines recovered up to 10 fixed points but produced 8–31 spurious attractors. Robustness to λ within a practical range (≤0.01) observed, indicating stability of both performance and inferred network structure.

Conclusion: The proposed differentiable learning framework effectively enforces prescribed fixed-point dynamics and yields stable, sparse, binary threshold networks with superior attractor quality compared to standard classifiers, suggesting broad applicability to dynamical constraint-guided gene network inference.

Abstract: We present a learning algorithm for inferring threshold Boolean networks (TBNs) with a prescribed set of fixed points. The proposed method employs a custom differentiable loss function that jointly enforces fixed point preservation, penalizes spurious attractors, encourages binary outputs, and promotes sparsity through L1 regularization. Applied to the FOS-GRN model of Arabidopsis thaliana, the approach achieved perfect reconstruction (i.e., all 10 desired fixed points and no spurious ones) in 5 out of 30 independent runs, recovering on average 8.53 $\pm$ 0.90 correct fixed points with no spurious attractors. In contrast, standard methods such as the Perceptron and Logistic Regression recovered up to 10 fixed points but introduced between 8 and 31 spurious ones. An additional analysis varying the sparsity coefficient ($λ$) confirmed that the method's performance and the structural properties of the inferred networks remain robust within a practical range (up to 0.01) of regularization strengths. Overall, the results demonstrate the effectiveness and stability of the proposed algorithm in capturing meaningful network dynamics under prescribed dynamical constraints.

</details>


### [179] [Improving Generalization and Robustness in Offline Reinforcement Learning via Boundary-Aware Data Augmentation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20300)
*Gong Gao,Weidong Zhao,Xianhui Liu*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: BADA is a boundary-aware data augmentation method for offline RL that uses neighboring states to create interpolation boundaries and generate synthetic data, improving generalization and robustness and achieving state-of-the-art results on limited offline datasets.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Offline RL models tend to overfit and exhibit poor in-distribution generalization and robustness under distribution shifts. Regularization techniques from CV are not sufficient due to high sensitivity of low-level physical signals to shifts. A distribution-preserving augmentation guided by state geometry is needed.

Method: The paper provides a theoretical analysis of error bounds for the behavior policy and Q-function under random episode interpolation, showing the error scales with state-distance. Based on this, BADA constructs interpolation boundaries using neighboring states to generate synthetic samples that respect the original data distribution. Qualitative studies in a toy environment assess policy smoothness and multimodal value distributions; extensive experiments on limited offline datasets demonstrate strong performance.

Result: BADA achieves state-of-the-art performance across diverse offline RL benchmarks; it produces mixed samples that preserve desirable policy smoothness and accurately reconstruct multimodal value distributions, indicating improved in-distribution generalization and robustness in data-scarce regimes.

Conclusion: Boundary-aware data augmentation provides a distribution-preserving mechanism for improving offline RL stability and performance, suggesting that leveraging local state geometry to constrain synthetic data is an effective strategy for in-distribution generalization and robustness.

Abstract: Current offline reinforcement learning (ORL) algorithms tend to overfit the training dataset and exhibit poor in-distribution generalization and robustness performance when deployed to real environments, thus compromising their effectiveness. Existing methods typically enhance in-distribution generalization and robustness by leveraging regularization techniques widely used in computer vision. However, due to the high sensitivity of low-level physical signals to distributional shifts, these methods still suffer from notable limitations in in-distribution generalization and robustness, making it difficult to achieve stable performance in complex environments. To address this issue, we theoretically analyze the error bounds of the behavior policy and action-value function trained with random episode interpolation, revealing that the error scales positively correlated with the distance between states. Based on this insight, we propose a method called $\bf{B}$oundary-$\bf{A}$ware $\bf{D}$ata $\bf{A}$ugmentation (BADA), which leverages neighboring states to construct interpolation boundaries, enabling the generation of synthetic data that more faithfully preserves the original data distribution. We first conduct qualitative studies in a toy environment, showing that BADA generates mixed samples that preserve desirable policy smoothness while accurately reconstructing multimodal value distributions. Extensive experiments on limited offline datasets further demonstrate that BADA attains state-of-the-art performance across diverse benchmarks.

</details>


### [180] [SAGG: Sample-Adaptive Gradient Gating for Robust Multimodal Learning under Heterogeneous Corruption](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20302)
*Wentao Zhang,Yifan Zhu,Yutong Zhang,Wentao Mo*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Under sample-heterogeneous corruption in multimodal learning, batch-level, shared-modulation gradient methods introduce an irreducible bias; per-sample all-or-nothing gating is unbiased. The authors propose SAGG, a sample-adaptive gradient gating mechanism with online feature-norm testing and truncation, proving convergence to clean-loss stationary points at O(1/√T) and establishing a robustness certificate for independent encoders. Empirically, SAGG outperforms existing methods on Kinetics-Sounds and UCF-101 under noise, missing modalities, and imbalance, especially at high corruption.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To address bias introduced by batch-level, sample-agnostic gradient modulation under heterogeneous corruption, which undermines learning in multimodal models; aim to design a method that adaptively gates samples to align with clean gradients and provide theoretical guarantees.

Method: 1) Theoretical analysis showing irreducible bias for batch-level linear estimators with shared modulation under sample-heterogeneous corruption. 2) Propose Sample-Adaptive Gradient Gating (SAGG): per-sample binary retain/discard decisions via online feature-norm quality test and a truncation mechanism for variance control. 3) Theoretical results: SAGG-SGD converges at O(1/√T) to stationary points of the clean loss without corruption-dependent error floor. 4) Derive a certified robustness radius for the independent-encoder architecture linking per-modality Lipschitz constants to classification margin. 5) Empirical evaluation on Kinetics-Sounds and UCF-101 with Gaussian noise, missing modalities, and contribution imbalance. 

Result: SAGG eliminates the corruption-induced bias that plagues batch-level, shared-modulation gradient methods by gating samples at the individual level. It achieves standard SGD convergence rates to the clean loss and provides a robustness certificate for architectures with independently encoded modalities. Empirically, SAGG consistently outperforms ten baselines, with the largest gains in high-corruption regimes.

Conclusion: Per-sample gating is essential to avoid irreducible bias from batch-level modulation under heterogeneous corruption. SAGG provides a principled online gating strategy with variance control, guaranteed convergence, and robustness, backed by strong empirical gains on large video datasets under various corruptions.

Abstract: Multimodal gradient balancing methods modulate encoder gradients with a shared scalar per modality, implicitly assuming that corruption is uniform across the training batch. In practice, corruption is sample-heterogeneous: within a single mini-batch, different samples may have different modalities corrupted. We prove that under this heterogeneous corruption model, any batch-level sample-agnostic linear estimator with a shared modulation parameter incurs an irreducible bias with respect to the clean-data gradient, and that sample-level all-or-nothing gating is the unique unbiased strategy within a natural distribution-free estimator class. Motivated by this result, we propose Sample-Adaptive Gradient Gating (SAGG), which makes a binary retain-or-discard decision per sample via an online feature-norm quality test and incorporates a truncation mechanism for variance control. We prove that SAGG-based SGD converges at the standard O(1/sqrt(T)) rate to stationary points of the clean loss without a corruption-dependent error floor, and derive a certified robustness radius for the independent-encoder architecture that connects per-modality Lipschitz constants to the classification margin. Experiments on Kinetics-Sounds and UCF-101 under Gaussian noise injection, partial modality missing, and natural contribution imbalance show that SAGG consistently outperforms ten existing methods, with the largest gains in high-corruption regimes where batch-level bias is most severe.

</details>


### [181] [Hypernetwork-Parameterized Spatially Adaptive Neural Operators for PDE Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20309)
*Jiaquan Zhang,Chaoning Zhang,Shuxu Chen,Meng Ye,Xiaofeng Zhang,Qiang He,Weifeng Huang,Guoqing Wang,Yang Yang,Caiyan Qin*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A spatially adaptive neural operator (SANO) introduces a continuous field of location-dependent operator parameters to better model spatial heterogeneity in PDEs, using Fourier-encoded coordinates, a coordinate-conditioned hypernetwork, Hyper-Neural Element interpolation, and partition-of-unity assembly, achieving consistent gains over baselines across 1D–3D PDEs and perforated domains.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To address underfitting in spatially shared neural operators, especially near boundaries and high-gradient regions in spatially heterogeneous PDEs, by enabling locally varying update rules that adapt across space.

Method: SANO replaces a single global operator with a spatially continuous field of operator parameters generated by a coordinate-conditioned hypernetwork using Fourier-encoded coordinates. It introduces Hyper-Neural Elements (HNE) to interpolate these operator-conditioning codes within local subregions, coupling neighboring operators. Overlapping local predictions are assembled via partition-of-unity weights.

Result: Empirical evaluation on 1D, 2D, 3D PDEs and perforated-domain elliptic benchmarks shows that SANO consistently outperforms competitive neural-operator, hypernetwork-based, and physics-informed baselines.

Conclusion: Spatially varying operator update rules, realized through a coordinate-conditioned hypernetwork and HNE interpolation with partition-of-unity assembly, yield improved accuracy for spatially heterogeneous PDEs across diverse settings.

Abstract: Spatially heterogeneous partial differential equations (PDEs) exhibit location-dependent dynamics arising from variations in geometry and physical coefficients. Existing neural operators improve localized modeling through multiscale features, attention mechanisms, or domain decomposition, yet their update rules often remain spatially shared. Hypernetwork-based methods adapt parameters across PDE instances but typically generate only one global parameterization per instance. Consequently, shared operators may underfit boundaries and high-gradient regions, with these localized errors accumulating during autoregressive rollout. We propose a spatially adaptive neural operator (SANO), which replaces this spatially shared parameterization with a spatially continuous field of location-dependent operator parameters. SANO uses Fourier-encoded coordinates and a coordinate-conditioned hypernetwork to generate spatial operator-conditioning codes at sampling points. A Hyper-Neural Element (HNE) mechanism interpolates these codes within local subregions, coupling neighboring operators while allowing their update rules to vary across space, and partition-of-unity weights assemble the overlapping local predictions. Experiments on one-, two-, and three-dimensional PDEs and two perforated-domain elliptic benchmarks show that SANO consistently outperforms competitive neural-operator, hypernetwork-based, and physics-informed baselines.

</details>


### [182] [ZeroHAT: Behavior-Conditioned Zero-Shot Human Activity Trace Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20310)
*Rongchao Xu,Dahai Yu,Lin Jiang,Guang Wang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: ZeroHAT is a zero-shot framework that generates synthetic human activity traces for a target region by transferring behavioral patterns from source regions and leveraging public contextual information. It focuses on consistency-aware intent extraction, cross-region behavioral cloning, and behavior-conditioned activity realization, achieving substantially higher downstream utility and fidelity than baselines across a ten-city benchmark.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Large-scale human activity traces (HATs) are costly and privacy-sensitive, and many regions lack real HAT data. Zero-shot synthetic HAT generation aims to enable data availability for new regions without region-specific training data by transferring patterns from other regions and using publicly available contextual information.

Method: ZeroHAT comprises three components: (i) a multidimensional consistency-aware intent extractor to infer user intents across dimensions, (ii) a cross-region behavioral cloning module to transfer learned patterns from source to target regions, and (iii) a behavior-conditioned activity realization module to generate activities conditioned on inferred intents and regional context. Evaluation is conducted on a ten-city benchmark comparing against baselines.

Result: ZeroHAT achieves 4.5-6.4x the normalized downstream utility of the strongest baseline and improves average fidelity by 15.6%-40.8% across target regions.

Conclusion: The framework demonstrates effective zero-shot synthetic HAT generation by leveraging cross-region behavioral patterns and contextual information, offering substantial utility gains and fidelity improvements over existing methods, and enabling data synthesis for regions lacking real HAT data.

Abstract: Human activity traces record individuals' timestamped visits to points of interest and are essential for applications such as mobility prediction and urban simulation. However, accessing large-scale HATs is challenging due to high collection costs and privacy concerns. Synthetic HAT generation offers a promising way to make such data available and has attracted growing interest from both industry and academia. Although many efforts have been devoted to this topic, most of them rely on real data from a region to generate synthetic data for the same region, which is infeasible for the many regions where real HATs are unavailable. To fill this gap, we propose ZeroHAT, a behavior-conditioned framework that generates synthetic HATs for a target region in a zero-shot manner by transferring behavioral patterns learned from real HATs in source regions and adapting them with publicly available contextual information about the target region. ZeroHAT has three key novel components: (i) a multidimensional consistency-aware intent extractor; (ii) a cross-region behavioral cloning module; and (iii) a behavior-conditioned activity realization module. We evaluate ZeroHAT on a ten-city benchmark, where extensive experiments show that ZeroHAT achieves 4.5-6.4x the normalized downstream utility of the strongest baseline and improves average fidelity by 15.6%-40.8% across target regions.

</details>


### [183] [EviRec: Continual Evidence Learning for Dual Cold-Start POI Recommendation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20313)
*Rongchao Xu,Lin Jiang,Guang Wang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: EviRec presents a continual evidence-learning approach for dual cold-start POI recommendation, leveraging per-candidate evidence reliability with three views, achieving strong gains, especially in cold-start settings.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: POI systems suffer from POI churn, user turnover, category drift, and memory decay; conventional static models fail to adapt to evolving environments, motivating continual dual cold-start recommendation.

Method: Proposes EviRec, which estimates per-candidate evidence, scoring candidates via three views: matching (recent mobility), transition-memory (repeated routines), and lifecycle (candidate maturity); applies a reliability gate based on observation state to route between transition-memory and lifecycle evidence.

Result: Evaluated on a year-long five-city POI check-in dataset with 30k+ users and 684k trajectories; EviRec outperforms baselines, with notable gains in cold-start queries; NDCG@10 improves by 20.4% on Dual-New cases; analysis attributes gains to the reliability gate and preserving mobility routines.

Conclusion: EviRec is effective for continual dual cold-start POI recommendation, demonstrating the value of candidate-specific reliability gating and multi-view evidence integration to adapt to evolving POI and user dynamics.

Abstract: Point-of-Interest (POI) recommendation is a core task in location-based services, yet most existing methods assume a fixed user population and POI catalog. Through a large-scale data-driven analysis of 10 U.S. cities, we identify substantial POI churn, user turnover, category drift, and decay in static POI memory, motivating the study of continual dual cold-start POI recommendation. To address this setting, we propose EviRec, a continual evidence-learning framework that estimates how much historical evidence should be trusted separately for each candidate POI. EviRec scores each visible candidate from three complementary views: a matching view based on the user's recent mobility profile, a transition-memory view that captures repeated mobility routines, and a lifecycle view that reflects candidate maturity. Because a near-zero transition score may indicate either irrelevance or insufficient observation, EviRec qualifies the evidence using each candidate's observation state and applies a reliability gate to adaptively route between transition-memory and lifecycle evidence. We evaluate EviRec on a full-year, five-city POI check-in dataset containing more than 30,000 users and 684,200 trajectories. Experimental results show that EviRec consistently outperforms state-of-the-art baselines, with the largest gains concentrated on cold-start queries. In particular, EviRec improves NDCG@10 by 20.4\% on Dual-New cases over the strongest baseline. In-depth analyses further confirm that these gains arise primarily from candidate-specific reliability gating while largely preserving previously learned mobility routines.

</details>


### [184] [Sharp Reconstruction Bounds for Autoencoders Using the Same Forward Map](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20333)
*Patricia Medina,Hy P. G. Lam*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Sharp bound on the uniform reconstruction-derivative error for autoencoders with the same forward map before/after zeroing observed coordinates; the bound depends on the Jacobian singular values [m,M] and is attained by affine maps; a translated radial rotation can reconstruct balls exactly with singular values near 1; LiDAR experiments validate the bound and show dramatic improvement when adding one hidden coordinate.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Characterize fundamental limits on reconstruction under coordinate masking and spectral constraints on the forward map; understand how Jacobian singular values constrain reconstruction error and the necessity of extra conditions for finite-data bounds.

Method: Theoretical analysis for equal odd input and hidden dimensions d≥3, considering orientation-preserving diffeomorphisms with Jacobian singular values in [m,M]. Derives the worst-case reconstruction-derivative error as max{1 - M(M - m)/2, 0}, with affine maps attaining the bound at arbitrary depth. Demonstrates that a translated radial rotation can realize exact ball reconstruction with singular values arbitrarily close to 1. Proposes conditions for finite-data bounds and validates predictions on a 798,452-point LiDAR forest scan; reports scale-based empirical results.

Result: The least uniform reconstruction-derivative error is max{1 - M(M - m)/2, 0}. Affine maps attain this bound at every depth. A translated radial rotation can reconstruct any ball exactly with singular values near 1. In LiDAR data at input scale 0.05, the theoretical mean bound is 0.155, about 84% of the mean training error 0.185 across regions, depths, and seeds; adding one hidden coordinate reduces the mean reconstruction error to below 6×10^-6.

Conclusion: The work establishes sharp, scale-invariant bounds on reconstruction error under specified Jacobian spectral constraints, with affine maps achieving the bound and more expressive operators capable of exact local reconstructions under near-identity spectral conditions. Finite-data generalization requires additional regularity beyond the Jacobian-spectral assumptions; empirical results corroborate the theory and highlight the impact of hidden-dimension augmentation.

Abstract: We study reconstruction in autoencoders that apply the same forward map before and after setting the observed coordinates to zero. For equal odd input and hidden dimensions $d\geq 3$, among orientation-preserving diffeomorphisms whose Jacobian singular values lie in $[m,M]$, we show that the least uniform reconstruction-derivative error is $\max\{1-M(M-m)/2,0\}$, with affine maps attaining this sharp bound at every prescribed depth. A translated radial rotation can nevertheless reconstruct any prescribed ball exactly with singular values arbitrarily close to one, motivating additional conditions for a finite-data bound. We test this prediction on a 798,452-point terrestrial LiDAR forest scan. At input scale $0.05$, the mean theoretical bound is $0.155$, about $84\%$ of the mean normalized training error $0.185$ across four spatial regions, two depths, and three seeds. At this scale, adding one hidden coordinate reduces the mean reconstruction error below $6\times10^{-6}$.

</details>


### [185] [COMPASS: Ordered Clustered Routing at 100K Scale](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20352)
*Ido Greenberg,Hugo Linsenmaier,Piotr Sielski,Shie Mannor,Alex Fender,Gal Chechik,Eli Meirom*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: COMPASS is a learning-accelerated, parallel sub-solver approach for the Ordered Clustered Traveling Salesman Problem (OCTSP). It scales by exploiting cluster structure, can reach exact solutions with time exponential in cluster size, and empirically outperforms alternatives on large synthetic and real asymmetric-distance data.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: OCTSP arises in large-scale routing where clusters must be visited in a prescribed order. Independent cluster optimization misses non-local dependencies; there is a need for scalable solvers that can handle general distance matrices and leverage structure as compute grows.

Method: COMPASS orchestrates parallel sub-solvers with a learning-augmented search component, enabling learning-accelerated routing. It exploits the clustered structure, uses general distance matrices (not limited to coordinates), and yields solutions with no predefined quality ceiling. Exact solutions are theoretically reachable with time exponential in cluster size rather than instance size.

Result: Empirically, COMPASS consistently outperforms alternative methods. It scales to 100k synthetic nodes and 28.5k real e-commerce nodes, achieving the largest reported routing solution over asymmetric distances (9x beyond established ATSP benchmarks).

Conclusion: COMPASS provides a scalable, general OCTSP solver with improving solution quality as compute increases, capable of exactness within cluster-size-exponential time and applicable beyond coordinate-based inputs.

Abstract: Large-scale routing often requires visiting clusters of nodes in a prescribed order, giving rise to the Ordered Clustered Traveling Salesman Problem (OCTSP). Optimizing each cluster independently seems natural, but misses non-local dependencies. We introduce the COMPASS algorithm for OCTSP, which combines search with learning-accelerated routing by orchestrating parallel sub-solvers. COMPASS has no quality ceiling and its solutions keep improving with compute. It exploits the clustered structure, and can reach exact solutions in time exponential in cluster size rather than instance size. Empirically, COMPASS consistently outperforms alternative methods. Unlike common large-scale routing solvers, COMPASS consumes general distance matrices and is not limited to coordinate inputs. We demonstrate scaling to 100K synthetic nodes and to 28.5K real e-commerce nodes. To our knowledge, the latter is the largest reported routing solution over asymmetric distances, 9x beyond established ATSP benchmarks.

</details>


### [186] [Minimax-Optimal Online Contract Design with Unrestricted Bounded Contracts](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20353)
*Rui Ai,David Simchi-Levi,Han Zhong*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Minimax regret in repeated principal–agent contracts with outcome-only signals scales as T^{m/(m+1)} for m outcomes (up to logs); using dimension reduction and revealed preference, a learning policy with Lipschitz parametrization achieves this rate under arbitrary actions and agent heterogeneity; each extra outcome increases learning cost.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Characterize learnability of contract design when the principal cannot observe agent actions, only outcomes, and quantify how outcome dimensionality affects regret.

Method: Derive an upper bound via effective-dimension reduction and normalization of the benchmark; show that revealed preference yields a monotone response map in payment-difference coordinates; construct a Lipschitz-parametrized learning policy based on observed outcome categories; extend to arbitrary action spaces and heterogeneous agents without smoothness/monotone-surplus assumptions. Prove a matching lower bound that captures accumulation of incentive losses across outcome dimensions.

Result: Regret over T rounds is of order T^{m/(m+1)} (up to logarithmic factors) for any m≥2; upper bound applies without smoothness or monotone-surplus assumptions; lower bound shows each additional contractible outcome raises the worst-case learning cost; effective-dimension reduction enables normalization even without shift-invariance.

Conclusion: Efficient learning in complex principal–agent settings is feasible with outcome-based payments by exploiting a monotone response structure in transformed coordinates; increasing the number of contractible outcomes inherently makes learning harder, delineating the fundamental cost of richer outcome spaces.

Abstract: We study repeated contract design when a principal observes outcomes but not the actions that generate them. The principal may use any bounded outcome-contingent payment vector, and the agent's best response can make expected profit discontinuous in those payments. For every fixed number $m\ge2$ of outcomes, the minimax regret over $T$ rounds is of order $T^{m/(m+1)}$, up to logarithmic factors. The upper bound allows arbitrary action spaces and agent heterogeneity, without smoothness or monotone-surplus assumptions. Its key is an effective-dimension reduction that the benchmark can be normalized even when fixed tie-breaking is not shift invariant, after which revealed preference yields a monotone response map in payment-difference coordinates. A learning policy built on a Lipschitz parametrization of this map attains the rate using only observed outcome categories. The lower-bound construction accounts for how incentive losses accumulate across outcome dimensions. It shows that each additional contractible outcome creates a precise and unavoidable increase in the worst-case cost of learning.

</details>


### [187] [Learning Principal-Agent Contracts for Equitable Smallholder Carbon Farming under Moral Hazard and Adverse Selection](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20404)
*Rishi Bharadwaj,Yadati Narahari*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Dynamic POMDP-based contract design with RL reveals that aggregators' pooled contracts exacerbate exclusion of smallholders in carbon farming; MRV costs drive disparity; area-proportional MRV could mitigate; policy implications.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Unlock the carbon sequestration potential of agricultural soils by engaging smallholder farmers. Despite their central role in South Asia and sub-Saharan Africa, real-world carbon programs often fail to reach them. The study models adverse selection (private adoption costs) and moral hazard (unobserved effort) in a multi-season context to inform contract design.

Method: Formulate the evolving contracting problem as a partially observable Markov decision process (POMDP) and apply reinforcement learning to learn a dynamic, profit-maximising contract. Perform simulations under varying conditions (farm size, MRV cost structure, counterfactuals) to assess performance.

Result: A profit-maximising aggregator does not merely exclude smallholders but amplifies exclusion: about 87.7% adoption on large farms vs 8.2% on smallholdings. MRV costs per hectare fall with farm size, and pooling contracts worsen this gradient. A counterfactual with purely area-proportional MRV costs eliminates the disparity.

Conclusion: Contract and policy design should account for heterogeneity and MRV cost structures to avoid systematically excluding smallholders. Dynamic, data-driven contracting informed by POMDP/RL can help broaden smallholder access to carbon income while enabling scalable soil carbon mitigation.

Abstract: Agricultural soils are a major untapped carbon sink. Carbon farming is emerging as a promising practice for tapping this potential. Smallholder farmers, who dominate agriculture across South Asia and sub-Saharan Africa, are key to scaling climate mitigation via carbon farming. It is ironic that real-world carbon programs largely fail to reach them. We study this important gap through the lens of contract design. An aggregator offers a single pooled contract to a heterogeneous population of smallholder farmers who have private adoption costs (adverse selection) and exert unobserved effort (moral hazard), with agronomic outcomes evolving over multiple seasons. We formulate this evolving contracting problem as a POMDP and use reinforcement learning to learn a dynamic profit-maximising contract. We analyse the performance of the aggregator under various conditions. We find that a profit-maximising aggregator does not merely inherit the exclusion of smallholders, it amplifies it. On large farms the aggregator realises 87.7% of achievable adoption, against only 8.2% on smallholdings. Per-hectare Measurement, Reporting and Verification (MRV) costs fall as farm size rises, and the aggregator's pooling contract compounds this gradient rather than offsetting it. A counterfactual that makes MRV costs purely area-proportional eliminates this disparity. Our results and simulation can guide contract and policy design that opens carbon income to smallholders while enabling agricultural soils to contribute to climate mitigation at scale.

</details>


### [188] [The Bias of Nonlinear Two-Time-scale Stochastic Approximation under Constant Step-Sizes](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20409)
*Djamel Rassem Lamouri,Dorian Baudry,Nicolas Gast*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: For nonlinear two-timescale stochastic approximation with fast step α and slow step β (α ≫ β) under standard assumptions, the mean-squared error and bias of both iterates around their equilibria are bounded by O(α + β^2/α^2); this bound is tight when β ≤ α^{3/2}. The analysis isolates contributions from initial conditions, fast-timescale tracking, Markovian noise, and coupling, revealing finite-time effects unique to nonlinear dynamics that are absent in the linear TTSA setting.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Finite-time guarantees for nonlinear two-timescale stochastic approximation with constant step-sizes are challenging and important for understanding and designing coupled learning/optimization algorithms in RL, control, and related fields.

Method: The authors study nonlinear TTSA with α ≫ β under standard stability, regularity, and Markovian noise assumptions. They derive upper bounds on the mean-squared error and bias for both iterates around their limiting equilibria, decomposing the error into contributions from initial conditions, fast-timescale tracking, Markovian dependence, and timescale coupling; they also establish a tightness result for β ≤ α^{3/2}.

Result: The mean-squared error and bias scale as O(α + β^2/α^2). The derived bound is tight in the regime β ≤ α^{3/2}, and the analysis clarifies that a β^2/α^2 term arises from the interaction of initial conditions, fast tracking, and noise under nonlinear dynamics. This reveals qualitative differences from the linear TTSA setting, where such finite-time effects may be absent.

Conclusion: Nonlinear TTSA exhibits finite-time effects not present in the linear case, due to nonlinear dynamics and timescale coupling. The results provide precise error decomposition and guidance on step-size selection (α, β) to balance bias and variance in nonlinear two-timescale algorithms.

Abstract: Two-timescale stochastic approximation (TTSA) is a fundamental tool for analyzing coupled iterative algorithms in reinforcement learning, optimization, and stochastic control. However, finite-time guarantees for nonlinear two-timescale schemes remain difficult to obtain, especially under constant step-sizes. In this paper, we study nonlinear TTSA with step-sizes $α\ggβ$. Under standard stability, regularity, and Markovian noise assumptions, we upper bound the mean-squared error and the bias of both iterates around their limiting equilibria. Our bounds scale as $O(α+β^2/α^2)$, which we prove to be tight when $β\leα^{3/2}$. The analysis separates the contributions of initial conditions, fast-timescale tracking error, Markovian dependence, and timescale coupling, thereby clarifying the origin of the $β^2/α^2$ term. Our results reveal qualitative differences from the linear TTSA setting previously studied, showing that nonlinear dynamics introduce additional finite-time effects that are absent in the linear case.

</details>


### [189] [SCGFM-ART: Amortized Relational Transport for Structure-Centric Graph Foundation Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20419)
*Xiaodong He,Xincheng Wang,Zhao Kang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: SCGFM-ART introduces a structure-centric GFM that maps heterogeneous graphs onto a shared relational atlas via Amortized Relational Transport, enabling robust cross-domain transfer with fast test-time inference by avoiding iterative alignment.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Severe domain shifts in topology, scale, and feature semantics hinder a unified, domain-agnostic representation space across graphs; a universal relational atlas and end-to-end transport plans can unify representations.

Method: Define a finite relational atlas of landmarks (bases). Train a model to predict end-to-end transport plans from graphs to the atlas (amortized). Represent each graph globally via coordinates to the atlas and locally via node-to-role correspondences. Model graphs and atlas bases as finite measured relational spaces, derive coordinate fidelity, stability, and amortized coverage bounds; bypass iterative Gromov-Wasserstein optimization at test time.

Result: Achieves state-of-the-art transferability on 14 cross-domain tasks, with average ranks of 2.29 (transferability) and 1.14 (node-level). Topological perturbation shows node-role transport preserves local structure beyond global coords. Amortized inference yields 44.2–85.1x faster frozen target-domain inference by avoiding iterative alignment.

Conclusion: SCGFM-ART delivers a scalable, interpretable, and fast framework for cross-domain graph representation learning, with theoretical guarantees and strong empirical transferability, leveraging a universal relational atlas and amortized transport to align heterogeneous graphs.

Abstract: Graph foundation models (GFMs) aim to learn transferable representations across severely heterogeneous graph domains. However, severe domain shifts in topology, graph scale, and feature semantics impede the construction of a unified, domain-agnostic representation space. To address this, we propose SCGFM-ART, a structure-centric GFM framework that aligns arbitrary graphs onto a shared relational atlas via Amortized Relational Transport (ART). The relational atlas serves as a universal coordinate system defined by a finite set of relational landmarks (bases), while ART directly predicts reusable, end-to-end graph-to-base transport plans, bypassing costly runtime Gromov-Wasserstein optimizations. Under this formulation, SCGFM-ART decomposes a graph into a unified representation: globally via its relational response coordinates relative to the atlas, and locally via its node-to-role structural correspondences. These correspondences project disparate node attributes into a canonical role space, resolving structural and semantic heterogeneity within a singular alignment interface. Rigorously modeling graphs and atlas bases as finite measured relational spaces, we establish coordinate fidelity bounds, prove stability under predicted transport plans, and derive an amortized coverage bound that guarantees our learning objective tightly surrogates ideal relational coverage. Benchmarked across 14 cross-domain graph- and node-level classification tasks, SCGFM-ART achieves state-of-the-art transferability, securing superior average ranks of 2.29 and 1.14, respectively. Topological perturbation analyses demonstrate that node-role transport retains fine-grained structural nuances beyond global coordinates. On real-world benchmarks, the amortized formulation yields 44.2 to 85.1 times faster frozen target-domain inference by avoiding iterative alignment at test time.

</details>


### [190] [Seismic Site Response Prediction from Sparse Observations Using Finite-Element-Pretrained Latent Dynamics](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20451)
*Yi Zhu,Su Chen,Xiaojun Li*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A data-efficient framework (FLARE-T) uses a transfer-enabled latent autoencoder to learn low-dimensional input–output dynamics from dense simulations and calibrate them with limited field records for improved multi-depth site-response predictions.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Numerical site-response models often misfit observations due to limited sensor coverage and events; there is a need for data-efficient calibration that leverages simulations and sparse field data.

Method: FLARE-T learns a low-dimensional response manifold and input-driven dynamics from dense FE simulations, trains a sparse encoder to map simulated sensor responses into the latent coordinates, and calibrates the dynamics using limited records. A short response window initializes predictions while full base motion drives the response.

Result: On layered-soil centrifuge tests and Lotung vertical array, FLARE-T improves multi-depth acceleration histories and 5%-damped pseudoacceleration spectra versus original FE models, reducing errors at all sensors across motion intensities; comparable accuracy with different Lotung constitutive parameters suggests reduced dependence on precise prior calibration.

Conclusion: FLARE-T provides a data-efficient approach that fuses dense numerical response information with sparse field data to enhance future site-response predictions.

Abstract: Numerical site-response predictions often deviate from observations, yet correcting these discrepancies is difficult because records are limited in both sensor coverage and number of events. This study proposes the Transfer-Enabled Forced Latent Autoencoder for Response Equations (FLARE-T) to improve these predictions by learning and calibrating low-dimensional latent dynamics that connect the base acceleration input to acceleration outputs at multiple depths. FLARE-T learns a low-dimensional response manifold and input-driven dynamics from dense finite-element simulations. It then trains a sparse encoder to map simulated sensor responses into the learned coordinates and uses limited records to calibrate the dynamics within them. A short response window initializes each prediction, while the complete base motion drives the response. The framework was evaluated using a layered-soil centrifuge test and the Lotung field vertical array. Test-set results show that FLARE-T improved multi-depth acceleration histories and 5%-damped pseudoacceleration response spectra relative to the original finite-element models, reducing errors at every evaluated sensor for motions of different intensities and, at Lotung, for both horizontal components. Two Lotung source models with different constitutive parameters achieved comparable test-set accuracy, indicating reduced dependence on precise prior calibration. FLARE-T therefore provides a data-efficient means of combining dense numerical response information with limited field records to improve future site-response predictions.

</details>


### [191] [Training Neural Networks to Approach the Optimum Bayes Estimator in Dense Multi-Emitter Localization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20465)
*Yi Sun,Mona Sharifi,Muzna Yumman*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Neural networks trained on synthetic frames can approximate the Bayes-optimal estimator for dense emitter localization, supporting the potential of data-driven approaches for high-throughput, large-FOV super-resolution SMLM.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Address the challenge of accurate, scalable emitter localization in dense, fast-changing scenes and enable high-throughput, large field-of-view super-resolution imaging by approximating the Bayes estimator with learned models.

Method: Supervised training of neural networks on simulated microscopy frames with known emitter positions, aiming to minimize localization error and approximate the Bayes estimator under dense emitter conditions.

Result: Demonstrates that neural networks can approach Bayes-optimal localization performance on synthetic data, justifying further development toward scalable, high-throughput SMLM.

Conclusion: Training neural networks on synthetic frames is a promising path toward achieving high-throughput, large-FOV, super spatiotemporal resolution SMLM; motivates future work to refine models and assess real-data performance.

Abstract: We train neural networks on synthesized frames to approach the optimum Bayes estimator for dense emitter localization. The result justifies the future work on training neural networks to achieve high-throughput large-FOV super spatiotemporal resolution SMLM.

</details>


### [192] [Deep Learning-Based Classification of Cognitive and Resting States Using Electroencephalography Signals](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20467)
*K. A. Januka S. Fernando,Harshit Srivastava*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A CNN-GRU deep learning framework with time-frequency features classifies resting vs cognitive EEG states (math, memory, music) and outperforms baseline methods, achieving ~83% accuracy for resting vs math/music and ~76% for resting vs memory.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Understand fluctuations between resting and task-related brain activity and enable automated pattern extraction from EEG using deep learning.

Method: A CNN stacked with a GRU extracts features from EEG; time-frequency analysis performed; features evaluated with conventional deep learning/machine learning classifiers, including a proposed 2D-Net architecture.

Result: Resting-versus-mathematical task: 83.177% accuracy; resting-versus-memory task: 76.107%; resting-versus-music task: 83.432%. The approach outperforms evaluated comparative methods.

Conclusion: Integrating signal processing with deep learning is effective for distinguishing resting from cognitive states in EEG.

Abstract: The categorization of cognitive and resting states derived from electroencephalography (EEG) signals is crucial for comprehending fluctuations in brain activity linked to various mental states. EEG provides a non-intrusive approach for documenting brain function in both resting and task-oriented cognitive conditions, whilst deep learning techniques enable the automatic extraction of significant patterns from intricate EEG data. This study presents a deep learning framework to distinguish between resting and cognitive states through EEG records. The proposed framework integrates a Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) stacked with a Gated Recurrent Unit (GRU) for the extraction of features from EEG signals. Time-frequency analysis is conducted to explore the salient aspects of signals, and the derived features are then assessed utilizing conventional deep learning and machine learning classifiers, including the suggested 2D-Net architecture. The proposed approach and feature extraction strategy outperform the evaluated comparative methods, achieving accuracies of 83.177% for resting-versus-mathematical task classification, 76.107% for resting-versus-memory task classification, and 83.432% for resting-versus-music task classification. The findings illustrate the efficacy of integrating signal processing with deep learning methodologies to discriminate resting from cognitive states utilizing EEG signals.

</details>


### [193] [Distributionally Robust Federated Learning with Multi-Source Data](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20501)
*Yingzhu Liu,Zhongkui Li,Pengcheng You,Ashish Cherukuri*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Federated learning robust to cross-client mixture uncertainty and within-client distributional ambiguity by constructing a global ambiguity set as a union of local mixtures, enabling a separable reformulation, a penalty-based algorithm with convergence guarantees, and high-probability generalization bounds; validated by simulations.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Data heterogeneity across clients and finite samples render the true mixture unknown and local distributions uncertain; existing worst-case approaches assuming accurate client-wise distributions can be brittle; a framework that handles both cross-client and within-client uncertainty with client-specific radii and scalable optimization is needed.

Method: Define a global ambiguity set as the union of admissible mixtures of local ambiguity sets (with client-specific radii); derive a client-wise separable reformulation; develop a penalty-based federated optimization algorithm; prove convergence under mild regularity conditions; establish high-probability out-of-sample guarantees.

Result: The approach yields a high-probability performance bound and simulations demonstrate the method’s effectiveness in robust federated learning under distributional uncertainty.

Conclusion: The proposed union-ambiguous federated framework provides robust performance and scalable optimization with provable guarantees under cross-client and within-client distributional ambiguity.

Abstract: Federated learning trains a shared model from private client data. In practice, data-generating distributions may differ, and the true mixture across clients is often unknown, making the underlying group distribution difficult to specify. Existing approaches address cross-client mixture uncertainty by optimizing against the worst-case mixture, yet assume accurate client-wise distribution estimates. However, these estimates can be unreliable when based on finite samples. To handle both cross-client mixture uncertainty and within-client distributional ambiguity, we construct a global ambiguity set as the union of admissible mixtures of local ambiguity sets. The construction allows client-specific ambiguity radii and admits a client-wise separable reformulation. Leveraging this structure, we establish a high-probability out-of-sample performance guarantee. We further develop a federated algorithm for a penalty-based reformulation and prove its convergence under milder regularity conditions. Simulations validate the algorithm's effectiveness.

</details>


### [194] [Radio Frequency Detection and Classification of Microplastics in Water](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20507)
*Jaden Tolbert,Md Saiful Islam,Pingshan Wang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: ML-assisted RF dielectric spectroscopic cytometry enables label-free, single-particle classification of microplastics; robust multi-class performance (macro-F1, precision, recall > ~0.71) in DI water and saline media across 0.2–9 GHz.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Growing prevalence of micro- and nano-plastics and the need for rapid, label-free detection methods; conventional optical/spectroscopic techniques face throughput and sample-prep challenges at low micrometer sizes; RF dielectric sensing with ML could enable high-throughput, non-invasive MP classification.

Method: Dielectric DiSC platform measures RF scattering (S-parameters) of single MP particles across 0.2–9 GHz, relative to carrier medium. Eight MP classes (~10 μm) in DI water; features derived from S-parameters used to train supervised ML models for material classification, including mixed samples and saline environments. Evaluation uses macro-averaged F1, precision, and recall; results stated for DI water and saline conditions.

Result: In DI water, macro-average F1, precision, and recall for eight MP classes exceed 0.71. PET classification remains robust in saline media with 3.3% and 6.6% sea salt, indicating environmental robustness of the approach.

Conclusion: Demonstrates feasibility of ML-assisted RF DiSC for rapid, single-particle MP classification in aqueous environments; future work to improve calibration, broaden spectral coverage, expand training data, and validate with environmentally aged and biologically contaminated microplastics.

Abstract: Micro- and nano-plastic particles (MPs/NPs) are ubiquitous environmental contaminants whose increasing abundance and potential health impacts have created an urgent need for rapid, label-free detection methods. As particle size decreases to the low-micrometer range, conventional optical and spectroscopic techniques become increasingly challenging because of limited throughput and/or complex sample preparation. In this work, we present a machine learning (ML)-assisted radio-frequency (RF) dielectric spectroscopic cytometry (DiSC) platform for the label-free detection and classification of MPs. Eight types of $ 10 $ μm nominal-diameter MP particles suspended in deionized (DI) water were characterized at four frequencies spanning $ 0.2\text{-}9\text{ GHz} $. The measured alterations in RF scattering parameters (S-parameters), referenced to the carrier medium, were used to train supervised ML models for material classification, including the identification of MPs in mixed samples and saline-water environments. For eight MP classes suspended in DI water, the proposed method achieved macro-average F1-score, precision, and recall values exceeding $ 0.71 $. Furthermore, PET classification performance was largely maintained in saline carrier media containing $3.3\% $ and $ 6.6\% $ sea salt. These results demonstrate the feasibility of ML-assisted RF DiSC for rapid, single-particle MP classification in aqueous environments. Future work will focus on improving classification performance through enhanced RF calibration, increased spectral coverage, larger training datasets, and validation using environmentally aged and biologically contaminated microplastics.

</details>


### [195] [When EOS Tokens Disagree: Understanding Length Inflation in On-Policy Distillation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20511)
*Yuxiao Yang,Tianrun Yu,Shangzhe Li,Kaixiang Zhao,Xuchao Zhang,Chetan Bansal,Huaxiu Yao,Taylor W. Killian,Weitong Zhang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: In on-policy distillation, termination-token mismatch between base students and post-trained teachers can cause length inflation; aligning functionally equivalent EOS tokens as a shared stopping action mitigates this across Qwen3, Llama, and Gemma; stage-wise training reveals shifting termination preferences and late-length inflation; an implementation of termination-handling corrections is released.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Address unexplained length inflation in OPD; prior work focusing on stopping-set alignment is insufficient; identify termination mismatch as a key source and propose a semantic sharing approach.

Method: Empirical analysis across three model families (Qwen3, Llama, Gemma); examine EOS/token stopping behavior; propose treating functionally equivalent EOS tokens as a single semantic stopping action; perform stage-wise (K2-Horizon) training analysis; provide a practical implementation.

Result: Stopping-set alignment alone is insufficient; semantic sharing of EOS tokens reduces length inflation across all models; training-stage analysis reveals substantial shifts in termination preferences and a persistent late-length inflation; termination mismatch identified as an important but not exhaustive source of OPD length dynamics.

Conclusion: Termination mismatch is a key contributor to OPD length dynamics; the proposed termination-handling corrections mitigate the issue; an implementation is released.

Abstract: We study length inflation in on-policy distillation (OPD), where student responses can become excessively long and even exhaust the generation budget.
