We identify \emph{termination-token mismatch} between base students and post-trained teachers as an important source of this behavior. Across Qwen3, Llama, and Gemma, the two models can place their stopping probability on different EOS tokens, even when their declared stopping sets are identical. This mismatch can suppress the student's preferred termination action without reliably transferring the teacher-preferred alternative. We show that aligning the decoding stopping set alone is insufficient, while treating functionally equivalent EOS tokens as a shared semantic stopping action substantially mitigates mismatch-induced length inflation across all three model families. To further understand how termination behavior evolves over training, we study OPD across different K2-Horizon training stages. This stage-wise analysis shows that termination preferences can shift substantially during training, while also revealing a distinct length inflation late in the OPD run that persists beyond termination alignment. Together, these results identify termination mismatch as an important, but not exhaustive, source of OPD length dynamics. We release an implementation incorporating the proposed termination-handling corrections.

</details>


### [196] [Parallelism, critical windows, and separations among diffusion language models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20539)
*Sitan Chen,Liye Wang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper provides a fine-grained, theory-driven comparison of parallel sampling across the three main dLLM diffusion paradigms (masked, uniform, Gaussian). It proves a fundamental separation in their sampling efficiency, linking forward passes to intrinsic distributional complexity.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To move beyond empirical claims and establish principled, quantitative limits on parallelism for diffusion-based language models, using information-theoretic measures and sampling-window analysis.

Method: The authors perform a theoretical analysis of forward-pass complexity for sampling with uniform, Gaussian, and masked diffusion. They show sampling efficiency scales with the dual total correlation of the distribution (for uniform/ Gaussian) and derive tight bounds under a family of random empirical measures. They compare required forward passes across paradigms and identify the critical sampling windows that govern parallelism.

Result: Uniform and Gaussian diffusion can sample in a number of forward passes that scales with the dual total correlation (often much smaller than the context length). For some random empirical measures, ~Θ~(√d) passes are necessary and sufficient for uniform/ Gaussian diffusion, while masked diffusion can require ~Ω(d) passes for certain approximate score oracles, establishing the first provable separation in parallelism among the three paradigms. The separation stems from narrower critical windows in masked diffusion rather than token-commitment. 

Conclusion: The study reframes parallelism across diffusion paradigms by tying efficiency to intrinsic distributional complexity and sampling-window properties. It predicts a pronounced performance gap: uniform/ Gaussian diffusion can be significantly more parallelizable than masked diffusion in certain regimes, guiding design choices for dLLMs and informing future theoretical and empirical work.

Abstract: A popular selling point of diffusion large language models (dLLMs) is their capacity for parallelism: the ability to generate sequences of text far more efficiently than autoregressive models, which require one forward pass per token. Yet among the many competing paradigms for dLLMs, from masked to uniform to Gaussian diffusion, principled understanding of how these different proposals compare in parallelism remains limited. In this work, we initiate a fine-grained comparison of the capacity for parallelism among these three leading approaches and prove the following:
  - Uniform and Gaussian diffusion can sample in a number of forward passes which scales with the dual total correlation of the underlying distribution, a measure of intrinsic complexity which can be much smaller than the context length. Previously, it was only known how to achieve this using masked diffusion.
  - For a certain family of random empirical measures, we show that $\widetildeΘ(\sqrt{d})$ forward passes are necessary and sufficient to sample using uniform or Gaussian diffusion, yet there exist approximate score oracles for which $\widetildeΩ(d)$ forward passes are needed for masked diffusion. This establishes the first provable separation in parallelism between the three prevailing dLLM paradigms.
  Contrary to popular intuition that masked diffusions are harder to parallelize because they must commit to token values, the latter separation instead comes from the fact that the critical windows in masked diffusion sampling are asymptotically narrower than those in uniform and Gaussian diffusion sampling.

</details>


### [197] [Mitigating Retaliatory Algorithmic Collusion in Repeated Games](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20548)
*Karthik Sivachandran,Rohan Paleja*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: CURB is a reward-shaping framework that detects and unwinds collusive equilibria in repeated games by penalizing policy dependence evidenced by the TV distance between an agent's cooperation and defection histories, converting SPC-induced equilibria to trivial, and reducing collusion in Q-learning and Deep Q-Networks in Bertrand and Cournot settings.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Address generalization gap in collusion mitigation beyond specific economic settings; connect empirical Q-learning collusion to Simple Penal Codes, and provide a general intervention method.

Method: Formalize link between SPCs and conditional dependence in agents' policies; use Total Variation distance between action distributions across history types as a signal; introduce CURB via reward shaping and belief injection that penalizes TV-distance; prove fixed-point conversion; apply to tabular Q-learning and extend to DQN.

Result: Empirically reduces collusion in Bertrand and Cournot repeated games for Q-learning; extends to deep Q-networks; evidence that CURB generalizes beyond tabular settings.

Conclusion: CURB offers a general, theoretically grounded intervention to unwind collusion in repeated-agent learning, scalable to more complex architectures, by penalizing history-dependent policy signals that sustain collusive equilibria while preserving learning dynamics.

Abstract: Reinforcement learning agents trained to maximize their own reward in repeated interactions can converge to supra-competitive outcomes resembling explicit collusion, without communication or shared design. Existing mitigation approaches are largely tied to specific economic settings, like two-sided platforms and auctions, leaving open how to design interventions for general repeated games. We address this gap by formalizing the connection between empirical observations from prior work on Q-learning collusion and classical theory of Simple Penal Codes (SPCs). We show any non-trivial SPC induces a quantifiable conditional dependence in agents' policies, detectable via the total variation distance between an agent's action distributions across cooperation and defection histories. Building on this connection, we propose CURB (Collusion Unwinding via Reward shaping and Belief injection), a reward-shaping framework that penalizes this Total Variation (TV) distance signal during Q-learning and is guaranteed to convert any SPC fixed point of the dynamics into a trivial one, thus precluding collusive equilibria sustained by punishment threats. Empirically, CURB substantially reduces collusion by Q-learning agents in both Bertrand and Cournot Competition Repeated Games. We further demonstrate that CURB extends to deep Q-network agents in Bertrand competition, suggesting the mechanism generalizes beyond tabular Q-learning.

</details>


### [198] [CrystalMO-TuRBO: Multi-Objective Trust-Region Bayesian Optimization for High-precision Joint Crystal Structure Refinement](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20592)
*Joseph Agada,Yishu Wang,Arpan Biswas*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Multi-objective Bayesian optimization (CrystalMO-TuRBO) for joint X-ray and neutron crystal-structure refinement using a two-phase trust-region approach to separate global search from local refinement, improving convergence and parameter precision.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Joint refinement of X-ray and neutron data is challenging due to non-convex, noisy, and highly correlated parameters; scalarized combinations of modalities with manual weighting lead to suboptimal solutions.

Method: Model X-ray and neutron discrepancies as separate objectives in a normalized maximization setting; Phase 1 global exploration with parallel TuRBO across multiple scalarizations; Phase 2 localized refinement within shrinking trust regions; explicit separation of global search and fine-tuning; evaluation on Ho2Ti2O7 diffraction data.

Result: Demonstrates improved convergence, robustness, and parameter precision compared to classical refinement methods and Bayesian baselines for a single-crystal pyrochlore system.

Conclusion: CrystalMO-TuRBO provides an effective multi-objective, two-phase optimization framework for joint diffraction data refinement, offering more accurate and robust parameter estimation than traditional single-objective or scalarized approaches.

Abstract: Crystal structure refinement is a fundamental inverse problem in materials characterization, where structural parameters are optimized to reproduce experimental diffraction data. Conventional approaches, such as least-squares and likelihood-based optimization, rely on local search and often struggle with non-convex, noisy, and highly correlated parameter landscapes, particularly when integrating multiple diffraction modalities. Joint refinement of X-ray and neutron data is especially challenging due to their complementary but competing sensitivities, which are typically combined through scalarized objectives requiring manual weighting and leading to suboptimal solutions. We propose CrystalMO-TuRBO, a multi-objective trust region Bayesian optimization architecture for joint crystal structure refinement. The method models X-ray and neutron discrepancies as separate objectives and transforms the problem into a normalized maximization setting. A two-phase optimization strategy is introduced: Phase 1 performs global exploration using parallel trust-region Bayesian optimization across multiple scalarizations to identify promising regions of the parameter space, while Phase 2 conducts localized refinement within a shrinking region to achieve high-precision solutions. This design explicitly separates global search from fine-grained optimization, addressing the unique accuracy requirements of refinement tasks. We evaluate the proposed method on experimentally collected X-ray and neutron diffraction data from single-crystal Ho2Ti2O7. Results demonstrate improved convergence, robustness, and parameter precision compared to classical refinement methods and Bayesian optimization baselines on refinement of a single-crystal pyrochlore material system.

</details>


### [199] [Recursive Quantum Long Short-Term Memory for Stable Short-Horizon Temperature Forecasting](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20594)
*Mu-En Lee,Yen-Ku Liu,Samuel Yen-Chi Chen,Yun-Cheng Tsai*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Recursive QLSTM improves stability and out-of-sample accuracy for weather time series forecasting compared to standard QLSTM in one-step-ahead daily temperature prediction.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Optimization variability due to random initialization and different temporal contexts in quantum recurrent models motivates exploring a recursive quantum feature transformation to enhance stability and generalization in compact quantum-classical temporal architectures.

Method: Compare recursive QLSTM against standard QLSTM on one-step-ahead prediction of daily min/max temperatures from Toronto data. Use identical training settings, 20 random seeds, and input windows of 8, 16, and 32 days. Evaluate convergence, predictive accuracy, and generalization with MAE, RMSE, and test loss.

Result: The recursive model consistently reaches near-optimal test loss earlier, reduces MAE and RMSE, and exhibits a smaller generalization gap compared to the standard QLSTM across tested window sizes and seeds.

Conclusion: Recursive quantum feature transformations can improve stability and out-of-sample performance for compact hybrid quantum–classical temporal models, suggesting a practical advantage of recursion in QLSTM architectures for time-series forecasting.

Abstract: Quantum long short-term memory (QLSTM) models extend recurrent sequence learning with variational quantum circuits, but their optimization behavior can vary substantially across random initializations and temporal contexts. This paper evaluates a recursive QLSTM architecture against a standard QLSTM for one-step-ahead prediction of daily minimum and maximum temperature. Using daily weather observations from Toronto and identical training settings, we compare convergence, predictive accuracy, and generalization across input windows of 8, 16, and 32 days over 20 random seeds. The recursive model consistently reaches a near-optimal test loss earlier, reduces mean absolute error and root mean squared error, and exhibits a smaller generalization gap. These results indicate that recursive quantum feature transformations can improve stability and out-of-sample performance for compact hybrid quantum--classical temporal models.

</details>


### [200] [COIN-GP: Cooperative Online Learning in Networked Distributed Systems with Partial Measurements via Gaussian Process Regression](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20598)
*Zewen Yang,Xiaobing Dai,Zhenxiao Yin,Hang Zhao,Zhijun Li,C. C. Chan*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Proposes an observer-based cooperative learning framework with online distributed GP regression and a data collection strategy to jointly estimate states and partially unknown dynamics under partial observability, with provable error bounds and superior simulation performance.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To enable accurate joint estimation of system states and unknown dynamics in distributed, sensor-rich networks when measurements are incomplete and GP models are imperfect.

Method: An observer-based dynamic cooperative learning framework integrating online distributed Gaussian Process regression, plus a novel data collection strategy with theoretical feasibility conditions; derives deterministic error bounds for both state and model estimation.

Result: Derives an upper bound on the combined state and model estimation error leveraging GP deterministic bounds; simulations demonstrate improved accuracy over existing distributed GP-based methods.

Conclusion: The framework enables accurate joint state and dynamics estimation in distributed settings with partial measurements and partial GP knowledge, supported by theoretical error bounds and empirical validation.

Abstract: In this paper, we tackle the problem of jointly estimating the system states and partially unknown dynamics within distributed sensor-equipped networks, particularly in scenarios where only partial state observations are available. To address this issue, we propose an observer-based dynamic cooperative learning framework incorporating online distributed Gaussian Process (GP) regression, which enables accurate estimation despite incomplete in measurements and deficient GP models. In addition, a novel data collection strategy is introduced, with theoretical conditions ensuring feasible data acquisition. Moreover, we also derive an error upper bound encompassing state estimation and model estimation, leveraging the deterministic error bounds of GPs. Empirical simulations demonstrate the superiority of our approach compared to existing distributed GP-based methods.

</details>


### [201] [Multi-center Medical Data Mining with FL-Net - A One-stop Shop for Federated Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20650)
*Simon Süwer,Julian Klemm,Elisa Acitelli,Mathieu Almeida,Lucia Altucci,Zsolt Bagyura,Michelangela Barbieri,Zsolt-Zoltán Bedő,Rosaria Benedetti,Béla Bihari,Csongor Csalóka,Lucia Dicunta,Stanislav Ehrlich,Bjoern M. Eskofier,Sándor-József Fejér,Georg Fröwis,Walter Hötzendorfer,Alexandra Kautzky-Willer,Jens Johann Georg Lohmann,Marianna Maranghi,Lorenzo Marconi,Rudolf Mayer,Wouter Leonard Megchelenbrink,Monika Moga,Adham Mottalib,Sanjeev Mehta,Madeleine Müller,Thomas Nyström,Balázs-Attila Orbán,Paul O'Toole,Giuseppe Paolisso,Paolo Parini,Matteo Pedrelli,Enrico Petrillo,Philipp Poindl,Niklas Probul,Anastasia Pustozerova,Tanja Šarčević,Lukas Weilguny,Jan Baumbach,Andreas Maier*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: FL-Net is a federated clinical research framework aimed at satisfying five literature-derived requirements. It integrates modular data harmonization, data discovery, disclosure control, versioned FL-Net-Tools, and containerized federated workflow execution into a persistent network to enable reusable harmonized data and workflows across studies.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Address the gap in clinical FL frameworks by delivering end-to-end, interoperable, reproducible, and privacy-preserving multicenter research capabilities that go beyond simulations.

Method: Develop modular components: data harmonization, data discovery, disclosure control, securely versioned FL-Net-Tools, and containerized federated workflow execution; assemble into a persistent network; evaluate via harmonization tasks, cross-study patient discovery (MIMIC and US-130), and reproducible/audited federated workflows with up to 50 concurrent clients.

Result: Demonstrated end-to-end FL-Net capabilities, enabling reuse of harmonized data and workflows; successful cross-study discovery between MIMIC and US-130; reproducible, audited federated workflows; supports up to 50 concurrent clients.

Conclusion: FL-Net offers a practical foundation for interoperable, reproducible, and privacy-preserving multicenter clinical research, currently under development in EU projects and targeting 800k patients across 10 hospitals in 9 countries, covering longitudinal and point-in-time data.

Abstract: Federated learning enables collaborative training without sharing patient-level data, but most studies remain simulations. Based on five requirements derived from the literature, we analyzed 14 FL frameworks and found that none fully satisfied these requirements. We present FL-Net, a novel federated clinical research framework to fulfill all requirements. It integrates modular data harmonization, data discovery, disclosure control, securely built versioned FL-Net-Tools and containerized federated workflow execution into a persistent network. It enables the re-use of harmonized data and workflows across studies. FL-Net's end-to-end capabilities were evaluated through harmonization, cross-study patient discovery across MIMIC and US-130, and reproducible, audited federated workflows with up to 50 concurrent clients. FL-Net is being developed within the dAIbetes and Microb-AI-ome EU projects and will cover over 800,000 patients across 10 hospitals in 9 countries covering longitudinal and single point in time data, FL-Net provides a practical foundation for interoperable, reproducible, and privacy-preserving multicenter clinical research.

</details>


### [202] [Epidemiological Causal Graph Identification: Challenges, Identifiability and Algorithms](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20676)
*Sambit Mishra,Yingying Wang,Christine K. Johnson,Urbashi Mitra*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Edge direction between ordinal and exponential-family nodes is identifiable; introduces score-based exhaustive search and DAGMA-based masked optimization for mixed-type DAGs; extends ordinal-Poisson results to the broader exponential family; numerics show recovery of orientations within Markov equivalence classes not identifiable by classical SEMs.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Causal discovery with mixed data types (ordinal and continuous/exponential-family) is under-addressed; existing identifiability results largely focus on continuous variables with additive noise or ordinal-Poisson settings. This work aims to establish distributional identifiability and provide practical algorithms for mixed-type DAGs.

Method: Theoretically proves distributional identifiability of the edge direction for a pair of nodes where one is ordinal (via an ordered logit model) and the other follows a one-parameter exponential family, for generic parameter values; generalizes Ordinal-Poisson results to arbitrary one-parameter exponential families. Computationally, develops a score-based exhaustive search and a masked continuous optimization framework using DAGMA to scale to larger graphs.

Result: Demonstrates that the ordinal–exponential edge direction is identifiable under generic parameters and generalizes to broader exponential families; numerical experiments validate the theory by recovering edge orientations that lie within a Markov equivalence class, which are unidentifiable under classical SEMs.

Conclusion: Extends identifiability results from purely continuous or Poisson-like settings to mixed ordinal and exponential-family data, and provides practical algorithms (score-based search and DAGMA-based masking) for causal discovery in larger graphs.

Abstract: Causal discovery from observational data is fundamental to statistics and machine learning, yet determining causal direction without interventions necessitates structural assumptions. Existing identifiability research primarily focuses on continuous variables under additive noise models, often neglecting mixed datasets containing ordinal scales, counts, and continuous measurements. This paper investigates causal discovery in Directed Acyclic Graphs (DAGs) where nodes follow either an ordinal distribution (via an ordered logit model) or a regular one-parameter exponential family distribution. We prove that the edge direction between an ordinal and an exponential family node is distributionally identifiable for generic parameter values. Our findings generalize previous Ordinal-Poisson results to the broader exponential family. Computationally, we introduce a score-based exhaustive search and a masked continuous optimization framework using DAGMA for larger graphs. Numerical results validate the theory, recovering edge orientations within a Markov equivalence class that are unidentifiable under classical structural equation models.

</details>


### [203] [RISC-V and machine learning: a survey](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20677)
*Shriman Keshri,Apparna Singh,Chinmaya Kumar Palo,Shreya Adya,Subhankar Mishra*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A survey of RISC-V in ML, proposing a unified taxonomy and evaluating implementations, toolchains, and applications; highlights trade-offs and trends, and outlines four future research directions.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: RISC-V's openness and configurability alongside ML demand require a comprehensive assessment of current capabilities, gaps, and roadmap to guide future ISA extensions, core designs, and software ecosystems.

Method: Comprehensive literature survey of academic and commercial RISC-V ML implementations, software frameworks, and deployment scenarios; development of a unified taxonomy of ML-enabled RISC-V designs; comparative performance and design trade-off analysis; assessment of toolchain maturity and deployment strategies; identification of emerging trends.

Result: Proposes a unified taxonomy of RISC-V ML implementations; provides a comparative analysis of performance, design trade-offs, and ecosystem maturity; evaluates software toolchains and deployment strategies; identifies trends in specialized instructions and accelerators; reports progress in energy efficiency and framework integration while noting standardization, verification, and ecosystem fragmentation challenges.

Conclusion: Four research directions are proposed: specialized neural processing extensions; adaptive and modular processor architectures; security frameworks; and energy-efficient multi-domain architectures; these provide a roadmap for advancing RISC-V as a platform for next-generation ML systems.

Abstract: The intersection of open-source processor architectures and machine learning is driving the demand for customizable, efficient, and accessible hardware. This survey examines the state of the RISC-V ISA in machine learning applications, analyzing current capabilities, challenges, and future directions based on recent research. The analysis covers academic and commercial implementations, software frameworks, and real-world applications. The RISC-V machine learning ecosystem is evaluated, from instruction set extensions and core implementations to compiler optimizations and deployment strategies. Key contributions include a unified taxonomy of RISC-V ML implementations, a comparative analysis of performance and design trade-offs, an evaluation of software toolchain maturity, and the identification of emerging trends in instruction set extensions and specialized accelerators. Findings reveal progress in energy efficiency, specialized instruction development, and framework integration, while highlighting challenges in standardization, verification complexity, and ecosystem fragmentation. The analysis proposes four research directions to address current limitations: specialized neural processing extensions, adaptive and modular processor architectures, security frameworks, and energy-efficient multi-domain architectures. These directions provide a roadmap for advancing RISC-V as a foundational platform for next-generation machine learning systems.

</details>


### [204] [Don't Mask the Environment: Observation Supervision Changes How Agents Explore Under RL](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20715)
*Juzheng Zhang,Disha Makhija,Manoj Ghuhan Arivazhagan,Vinayshekhar Bannihatti Kumar,Rashmi Gangadharaiah*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: ActObs jointly supervises both action and observation tokens in trajectories during SFT/RL, improving RL initialization, exploration, and cross-domain generalization by maintaining environment consequence modeling without extra data or computational cost.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Standard supervised fine-tuning (SFT) uses only agent-authored action tokens, treating observations as context. This may bias the policy toward action-leading representations and degrade environment understanding for downstream RL. ActObs investigates whether supervising observations can better initialize RL.

Method: Introduce ActObs to supervise the observation tokens that appear in each trajectory in addition to action tokens. No extra data, parameters, or forward passes are required. Compare ActObs against the action-only baseline across SFT-to-RL pipelines, using GRPO on Qwen3-4B and Qwen3-8B, Terminal-Bench 2.0, and cross-domain code editing on aider-polyglot.

Result: ActObs and action-only baselines perform similarly after SFT, but ActObs consistently outperforms after GRPO: higher pass@k across budgets on Qwen3-4B; modest trade-off between pass@1 and higher pass@16 on Qwen3-8B; gains in unseen tasks in aider-polyglot (+4.2 pp at pass@1). ActObs preserves higher entropy during RL with less policy movement, keeping the policy closer to the SFT initialization. Gradient analysis indicates action and observation gradients become orthogonal under action-only training and residual observation gradients degrade environment prediction; joint supervision prevents this specialization and preserves consequence prediction for better exploration.

Conclusion: Joint supervision of actions and observations (ActObs) yields a better RL initialization that preserves environment modeling, maintains linkage to SFT, and enhances downstream exploration and cross-domain performance. ActObs is beneficial across model sizes and domains, and mitigates gradient misalignment seen in action-only training.

Abstract: Agent trajectories record what an agent does and what happens next. Yet standard supervised fine-tuning (SFT) applies loss only to agent-authored action tokens, using environment observations as context but not as prediction targets. We ask whether this convention provides the best initialization for subsequent reinforcement learning. We introduce ActObs, which also supervises the observation tokens already present in each trajectory. Although deployed agents never generate observations, learning to predict them encourages the policy to model action consequences without adding data, parameters, sequence tokens, or forward passes. The methods perform similarly after SFT but diverge after GRPO. On Qwen3-4B, GRPO from ActObs achieves higher pass@k at every evaluated sampling budget than its action-only counterpart on Terminal-Bench 2.0. On Qwen3-8B, it trades some pass@1 reliability for higher pass@k (+3.4 pp at pass@16) and solves more distinct tasks. The advantage extends to cross-domain code editing on aider-polyglot (+4.2 pp at pass@1 at 4B), whose tasks are unseen during SFT and RL. ActObs retains more entropy during RL while requiring less policy movement, leaving the final policy closer to its SFT initialization. Our analysis traces this difference to SFT: action and observation gradients rapidly become orthogonal, while action-only training leaves a large residual observation gradient and degrades environment prediction below the base model. Joint supervision prevents this one-sided specialization, preserving consequence prediction and preparing the policy for downstream exploration.

</details>


### [205] [Video DeltaNet: A Video-Native Hybrid Attention for Livestream Video Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20744)
*Haocheng Xi,Yiming Xie,Hexu Zhao,Yiwen Zhang,Michael Liu,Thomas Creavin,Kurt Keutzer,Xiuyu Li,Zhaoyang Lv,Chenfeng Xu,Haiwen Feng*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: VDN introduces Video DeltaNet, a hybrid attention architecture that combines local Softmax attention with a bidirectional linear memory (Video Delta Attention) to accelerate long-range video diffusion while preserving fine-grained video interactions. Uses staged teacher-alignment and 8-step distillation on MiniMax H3, achieving 14.5x speedups (6.70s denoise of a 14.3s 768p video on 8 GPUs) over a 50-step dense baseline; maintains Softmax for multimodal (text/audio) interactions.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Video diffusion models process long spatiotemporal token sequences, making attention a computational bottleneck. Linear attention helps, but directly applying it to video can lose fine-grained interactions essential for high-quality generation. A hybrid approach aims to retain important interactions while speeding up inference.

Method: Introduce Video DeltaNet (VDN) that blends local Softmax attention with a bidirectional linear memory for long-range video context. The linear branch adds Video Delta Attention (VDA), updating memory once per frame by jointly incorporating spatial tokens. Use separate output projections and learnable gates to calibrate the two branches. Apply a staged teacher-alignment procedure to retrofit pretrained models. Instantiate on MiniMax H3, applying the hybrid to video-to-video interactions while keeping Softmax for text/audio interactions. Use eight-step distillation and an optimized SGLang serving stack for efficient inference.

Result: VDN-H3 denoises a 14.3-second, 768p video in 6.70 seconds on eight NVIDIA B200 GPUs, achieving a 14.5x speedup over the 50-step dense H3 baseline on the same hardware.

Conclusion: VDN provides an effective, scalable acceleration for diffusion-based video generation by preserving crucial video-to-video interactions through a hybrid attention architecture and a staged retrofit strategy, enabling faster vide generation without sacrificing multimodal interaction quality.

Abstract: Video diffusion models repeatedly process long spatiotemporal token sequences during denoising, making attention a major computational bottleneck. Linear attention offers an appealing alternative and has been widely adopted in recent large language models, but directly applying it to video models often fails to preserve the fine-grained interactions required for high-quality generation. We present Video DeltaNet (VDN), which combines local Softmax attention with bidirectional linear memory for long-range video context. Its linear branch introduces Video Delta Attention (VDA), which updates memory once per frame by jointly incorporating its spatial tokens. Separate output projections and learnable gates calibrate the two branches, while a staged teacher-alignment recipe progressively introduces the new pathway into pretrained models. We instantiate VDN on MiniMax H3, applying the hybrid to video-to-video interactions while retaining Softmax for interactions involving text or audio. With eight-step distillation and an optimized SGLang serving stack, VDN-H3 completes DiT denoising for a 14.3-second, 768p video in 6.70 seconds on eight NVIDIA B200 GPUs, corresponding to a 14.5x speedup over the 50-step dense H3 baseline on the same GPU count.

</details>


### [206] [Calibrated RF-Fingerprinting Under Interference With Heterogeneous Transmission Protocols](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20765)
*Tariq Abdul-Quddoos,Xiangfang Li,Lijun Qian*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A multi-label RF fingerprinting framework using 1D CNNs to handle co-channel interference, with calibrated thresholds that bound average false negatives, validated on POWDER 5G data across Wi-Fi, LTE, and 5G NR; shows high accuracy (up to 97%) under favorable conditions and lower performance (down to 73%) under challenging channels, with robust calibration to out-of-distribution interference.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Address the gap in RF fingerprinting research which typically assumes single-transmitter scenarios; extend to co-channel interference to reflect real-world spectral environments and provide confidence guarantees on not missing true policy violations.

Method: Formulate as a multi-label classification problem using a 1D CNN to extract features from RF signals. Implement calibration of label probabilities to derive confidence thresholds, with guarantees on the upper bound of the average number of False Negatives. Validate on real-world POWDER 5G data containing devices transmitting 802.11a, LTE, and 5G NR.

Result: Achieves accuracies ranging from 97% to 73% depending on channel conditions after calibration. Calibration yields micro recall scores near (1 - calibrated FNs) and remains robust to out-of-distribution interference, suggesting feasibility in high-contest wireless environments.

Conclusion: The proposed multi-label, calibrated 1D-CNN RF fingerprinting approach shows promise for realistic spectrum monitoring with multiple concurrent transmitters, offering accuracy under varying channel conditions and calibrated confidence guarantees for not missing true policy violations.

Abstract: Radio Frequency(RF)-Fingerprinting is a spectrum monitoring technique that identifies specific transmitters based on hardware impairments imprinted within the emitted signal. Although widely researched, studies almost exclusively consider scenarios where only one transmitter is emitting at a time, limiting real world applicability. In this work, we further the study of RF-Fingerprinting by considering co-channel interference, with multiple emitted signals interfering with each other, overlapping in time and frequency. Specifically, we formulate this problem as a multi-label classification problem and employ a 1D convolutional neural network (CNN). Furthermore, the models are calibrated such that the confidence thresholds for the label probabilities are derived, with guarantees on the upper bound on the average number of False Negatives, providing a degree of confidence in not missing a true spectrum policy violation. The proposed method is validated using real world data from the POWDER 5G testbed on devices transmitting 802.11a(Wi-Fi), 4G LTE, and 5G NR waveforms. The results show accuracy as high as 97% and as low as 73% after calibration depending on channel conditions. Also calibrating for various average false negatives upper bounds achieves micro recall scores of approximately (1 - calibrated false negatives) with the calibration robust to out-of-distribution interference, demonstrating the potential of the proposed method in a realistic high contention wireless environment

</details>


### [207] [PosteriorBench: From Point Estimates to Posterior Matching in Evaluating Generative Inverse Solvers](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20794)
*Jiachen Yao,Zi-Siang Hsu,Xi Deng,Aditi Gupta,Xin Ju,Sally M Benson,Gege Wen,Anima Anandkumar*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: PosteriorBench introduces a distribution-focused benchmark for generative inverse solvers across four physics-based ill-posed problems, using high-fidelity posterior references and a five-metric evaluation suite to assess distributional accuracy and uncertainty calibration.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Ill-posed inverse problems yield multiple plausible solutions; traditional evaluations focusing on pointwise accuracy miss the full posterior. There is a need for benchmarks that quantify distributional fidelity and uncertainty calibration.

Method: Construct high-fidelity reference posteriors using rejection sampling and MCMC for four tasks (Darcy flow inversion, Poisson source recovery, carbon capture and storage, light transport material inference). Develop PosteriorBench with a five-metric suite: posterior-mean error, posterior-standard-deviation error, maximum mean discrepancy, sliced Wasserstein distance, radially averaged power-spectrum error. Provide a unified pipeline for distribution matching and uncertainty quantification; evaluate across varying sensing regimes, nonlinear forward models, noise levels, and multimodal priors; compare solvers including neural operators; analyze effects of guidance weights and generation noise on posterior variance calibration.

Result: Empirical evaluation reveals substantial distribution-matching gaps in current solvers; neural operators improve resolution robustness; tuning guidance weights and generation noise is crucial for proper posterior-variance calibration.

Conclusion: PosteriorBench enables direct assessment of full posterior recovery in generative inverse solvers, highlighting current shortcomings and guiding improvements in model architectures and training strategies to better capture uncertainty and multimodal solutions.

Abstract: Generative models are increasingly used to solve scientific inverse problems, but existing evaluations still focus primarily on whether a method can produce a single plausible reconstruction. This is insufficient for ill-posed problems, where multiple solutions may be consistent with the same sparse or noisy observations. In these settings, a method can achieve strong pointwise accuracy while still failing to capture the true posterior through mode collapse, overconfident uncertainty, or averaging incompatible solutions. We introduce PosteriorBench, a benchmark for evaluating the distributional accuracy of generative inverse solvers. PosteriorBench evaluates four physics-based inverse problems: Darcy flow inversion, Poisson source recovery, carbon capture and storage, and light transport material inference. For each task, we construct high-fidelity reference posteriors using computationally heavy but established procedures such as rejection sampling and Markov chain Monte Carlo, enabling direct assessment of whether solvers recover the full set of solutions rather than the single best sample. We pair these references with a five-metric posterior evaluation suite: posterior-mean error, posterior-standard-deviation error, maximum mean discrepancy, sliced Wasserstein distance, and radially averaged power-spectrum error. These metrics assess pointwise accuracy, marginal uncertainty, distributional alignment, and global frequency fidelity. The benchmark spans sparse sensing, low-resolution observations, nonlinear forward models, varying noise levels, and multimodal priors, with a unified pipeline for distribution matching and uncertainty quantification. Our experiments reveal substantial distribution-matching gaps across current solvers, while showing that neural operators improve resolution robustness, and guidance weights and generation noise are key to posterior-variance calibration.

</details>


### [208] [Score Centering Stabilizes Off-policy Reinforcement Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20807)
*Martin Marek,Max Ryabinin*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: An additive score-centering correction stabilizes RL under training-inference mismatch (TIM) by canceling drift, matching or outperforming importance-sampling baselines, and composing with IS to further improve performance under TIM and staleness.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: TIM causes instability in RL for large language models; fully eliminating TIM is impractical due to rollout inefficiency; the instability is largely due to drift between training and inference engines that accumulates with training.

Method: Derivation and application of an additive 'score centering' correction term to cancel drift under TIM; evaluation across models from 0.6B to 30B parameters; comparison to importance sampling (IS) under quantization; examination of additive composition with IS in staleness experiments.

Result: Score centering alone matches or outperforms IS-based methods under quantization; the performance gap grows as TIM becomes more severe; because the correction is additive, it composes with IS, and their combination outperforms pure IS baselines in staleness experiments.

Conclusion: Score centering provides a simple, scalable, additive stabilization technique for RL under TIM, compatible with IS approaches, and effective across a wide range of model sizes.

Abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) of large language models is notoriously sensitive to small differences between training and inference engines, often referred to as the training-inference mismatch (TIM). However, completely eliminating TIM is impractical, as it would come at a major cost to rollout efficiency. In this paper, we show that the instability of RL under TIM is primarily caused by drift: a persistent bias between training and inference engines that accumulates with every training step. We derive an additive "score centering" correction term that stabilizes RL under TIM by canceling drift. When training models from 0.6B to 30B parameters, score centering alone matches or outperforms methods based on importance sampling under quantization, with the gap growing as the mismatch becomes more severe. Because the correction is additive, score centering also composes with importance sampling -- their composition outperforms pure importance-sampling baselines in our staleness experiments.

</details>

### [209] [AthenaZero: A low-inertia, bimanual robot for dynamic manipulation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.19194)
*Andrew S. Morgan,Gregory Xie,Capprin Bass,Rachel Thomasson,Chunpeng Wang,Erfan Shahriari,Harrison Busa,Oluwaseun Araromi,Joseph Aronov,Michael Burgess,Velin D. Dimitrov,Matthew A. Estrada,Faris Hamdi,Samuel Kendig,Taeyoon Lee,Jose Oscar Mur-Miranda,Emma Sommers,Paul Titchener,Margaret Wang,Achu Wilson,Mark Yeatman,Osman Dogan Yirmibesoglu,Alfred A. Rizzi,Annan Mozeika,Nicolas Rojas,Lael Odhner*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: A bimanual, low-inertia manipulator (AthenaZero) with quasi-direct drive achieves human-like endpoint dynamics and high torque transparency, enabling rapid baseball-inspired actions (throwing >30 m/s, catching/batting >14 m/s over 7.3 m) and robot/human collaborations.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Enable dynamic manipulation tasks requiring high acceleration and human-scale timing by minimizing effective endpoint mass while preserving control authority.

Method: Design and fabricate a bimanual manipulator using quasi-direct drive actuation and transmission remotization to reduce inertia and improve torque transparency; describe the design methodology and validate on baseball-inspired tasks (throw, catch, bat).

Result: AthenaZero achieves an endpoint mass comparable to humans (roughly an order of magnitude lower than conventional robots) and high acceleration capability, throwing speeds >30 m/s and catching/batting >14 m/s over 7.3 m. Demonstrated in robot-robot and human-robot interactions, illustrating adaptability for dynamic tasks.

Conclusion: Low inertia and torque transparency enable high-speed, dynamic manipulation on human-comparable timescales, with demonstrated efficacy across partner configurations; system suitable for tasks demanding rapid interaction and high acceleration.

Abstract: AthenaZero is a bimanual manipulator designed to minimize inertia without compromising control authority. By utilizing quasi-direct drive actuation and transmission remotization techniques, the system achieves an effective endpoint mass comparable to that of a human---about an order of magnitude less than conventional robot manipulators. This characteristic, combined with its inherent torque transparency, makes AthenaZero exceptionally well-suited for dynamic manipulation. We describe the methodology} that led to this design and demonstrate the robot's capabilities on three baseball-inspired tasks: throwing, catching, and batting, which showcase complex interactions on human-comparable timescales where milliseconds matter. AthenaZero was capable of throwing at speeds in excess of 30 m/s, with catching and batting at speeds in excess of 14 m/s over a short 7.3 m distance. Batting practice and a game of catch were subsequently performed in robot-to-robot and human-to-robot variations, showcasing the efficacy and adaptability of our system in tasks that require high acceleration.

</details>


### [210] [DITTO: Dexterous Interface for Transparent TeleOperation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.19196)
*Joaquin Palacios,Katelyn Lee,Cheng Zhang,Zhanpeng He,Matei Ciocarlie*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: DITTO enables handheld in-the-wild data collection and bilateral teleoperation for high-DOF manipulation with a 7-DOF dexterous hand linked 1-to-1 to a motorized exoskeleton.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Data collection for high-DOF manipulation must balance natural force feedback and deployment consistency. Teleoperation lacks force feedback; handheld systems lack stable embodiment during deployment, causing a gap between training and real-world use.

Method: An anatomically informed co-design of a 7-DOF robotic hand and a kinematically equivalent motorized exoskeleton with a 1-to-1 actuator mapping, enabling handheld data collection and bilateral teleoperation with joint-level force feedback in a single platform.

Result: The exoskeleton covers the operator's index-to-thumb workspace; DITTO demonstrates dexterous capabilities via learned policies on contact-rich tasks.

Conclusion: DITTO unifies handheld data collection and bilateral teleoperation with force feedback, enabling natural data generation for learning dexterous manipulation in contact-rich scenarios.

Abstract: Collecting data for manipulation with high-DOF hands is challenging, as interfaces must capture rich hand motion while rendering the contact interactions essential for precise manipulation. Existing data collection approaches face a trade-off: teleoperation ensures deployment consistency but lacks force feedback, while handheld (in-the-wild) systems provide natural force transparency but introduce a visual embodiment gap at deployment. We present DITTO, a Dexterous Interface for Transparent TeleOperation, which resolves this through the anatomically informed co-design of a dexterous 7-DOF robotic hand and a kinematically equivalent motorized exoskeleton. A 1-to-1 actuator mapping between the exoskeleton and robotic hand enables handheld (in-the-wild) data collection and bilateral teleoperation with joint-level force feedback unified in a single platform. We demonstrate that the DITTO exoskeleton spans the operator's natural index-to-thumb workspace, and showcase DITTO's dexterous capabilities via learned policies on contact-rich tasks.

</details>


### [211] [ULOHA: An Underwater Bimanual Robot System for Robot Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.19200)
*Masato Kobayashi,Takeru Tsunoori*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: ULOHA: a unified underwater bimanual learning platform enabling end-to-end demonstration, policy training, and deployment; showing cross-method evaluation and cross-media transfer.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Address the gap in underwater bimanual learning research and the transferability of air-trained policies to water, due to challenging perceptual and physical dynamics.

Method: Develop leader-follower hardware, extend LeRobot software, integrate teleoperation, multi-view sensing, demonstration collection, policy training, autonomous deployment; perform real-robot experiments; evaluate ACT, Diffusion Policy, SmolVLA; study cross-media transfer via single-arm experiments.

Result: Demonstrated coordinated underwater bimanual behaviors (inter-arm transfer, shared-object manipulation, buoyancy-driven interception); characterized effects of underwater dynamics; cross-media demonstrations enable execution in air and water; provided a unified platform.

Conclusion: ULOHA provides a practical research platform for underwater bimanual learning, enabling systematic study of perceptual/physical coupling and method transfer; supports future development in underwater autonomy.

Abstract: Underwater visuomotor policy learning has focused primarily on single manipulators, while bimanual imitation learning has been studied largely in air. We present ULOHA, an underwater bimanual robot learning platform that combines custom-designed leader--follower hardware with software extensions to LeRobot, integrating teleoperation, multi-view sensing, demonstration collection, policy training, and autonomous deployment. Real-robot experiments demonstrate a range of coordinated underwater bimanual behaviors, including inter-arm transfer, shared-object manipulation, and buoyancy-driven interception. We evaluate ACT, Diffusion Policy, and the vision--language--action model SmolVLA on the platform. We investigate how learning methods and execution strategies developed for manipulation in air perform underwater, examining bubble disturbances, buoyancy-driven object motion, action-execution horizons, and real-time chunking. A separate single-arm study examines policy transfer between air and water and shows that demonstrations spanning both media support execution in both under the tested conditions. ULOHA provides a unified experimental platform for studying underwater bimanual robot learning under the coupled perceptual and physical effects of underwater environments. Additional material: https://mertcookimg.github.io/uloha/

</details>


### [212] [REACT: A Fully Spiking State-Space Model for Real-Time Event-Driven Temporal Perception](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.19204)
*Geoffroy Keime,Nicolas Cuperlier,Benoit R. Cottereau*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: REACT is a fully spiking state-space model for event-driven perception that processes raw events individually (no temporal accumulation) using complex-valued spiking neurons, achieving ultra-low latency TTC estimation with good accuracy and energy efficiency, and showing strong generalization and quantization benefits.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Event cameras offer microsecond temporal resolution but most methods rely on accumulating events into frames, introducing latency that hinders fast reactive control. A continuous-time, event-by-event processing model could dramatically reduce latency for temporal perception tasks like TTC estimation.

Method: REACT employs a complex-valued spiking neuron (C-SiLIF) whose continuous-time dynamics are driven by inter-event intervals. The model processes each incoming event serially, without framing or time-binning, and operates end-to-end on full-field event streams without requiring target bounding boxes or localization inputs. The approach supports anytime TTC prediction, zero-shot transfer, and INT8 quantization.

Result: On the EvTTC dataset, REACT achieves 9.59% relative TTC error with 4.6 ms end-to-end latency, within 0.15 percentage points of the best learned method, and needs no target prior. At mean approach speed, the latency corresponds to ~4 cm of vehicle motion, far better than the 1 m required by competing methods. Energy consumption drops from 18.5 mJ to 2.8 mJ per 32,768 events with INT8 quantization.

Conclusion: Event-driven, continuous-time spiking state-space dynamics enable low-latency, continuously updated temporal perception for reactive robotic systems. The approach demonstrates strong performance without target priors, robust transfer capabilities, and significant energy efficiency, highlighting the potential of neuromorphic, event-driven perception for time-critical robotics.

Abstract: Robotic systems operating in dynamic environments require visual perception that evolves continuously with the incoming sensory stream. Event cameras provide microsecond temporal resolution and asynchronous sensing, but most learning-based methods accumulate events into frames or temporal bins, introducing an integration delay that can limit fast reaction. Here we propose REACT, a fully spiking state-space model for event-driven temporal perception that processes raw events one by one, without temporal accumulation. REACT uses a complex-valued spiking neuron, C-SiLIF, whose continuous-time dynamics are driven by the physical inter-event interval, allowing its internal state to evolve at the temporal resolution of individual events. We evaluate REACT on gesture recognition and time-to-collision (TTC) estimation from full-field event streams, without a target bounding box or localization input. On EvTTC, REACT achieves a 9.59% relative TTC error with 4.6 ms end-to-end inference latency, within 0.15 percentage points of the best learned method while requiring no target prior. At the dataset's mean approach speed, this latency corresponds to only 4 cm of vehicle motion, compared with 1 m for the fastest competing learned method. REACT further supports anytime TTC prediction, zero-shot transfer to a different driving sequence, and INT8 quantization, reducing the estimated energy consumption from 18.5 to 2.8 mJ per 32,768 events. These results show that event-driven spiking state-space dynamics can provide low-latency, continuously updated temporal perception for reactive robotic systems.

</details>


### [213] [4D Radar Perception Algorithms for Autonomous Driving: A Review](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.19216)
*Xumin Wu,Jun Zhou,Jilin Mei,Chen Min,Yu Hu*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: Comprehensive review of 4D millimeter-wave radar perception for autonomous driving, organizing tasks and algorithms, and outlining datasets, challenges, and future directions.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: 4D radar offers rich spatial and motion cues (elevation, Doppler, priors) robust to weather and lighting; yet the field lacks a unified taxonomy and benchmarks to drive progress.

Method: Systematic literature survey organized by perception tasks and algorithm families (radar-only, radar-cam fusion, cross-modal supervision); examine data representations, quality enhancement, and the role of radar priors; survey datasets and evaluation protocols; discuss challenges and future directions.

Result: A task-oriented framework linking perception tasks to appropriate algorithms and data representations; synthesis of how radar priors and Doppler/elevation are exploited; identification of dataset coverage and evaluation gaps; roadmap for future research.

Conclusion: This review provides a cohesive map for transitioning from sparse object perception to dynamic spatial understanding with 4D radar, emphasizing standardization, robust fusion, and advanced scene understanding.

Abstract: Research on 4D millimeter-wave radar perception algorithms has flourished in recent years, extending from signal processing and object detection to semantic segmentation, motion estimation, occupancy prediction, and dynamic scene reconstruction. This review organizes the field according to the evolution of perception tasks and algorithms. It first introduces radar fundamentals, data representations, and quality-enhancement methods, and then reviews object-level perception, motion and localization, local and dense spatial perception, and dynamic scene understanding. Across these directions, we compare radar-only learning, multimodal fusion, and cross-modal supervision and knowledge distillation. Particular attention is paid to how elevation, Doppler measurements, and radar physical priors are exploited across tasks. We further summarize the task coverage, input data, annotations, and evaluation protocols of existing datasets, clarifying the empirical support for different research directions. Finally, we discuss the common challenges and future directions of 4D radar perception for autonomous driving. This review provides a task-oriented perspective on the transition from sparse object perception to dynamic spatial understanding.

</details>


### [214] [Grasping by interconnection: robust closing motions from coarse object templates](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.19228)
*Julien Vanderheyden,Guillaume Drion,Fulvio Forni,Pierre Sacré*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: A non-feedback closing-motion planner for dexterous grasping using four principles; robust to size ~1 cm and pose errors; outperforms a data-driven planner in most cases; achieved 82.5% success on 80 everyday objects; robustness designed into closing motion; future work to pair with adaptive feedback.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Quantify how much inaccuracy a self-contained closing motion can tolerate in dexterous grasping and reduce reliance on precise object models or feedback.

Method: Planner based on four principles: a coarse object template, human grasp types, object-centric interaction, and compliant, sliding contacts; implemented via virtual model control; evaluated on Shadow Dexterous Hand with no feedback.

Result: Without feedback, planned motions tolerated size errors of about 1 cm and pose errors of several centimeters and tens of degrees; outperformed a state-of-the-art data-driven planner in 25 of 27 conditions; grasped 82.5% of 80 everyday objects; succeeded within an autonomous pipeline.

Conclusion: Robustness can be designed into the closing motion itself, enabling reliable manipulation in uncertain settings; future work to combine with adaptive feedback control on the physical hand.

Abstract: Dexterous robot hands must often grasp objects whose shape, size, and pose are known only approximately. Grasp planners typically require accurate object models or correct errors with feedback, but how much inaccuracy a closing motion can tolerate on its own remains unclear. To address this question, we designed a motion planner based on four principles: a coarse template of the object, human grasp types, an object-centric interaction, and compliant, sliding contacts instead of prescribed contact points. This paper presents the planner, implemented through virtual model control, and its evaluation on a Shadow Dexterous Hand. Without feedback, the planned closing motions tolerated size errors of about 1cm and pose errors of several centimeters and tens of degrees, a wider range than a state-of-the-art data-driven planner in 25 of 27 tested conditions. They also grasped 82.5% of 80 everyday objects and succeeded within an autonomous pipeline. Robustness can thus be designed into the closing motion itself, rather than left only to feedback. This planner opens a path toward reliable manipulation in uncertain settings, which we will pursue by combining it with adaptive feedback control on the physical hand.

</details>


### [215] [Learning Safe Humanoid Navigation from Reduced Order Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.19272)
*William D. Compton,Zachary Olkin,Ryan Bena,Aaron D. Ames*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: A two-stage RL navigation approach (RoM-Nav) enables scalable multi-floor humanoid navigation by first training in reduced-order dynamics with full 3D LiDAR, then bootstrapping to full-order humanoid dynamics with a frozen locomotion policy, augmented by a Poisson safety filter to handle unsafe or out-of-distribution obstacles; demonstrated on Unitree G1 with significant vertical displacement and path length.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Single-stage RL navigation struggles to scale to multi-level/humanoid terrains (e.g., stairs). A staged approach leveraging reduced-order dynamics can learn robust navigation policies that generalize to full-body dynamics while maintaining safety.

Method: 1) Train a navigation policy on reduced-order dynamics using full 3D LiDAR to handle complex, multi-story terrain. 2) Kickstart a full-order humanoid navigation policy by initializing with the learned reduced-order policy and keep a frozen locomotion policy in the loop. 3) Apply a Poisson safety filter to the navigation outputs to ensure safety with out-of-distribution obstacles, without sacrificing navigation success. 4) Validate with RoM-Nav on a Unitree G1 for mapless multi-floor navigation across >10 m vertical and >100 m path.

Result: Demonstrates RoM-Nav successfully enabling mapless multi-floor navigation on a Unitree G1, achieving substantial vertical displacement and path length.

Conclusion: A two-stage RoM-Nav framework effectively scales humanoid navigation to multi-story environments, combining reduced-order learning, bootstrapping to full dynamics, and a Poisson safety filter to maintain safety under out-of-distribution obstacles.

Abstract: Research in humanoid robotics has achieved rapid progress in locomotion, and recent results have pushed the boundary on autonomous navigation. We demonstrate that a standard single-stage RL navigation pipeline struggles to scale to multi-level and multi-story terrain, limited by the difficulty of complex humanoid terrain interactions such as stairs. To overcome this challenge, we decompose the navigation problem into two pieces. First, we train a policy operating on the reduced order dynamics but with full 3D LiDAR observations to navigate complex, multi-story terrain. We then utilize this navigation knowledge to kickstart a policy operating on the full-order humanoid dynamics, with a frozen locomotion policy in the loop. Additionally, we demonstrate that applying a Poisson safety filter to the navigation policy output recovers safety in the presence of out-of-distribution obstacles, without dropping navigation success rate. We demonstrate the resulting RoM-Nav policy on a Unitree G1, accomplishing mapless multi-floor navigation covering trials with over 10m of vertical displacement and over 100m of path length. Project page with videos https://wdc3iii.github.io/rom-nav/ .

</details>


### [216] [OHRID-Retail: An Open Multimodal Dataset of Human Activity in Retail Environments](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.19302)
*Xiangrui Wang,Yuetong Wu,Jalen Beeman,Robert Cook,Yu Gu,Nathanial Pearson,Trevor Smith,Read Hayes,Boyi Hu*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: Open multimodal dataset (OHRID Retail) with 16 adults performing simulated shelf-picking under three robot guidance conditions; full-body kinematics (17 IMUs) and 10-site EMG; open data and reproducible tools for HRI/ergonomics research.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Fill the gap of open, human-centered datasets in shared-workspace robot contexts, enabling research in activity recognition, sensor fusion, and human-robot interaction in retail-like environments.

Method: Within-subject design: each of 16 participants completed two trials per condition across three conditions (no robot, low-speed robot, high-speed robot). Data collected with 17 Xsens Awinda IMUs for full-body kinematics and 10-site Delsys EMG; results include descriptive analyses of movement intensity and muscle activation; dataset released with raw, processed, documentation, and reproducible analysis resources.

Result: Descriptive analyses show systematic variation in movement intensity and muscle activation by robot guidance condition and anatomical location; dataset is openly available with comprehensive documentation and analysis resources.

Conclusion: OHRID Retail provides a valuable open benchmark for multimodal human behavior research in human-robot shared environments, supporting HRI, activity recognition, ergonomics, and robot navigation research in retail contexts.

Abstract: Open datasets describing human behavior in environments shared with mobile robots remain limited, particularly for retail activities that combine locomotion, reaching, object handling, and robot guided movement. This paper introduces OHRID Retail, an open, human centered multimodal dataset collected from 16 healthy adults performing a simulated shelf picking task under three within participant conditions: no robot, low speed robot guidance, and high speed robot guidance. Each participant completed two trials per condition. Whole body kinematics were recorded using 17 Xsens Awinda inertial sensors and muscle activity was measured at 10 locations using Delsys Trigno surface electromyography sensors. Descriptive analyses demonstrate variation in whole body movement intensity and muscle activation across robot interaction conditions and body locations. OHRID Retail provides openly available raw recordings, processed measures, documentation, and reproducible analysis resources. The dataset can support research in human activity recognition, multimodal sensor fusion, occupational biomechanics, ergonomics, human aware robot navigation, and human robot interaction in retail and related shared environments.

</details>


### [217] [GAVEL: Graph World Models for Verified and Efficient Long-Horizon LLM Task Planning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.19315)
*Ruiyang Wang,Hao-Lun Hsu,Swarajh Mehta,Jiwoo Kim,Zhihao Dou,Miroslav Pajic*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: GAVEL uses an explicit graph world model to verify and repair long-horizon LLM plans, predicting consequences, correcting violations, and re-planning only when semantic reasoning is needed; it significantly improves task success and efficiency on BEHAVIOR-1K.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLM-planned long-horizon robotic tasks often violate embodiment constraints, fail to recover from planning errors, and struggle under partial observability. A verification/repair framework with a belief-aware world model can improve reliability and efficiency, and reduce unnecessary replanning.

Method: Construct an explicit graph world model capturing object relations, action preconditions/effects, and probabilistic beliefs over unobserved object locations. Use it to predict action consequences before execution, detect violations, and repair them via world-model-consistent corrections. Replanning is reserved for semantic errors. For multi-task instructions, perform distributional belief reasoning over possible object locations to reorder remaining subtasks to minimize expected search cost. Evaluated on BEHAVIOR-1K with Qwen3-8B (100 single-task tasks, 500 multi-task instructions).

Result: Single-task success improved from 41.2% to 91.8%; multi-task success from 19.9% to 92.6%; distributional belief reasoning reduces travel distance by ~5.4% over a static variant.

Conclusion: An explicit graph world model can substantially improve reliability and efficiency of long-horizon embodied planning across both compact and frontier-hosted LLMs.

Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) provide a flexible interface for long-horizon robot planning, but generated plans often fail to respect embodiment constraints, recover from planning errors, or reason effectively under partial observability. We present GAVEL, a framework for verifying and repairing long-horizon LLM planning built around an explicit graph world model. The graph represents relevant object-relations, action pre-conditions and effects, and probabilistic beliefs over unobserved object locations. This model can predict the consequences of LLM-generated actions before execution, detect violations, and repair those whose corrections follow directly from the world model. This method also reserves LLM replanning solely for errors requiring semantic reasoning. For multi-task instructions, GAVEL reasons over distributions of possible object locations to reorder remaining subtasks and minimize expected search cost. We evaluate GAVEL on BEHAVIOR-1K across 100 single long-horizon tasks and 500 multi-task instructions. With Qwen3-8B, GAVEL improves single-task success from 41.2% to 91.8% and multi-task success from 19.9% to 92.6%. Distributional belief reasoning also reduces travel distance by approximately 5.4% compared with a static variant. These improvements show that an explicit graph world model harness can substantially improve the reliability and efficiency of long-horizon embodied planning across compact and frontier hosted LLM capabilities.

</details>


### [218] [A Morphing Aerial Robot With Thruster-Integrated Flexible Continuum Links for Shape Adaptive Aerial Manipulation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.19328)
*Eri Sawada,Kazuki Sugihara,Ayano Miyamichi,Kunio Kojima,Kei Okada*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: A morphing rotor-distributed aerial robot with flexible continuum links and integrated thrusters enables both high shape adaptability and expanded wrench space, using a composite leaf-spring for vibration suppression, demonstrated in stable flight and manipulation tasks; claimed to be the first integration of flexible links with thrusters for aerial manipulation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Aerial manipulation requires both environmental adaptability (soft manipulators) and a large feasible wrench space (distributed thrust along the manipulator). Existing systems typically optimize one aspect but not both; there is a gap for an integrated solution.

Method: Design of a morphing rotor-distributed aerial robot featuring flexible continuum links acting as soft manipulators with thrusters distributed along the links to enlarge the wrench space. Develop a composite leaf-spring structure to provide high torsional and vertical stiffness and implement vibration-suppressing control methods. Validate through experiments demonstrating stable flight and manipulation.

Result: Successful stable flight and a range of aerial manipulation tasks are demonstrated, confirming viability of the integrated soft links with distributed thrusters.

Conclusion: First reported work to realize aerial manipulation using flexible links with integrated thrusters; shows potential to combine high shape adaptability with expanded interaction capabilities.

Abstract: In recent years, aerial manipulation has attracted increasing attention as a key to expand the application of aerial robots. In this work, we focus on two major research directions for achieving versatile aerial manipulation: (i) acquiring high environmental adaptability using soft manipulators, and (ii) expanding the feasible wrench space by distributing thrusters along the manipulator. However, no aerial robot has simultaneously satisfied these two requirements. Therefore, in this paper, we propose a morphing rotor-distributed aerial robot with flexible continuum links that achieves both high shape adaptability and an expanded wrench space. The flexible continuum links function as soft manipulators, passively conforming to the shape of the environment, while the thrusters distributed along the continuum links expand the feasible thrust wrench space and enable the end-effector to exert large interaction forces. To realize the proposed robot, it is essential to suppress vibrations of the lightweight continuum links. Thus, we develop a composite leaf-spring structure that provides both high torsional and vertical stiffness, and vibration-suppressing control methods. Using these implementations, we demonstrate stable flight and a variety of aerial manipulation tasks. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first work to realize aerial manipulations using flexible links with an integrated thruster.

</details>


### [219] [SemSafe-3DGS: Semantic Risk-Aware Active Navigation in Uncertain 3D Gaussian Splatting Maps](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.19330)
*Amirhossein Mollaei Khass,Athanasios Cosse,Nader Motee*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: A semantic risk-aware safe-active perception framework for navigation in attributed 3D Gaussian maps, using AVaR-based collision clearance with semantic weights, integrated in a CBF-QP to enforce safety while guiding information gathering.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Safety in partially observable environments is not solely geometric; semantic consequences of obstacles affect risk and planning. Conventional geometry-focused formulations may mis-prioritize similar-looking elements.

Method: Construct attributed 3D Gaussian maps with semantic attributes; modulate an Average Value-at-Risk (AVaR) collision clearance by class-dependent risk weights; aggregate into a weighted clearance feeding a control barrier function (CBF); introduce a trajectory-relevant active perception barrier to reduce map uncertainty along predicted motion; solve a unified CBF-QP that enforces semantic risk-aware collision avoidance as a hard constraint while permitting information acquisition when it does not compromise safety or progress.

Result: Efficient satisfaction of safety constraints; improved navigation via active perception; trajectory adaptation guided by semantic risk; validated on real robot with Ackermann dynamics.

Conclusion: Semantic risk-aware integration with Gaussian-map representations and AVaR-based clearance enables safer, more informative navigation in partially observed environments, with potential generalization to broader robotic dynamics and perception models.

Abstract: Autonomous robots operating in partially observed environments must navigate safely while acquiring observations that improve future planning. Existing safety formulations generally reason primarily about geometry. Consequently, geometrically similar scene elements may induce comparable control responses despite having different semantic consequences. We present a semantic risk aware safe-active perception framework for navigation in attributed 3D Gaussian maps. Semantic attributes modulate an Average Value-at-Risk collision clearance model through class dependent risk weights, allowing safety-critical Gaussian primitives to receive greater influence in the composite barrier. The resulting weighted clearances are aggregated into a control barrier function, while a trajectory-relevant active perception barrier promotes observations that reduce geometric map uncertainty along the robot's anticipated motion. Both objectives are integrated in a unified CBF-QP that enforces semantic risk-aware collision avoidance as a hard constraint while relaxing information acquisition when it conflicts with safety or task progress. Experiments demonstrate efficient safety constraint, improved navigation through active perception, semantic dependent trajectory adaptation, and real-robot execution under Ackermann dynamics.

</details>


### [220] [Dynamic-LIVO: A Dynamic-Aware LiDAR-Inertial-Visual Odometry System Using Spatio-Temporal Normals](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.19336)
*Zhixin Zhang,Samuel Ahiwe,Matthew Hale,Liang Zhao,Pawel Ladosz*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: Dynamic-LIVO is a dynamic-aware LIVO system that uses spatio-temporal normals to detect dynamic LiDAR points and a time-delayed re-evaluation to improve classification in sparse/new regions, yielding better localization and static colored maps in dynamic scenes.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Dynamic environments cause dynamic measurements to corrupt state estimation and mapping. Spatio-temporal normal analysis can fail in newly observed or spatially sparse areas due to insufficient observations, leading to unreliable dynamic/static classification and degraded performance.

Method: 1) Use Spatio-Temporal normal analysis to identify dynamic LiDAR points and propagate this classification to LiDAR-inertial and visual-inertial updates so dynamic data does not contaminate estimation or mapping. 2) Introduce a time-delayed S-T normal estimation strategy that defers classification for points with insufficient constraints and reevaluates them as more observations become available, preserving valid static points for map construction and improving reliability.

Result: Experiments on public and self-collected datasets with diverse sensor configurations show improved localization accuracy and cleaner static colored maps in challenging dynamic environments, demonstrating the effectiveness of Dynamic-LIVO.

Conclusion: The time-delayed re-evaluation strategy enhances dynamic classification reliability while maintaining accurate static mapping; the approach achieves robust state estimation in dynamic scenes and will release source code and dataset upon acceptance.

Abstract: This paper proposes Dynamic-LIVO, a dynamic-aware LiDAR-Inertial-Visual Odometry (LIVO) system for robust state estimation and static colored mapping in dynamic environments. Dynamic-LIVO employs Spatio-Temporal (S-T) normal analysis to identify dynamic LiDAR points and propagates the resulting classification to both LiDAR-inertial and visual-inertial updates, preventing dynamic LiDAR measurements and their associated visual observations from affecting state estimation and mapping. However, S-T normal estimation can be unreliable in newly observed and spatially sparse regions due to insufficient spatio-temporal observations. To address this issue, we introduce a time-delayed S-T normal estimation strategy that defers the classification of insufficiently constrained points and re-evaluates them as additional observations become available. This strategy improves dynamic classification reliability while preserving valid static points for map construction. Extensive experiments on public and self-collected datasets with diverse sensor configurations demonstrate that Dynamic-LIVO improves localization accuracy and produces cleaner static colored maps in challenging dynamic environments. The source code and self-collected dataset will be publicly released upon acceptance.

</details>


### [221] [ViLoMan: Learning Visual-Proprioceptive Whole-Body Loco-Manipulation Skills for Humanoid Robots](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.19340)
*Zejie Tian,Ruibing Hou,Bingpeng Ma,Börje F. Karlsson,Shiguang Shan*

Main category: cs.RO
