TL;DR: ViLoMan is a scalable method that learns a unified whole-body loco-manipulation policy for humanoids by converting human demonstrations into executable robot trajectories and distilling them via teacher-student learning, enabling on-board depth/proprioception control for door-closing with sim-to-real transfer.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Address data scarcity for diverse, physically executable humanoid loco-manipulation and the challenge of learning from onboard observations without reference motions.

Method: Convert partial human-object interaction demonstrations into complete robot trajectories; use teacher-student distillation to learn a unified policy that maps egocentric depth and proprioception to joint-level actions; deploy without reference motions or commands.

Result: Single policy on Unitree G1 achieves successful door closure across configurations in simulation and real world using only onboard sensing; robust generalization to task variations and successful sim-to-real transfer.

Conclusion: ViLoMan demonstrates scalable, end-to-end learning of unified loco-manipulation policies that can operate from onboard observations, enabling robust humanoid manipulation with reduced reliance on predefined reference motions.

Abstract: Humanoid loco-manipulation requires adaptive whole-body coordination to seamlessly integrate locomotion and physical interaction. Despite recent advances, learning autonomous loco-manipulation remains challenging due to the scarcity of diverse, physically executable robot-object interaction data and the difficulty of learning unified whole-body control directly from onboard observations. We present ViLoMan, a scalable framework for autonomous humanoid loco-manipulation. ViLoMan first transforms partial kinematic demonstrations of human-object interactions into complete, physically executable robot trajectories. It then leverages these trajectories within a teacher-student distillation framework to learn a unified policy that maps egocentric depth observations and proprioceptive measurements directly to joint-level whole-body actions. During deployment, the policy requires neither reference motions nor intermediate commands. We evaluate ViLoMan on door-closing tasks across diverse door configurations and robot initial conditions in both simulation and the real world. Experimental results demonstrate that a single policy enables a Unitree G1 humanoid to complete the full task using only onboard depth sensing and proprioception, while generalizing robustly across task variations and transferring effectively from simulation to reality. Project page: viloman-anonymous.pages.dev.

</details>


### [222] [Kinematics-Grounded Agentic AI for Robotic Additive Manufacturing Process Planning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.19347)
*Jingzhan Ge,Ruimin Chen,Azadeh Haghighi,Jiong Tang,Farhad Imani*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: An agent-specialist-tool framework (A-RAM) that integrates LLM-driven intent interpretation with a deterministic planning agent and domain tools to produce execution-ready, traceable plans for robotic additive manufacturing; shows substantial reductions in Joint-6 jerk and shorter trajectories/print times across three case studies in a six-axis robotic-arm AM cell.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Slicer decisions, part orientation, and workspace placement are tightly coupled with robot kinematics; naive planning can yield infeasible or suboptimal plans. Existing tools lack integrated pre-execution evaluation of these coupled decisions.

Method: The LLM interprets manufacturing objectives and constraints, identifies prescribed and searchable planning variables, and encodes this reasoning in a schema-constrained request. A deterministic Planning Agent instantiates the corresponding search workflow, while domain tools compute quantitative evidence for slicing, placement, inverse kinematics, trajectory timing, Joint-6 jerk, and extrusion. Evaluation occurs on a six-axis robotic-arm AM cell via three case studies: expert-specified planning, goal-only planning, objective-dependent infill screening, and geometry-dependent orientation-placement selection.

Result: Selected plans achieve up to 53.5% lower maximum Joint-6 jerk and 48.3% lower mean absolute Joint-6 jerk than the least favorable valid candidates. Objective-specific infill screening yields motion-plan completion times up to 40.1% shorter and extrusion paths up to 12.7% shorter than the corresponding least favorable screened patterns.

Conclusion: Demonstrates an integrated, traceable, and execution-ready planning pipeline for robotic additive manufacturing (A-RAM) that combines LLM-based decision support, a deterministic planner, and domain-tools to reduce kinetic penalties and enhance efficiency.

Abstract: Robotic additive manufacturing (AM) extends material-extrusion printing beyond gantry kinematics but makes process planning robot-dependent. A slicer-generated plan that appears favorable in part coordinates can become infeasible or robotically unfavorable on a manipulator because slicer-process decisions and part orientation determine the generated path, while part orientation and workspace placement affect its kinematic realization. Existing AM tools, large language model (LLM)-based decision-support methods, and digital-shadow systems do not provide integrated pre-execution evaluation of these coupled decisions. This paper presents agentic robotic additive manufacturing (A-RAM), an agent-specialist-tool framework that converts user intent and a part file into traceable, execution-ready plans. The LLM interprets manufacturing objectives and constraints, identifies prescribed and searchable planning variables, and encodes this reasoning in a schema-constrained request; a deterministic Planning Agent instantiates the corresponding search workflow, while domain tools compute quantitative evidence for slicing, placement, inverse kinematics, trajectory timing, Joint-6 jerk, and extrusion. The framework is evaluated on a six-axis robotic-arm AM cell through three case studies covering expert-specified planning, goal-only planning, objective-dependent infill screening, and geometry-dependent orientation-placement selection. Across the evaluated candidate sets, selected plans achieve up to 53.5% lower maximum Joint-6 jerk and 48.3% lower mean absolute Joint-6 jerk than the least favorable valid candidates, while objective-specific infill screening yields motion-plan completion times up to 40.1% shorter and extrusion paths up to 12.7% shorter than the corresponding least favorable screened patterns.

</details>


### [223] [Design and Experimental Validation of a 3D Printed Torsional Series Elastic Actuator for Safe Human Robot Interaction](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.19367)
*Joel Hidalgo Pisco,Melissa Cobos Condo,Luigi Miranda,Dennys Paillacho*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: Low-stiffness, 3D-printed TPU torsional spring for SEAs; validated by FEA and experiments; exhibits near-linear torque response and safe pHRI via a hybrid controller with torque-threshold switching; TPU damping provides passive filtering for stable operation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Enable intrinsic safety in physical human-robot interaction with a compliant, manufacturable alternative to traditional metallic SEAs; address complexity and multi-part assemblies by using 3D-printed TPU.

Method: Design and fabricate a low-stiffness TPU torsional spring for SEAs; perform finite element analysis (FEA); implement a hybrid position controller with torque threshold switching to accommodate external interactions; conduct experimental validation including trajectory tracking and disturbance rejection; analyze damping effects of TPU on high-frequency oscillations.

Result: KS = 0.066 Nm/deg with <3% deviation from numerical predictions; deviation attributed to FDM anisotropy; successful tracking of non-stationary trajectories; safe yield to external disturbances; TPU damping acts as a passive low-pass filter during control transitions.

Conclusion: The architecture offers a cost-effective, reliable, and easily manufacturable solution for safe physical human-robot interaction, leveraging 3D-printed TPU compliant elements and a hybrid control scheme.

Abstract: Ensuring intrinsic safety in physical human robot interaction (pHRI) is a critical requirement for social and service robots. While Series Elastic Actuators (SEAs) offer hardware based compliance, traditional metallic designs often require complex, multi part assemblies. This paper presents the design, finite element analysis (FEA), and experimental validation of a low stiffness, torsional spring for SEAs, manufactured via 3D printed thermoplastic polyurethane (TPU). The compliant element exhibits a highly linear torque deformation response (Ks = 0.066 Nm/degree), matching numerical predictions with under 3% deviation, a variance attributed to FDM structural anisotropy. To accommodate external interactions using standard position limited servomotors, a hybrid position controller with torque threshold switching was implemented. Experimental evaluations demonstrate the system ability to accurately track non stationary trajectories and safely yield to external disturbances. Furthermore, the inherent material damping of the TPU acts as a passive low pass filter, preventing high frequency oscillations during control mode transitions. The proposed architecture offers a cost effective, reliable, and easily manufacturable solution for safe pHRI.

</details>


### [224] [Enhancing the Perception of Safety and Comfort during Physical Human-Robot Handshake Interactions by Integrating Flexible Elements into a Robotic Arm](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.19375)
*Joel Hidalgo,Dennys Paillacho,Melissa Cobos,Luigi Miranda*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: Using series elastic actuators (SEA) in robotic arms during handshakes improves perceived safety and comfort compared to rigid joints; experimental study with 10 volunteers showed SEA enhances safety perception and interaction experience.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Address safety and comfort in human-robot physical interactions, particularly in natural gestures like handshakes, by employing SEAs to absorb impacts and reduce rigidity.

Method: Experimental comparison between rigid-joint and SEA-equipped robotic arms. 10 volunteers (6 men, 4 women) performed two handshakes per arm. Collected objective end-effector trajectory data and subjective perception data via surveys focusing on safety, naturalness, and confidence.

Result: SEA-equipped arm yielded higher perceived safety and comfort during handshakes, supporting SEAs as a design strategy to enhance safety and social acceptance in HRI.

Conclusion: Incorporating SEAs in robotic arms can improve safety perceptions and social acceptance in everyday human-robot hand interactions, validating SEAs as a practical approach for safer HRI.

Abstract: Safety and comfort in human-robot physical in-teractions are essential aspects in the development of social technologies, where natural gestures, such as handshakes, represent a challenge due to their direct physical contact. The implementation of series elastic actuators (SEA) to absorb impacts is proposed as a design strategy that favors safer interactions. This paper presents an experimental study aimed at evaluating how the incorporation of SEAs in robotic arms influences perceived safety and the interaction experience dur-ing handshaking. The design allows a direct comparison of the effect of rigidity versus the incorporation of elastic elements, in order to identify the advantages of SEAs in improving the physical safety and social acceptance of robotic systems in everyday contexts. The experiment was carried out with 10 volunteers (6 men and 4 women), who performed two interactions with each robotic arm: one with rigid joints and the other with flexible joints using SEA. During testing, objective data on end-effector trajectories were collected, as well as subjective information through a perception survey focused on safety, naturalness, and confidence during the handshake. The survey results show increased perceptions of safety and comfort with the SEA-equipped arm, supporting its potential to facilitate safer and more socially accepted human-robot interactions.

</details>


### [225] [Task-Oriented Active Learning of Residual Dynamics for Model Predictive Path Integral Control](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.19378)
*Nobuaki Aoki,Hojin Lee,Stefan Sosnowski,Sandra Hirche*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: Task-Oriented Information Acquisition (ToIA) for MPPI with online GP residual learning improves task performance by prioritizing informative observations that reduce downstream uncertainty in states relevant to the objective; yields substantial gains over passive and task-agnostic baselines and supports real-time control.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Passive data collection may not cover states important for later task phases; task-agnostic active learning may focus on information that does not improve task performance.

Method: For each MPPI control sequence, ToIA estimates the potential reduction in predictive uncertainty at future states if an observation is obtained early in the rollout, and weights it by the route's task relevance. This score is computed using the existing rollout batch without simulating future observations or re-optimizing controls. Applied to online GP residual learning within MPPI.

Result: In simulated off-road navigation across held-out maps with heterogeneous terrain, ToIA increased goal-reaching success rate by 19.3 and 27.4 percentage points over passive GP learning, and outperformed task-agnostic active-learning baselines across both dense and sparse online-learning intervals. An ablation shows task relevance drives gains, especially when model updates are infrequent.

Conclusion: ToIA provides an effective, low-overhead, task-aware information criterion for active learning in MPPI with online GP residuals, enabling higher success rates and real-time control at 20 Hz on a standard GPU.

Abstract: Online residual learning can reduce model mismatch in predictive control, but passive data collection may fail to adequately cover states that become important later in the task. Task-agnostic active learning targets uncertain or informative regions, but information acquired in such regions does not necessarily improve task performance. This paper introduces Task-Oriented Information Acquisition (ToIA), an active-learning criterion for model predictive path integral control (MPPI) with online Gaussian process (GP) residual learning. For each sampled control sequence, ToIA estimates how much an observation obtained early in the rollout would reduce predictive uncertainty at later states on the same rollout, and weights this reduction by the rollout's relevance to the task. The score is evaluated over the existing MPPI rollout batch without sampling future observations or re-optimizing control under hypothetical posterior updates. In simulated off-road navigation across held-out maps with heterogeneous terrain, ToIA improved the goal-reaching success rate over passive GP learning by 19.3 and 27.4 percentage points and outperformed task-agnostic active-learning baselines across dense and sparse online-learning intervals. An ablation study indicates that task relevance is particularly important under sparse model updates. The implementation supports online control at 20 Hz on an NVIDIA RTX 2080 Ti.

</details>


### [226] [From Rollout to Reset: A Graph-Based Harness for Autonomous Long-Horizon Manipulation Evaluation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.19413)
*Jing Jiang,Yue Yang,Xinkai Jiang,Gedas Bertasius,Daniel J. Szafir,Rudolf Lioutikov*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: HALTER automates long-horizon robot evaluation by planning resets from a library of learned atomic skills using a scene graph and LLM, achieving higher restoration and verification accuracy with lower human effort.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Single-step eval systems like AutoEval fail to scale to long-horizon tasks due to combinatorial terminal states; need scalable, automated reset and scoring.

Method: Build a library of atomic reset skills; online scene graph from point clouds and vision foundation models; LLM reasons over the graph to plan resets, score rollouts, and verify resets without labeled success images.

Result: Restores scene in 76% of episodes (vs 52% AutoEval, 65% motion planning). Completed-skill fraction estimated correctly in 90% (vs 76%). Reset-verification verdict 91% correct (vs 78%). Reduces operator time by 72%. In compositional generalization tests, HALTER resets 74.7% vs 1.3% for per-task reset. Ablations show importance of scene representation and graph update rate.

Conclusion: HALTER provides scalable, autonomous long-horizon evaluation with improved restoration, accuracy, and efficiency, enabling better reproducibility and broader generalization.

Abstract: Robot manipulation policies are improving quickly, and real-robot evaluation remains the standard evidence for that progress. It still relies on a human to reset the scene between rollouts, which consumes operator time and leaves the initial state distribution unspecified, so results reproduce poorly. A recent system, AutoEval, automates both reset and scoring, but only for single-step tasks, because a long-horizon rollout can terminate in combinatorially many configurations that no single learned reset policy covers. We present HALTER, a Harness for Autonomous Long-horizon Task Evaluation and Reset, which restores the scene by planning over a library of learned atomic reset skills, so demonstration cost scales with the size of that library rather than with the number of terminal states. HALTER builds a spatial scene graph online from point clouds and vision foundation models, and an LLM reasons over this graph to score the rollout, plan the reset, and verify that the reset succeeded, without collecting labeled success images for any task. On four long-horizon tasks on a Franka arm, HALTER restores the scene in 76% of episodes, against 52% for AutoEval and 65% for a motion-planning reset, and it estimates the completed-skill fraction correctly in 90% of episodes, against 76%. Its reset-verification verdict is correct in 91% of episodes, compared with 78% for AutoEval. It also cuts the operator time of an evaluation campaign by 72% relative to manual reset. We further measure compositional generalization on three held-out tasks, where HALTER resets 74.7% of episodes against 1.3% for a per-task reset policy, and we ablate the scene representation and the graph update rate.

</details>


### [227] [Predict Before You Deploy: Offline Prediction of Quantization-Induced Task Degradation for World Action Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.19441)
*Jiuyi Xu,Jinjia Guo,Meida Chen,Jing Du,Yangming Shi*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: PreDE is a policy-calibrated method to predict quantization-induced task degradation in World Action Models (WAMs) using offline development data. It calibrates two thresholds to accept, reject, or defer new quantization configurations based on a fixed observation log, reducing the need for expensive closed-loop testing while maintaining performance on held-out configurations and predicting degradation on high-deviation configurations.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To reduce memory and compute for video-generation backbones in WAMs by exploring quantization configurations efficiently. Exhaustive closed-loop evaluation of all bit-width/group/quantizer choices is impractical due to the large configuration space and deployment cost.

Method: Use offline development data to calibrate two decision thresholds under a within-setting label-ordering assumption. For a new configuration, PreDE compares observed offline deviations to the calibrated thresholds and decides to accept, reject, or defer, using a fixed observation log of prior configurations. Only configurations where the thresholds agree across the development labels are issued as decisions.

Result: Across five WAMs and four benchmark settings, quantization effects on task performance vary with configuration and cannot be explained by bit width alone or a single deviation threshold. In 28 held-out configurations from two policies, PreDE made 21 decisions (75% coverage) matching observed outcomes. Deferred candidates included both acceptable and substantially degraded cases (33-percentage-point loss). In 450 trials with two fine-tuned policies, high-deviation configurations degraded significantly, while low-deviation configurations did not show significant degradation. On a real robot, W4A4 achieved 1.37x action-query speedup and ~44% lower peak memory. Code is available at the provided GitHub URL.

Conclusion: Policy-specific behavioral calibration is effective for selecting promising quantization configurations while flagging candidates that require closed-loop testing. PreDE can substantially reduce search cost for deployment-friendly quantization in WAMs.

Abstract: World action models (WAMs) rely on video-generation backbones, requiring substantial memory and compute for deployment. Post-training quantization reduces memory and can accelerate inference, but bit width, grouping, and quantizer choice define a large configuration space. Identifying configurations that preserve task performance through exhaustive closed-loop evaluation is costly. We propose PreDE (Predict Before You Deploy), a policy-calibrated framework for predicting quantization-induced task degradation from offline action deviations. Using closed-loop outcomes from a small development set, PreDE calibrates two thresholds and accepts, rejects, or defers new configurations using a fixed observation log. Under a within-setting label-ordering hypothesis, the rule issues decisions where all thresholds consistent with the development labels agree. Across five WAMs and four benchmark settings, quantization produces configuration-dependent task losses that cannot be explained by bit width alone or a shared deviation threshold. Across 28 held-out configurations from two policies, PreDE issued 21 decisions before observing closed-loop outcomes (75% coverage), all matching the observed acceptable or degraded labels. Deferred candidates included both acceptable outcomes and a 33-percentage-point loss. In 450 Franka Research 3 trials across two independently fine-tuned policies, all configurations assigned to high-deviation groups before testing showed significant degradation, while low-deviation comparisons showed no statistically significant degradation. On the real robot, W4A4 achieved a 1.37x action-query speedup and approximately 44% lower peak memory. These results support policy-specific behavioral calibration for quantization configuration selection while identifying candidates that require closed-loop evaluation. The code is available at https://github.com/jiuyixu25/PreDE.

</details>


### [228] [From Wizard-of-Oz Human-Robot Dialogue Collection to a Taxonomy of Robot Response Decisions: A Retrospective Analysis of Assistive Pilot Interactions](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.19447)
*Guangping Liu,Nicholas Hawkins,Tipu Sultan,Flavio Esposito,Madi Dian*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: A study derives a hierarchical taxonomy for robot dialogue in natural-language instruction following, validated on pilot Wizard-of-Oz data, showing reliable annotations and feasibility of training vision-language models with taxonomy labels; it also highlights boundary cases and suggests protocol improvements for data collection.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To address the gap between real-world instruction following and incomplete human utterances by providing practice-grounded criteria for when a robot should act, confirm, clarify, or refuse, supported by real-world situated dialogue data.

Method: Retrospective analysis of 40 episodes (five participants) where a wheelchair-mounted mobile manipulator operated under Wizard-of-Oz guidance without a formal policy. Developed a six-mode, four-ambiguity taxonomy; two human annotators and an AI annotator applied it. Measured inter-annotator agreement (Cohen's kappa 0.72–0.95) and clean-label rates (89–91%). Fine-tuned LLaVA-1.6-7B on ACT/CLARIFY labels to test feasibility of taxonomy-based training.

Result: Established a hierarchical taxonomy: six response modes (ANSWER, REPORT_DONE, REFUSE, CONFIRM, CLARIFY, ACT) and four ambiguity types (intent, referential, spatial, intelligibility). Achieved high annotation reliability and demonstrated that taxonomy-derived labels can train vision-language models. Identified boundary cases that motivate a constrained dialogue-collection protocol for more consistent data.

Conclusion: An explicit decision policy grounded in a taxonomy can improve consistency in robot dialogue management for incomplete instructions. The approach yields reliable annotations, supports model training, and points to protocol refinements needed to handle remaining boundary cases and enhance data collection for future studies.

Abstract: Robots that follow natural-language instructions in everyday indoor environments must act on incomplete human utterances. Instructions often omit essential information, such as the identity of an out-of-view object, an intended destination, or the user's goal. Existing datasets contain little real-world situated dialogue and provide few practice-grounded criteria for deciding when a robot should act, confirm, clarify, or refuse. We retrospectively analyze a pilot Wizard-of-Oz study in which five participants performed everyday indoor tasks, including door opening, drawer opening, feeding, drinking, and cleaning, with a wheelchair-mounted mobile manipulator while the wizard responded without a formal communication policy. This preserved authentic user behavior but produced inconsistent robot-side decisions, motivating an explicit decision scheme. From 40 episodes, we derived a hierarchical taxonomy of six response modes (ANSWER, REPORT_DONE, REFUSE, CONFIRM, CLARIFY, ACT) and four ambiguity types (intent, referential, spatial, intelligibility). Two human annotators and an AI annotator applied the scheme to the pilot data. Clean-label rates were 91% and 89%, and Cohen's ranged from 0.72 to 0.95 across decision-point, mode, and ambiguity levels for both human-human and human-AI comparisons. Fine-tuning LLaVA-1.6-7B on taxonomy-derived labels for ACT and CLARIFY indicates the feasibility of training vision-language models using annotations from our taxonomy. Remaining boundary cases in decision-point identification and REPORT_DONE motivate a constrained protocol for more consistent dialogue collection.

</details>


### [229] [Winning a Won Game: Strict Reach-Avoid-Stay Control Barrier Functions for High-Dimensional Black-Box Systems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.19449)
*Donggeon David Oh,Duy P. Nguyen,Gongkai Yuan,Qingchen Li,Jaime Fernández Fisac,Haimin Hu*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: Introduces a robust discrete-time CBF framework (sRAS) with stay and reach-avoid values, lifted to state-action Q-functions for runtime safety in black-box, uncertain, high-dimensional systems; validated on quadruped gap jumping and simulated races.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Safety-critical control requires guaranteeing reaching a target and then remaining safely forever under bounded uncertainty, without reliance on known dynamics or hand-crafted barriers.

Method: Constructs a stay value encoding safe permanent residence in a target subset and a reach-avoid value encoding safe reachability while avoiding non-guaranteed target states; proves these yield a valid robust discrete-time CBF; lifts them to state-action Q-functions for runtime intervention; uses reachability-based adversarial RL for scalable value approximation using black-box interactions; does not require known dynamics, affine structure, value derivatives, or hand-designed barriers.

Result: Exact sRAS values and a measure-zero condition ensure feasibility from almost every winnable initial state and safety after first entry under all admissible uncertainties; validated in simulation and hardware for quadruped gap jumping and in simulated F1TENTH races for safe overtaking and lead retention.

Conclusion: The framework provides a scalable, model-free method to enforce strict reach-avoid-stay safety for high-dimensional, uncertain systems, enabling safe operation and long-term stability with only black-box interactions.

Abstract: Robots must complete their tasks and maintain the achieved outcomes while avoiding safety failures at all times. Strict reach-avoid-stay (sRAS) formalizes this requirement: safely reaching a target and remaining there indefinitely after first entry. We propose an sRAS Q-control barrier function (CBF) safety filter for high-dimensional black-box systems under bounded uncertainty. Our construction combines a stay value encoding safe permanent residence in a target subset with a reach-avoid value encoding safe reachability of this subset while avoiding target states from which safe permanent residence cannot be guaranteed. We prove that these values jointly yield a valid robust discrete-time CBF and lift them to state-action Q-functions for runtime intervention. For exact values and under a measure-zero condition, our filter preserves sRAS feasibility from almost every winnable initial state and keeps the system safely within the target after first entry, against all admissible uncertainty realizations. We adopt reachability-based adversarial reinforcement learning for scalable value approximation using only black-box interactions. Notably, neither synthesis nor deployment of our filter requires known dynamics, affine structure, value derivatives, or hand-designed barriers. We validate our framework in quadruped gap jumping in simulation and hardware, where the robot crosses the gap, lands safely, and remains safe afterward. Simulated F1TENTH races further demonstrate safe overtaking and lead retention.

</details>


### [230] [GLAMDRING: Gait Learning And Morphology co-Design via Reinforcement LearnING of CPGs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.19452)
*Amogh Joshi,Kaushik Roy*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: GLAMDRING jointly designs robot morphology and gait policy, optimizing for speed, energy efficiency, or payload margin in unstructured environments; demonstrates co-design necessity, actuator-envelope feasibility, and emergent canonical gaits with real-world validation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Robots must operate in unstructured environments where suitable off-the-shelf morphologies do not exist; a framework is needed to select an optimal body (link geometry and actuators) and jointly learn a capable gait.

Method: Synthesize a quadruped morphology under forward-velocity bounds, per-actuator power budget, an actuator library, and payload need. Use Hopf-oscillator CPGs as gait policy and train a small set of policies via reinforcement learning across candidate morphologies, co-learning gait with hardware. Resolve link lengths and actuators post-hoc from policy envelope to keep synthesis cost low (few RL runs). Rank feasible designs by target objective (max speed, min CoT, or max payload margin).

Result: Co-design of body and gait is essential to meet locomotion constraints; actuator envelopes, not just motion success, cap payload; canonical animal gaits arise from morphology and constraints; real-world demonstration validates practicality.

Conclusion: GLAMDRING enables joint optimization of robot morphology and locomotion policy, reducing synthesis cost and yielding designs that satisfy performance constraints in unstructured environments.

Abstract: Robots are moving out of the structured factory floor and into unstructured environments such as disaster sites, planetary surfaces, and agricultural fields, for which the right robot often does not yet exist. We present GLAMDRING, a framework that synthesizes the optimal robot for a locomotion task and, jointly, learns the controller that drives it. For the given specifications of forward-velocity bounds, a per-actuator power budget, an actuator library, and a payload requirement, GLAMDRING returns a matched quadruped morphology (link geometry and per-joint actuators) and a Hopf-oscillator Central Pattern Generator (CPG) gait policy. We rank feasible designs against a target design objective, viz., maximum speed, minimum Cost of Transport (CoT), or max Payload Margin. Because body and locomotion are coupled, the optimal morphology dictates how a robot is driven, while optimal gait depends on the physical body. We train a small number of CPG policies by reinforcement learning across the space of candidate morphologies, co-learning the gait with the underlying robot hardware. Link lengths and actuators are then resolved post-hoc from the policy's logged operating envelope, reducing synthesis cost to a small, fixed number of reinforcement-learning runs instead of one per candidate. Our experiments show three key findings: co-designing body and gait is necessary to satisfy locomotion constraints; actuator-envelope feasibility, rather than locomotion success alone, determines realizable payload capacity; and canonical animal gaits emerge naturally in most designs from morphology and constraints alone. A real-world demonstration further highlights the efficacy of our work.

</details>


### [231] [Pose-aware Legged Robot Semantic Exploration with Omnidirectional Perception in Confined Unknown Environments](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.19460)
*Xiaoyang Zhan,Shiyu Chen,Kenji Shimada*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: POSE enables pose-aware, vision-guided semantic exploration on legged robots by exploiting body pitch/roll with an omnidirectional camera-LiDAR. It combines pose-aware viewpoint sampling, aim-aligned execution, and VLM-assisted, BEV-based pruning to reduce redundant inspections and improve coverage and efficiency. validated in simulation and a real machine-shop experiment; code to be released.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Planar viewpoints and fixed stances in legged systems limit visibility of upper object surfaces, especially in confined environments with restricted standoff. Tilting can improve coverage but increases mission time. A method that smartly selects body postures and prunes redundant inspections can improve the coverage-time trade-off in semantic exploration.

Method: Introduce POSE with: (1) a pose-aware viewpoint sampling module that selects body postures from partial object maps based on expected coverage gain; (2) aim-aligned execution to minimize unnecessary body reorientation; (3) an object-centric viewpoint pruning strategy aided by a vision-language model (VLM) using persistent observation history and bird's-eye-view maps; (4) integration of semantic viewpoints with geometric exploration viewpoints in a global planner.

Result: In simulation, POSE increases final target-surface coverage by 8–10 percentage points and reduces exploration time by 17–32%, achieving the highest mean object coverage AUC among baselines. Real-world tests with a legged robot carrying an omnidirectional camera-LiDAR setup in a machine shop demonstrated applicability.

Conclusion: Adaptive body-posture planning enhances the coverage-efficiency trade-off in legged robot semantic exploration and is suitable for real-world deployment; code release is planned for community use.

Abstract: Semantic exploration in confined environments requires both environment mapping and detailed observation of target objects. For ground robots, limited sensor vertical fields of view and restricted standoff distances can leave upper object surfaces unobserved from planar viewpoints. Body tilting can improve coverage, but additional observations and posture transitions increase mission time. To address this trade-off, we present POSE, a pose-aware semantic exploration system that exploits a legged robot's intrinsic body pitch and roll with omnidirectional camera-LiDAR perception. The proposed pose-aware viewpoint sampling module selects body postures from partial object maps according to expected coverage gain, while aim-aligned execution reduces unnecessary body reorientation. Further, we introduce an object-centric viewpoint pruning strategy assisted by a vision-language model (VLM), which uses persistent observation history and bird's-eye-view (BEV) maps to reduce redundant inspection visits. The resulting semantic viewpoints are combined with geometric exploration viewpoints in a global exploration planner. Simulations show that POSE improves final target-surface coverage by 8-10 percentage points over the planar planning baseline while reducing exploration time by 17-32%, and achieves the highest mean object coverage AUC among the evaluated baselines. Real-world experiments with a legged robot carrying an omnidirectional camera-LiDAR suite in a machine shop further demonstrate the system's applicability. These results support adaptive body-posture planning for improving the coverage-efficiency trade-off in legged robot semantic exploration. We plan to release the code for community benefit in the future.

</details>


### [232] [FASA: Feedback-Aware Sampling Adaptation for Efficient Diffusion-Based VLA Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.19475)
*Yuchen Han,Jianhan Wu,Xiaoyang Qu,Lingwei Kong,Shiyi Li,Jianzong Wang*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: Training-free runtime adaptation for diffusion-based Vision-Language-Action models using feedback signals to adapt sampling range and step within range, yielding up to 1.45x speedup with competitive accuracy.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Diffusion-based VLA models incur heavy iterative sampling costs, hindering real-time deployment on edge devices. Existing acceleration methods rely on costly training or static pruning that fails to adapt to dynamic robotic workloads.

Method: Introduce FASA (Feedback-Aware Sampling Adaptation): a training-free framework with two co-designed adapters: an interaction-driven range adaptor uses visual and gripper-force feedback to modulate the global sampling-step budget; a proprioception-aware step adaptor selects the optimal step within the adapted range. This enables hardware to adapt to workload demands across execution phases.

Result: Empirical evaluations show inference speed improvements up to 1.45× on multiple benchmarks while maintaining competitive success rates, demonstrating a dynamic runtime architecture for deploying heavy generative embodied AI on resource-constrained platforms.

Conclusion: FASA enables a novel dynamic runtime paradigm for diffusion-based VLA that leverages multimodal feedback to adapt sampling in real time, reducing compute demands without sacrificing performance.

Abstract: Diffusion-based Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models achieve strong performance in embodied tasks, but their iterative sampling imposes heavy computational and memory-access cost, blocking real-time deployment on edge platforms. Existing acceleration methods either require expensive training (e.g., distillation, flow matching) or degrade perception via statically scheduled pruning and caching, ignoring the dynamic workload variance of robotic interactions. This paper presents FASA (Feedback-Aware Sampling Adaptation), a training-free runtime framework that treats real-time multimodal feedback as a control signal for the denoising pipeline: an interaction-driven range adaptor modulates the global sampling-step budget based on visual and gripper-force feedback, and a proprioception-aware step adaptor pinpoints the optimized step within the adapted range. This co-designed framework allows the underlying hardware architecture to adaptively match the workload demands of different execution phases. Comparative evaluations across several benchmarks show that the inference speed can be increased by up to 1.45$\times$ while maintaining competitive success rates, providing a novel dynamic runtime architecture paradigm for deploying heavy generative embodied AI workloads onto resource-constrained computing platforms.

</details>


### [233] [Self-excited actuation enables adaptive and resilient flapping-wing flight](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.19480)
*Rundong Yang,Ethan S. Wold,Ellen Liu,James Lynch,Wei Zhou,Mark Jankauski,Simon Sponberg,Nick Gravish*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: First flight-capable flapping wing robot actuated asynchronously; demonstrates fast, collision-responsive wingbeats and improved stability versus synchronous actuation, suggesting asynchronous actuation as a robust blueprint for future flying robots.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Biological inspiration from insect flight muscles: asynchronous muscles enable intrinsic resonance and rapid, autonomous responses. Most flapping robots use synchronous actuation, which may limit speed and robustness; the work seeks to exploit asynchronous actuation to enhance embodied control.

Method: Design and implementation of a flight-capable flapping wing robot employing asynchronous actuation. The study analyzes how wings adapt to changes in resonant body mechanics without control input and how wings react to obstacle collisions without extrinsic sensing. Comparative flight tests against synchronous actuation in cluttered environments.

Result: Asynchronous actuation yields instantaneous response to collisions and adaptation to resonant mechanics without external control input. Flight tests show significantly improved stability and performance with asynchronous actuation compared to synchronous actuation.

Conclusion: Emulating asynchronous insect muscles enables fast, reactive actuation and supports a division of control between low-level actuation dynamics and high-level sensorimotor systems. This approach provides a blueprint for more robust and responsive flying robots.

Abstract: The muscles that power insect flight fall into one of two categories: 1) synchronous muscles that contract under direct control from the nervous system, and 2) asynchronous muscles which have an intrinsic stretch activation response that spontaneously generates wingbeats without the need for signaling from the brain. It is thought that the emergent nature of asynchronous wingbeats provides both adaptive and responsive capabilities for flight control. To date, most flying robots use synchronous actuation. In this paper we develop the first flight-capable flapping wing robot that uses asynchronous actuation. We demonstrate that asynchronous actuation allows wings to respond to changes in the resonant mechanics of the body without control input, and wings can react instantaneously to collisions with obstacles with no extrinsic sensing needed. Flight tests within cluttered environments demonstrate that asynchronous actuation significantly improves stability and performance when compared to synchronous actuation. In total this work demonstrates that a flapping wing robot actuation strategy that emulates the asynchronous muscles of flying insects can provide fast, reactive actuation responses before a control system would need to intervene. This partitioning of embodied control to both the low-level actuation dynamics and and high-level sensorimotor system provides a compelling blueprint for new flying robots.

</details>


### [234] [PIVOT: Perception-aware Independent Viewpoint Online Optimization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.19510)
*Yuyang Chen,Shekoufeh Sadeghi,Charuvahan Adhivarahan,Elton Lemos,Chen Wang,Sanjeev J. Koppal,Karthik Dantu*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: PIVOT is a lightweight iterative method to optimize sensor viewing direction along a fixed translation to maximize feature visibility; achieves 76–85× speedup with ~98–100% of brute-force visibility; validated in simulation and on a quadruped robot.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Robotic perception often assumes a fixed field of view (FoV); motion-decoupled sensors enable dynamic viewpoint control but require efficient online direction selection in feature-dense environments to maintain robust localization.

Method: Under a conical FoV model, visibility depends solely on the optical axis, reducing the optimization to two degrees of freedom on the viewing sphere S^2. The method uses coordinate-free SO(3) exponential-map updates for continuous optimization, avoiding explicit angular parametrizations or exhaustive sphere search. It performs iterative optimization of the viewing direction along a fixed translation trajectory.

Result: Monte Carlo evaluations show 98.1–99.6% of brute-force visibility with a 76–85× speedup. Photorealistic simulation and real-world experiments demonstrate improved visual localization robustness and practical viewpoint control on a quadruped robot.

Conclusion: PIVOT enables efficient, near-optimal online viewpoint optimization for motion-decoupled sensors, improving localization robustness and enabling practical control of sensor direction in dynamic, feature-dense environments.

Abstract: A fundamental assumption in robotic perception is that the sensor's field of view (FoV) is fixed relative to the robot body. Motion-decoupled sensors, such as gimbal-mounted cameras and MEMS-based LiDARs, instead allow sensing direction to be controlled independently at runtime. This freedom creates a computational challenge: efficiently selecting useful viewing directions online in feature-dense environments. We propose PIVOT, a lightweight iterative method that optimizes sensor viewing direction along a fixed translation trajectory to maximize feature visibility. Under a conical FoV model, visibility depends only on the optical axis, yielding a two-degree-of-freedom optimization on the viewing sphere $S^2$. Coordinate-free $SO(3)$ exponential-map updates enable efficient continuous optimization without explicit angular parameterizations or exhaustive viewing-sphere search. Monte Carlo evaluations retain 98.1--99.6% of brute-force visibility with a 76--85x speedup. Photorealistic simulation and real-world experiments further demonstrate improved visual localization robustness and practical viewpoint control on a quadruped robot.

</details>


### [235] [CoreSense: Traceable Failure Recall and Conflict-Aware Belief Gating for Auditable Robot Decisions](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.19512)
*Zoe Li*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: CoreSense provides an auditable, conflict-aware gate for robot memory evidence, achieving near-zero unsafe actions across offline, simulated, and cloud deployments; however, it does not enable autonomous recovery or safety certification.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Address the mismatch between recalling past failures and current observations, ensuring decisions are bounded, justifiable, and auditable rather than blindly autonomous.

Method: Propose CoreSense architecture: a traceable episodic-evidence store coupled with a conflict-aware belief gate that evaluates scope, provenance, time, contradiction, and support before choosing PROCEED, re-observe, abstain, or escalate. Evaluation spans three layers (offline real-robot data, frozen signal-level simulation, live cloud path) with datasets CableTrace-120 and BotFails-200, plus public data and cloud deployment tests. Additional components include disjoint raw-video policies, ViFailback-BotFails detectors, UR3 telemetry for protective stops, grip-loss transfer, controlled physical corroboration, and conflict-aware fusion, culminating in a CockroachDB Cloud–Amazon Bedrock deployment path.

Result: Belief gating reduces protocol-defined unsafe proceeds to 0% on CableTrace-120 and BotFails-200 (from 20% and 40%). A raw-video policy achieves 0% unsafe proceed but overblocks all nominal episodes. On public data, ViFailback-BotFails detector attains AUROC 0.778 yet remains all-blocking; UR3 telemetry yields 0% unsafe proceed with 36.1% overblocking and 61.9% coverage; grip-loss transfer is negative. Controlled physical corroboration shows 3.3%, 0%, and 42.0%; conflict-aware fusion shows 4.7%, 0%, and 42.8%. Cloud recalls (20/20) validate a CockroachDB Cloud–Amazon Bedrock deployment path.

Conclusion: The evidence supports an auditable integration pattern for evidence-based robotic decision-making, rather than autonomous recovery or formal safety certification.

Abstract: Robots can recall prior failures without knowing whether recalled evidence remains valid, conflicts with current observations, or is sufficient to guide a decision. We present CoreSense, a robot-system integration architecture that combines traceable episodic evidence with a conflict-aware belief gate and bounded, auditable recommendations. The gate checks scope, provenance, time, contradiction, and support before it permits PROCEED, requests re-observation, abstains, or escalates. Evaluation follows three complementary layers without commanding a physical robot: offline public real-robot data, a frozen signal-level simulation, and a live cloud deployment path. On CableTrace-120 and BotFails-200, belief gating reduces protocol-defined unsafe proceeds from 20% and 40% to 0%. A disjointly calibrated raw-video policy also reaches 0% unsafe proceed, but overblocks every nominal episode. On public data, a ViFailback-BotFails visual detector reaches 0.778 AUROC yet remains all-blocking, whereas cycle-disjoint UR3 telemetry for protective stops yields 0% unsafe proceed, 36.1% overblocking, and 61.9% coverage; grip-loss transfer remains a negative result. Controlled physical corroboration yields 3.3%, 0%, and 42.0%, while conflict-aware fusion yields 4.7%, 0%, and 42.8%. Finally, 20/20 cloud recalls validate a CockroachDB Cloud-Amazon Bedrock deployment path. The evidence supports an auditable integration pattern, not autonomous recovery or certified safety.

</details>


### [236] [AURORA: A Natural Language-Driven Agentic Framework for Understanding, Reasoning, and Orchestrating Reliable Air-Ground Co-Simulation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.19527)
*Keshu Wu,Hao Zhang,Rui Gan,Xiangbo Gao,Xiaopeng Li,Zhengzhong Tu,Yang Zhou*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: AURORA uses a natural-language-driven framework and the Air-Ground Scenario Graph (AGSG) to compile, verify, and repair air-ground co-simulation scenarios, improving reliability and faithfulness to user requests.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Reduce labor-intensive scenario construction and validate cross-domain relationships (spatial, temporal, communication, behavioral) to ensure user-requested interactions are realized, not just executable code.

Method: Introduce AGSG as a typed intermediate representation linking agents, missions, events, links, success conditions, and dependencies. Enable simulator-grounded parsing, joint road-airspace grounding, temporal planning, pre-execution feasibility checking, trace-based runtime verification, failure localization, and bounded repair within a unified workflow. Develop AURORA-Bench to evaluate both executability and faithfulness to interactions across multiple language models.

Result: Structured execution and runtime verification significantly improve reliability; silent failures are exposed by runtime checks; localized repairs fix violations without regenerating entire scenarios; explicit intermediate representations enable verifiable and repairable language-driven co-simulation.

Conclusion: Explicit intermediate representations and runtime verification are essential for reliable language-driven co-simulation, enabling not only executable code but verified realized behavior and repairability.

Abstract: Air-ground transportation research increasingly relies on co-simulation, yet constructing scenarios remains labor-intensive and difficult to validate. More importantly, a generated scenario may execute successfully while failing to realize the spatial, temporal, communication, or behavioral relationships requested by the user. This paper presents AURORA, a natural-language-driven agentic framework that treats air-ground scenario generation as a process of compilation with verification. Central to AURORA is the Air-Ground Scenario Graph (AGSG), a typed intermediate representation that explicitly connects agents, aerial missions, events, communication links, success conditions, and their cross-domain dependencies. This shared representation enables simulator-grounded parsing, joint road-airspace grounding, temporal planning, pre-execution feasibility checking, trace-based runtime verification, failure localization, and bounded repair within a unified workflow. We further introduce AURORA-Bench to evaluate not only whether generated scenarios execute, but whether they faithfully realize the requested interactions. Experiments across multiple language models show that structured execution substantially improves reliability, while runtime verification exposes silent failures that completion-based evaluation overlooks. Localized repair further resolves many violations without regenerating the entire scenario. The results show that reliable scenario generation requires verifying realized behavior, not merely executable code, and demonstrate the value of explicit intermediate representations for verifiable and repairable language-driven co-simulation.

</details>


### [237] [SLAMSqueezeBench: Comparing SLAM Systems under Resource Constraints](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.19533)
*Mohamed Hefny,Karthik Dantu,Steven Y. Ko*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: SLAMSqueezeBench offers a framework to benchmark SLAM systems under realistic edge-resource constraints, including compute/memory limits and frame-drop simulation, across nine SLAM methods; aims to standardize evaluation and will be community-accessible.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing SLAM benchmarks do not evaluate performance under realistic, co-located resource constraints on edge hardware where SLAM runs alongside other tasks; a common, constrained evaluation framework is needed.

Method: Developed SLAMSqueezeBench that enforces compute and memory limits on the SLAM process and simulates camera frame acquisition with a finite buffer that can drop frames; used to compare nine SLAM systems spanning classical, learning-based, and Gaussian-splatting approaches.

Result: Applied the framework to perform a comparative evaluation of nine SLAM systems, illustrating its ability to test under realistic workloads; the framework will be released for community use upon publication.

Conclusion: SLAMSqueezeBench enables standardized, realistic benchmarking of SLAM on edge hardware and is planned for public release, addressing a gap in current benchmarking practices.

Abstract: Simultaneous localization and mapping (SLAM) is one of the services running on an autonomous robot. It is typically run to assist other tasks such as planning, manipulation, etc. All these tasks are run on edge hardware and are subject to severe resource constraints. However, most SLAM systems are built and tested in isolation, and their performance is reported as if they are the only task running on a system. We observe that existing benchmarks lack a common mechanism for comparing SLAM systems under realistic resource constraints. To address this limitation, we have developed SLAMSqueezeBench, a framework that allows testing of SLAM systems under realistic workloads on edge hardware. It does so by imposing constraints on compute and memory resources available for the SLAM system during execution. It also simulates realistic camera frame acquisition with frame drops when a finite buffer is full. Using SLAMSqueezeBench, we compare nine SLAM systems spanning classical systems, learning-based systems, and approaches for Gaussian splatting. Our testing framework will be available for use by the community upon publication.

</details>


### [238] [Navigate or Relocate? Planning Among Movable Obstacles in Unknown Environments](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.19541)
*Yuqing Zhang,Haoyu Zhu,Yiannis Kantaros*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: An online NAMO framework for unknown environments that jointly considers navigation and object relocation, using interdependent relocation sequences and LLM-guided sampling to handle ambiguity and improve plan quality.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To overcome planning failure when all collision-free paths are blocked in unknown environments, by enabling online decisions between navigating and relocating movable objects, including interdependent relocations.

Method: The framework alternates between treating discovered movable objects as obstacles or as removable. Navigation uses existing motion planners; relocation uses a sampling-based search that considers interdependencies among relocations and employs a language model to bias sampling. It operates online with onboard sensing to reveal unknown space and determine whether relocation is necessary.

Result: Demonstrates scalability to cluttered environments requiring interdependent relocations and achieves improved plan quality over existing baselines in numerical experiments.

Conclusion: The proposed online NAMO framework effectively resolves ambiguity between navigating and relocating in unknown environments and outperforms prior approaches, suggesting potential for broader applicability in robot motion planning under partial observability.

Abstract: Conventional robot planning methods seek collision-free paths to a goal but fail when all paths are blocked. In these cases, the robot must determine which objects to relocate, in what order, and where to place them to clear a path---a problem known as Navigation Among Movable Obstacles (NAMO). Most NAMO planners assume a known environment, while existing approaches for unknown environments typically reason locally about relocations and cannot plan interdependent relocation sequences. We consider NAMO in unknown environments revealed through onboard sensing, where the robot must decide whether a blocked route requires relocation or a feasible path may exist through unexplored space. We propose an online framework that addresses this ambiguity by selecting between navigation and relocation using shortest paths that treat discovered movable objects as obstacles or as removable. Navigation relies on existing motion planners, while relocation uses a sampling-based approach that, unlike existing approaches for unknown environments, searches over \textit{interdependent} relocation sequences and uses an LLM to bias sampling. Numerical experiments demonstrate scalability to cluttered environments requiring interdependent relocations and improved plan quality over existing baselines.

</details>


### [239] [VABench: Measuring Embodied Spatial Intelligence through Visual Demonstrations, Active Perception, and Metric Control](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.19554)
*Zhongbo Zhang,Jiayi Jin,Yifan Wang,Zaibin Zhang,Haiwen Diao,Lijun Wang,Huchuan Lu*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: VA-Bench evaluates the complete observe-reason-act-revise loop for embodied spatial tasks using RGB-only demonstrations and active viewpoint control, across 14 base task families, held-out geometries, and a long-horizon five-object track; results show strong target localization but limited long-horizon success, with active vision boosting performance and geometry transfer causing significant drops.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Quantify whether general-purpose multimodal LLMs can autonomously acquire missing spatial evidence, reason over a common frame, and act via a model-agnostic controller without privileged priors.

Method: Introduce VA-Bench with 14 base task families (11 single-arm, 3 dual-arm), 7 held-out geometry/layout variants, and a long-horizon five-object track. Evaluate 12 model conditions across 3 runs with 20 seeds each, measuring terminal success, trajectory diagnostics, and subtask progress. Features include RGB-only demonstrations, active camera control, metric Cartesian commands, and revision from execution feedback, with no oracle trajectories or learned action heads.

Result: Best model achieves 100% target localization and 78.9% spatial-relations accuracy; three-run macro-average task success is 53.93% ± 3.17%. Active camera control raises success from 27.86% to 57.50% in a matched comparison; held-out geometry transfer reduces task success by >30 percentage points; no model completes a strict long-horizon episode.

Conclusion: VA-Bench robustly probes teaching an observe-reason-act-revise loop with general-purpose MLLMs: while models can leverage demonstrations and active sensing to perform embodied tasks, they struggle to generalize across held-out geometries and to complete long-horizon episodes, highlighting the need for deeper integration of perception, planning, and control.

Abstract: Spatial intelligence requires more than describing object locations. Under incomplete observation, models must identify and acquire missing evidence, interpret it in a common spatial frame, and act on it. We introduce VA-Bench to evaluate the complete observe-reason-act-revise loop. General-purpose MLLMs learn procedural context from RGB-only demonstrations, actively select camera viewpoints, issue metric Cartesian commands, and revise them from execution feedback. Models receive no privileged object poses, oracle trajectories, or learned action heads. A fixed model-agnostic controller executes only model-specified targets. VA-Bench contains 14 base task families (11 single-arm and three dual-arm), seven held-out geometry/layout variants, and a long-horizon five-object composition track. We evaluate 12 primary model conditions in three independent runs over the same 20 physically verified seeds per base task, reporting terminal success, nine trajectory-level behavioral diagnostics, and subtask progress. First, the best-performing model scores 100.0% on target localization and 78.9% on spatial relations in the annotated run. Its three-run macro-average task success is only 53.93+/-3.17%. Second, active camera control significantly improves task success over passive multi-view observation. In one matched comparison, success rises from 27.86% to 57.50%. Third, held-out geometric transfer can reduce task success by over 30 percentage points. No model completes a strict long-horizon episode, despite substantial partial progress. VA-Bench thus tests whether general-purpose MLLMs can turn visual demonstrations and actively acquired evidence into successful embodied action.

</details>


### [240] [Tele-Traversability: Rethinking Traversability for Teleoperated Ground Robots in Terrain Navigation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.19577)
*Lewei Feng,Qi Chen,Wenshuo Wang,Xianghao Meng,Minh Kieu,Haijie Guan,Jin Wu,Fuchun Sun,Junqiang Xi*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: Proposes tele-traversability, integrating operator cognitive states into traversability assessment for teleoperation to align human and robot judgments; provides definitions, framework, and future challenges.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Discrepancy between human-in-the-loop feedback and robot onboard sensing in teleoperation; need human-centric traversability considering attention, workload, and risk tolerance.

Method: Literature reframing and extension of traversability definitions from robot-centric to teleoperation; conceptual framework bridging human factors with robot perception; analysis of roles and definitions; literature synthesis and identification of trends.

Result: A conceptual extension; formalizes tele-traversability, outlines operators' cognitive factors affecting judgment, and proposes direction for human-centric teleoperation research; not empirical results.

Conclusion: Tele-traversability as a step toward human-centric teleoperation; outlines future trends and open challenges in aligning human and robot traversability, enabling fluent tele-navigation.

Abstract: Teleoperation, a human-in-the-loop control scheme, allows a human operator to remotely command and guide a mobile robot to navigate in off-road environments, yet fluent and user-friendly tele-navigation requires an alignment of traversability evaluation between human and robot. In the teleoperation system, the human operator typically utilizes off-site incomplete and delayed feedback via a human-machine interface to make a judgment of traversability, while the robot makes such an evaluation based on in situ onboard sensory information, which could cause divergent traversability estimation and thus generate mismatched decisions and actions. Existing approaches for traversability modeling, estimation, and prediction are mainly derived from the view of robots, i.e., robot-centric, and are practically suitable for fully autonomous mobile robots, but neglect the influence of human operators. To address this problem, this paper extends the concept of traversability from robot-centric to human-centric by accounting for the operator's cognitive states, such as attention, workload, and risk tolerance or awareness, termed tele-traversability. We first revisit the definitions and roles of traversability in robotics and then extend them to teleoperation settings. Finally, we highlight future trends and open challenges of tele-traversability toward human-centric teleoperation systems.

</details>


### [241] [Recovering Aggressively Pruned Vision-Language-Action Models with Offline Hidden-State Distillation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.19579)
*Chiyoung Kim,Sanghyuk Roy Choi,Minhyeok Lee*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: Offline, width-pruned VLA backbones with hidden-state distillation recover most teacher-level performance without online rollouts, enabling faster on-board execution and smaller memory footprint.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Enable deployment of large vision-language-action models on robot hardware by reducing model size and compute while preserving task performance.

Method: Apply width pruning that reduces channel dimensions while keeping the residual stream size; train the student against a cache built from a single teacher pass (no projector required) and perform hidden-state distillation. Sweep pruning ratios to identify when the recovery objective matters; compare against supervised recovery and reinforcement-learning–based restoration. Evaluate on OpenVLA-OFT, CogACT, and a 6-DoF manipulator.

Result: 63% pruning lifted to within 3.5 points of the teacher after ~8 GPU-hours of offline training. OpenVLA-OFT shows no significant difference up to ~45% pruning; hidden-state distillation adds 2.1–4.5 points (63–87% pruning) and CogACT adds 9.4–22.1 points (63% onward). At 81% pruning on CogACT, the gap is ~3.9 points; supervised recovery lags by >20 points. With matched compression, width pruning improves success while depth pruning reduces latency. On a 6-DoF manipulator, the distilled student at 72% reduction achieves 77.5% success vs 59.5% for supervised recovery, runs 2.23× faster on-board, and uses 62% less memory.

Conclusion: Offline hidden-state distillation with width pruning can effectively recover teacher performance for VLA robots, offering substantial gains in accuracy over supervised recovery, reduced latency, and memory efficiency. The approach scales across tasks and enables practical on-board deployment at high compression.

Abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models let robots follow language instructions, but their language backbones of several billion parameters are the main obstacle to running them on robot hardware. Structured pruning reduces that backbone, and removing 63% of it from OpenVLA-OFT drops LIBERO-Long success from 93.2% to 0.8%. A recent approach restores such a model with supervised fine-tuning followed by reinforcement learning, which needs online rollouts and hundreds of GPU-hours. We recover most of the lost success entirely offline. Width pruning narrows the blocks but keeps the residual stream at its original size, so teacher and student hidden states have the same shape and are matched directly, without a projector. Training against a cache built in one teacher pass lifts the 63%-reduced student to within 3.5 points of the teacher in about 8 GPU-hours. A sweep over nine ratios locates where the recovery objective starts to matter. Up to 45% reduction the two do not differ significantly on OpenVLA-OFT. Hidden-state distillation then adds +2.1 to +4.5 points there between 63% and 87%, and +9.4 to +22.1 points on CogACT from 63% onward. At 81% on CogACT, a tripled recovery budget narrows the distilled student's gap to the teacher to 3.9 points on average, while supervised recovery stays more than 20 points below. At matched compression, width pruning yields higher success and depth pruning lower latency. On a 6-DoF manipulator, the distilled student at 72% reduction reaches 77.5% success against 59.5% for supervised recovery, runs 2.23x faster on-board than the teacher, and uses 62% less memory.

</details>


### [242] [OmniCalib: Target-Free, Task-Structured Self-Calibration for Humanoid Robots](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.19582)
*Kaixiang Lu,Haiyu Lan,Chunxiao Qiao,You Li,Enyu Li,Yehao Lu,Jiarui Yang,Peiwen Lin,Chuang Wang*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: OmniCalib is a target-free, robot-native calibration workflow that jointly calibrates full upper and lower limbs and multi-camera head rig on humanoids, using depth ICP and onboard sensing to estimate joint zeros and camera extrinsics with high accuracy and without fiducials.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To address drift and miscalibration caused by assembly, wear, and replacement, and to remove dependence on calibration targets by leveraging only onboard sensing and native robot motions.

Method: A modular, observability-checked pipeline where each observable block corresponds to a robot-native task. Depth ICP recovers 14 arm joint zeros and calibrates RGB-D extrinsics; head rig uses visual/legged odometry with a live ROS transform tree. All corrections are written back to the CAD model only if observable and supported.

Result: Extrinsic corrections relative to CAD: left wrist 10.56 mm / 1.74°, right wrist 6.33 mm / 1.25°, chest RGB-D 9.81 mm / 0.929°. ICP point-to-plane residual 2.09 mm. ICP and ArUco recover joint zeros within encoder resolution. Lower-limb joints: RMS error 0.063° for 12 zeros on AGIBOT A3 Ultra. Head module achieves mean SO(3) error 1.061°, best sequence 0.775°. Rig-relative angles repeat within 0.140°. Validation via injection tests and held-out data.

Conclusion: The OmniCalib framework enables accurate, target-free, multi-robot calibration of all limb joints and camera extrinsics with strong observability guarantees, competitive to iKalibr, and demonstrates robust performance across walking and varied sequences.

Abstract: Assembly, wear, and component replacement perturb the sensor extrinsics and joint zeros encoded by a humanoid CAD model. Existing procedures calibrate one sensor pair or require external fiducials. Using only robot-native motion and onboard sensing, we present OmniCalib, a target-free workflow that calibrates the full upper limbs---all 14 arm joint zeros and the extrinsics of both wrist and chest cameras---as well as lower limbs and the multi-camera head rig. Each module matches a robot-native task to a parameter block, checks observability, and writes only supported corrections to the CAD model. Our depth ICP method recovers all 14 arm joint zeros and calibrates all RGB-D camera extrinsics without any calibration target. Relative to CAD, the estimated extrinsic corrections are 10.56 mm and 1.74 degrees for the left wrist, 6.33 mm and 1.25 degrees for the right wrist, and 9.81 mm and 0.929 degrees for the chest RGB-D camera. ICP point-to-plane residual is 2.09 mm. On the same injected offsets, ICP and ArUco recover all 14 joint zeros below the 0.1-degree encoder-resolution reference. On an AGIBOT A3 Ultra humanoid, four static double-support stances recover all 12 lower-limb joint-zero offsets injected with an RMS error of 0.063 degrees. The head module combines multi-camera visual odometry with legged odometry and dynamic compensation through the live ROS transform tree. Using only planar walking, it attains a mean SO(3) error of 1.061 degrees across three sequences. The best sequence reaches 0.775 degrees, competitive with iKalibr at 0.902 degrees from rich 6-DOF excitation. Rig-relative angles repeat within 0.140 degrees. Injection recovery and held-out tests validate each observable block.

</details>


### [243] [Quantifying Mechanical Intelligence in Legged Robots with Information Theory](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.19588)
*Zach J. Patterson*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: Proposes information-theoretic metrics to quantify mechanical intelligence in legged robots, treating body dynamics as computation and communication channels, and analyzes how compliance vs. low-gear transmissions influence information processing across simple to complex robotic systems.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: There is a gap between engineering achievements in mechanical intelligence and a rigorous theoretical framework; quantitative, information-theoretic measures are needed to characterize embodied computation in robots.

Method: Develop information-theoretic metrics for mechanical intelligence and apply them to models of increasing complexity: (1) a linear robot-leg transmission, (2) a nonlinear single-leg simulation, (3) simulated quadrupeds with learned locomotion policies on challenging terrain; view mechanical modes as processors/channels and quantify information flow (bits) across coordinates and modes; compare effects of series-elastic actuation (compliance) versus proprioceptive, low-gear-ratio transmissions.

Result: Demonstrates a viable framework for quantifying mechanical intelligence with information theory, showing how existing legged-robot engineering insights map to information-theoretic terms and how information processing occurs within mechanical modes and coordinate spaces; establishes groundwork for broader study of robot mechanisms as embodied computation.

Conclusion: Provides a foundational framework to measure and compare embodied computation in robotic systems, enabling principled design choices for actuation and control; future work includes expanding to more diverse robots, terrains, and learning policies, and validating the metrics experimentally.

Abstract: Mechanical intelligence, loosely defined as the reduction in control burden afforded by a robot's physical form, has become a prominent concept in robotics, with instantiations in bioinspired robotics, soft robotics, robotic swarms, and many other areas. However, rigorous theoretical understanding and quantitative measures of mechanical intelligence have lagged behind the engineering systems that the community has developed. In this work, using modern legged robots as a benchmark and exemplar, we propose several information-theoretic metrics for quantifying mechanical intelligence. By viewing body dynamics as both a computational process and a communication channel, we show that several prior insights in legged-robot engineering can be described using information theory, and we quantify how bits are processed by mechanical modes and across robot coordinates. Specifically, we examine the trade-off between explicitly incorporating compliance through series-elastic actuation and using so-called proprioceptive, low-gear-ratio transmissions, and we explore how these mechanisms interact with control policies during locomotion. We develop these results on systems of increasing complexity: a simplified linear model of a robot-leg transmission, a nonlinear single-leg simulation, and simulated quadruped robots controlled by a learned policy while navigating challenging terrain. These results lay the groundwork for broader study of robot mechanisms and their role in embodied computation.

</details>


### [244] [WorldContact: A Contact-Centric World Model for Scalable Robot Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.19600)
*Caoliwen Wang,Mengdi Wang,Heng Zhang,Shixun Huang,Siyuan Chen,Chao Liu,Anpei Chen,Zhendong Wang,Peter Yichen Chen,Huamin Wang*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: WorldContact: a contact-centric deformable-object model built from limited high-quality trajectories that enables faster data generation (10x) and improves real-robot policy adaptation (bag lifting from 65% to 95%).


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Robots require interaction data to adapt to new objects/tasks, but collecting such data is costly. Deformable objects like bags complicate simulation and require tiny time steps to avoid interpenetration; a data-efficient model is needed to generate training data quickly for policy adaptation.

Method: Construct WorldContact from a small set of trajectories; predict dynamics at larger time steps than the simulation, while ensuring fidelity; evaluate on 16 shopping-bag tasks; use state-rollouts on an H100 GPU; fine-tune an existing vision-language-action policy with the generated data; deploy on real robot.

Result: 10x GPU speedup over the source simulator (excluding rendering/disk I/O); improved bag-lifting success from 65% (source sim data only) to 95% (with WorldContact-expanded data).

Conclusion: WorldContact enables efficient data generation for deformable-object manipulation, enabling better policy adaptation with limited high-quality trajectories.

Abstract: Adapting robots to new objects and tasks requires interaction experience that can be costly to obtain. We present WorldContact, a contact-centric world model for deformable-object manipulation, constructed from a limited set of high-quality trajectories to generate additional training data efficiently. It predicts object dynamics using larger time steps than the source numerical simulator, which requires small integration steps to resolve rapid motion and prevent interpenetration. We evaluate WorldContact across 16 shopping-bag manipulation tasks. State-rollout measurements on a single H100 GPU show a $10\times$ speedup over the source simulator, excluding rendering and disk I/O. We use the generated data to fine-tune an existing vision-language-action policy and deploy it directly on a real robot. In bag lifting, the same policy achieves 65% single-attempt success when fine-tuned on source simulation data alone, compared with 95% when fine-tuned on the dataset expanded with WorldContact. These results support efficient data generation with WorldContact for robot policy adaptation.

</details>


### [245] [TacSushi: Tactile-Grounded World-Action Modeling for Dexterous Sushi Manipulation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.19613)
*Haodi Hu,Kaen Kogashi,Toshiaki Koike-Akino*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: TacSushi is a tactile-grounded, Cosmos3-based world-action policy for dexterous food manipulation that uses a future-consequence predictive decoder with feature-wise gated tactile fusion, trained on real-robot data, delivering superior in-distribution and out-of-distribution performance compared to baselines.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Address manipulation under deformation, occlusion, and uncertain contact in food tasks by grounding control in tactile sensing and by leveraging predictions of future consequences during training to improve sample efficiency and generalization.
