Method: Cosmos3-based world-action policy with a backbone that encodes current RGB, language, and hand state. Feature-wise gated fusion integrates fingertip tactile features into the action representation. A decoder conditioned on demonstrated action chunks predicts logged future visuals, task progress, contact risk, and tactile summaries during training; the decoder is discarded at deployment. Consequence supervision comes from failed trials, which are excluded from imitation. The model is trained on 340 successful and 50 failed real-robot trials and evaluated across 600 rollouts on three in-distribution tasks and two out-of-distribution ingredient variants. Evaluation uses an anchored visual-quality protocol combining five human ratings and three vision-language-model ratings per rollout. Six baselines are compared, including omitting future-consequence supervision and using direct tactile concatenation instead of gated fusion.

Result: TacSushi achieves 68.3% average in-distribution success and 37.5% out-of-distribution success. Baselines: without future-consequence supervision 36.7%/10.0%, and with direct tactile concatenation instead of gated fusion 25.0%/17.5%. The results support that feature-wise gated tactile fusion and training-time predictive supervision provide complementary benefits.

Conclusion: Combining feature-wise gated tactile fusion with training-time predictive supervision improves dexterous food manipulation performance and generalization, highlighting the value of integrating tactile grounding and future-consequence modeling in policy learning.

Abstract: Dexterous food manipulation requires control under deformation, occlusion, and uncertain contact. We present TacSushi, a tactile-grounded, Cosmos3-based world-action policy that learns from recorded future consequences while acting on current observations. The backbone encodes current RGB, language, and hand state, and feature-wise gated fusion incorporates fingertip tactile features into the action representation. During training, a decoder conditioned on demonstrated action chunks predicts logged future visual observations, task progress, relative contact risk, and tactile summaries; this decoder is removed at deployment. Failed trials provide consequence supervision, but their actions are excluded from imitation. We train TacSushi on 340 successful and 50 failed real-robot trials and compare six methods in 600 separate rollouts across three in-distribution tasks and two out-of-distribution ingredient variants. To assess food quality beyond a single geometric threshold, we score terminal outcomes using an anchored visual-quality protocol that equally weights five human ratings and three vision-language-model ratings per rollout. Full TacSushi achieves 68.3% average in-distribution success and 37.5% out-of-distribution success, compared with 36.7%/10.0% without future-consequence supervision and 25.0%/17.5% with direct tactile concatenation in place of gated fusion. These comparisons support complementary benefits of feature-wise gated tactile fusion and training-only predictive supervision.

</details>


### [246] [EmbodiedMind: Adaptive Data Curation and Prefix-Tree Reinforcement Learning for Efficient Embodied Intelligence](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.19659)
*Feifan Wang,Zongbing Zhang,Yu Zhang,Lingfeng Wang,Yurui Zhu,Jin Deng,Mingliang Zhang,Zhengguang Gao,Yongcheng Wang,Jin Xu,Ri Yang*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: Efficient embodied learning via a three-stage pipeline (RSFT, IR-GRPO, Trie-GRPO) to improve data efficiency, gradient balance, and long-horizon credit assignment, achieving 70.02% average on 18 benchmarks and better long-horizon planning; reproducible.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Address three core limitations in training embodied foundation models: (1) low information value of many samples leading to inefficient sample utilization; (2) imbalanced gradient contributions across heterogeneous tasks within RL settings; (3) poor credit assignment in long-horizon planning where trajectory rewards penalize tokens indiscriminately.

Method: Three-stage approach: (1) RSFT filters low-informative samples via rejection sampling during fine-tuning to build robust behavioral priors without distributional collapse; (2) IR-GRPO uses task-specific, difficulty-stratified queues to balance datasets across RL iterations and employs a hybrid reward mechanism for cross-task feedback; (3) Trie-GRPO introduces action prefix trees to enable step-level advantage estimation for long-horizon planning, isolating intermediate correct decisions from downstream errors and balancing exploration depth with efficiency.

Result: EmbodiedMind achieves a state-of-the-art average performance of 70.02% across 18 benchmarks and markedly improves long-horizon task planning accuracy compared to other embodied foundation models.

Conclusion: The proposed RSFT–IR-GRPO–Trie-GRPO paradigm jointly enhances data efficiency, task balance, and credit assignment in embodied learning, yielding superior average performance and better long-horizon planning; results are set for reproducibility.

Abstract: Training embodied foundation models typically requires massive-scale datasets and extensive computational resources, yet often suffers from three critical limitations: (1) inefficient sample utilization due to low-informative samples; (2) imbalanced gradient contributions across heterogeneous tasks; and (3) severe credit assignment problem in long-horizon planning, where trajectory-level rewards indiscriminately penalize all tokens. To address these issues, we propose an efficient training paradigm that achieves state-of-the-art average performance through strategic data selection and hierarchical policy optimization. Our approach consists of three synergistic stages. First, Rejection Sampling-based Fine-Tuning (RSFT) filters out low-informative samples to establish robust behavioral priors while preventing distributional collapse. Second, Iterative Rejection GRPO (IR-GRPO) employs task-specific queues stratified by difficulty to keep datasets balanced across reinforcement learning iterations, coupled with a hybrid reward mechanism for precise cross-task feedback. Third, to enhance long-horizon task planning, we introduce Trie-GRPO, a novel reinforcement learning algorithm based on action prefix trees, which enables step-level advantage estimation. This resolves the credit assignment problem by isolating intermediate correct decisions from downstream errors, while effectively balancing exploration efficiency and depth compared to conventional search trees. As a result, EmbodiedMind achieves a state-of-the-art average performance of 70.02% across 18 benchmarks, and significantly outperforms other embodied foundation models in long-horizon task planning accuracy. Our project will be released for reproducibility.

</details>


### [247] [ReShoot: Generative Visual Domain Randomization of Recorded Robot Demonstrations for Visuomotor Policy Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.19661)
*Chiyoung Kim,Min Sung Choi,Jinho Ju,Chanhoe Gu,Donghwan Hwang,Wonseok Choi,Woongsun Jeon,Minhyeok Lee*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: ReShoot synthesizes visual diversity by re-rendering demonstrations with altered appearances to improve imitation-learning policies without additional data collection.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Imitation policies overfit to training visual conditions; reducing data collection burden by generating diverse visuals can improve robustness.

Method: 1) Caption scene with a vision-language model; 2) Edit targeted attributes (background, color, material); 3) Edge-conditioned video generator re-renders camera views; 4) Update instruction; 5) Copy action sequence and proprioception verbatim; generated episodes retain recorded labels.

Result: On LIBERO, mixed (recorded + re-rendered) demonstrations match recorded-only training (96.5% vs 96.9%). On LIBERO-Plus, robustness to perturbations improves (85.5% vs 82.3%). In physical robots (two platforms), with 43 and 100 demonstrations, recolored-object success rises from 0.0% to 42.9% and 47.5%, while original appearance performance is preserved.

Conclusion: ReShoot reduces data-collection needs by generating diverse visual contexts, preserves action labels, and yields comparable or improved performance and robustness across sim-to-real settings.

Abstract: Imitation-learned robot policies are frequently overfit to the visual conditions present in their training demonstrations. Consequently, variations in object color or background appearance often induce substantial performance degradation. A common mitigation strategy is to acquire additional demonstrations in each novel visual context; however, this approach is resource-intensive, requiring repeated access to a robot, a controlled environment, and human operation for every appearance condition to be covered. We introduce ReShoot, a framework that synthesizes visual diversity by re-rendering previously recorded demonstrations under altered appearances, thereby shifting the burden from data collection to generation. A vision-language model captions the scene, edits a targeted attribute (e.g., background, object color, or material), and an edge-conditioned video generator re-renders both camera views to match. The instruction is updated accordingly. The action sequence and proprioceptive trajectory are copied verbatim without relabeling, so each generated episode retains the recorded action and proprioceptive labels. On LIBERO, a policy trained on an equal mixture of recorded and re-rendered demonstrations matches the performance of recorded-only training (96.5% vs. 96.9%). Moreover, the mixed training set improves robustness to scene perturbations on LIBERO-Plus (85.5% vs. 82.3%). Across two physical robotic platforms, deploying ReShoot with 43 and 100 pre-collected demonstrations increased the success rate on recolored objects from 0.0% to 42.9% and 47.5%, respectively, while maintaining performance under the original recorded appearance.

</details>


### [248] [Runtime Safety Filtering for Two-Terminal Hazards in Robotic Battery Recycling](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.19665)
*Yuxin Cao,Wei Song,Xianglin Yang,Fusen Guo,Lin Li,Xiao Cheng,Jin Song Dong*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: Margin and fallback strategy dominate safety-utility trade-offs for proximity-defined hazards; predicate structure (conjunctive vs. two-site vs. composite) has little impact when margins are tuned.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Proximity hazards depend on joint spatial relations and cannot be adequately captured by simple object-wise keep-out regions; understanding how predicate structure, margin, and fallback affect runtime safety filters for learned manipulation policies.

Method: Evaluate runtime safety filters for LIBERO with frozen OpenVLA policies across three predicate families (conjunctive, two-site, composite) and four fallbacks (holding, retreat, sampled search, continuous-action barrier projection); vary geometric margin; test across three workcells; map safety-utility frontiers.

Result: All three predicate families produce nearly identical safety-utility frontiers once margins are tuned. The fallback strategy drives much of the trade-off: holding lowers task success versus retreat without reducing hazard; minimally invasive fallbacks leave more residual hazard. The ordering holds across a second policy; retreat-based filtering remains robust to standing clearance errors, but correlated payload-size errors are particularly damaging.

Conclusion: For proximity-defined manipulation hazards, margin selection and fallback strategy are more critical than predicate structure in determining the safety-utility trade-off of runtime filters; focus on margin calibration and choice of fallback over predicate design.

Abstract: Runtime safety filters for learned manipulation policies typically define unsafe states as unions of object-wise keep-out regions. This representation can be unnecessarily restrictive for hazards that depend on a joint spatial relation, such as battery recycling, where a conductive payload can short a charged cell only when it approaches both terminals simultaneously. We study runtime filtering for this two-terminal hazard in LIBERO using frozen OpenVLA policies. We factor a runtime filter into three design choices: the predicate structure, its geometric margin, and the fallback action applied when a commanded action is rejected. We compare a conjunctive predicate, a conventional two-site keep-out, and a composite of the two. For each predicate, we vary its margin to obtain a frontier between task success and residual hazard. We then compare four fallback strategies at matched operating points: holding, retreat, sampled search, and a continuous-action barrier projection. Across three workcells, the three predicate families trace nearly identical safety--utility frontiers once each is evaluated over its own margin. In contrast, the fallback strategy has a substantially larger effect: holding reduces task success by up to 0.302 relative to retreat without reducing hazard, while both minimally invasive fallbacks leave substantially more residual hazard. This ordering transfers to a second policy and task suite, while retreat-based filtering remains effective under standing errors in the clearances available to the filter, although correlated error in the estimated payload size is more damaging than larger independent errors in terminal position. These results show that, for proximity-defined manipulation hazards, margin selection and fallback strategy can matter more than predicate structure in determining the safety--utility trade-off of a runtime filter.

</details>


### [249] [Towards High-DoF Dexterous Manipulation through VLA Post-Training](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.19666)
*Junlei Zhu,Shenzhe Yao,Chaogui Huang,Wenkai Zhu,Jingwei Peng,Guanqi He,Soren Schwertfeger,Jiahao Chen,Yide Liu*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: A four-step post-training pipeline enables adapting imitation-learned VLA foundation models to dexterous hands, achieving reliable real-world manipulation across five tasks with 100% success on 20 trials per task.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Dexterous manipulation with high-DoF hands faces a mismatch between open-source VLA interfaces and actionable control, make retuning difficult due to gesture discontinuities in DAgger, and inefficient exploration in raw joint-space RL.

Method: A unified pipeline: (1) learn a temporal hand-action codec to map VLA outputs to absolute dexterous-hand commands, (2) supervised fine-tuning of the codec, (3) DAgger with buffered rollback, pose alignment, and smooth command blending to allow continuous hand-control corrections, (4) latent residual RL to explore in a restricted, codec-consistent space.

Result: Evaluated on five real-world tasks (bimanual transfer, in-hand reorientation, tool use). Within the reported post-training budgets, policies achieved 100% success on every task across 20 trials each.

Conclusion: The workflow offers a practical path to reliably deploy VLA foundation models for real-world dexterous manipulation, balancing data efficiency, stability, and safety while maintaining broad behavioral capabilities.

Abstract: Imitation-learned vision--language--action (VLA) foundation models acquire broad manipulation capabilities by scaling robot data across tasks and embodiments, but reliable deployment on a specific downstream task and hardware platform still requires post-training. Dexterous hands make this adaptation particularly difficult: their broad behavioural repertoire and high degree of freedom create a large and structured action space. Three obstacles are central: open-source VLAs do not natively provide an action interface for high-DoF hands; gesture mismatch during human-gated DAgger takeover creates command discontinuities and contaminates corrective trajectories; and reinforcement learning in the raw joint space is sample-inefficient. We present a unified four-step post-training pipeline comprising a learned temporal hand-action codec, supervised fine-tuning, DAgger, and real-world residual reinforcement learning. The codec adapts a pretrained VLA to absolute dexterous-hand commands. Buffered rollback, pose alignment, and smooth command blending enable continuous, task-relevant DAgger corrections, while latent residual RL confines exploration to coordinated hand motions captured by the codec. We evaluate the pipeline on five diverse real-world tasks spanning bimanual transfer, in-hand reorientation, and tool use. Within the reported post-training budgets, the resulting policies achieve 100\% success on every evaluated task over 20 trials per task. These results provide a practical path for adapting VLA foundation models to reliable real-world dexterous manipulation.

</details>


### [250] [VAST: V2X/Dynamic Map-Aware Autonomous Driving Systems Validation Toolchain](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.19681)
*Shunsuke Ito,Takuya Azumi*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: VAST provides an interoperable validation pipeline for cooperative autonomous driving, integrating Scenic, Scenario Simulator v2, AWSIM, Autoware, and SIM-LDM to validate CPS across IoT/Edge/Cloud, improving edge-case discovery and reducing collision rates via Dynamic Map integration.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Addresses interoperability challenges across simulation and software stacks in V2X/cooperative autonomous driving and demonstrates a practical, cross-stack validation infrastructure.

Method: Connects Lanelet2 to Scenic, ROS 2 co-simulation via SS2, Dynamic Map object injection into Autoware, and data collection of TTC, PET, collisions, timeouts, and performance. Performs constrained sampling in occluded intersections to boost edge-case discovery; compares scenarios with and without Dynamic Map; includes throughput study with 1-16 NPCs.

Result: Edge-case discovery rate under occlusion doubles from 40% to 80%, and average time per edge case halved (259.7s to 110.4s). Dynamic Map availability halves collision rate (78% to 40%) and doubles non-collision outcomes (22% to 60%), with TTC/PET shifts being statistically significant. Throughput with 1-16 NPCs shows sampling <0.1s; simulator execution and restart overhead dominate runtime.

Conclusion: VAST is a practical validation infrastructure for cooperative autonomous-driving CPSs, enabling interoperable, end-to-end validation across vehicle, infrastructure, edge, and cloud components.

Abstract: Cooperative autonomous driving in the IoT-to-Edge-to-Cloud continuum requires system-level validation across vehicles, infrastructure sensors, edge-side Dynamic Map services, and in-vehicle autonomous-driving stacks. This paper presents VAST, a V2X/Dynamic Map-aware validation toolchain that connects Scenic, Scenario Simulator v2, AWSIM, Autoware, and SIM-LDM. VAST does not introduce a new search algorithm; instead, it addresses interoperability challenges, including Lanelet2-to-Scenic mapping, ROS 2-based co-simulation through SS2, Dynamic Map object injection into Autoware, and collection of TTC, PET, collision, timeout, and performance measurements. In occluded-intersection scenarios, Lanelet2-compatible constrained sampling increases the edge-case discovery rate from 40.0% to 80.0% and reduces the average time per discovered edge case from 259.7 s to 110.4 s. Under the same generated scenario distribution, Dynamic Map availability reduces the collision rate from 78.0% to 40.0% and increases non-collision outcomes from 22.0% to 60.0%, with statistically significant TTC/PET shifts. A throughput study with 1-16 NPCs shows that sampling remains below 0.1 s, whereas AWSIM/Autoware execution and restart overhead dominate runtime. These results position VAST as a practical validation infrastructure for cooperative autonomous-driving CPSs.

</details>


### [251] [LYRIC: Language-Driven Physics-Based Character Control for Contact-Rich Whole-Body Object Interaction](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.19688)
*Zeyu Han,Zichong Meng,Julian Tanke,Minami Matsumoto,Sergey Bashkirov,Yingruo Fan,Selim Engin,Dongseok Shim,Takashi Shibuya,Yuki Mitsufuji,Huaizu Jiang*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: LYRIC is a language-driven, flow-matching controller for contact-rich physics-based interaction; it decomposes planning and action generation, achieving higher task success on OMOMO and held-out splits, with zero-shot transfer and test-time guidance.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Enable simulated characters to perform contact-rich whole-body object interactions from free-form language instructions, leveraging imperfect motion-capture data.

Method: Factorize control into a task-level planner predicting short-horizon object and humanoid-root trajectories and an action generator that resolves full-body motion and contacts in closed loop. Train via behavior cloning, freeze the planner, and post-tune the action generator using planner-based supervision. Use geometry-conditioned interaction rewards and relaxed reference tracking near hand-object contact; test-time object-waypoint guidance; evaluated on OMOMO with improved metrics.

Result: Tracker achieves 64.3% success vs 53.2% for InterMimic; unified policy 76.5% on full OMOMO; held-out LYRIC 90.3% vs 74.2% for strong baseline; qualitative results show robust, natural contact-rich interactions and zero-shot transfer; web page provided.

Conclusion: LYRIC advances language-driven control for contact-rich, whole-body interactions with improved success and motion quality, supports test-time guidance, and demonstrates strong transfer to novel object shapes.

Abstract: We present LYRIC, a generative flow-matching controller for language-driven physics-based contact-rich interaction control, that enables simulated characters to perform contact-rich whole-body object interactions from a free-form language instruction and a sparse terminal object goal. To obtain reliable expert trajectories from imperfect motion-capture references, a single tracking policy is trained using geometry-conditioned interaction rewards and relaxed reference tracking near hand-object contact. To guide interaction progress without prescribing a full-body kinematic reference, we factorize the controller into a task-level planner that predicts short-horizon object and humanoid-root trajectories, and an action generator that resolves whole-body motion and contacts in closed loop. After behavior cloning, we freeze the planner and post-tune the action generator on policy using the planner's predictions as stable supervision for intermediate task progression. In a controlled OMOMO evaluation, our tracker achieves 64.3% success compared with 53.2% for an InterMimic reimplementation, while a unified policy achieves 76.5% on the full OMOMO dataset. On the held-out split, LYRIC achieves 90.3% task success, compared with 74.2% for the strongest matched kinematic-planner baseline, with better semantic alignment and motion quality. Without retraining, the controller also supports test-time object-waypoint guidance. Qualitative results further demonstrate robust, natural contact-rich interactions and zero-shot transfer to novel object shapes. The webpage is available at https://neu-vi.github.io/LYRIC/

</details>


### [252] [UniExo: Unified Multi-Skill Policies for Musculoskeletal Locomotion and Co-Adaptive Exoskeleton Control](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.19690)
*Yifei Yuan,Jakob Wolf,Ghaith Androwis,Xianlian Zhou*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: UniExo unifies multiple locomotion skills into a single exoskeleton controller via a two-stage learning framework: distill four single-skill human policies into a shared latent policy and co-train an exoskeleton controller with RL across transitions, enabling seamless skill switching without explicit mode labels.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To replace activity-specific exoskeleton controllers and reduce explicit mode-switching by enabling a unified, user-specific controller that handles diverse locomotion tasks and transitions.

Method: 1) Train four single-skill imitation experts for walking, turning, running, and backward walking. 2) Distill them into a single network structured by a skill latent. 3) Fine-tune via reinforcement learning on transition sequences. 4) Initialize a hip exoskeleton controller from hip moment predictions of the human policy and co-adapt with it through multi-agent RL across the four skills. 5) Evaluate on unseen clips, multiple treadmill speeds, and cross-participant routes without skill labels.

Result: The unified human policy achieves a mean tracking success rate of 94.7% on unseen clips across the four skills and shows greater robustness to perturbations than its component experts. The exoskeleton controller shifts assistance timing and increases positive work at the hip. In experiments with six participants, the UniExo controller generalizes to four treadmill speeds and a continuous route through all four skills and transitions without skill labels or explicit mode switching.

Conclusion: UniExo demonstrates progress toward activity-general, unified exoskeleton control by bridging per-skill policies with a shared latent representation and cooperative learning, enabling robust, label-free transitions across diverse locomotor tasks.

Abstract: Daily locomotion encompasses diverse activities and frequent transitions between them, yet most exoskeleton controllers are designed for a single activity or a narrow set of related movements. Changes in activity therefore typically require explicit mode switching and separately tuned or retrained controllers. Simulation-based learning reduces the need for hardware-based tuning but generally retains this limitation. Here we present UniExo, a framework that first constructs a multi-skill musculoskeletal human policy and then jointly trains an exoskeleton control policy with it. Four single-skill imitation experts for walking, turning, running and backward walking are distilled into a single network structured by a skill latent and subsequently fine-tuned through reinforcement learning on transition sequences. The resultant unified human policy achieves a mean tracking success rate of 94.7% on unseen clips of the four skills and exhibits greater robustness to perturbations than its constituent experts. A single hip exoskeleton controller (UniExo) is initialized from hip moment prediction of the human policy and co-adapted with it through multi-agent reinforcement learning across the four skills. This co-adaptation shifts the timing of the assistance torque and raises the fraction of positive work delivered to the hip. When deployed on a custom hip exoskeleton, the controller generalizes across four treadmill speeds in six participants and assists one participant through a continuous route of all four skills and their transitions, without skill labels or explicit mode switching. UniExo thus provides a step towards replacing activity-specific controllers with unified, user-specific controllers that support diverse locomotor activities and the transitions between them.

</details>


### [253] [Decoupling Physical Speed from Path Parameterization in Singularity-Free Guiding Vector Fields](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.19726)
*Zhouru Xiao,Sha Luo,Yang Lu,Mingliang Xiao,Weijia Yao,Bohuan Lin,Xianzhe Cheng,Yaonan Wang*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: Introduces a singularity-free guiding vector field with prescribed physical speed (PPS) to overcome speed-specification and normalization-induced singularity issues in SF-GVF, achieving exponential convergence to the path and PPS tracking, with a saturated acceleration controller, validated by simulations and quadrotor experiments.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To address limitations of existing SF-GVF methods: (1) although an auxiliary virtual coordinate removes singularities, the along-path speed is constrained by path parameterization; (2) partial normalization to enforce a user-defined speed can introduce new singularities; (3) there is a need for guaranteed convergence while enforcing a prescribed physical speed along the path.

Method: Develop a new SF-GVF in a higher-dimensional space that prescribes the physical speed (PPS). Prove exponential convergence of integral curves to the desired path, ensure the physical speed converges to PPS, and maintain path-error dynamics invariant under reparameterizations. Add a saturated acceleration control law for second-order kinematic models and validate via simulations and 3D quadrotor experiments.

Result: The integral curves converge exponentially to the desired path from any initial condition in the augmented space; the robot's physical speed converges to the PPS; path-error dynamics are invariant to path reparameterizations; the approach is validated by comparative simulations and 3D quadrotor experiments under various PPS profiles.

Conclusion: The proposed PPS-SF-GVF resolves the speed-specification and singularity issues of conventional SF-GVF, providing guaranteed convergence to the path with a prescribed speed and feasible acceleration, backed by simulations and real-world quadrotor tests.

Abstract: The existing singularity-free guiding vector field (SF-GVF) with an additional virtual coordinate can eliminate singular points (i.e., points where the vector field vanishes) inherent in conventional GVFs and guarantee global convergence of robot trajectories to closed and self-intersecting desired paths. However, the desired speed given by the GVF along the desired path in the original lower-dimensional space cannot be arbitrarily specified but depends on path parameterizations. One possible workaround is to partially normalize the physical projection of the SF-GVF and assign a user-designed speed. However, we show that this workaround may introduce new singularities since the normalization denominator can become zero. To address this issue, we propose a new SF-GVF with prescribed physical speed (PPS). The integral curves of the new SF-GVF converge exponentially to the desired path from any initial condition in the higher-dimensional space (including virtual dimension); more importantly, the robot's physical speed converges to the PPS, while the path-error dynamics remain invariant under regular reparameterizations of the desired path. We further develop a saturated acceleration control law for second-order kinematic models. Finally, comparative simulations and 3D path-following experiments with a quadrotor under different PPS profiles validate the theoretical results and demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed approach.

</details>


### [254] [Equivariant Filter Design for Acoustic and Depth Aided Inertial Navigation Systems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.19742)
*Arihant Lunawat,Pieter van Goor,Frank Dellaert,Stefan B. Williams*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: Equivariant Filtering on Lie groups (TG-EqF) for AUV navigation improves accuracy and covariance consistency by embedding IMU biases in the state geometry via Tangent-Group symmetry; outperforms IEKF variants in simulations and field data.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Autonomous underwater navigation without GPS requires fusing IMU, DVL, and depth; standard IEKF-based filters degrade covariance due to treating biases as Euclidean perturbations, breaking exact log-linear error dynamics on the Lie group. A filter that preserves group structure and biases within the geometry can improve accuracy and consistency.

Method: Develop TG-EqF using Tangent-Group symmetry to maintain zero linearization error in nav states and second-order bias error; create an equivariant DVL output model with third-order linearization error and a direct pressure output; compare against Two-Frame-Group IEKF and Multiplicative EKF via Monte Carlo simulations and offline field data.

Result: Attitude, velocity, and position errors reduced by 18–25% relative to baselines; ANEES statistics stay nearer to 1, indicating improved covariance consistency; field data corroborates reduced position drift and overall improved navigation performance.

Conclusion: TG-EqF preserves the Lie-group structure and the associated log-linear error dynamics by embedding biases in the state geometry, yielding lower estimation error and more reliable covariance estimates for AUV navigation; shows superior performance to existing IEKF-based methods in both simulated and real data.

Abstract: Autonomous Underwater Vehicles (AUVs) navigating without GPS typically fuse inertial measurements with acoustic Doppler Velocity Log (DVL) velocities and pressure-derived depth. Posing the navigation state on a Lie group improves accuracy and consistency. However, state-of-the-art filters based on the Invariant Extended Kalman Filter (IEKF) append the Inertial Measurement Unit (IMU) biases as a Euclidean extension, which breaks the group-affine structure required for exact log-linear error dynamics, causing the reported covariance to degrade alongside the estimate. We apply the Tangent-Group (TG) symmetry, which carries the biases within the geometry of the state space, to derive an Equivariant Filter (EqF) for this system, leaving zero linearization error in the navigation states and second-order error only in the biases. We develop an equivariant output model for the DVL, whose update incurs only third-order linearization error, together with a direct pressure output. Monte Carlo simulations benchmark the TG-EqF against a Two-Frame-Group IEKF and a Multiplicative EKF. The TG-EqF reduces error by 18--25\% against both alternatives in each of attitude, velocity, and position. The main benefit is in the covariance it estimates: its Average Normalized Estimation Error Squared (ANEES) stays closer to its nominal value of one than that of the others. Offline analysis on AUV field data corroborates the findings of the simulations, demonstrating reduced position drift.

</details>


### [255] [LIFD: Anchored Diffusion for 3D-Aware Scene Memory in Robotic Manipulation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.19796)
*Wenbo Li,Yiteng Chen,Wenhao Li,Qingyao Wu*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: LIFD provides a persistent, 3D-aware scene memory for robotic manipulation under partial observability by learning a scene-token representation from multi-view agreement and completing it from a single RGB view with recurrent memory, yielding improved success on LIBERO, MetaWorld, and UR5e tasks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Partial observability in robotic manipulation breaks geometric perception as views change; geometry-aware RGB features lose past information when regions disappear. There is a need to maintain a memory of observed structure and infer missing content in a way that remains grounded in visible evidence.

Method: LIFD (Look, Imagine, Focus, and Do) learns a scene-token representation from multi-view agreement; uses a rectified-flow model to generate tokens and Anchor-Guided Cross-Attention to condition completion on current geometric features; connects tokens to a manipulation policy via compact slot features. Training uses multi-view and geometric supervision; deployment uses a single RGB camera, proprioception, and a task instruction.

Result: Quantitative results show strong performance: LIFD (Staged) achieves 91.6% average success on LIBERO and 79.8% on MetaWorld, improving LIBERO by 3.1 points over Joint training. On UR5e with ten demonstrations per task family, mean success is 56.0% versus 40.5% for OpenVLA-7B.

Conclusion: LIFD enables persistent, 3D-aware scene representations that stay grounded to visible evidence while inferring hidden content, enabling more robust manipulation under partial observability and outperforming relevant baselines on standard benchmarks.

Abstract: Robotic manipulation under partial observability requires spatial information that extends beyond the current view. Geometry-aware RGB features describe visible structure, but previously observed regions may disappear as the robot or scene moves. Maintaining a useful scene representation therefore requires retaining observation history while inferring missing content without losing its connection to visible evidence. We introduce LIFD (Look, Imagine, Focus, and Do), a framework for persistent, 3D-aware scene memory. LIFD learns a scene-token representation from multi-view agreement and completes it from a single RGB view and recurrent memory. A rectified-flow model generates the tokens while Anchor-Guided Cross-Attention conditions completion on current geometric features. Compact slot features connect this representation to a manipulation policy. Multi-view and geometric supervision are used during representation learning; deployment requires one RGB camera, proprioception, and a task instruction. LIFD (Staged) reaches 91.6% average success on LIBERO and 79.8% on MetaWorld, improving LIBERO average success by 3.1 percentage points over Joint training. On four UR5e task families with ten demonstrations per family, it achieves 56.0% mean success, compared with 40.5% for OpenVLA-7B.

</details>


### [256] [Affective Shared Autonomy: Temporal Affect Dynamics and Subjective Evaluation in Bimanual Teleoperation Tasks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.19802)
*Zhengji Liang,Guiyin Tian,Sijin Qu,Hainan Liu,Shiyan Hu*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: Affective-aware shared autonomy for teleoperation using multimodal signals to modulate assistance; reports increased productive states and a new multimodal dataset; outperforms zero-shot baselines.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Address cognitive workload and misaligned interventions in traditional task-based shared autonomy that overlook operator affect.

Method: Real-time estimation of operator affect from synchronized facial video, cardiac signals, and bilateral arm kinematics; outputs a seven-state affective distribution and a three-category operational state; triggers assistance only in continuous adverse states; empirical study with N=30; dataset of multimodal signals during bimanual teleoperation; multimodal fusion model evaluated against zero-shot baselines (Qwen, MiniCPM-V).

Result: Productive states increased by up to 39.7% without reducing user agency; dataset is first to provide continuous visual, physiological, and bilateral motion tracking of temporal affective state shifts; model outperforms zero-shot baselines in tracking temporal dynamics.

Conclusion: Presents a human-centric, multimodal framework for physical human-robot interaction that integrates vision, physiology, and motion tracking for affect-aware control; demonstrates real-world deployment and contributes a valuable dataset.

Abstract: Physical teleoperation integrates human cognitive flexibility with robotic precision, yet demanding manipulation tasks frequently induce severe cognitive workload, acute frustration, and execution breakdown. Conventional shared autonomy paradigms rely primarily on task-based rules, such as spatial error boundaries, which disregard the operator's transient affective state and risk misaligned control interventions. To address this limitation, we propose an affect-aware shared autonomy teleoperation framework that dynamically modulates robotic assistance based on real-time operator state estimation. The system estimates operator affective states from synchronized facial video, cardiac signals, and bilateral arm kinematics, outputting a seven-state affective distribution and a three-category operational abstraction (neutral, productive, adverse). Affect-aware assistance is selectively triggered when the user is detected in a continuous adverse state, preserving task-positive engagement without unnecessary disruption. The empirical user study ($N = 30$) confirms that the proposed affective assistance increases the productive states by up to 39.7% without compromising user agency. The collected dataset represents the first multimodal dataset that provides continuous visual, physiological, and operator's bilateral motion tracking of temporal affective state shifts during bimanual teleoperation. Our multimodal fusion model outperforms zero-shot baselines (Qwen, MiniCPM-V) in tracking temporal state dynamics. This real-world deployment offers a new human-centric framework that integrates visual, physiological, and motion tracking for physical human-robot interaction.

</details>


### [257] [HEROIC: Heterogeneous Evidential Reasoning for Open-Vocabulary Identification and Cross-Robot Collaboration](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.19803)
*Mihir Chauhan,Aarav Jain,Addison Zucek,Manmeet Dang,Damon Conover,Aniket Bera*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: HEROIC enables language-only, decentralized coordination of heterogeneous air-ground agents for open-world search, with dynamic role reallocation based on sensor capabilities and a scale-law, achieving higher success and faster target arrival than baselines.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To overcome fixed roles and hand-written capability tags in language-tasked multi-agent teams, enabling open-vocabulary natural language communication for flexible, robust search in uncertain environments.

Method: Derive initial roles from sensor properties and a target detectability scale law; determine aerial altitude and sweep spacing from mission prompt; re-task aerials to triage/escort/route-guide when height would be unsafe; maintain evidential belief over the search area using bearing rays for positive evidence and log-odds for negative evidence; gate arrival on close-range verification; operate in a fully decentralized framework with natural-language communication.

Result: In full-stack experiments, HEROIC reached the target 84% across 6 scenes, outperforming baselines at 35–54% and arriving 2–4x faster.

Conclusion: Natural-language-only coordination in a decentralized open-vocabulary framework substantially improves open-world search performance for heterogeneous air-ground teams through dynamic tasking and evidence-based gating.

Abstract: Multi-agent heterogeneous air-ground robot teams are attractive for open world search, with applications for reconnaissance, urban search and rescue missions (USAR), disaster response and recovery, and hazardous environments. These two platforms have different failure modes: aerial robots cover ground quickly but cannot resolve small or occluded targets from altitude, while ground robots can identify objects-of-interest, such as people or hazardous objects, at close range but cover less area. Existing language-tasked teams either have roles fixed prior, or have a language model assign them from hand-written capability tags, so the team is unable to know when within a mission an asset is no longer useful. We present HEROIC, a decentralized heterogeneous multi-agent open-vocabulary search coordination framework that requires agents to communicate in natural language only. HEROIC's initial agent role assignment is derived from sensor properties and a scale law to determine whether targets can be detected with a high confidence. From the mission's natural language prompt alone, this law assigns aerial flight altitudes and sweep spacing. When this calculated height falls below the altitude for safe flight, aerial agents re-task themselves from searcher to aerial triage, escort, and route guide for ground agents. Both robots maintain an evidential belief over the search area (bearing rays for positive evidence, a log-odds posterior for negative evidence) and gate any arrival on close-range verification. In full-stack experiments, HEROIC reaches the target 84% of the time across all 6 scenes, compares to 35-54% for vision-language frontier baselines, frontier-based search, lawnmower, and random-walk running the same perception, all while being 2-4x sooner to arrive at the target.

</details>


### [258] [Vehicle Trajectory Prediction via Neural Fusion of Multiple EKF-Based Trajectory Candidates](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.19813)
*Seong-Jun Kim,Seung-Hyun Kong*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: Fuse Trajectron++ predictions with EKF-generated trajectory candidates at a late stage, improving prediction accuracy on nuScenes without changing the neural baseline.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Neural predictors may produce physically infeasible trajectories in regimes like acceleration, deceleration, and turning; integrate physics-informed EKF candidates to enforce feasibility.

Method: Late-stage fusion of Trajectron++ outputs with multiple EKF-based trajectory candidates, using EKF to generate alternative plausible paths; no changes to baseline architecture.

Result: On nuScenes, AED reduced by 13.7% and FDE reduced by 14.6% relative to Trajectron++ baseline.

Conclusion: EKF-based trajectory candidates effectively complement neural trajectory prediction through learned fusion, offering improved accuracy without rearchitecting the neural predictor.

Abstract: Predicting the future trajectories of surrounding vehicles in autonomous driving is important for collision risk assessment and safe ego-vehicle path planning. Conventional neural network-based trajectory predictors typically achieve strong prediction performance by exploiting agent history, dynamic scene graphs, and semantic maps. However, in specific motion regimes such as acceleration, deceleration, and turning, these predictors may fail to reflect physically feasible trajectories. To address this issue, this study proposes a framework that fuses the output of Trajectron++, a neural network-based trajectory predictor, with extended Kalman filter (EKF)-based multiple trajectory candidates at a late stage. On the nuScenes dataset, the proposed method reduces the average displacement error and final displacement error of the Trajectron++ robot baseline by 13.7% and 14.6%, respectively, without modifying the baseline architecture. These results indicate that EKF-based trajectory candidates can effectively complement neural trajectory prediction through learned fusion.

</details>


### [259] [RotateIt! Fast and Reliable Single-Arm Garment Unfolding via Online-Adaptive Dynamic Rotation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.19817)
*Zeqing Zhang,Zuokun Xie,Ao Fang,Bin Dai,Zhengjie Shu,Yifeng Tang,Ziwei Wang*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: Single-arm dynamic garment unfolding via adaptive axial rotation (RotateIt!) improves robustness and sim-to-real transfer compared to quasi-static methods.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Quasi-static unfolding requires many actions; existing dynamic methods rely on bimanual flinging; need a single-arm, efficient primitive that can generalize to unseen garments.

Method: From random tabletop state, select rotation-effective grasp (anchor) with a grasp ranker; rotate lifted garment about anchor to induce inertial tension that separates layers; online residual policy adapts rotation extent and speed and determines release timing; evaluates on seen/unseen simulated garments and eight unseen real garments; sim-trained policies transfer zero-shot to real.

Result: RotateIt! improves success within three attempts by 44.0–61.0 percentage points over quasi-static pick-and-place; real-world zero-shot success 75.6%, +41% first-attempt coverage, +26% final coverage.

Conclusion: Dynamic axial rotation is a viable primary manipulation primitive for garment unfolding, enabling subsequent autonomous folding without manual rearrangement.

Abstract: Robotic garment unfolding is essential for downstream tasks, yet quasi-static methods require repeated actions, while existing dynamic approaches predominantly rely on bimanual flinging. We present RotateIt!, a single-arm framework that uses adaptive axial rotation for dynamic garment unfolding. To the best of our knowledge, it is the first unfolding framework to employ dynamic axial rotation as its primary manipulation primitive. From a randomly initialized tabletop configuration, the robot selects a rotation-effective grasp and rotates the lifted garment about an approximately fixed anchor, generating inertial tension that separates overlapping layers within a compact workspace. A grasp ranker selects the anchor, while an online residual policy adapts the rotation extent and speed, thereby determining the release timing. Across seen and unseen simulated garments and eight unseen real garments, RotateIt! improves success within three attempts by 44.0-61.0 percentage points over quasi-static pick-and-place. The simulation-trained policies transfer zero-shot to the real world, achieving 75.6% success, 41% higher first-attempt coverage, and 26% higher final coverage. The resulting states further enable autonomous robotic folding without manual rearrangement.

</details>


### [260] [TADreamer: Zero-Shot Language-Guided 3D Navigation for Terrestrial-Aerial Bimodal Robots via Video Imagination](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.19824)
*Xiangyu Li,Tiancheng Lai,Xijie Huang,Ruitian Pang,Siqi Shen,Juncheng Chen,Zaisheng Pan,Chao Xu,Fei Gao,Yanjun Cao*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: TADreamer: a zero-shot framework grounding video-imagined navigation to measured geometry for terrestrial–aerial robots; uses vision–language prompts, 3D reconstruction, two-stage calibration, and geometry-aware planning; achieves fast usable videos and substantial depth-error reductions vs NavDreamer.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Deriving metrically consistent navigation references from generated videos is hard due to scale ambiguity and axis distortions; need to ground video-motion to real-world geometry without task-specific training.

Method: A vision–language model generates and selects video candidates based on onboard observations and instructions, then provides corrective feedback. The chosen video is reconstructed into 3D waypoints with terrestrial/aerial mode labels. A two-stage calibration initializes scale via field-of-view constraints and refines axis scales, rotation, and translation by registering the point cloud to measured geometry. A planner uses the calibrated waypoints and mode labels with measured geometry for execution.

Result: Experiments across seven indoor/outdoor scenarios show usable videos in at most two rounds with five candidates per round. Calibration-based evaluation reports 87.7% reduction in mean absolute depth error and 86.3% reduction in mean absolute relative depth error versus NavDreamer.

Conclusion: Zero-shot grounding of video-imagined navigation to measured geometry is effective, enabling metric-consistent navigation for terrestrial–aerial robots without task-specific training.

Abstract: Language-guided navigation for terrestrial-aerial bimodal robots requires selecting routes and locomotion modes that match scene context and task intent. Generated videos can represent such motion sequences, but recovering metrically consistent navigation references from them is challenging because of scale ambiguity and axis-dependent geometric distortions. We present TADreamer, a zero-shot framework that grounds video-imagined navigation in measured geometry without task-specific training or fine-tuning. A vision-language model translates onboard observations and instructions into navigation prompts, selects valid generated videos, and provides corrective feedback when regeneration is needed. The selected video is reconstructed into 3D waypoints annotated with terrestrial or aerial modes. A two-stage calibration procedure uses field-of-view constraints to initialize scale estimation, then refines axis-dependent scales, rotation, and translation by registering the reconstructed point cloud to measured geometry. The calibrated waypoints and mode labels guide a planner that incorporates measured geometry for robot execution. Real-world experiments demonstrate navigation across seven indoor and outdoor scenarios. With five candidates per round, usable videos are obtained within two rounds in all seven scenarios. On the calibration observations, our method reduces mean absolute depth error by 87.7% and mean absolute relative depth error by 86.3% compared with NavDreamer.

</details>


### [261] [Improving Cross-embodiment Transfer in Latent Action Models with Action-Similarity Supervision](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.19846)
*Maxime Alvarez,Renzo Caballero,Tatsuya Matsushima,Yusuke Iwasawa,Yutaka Matsuo*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: Action-similarity supervision for latent-action models (LAMs) improves cross-embodiment transfer by aligning latent actions with similarities in ground-truth action sequences, outperforming auxiliary-action-prediction losses; end-effector similarities across robots yield the best results, enabling better generalization without predicting embodiment-specific actions.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LAMs benefit from sharing demonstrations across embodiments, but are sensitive to background noise and embodiment-specific latents. The goal is to align latent actions with human/robot action similarities without forcing the LAM to predict ground-truth actions.

Method: Train LAMs with latent actions. Compute pairwise similarities between latent actions and supervise them to match pairwise similarities of the corresponding ground-truth action sequences. Compare supervision via end-effector motion vs joint-space motion and two cross-embodiment robots (RoboTwin 2.0) with disjoint task sets. Train a single policy on all demonstrations; evaluate cross-embodiment transfer where each robot is only evaluated on the tasks demonstrated by the other.

Result: Predicting latent actions yields more than a 2x increase in cross-embodiment success compared to predicting ground-truth actions. Similarity supervision transfers better than an auxiliary loss that predicts ground-truth actions. Using end-effector motion for similarity, and allowing latent-action similarity to cross-robot, delivers the best performance.

Conclusion: Action-similarity supervision effectively reduces embodiment-specific bias in LAMs and enhances cross-embodiment generalization. End-effector-based similarity across robots is particularly effective, suggesting a scalable way to share demonstrations across diverse embodiments without requiring ground-truth action predictions.

Abstract: As generalist robot policies gain vision and language from web-scale pretraining, demonstrations remain costly to collect and tied to the robot that recorded them. Latent action models (LAMs) address both by learning latent actions from action-free videos that can be shared across embodiments, however, in practice, LAMs are sensitive to background visual noise, and the same motion from two different robots may be encoded with different latents. One solution to the background visual noise is to add an auxiliary loss predicting the robot action from the latent action, further associating the latent action space to the embodiment specific robot action space. We study a different use of the same labels, through action-similarity supervision. The similarity between any two latent actions is trained to match the similarity of the two ground-truth robot action sequences. The ground-truth actions are never predicted by the LAM, so the latent action does not need to encode embodiment specifics. We evaluate cross-embodiment transfer on RoboTwin 2.0 in a controlled setup, two bimanual robots demonstrate disjoint task sets, a policy is trained on all the demonstrations, and each robot is evaluated closed-loop on the tasks only the other demonstrated. With the policy architecture and its hyperparameters, the dataset, and the evaluation protocol fixed, predicting latent actions instead of ground-truth actions more than doubles cross-embodiment success. Given the same ground-truth actions, similarity supervision transfers better than an auxiliary loss that predicts the ground-truth action during the LAM training. Computing the similarities on end-effector motion rather than joint-space motion, and letting the loss compare latent actions across the two robots, gives the best approach of the study.

</details>


### [262] [GR2PO: Group Relative Return Policy Optimization for Continuous Robot Control](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.19850)
*Pengqin Wang,Qiming Zhang,Shaojie Shen,Jun Ma*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: GR2PO is a critic-free reinforcement learning framework for continuous control that estimates discounted returns from parallel rollout trajectories using group normalization and relative advantages with clipped targets, achieving competitive performance to actor-critic methods and enabling edge deployment.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Overcome the computational overhead and error-prone value estimation of critic-based methods, and address the poor long-horizon credit assignment of existing critic-free approaches in dense-reward environments.

Method: Collect parallel rollout trajectories, estimate discounted returns without a critic, apply group normalization at each rollout time index, and update the policy using relative advantages and clipped targets. The framework is instantiated in simulation and on real hardware (edge device); ablation studies examine group size, return estimation methods, and clipping ratio.

Result: GR2PO significantly outperforms critic-free baselines that rely on immediate rewards and is competitive with state-of-the-art actor-critic methods. It demonstrates efficient training and feasible deployment on NVIDIA Jetson TX2, with ablations revealing the impact of parallel group size, return estimation method, and target clipping ratio on learning performance.

Conclusion: GR2PO provides a practical, competitive critic-free approach for continuous control, offering efficient training and edge-deployment feasibility, with public release planned to support future research.

Abstract: Actor-critic architecture has been widely used in continuous robot control. However, they rely on learning a value network, introducing additional computational overhead during training. Moreover, policy learning may also be affected by the approximation error of value estimation. Critic-free group relative policy optimization methods provide a simpler training approach by removing the need for a critic. However, they fail to learn long-term action outcomes when directly applying immediate rewards to policy optimization in dense-reward environments. To address these problems, we propose Group Relative Return Policy Optimization (GR2PO), a critic-free reinforcement learning framework for continuous robot control. GR2PO estimates the discounted returns from the parallelly collected trajectories, performs group normalization at each rollout time index, and uses relative advantages and clipped targets to update the policy. To evaluate the effectiveness of the proposed framework, we instantiate it on robot control simulation environments and deploy the model to a real-world edge device. The results show that GR2PO significantly outperforms critic-free baselines that use immediate rewards and performs competitively against state-of-the-art actor-critic methods. Furthermore, GR2PO demonstrates competitive training efficiency. Inference tests on NVIDIA Jetson TX2 demonstrate the feasibility of deploying the learned policies on edge platforms. Further ablation experiments analyze the effects of parallel group size, return estimation methods, and target clipping ratio on learning performance. To support follow-up research, we will make the complete code publicly available after the paper is accepted, including the framework implementation, experimental configuration, and training and evaluation scripts.

</details>


### [263] [Feeling Terrain Before Crossing: World Models for Off-Road Navigation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.19863)
*E-In Son,Dong-Wook Kim,Ji-Hoon Hwang,Kangsun Lee,Jisung Bae,Jung-Taak Kim,Seung-Woo Seo*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: Feel-WM is a proprioception-conditioned off-road navigation world model that predicts both future camera observations and robot proprioception with a failure risk, enabling onboard planning and improved rough-terrain navigation; outperforms visual-only models and enables successful mountain-trail navigation on a Husky.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Off-road navigation requires predicting the robot–terrain interaction (slip, tilt, shake). Visual predictions alone are insufficient; proprioception provides essential dynamic information for forecasting physical outcomes and safe planning.

Method: Introduce Feel-WM, a proprioception-conditioned world model that forecasts future proprioceptive state and a failure risk, conditioned on proprioceptive inputs. A planner rolls out both scene and physical futures and scores them by separating failure risk from goal similarity. Training uses robot experience without human labels. Evaluated on real off-road data and simulation across wheeled and legged platforms; deployed onboard for rough-terrain navigation.

Result: Feel-WM outperforms visual-only navigation world models in open-loop planning and closed-loop rough-terrain navigation across wheeled and legged platforms; deployed on a Husky on mountain trails, it predicts rough ground ahead and steers around it, completing courses that an end-to-end policy fails.

Conclusion: Proprioception-conditioned world models enable accurate physical future predictions essential for safe, robust off-road planning, demonstrated via real-world deployment and cross-platform evaluation.

Abstract: Navigation world models plan by foresight, predicting the future that each candidate action sequence produces and selecting the best, rather than mapping observations to actions directly. Unlike urban settings where a predicted scene is a sufficient proxy, off-road navigation hinges on the robot--terrain interaction, so the prediction must cover not only what the camera will see but what the robot will feel. However, existing scene-focused models do not predict how much the robot will slip, tilt or shake along a planned trajectory. Proprioception captures these dynamics directly and, when used as input, improves the prediction of the physical future. We present Feel-WM, the first off-road navigation world model that conditions on proprioception and predicts what the robot will feel alongside what the camera will see. The physical future takes the form of a future proprioceptive state and a failure risk, both learned from the robot's own experience without human labels. The planner rolls out the physical future alongside the scene and weighs the predicted failure risk against goal similarity in a separable score. Experiments on real off-road data and in simulation demonstrate that Feel-WM outperforms visual-only navigation world models in open-loop planning and closed-loop rough-terrain navigation across wheeled and legged platforms. Deployed on a Husky on mountain trails, Feel-WM plans onboard, predicts rough ground ahead and steers around it, completing courses that an end-to-end policy fails.

</details>


### [264] [Learning Reliable Parking Policies via Offline Reinforcement Learning with Quantized Action Representations](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.19894)
*Zewei Yang,Zengqi Peng,Jun Ma*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: A waypoint-level offline RL framework for interaction-aware autonomous parking, combining hierarchical expert rollouts with rotational augmentation, FiLM-adapted LiDAR features, a state-conditioned tokenizer to discretize waypoint sequences, and conservative Q-learning; evaluated in CARLA with superior parking success and generalization to unseen slots.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Parking in urban environments is cluttered and weakly structured, with interactive uncertainty from surrounding vehicles. Existing planners struggle with reliability and distributional shift; offline RL with robust representation learning and action discretization may improve safety and generalization.

Method: 1) Build a parking dataset from hierarchical expert rollouts with rotational waypoint augmentation (covering non-interactive and interactive scenarios). 2) Condition the policy on a compact state representation. 3) Adapt LiDAR obstacle features to the target pose via feature-wise linear modulation (FiLM). 4) Use a state-conditioned tokenizer to quantize continuous waypoint sequences into discrete action tokens. 5) Apply conservative Q-learning on the discrete tokens to mitigate value overestimation for poorly supported actions.

Result: Closed-loop experiments in CARLA show the approach achieves the highest parking success rate among baselines and generalizes to unseen parking slots.

Conclusion: The proposed offline RL framework effectively handles interaction-aware parking under clutter and uncertainty, with FiLM-based perception, tokenized action space, and conservative Q-learning contributing to robust performance and transferability.

Abstract: Parking is a routine yet safety-critical task for autonomous vehicles operating in urban environments. However, cluttered and weakly structured parking spaces, compounded by the interactive uncertainty from surrounding vehicles, hinder reliable maneuver generation. To address these challenges, we develop a waypoint-level offline reinforcement learning framework for interaction-aware autonomous parking. Specifically, a dedicated parking dataset is constructed from hierarchical expert rollouts with rotational waypoint augmentation, covering both non-interactive scenarios and interactive ones. The policy is then conditioned on a compact state representation, in which LiDAR-based obstacle features are adapted to the target pose via feature-wise linear modulation. A state-conditioned tokenizer further quantizes continuous waypoint sequences into discrete action tokens, over which conservative Q-learning is performed to suppress value overestimation on poorly supported actions. Extensive closed-loop experiments are conducted in the high-fidelity CARLA simulator. The proposed framework attains the highest parking success rate among all baselines and transfers reliably to unseen parking slots.

</details>


### [265] [Learning and Transferring Closed-Loop Robot Software](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.19906)
*So Kuroki,Yujin Tang*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: Execution-improved reusable closed-loop implementations serve as a policy-learning resource; archival optimization enhances transfer to new tasks in RoboCasa.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Assess whether improved complete implementations can facilitate policy acquisition on unseen tasks, reducing manual tuning and enabling zero-shot/few-shot transfer with execution feedback.

Method: 1) For each source task, a coding agent generates policy code from few demonstrations; 2) iteratively improves via simulation feedback; 3) validated implementations are archived; 4) for new tasks, agent uses archived implementations, target demonstrations, and execution feedback to create/improve policies; 5) final policy frozen for execution without model calls; measured across four source tasks and nine target tasks with three runs.

Result: Source tasks: mean success 28.3% -> 64.2%. Target tasks: mean success across three runs: 45.2% no refs, 41.5% with initial, 57.0% with optimized; optimized references beat initial with 15.6 pp gain on nine-task average. Initial references better on two target tasks when averaged across runs.

Conclusion: Execution-improved software can materially improve policy acquisition for new tasks; remains best in some cases and is not universally superior to initial references; highlights value of reuse and iterative optimization with execution feedback.

Abstract: Closed-loop robot policies require observation processing, state management, and situation-dependent branching, making them costly to design and tune manually. Although coding agents increasingly support control-code generation and optimization, it remains unclear whether implementations improved on source tasks also support policy acquisition for new tasks. We study this question by treating complete closed-loop implementations as reusable execution experience. For each source task, a coding agent generates policy code from a few successful demonstrations and iteratively improves it using simulation feedback. The validation-selected implementations are retained in a software archive. For new tasks, the agent generates and improves policies using archived implementations, target demonstrations, and execution feedback. The resulting policy is then frozen and executes without further model calls. Across four source tasks in RoboCasa, iterative optimization increases mean success from 28.3% to 64.2%. Across nine target tasks and three independent runs, mean success is 45.2% without references, 41.5% with initial source code, and 57.0% with optimized source code. Optimized references outperform initial references in all three runs on the nine-task average, with a mean gain of 15.6 percentage points. These results demonstrate the value of execution-improved software as a resource for acquiring new policies in this setting, although initial references remain better on two target tasks when averaged across runs.

</details>


### [266] [Distributed Model Predictive Control with Connectivity-based Contracts](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.19912)
*Jorit Geurts,Danilo Saccani,Melanie N. Zeilinger,Andrea Carron*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: A scalable DMPC framework that enforces connectivity via local connectivity contracts, enabling each agent to optimize independently while preserving team connectivity and collision avoidance.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Ensure guaranteed network connectivity in distributed MPC for multi-robot teams, overcoming nonconvex connectivity constraints that hinder real-time scalability.

Method: Assign each agent a connectivity contract—a local region for its predicted horizon. If all agents stay within their contracts, the team remains connected. Contract graphs are built via a single exchange with neighbors; agents then solve independent DMPC problems. Theoretical proofs ensure connectivity, collision avoidance, and constraint satisfaction.

Result: The approach guarantees connectivity, avoids collisions, and respects local constraints; validated through simulations and hardware experiments on miniature car-like robots.

Conclusion: Connectivity guarantees in DMPC can be achieved with minimal inter-agent communication through local contracts, enabling scalable, real-time coordination in multi-robot systems.

Abstract: Teams of mobile robots rely on continuous communication with their neighbors for coordination, yet most distributed model predictive control (DMPC) schemes assume the communication network stays connected rather than actively enforcing it. Adding such a guarantee is hard since the usual mathematical condition for connectivity is nonconvex and links every agent to every other, which is incompatible with a scalable distributed real-time controller. We propose a DMPC framework in which each agent is assigned a connectivity contract: a local region prescribing where its predicted positions may lie over the prediction horizon. The contracts are designed so that, as long as every agent stays within its own contract, the team is guaranteed to remain connected. Given the maintained contract graph, an agent builds its contract from a single exchange with its immediate neighbors, after which every agent solves its own optimization problem independently. We prove that the resulting closed-loop system maintains connectivity, avoids collisions, and respects local state and input constraints. Simulation and hardware experiments on miniature autonomous car-like robots demonstrate the approach.

</details>


### [267] [Co-VLA: Consensus-based Federated Training for Vision-Language-Action Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.19923)
*Haolong Li,Guner Dilsad Er,Michael Muehlebach,Joerg Stueckler*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: Co-VLA uses ADMM-based consensus optimization to federate vision-language-action model training across heterogeneous robot clients, enabling both full-model training and parameter-efficient fine-tuning with fixed-rank or rank-adaptive adapters, achieving centralized-like performance without data sharing.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Centralized collection of robot data is costly and often impractical due to distribution across robots, tasks, and locations. Federated learning offers a path to leverage decentralized data while respecting privacy and reduce data movement, but heterogeneity across clients poses challenges for VLA training.

Method: Apply consensus optimization via the Alternating Direction Method of Multipliers (ADMM) to federated VLA training. The framework supports both full-model training and parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) using adapters that can be fixed-rank or rank-adaptive.

Result: Empirical results show Co-VLA achieves performance comparable to centralized training in both full-model training and PEFT settings, despite data heterogeneity across clients.

Conclusion: Co-VLA demonstrates that federated training of VLAs via ADMM-based consensus optimization is feasible and effective across heterogeneous robot data, with flexibility to switch between full-model and PEFT approaches, while preserving data locality.

Abstract: Vision-language-action models (VLAs) have emerged as a promising paradigm for general-purpose robot learning, with performance improving as models and datasets scale. Scaling robot data collection, however, remains challenging because data are naturally distributed across robots, tasks, and locations, making centralization costly or impractical. Federated learning offers a way to train on decentralized robot data, but applying it to VLAs requires accounting for heterogeneous robot client data distributions. We present Co-VLA, which applies consensus optimization using the Alternating Direction Method of Multipliers~(ADMM) to federated VLA training. We show that the same algorithm supports both full-model training and parameter-efficient fine-tuning with both fixed-rank and rank-adaptive adapters. The name Co-VLA reflects both consensus and collaboration: clients with different local robot datasets collaboratively train a shared model without sharing their data. Our experiments demonstrate that Co-VLA achieves performance comparable to centralized training in both full-model training and parameter-efficient fine-tuning settings.

</details>


### [268] [Execution-Aware Pre-Execution Ranking for Grasp-Conditioned Robotic Placement](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.19946)
*Tianyuan Liu,Rutherford Agbeshi Patamia,Benjamin Champion,Richard Dazeley,Akansel Cosgun*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: A pre-execution grasp–placement ranking model uses a typed target-conditioned point cloud with pose descriptors and hierarchical heads to predict planning and execution success, achieving strong cross-d dataset performance and zero-retraining transfer to xArm/MoveIt.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Geometric validity at pose level does not guarantee executability due to end-effector pose constraints, collision geometry, and transport motion. The process benefits from ranking candidate grasps/placements before planning to improve planning efficiency and end-to-end success, evaluated on a large 30-object, 1,235-scene dataset with scene-group held-out splits.

Method: A model combines a typed target-conditioned point cloud with three pose descriptors and hierarchical heads for planning success and execution success conditioned on planning, enabling joint-ranking and fixed-target ranking of candidate pairs.

Result: Three-seed top-1 success on covered test groups: joint selection 85.63% ±1.08, fixed-target 79.84% ±0.16. Frozen seed-42 improves top-1 from 72.84% to 85.78% (joint) and 59.65% to 79.67% (fixed-target) over full-pool cuMotion. Frozen transfer to xArm7/MoveIt requires no retraining. Among 27 locked cases, 13 complete end-to-end (48.15%). Of 16 preflight-pass cases that begin execution, 13 succeed (81.25%). Deployment-feasibility prediction: 81.25% recall, 85.20% specificity, 83.23% balanced accuracy.

Conclusion: The proposed pre-execution ranking and deployment-feasibility prediction achieve high end-to-end success and robust zero-shot transfer to new hardware without retraining, demonstrating strong generalization across objects/scenes and reliable decision-making for deployment.

Abstract: A geometrically valid placement can still be difficult to execute because the selected grasp changes the required end-effector pose, collision geometry, and transport motion. Placement is formulated as a pre-execution ranking problem in which supplied grasp-placement candidates are scored before planning. The model combines a typed target-conditioned point cloud with three pose descriptors and hierarchical heads for planning success and execution success conditioned on planning. On a 30-object, 1,235-scene dataset with scene-group-held-out splits, three-seed top-1 success on covered test groups reaches 85.63 +/- 1.08% for joint selection and 79.84 +/- 0.16% for fixed-target ranking. For the designated frozen seed-42 checkpoint, top-1 success improves from 72.84% to 85.78% over full-pool cuMotion for joint ranking and from 59.65% to 79.67% for fixed-target ranking. Frozen transfer to xArm7/MoveIt requires no xArm-specific retraining. Across 27 locked cases, 13 complete end to end (48.15%). Of the 16 cases that pass Top-5 preflight and begin execution, 13 succeed (81.25%). Candidate-level deployment-feasibility prediction reaches 81.25% recall, 85.20% specificity, and 83.23% balanced accuracy.

</details>


### [269] [LapaTrack-3D: 6 DoF pre-operative shape tracking for laparoscopic surgery](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.19954)
*Jingwei Song,Javid Hussain Jakir,Ray Zhang,Wenwei Zhang,Hao Zhou,Xiaomeng Xian,Maani Ghaffari*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: A real-time monocular 6-DoF tracking framework (LapaTrack-3D) for laparoscopic surgery, extending ORB-SLAM2 with four priors: fast initialization from primitive 3D shapes, pseudo-segmentation, 3D geometric prior in pose graph, and MSRCP-based image enhancement; achieves 13 Hz at 1280x720 and robustly handles common laparoscopic challenges, validated in vivo/ex vivo.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Intraoperative-to-preoperative data alignment in monocular laparoscopic settings is critical due to lack of tactile feedback and complex organ motion; existing SLAM approaches struggle with illumination, occlusion, and organ-background motion.

Method: Four major modifications to ORB-SLAM2: (1) primitive 3D shape enables fast initialization of monocular mode; (2) pseudo-segmentation separates target organ from background for tracking; (3) the 3D shape is incorporated as a geometric prior in pose graph optimization; (4) the MSRCP algorithm (modified) enhances images under challenging illumination; integrates as a prior-based 3D tracking framework; reported at real-time speeds (~13 Hz).

Result: In-vivo and ex-vivo experiments validate 3D tracking robustness; handles poor illumination, fast motion, out-of-field-of-view scenarios, partial visibility, and organ-background relative motion.

Conclusion: LapaTrack-3D provides robust, real-time prior-based 3D tracking for monocular laparoscopy, enabling improved alignment with preoperative data and resilience to common surgical imaging challenges.
