Abstract: This work proposes a real-time 6 Degree-of-Freedom (6 DoF) tracking algorithm for monocular laparoscopic surgery. It provides alignment between intra-operative video and pre-operative data (e.g., CT). The 6 DoF tracking offers a solution for accurately locating the internal anatomy of the target organ despite the lack of tactile feedback and transparency. The ORB-SLAM2 framework is adopted and modified for prior-based 3D tracking with four major modifications. First, the primitive 3D shape is used for fast initialization of the ORB-SLAM2 monocular mode. Second, a pseudo-segmentation strategy is employed to separate the target organ from the background for tracking. Third, the 3D shape is incorporated as a geometric prior in its pose graph optimization. Fourth, the Multi-Scale Retinex with Chromaticity Preservation (MSRCP) algorithm is leveraged and modified for image enhancement in challenging illumination scenarios. In-vivo and ex-vivo experiments validate that LapaTrack-3D provides robust 3D tracking and effectively handles typical challenges such as poor illumination, fast motion, out-of-field-of-view scenarios, partial visibility, and ``organ-background'' relative motion. LapaTrack-3D achieves a processing rate of 13 Hz for 1280*720 pixel video.

</details>


### [270] [Hybrid Residual Reinforcement Learning for Contact-Rich Robotic Book Insertion](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.19962)
*Tianyuan Liu,Rutherford Agbeshi Patamia,Benjamin Champion,Akansel Cosgun,Richard Dazeley*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: Hybrid control for inserting a grasped book uses a nominal geometry-based controller augmented by a bounded residual PPO; achieves major gains in success rate and robustness over nominal control in both simulation and hardware, by offloading contact-sensitive behavior to learning while preserving task structure.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Tight-contact manipulation tasks require millimeter-scale precision; combining known geometry with learning can improve reliability and robustness where fixed rules struggle, especially in the critical final-insertion phase.

Method: Maintain a structured task-space controller for insertion and seating; learn bounded local corrections with PPO to handle contact dynamics; the release decision is learned; only a brief open-retreat-reclose transition is scripted; evaluation includes deployment-matched simulation over 512 fixed conditions and hardware trials on an xArm7.

Result: Simulation: 98.50% mean success (SD 0.23) across 3 training runs vs 37.89% with nominal control. Hardware (xArm7): 60 trials over 30 conditions show success improving from 26.7% (nominal) to 63.3% with residual control; failures reduced from 22 to 11; 13 of 15 matched conditions favored the residual controller. Robustness: performance stays above 87% under initialization perturbations up to 1.5x; very tight clearances reveal geometric limits of local correction.

Conclusion: A hybrid geometry-and-learning design preserves task structure while letting learning handle contact-sensitive behavior, yielding higher reliability and robustness than fixed-rule control in tight-insertion tasks.

Abstract: Placing a grasped book into a tight shelf is a compact but difficult contact-rich control problem: millimetre-scale pose error can turn a geometrically valid approach into jamming, failed release, or incomplete seating. We study this final phase after grasp acquisition and global approach, and ask how control authority should be divided between known geometry and learned behaviour. Our method retains a nominal task-space controller for structured insertion and seating, while residual PPO supplies bounded local corrections and decides when to release. Only the brief open-retreat-reclose transition is scripted. For the final policy used on hardware, a deployment-matched simulation evaluation over 512 fixed conditions yields 98.50 percent mean success (0.23 percentage-point sample SD) across three independent training runs, compared with 37.89 percent for nominal control. On the physical xArm7, 60 trials over 30 matched conditions show the same qualitative advantage: residual control raises success from 26.7 percent to 63.3 percent, reduces failures from 22 to 11, and wins 13 of the 15 matched conditions in which the two controllers differ. Robustness tests show that performance remains above 87 percent under initialization perturbations up to 1.5x, while very tight clearances expose the geometric limit of local correction. These results support a hybrid design in which geometry preserves reliable task structure and learning is concentrated on the contact-sensitive behaviour that fixed rules handle poorly.

</details>


### [271] [MaskHarness-WAM: Instance-Grounded Harnessing for Long-Horizon Robot Manipulation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.19974)
*Zitai Huang,Taiyi Su,Jian Zhu,Jianjun Zhang,Chong Ma,Tianbin Liu,Weiyi Lu,Yi Xu,Hanli Wang*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: Instance-grounded long-horizon manipulation that links high-level planning to low-level policies via per-subtask target masks, enabling sequential multi-object manipulation with reliable long-horizon execution.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Long-horizon manipulation with identical-looking objects requires continuous perception, instance tracking, and robust subtask sequencing; limited-horizon policies struggle to decide which instance to act on and when to transition between subtasks.

Method: MaskHarness-WAM connects task planning and manipulation through target masks. At each subtask boundary, it re-observes the scene, generates and verifies a new initial target mask for the next object, and uses this updated instance-level spatial condition in the low-level policy. The system switches target instances based on verified subtask completion to progress the manipulation.

Result: Real-robot experiments show substantial improvement over limited-horizon policies in sequential multi-object manipulation, demonstrating effective extension of local manipulation skills to reliable long-horizon execution.

Conclusion: The approach provides an effective architecture for instance-grounded long-horizon manipulation by integrating visual feedback and mask-based instance specification with task planning; extensions may include more robust mask generation, scaling to complex task graphs, and improved generalization across object types.

Abstract: Long-horizon robot manipulation requires not only stable local visuomotor control, but also continuous target tracking and reliable task progress assessment throughout execution. This challenge becomes particularly critical when multiple objects share identical appearances and must be manipulated in a prescribed order. In such scenarios, relying solely on a limited-horizon manipulation policy is often insufficient to determine which instance should be operated on and when the task should transition to the next stage. To address this challenge, we propose MaskHarness-WAM, an instance-grounded harness for long-horizon manipulation. The proposed system connects high-level task planning with low-level manipulation policies through target masks, while leveraging visual feedback for subtask scheduling and continuous execution. Since each subtask corresponds to a different target instance, the low-level policy requires a newly established initial target mask under the updated scene at each subtask transition. The harness continuously re-observes the environment, generates, and verifies the target mask at subtask boundaries, thereby updating the instance-level spatial condition provided to the low-level policy. Furthermore, the system advances the manipulation process by switching target instances according to the verified completion status of each subtask. Experiments on a real robot platform demonstrate that MaskHarness-WAM substantially outperforms limited-horizon policies on sequential multi-object manipulation, showing its effectiveness in extending local manipulation skills to reliable long-horizon execution.

</details>


### [272] [Compliance for Free: Learning Identifiable Impedance via Bilateral Teleoperation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.19976)
*Harsha Guda,Adrià Colomé,Carme Torras*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: A four-channel bilateral teleoperation framework identifies per-axis stiffness without annotations and uses these labels to fine-tune a vision-language-action (VLA) model to output stiffness alongside pose, demonstrated on a Franka wiping task where force increases with a “firm” instruction.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Contact-rich manipulation requires knowing not just where to move but how hard to push (compliance). Standard interfaces fail to identify operator intent for stiffness due to identifiability between equilibrium and stiffness. The work provides a zero-labeled, hardware-supported method to supervise compliance for VLA models.

Method: Employ four-channel bilateral teleoperation to treat the leader arm as a measurement of intended equilibrium; infer per-axis stiffness via regression on existing joint-torque sensing, granting per-timestep, direction-dependent compliance labels without extra annotation; fine-tune a VLA model to emit both pose and stiffness.

Result: On the Franka Research 3 wiping task, the proposed policy uniquely shows a change in contact force when switching from normal (6.4 N) to firm (9.1 N) wipe (RMS), with Cohen's d = 0.89 and p = 0.023 among five policies.

Conclusion: Zero-annotation compliance supervision via bilateral teleoperation can supply reliable stiffness labels to a VLA, enabling explicit control of contact stiffness and improving task-specific compliance behavior; broader validation across tasks and robustness considerations remain for future work.

Abstract: Vision-language-action models tell a robot where to move, but not how hard to push. Contact-rich tasks depend on that second quantity, compliance, yet no widely used demonstration interface records it. The obstacle is identifiability as realized pose and measured force cannot separate the operator's intended equilibrium from their stiffness, so VR controllers, SpaceMouse and handheld grippers cannot supply compliance supervision even in principle. Prior compliance-output policies work around this with hand-specified task structure, privileged simulation contact state, or dedicated force and tactile hardware. Four-channel bilateral teleoperation removes the ambiguity directly by using the leader arm as a separate measurement of the intended equilibrium, making per-axis stiffness identifiable by regression using only the joint-torque sensing already on the manipulator. This yields per-timestep, direction-dependent compliance labels at zero annotation cost, which we use to fine-tune a VLA to emit stiffness alongside pose. On a Franka Research 3 wiping task, ours is the only policy of five whose contact force changes when the instruction asks for a firm wipe rather than a normal one (6.4N (normal) to 9.1N (firm) RMS, Cohen's d = 0.89, p = 0.023

</details>


### [273] [DR-MPC: Fast and Feasible Dynamics-Relaxed Model-Predictive Control for Legged Locomotion](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20035)
*Run Wang,Alapati Tuerxun,Shuo Liu,Wei Xiao,Ján Drgoňa,Yilin Mo,Liang Wu*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: DR-MPC: a dynamics-relaxed MPC for legged locomotion with a tailored interior-point solver. It relaxes dynamics into penalties, uses box constraints, and exploits a Schur complement to reduce the problem, achieving large speedups and real-time onboard performance on a quadruped.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To enable real-time, online MPC for legged locomotion by reducing computational burden while maintaining feasibility and contact-awareness.

Method: Formulate the MPC as a box-constrained QP with a block-arrow Hessian; relax dynamics and affine input constraints into quadratic penalties, retaining only box constraints. Eliminate state and affine-output directions via Schur complement; perform swing-force elimination and contact-aligned move blocking; solve a reduced control system with an interior-point method.

Result: Median speedups: 16.0x vs HPIPM and 4.4x vs OSQP; end-to-end onboard MPC time 4.4 ms; comparable locomotion performance in simulation; validated on Unitree Go1; code to be released open-source after publication.

Conclusion: The DR-MPC formulation combined with a specialized IPM solver substantially accelerates legged MPC to real-time onboard levels while maintaining comparable locomotion performance, enabling practical deployment and further research.

Abstract: This paper presents dynamics-relaxed model predictive control (DR-MPC), a novel MPC formulation for legged locomotion, and a tailored interior-point method (IPM) solver. The formulation combines online optimization feasibility by construction with a contact-aware input parameterization. DR-MPC moves the dynamics equality and affine input constraints into quadratic penalties and retains only nonempty box constraints. The resulting box-constrained quadratic program (QP) has a block-arrow Hessian that enables the state and affine-output directions to be eliminated through a Schur complement. The solver factors only the reduced control system after swing-force elimination and contact-aligned move blocking. For the evaluated implementations using the same DR-MPC formulation, our method achieves median end-to-end MPC speedups of $16.0\times$ over HPIPM and $4.4\times$ over OSQP, with comparable locomotion performance in simulation. DR-MPC achieves a median onboard MPC end-to-end time of $4.4$ ms and is validated on a Unitree Go1 quadruped. Open-source code will be made available after publication.

</details>


### [274] [Mechanical Precision Weeding with a Quadruped Robot](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20048)
*Ruben Beumer,Tom Janssen,René van de Molengraft,Duarte Antunes*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: A small-scale autonomous weeding system using a Spot quadruped with a milling weed-removal tool, designed to reduce soil compaction and improve scalability of mechanical weeding; evaluates performance indoors and outdoors and outlines future improvements.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Herbicide-based weed control is unsustainable due to resistance and environmental impact; large mechanical weeding causes soil compaction; a low-impact, scalable alternative is needed.

Method: Deploy a custom milling-based weed removal tool attached to the robot base of a Boston Dynamics Spot quadruped. The robot uses leg actuation to drive the tool while feet remain stationary, leveraging the robot's DOF. Develop a software architecture for autonomous weed removal and integrate all required subsystems. Conduct indoor and outdoor experiments to assess accuracy and efficiency and compare to existing automated mechanical weeding approaches.

Result: Proof-of-concept is evaluated for accuracy and efficiency in both indoor and outdoor settings. The study provides recommendations for improving accuracy and efficiency in future work.

Conclusion: The approach demonstrates potential as a scalable, low-compaction mechanical weeding solution; further work is needed to enhance accuracy, robustness, and field practicality, including perception, control, and energy considerations.

Abstract: Herbicide-based weed control is increasingly unsustainable due to rising weed resistance and the adverse environmental impacts of chemical use. While mechanical weed control avoids these drawbacks, it is typically implemented using large machines that cause soil compaction. We propose a novel alternative based on small mobile robots for mechanical weeding. Compared with existing automated mechanical weeding approaches, the proposed method offers reduced soil compaction, simpler automation, and improved scalability. Our solution involves a Boston Dynamics Spot quadruped robot equipped with a custom weed removal tool featuring a milling bit at its end. The tool is rigidly attached to the robot and uses the degrees of freedom of the robot base by actuating the legs, while keeping the feet stationary. We develop a software architecture that enables autonomous weed removal and integrate this system with all other required components. We analyze the accuracy and efficiency of the current proof of concept both in an indoor and outdoor environment and provide recommendations for future work to make the system more accurate and efficient.

</details>


### [275] [FlipToSee: A Probabilistic Stable Placement Prior for Active Visual Exploration via Regrasping](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20078)
*Chang Shu,Sushil Samuel Dinesh,Shinkyu Park*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: Proposes FlipToSee, a probabilistic framework for predicting stable placements of tabletop objects by modeling orientation via unit normals on the sphere and a von Mises–Fisher mixture, with candidate extraction and reranking; achieves high success in simulation and validates on a real robot.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Efficiently identifying stable object placements from a single-view point cloud to enable active visual exploration of occluded surfaces. Conventional 6-DoF regression is ambiguous due to multimodality and orientation redundancy; a robust multimodal prior over placements is needed.

Method: Parameterize placements as normals on S^2; model the multimodal distribution with a von Mises–Fisher mixture density network; deterministically extract a compact candidate set from mixture components and apply robustness-aware reranking via an auxiliary head trained with candidate-aligned supervision; validate in simulation and demonstrate on a physical robot integrated with grasp and motion planning for exploratory regrasping.

Result: In simulation, 98.4% first-proposal success on in-distribution shapes, 95.3% on out-of-distribution shapes, and 90.0% under zero-shot transfer to household YCB objects. Demonstrated on a physical robot by integrating with grasp and motion planning for exploratory regrasping.

Conclusion: FlipToSee eliminates representational ambiguity and captures multimodality in stable-object placement, delivering robust, high-probability placement proposals suitable for active exploration in both simulation and real-robot settings.

Abstract: Active visual exploration of tabletop objects often requires reorienting an unknown resting object onto a different stable support face to expose occluded surfaces. To identify such placements without exhaustive physical search, we learn a probabilistic placement prior from a single-view point cloud. Stable placement prediction is inherently multimodal, and conventional 6-DoF regression introduces further ambiguity by modeling translation and in-plane yaw. We therefore propose FlipToSee, a probabilistic framework that removes this representational ambiguity by parameterizing placements as unit support normals on $S^2$ while modeling their multimodal conditional distribution via a von Mises--Fisher mixture density network. To decouple mode diversity from physical robustness, FlipToSee deterministically extracts a compact candidate set from the mixture components and applies robustness-aware reranking using an auxiliary head trained with candidate-aligned supervision. In simulation, FlipToSee achieves $98.4\%$ first-proposal success on in-distribution objects, $95.3\%$ on out-of-distribution shapes, and $90.0\%$ under zero-shot transfer to household YCB objects. We further demonstrate the learned placement prior on a physical robot by integrating it with grasp and motion planning for exploratory regrasping.

</details>


### [276] [Graph-Based Design of Soft Grippers with Multi-Objective Quality-Diversity Optimisation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20087)
*Andre Farinha,Ge Shi,Harry Bowman,Brendan Tidd,David Howard,Josh Pinskier*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: Diversity-driven, graph-based optimization yields generalizable soft grippers when trained across diverse grasping tasks; emergent generalization improves robustness to unseen objects and contact conditions.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Soft grippers have rich design spaces and tend to overfit to specific tasks; there is a need for mechanisms that promote generalization by leveraging task diversity and explicit diversity in design optimization.

Method: Represent soft structures as graphs and perform a multi-objective genetic optimization that explicitly promotes design diversity. Evaluate across multiple grasping scenarios during optimization to study how task diversity impacts generalization to unseen objects and contact conditions.

Result: Optimizing over a sufficiently diverse set of grasping cases produces designs capable of generalization, showing improved robustness on novel scenarios compared with task-specific solutions.

Conclusion: Diversity-driven optimization offers a principled approach for developing general-purpose soft grippers, aligning with the adaptable nature of soft robotics.

Abstract: Effective manipulation across diverse objects is critical for applications ranging from agricultural harvesting to laboratory and domestic automation. While the inherent compliance of soft robotics is well suited to this challenge, designing grippers that generalize across tasks remains difficult due to the vast design space of continuum mechanics and the risk of overfitting to specific scenarios.
  We propose a graph-based design space for representing soft structures and mechanisms, coupled with a multi-objective, diversity-driven genetic optimization framework that explicitly promotes solution variety throughout the design process. Using multiple grasping scenarios during optimization, we study how task diversity influences the emergence of generalization to unseen objects and contact conditions.
  Our results show that optimization over a sufficiently diverse set of grasping cases leads to designs with emergent generalization, exhibiting improved robustness compared to task-specific solutions on novel scenarios. These findings suggest that diversity-driven optimization offers a principled pathway toward general-purpose soft grippers, aligned with the adaptable nature of soft robotics.

</details>


### [277] [Safety-Critical Scenanrio Emerges from Initial Scene](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20103)
*Yin Wu,Jiarong Wei,Carl Esselborn,Shubham Phoolari,Ahmed Abouelazm,Daniel Slieter,J. Marius Zöllner*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: AdvScene introduces a conditional latent diffusion framework to generate safety-critical driving initial scenes, using RL-tuned adversarial agents to increase critical interactions; achieves higher ego-fault collision and TTC<3s events on Waymo data.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Traditional approaches start from real driving scenes and modify surrounding agents, which limits discovering failures due to sparse critical interactions and many static ego frames; an initialization-based approach is needed to reveal safety-critical scenarios.

Method: AdvScene is a two-stage, conditional latent diffusion model trained first on naturalistic driving data, then post-trained for adversarial-agent generation via reinforcement learning using feedback from closed-loop simulator rollouts. It conditions on ego displacement to prevent static ego and uses RL to optimize non-differentiable safety metrics, enabling realistic, critical initial scenes.

Result: Experiments on Waymo across 12 combinations of ego and traffic policies show AdvScene substantially increases the rate of ego-fault collision events and TTC<3s events.

Conclusion: Initialization-based safety-critical scenario generation with diffusion models and RL feedback effectively uncovers critical interactions beyond data-driven scenes, generalizing across policy combinations and enhancing safety validation.

Abstract: Safety-critical driving scenario generation has largely focused on manipulating the behavior of surrounding agents while starting from an initial scene from driving data. This assumption can limit the space of discoverable failures, since driving data can provide little opportunity for meaningful interaction. For example, in the Waymo Open Motion Dataset, 20.44% of recorded slices feature a stationary ego vehicle that never moves, and 30.39% of initial frames contain no nearby traffic participants within 10 meters. We instead study safety-critical scenario generation as an initialization problem: given agnostic black-box driving policies, we learn to generate realistic initial scenes that are more likely to evolve into critical interactions. We propose AdvScene, a conditional latent diffusion model that is trained in two stages. Starting from pretraining on naturalistic driving data, we post-train the adversarial-agent generation branch using reinforcement learning with feedback from closed-loop simulator rollouts. Conditioning on ego driving displacement prevents the ego from remaining static, and RL finetuning induces criticality directly with non-differentiable safety-critical metrics. Experiments on the Waymo dataset across 12 combinations of ego and traffic policies show that our AdvScene substantially increases the rate of ego-fault collision events and TTC<3s events.

</details>


### [278] [AnyViewDex: View-Invariant Dexterous Manipulation from RGB Observations](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20107)
*Soham Patil,Om Sanjay Gunjal,Sourabh Bhosale,Arhan Chavare,Ramandeep Singh Hora,Spandan Roy*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: AnyViewDex enables view-invariant dexterous manipulation with monocular RGB by embedding geometric grounding during simulated training; zero-shot deployment without test-time depth, achieving 76.7% success on unseen objects/viewpoints.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Viewpoint shifts undermine visuomotor policies; 3D sensing adds hardware/calibration challenges; aim to remove test-time depth while maintaining invariance.

Method: Asymmetric training: multi-view contrastive alignment + privileged 3D geometric supervision; regress absolute 3D coordinates during simulation to provide grounding; apply RL and distillation; zero-shot deployment with monocular RGB + proprioception.

Result: Hardware evaluation on xArm7 + LEAP Hand: 76.7% grasping success across 8 unseen objects and 6 uncalibrated viewpoints; 480 trials; 2,400 across ablations.

Conclusion: Geometric grounding during training enables view-invariant policies without test-time 3D sensing; reduces hardware dependencies and sensor noise vulnerability; demonstrated across RL and distillation, with strong zero-shot transfer.

Abstract: Visuomotor policies for multi-fingered dexterous manipulation are highly sensitive to camera viewpoint shifts. To achieve view invariance, recent methods increasingly rely on explicit 3D modalities like RGB-D or point clouds, which can introduce hardware dependencies, calibration requirements, and vulnerability to sensor noise during real-world deployment. In this work, we show that view-invariant control can be achieved without explicit test-time 3D sensing by encoding geometric knowledge into the visual representation during simulation. We present AnyViewDex, an asymmetric training pipeline that combines multi-view contrastive alignment with privileged 3D geometric supervision. By regressing absolute 3D object coordinates during simulated training, this auxiliary objective provides a geometric grounding signal that mitigates the spatial collapse of the globally pooled contrastive embedding. At deployment, the policy operates zero-shot using only uncalibrated monocular RGB and proprioception. We validate this approach across both reinforcement learning and student-teacher distillation. In hardware evaluation on an xArm7 with a 16-DoF LEAP Hand, AnyViewDex reaches 76.7% grasping success across eight unseen objects and six uncalibrated viewpoints (480 trials; 2,400 across all ablation conditions), indicating that geometrically grounded monocular policies transfer zero-shot without test-time depth. Project Page: https://anyviewdex.github.io/

</details>


### [279] [Universal Navigation Interface: Robot-Free Data for Wheeled Robot Navigation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20114)
*Sarvesh Prajapati,Ananya Trivedi,Lorena Maria Genua,Drake Moore,Bruce Maxwell,Taskin Padir*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: UNI uses a rollator-based, robot-free data collection method to gather real-world navigation demonstrations for training; yields reduced trajectory error and enables transfer to target robots at low cost, though demonstrations bias toward wheeled-feasible routes.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Address scalability and cost of collecting real-world navigation data requiring platform-specific teleoperation; enable large-scale supervision for goal-conditioned navigation models without the target robot.

Method: Collect demonstrations using a four-wheeled rollator and smartphone (UNI). Rollator imposes physical constraints (no stairs, no uncut curbs, no narrow gaps) leading to biased but practically relevant data. Recover metric trajectories from demonstrations to supervise models. Fine-tune visual-navigation models on UNI data. Evaluate on held-out UNI data and other datasets; demonstrate closed-loop transfer to a powered wheelchair in curb/staircase/curb-cut scenarios.

Result: UNI-enabled fine-tuning reduces trajectory prediction error by 17.4-24.8% on held-out UNI demonstrations. 37.2 km of data collected. Benefits on other datasets vary by dataset and metric. Demonstrated closed-loop transfer to powered wheelchair in curb, staircase, curb-cut tasks.

Conclusion: Low-cost physical proxy data collection is a practical source of navigation supervision that can scale up training without the target robot; UNI offers bias toward wheeled-feasible routes that can still generalize across datasets, with some transferability to related platforms.

Abstract: Collecting real-world navigation data for mobile robots typically requires platform-specific teleoperation, making large-scale collection expensive and difficult to scale. We introduce Universal Navigation Interface (UNI), a robot-free data collection paradigm that uses a four-wheeled rollator walker (rollator) and smartphone to collect physically constrained human demonstrations. Because the rollator cannot climb stairs, negotiate uncut curbs, or pass through narrow gaps, demonstrations are naturally biased toward wheeled-feasible routes. Using UNI, we collect 37.2 km of real-world navigation data and recover metric trajectories that directly supervise goal-conditioned navigation models. Fine-tuning visual-navigation models on UNI reduces trajectory prediction error by 17.4-24.8% on held-out UNI demonstrations. Evaluation on other navigation datasets shows benefits that vary by dataset and metric. We further demonstrate closed-loop transfer to a powered wheelchair in curb, staircase, and curb-cut scenarios. These results support low-cost physical proxies as a practical source of navigation supervision collected without the target robot.

</details>


### [280] [GPT-6-Astra in a Navigation Workflow: Behavioral Analysis in Zero-Shot Vision-and-Language Navigation in Continuous Environments](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20116)
*Guangzhao Dai,Qi Wu,Bin Zhu*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: A zero-shot VLN-CE system using GPT-6-Astra to interpret instructions, plan, and execute in a continuous environment, evaluated end-to-end without an agent harness or task-specific fine-tuning; results show moderate success but reveal a gap between understanding and sustained progress and stopping.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To understand how a large-language-model-based agent performs in end-to-end Vision-and-Language Navigation in Continuous Environments without task-specific fine-tuning or a packaged navigation agent, emphasizing context management and action control.

Method: Zero-shot VLN-CE loop: interpret observations, reason and decide actions, execute via direct model API calls; retain progress/history to link landmarks and actions to instructions; evaluate on 50 val-unseen episodes from Open-Nav's R2R-CE; metrics include success rate, SPL, and nDTW; termination via workflow-accepted STOP or step-limit distance criterion.

Result: SR 52.0%, SPL 48.9%, nDTW 70.8%; 36.0% succeed with a STOP; 16.0% meet distance criterion at the step limit; qualitative findings: (1) responses link landmarks and earlier actions to instructions using observations/history, (2) reviews request additional views and revisions, (3) unfinished crossings are identified while rotation continues.

Conclusion: Highlights the central challenge of translating correct local judgments into sustained progress and appropriate stopping; suggests a gap between task understanding and autonomous completion, indicating the need for improved stopping criteria and action-flow design in zero-shot LM-based VLN-CE systems.

Abstract: We study GPT-6-Astra in a zero-shot Vision-and-Language Navigation in Continuous Environments (VLN-CE) system, where it interprets instructions, assesses its surroundings, and proposes actions. The system uses a common observation--decision--execution workflow with direct model API calls, without a packaged agent harness or navigation-specific fine-tuning. In this workflow, each request receives selected observations, execution feedback, and retained progress records. Evaluation covers the complete system, including context management and action control. We evaluate the system on 50 of the 100 R2R-CE val-unseen episodes used by Open-Nav. It achieves a success rate of 52.0\%, an SPL of 48.9\%, and an nDTW of 70.8\%. Our analysis highlights three findings. First, recorded responses link landmarks and earlier actions to instructions using observations and supplied history. Second, reviews include requests for additional views and revisions of uncertain judgments. Third, the results suggest a gap between task understanding and autonomous completion: an unfinished crossing is recognized while rotation continues. At termination, 36.0\% of episodes succeed with a workflow-accepted STOP, while another 16.0\% meet the distance criterion at the step limit. These results highlight a central challenge: translating correct local judgments into sustained progress and appropriate stopping.

</details>


### [281] [VLN on the Fly: An Onboard Vision-Language Navigation Stack for Aerial Robots](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20191)
*Marco S. Tayar,Felipe Tommaselli,Gianluca Capezutto,Pedro Antonio Rabelo Saraiva,Pedro H. V. de Freitas,Lucas Kido,Guilherme Sonego,Ricardo V. Godoy,Marcelo Becker*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: Modular onboard VLN stack for aerial robots (VLN on the Fly) keeps grounding, planning, and control as separate, inspectable stages, enabling real-time navigation with limited compute and safety checks preserved.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: End-to-end or onboard single-stage vision-language navigation is challenging on aerial platforms due to limited compute and the difficulty of isolating errors during flight; a modular onboard pipeline can improve observability, safety, and robustness.

Method: An onboard stack uses: (1) a quantized vision-language model to ground instructions to an image cell; (2) depth estimation to lift the grounded target to a 3D goal; (3) a fast B-spline planner to generate a feasible trajectory; (4) a pretrained reinforcement learning policy to execute motor commands on quadrotors. Evaluated on 15 onboard flights across three referents in a controlled indoor volume, achieving 13/15 success with 5.72 cm mean error and 39.3% GPU utilization; plus 6 cluttered-environment trials showing collision-free trajectory tracking with onboard perception.

Result: Success in 13 of 15 trials indoors with a 5.72 cm mean goal error and modest GPU load (39.3%); additional cluttered-environment trials demonstrate collision-free trajectory tracking under onboard perception gating.

Conclusion: A structured onboard VLN stack yields observable, debuggable, and reliable navigation for aerial robots, balancing performance with safety and resource constraints; the approach appears effective across multiple quadrotors and referents, with room to improve success rate and compute efficiency.

Abstract: Running vision-language navigation fully onboard an aerial robot is hard, since grounding, planning, and control must share limited compute and a single-stage error is difficult to isolate in flight. End-to-end aerial policies fuse these stages into one network, giving up the observability and safety checks a modular stack keeps available. We propose VLN on the Fly, an onboard stack that keeps grounding, planning, and control as separate, inspectable stages. A quantized VLM grounds an instruction to a coarse image cell, depth lifts it to a 3D goal, a fast B-spline planner returns a feasible trajectory, and a pretrained reinforcement learning policy tracks it to motor commands across quadrotors. Across 15 onboard flights over three everyday referents in a controlled indoor volume, the stack reaches the target in 13 of 15 trials with 5.72 cm mean goal error and 39.3% average GPU utilization. In 6 additional cluttered-environment trials, the stack tracks collision-free trajectories under onboard perception gating.

</details>


### [282] [Strategic Transformer for Resource-Constrained Multi-Object Navigation in Ultra-Large-Scale Environments](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20227)
*Daiki Iwata,Kanji Tanaka,Senta Hishida*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: Strategic Transformer for resource-constrained multi-object navigation reformulates the problem as a Set Orienteering Problem (SOP) to manage exploitation and exploration under resource limits, achieving real-time, onboard-ready performance with a 94× speedup and 41.03 ms inference by combining macro-planning with a bounded 2-opt refinement, validated on ProcTHOR with Progress weighted by Path Length (PPL).


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Real-time navigation in large indoor spaces is NP-hard under resource constraints. Conventional baselines either plan rigidly or act myopically. There is a need for a unified framework that balances exploration and exploitation efficiently and can run onboard.

Method: Formulate as SOP with exploitation guided by SOP and exploration controlled by a heuristic switcher. Introduce the Strategic Transformer as a lightweight priority planner that internalizes expert combinatorial logic into a predictable 41.03 ms forward pass, uses geometric attention biases to model long-range dependencies, and couples a macro-plan with a bounded iterative 2-opt local refinement on a capped candidate graph. Employ teacher–student distillation to reduce information asymmetry and achieve real-time performance (≈94× faster than heavy meta-heuristics).

Result: The approach achieves real-time, bounded-latency inference suitable for onboard deployment. It yields a 94× speedup over heavy meta-heuristics and a 41.03 ms forward pass. On ProcTHOR, it outperforms re-implemented baselines in the Progress metric weighted by Path Length (PPL), establishing a new benchmark for scalable, resource-constrained navigation.

Conclusion: Strategic Transformer effectively bridges exploration and exploitation for SOP-based navigation, enabling scalable, resource-constrained indoor navigation with real-time performance and competitive accuracy on ProcTHOR; the framework sets a new bottleneck: real-time planning under NP-hard SOP under resource constraints.

Abstract: Resource-constrained multi-object navigation in vast indoor environments ($>2,000\text{ m}^2$) poses significant challenges for efficiency and strategic planning. To tackle this, we reformulate the task as a Set Orienteering Problem (SOP), providing an optimization framework under resource constraints where exploitation is governed by the SOP model and exploration is managed by a separate heuristic switcher. Conventional baselines suffer from either rigid planning or myopic behaviors. To overcome these limitations and resolve the NP-hard computational challenges of SOP for real-time navigation, we develop the Strategic Transformer. This lightweight architecture functions as a priority planner that internalizes expert combinatorial logic into a predictable $41.03\text{ ms}$ forward pass while reducing teacher-student information asymmetry. Incorporating geometric attention biases allows the network to effectively model long-range structural dependencies. By coupling the Transformer's macro-plan with a bounded iterative 2-opt local refinement on a capped candidate graph, our framework achieves a $94\times$ speedup compared to heavy meta-heuristics, ensuring bounded-latency inference suitable for onboard deployment. Experiments on ProcTHOR validate that our method successfully bridges the gap between exploration and exploitation, outperforming carefully re-implemented baselines under Progress weighted by Path Length (PPL) and establishing a new benchmark for scalable, resource-constrained navigation.

</details>


### [283] [LLM-Guided Transformation of Non-Critical Driving Scenes into Safety-Critical Scenarios Using Augmented Reality](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20318)
*Noura Fady,Farah Khaled,Catherine M. Elias*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: Automated pipeline to convert safe driving scenes into safety-critical ADS scenarios using CV, LLMs, and AR; validated on nuScenes with high safety classification accuracy.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Addresses the need for realistic, safety-critical data for ADS testing without the risks and costs of real-world data collection by generating challenging scenarios systematically.

Method: Detect and track road users; extract safety features (distance, velocity, motion direction, Time-to-Collision); assess scene criticality; an LLM generates collision-inducing objects/behaviors; integrate into the scene via Augmented Reality; evaluate on nuScenes.

Result: Achieved 97.52% safety classification accuracy; generated realistic scenarios such as pedestrian crossings, rear overtaking, and sudden-stop events; demonstrates an effective, flexible pipeline for automated safety-critical scenario generation for ADS testing.

Conclusion: Proposes a scalable, adaptable approach to automatically generate safety-critical driving scenarios, enhancing testing/validation of autonomous driving systems by bridging safe scenes with realistic critical events.

Abstract: Testing Autonomous Driving Systems (ADS) requires realistic safety-critical scenarios, but collecting such data from real-world driving is costly and unsafe. This paper presents an automated pipeline that transforms safe driving scenes into safety-critical scenarios by combining computer vision, Large Language Models (LLMs), and Augmented Reality (AR). The system detects and tracks road users, extracts safety features including distance, velocity, motion direction, and Time-to-Collision (TTC), and assesses scene criticality. Safe scenes are modified by an LLM, which generates realistic collision-inducing objects and behaviors that are integrated into the original scene using AR. The proposed pipeline was evaluated on the nuScenes dataset, achieving 97.52% safety classification accuracy and successfully generating realistic scenarios such as pedestrian crossings, rear overtaking vehicles, and sudden-stop events. The results demonstrate an effective and flexible approach for automated generation of safety-critical scenarios to support the testing and validation of autonomous driving systems.

</details>


### [284] [Implementation of Tightly-Coupled SLAM Fusion of GPS, IMU, and LiDAR for Autonomous Vehicles](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20321)
*Amr O. Elmehrath,Farah Khaled,Rana Nahas,Catherine M. Elias*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: Tightly-coupled 3D SLAM fusion integrating LiDAR, IMU, and GPS with iterative EKF and pose-graph optimization to deliver robust HD maps.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Sensor fragility in featureless or challenging environments (featureless corridors for LiDAR, IMU drift, GPS dropouts) necessitates a robust, continuous mapping system for autonomous navigation.

Method: Phased development: start with 2D hardware/geometry validation; progress to full 3D using FAST-LIO2. Fuse dense 3D LiDAR data with high-rate IMU via Iterated Error-State Kalman Filter (IESKF); incorporate GPS; and apply GTSAM pose-graph optimization for loop closures to mitigate drift.

Result: Demonstrates that tight 3D fusion mitigates individual sensor blind spots, yields detailed point clouds, enabling HD maps for downstream planners; validated in simulation and real-world deployments.

Conclusion: A robust, multi-modal SLAM framework that combines dense LiDAR, high-frequency IMU, and GPS with iterated EKF and loop-closure back-end to provide continuous, accurate localization and mapping for autonomous systems.

Abstract: Autonomous vehicles depend entirely on Simultaneous Localization and Mapping (SLAM) to navigate safely in unknown environments. However, relying on a single sensory modality introduces critical failure points: LiDAR systems degrade in featureless corridors, Inertial Measurement Units (IMUs) accumulate mathematical drift, and GPS drops frequently in urban canyons. This paper presents the implementation of a tightly-coupled SLAM fusion architecture that integrates a Velodyne 3D LiDAR, a high-frequency IMU, and GPS to achieve continuous spatial awareness. Utilizing a phased development methodology, we establish a 2D baseline to validate hardware synchronization and transform geometries before upgrading to a full 3D architecture driven by FAST-LIO2. This advanced approach uses an Iterated Error-State Kalman Filter (IESKF) to process dense 3D laser points alongside continuous inertial data, eliminating motion blur at high speeds. To eradicate long-term drift, a GTSAM pose-graph optimization back-end executes multi-modal loop closures. Evaluated across simulated environments and physical deployments, the results demonstrate that tightly-coupled 3D fusion effectively overcomes individual sensor blind spots to generate highly detailed point clouds, providing the foundational High-Definition (HD) maps required for advanced downstream autonomous planners.

</details>


### [285] [RoboFind: Multi-Agent Personalized Object Search for People Who Are Blind or Have Low Vision](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20330)
*Ruiping Liu,Shaofang Quan,Qian Yin,Jingqi Zhang,Junwei Zheng,Yufan Chen,Di Wen,Weijia Fan,Kailun Yang,M. Saquib Sarfraz,Tamim Asfour,Kunyu Peng,Rainer Stiefelhagen*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: RoboFind uses a multi-agent system to personalize object search for blind/low-vision users, achieving high success and reliable verification via stored semantic references.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Solves the challenge of locating a specific personal object rather than any instance, requiring mobile exploration and an accessible user interface to teach the robot and verify identity.

Method: A smartphone-based Target Teaching Agent creates a semantic target profile and a reusable multi-view reference bank. Runtime involves Navigation, Verification, and Coordination/Recovery Agents controlling a quadruped robot, with AR guidance, speech/haptic feedback, and screen-reader support. Evaluated over 32 real-robot missions (10 targets) against a reconstructed baseline and GPT-6 Astra-only trials.

Result: Achieves 85.0% success (32 missions) vs 25.0% baseline; reduces false success from 75.0% to 5.0%. On six shared targets, 10/12 successes vs 5/12 for Astra-only. Demonstrates reliability by verifying identity before declaring completion.

Conclusion: The multi-agent design matches the demands of personalized object search for visually impaired users; explicit identity verification via a stored reference bank improves reliability and user trust; the approach supports scalable, accessible teaching and robust search in real environments.

Abstract: Blind and low-vision users often need to locate a specific personal object rather than an arbitrary instance of the same category. The task calls for a robot that can move through the space and reach viewpoints the user cannot, and for an accessible interface where the user says which object is meant and learns whether the right one was found. We present RoboFind, a multi-agent framework in which a smartphone teaches the target and a quadruped robot carries out the search. A Target Teaching Agent converts guided smartphone recordings into a semantic target profile and a reusable multi-view reference bank through an accessible capture flow with AR guidance, speech and haptic feedback, and screen-reader support, so later missions refer to a stored object without repeating the teaching process. At runtime, a Navigation Agent explores the environment and proposes candidate targets, a Verification Agent checks each candidate against the stored references, and a Coordination and Recovery Agent completes the mission or triggers recovery and continued search. Across 32 real-robot missions, RoboFind reaches 85.0% success against 25.0% for a reconstructed sequential first-stop baseline over 20 trials with ten targets, and reduces false success from 75.0% to 5.0%. On six shared targets it succeeds in 10/12 trials, against 5/12 for 12 independently executed GPT-6 Astra-only trials. These results show that the multi-agent design fits the demands of personalized object search, where verifying object identity before declaring completion is what makes the outcome something a user can rely on.

</details>


### [286] [Navi-Agent: Unlocalized Monocular Navigation Agent](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20388)
*Wenyuan Xie,Mengyang Hong,Yongzhong Wang,Yanbiao Ji,Yijin Zhou,Shaokai Wu,Shalayiding Sirejiding,Huayi Zhou,Yi-Chao Chen,Ma Ling,Yue Ding,Hongtao Lu*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: Navi-Agent builds a coordinate-free navigation topology from visual observations and action history to enable self-localization, progress verification, and recovery in zero-shot VLN-CE, achieving state-of-the-art among geometry-constrained methods.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: VLN-CE requires persistent spatial awareness and place-level localization without global coordinates; coordinate-based or depth-based methods struggle with confirmation, progress tracking, and recovery in unseen environments.

Method: Constructs a navigation topology where nodes are visually observed places and edges are motion transitions; supports observation-based self-localization, progress verification, and revisitation-based recovery; performs closed-loop navigation by decomposing instructions into sub-goals, executing local visual navigation, and verifying visited places against the topology.

Result: Achieves state-of-the-art performance among geometry-constrained zero-shot VLN-CE methods and remains competitive with coordinate-based approaches on real-world robots.

Conclusion: A coordinate-free topology provides persistent spatial state for VLN-CE without global localization, enabling robust place confirmation and recovery and suggesting a viable direction for geometry-constrained navigation in unknown environments.

Abstract: Vision-Language Navigation in Continuous Environments (VLN-CE) requires an embodied agent to execute long-horizon instructions in unknown environments. Existing zero-shot VLN-CE systems typically maintain spatial states through geometric localization or coordinate-based representations. Recent geometry-constrained navigation removes depth and globally consistent coordinates, but maintaining persistent spatial awareness for place confirmation, progress verification, and recovery remains challenging. We present Navi-Agent, a zero-shot VLN-CE agent that constructs a coordinate-free spatial state from visual observations and executed motion histories. Navi-Agent organizes this state as a navigation topology, where nodes represent visual places and edges represent motion transitions. This representation enables observation-based approximate self-localization, task progress verification, and visual revisitation-based recovery. Navi-Agent performs closed-loop navigation by decomposing instructions into sub-goals, executing local visual navigation, and verifying visited places through the constructed spatial state. Experiments on zero-shot VLN-CE benchmark and real-world robot platforms show that Navi-Agent achieves state-of-the-art performance among geometry-constrained methods while remaining competitive with approaches relying on geometric localization.

</details>


### [287] [Imagine-TAMP: Imagination-Guided Task and Motion Planning in Partial Observability](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20396)
*Antareep Singha,Shivaram Kumar,Yoonwoo Kim,Yoonchang Sung*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: Imagine-TAMP interleaves planning and execution by imagining both semantic relations and plausible unobserved geometry to evaluate alternative task strategies under partial observability, guiding selection of a plan skeleton before costly motion planning.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: In cluttered, partially observable environments, it is unclear whether to spend resources on sensing to reveal the target or to manipulate occluders first. Conventional TAMP relies on symbolic or expensive geometric evaluation that may not capture the likelihood that an observation will reveal the target.

Method: The approach uses a vision-language model to shape a particle belief over target locations via commonsense relations between the target and visible objects, and a generative scene model to estimate plausible geometry in unobserved regions. It generates multiple symbolic plan skeletons with non-unit costs that reflect manipulation effort and the value of sensing actions. A selected skeleton is refined into a feasible continuous plan and executed, with belief updates and replanning triggered by new observations.

Result: In viewpoint-constrained shelf scenes, non-unit geometric evaluation raised success from 46.0% to 84.0%. Semantic belief shaping further reduced manipulation and replanning. On a real robot, the complete system cut planning time by 32% versus a geometry-only ablation.

Conclusion: Imagination-guided evaluation improves decision-making under partial observability by integrating semantic and geometric reasoning into TAMP, enabling better observation-versus-manipulation choices and faster planning.

Abstract: Robots operating in cluttered environments must often manipulate objects whose locations are only partially observable. A central challenge is deciding whether to acquire another observation or to first manipulate objects that may occlude the target. Conventional task and motion planning (TAMP) approaches typically make this decision using symbolic action costs or expensive geometric planning, neither of which adequately captures how likely an observation is to reveal an occluded target. We introduce Imagine-TAMP, an interleaved planning and execution framework that uses semantic and geometric imagination to compare alternative task-level strategies under partial observability before committing to expensive motion planning. A vision-language model shapes a particle belief over target locations using commonsense relationships between the target and visible objects, while a generative scene model estimates plausible geometry in unobserved regions. Given a target hypothesis and imagined scene, Imagine-TAMP generates multiple symbolic plan skeletons and assigns non-unit costs that approximate both manipulation effort and target visibility from sensing actions, distinguishing a short but poorly informative observation strategy from a longer strategy that first manipulates an occluder to better expose the target. The selected skeleton is then refined into a feasible continuous plan and executed, with new observations updating the belief and triggering replanning when necessary. Experiments show that imagination-guided evaluation improves observation-versus-manipulation decisions: in viewpoint-constrained shelf scenes, non-unit geometric evaluation increases success from 46.0% to 84.0%, while semantic belief shaping further reduces manipulation and replanning. On a real robot, the complete system reduces planning time by 32% relative to a geometry-only ablation.

</details>


### [288] [Resilient Motion Planning for Free-Flying Space Robots under Actuator Failures](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20407)
*Nicolas de Maddalena,Joris Verhagen,Jana Tumova*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: A probabilistic, proactive planner for free-flying space robots that anticipates actuator failures, using Markov-model failures, precomputed reachable sets and RRT* to maximize the probability of reaching the goal across a horizon; validated on a real platform with injected failures.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Actuator failures threaten control authority in free-flying space robots; traditional planners neglect stochastic failure modes and the passive straight-line drift in absence of actuation. A resilient planner can improve mission success by accounting for failure probabilities and exploiting dynamics.

Method: Model actuator failures as a Markov chain; propagate the probability of successfully reaching the goal over the planning horizon. Precompute reachable sets for capability under potential failures. Use an RRT*-based planner to assemble a sequence of waypoints that maximize the overall target-reaching probability.

Result: Experimental validation on a physical free-flyer platform with injected actuator failures, demonstrating feasibility of the probabilistic robust planning approach.

Conclusion: The framework yields maximally resilient motion plans by explicitly incorporating failure dynamics and free-flying characteristics, showing promise for space robotics applications.

Abstract: Free-flying robots rely on multiple thrusters to maneuver in space. If one or more of these thrusters fail, the robot may lose control authority and risk mission failure. At the same time, their free-flying nature implies that, even in the absence of actuation, they continue along (locally) straight-line trajectories. In this work we present a probabilistic, proactive, motion planning framework that explicitly accounts for actuator failures in space. We model actuator failure modes as a Markov chain and propagate the probability of successfully reaching the goal along the planning horizon. Precomputed reachable sets evaluate the robot's capabilities of reaching waypoints under potential failures and an RRT$^*$-based planner concatenates these waypoints. The resulting algorithm maximizes the overall target-reaching probability, providing maximally resilient motion plans utilizing free-flying properties. We validate our approach experimentally on a physical free-flyer platform with injected actuator failures.

</details>


### [289] [Time-Efficient Iterative Learning Planning for Safety-Critical Dynamic Obstacle Avoidance](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20435)
*Zhiyi Chen,Shuli Lv,Chen Min,Yong Xu,Jian Sun,Quan Quan*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: Extends Iterative Learning Planning (ILP) with an anticipatory risk-blended CBF (ARB-CBF) for safety-critical dynamic obstacle avoidance in dynamic environments, yielding safe, time-efficient planning with low computational overhead.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To achieve reliable, real-time navigation on resource-constrained platforms by combining lightweight ILP planning with formal safety guarantees for dynamic obstacles.

Method: Extend ILP by integrating ARB-CBF. ILP learns traversal-speed and steering-bias via a fractional-power update based on local obstacle risk, generating nominal commands; ARB-CBF modifies these commands at runtime to ensure safety. Algorithmic analysis shows ILP replanning scales as O(kN) for k iterations and N waypoints; ARB-CBF runs in linear complexity. Validation via simulations and real-world experiments.

Result: ILP+ARB-CBF achieves superior temporal efficiency and safety with lower computational overhead compared to optimization-based baselines.

Conclusion: The proposed framework enables safe, efficient navigation in dynamic environments on resource-constrained platforms by coupling light-weight planning with real-time safety guarantees.

Abstract: Autonomous mobile robots require timeefficient planning and safety-critical dynamic obstacle avoidance under constrained onboard computation. While Iterative Learning Planning (ILP) offers lightweight and efficient traversal planning, it lacks explicit mechanisms for dynamic obstacle perception and avoidance. This article extends ILP to safety-critical navigation in dynamic environments by integrating an anticipatory risk-blended control barrier function (ARB-CBF). The extended ILP learns traversal-speed and steering-bias profiles via a fractionalpower update based on local obstacle risk, generating nominal control commands that ARB-CBF modifies at runtime for real-time safety guarantees. Algorithmic analysis demonstrates that the ILP replanning stage scales at O(kN) for k iterations and N waypoints, while ARB-CBF executes with linear complexity. Comprehensive simulations and real-world experiments validate the framework, demonstrating superior temporal efficiency and safety with lower computational overhead compared to optimizationbased baselines, making it highly suitable for resourceconstrained platforms.

</details>


### [290] [Spatial-Semantic Uncertainty in VLM-Based Target Search: Balancing Exploration and Identification](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20443)
*Alkesh K. Srivastava,Jonathan Diller,Vijay Kumar,Philip Dames*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: A spatial-semantic uncertainty formulation for VLM-based search that separately reasons about where to search and which candidate is the target, using a probabilistic identity posterior with an 'undiscovered target' mass; an information-theoretic planner uses spatial and semantic EIG to guide exploration vs identification; evaluated on 500 synthetic targets; semantic emphasis reduces exploration while maintaining accuracy; results highlight distinct roles of uncertainty representation and planning.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Address conflation of spatial and semantic uncertainty in vision-language model guided searches; require separate belief representations to enable principled trade-offs between discovering new candidates and disambiguating the target.

Method: Decompose uncertainty into spatial and semantic components; integrate VLM evidence into a global target-identity posterior including mass for undiscovered targets; compute spatial and semantic Expected Information Gain (EIG) to guide planning; evaluate six VLM uncertainty-elicitation interfaces on 500 synthetic targets; compare EIG-based planners to Random search; test behavior under degraded observations.

Result: EIG-based planners reach confident decisions in 75.0%-92.5% of trials vs 20% for Random; varied spatial-semantic weightings yield comparable identification accuracy once confident; higher semantic emphasis reduces unnecessary exploration and VLM queries.

Conclusion: Explicit planning over semantic uncertainty, combined with a spatial-semantic uncertainty representation, accelerates target resolution without sacrificing decision quality, highlighting the importance of uncertainty representation and uncertainty-driven planning in embodied VLM systems.

Abstract: Robots searching for a target from a natural-language description must determine not only where to search, but also which observed candidate is the desired target. These decisions reflect two distinct sources of uncertainty - spatial uncertainty over candidate locations and semantic uncertainty over target identity - that are often conflated in VLM-based search systems. We introduce a spatial-semantic uncertainty formulation that maintains separate beliefs over each component and integrates probabilistic VLM evidence into a global target-identity posterior, including probability mass for undiscovered targets. This decomposition allows an information-theoretic planner to independently value candidate discovery and target disambiguation through spatial and semantic expected information gain (EIG), providing an explicit mechanism for trading broader exploration against earlier identification. We evaluate six VLM uncertainty-elicitation interfaces on 500 synthetic targets and show that similar recognition accuracy can conceal substantial differences in calibration and false confidence. In degraded-observation search-and-identify experiments, EIG-based planners reach confident decisions in 75.0%-92.5% of trials, compared with 20.0% for Random search, while different spatial-semantic weightings achieve comparable identification accuracy once confidence is attained. Increasing semantic emphasis reduces unnecessary exploration and VLM queries, demonstrating that explicitly planning over semantic uncertainty can accelerate target resolution without sacrificing decision quality. These results highlight the distinct roles of uncertainty representation and uncertainty-driven planning in embodied VLM systems.

</details>


### [291] [Visual Sim-to-Real Learning for Robotic Insertion under Geometric Variations: Application to Rebar Installation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20477)
*Tao Sun,Beining Han,Patrick Yin,Rui Xu,Harry He,Abhishek Gupta,Szymon Rusinkiewicz,Yi Shao*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: A visual sim-to-real framework (RebarSim) for robotic rebar insertion; teacher-student distillation with domain randomization enables zero-shot real-world transfer with 91.3% success; design diversity and pretraining improve performance, and adaptation to new designs requires fewer distillation samples.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Address the data-hungry, contact-rich nature of rebar insertion under 1.4 mm clearance and design/fabrication tolerance variability; enable robust real-world operation with minimal real data.

Method: Train a privileged state-based RL teacher in simulation over procedurally generated geometries; distill to a multi-view student mapping RGB and proprioception to actions; intensive appearance randomization and DAgger integration; evaluate zero-shot transfer and adaptation to new designs; analyze impact of design diversity and pretraining.

Result: Zero-shot transfer achieves 91.3% real-robot rollout success; diversity and pretraining improve zero-shot performance; student outperforms single-design specialist; adaptation to a new design requires 4–6x fewer distillation samples; removing appearance randomization or DAgger degrades performance.

Conclusion: Appearance randomization and DAgger are crucial for visual sim-to-real; training across diverse nominal designs enhances zero-shot transfer; distillation from a simulated teacher to a student offers practical, data-efficient real-world deployment in construction automation.

Abstract: Rebar insertion is among the most repetitive and physically demanding tasks on construction sites, and a contact-rich problem at 1.4 mm clearance. The parts, however, vary at two levels: a nominal design per structural member, and fabrication tolerance around each nominal design. Real-world data therefore has to be re-collected as designs and batches change. We present RebarSim, a visual sim-to-real system trained entirely in simulation. A privileged state-based teacher is trained with reinforcement learning over procedurally generated rebar geometries, then distilled into a multi-view student that maps raw RGB and proprioception directly to actions under extensive domain randomization. The student transfers to the real world zero-shot, seating rebars taken from a real factory production run in 91.3% of real-robot rollouts. Underlying that result, geometry diversity and pretraining both bring benefits. Training across a diverse set of nominal designs rather than one lifts the zero-shot success of both the teacher and the student on unseen designs, and the student policy outperforms a single-design specialist on that specialist's own design. A pretrained student then adapts to a new design with 4--6x fewer distillation samples than one trained from scratch. Visual sim-to-real transfer depends on appearance randomization and the DAgger mixture: removing either one sharply lowers success. Videos, code, and task assets are available at https://rebarsim.github.io.

</details>


### [292] [Worst-Case Hidden-Vehicle Trajectory Search in Spatiotemporal Occlusion Regions](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20480)
*Ruichen Tan,Zengxiang Lei,Satish Ukkusuri*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: HC-MTS introduces a history-conditioned minimax trajectory search that reasons about finite hidden-state modes under multi-frame occlusion constraints, using a bilevel game to optimize ego score against worst-case hidden-vehicle trajectories; empirical results on Waymo show reduced retained hidden seeds and identification of avoidable counterexamples within a fixed search budget.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Occlusions create fundamental uncertainty in autonomous driving; existing methods either propagate frame-wise hypotheses or rely on predetermined hidden-agent predictions, leaving long-horizon, history-consistent interactions underexplored.

Method: Construct finite hidden-state modes certified by backward witnesses with multi-frame visibility, occupancy, semantic-map support, and class-specific kinematic constraints. Solve a bilevel minimax: inner oracle maximizes ego driving score over destinations and ride comfort; outer search selects a legal hidden-vehicle trajectory that minimizes the inner best-response value, under a finite search budget.

Result: Across eight Waymo Open Motion Dataset scenarios, increasing the visibility-memory horizon from K=1 to K=20 reduces mean retained hidden-seed counts for vehicles, pedestrians, and total by 18.12%, 21.67%, and 18.45%, respectively. HC-MTS identifies six avoidable counterexamples; no legal collision-producing attacker is found in the remaining two scenes within the finite budget.

Conclusion: History-conditioned, response-aware minimax search effectively reasons about occluded interactions, reduces unnecessary retention of hidden seeds, uncovers avoidable failure cases, and demonstrates robustness within a finite search budget on real-world data.

Abstract: Occlusion creates fundamental uncertainty in autonomous driving. Existing methods often propagate frame-wise hypotheses or optimize ego behavior against prescribed hidden-agent predictions, leaving the worst history-consistent interaction unexplored. We introduce History-Conditioned Minimax Trajectory Search (HC-MTS), which combines temporal occlusion reasoning with response-aware search. First, HC-MTS constructs finite hidden-state modes, each certified by a backward witness satisfying multi-frame visibility, occupancy, semantic-map support, and class-specific kinematic constraints. It then solves a bilevel minimax problem: an inner finite oracle maximizes the ego driving score over destination attainment and ride comfort, while the outer search selects the legal hidden-vehicle trajectory that minimizes this best-response value. Across eight Waymo Open Motion Dataset scenarios, increasing the visibility-memory horizon from K=1 to K=20 reduces the mean per-scenario vehicle, pedestrian, and total retained hidden-seed counts by 18.12%, 21.67%, and 18.45%, respectively. HC-MTS identifies six avoidable counterexamples, while no legal collision-producing attacker is found in the remaining two scenes within the finite search budget.

</details>


### [293] [Towards AI-enhanced control: a numerical technique for trajectory smoothing of a parallel robot for pancreatic surgery](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20499)
*Iosif Birlescu,Alexandru Pusca,Bogdan Gherman,Calin Vaida,Ionut Zima,Damien Chablat,Doina Pisla*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: A real-time, master-slave controlled parallel robot for minimally invasive pancreatic surgery uses S-curve velocity profiles to smooth end-effector trajectories, driven by a 3D space mouse; this reduces tissue trauma by controlling accelerations. The approach segments S-curves to enable real-time control, with a constant acceleration-time variant; numerical results show smooth transitions in end-effector and joint spaces, supporting feasibility and stability. Future work includes experimental validation and AI-based training integration.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To enable smooth, real-time trajectory execution for a parallel robot in minimally invasive pancreatic surgery, minimizing tissue trauma while providing intuitive 3D input and ensuring stable control in a master-slave configuration.

Method: Generate S-curve velocity profiles in end-effector space, segmented in response to commands from a 3D space mouse, for real-time velocity control in a master-slave parallel robot. Consider a special case with constant acceleration time. Validate via numerical simulations showing stability in end-effector and joint-space trajectories.

Result: Numerical results show stable, non-abrupt transitions in both end-effector and active joint parameter spaces, indicating the approach yields smooth trajectories suitable for MIS applications.

Conclusion: The proposed S-curve based trajectory smoothing supports real-time, smooth end-effector motion for MIS parallel robotics, reducing tissue trauma; future work involves experimental validation and integration with AI-based training modalities.

Abstract: The paper presents a numerical approach for the end-effector trajectory smoothing of a parallel robot designed for minimally invasive pancreatic surgery. The approach is tailored for real-time master-slave control architecture and uses a 3D space mouse for command input for velocity control. The trajectory smoothing is achieved by generating S-curves in the end-effector velocity fields, thus controlling the accelerations, which in turn reduces tissue trauma in the minimally invasive procedures. Real-time control is enabled by segmenting the S-curves based on the command inputs from the 3D space mouse. A special case is considered where the acceleration time is constant for all command inputs. Numeric results demonstrate stable transitions (without abrupt changes) in both the end-effector parameter space and in the active joints parameters, thereby validating the proposed approach. Further work aims to test the approach on an experimental model and integrate it into AI-based training modules.

</details>


### [294] [Integrated Guidance and Control of a Mother-Child UAV-UGV System for Cooperative Missions](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20540)
*Aashish Sahu,R. Prasanth Kumar*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: A field-validated autonomy framework for autonomous recovery of a small multirotor onto a hovering carrier, achieving 85% success across 20 outdoor missions with quantified alignment, distance, and vertical separation metrics.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Enable autonomous recovery onto an actively controlled aerial platform, addressing the unique challenges of a moving, thrust-limited recovery surface and the need for reliable, field-tested autonomy.

Method: Integrated stack combining jerk-bounded reference generation, disturbance-observer-augmented planar tracking, feasibility-aware vertical control, a discrete-time barrier-based safety filter for relative vertical geometry, and communication-aware carrier-state prediction. Implemented on a PX4-ROS 2 architecture with RTK GNSS/IMU/barometer fusion; mothership uses 1D lidar as auxiliary cue; RTK-fixed positioning maintained. Field validation across 20 outdoor missions with 17 successes (85%); deployment, sortie, recovery, and synchronous descent stages.

Result: 17/20 mission success; mean terminal-alignment time 6.3 s; mean planar alignment error at acceptance 0.18 m; max terminal planar deviation 0.32 m within 0.40 m capture radius; minimum logged relative vertical separation during descent 0.41 m; mothership planar station-keeping RMS 0.25 m.

Conclusion: The study demonstrates practical, field-validated autonomous aerial recovery onto a hovering multirotor within the tested envelope, showing a viable approach for autonomous rover-mothership-child operations.

Abstract: Autonomous recovery of a small multirotor onto a hovering multirotor carrier differs from recovery onto ground or shipborne platforms because the recovery surface is itself an actively controlled, thrust-limited aerial vehicle. This paper presents a field-validated autonomy framework for a heterogeneous rover-mothership-child system executing rover supervision, mothership transit, child deployment and sortie, autonomous return, aerial recovery, and synchronized descent. The recovery stack combines jerk-bounded reference generation, disturbance-observer-augmented planar tracking, feasibility-aware vertical control, a discrete-time barrier-based safety filter for relative vertical geometry, and communication-aware carrier-state prediction. The contribution is the coordinated system-level integration of these methods for recovery onto a hovering multirotor and its full-scale outdoor validation. The framework is implemented on a PX4-ROS 2 architecture using RTK-enabled GNSS, IMU, and barometric fusion, with mothership-side 1D lidar used only as an auxiliary near-contact cue. RTK-fixed positioning was maintained throughout testing. Across 20 outdoor cooperative missions, 17 successfully completed deployment, sortie, and recovery, giving an observed mission success rate of 85%. For successful recoveries, mean terminal-alignment time was 6.3 s, mean planar alignment error at acceptance was 0.18 m, maximum terminal planar deviation was 0.32 m within a 0.40 m capture radius, and minimum logged relative vertical separation during coupled descent was 0.41 m. Mothership planar station-keeping RMS error was 0.25 m. The three unsuccessful trials occurred at different mission stages and are analyzed separately. Results demonstrate practical autonomous aerial recovery within the tested outdoor operating envelope.

</details>


### [295] [Learning Slope-Adaptive Whole-Body Locomotion for Humanoid Robots in Roofing Construction](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20558)
*Songyang Liu,Shuai Li*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: A scene-grounded, task-semantic framework learns roofer-style whole-body motions on a Unitree G1 by retargeting human demonstrations with a metric roof model, trajectory optimization, and execution-aware RL to preserve roof-related relations; achieves precise contact and clearance on roofing tasks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Roofing on pitched surfaces imposes strict contact constraints and balance; direct retargeting often misplaces feet/hands and violates nonpenetration; a scene-grounded approach is needed to enforce roof-relative references and work relations.
