Method: Capture human demonstrations; retarget to robot; supply spatial reference via metric roof model; perform trajectory-level optimization to ground contact/support relations to roof; train with execution-aware reinforcement learning to preserve relations under tracking errors; compare to pure RL and zero-shot teleoperation; evaluate with multi-motion tracking, roof-pitch coverage, nailgun ablation, cross-task hammering/pushing; physical experiments.

Result: Robot satisfies support, work-clearance, and nonpenetration across seeds; nailgun/hammering/pushing tasks achieve work-clearance errors 0.256–0.531 cm; 3/3 success per task; physical tests show uphill walking, nailgun, hammering, bending; mean base-frame motion errors <80 mm.

Conclusion: Scene-grounded human motion learning is a promising basis for construction-oriented humanoid motion primitives, enabling robust, safe, and accurate roofing motions on pitched surfaces.

Abstract: Roofing requires workers to coordinate locomotion, balance, and work-related body motions on pitched surfaces, creating a challenging application for humanoid robots. Directly retargeted human demonstrations, however, may preserve motion appearance while placing the robot's feet or hands incorrectly relative to the roof. This study presents a task-semantic scene-grounded framework for learning roofer-style whole-body motions on a Unitree G1. Human demonstrations are captured using a tracking system and retargeted to the robot, while a metric roof model supplies the spatial reference unavailable from the tracking system. A trajectory-level optimization grounds inferred support contacts and annotated work relations to the roof, and execution-aware reinforcement learning encourages the resulting policy to preserve these relations under dynamic tracking errors. The framework is evaluated through a multi-motion tracking study, a roof-pitch coverage matrix, a five-way nailgun ablation, cross-task experiments on hammering and lateral pushing, and comparisons with pure reinforcement learning and zero-shot teleoperation. Our method enables the robot to satisfy support, work-clearance, and nonpenetration criteria across all evaluated seeds. Across nailgun, hammering, and pushing, it achieves work-clearance errors between 0.256 and 0.531 cm and 3/3 successful evaluations per task. Physical experiments reproduce uphill walking, nailgun, hammering, and bending motions with mean base-frame motion errors below 80 mm. These findings establish scene-grounded human motion learning as a promising basis for construction-oriented humanoid motion primitives.

</details>


### [296] [OmniMimic: Dynamics-completed Motion Augmentation for Multi-style Omnidirectional Quadruped Locomotion](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20566)
*Sheng Wu,Guoqiang Zhao,Zhe Yang,Fei Teng,Zhikun Zhou,Yanlin Yang,Zheng Fang,Hong Zheng,Yaonan Wang,Kailun Yang*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: OmniMimic learns a single multi-gait policy from directionally limited animal demonstrations by augmenting supervision through temporal reversal, constrained dynamics completion, and sagittal reflection, then progressively expands command space with a shared actor and gait-specialized residual experts; it substantially improves trajectory and velocity-tracking accuracy over APEX in simulation across four gaits.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To address the narrow directional coverage of animal demonstrations that restricts natural gait styles to a limited set of directions, hindering the learning of robust, direction-general quadruped locomotion.

Method: 1) Construct robot-specific supervision beyond observed directions using temporal reversal, constrained dynamics completion, and sagittal reflection. 2) Expand commands progressively from the demonstrated velocity distribution toward target per-axis bounds. 3) Use a shared actor with soft-gated, gait-specialized residual experts to balance reusable locomotion skills with gait-specific corrections. 4) Evaluate across four gaits in simulation and compare to a matched APEX baseline.

Result: Compared with APEX, OmniMimic reduces mean foot-position RMSE at forward and backward reference velocities by 12.9% and reduces velocity-tracking RMSE on a uniform Cartesian command grid by 63.1%. These gains occur across four gaits in simulation.

Conclusion: OmniMimic enables a directionally limited set of demonstrations to yield a single, versatile multi-gait policy that generalizes to broader command spaces, delivering notable improvements in trajectory accuracy and command tracking over a strong baseline.

Abstract: Animal demonstrations provide quadruped robots with natural and distinctive gait styles that are difficult to specify through hand-crafted rewards. However, their narrow directional coverage leaves little style-consistent supervision for backward, lateral, and turning commands. We present OmniMimic, a training framework that turns directionally limited animal demonstrations into a single multi-gait policy over target per-axis velocity ranges. OmniMimic first combines temporal reversal, constrained dynamics completion, and sagittal reflection to construct robot-specific kinematic and physical supervision beyond the observed directions. It then expands commands progressively from the demonstrated velocity distribution toward the target per-axis bounds, and uses a shared actor with soft-gated, gait-specialized residual experts to balance reusable locomotion skills with gait-specific corrections. Across four gaits in simulation, OmniMimic reduces mean foot-position RMSE at forward and backward reference velocities by 12.9% and velocity-tracking RMSE on a uniform Cartesian command grid by 63.1%, compared with the matched APEX baseline. The project page is at https://OmniMimic.github.io.

</details>


### [297] [Walking on the Slope: Stable Bipedal Gaits with Genetic-Algorithm-Optimized Trajectories](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20570)
*Madhav Rijal*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: An 8-DOF biped robot is modeled and controlled to achieve stable walking on flat and inclined terrains, with trajectory generation via cubic splines, inverse kinematics mapping, Newton-Euler torque computation, ZMP-based stability analysis, and GA-based optimization of hip height, swing-foot lift, and tilt. MATLAB simulations show ZMP stability up to 0.5 s step times and 22.5° slopes; instability beyond these limits requires geometry/trajectory adjustments; stability is more sensitive to mass distribution among links than total mass.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To develop a complete planning, control, and stability framework for 8-DOF bipeds on varied terrain, enabling stable walking under ZMP constraints while reducing actuator work.

Method: Kinematics: forward using DH parameters and homogeneous transforms; inverse kinematics solved in closed form for hip and swing-foot Cartesian trajectories (cubic splines to joint angles). Dynamics: joint torques via Newton-Euler iterative method. Stability: ZMP criterion with feasibility penalty. Optimization: genetic algorithm tuning hip height, maximum swing-foot lift, and frontal-plane tilt to minimize joint work subject to ZMP feasibility.

Result: Nominal 8-DOF model remains ZMP-stable for step times down to 0.5 s and slope inclinations up to 22.5 degrees with the specified foot geometry. Beyond these limits, ZMP exits the support polygon unless foot dimensions or trajectory parameters are modified. Stability is governed more by mass distribution among links than by total mass.

Conclusion: The work highlights the critical role of link mass distribution in ZMP stability, demonstrates a complete modeling–control–optimization pipeline for stable walking on varied terrain, and provides design guidelines (foot geometry and trajectory design) to maintain ZMP feasibility for faster steps or steeper inclines.

Abstract: This paper presents the kinematic and dynamic modeling, trajectory generation, and stability analysis of an 8-degree-of-freedom (DOF) biped robot walking on flat and inclined terrain. Denavit-Hartenberg (DH) parameters and homogeneous transformations are used to derive the forward kinematics, while closed-form inverse kinematics maps the desired hip and swing-foot Cartesian trajectories, generated with cubic splines, to joint angles. Joint torques are computed using the Newton-Euler iterative algorithm, and dynamic stability is evaluated using the zero moment point (ZMP) criterion. A genetic algorithm (GA) optimizes the hip height, maximum swing-foot lift, and frontal-plane tilt angle by minimizing the work done by the joints subject to a ZMP feasibility penalty. Simulation results in MATLAB show that the nominal 8-DOF model remains ZMP-stable for step completion times down to 0.5 s and for slope inclinations up to 22.5 degrees with the given foot geometry. Beyond these limits, the ZMP leaves the support polygon, and either the foot dimensions or the trajectory parameters must be modified. The results also show that ZMP stability is governed by the mass distribution among the links rather than the total mass of the robot.

</details>


### [298] [Accelerating Visual Policy Learning with Sampling-Based Model Predictive Control](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20575)
*Yilang Liu,Haoxiang You,Qian Wang,Daniel Rakita,Ian Abraham*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: SGPS fuses sampling-based MPC with first-order policy gradients to stabilize training of visual, contact-rich policies and enable zero-shot transfer to real robots.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Reduce training cost and memory for differentiable simulations, avoid local optima in FoPG contact patterns, and enable learning directly from depth without a policy teacher.

Method: Behavior cloning initializes the policy from sampled actions; training alternates sampling-based refinement with short-horizon FoPG updates under perturbed initial states and randomized dynamics. A decoupled FoPG for visual policy excludes rendering from the computation graph, enabling learning from depth observations without a state-policy teacher. Trains on simulated Unitree Go2 and G1 for locomotion, obstacle traversal, crate pushing, and bimanual carrying on a single GPU; evaluates zero-shot transfer to a real Go2 using onboard depth.

Result: Policies learned for locomotion, obstacle traversal, crate pushing, and bimanual carrying. Refinement improves policy learning beyond initialization and tracking alone. Distilled policy transfers zero-shot to a real Go2 and autonomously performs trot, crawl, hurdle clearance, and behavior switching using onboard depth.

Conclusion: SGPS reduces training cost and mitigates local optima in visual policy learning by coupling sampling-based refinement with FoPG; the decoupled FoPG enables efficient learning from depth without a teacher, enabling practical real-world deployment on legged robots.

Abstract: Learning visual policies for locomotion and manipulation requires coordinating contact with the environment and can incur substantial computation and GPU memory costs. First-order policy gradients (FoPG) reduce training cost through differentiable simulation, but local optimization can converge to unintended contact patterns. To address this shortfall, we propose Sampling-Guided Policy Search (SGPS), which couples recurring action-target refinement by sampling-based model-predictive control with first-order policy optimization. Behavior cloning initializes the policy from sampled actions; training then alternates sampling-based refinement with short-horizon FoPG updates under perturbed initial states and randomized dynamics. For visual policy training, we use a decoupled FoPG formulation that excludes rendering from the computation graph, enabling direct learning from depth observations without a state-policy teacher. On a single GPU, SGPS learns policies for locomotion, obstacle traversal, crate pushing, and bimanual carrying on simulated Unitree Go2 and G1 robots. Our experiments further show that refinement improves policy learning beyond initialization and tracking alone. For hardware deployment, the distilled policy transfers zero-shot to a real Go2 and uses onboard depth to autonomously trot, crawl, clear hurdles, and switch between these behaviors.

</details>


### [299] [V2-STRep: VLM-Grounded Structured Task Representations for Reusable Robot Skills Acquired from Generated Videos](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20582)
*Yexin Hu,Dongheui Lee*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: V2-STRep: a zero-shot framework converting video-generated demonstrations into reusable, geometry-aware robot skills via VLM-grounded structured task representations; enables cross-scene transfer and constrained trajectory optimization.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Video-driven demonstrations provide rich motion but are typically tied to a single scene; there is a need to extract explicit task structure, geometry, and constraints to enable reusable, instruction-agnostic robot skills across scenes.

Method: Introduce V2-STRep with structured task representations that specify motion phases, references, and constraints. Target geometry is represented by simple primitives (points, normals, axes, planes, 6D poses). Use VLM-derived 2D cues lifted to 3D from RGB-D to reconstruct task geometry and candidate grasps. Apply geometry-specific rules to transfer motion to new scenes. Use task-constrained trajectory optimization to couple grasp selection with full robot motion planning, respecting joint limits, and allow remaining rotational freedom. Update deployment grounding and constraints to reuse with new compatible instructions without re-generating video.

Result: Experiments on six real-world manipulation tasks show improved execution success over baselines, reliable cross-scene transfer of learned skills, and adaptation to changed deployment instructions.

Conclusion: The approach demonstrates zero-shot transfer of video-generated demonstrations into reusable, geometry-aware robot skills by combining 3D geometry reasoning, structured task representations, and optimization-driven planning, enabling flexible reuse across scenes and instructions.

Abstract: Human manipulation videos provide rich motion and interaction cues for acquiring robot skills without robot demonstrations. Video generation models synthesize such demonstrations from an initial scene image and task instruction, avoiding the need to record demonstrations for each task. However, the recovered motion captures only one scene-specific realization, leaving task structure, geometric relations, and constraints implicit. We present V2-STRep, a zero-shot framework that converts generated video motion into reusable robot skills through VLM-grounded structured task representations. The representation specifies motion phases, references, and task-relevant constraints, with targets described by minimal geometric structures: points, point-normals, axes, planes, and full 6D poses. VLM-provided 2D image-space cues are lifted into 3D using RGB-D observations to reconstruct task geometry and candidate grasp poses. Geometry-specific rules transfer motion to new scenes, while task-constrained trajectory optimization couples grasp selection with complete robot motion planning. It preserves task requirements while using remaining rotational freedom to accommodate joint limits. Updating deployment grounding and constraints enables reuse under new compatible instructions without generating another video. Experiments on six real-world manipulation tasks demonstrate improved execution success over baselines, reliable cross-scene transfer of successfully acquired skills, and adaptation to changed deployment instructions.

</details>


### [300] [CoRef-GS: Cooperative Referring Gaussian Splatting for Multi-Agent Scene Understanding](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20586)
*Zhikun Zhou,Kunyu Peng,Runyi Yang,Junhao Cai,Di Wen,Ruiping Liu,Danda Pani Paudel,Yi Zhou,Luc Van Gool,Kailun Yang*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: CoRef-GS enables cooperative language grounding on fused Gaussian maps across multiple agents, using cross-agent alignment and a view-conditioned relation graph, and introduces the CoQuad-Ref benchmark with strong quantitative gains.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To enable language grounding for referring expressions in cooperative multi-robot systems after map fusion, preserving geometric alignability, semantic comparability, and view-consistent relation reasoning.

Method: 1) Build local open-vocabulary instance-aware Gaussian maps for each agent. 2) Align partially overlapping maps via a cross-agent alignment module enforcing geometric and semantic consistency. 3) Ground queries with a view-conditioned mask relation graph. 4) Propose CoQuad-Ref, a dual-quadruped benchmark spanning real and simulated indoor scenes.

Result: In simulated scenes, rotation error reduces from 2.58° (coarse init) to 0.15° after refinement; real-world referring mIoU improves from 52.6% to 68.8% over ReferSplat.

Conclusion: CoRef-GS delivers a novel cooperative referring grounding framework for fused Gaussian maps, demonstrating substantial accuracy gains and providing the CoQuad-Ref benchmark and code release for community adoption.

Abstract: Referring scene understanding for embodied robots requires grounding object- and relation-centric language queries from a designated viewpoint. While a local semantic Gaussian map can support such grounding within one agent's observations, cooperative settings require this ability to remain effective after independently reconstructed maps are aligned and fused. In this setting, the referred target or its contextual landmark may come from another agent's observations, while spatial relations must still be interpreted from the querying robot's viewpoint. We formulate this problem as cooperative referring Gaussian grounding over fused maps, which requires geometric alignability, instance-level semantic comparability, and view-conditioned relation reasoning. Existing language-aware Gaussian methods mainly focus on single-map querying, whereas Gaussian registration methods optimize geometric or photometric alignment without preserving language-grounding-oriented semantic compatibility. We propose CoRef-GS, a cooperative referring Gaussian splatting framework. CoRef-GS constructs local open-vocabulary instance-aware Gaussian maps, then aligns partially overlapping maps with a cross-agent alignment module by geometric and semantic consistency, and grounds queries using a view-conditioned mask relation graph. We further introduce CoQuad-Ref, a dual-quadruped benchmark spanning both real-world and simulated indoor scenes. Experiments show that, on simulated scenes, CoRef-GS reduces the rotation error from 2.58° after coarse initialization to 0.15° after refinement, and improves real-world referring mIoU over ReferSplat from 52.6% to 68.8%. The established benchmark and source code will be publicly released at https://github.com/ruojiruoli17/CoRef-GS.git.

</details>


### [301] [Semantic SLAM in Precision Agriculture using Bayesian Inference](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20604)
*Ruben Beumer,Sander Doodeman,René van de Molengraft,Duarte Antunes*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: A real-time semantic world-modeling framework for precision agricultural robotics that fuses probabilistic object/semantic mapping with graph-based SLAM (g^2o), enabling GPS-independent localization and mapping of hundreds of plants using YOLOv8n perception; validated in Gazebo and indoor Spot experiments.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To enable accurate, semantic-aware mapping and localization for autonomous agricultural robots in GPS-denied environments by integrating object-level semantics with SLAM.

Method: Integrates probabilistic object mapping and semantic attributes updated via Bayesian inference with a graph-based SLAM framework using g^2o. Perception via YOLOv8n on depth-camera data extracts plant- and health-related semantic data. Validates in Gazebo simulations and indoor experiments with artificial crops using Spot.

Result: Real-time mapping and localization achieved for at least 400 plants in simulated and indoor experiments; demonstrates effective fusion of semantic information with SLAM, enabling autonomous task execution in agriculture.

Conclusion: The framework provides a viable, real-time, semantic-aware SLAM solution for precision agriculture that reduces GPS dependence and supports semantically guided autonomous farming tasks; further work may address outdoor deployment and broader semantic categories.

Abstract: This paper presents a real-time semantic world modeling framework specialized for precision agriculture using autonomous robots. The framework combines probabilistic mapping of objects and their semantic attributes, updated through Bayesian inference, with a graph-based Simultaneous Localization and Mapping (SLAM) approach implemented using $g^2o$, a general framework for graph optimization. This integration enables accurate mapping and localization without relying solely on GPS. By leveraging semantic information such as plant type, size, and health, the robot can perform tasks while mapping and localizing itself within a field of crops. The proposed framework was validated through Gazebo simulations and physical experiments on an indoor field with artificial plants using Boston Dynamics' robot dog Spot. A YOLOv8n object detection model was trained to extract object and semantic data from depth camera observations. These simulations and experiments demonstrate that the system can successfully perform real-time mapping of up to at least 400 plants.

</details>


### [302] [Bayesian Continuum Robot Dynamics and State Estimation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20605)
*James M. Ferguson,Tucker Hermans,Alan Kuntz*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: A physics-informed factor-graph framework for continuum robots that extends quasi-static estimators to dynamic regimes by embedding Cosserat-rod dynamics; inertia/damping are recast as applied loads, enabling stochastic forward simulation and joint estimation of kinematic/dynamic states and external loads, validated in simulation and tendon-driven experiments.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Quasi-static factor-graph methods fail to capture inertial effects during dynamic motions in continuum robots; there is a need for a physics-consistent approach that can perform forward simulation and state estimation under dynamic conditions.

Method: Model Cosserat rod dynamics and recast inertia and damping as equivalent applied loads so dynamic balance resembles the static form used in prior quasi-static work. Construct a factor-graph that either performs stochastic forward simulation (no backbone observations) or jointly estimates kinematic/dynamic states and external loads when observations exist.

Result: Demonstrated both stochastic forward simulation and state estimation on tendon-driven continuum robots, with validation through simulations and experiments.

Conclusion: A dynamics-aware, factor-graph framework extends continuum-robot state estimation into dynamic regimes, enabling simultaneous forward simulation and estimation of external loads; promising for improving accuracy in dynamically actuated continuum robots.

Abstract: Recent factor graph approaches to continuum robot state estimation have been successful for quasi-static applications and spatiotemporal estimation using white-noise kinematic motion priors. However, when inertial effects are significant, these approximations may fail to capture the underlying physics, limiting accuracy during dynamic motions. In contrast, our approach approximates the Cosserat rod dynamics of continuum robots. We write inertia and damping as equivalent applied loads, so that the dynamic balance retains the algebraic form of the static one from prior work with quasi-static robots. Without backbone observations, the framework reduces to a stochastic forward simulation of the robot's motion. Given observations, it jointly refines kinematic and dynamic states and infers external loads, among other states. We validate the approach through simulation and experiments, demonstrating stochastic forward simulation as well as state estimation on tendon-driven continuum robots.

</details>


### [303] [INSPECT: Learning Robot View Selection from Assistant Use](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20615)
*Di Wen,Kailun Yang,Wenhao Guo,Yitian Shi,Junwei Zheng,Yufan Chen,Ruiping Liu,Jiale Wei,Rania Rayyes,Kunyu Peng*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: INSPECT learns view preferences for egocentric assembly inspection from a smart-glasses assistant, using PI-TwinSwap calibration, claim-indexed supervision, and object-centered calibration to select views without candidate images. It improves verifiability and decision accuracy on gearbox assemblies and IMPACT data, and code is released.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Efficient verification of part presence and correct installation in assembly tasks requires robust, view-efficient policies that can adapt to robot poses and observation changes, without relying on target-domain labeled views.

Method: INSPECT includes: (1) presence-invariant TwinSwap (PI-TwinSwap) with paired identity interventions to calibrate evidence; (2) claim-indexed supervision separating evidence requirements from camera-driven changes; (3) object-centered calibration aligning relative view preferences to robot poses; (4) clause-level screening checking predicted evidence; (5) view selection using only current observation and known poses, no candidate images; evaluation uses annotated assistant-video replay to simulate state feedback; policy trained without target-domain view labels.

Result: Gearbox assemblies: highest view utility among non-oracle policies; human-rated full verifiability increases from 34.8% to 41.7% vs maintaining current view. IMPACT dataset (commercial angle grinders): transferred relative-view selector raises correct decision rate from 50.6% to 54.3% with frozen perception head. Open-source code at GitHub.

Conclusion: INSPECT demonstrates effective, transferable view-selection for egocentric assembly verification, reducing dependence on labeled target-domain views and improving verifiability and decision accuracy across tasks.

Abstract: Robots inspecting an assembly must determine which parts are present and whether they are correctly installed. During egocentric assembly assistance, head motion and workpiece handling reveal evidence for these checks, while spoken state confirmations link observations to procedural outcomes. We introduce INSPECT, which learns robot view preferences from records of a smart-glasses assistant that answers part queries and provides next-step guidance. Presence-Invariant TwinSwap (PI-TwinSwap) calibrates object evidence through paired identity interventions. Claim-indexed supervision separates evidence requirements from camera-reproducible observation changes. Object-centered calibration adapts relative view preferences to robot poses, while clause-level screening checks predicted evidence. The robot selects views using only its current observation and known poses, without candidate images. Evaluation uses annotated assistant-video replay to simulate state feedback, without target-domain view labels for policy training. On images of physical gearbox assemblies, INSPECT achieves the highest view utility among the compared non-oracle policies and raises human-rated full verifiability from 34.8% to 41.7% compared with keeping the current view. On commercial angle-grinder recordings in IMPACT, the transferred relative-view selector increases the correct decision rate from 50.6% to 54.3% with a frozen perception head. The source code is available at https://github.com/Kratos-Wen/INSPECT.

</details>


### [304] [A Simulation Platform for AUV Fault Recovery: Exploring LLM-Based Diagnostic Strategies](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20620)
*Khalid Halba,Kylie Cooper,James G. Bellingham*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: SPAR is a simulation framework that combines deterministic AUV control with an LLM-based diagnostic and recovery planner, enabling ensemble evaluation of LLM-assisted fault recovery under varied fault scenarios and prompts.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Autonomous underwater operations often suffer from communication blackouts and faults; LLMs offer reasoning capabilities for diagnosis and recovery planning, but their stochasticity requires systematic ensemble testing to assess reliability and safety.

Method: A closed-loop simulator that integrates real-time C vehicle software with an orchestration layer for physics-based fault injection, structured prompting, LLM interaction, mission file generation, execution, and LLM-judge scoring. SPAR supports varying fault realizations, prompting strategies, reasoning models, and mission conditions across 480 trials using multiple LLMs (frontier and three local models).

Result: Model choice dominates diagnostic success: frontier LLM places the CG-shift mechanism in its top-3 hypotheses in 85–90% of trials, while best local models achieve 60–78%. Local models that follow the full diagnostic procedure perform better; weaker models tend to prematurely conclude elevator failure even when actuator tracking aligns with commands. Diagnostic quality and operational decision-making appear decoupled in the dataset.

Conclusion: The work presents an architecture for unanticipated-fault recovery from detection to mitigation and introduces an ensemble methodology for evaluating LLM-assisted mission management on low-power AUVs.

Abstract: Autonomous underwater vehicles (AUVs) operating beyond reliable communications must recover from failures without human intervention. We investigate an architecture in which conventional deterministic layered control autonomy manages normal operations, while an invokable large language model (LLM) serves as a diagnostic and recovery planner when onboard anomaly detection identifies performance outside expected limits. Because language models are stochastic, rigorous evaluation requires ensemble testing rather than individual demonstrations. We present a closed-loop simulation architecture that couples real-time C vehicle software with a higher-level orchestration layer for physics-based fault injection, structured prompting, language-model interaction, mission file generation, validation, execution, and LLM-judge scoring. The framework, which we call SPAR (Simulation Platform for AUV Recovery), supports evaluation across fault realizations, prompt structures, reasoning models, and mission conditions. We vary these for a mass-shift fault over 480 SPAR trials, evaluating a frontier model and three off-the-shelf locally deployable LLMs. Model choice dominates diagnosis: the frontier model places the CG-shift mechanism in its top three hypotheses in 85-90% of trials, versus 60-78% for the best local model. Reasoning analysis indicates that local-model success is associated with following the complete diagnostic procedure, whereas weaker models often commit prematurely to elevator failure even though the actuator tracks its command. Diagnosis and operational decision performance do not appear to be coupled in this dataset. The contributions are an architecture extending unanticipated-fault recovery from detection to mitigation and an ensemble methodology for evaluating LLM-assisted mission management on low-power AUVs.

</details>


### [305] [SmellDiffusion: Diffusion-Based Quadruped Navigation with Olfactory Scene Graphs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20624)
*Faith Ogunwoye,Iana Zhura,Hajira Amjad,Timofei Kozlov,Didar Seyidov,Dmitrii Plotnikov,Fedor Fedorov,Dzmitry Tsetserukou*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: SmellDiffusion introduces a diffusion-guided, gas-aware planning pipeline that uses a peak-informed geometric gate and a shared scene-graph goal to robustly estimate gas sources and navigate to the target, achieving competitive performance with A* and improved localization.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Robustly identifying and localizing gas sources while preserving gas identity in varied wind conditions, using open-vocabulary gas representations and a unified goal across planning methods.

Method: SmellDiffusion pipeline with a peak-local geometric gate for selective source correction and diffusion-based, gas-guided trajectory generation. A source-independent geometric gate calibrated on the training split detects peak displacements. A precomputed forward-matching correction is gated to reduce error. All planners share a common scene-graph source estimate as the goal. Comparative evaluation against gas-guided A* and plain A* in Gazebo.

Result: Key quantitative findings: 424 source–wind configurations with 28 peaks displaced >0.5 m; gate detects 9 of 10 held-out displacements at 0.64 precision. Gating+correction reduces mean error on displaced cases from 1.468 m to 0.592 m (60%), using matching on 14/204 cases; all-case mean error drops from 0.205 m to 0.180 m. In controlled tests, best-of-ten diffusion yields mean gas exposure similar to gas-guided A* (0.0476 vs 0.0455). Single diffusion proposal: 41.7 ms; gas-guided A*: 72.3 ms. Plain A* fastest and shortest-path. In six Gazebo runs, robot-to-source errors: A*: 0.39 m; diffusion: 0.31 m.

Conclusion: Diffusion-based planning provides competitive exposure and improved source localization compared with A*, with favorable per-proposal latency and useful gating corrections; plain A* remains the fastest baseline, while diffusion offers robustness advantages in open-vocabulary gas scenarios through shared scene-graph goals.

Abstract: A robot sent to a named gas leak must preserve gas identity, estimate the source, and navigate to the resulting goal. We present SmellDiffusion, a simulation pipeline that represents species-specific gas zones in an open-vocabulary olfactory scene graph and shares the selected goal between classical and diffusion planners. Its key components are a peak-local geometric gate for selective source correction and diffusion-based, gas-guided trajectory generation. Among 424 unique source-wind configurations in solved flow, 28 have a concentration peak displaced more than 0.5m from the source. A source-independent geometric gate, calibrated only on the training split and evaluated at the observed peak, detects 9 of 10 held-out displacements at 0.64 precision. Gating a precomputed forward-matching correction reduces mean error on the displaced cases from 1.468m to 0.592m (60%), using matching for only 14/204 cases. All-case mean error falls from 0.205m to 0.180m. All planners receive the same scene-graph source estimate as their goal. In a controlled comparison, best-of-ten diffusion achieves mean gas exposure comparable to gas-guided A* (0.0476 versus 0.0455). A single diffusion proposal takes 41.7ms, compared with 72.3ms for gas-guided A*, although best-of-ten sequential sampling increases total runtime. Plain A* also reaches the same goal and remains the fastest and shortest-path method. Six matched Gazebo runs give mean robot-to-source errors of 0.39m for A* and 0.31m for diffusion.

</details>


### [306] [RTK-Vision PPO for Autonomous Micro UAV Recovery on an Airborne Carrier](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20629)
*Aashish Sahu,R Prasanth Kumar*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: RTK-vision-guided PPO reinforcement-learning framework enabling autonomous recovery of a micro UAV onto a moving carrier, with high simulation-to-hardware performance and strong outdoor success.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To enable a complete, reusable carrier-child deployment–recovery cycle by addressing the coupling of long-range rendezvous, close-range perception, carrier motion, aerodynamic interaction, and a discontinuous contact event.

Method: Integrate RTK-GNSS with a downward-facing camera and fiducial marker detector for alignment cues; train a PPO policy for the terminal recovery phase in a MuJoCo physics simulation with sensor noise, aerodynamic disturbance surrogate, and marker-latency randomization; transfer learned policy to hardware; PX4 handles stabilization; a deterministic safety gate governs descent.

Result: Simulation: PPO achieves 99.55% success over 2,000 terminal episodes vs 78.4% for a tuned PD baseline; median planar terminal error 6.62 cm. Outdoor trials: 13/14 successes (92.9%), covering near-region recovery and recovery after carrier translates away from release point.

Conclusion: Demonstrates a complete autonomous aerial deployment–and–recovery cycle, establishing a practical basis for reusable carrier–child operation in inspection, surveillance, and mobile-logistics applications.

Abstract: Autonomous recovery of a micro unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) onto a moving airborne carrier enables reusable deploy-mission-recover operation, but couples long-range rendezvous, close-range perception, carrier motion, aerodynamic interaction, and a discontinuous contact event. This paper presents an RTK-vision-guided reinforcement-learning framework in which a child UAV is physically transported by a larger carrier, takes off from the carrier while airborne, executes an independent sortie, returns to the carrier's current position, redocks, and subsequently descends with the carrier. Both vehicles carry RTK-GNSS, and the carrier continuously shares its navigation state with the child. Near the recovery deck, RTK remains active while a downward-facing camera with a fiducial marker detector provides marker-relative alignment cues. A proximal policy optimization (PPO) policy governing the terminal recovery phase is trained in a physics-based MuJoCo simulation environment with explicit sensor noise models, an aerodynamic disturbance surrogate, and marker-latency randomization, then transferred to hardware. PX4 retains low-level stabilization, and a deterministic safety gate authorizes descent independently of the learned policy. The PPO checkpoint achieves 99.55% success over 2,000 held-out randomized terminal episodes, compared with 78.4% for a tuned PD baseline under identical conditions, with a median planar terminal error of 6.62 cm. Across 14 outdoor trials, the full mission succeeds in 13 trials (92.9%), spanning both near-region recovery and recovery after the carrier translates away from the release point. The results demonstrate a complete autonomous aerial deployment-and-recovery cycle rather than an isolated landing maneuver, establishing a practical basis for reusable carrier-child operation in inspection, surveillance, and mobile-logistics applications.

</details>


### [307] [TraceFlow: Guiding Frozen Flow-Matching Robot Policies with Success and Failure Traces](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20646)
*Jiaxuan Zhang,Ruizhe Liu,Yu Zhang,Yanchao Yang*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: TraceFlow introduces a progress-aligned guidance field that modulates a frozen flow-matching action expert using success and failure traces stored in a TraceBank, using only terminal outcomes as labels. It leverages failed rollouts as negative evidence and shows performance gains on real-robot packing tasks and simulated tasks, with finite stacking gains and modest statistical significance in some settings.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To improve the robustness and sample-efficiency of vision-language-action policies by leveraging negative evidence from failed rollouts and a trace-based, terminal-outcome guided correction on a frozen policy.

Method: Compute per-step action densities for retrieved successful and failed rollouts; apply a bounded correction to a fixed flow-matching action expert based on a terminal outcome bit per rollout; maintain TraceBank of time-ordered traces with terminal labels, starting from target-task traces and later incorporating deployed rollouts.

Result: Real robot: order-based base 21/50; TraceFlow 39; one stacking round 47 without weight updates; wrong-sequence episodes reduced from 20 to 0. Simulation (per-suite settings): Sequence 78.92%→91.50%; Transferring 54.41%→62.00%; 26-task aggregate unchanged; Counting and Occlusion reduced by 1.12 and 1.42 points; LIBERO-Plus (Long) +1.27 points (p=0.0733). Stacking gains finite; all branches peak before round ten; bank's ratio predicts no retrieval allocation.

Conclusion: TraceFlow yields selective, finite gains by using failed rollouts as negative evidence and a trace-based correction to a frozen policy. Benefits occur in both real and simulated tasks, though gains depend on task settings and some statistical tests show modest significance.

Abstract: A vision-language-action (VLA) policy with a flow-matching action expert generates each action chunk (a short command sequence) by integrating a learned velocity field; once its weights are fixed, the success or failure of an earlier rollout cannot change the chunk generated now. Concurrent test-time methods give a frozen policy such an input from retrieved successes, a learned critic, a verifier, or a dynamics model, but none uses the robot's own failed rollouts as negative evidence with nothing but a terminal outcome bit. We introduce TraceFlow, a progress-aligned guidance field that turns the action densities of retrieved successful and failed rollouts into a bounded correction to a frozen flow-matching action expert, using one terminal outcome bit per rollout and no other label. Its TraceBank stores traces, time-ordered state-action records with a terminal label, starts from the target-task training traces, and later admits the deployed robot's own rollouts. On an ordered real-robot packing task the base completes 21 of 50 trials in order, TraceFlow 39, and one stacking round without any weight update 47, with wrong-sequence episodes falling from 20 to 0. In simulation the gain is selective: with per-suite selected settings, TraceFlow raises RoboMemArena Sequence from 78.92\% to 91.50\% task success and Transferring from 54.41\% to 62.00\% at stacking round 2, leaves the 26-task aggregate unchanged, lowers Counting and Occlusion by 1.12 and 1.42 points, and changes LIBERO-Plus (Long) by +1.27 points (p = 0.0733). Stacking gains are finite, every branch peaking before round ten, and the bank's success-to-failure ratio predicts no retrieval allocation.

</details>


### [308] [SkipVLA: Skipping VLA Steps with Classical Planning for Fast Robot Manipulation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20648)
*Kaivalya Agrawal,Md Ashiqur Rahman,Raymond A. Yeh,Zachary Kingston*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: Hybrid policy SkipVLA uses a classical motion planner for free-space motion and queries a frozen Vision-Language-Action (VLA) backbone only for contact-rich skills, predicting target poses for planned motions without extra demonstrations.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Address high test-time latency of Vision-Language-Action models on long-horizon tasks by delegating fast, collision-free motion planning to a classical planner and reserving VLA queries for semantically rich, contact-rich actions.

Method: Combine a pretrained, frozen VLA backbone with a classical motion planner. The planner provides collision-free trajectories; for each planned motion, the VLA predicts a target pose to guide the motion. The predictor is learned without additional demonstrations by leveraging representations learned by the large VLA; only VLA-derived targets are queried for contact-rich steps such as grasping and placing.

Result: Evaluated on 13 LIBERO tasks in simulation and 3 real pick-and-place tasks on a 6-DoF YAM arm. Achieved up to 2.5x faster task completion and significantly lower energy consumption while maintaining the same task success rate.

Conclusion: A practical hybrid approach that leverages fast planning for free-space motion and the semantic understanding of VLA for contact-rich actions can substantially improve speed and energy efficiency without sacrificing success rate across diverse tasks.

Abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models are a class of generalist robot policies that map camera images and language instructions directly to robot actions. While promising, these models remain slow at test time, particularly for long-horizon tasks that require many queries to the policy. Recent efforts reduce VLA latency by distilling smaller models, overlapping asynchronous action chunks, or pairing the VLA with a fast low-level policy, but still run a learned policy for the entire task. In contrast to VLA, classical motion planners quickly find collision-free motions, but require an explicit goal and have no semantic understanding of the task. In this work, we present SkipVLA, a hybrid policy that combines a pretrained VLA with a classical motion planner, using the planner for free-space motion and querying the VLA only for contact-rich skills such as grasping and placing. SkipVLA reuses the frozen vision-language backbone of the VLA to predict a target pose for each planned motion, and learns this predictor without additional demonstrations introduced into the system by using what was already learnt by the large VLA. We evaluate SkipVLA with three VLAs on 13 LIBERO tasks in simulation and three pick-and-place tasks on a physical 6-DoF YAM arm, demonstrating up to 2.5x faster task completion and significantly lower energy consumption while achieving the same task success rate.

</details>


### [309] [DexTouch-WM: Learning Action-Conditioned Tactile World Models from Human Touch for Dexterous Robot Manipulation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20649)
*Yan Qin,Yue Chen,Wenwei Lin,Shujia Liu,Chuqiao Lyu,Kailun Su,Chenze Yu,Ping Luo,Wenbo Ding,Tianxing Chen,Renjing Xu*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: Introduces DexTouch-WM, an action-conditioned world model trained with scalable human tactile data to predict future RGB and bilateral tactile dynamics, enabling synthetic trajectories and policy evaluation for dexterous manipulation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Dense tactile data for contact-rich dexterous manipulation is expensive to collect on real robots and often tied to embodiment-specific sensors. The work proposes leveraging scalable human tactile data with compatible sensing to transfer contact dynamics to robots.

Method: Use flexible piezoresistive arrays with a shared sensing layout on human and robot hands; retarget human motion to robot action space; couple a pretrained video world model with a lightweight tactile expert using anatomy-aware tactile tokens and aligned action conditioning; train with real-robot (5h) and large-scale human data (0–100h) supervision.

Result: With increasing human data while keeping robot supervision fixed, held-out robot-domain visual, geometric, and contact predictions improve substantially. The world model also serves as a surrogate environment for policy evaluation and a generator of synthetic trajectories for real-robot policy learning, demonstrating data-axis complementarity between human data and robot data.

Conclusion: Transferable contact dynamics can be learned when tactile observations and actions are aligned across humans and robots; scalable human tactile supervision effectively augments dexterous robot world models for better prediction and policy learning.

Abstract: Learning predictive models of contact-rich dexterous manipulation requires dense tactile interaction, but such data are costly to scale on real robots and remain tied to embodiment-specific sensors. We introduce DexTouch-WM, an action-conditioned world model that learns from scalable human touch to jointly predict future RGB observations and bilateral tactile dynamics. Our insight is that human and robot manipulation share transferable contact dynamics when their tactile observations and action spaces are made compatible. We deploy flexible piezoresistive arrays with a shared sensing layout on both human and dexterous robot hands, and retarget human motion into the robot action space so that human interaction can supervise the same dynamics model used for real-robot prediction. DexTouch-WM couples a pretrained video expert with a lightweight tactile expert using anatomy-aware tactile tokens and aligned action conditioning. In human-to-robot scaling experiments, we keep five hours of real-robot supervision fixed while increasing human interaction from 0 to 100 hours, and observe substantial improvements in held-out robot-domain visual, geometric, and contact prediction despite disjoint human and robot task sets. Beyond prediction, we evaluate the world models as surrogate environments for policy evaluation and as generators of synthetic trajectories for real-robot policy learning, showing that scalable human interaction provides a complementary data axis for learning dexterous robot world models.

</details>


### [310] [HIL-UMI: Bringing Human-in-the-Loop Post-Training of Vision-Language-Action Models to Universal Manipulation Interface](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20659)
*Zimu Han,Yiming Zeng,Jiyao Zhang,Zihao Zhao,Yuanfei Wang,Yixiang Jin,Shiqi Li,Shuangben Chen,Wei Huang,Ruodai Li,Hui Shen,Hao Dong*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: Policy-guided post-training for VLA models via HIL-UMI: interactive data collection and advantage refinement yield better manipulation performance with scalable, low-cost data collection.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: SFT on task-specific demonstrations suffers from limited coverage of out-of-distribution states and non-discriminative imitation objectives; interactive post-training helps but is often costly on real robots.

Method: During handheld UMI demonstrations, query the current policy on the same observation stream without executing; use Energy Score to detect and collect in out-of-distribution regions; a separate loop identifies segments with low online advantage to refine a progress-based advantage estimator; perform advantage-conditioned behavioral cloning on a balanced mix of base demonstrations and new policy data, decoupling collection from deployment.

Result: Four real-world tasks (long-horizon and precise manipulation) show consistent improvement over SFT; benefits from targeted data collection and advantage refinement; outperforms HG-DAgger on Clean Up Table with lower per-frame collection time.

Conclusion: HIL-UMI provides a scalable path for VLA post-training across operators and locations by maintaining policy-awareness while separating data collection from robot deployment.

Abstract: Large-scale vision-language-action (VLA) models provide powerful priors for robot manipulation, yet adapting them to a specific deployment remains challenging. Supervised fine-tuning (SFT) on task-specific demonstrations provides a step toward deployment, but faces two persistent limitations: static data provide limited coverage of out-of-distribution states, and standard imitation objectives do not distinguish progressing behavior from less useful data. Interactive post-training can address these limitations, but typically requires repeated policy execution and human intervention on a physical robot. We introduce HIL-UMI, a policy-guided Universal Manipulation Interface (UMI) framework for robot-free human-in-the-loop VLA post-training. During handheld UMI demonstrations, HIL-UMI queries the current policy on the same observation stream without executing its predictions. The Energy Score compares the human action trajectory with policy inference and triggers collection when their discrepancy indicates an out-of-distribution region. In a separate feedback loop, low online advantage predictions identify essential segments for refining a progress-based advantage estimator. The updated estimator then guides advantage-conditioned behavioral cloning using a balanced mixture of base demonstrations and new policy data. This design preserves the iterative and policy-aware nature of human-in-the-loop learning while decoupling data collection from robot deployment. Experiments on four real-world tasks spanning long-horizon and precise manipulation show that HIL-UMI achieves consistent improvement over SFT and benefits from both targeted collection and advantage refinement. Moreover, HIL-UMI outperforms HG-DAgger on Clean Up Table with lower per-frame collection time, suggesting a scalable path for VLA post-training across operators and locations.

</details>


### [311] [Learning Foresight without Explicit Trajectories for 3D Diffusion Policies](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20669)
*Zhongbo Zhang,Zaibin Zhang,Yifan Wang,Changbo Yan,Lijun Wang,Huchuan Lu*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: Movement Trend Guidance adds a compact latent forecast of interaction evolution to 3D diffusion policies, enabling future-oriented conditioning without explicit planning; yields notable accuracy gains with modest parameter overhead.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Fill the gap in diffusion-based manipulation policies where foresight into interaction direction is implicit; provide explicit but lightweight anticipatory conditioning to improve planning in manipulation tasks.

Method: From short observation history, learn a compact latent representation of interaction evolution; train with supervision from sparse future gripper states; at inference, use the latent as future-oriented conditioning alongside current observation; incorporate a gated FiLM branch at the UNet bottleneck; adds ~3.5% parameters to the base DP3 model.

Result: Consistent improvements across RoboTwin2.0, LIBERO-40, and DexArt datasets: 50-task RoboTwin2.0 mixed training: 62.8% vs. 56.1%; LIBERO-40: 71.93% vs. 37.08%; five real-robot tasks: 72.0% vs. 49.0%.

Conclusion: A diffusion policy benefits substantially from knowing the interaction's heading via a latent forecast, without requiring an explicit motion plan; preserves the original dense-action and receding-horizon formulation while delivering clear performance gains.

Abstract: 3D diffusion policies are strong at generating geometrically grounded actions from current observations, but successful manipulation requires not only knowing what motion is feasible now, but also anticipating where the interaction is heading. Existing policies largely leave such foresight to emerge implicitly from action learning. We introduce Movement Trend Guidance, a simple but effective way to provide this foresight without introducing an explicit plan. From a short observation history, the policy learns a compact latent representation of interaction evolution. During training, sparse future gripper states supervise this representation; at inference, only the latent is retained as future-oriented conditioning alongside the current observation. The latent provides global conditioning for action generation, while an additional gated FiLM branch is used only at the UNet bottleneck. Despite adding only 3.52% more parameters to DP3, our method preserves the original dense-action and receding-horizon formulation and consistently improves upon DP3 across RoboTwin2.0, LIBERO-40, and DexArt. It reaches 62.8% vs. 56.1% in 50-task RoboTwin2.0 mixed training, 71.93% vs. 37.08% on LIBERO-40, and 72.0% vs. 49.0% on five real-robot tasks. These results show that a diffusion policy can benefit substantially from knowing where an interaction is heading, without being told exactly where to move.

</details>


### [312] [MAGNETAR: Multipath-Guided Spatial Posteriors for Transmitter Pose Inference in the Upper Mid-Band](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20670)
*Haozhe Lei,Ruibin Chen,Yuhan Jiang,Ali Rasteh,Aditya Dhananjay,Sundeep Rangan*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: Grid-based joint posterior over transmitter position and heading using a conditioned 2D U-Net; outperforms position-only methods in multipath RF localization, with real-to-sim calibration and transfer to robotic measurements.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: In cluttered rooms, a single RF snapshot yields multiple plausible transmitter locations and headings due to multipath and directional antennas; a joint position-heading posterior can disambiguate candidates.

Method: MAGNETAR uses a shared 2D U-Net conditioned on each candidate heading to score a discretized position-heading grid. Five neural scorers jointly normalize scores into a joint posterior over position and heading, trained on real-to-sim-calibrated 10 GHz simulations with a small measured subset.

Result: Grid-based joint posteriors outperform parametric posteriors on held-out simulations. The heading-conditioned scorer transfers best to robotic measurements. Fusing joint posteriors provides improvements over fusing position-only marginals.

Conclusion: Joint grid-based posteriors over position and heading improve RF transmitter localization in multipath environments and transfer effectively to real robotic settings when trained with calibrated simulations and limited measurements.

Abstract: Robots that localize a radio transmitter need more than a point estimate: in cluttered rooms, one measurement is often consistent with several transmitter locations and, because upper-mid-band antennas are directional, several headings. We present MAGNETAR, which infers a joint posterior over planar transmitter position and heading from a single asynchronous radio-frequency (RF) multipath snapshot, represented by angle-of-arrival and signal-to-noise-ratio estimates, given the room layout and receiver pose. Among our five neural scorers, MAGNETAR adopts a shared 2D U-Net conditioned on each candidate heading, jointly normalizing scores over a discretized position-heading grid. Training uses real-to-sim-calibrated 10 GHz simulations and a small measured subset. Grid-based joint posteriors outperform parametric ones on held-out simulations, the heading-conditioned scorer transfers best to robotic measurements, and fusing joint posteriors improves on fusing position-only marginals.

</details>


### [313] [Towards Scaling Marine Perception with Synthetic Data](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20680)
*Haoyu Ma,Onur Bagoren,Anja Sheppard,Elias Fandi,Ashrith Edukulla,Tanner Aslan,Natasha Sieh,Jingyu Song,Katherine A. Skinner*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: Extends OceanSim with a Synthetic Data Generation pipeline to produce large, labeled, photorealistic underwater datasets for training and evaluating sim-to-real perception; evaluated on a sea urchin detection task; open-source code released.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Underwater ML is hindered by scarce labeled real-world data. Synthetic data can enable scalable, labeled datasets and enable controlled variation in appearance, scene structure, and sensor settings to study sim-to-real transfer.

Method: Integrate a Synthetic Data Generation (SDG) pipeline with the OceanSim (IsaacSim-based) underwater perception simulator to generate large, automatically labeled, photorealistic datasets with configurable scene appearance, structure, and sensor configurations. Evaluate the pipeline on a real-world sea urchin detection task and analyze how different synthetic scene variations affect sim-to-real performance; discuss limitations and future directions; release open-source code at GitHub.

Result: The pipeline produces large, automatically labeled datasets for underwater perception and enables systematic study of how synthetic scene variation influences sim-to-real transfer. Empirical results provide insights into the effectiveness and limitations of current rendering fidelity, scene diversity, and evaluation methods for sim-to-real generalization.

Conclusion: SDG-enabled OceanSim offers scalable underwater data generation for training and evaluating perception models, with demonstrated potential for sim-to-real transfer. The paper highlights current shortcomings in rendering fidelity and scene diversity and outlines future work to improve fidelity, diversify scenes, and strengthen sim-to-real evaluation; code is openly available at the provided GitHub repository.

Abstract: Scalable machine learning in challenging underwater environments is strongly limited by the lack of labeled real-world training data. This data is often expensive and laborious to gather, making large-scale real-world data challenging to gather and curate. However, simulated data can help close the gap, enabling many learning-based tasks for underwater perception. In this work, we extend OceanSim, an IsaacSim-based underwater perception simulator, with a Synthetic Data Generation (SDG) pipeline for training models to be used in underwater scenarios. The proposed pipeline enables users to generate large, automatically labeled, photorealistic datasets with configurable scene appearance, structure, and sensor settings. We evaluate the pipeline on a real-world sea urchin detection task and study how different forms of synthetic scene variation affect sim-to-real performance. Based on these experiments, we discuss findings on our results, main limitations of the current pipeline and identify future directions for improving underwater rendering fidelity, scene diversity, and the evaluation of sim-to-real generalization. The open-source code can be found at https://github.com/umfieldrobotics/OceanSim.

</details>


### [314] [Custom PX4 firmware for autonomous hybrid aerial-marine missions](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20691)
*Andrea Capuozzo,Fabio Ruggiero,Vincenzo Lippiello*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: A PX4 firmware extension enables hybrid aerial-amphibious navigation with manual and autonomous marine modes, integrated into the standard PX4 mission pipeline and QGroundControl, preserving flight safety while enabling unified planning for aerial and marine waypoints; simulations show stable surface navigation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: There is a need for versatile platforms that can map and monitor aquatic environments using both air and water surfaces. A unified software framework within PX4 would streamline mission planning and control for hybrid platforms.

Method: Extend PX4 firmware to add marine navigation modes (manual and autonomous) that integrate with the existing mission pipeline and QGroundControl. Maintain current flight safety mechanisms and enable differentiated aerial/marine waypoints within unified mission planning.

Result: The framework is implemented and validated in simulation, showing stable surface navigation under calm and wavy water conditions, while preserving existing flight functionalities.

Conclusion: The proposed framework enables seamless planning and execution of hybrid aerial-marine missions with distinct waypoint types, leveraging the PX4 ecosystem; simulations support feasibility, with potential for real-world testing.

Abstract: Mapping and monitoring aquatic environments can benefit from hybrid aerial-amphibious drones able to combine flight and water-surface navigation within the same mission. This paper presents a PX4 firmware extension for such platforms, introducing manual and autonomous marine navigation modes integrated with the standard PX4 mission pipeline and QGroundControl interface. The proposed framework preserves existing flight functionalities and safety mechanisms while enabling unified planning and execution of hybrid aerial-marine missions with differentiated aerial and marine waypoints. Simulated case studies validate the implementation and demonstrate stable surface navigation under calm and wavy conditions.

</details>


### [315] [HOPHY: A Hierarchical Hypergraph Representation for Off-Road Path and Mission Planning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20694)
*Pranay Meshram,Charuvahan Adhivarahan,Prithvi Poddar,Ehsan Tarkesh Esfahani,Chen Wang,Souma Chowdhury,Karthik Dantu*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: A hierarchical hypergraph-based terrain representation (HOPHY) enabling fast, near-optimal planning for off-road robotics across large maps, outperforming pixel grids and abstractions in speed and accuracy with real-robot validation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Repeated planning under changing terrain, agent types, and objectives; pixel-grid searches are expensive; semantic abstractions must preserve costs and connectivity.

Method: Construct GSNodes (geometrically connected semantic regions), Coarse Regions (connectivity-preserving critical regions), and typed hyperedges (terrain, agent, weather). Hyperedge intersections trigger selective state updates without hierarchy rebuild; evaluate on real maps; MRTA; hardware experiments.

Result: 100% planning success; median cost deviation <0.01% vs pixel A*; lower query/replanning latency vs pixel and abstraction baselines; MRTA computation reduced by 79x vs pixel A* and 7.2x vs fastest abstraction; mission makespan comparable to pixel A*; physical 1.5 km eight-task mission across mixed terrain with replanning.

Conclusion: HOPHY enables robust, scalable mission-level autonomy for disaster response and UGV operations, maintaining cost/connectivity under changing conditions and enabling significant compute savings; validated on real maps and hardware.

Abstract: Mission-level autonomy for disaster response, search and rescue, and tactical UGV operations requires repeated path and mission planning as terrain conditions, agent types, and objectives change. Pixel-grid search is costly for repeated kilometer-scale queries, while semantic abstractions must maintain valid costs and connectivity as conditions change. We present HOPHY (Hierarchical Off-Road Planning using Hypergraphs), a reusable hierarchical terrain representation that organizes map-scale terrain into geometrically connected semantic regions (GSNodes), connectivity-preserving critical regions (Coarse Regions), and typed hyperedges for terrain, agent, and weather context. Hyperedge intersections select affected regions and incident edges for state updates without rebuilding the hierarchy. Across real off-road maps spanning kilometer-scale areas, HOPHY achieves 100% planning success and less than 0.01% median cost deviation from the oracle (pixel A*), with substantially lower query and replanning latency than the evaluated pixel and abstraction baselines. Applied to a multi-robot task-allocation (MRTA) problem, these gains reduce total computation by 79x over pixel A* and 7.2x over the fastest abstraction baseline, with mission makespan comparable to pixel A*. Finally, we demonstrate HOPHY on a physical Clearpath Jackal that successfully executes a 1.5-km, eight-task mission across mixed-surface outdoor terrain and a blockage-triggered replanned route.

</details>


### [316] [MoWAM: Explicit Future Motion Prediction for Efficient World Action Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20709)
*Jiayu Wang,Bin Zhu,Yue Yu,Jingjing Chen*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: MoWAM eliminates high-cost future video generation in World Action Models by predicting explicit future motion with a Mixture-of-Transformer. This compact representation enables candidate-based inference-time scaling and maintains explicit future dynamics, yielding efficiency, robustness, and strong real-world performance.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To reduce the computational overhead of generating future videos in WAMs while preserving ability to reason about future dynamics and maintain robustness under distribution shifts.

Method: Train a Mixture-of-Transformer that learns future visual dynamics and jointly predicts motion and action. Replace full video reconstruction with a compact, explicit future motion representation. At inference, sample multiple motion–action candidates and use a motion-aware task-progress verifier to select among them, enabling video generation removal. The motion abstraction supports scalable inference without sacrificing dynamic awareness.

Result: On LIBERO, LIBERO-Plus, and real-world manipulation tasks, MoWAM achieves strong in-distribution performance, improved out-of-distribution robustness, and higher average real-world success than representative WAM baselines. Increasing the number of motion-action candidates improves performance, indicating explicit future motion as an effective basis for inference-time scaling.

Conclusion: Explicit future motion provides an efficient, scalable basis for WAM-based policy learning, matching or exceeding baseline performance while reducing inference-time cost. The approach offers improved robustness to distribution shifts and benefits from broader exploration of motion-action candidates; future work could refine motion abstractions and extend to additional modalities and tasks.

Abstract: World Action Models (WAMs) improve robot policy learning by incorporating future dynamics, yet explicitly generating future videos at inference introduces substantial computational overhead. Removing future generation improves efficiency, but leaves future dynamics only implicitly encoded in observation features, which can limit robustness under distribution shifts. We propose MoWAM, an efficient WAM that replaces future video generation with explicit future motion prediction. Instead of reconstructing the complete future scene, MoWAM models structured robot motion as a compact abstraction of the future, capturing how the robot is expected to evolve under the current scene and interaction constraints. A Mixture-of-Transformer architecture learns future visual dynamics during training while jointly predicting motion and action, allowing video generation to be removed entirely at inference while retaining an explicit representation of the future. The compact motion representation further enables efficient inference-time scaling by sampling multiple candidates of motion and action pairs and selecting among them with a motion-aware task-progress verifier. Experiments on LIBERO, LIBERO-Plus, and real-world manipulation tasks demonstrate that MoWAM achieves strong in-distribution performance, improved out-of-distribution robustness, and higher average real-world success than representative WAM baselines. In addition, performance improves as more candidates are explored, demonstrating that explicit future motion provides an effective and efficient basis for inference-time scaling.

</details>


### [317] [Underwater Visual Target Tracking with Target-Specific Depth Estimation and Adaptive Model-Fusion Predictive Control](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20731)
*Yuheng Zhou,Haiyang Cheng,Yanqi Feng,Pangkit Fong,Mei Xuan Lee,Marcus Gee,Chongrong Fang,Jianping He*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: Stereo visual-servoing for underwater AUVs: robust 3D state estimation via target-depth extraction and Kalman filtering, plus yaw-translation decoupled control with adaptive model-fusion MPC; validated by simulations and real-world experiments with superior performance.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Underwater vision tracking is hindered by unreliable depth measurements and unknown target motion, necessitating robust perception and real-time, adaptable control.

Method: Perception: construct a target-depth mask from color, disparity, and temporal cues; apply target-specific depth extraction and Kalman filtering to estimate a stable 3D relative state, with depth and image center filtered separately. Control: decouple yaw regulation from translational control to enable real-time translational MPC; translational controller uses adaptive model-fusion predictive control, combining constant-velocity and zero-velocity target models; weights updated from historical prediction errors; commands respect actuation, following-distance, and field-of-view constraints.

Result: Simulations and real-world experiments validate the framework, showing better performance than existing frameworks.

Conclusion: A robust stereo visual-servoing framework for AUVs that handles unreliable depth and varying target motion, enabling real-time decoupled yaw and translational control with adaptive model fusion and validated improvements.

Abstract: Vision-based underwater target tracking is challenged by unreliable depth measurements and unknown target motion. This paper proposes a stereo visual-servoing framework for an autonomous underwater vehicle (AUV). For perception, the framework derives a stable 3D relative state from stereo images through target-specific depth extraction and Kalman filtering. It constructs a target-depth mask from color, disparity, and temporal cues to select reliable target pixels, and then filters the resulting depth measurement and detected image center separately. For control, the framework decouples yaw regulation from translational control, avoiding computationally expensive coupled multi-DOF optimization and enabling real-time translational MPC. The translational controller employs adaptive model-fusion predictive control, combining constant-velocity and zero-velocity target models to accommodate different target-motion patterns. It updates the model weights using historical prediction errors and computes translational commands subject to actuation, following-distance, and field-of-view constraints. Through simulations and real-world experiments, we validate the effectiveness of the proposed framework and show it has better performance than existing frameworks.

</details>


### [318] [MILER: Semantic Mid-Level Representation for Sim-to-Real Reinforcement Learning in Unstructured Autonomous Driving](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20747)
*Thomas Steinecker,Denis Trescher,Alexander Bienemann,Thorsten Luettel,Mirko Maehlisch*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: MILERA demonstrates zero-shot sim-to-real transfer for unstructured autonomous driving via a semantic mid-level representation (MLR) simulator and trajectory-alignment, enabling end-to-end RL policies trained offline to operate on real vehicles with BEVFusion-aligned perception; validated on real tracks with 17.3 km across two vehicles on a 3.0 km track using on-board Jetson AGX Orin.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Overcome the sim-to-real gap in end-to-end RL for autonomous driving in unstructured environments by bridging perception and control through a consistent semantic representation and a trajectory-alignment deployment strategy.

Method: Train an RL policy offline in a custom MLR simulator; apply policy outputs to a bicycle model during training; at deployment, process camera/LiDAR with BEVFusion to produce a BEV semantic representation aligned with MLR; use a trajectory-alignment strategy rather than direct actuation to the real vehicle; deploy on Jetson AGX Orin.

Result: Extensive real-world evaluation on a challenging test track with obstacles, hairpin curves, and speeds up to 33.6 km/h; drove 17.3 km in 3.0 km track with two vehicles, without human intervention.

Conclusion: Zero-shot sim-to-real transfer of both perception and control is feasible for unstructured driving by combining MLR-based offline RL with perception–control alignment; practical, edge-deployable pipeline.

Abstract: Reinforcement learning constitutes a promising approach owing to its potential for superhuman performance and self-learned policies. However, its application to real-world autonomous driving remains scarce, particularly in unstructured environments, because of the challenges associated with sim-to-real transfer for unstructured environments. In this work, we present MILER, an end-to-end policy framework with zero-shot sim-to-real transfer. During offline training, we employ a custom semantic mid-level representation (MLR) simulator and train the policy network using reinforcement learning, with its control outputs applied directly to a bicycle model. During deployment on the real vehicle, camera and LiDAR data are processed by BEVFusion to generate a semantic bird's-eye-view representation consistent with that of the MLR simulator. The actions generated by the policy network are not applied directly to the real vehicle. Instead, we employ a trajectory-alignment strategy that enables zero-shot sim-to-real transfer of both perception and control. We extensively evaluate the proposed framework on a diverse test track comprising numerous challenges, including various obstacles, hairpin curves, velocities of up to 33.6 km/h, and off-road sections. In total, we drove 17.3 km with two different vehicles on a 3.0 km test track without human intervention, thereby demonstrating the effectiveness of our approach. Furthermore, the entire software stack runs on a Jetson AGX Orin.

</details>


### [319] [OPTED: On-Policy Fine-Tuning for End-to-End Driving using a Render-Free Teacher](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20756)
*Damiano Da Col,Maximilian Igl,Peter Karkus,Kashyap Chitta,Boris Ivanovic,Marco Pavone,Konrad Schindler,Christos Sakaridis*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: A privileged teacher-student framework OPTED for end-to-end driving; RL-trained teacher supervises a frozen student during post-training, achieving significant driving score gains with far fewer simulator interactions.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Diminishing returns from scaling pre-training data and safety concerns with closed-loop deployment; need efficient, data-efficient post-training that stays close to human priors.

Method: Train a privileged teacher with reinforcement learning on vectorized inputs (HD-map and bounding boxes). The teacher provides supervision to a pre-trained student during closed-loop post-training. Applied to two camera-based models (TransFuser and VaVAM), fine-tuning in AlpaSim with neural reconstructions (3DGS) of real driving logs.

Result: Driving scores improve by 1.6x and 9.5x for the two models. OPTED matches closed-loop RL performance with approximately three orders of magnitude fewer simulator interactions than direct RL post-training and stays closer to the human prior.

Conclusion: OPTED decouples RL from post-training to enable efficient, safer fine-tuning of end-to-end driving policies across camera-based models, with strong data efficiency and alignment to human behavior.

Abstract: As scaling pre-training data alone yields diminishing returns, post-training is becoming increasingly important across physical AI domains such as autonomous driving. End-to-end driving policies are pre-trained in open loop with behavior cloning on human demonstrations. However, compounding errors during closed-loop deployment can take the vehicle outside the training data distribution, increasing the risk of safety-critical incidents. Closed-loop post-training can mitigate this risk but requires costly simulation for sensor-based policies. We propose OPTED (on-policy fine-tuning for end-to-end driving) which decouples reinforcement learning from the post-training of the end-to-end policy: a privileged teacher is trained using RL on vectorized inputs (HD-map and bounding boxes). This teacher then provides supervision to the pre-trained student during closed-loop post-training. We apply OPTED to two camera-based models, TransFuser and VaVAM, and fine-tune them in AlpaSim, using neural reconstructions (3DGS) of real driving logs. Driving scores increase by factors of 1.6$\times$ and 9.5$\times$, respectively. In controlled experiments OPTED matches closed-loop performance with approximately three orders of magnitude fewer simulator interactions than direct RL post-training, while staying closer to the human prior. Project page: https://01dami23.github.io/opted/

</details>


### [320] [Agile-WAM: An Agile Tactile World Action Model for Contact-Rich Robot Control](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20761)
*Hanchu Zhou,Brendan Lynch,Raman Goyal,Dechen Gao,Begum Kasap,Boqi Zhao,Junshan Zhang*

Main category: cs.RO
