TL;DR: TARO is an agile tactile World Action Model that uses a shared visual-tactile latent and multi-horizon prediction to enable fast, robust contact-rich robot control, outperforming baselines with low inference latency.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Tactile WAMs often rely on large pretrained backbones that hinder inference efficiency and deployment flexibility; an lightweight, multimodal, high-frequency model is needed for real-world control.

Method: Encode visual and tactile observations into a common latent space; use a vision-tactile-to-action flow-matching process to jointly predict latent action chunks and future visual/tactile latents. Employ multi-horizon prediction: predict visual latent at a larger temporal offset and tactile latent in the next frame to capture coarse dynamics and fine contact changes.

Result: Outperforms the strongest baseline in success rate across 9 simulated and 5 real-world tasks. In 5 real-world experiments, achieves a 29.4% relative gain in success and an inference latency of 11.9 ms.

Conclusion: Demonstrates that multimodal WAMs can be designed with agile architectures to support precise, high-frequency control on both simulation and real-world tasks.

Abstract: World Action Models (WAMs) advance beyond conventional visuomotor policies by jointly predicting future world states and robot actions, enabling the policy to learn physical dynamics that support effective control. However, recent tactile WAMs often rely on large-scale pretrained generative backbones to capture contact-rich physical dynamics, which limit their inference efficiency and flexible deployment. In this paper, we present \ABBR{}, an agile tactile World Action Model for contact-rich robot control. \ABBR{} encodes visual and tactile observations into a shared latent that serves as the source of a direct vision-tactile-to-action flow-matching process, which can jointly generate latent representations of action chunks and future visual/tactile latents. A key observation is that vision and tactile signals evolve at inherently different timescales: adjacent visual frames are often highly similar, whereas tactile signals can change abruptly upon contact. We therefore introduce multi-horizon multimodal prediction in \ABBR{}, which provides supervision for visual latent at a larger temporal offset while predicting the tactile latent in the next frame to capture fine-grained contact dynamics. Across nine simulated and five real-world contact-rich manipulation tasks, \ABBR{} demonstrates strong and robust performance, outperforming the strongest baseline in success rate while maintaining low inference latency. In particular, in five real-world experiments, \ABBR{} yields a relative gain of $\textbf{29.4\%}$ in overall success rates while achieving inference latency of $\textbf{11.9 ms}$. These results demonstrate that multimodal WAM can be achieved with an agile architecture suitable for precise and high-frequency robot control. More details are available on our project page: https://hanchuzhou.github.io/TARO_project_page/.

</details>


### [321] [Coding Agents with an Obstacle-Aware Harness for Safe Robot Manipulation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20822)
*Bingxin Xu,Yuzhang Shang,Zhen Dong,Emilio Ferrara*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: SafeHarness improves safety compliance for coding agents in robot manipulation by obstacle-aware route planning and contact execution, achieving high task success and collision avoidance.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The study asks whether coding agents can satisfy explicit safety constraints in manipulation tasks and identifies planning as the source of safety failure, aiming to close the gap with obstacle-aware strategies.

Method: Decompose manipulation into route planning and contact execution. Introduce obstacle-grounded routing using bounding boxes to generate and verify candidate routes with replanning. Implement obstacle-aware contact execution to choose contact points that avoid the obstacle. Two harnesses guide planning and contact to respect safety constraints.

Result: 71.9% task success and 87.5% collision avoidance, surpassing previous SOTA by 6.5% and 27.0% respectively; improvements of 2.3x and 1.5x compared to the same agent without harnesses.

Conclusion: Obstacle-aware harnesses enable coding agents to prioritize safety constraints, improving safety without sacrificing task success; the approach highlights a practical path to safer grounding of language-model-based controllers in manipulation tasks.

Abstract: Coding agents have emerged as a promising paradigm for robot manipulation: a language model writes the robot controller as a program, and agents built in this way now operate robots without robot-specific training.Whether this paradigm is also safe, however, has not been asked. We evaluate coding agent under a safety constraint, where each task pairs a manipulation goal with an obstacle the robot must not touch. The agent pursues the goal but collides with the obstacle in most cases, treating task completion as its sole objective while neglecting safety. The agent reasons about the obstacle in its traces, and the prompt already forbids touching it, so neither perception nor instruction is at fault; the fault lies in the planning, where the stated constraint never becomes a priority. By decomposing manipulation into a route phase and a contact-rich moment, we locate the source of the failure. Along the route, the model cannot prioritize the safety constraint, having no notion of a clearing route and none of replanning once a chosen route becomes infeasible. At the contact, it is unaware that contact execution is bounded by the same constraint. To close this gap, we present SafeHarness, which equips the model with two obstacle-aware harnesses that enable it to prioritize the safety constraint. Obstacle-aware route planning grounds the objects as bounding boxes and draws candidate routes over them as sequences of waypoints. The agent then plans a route in advance, verifies it, replans when necessary, and only then executes it. Obstacle-aware contact execution instead selects the contact position so that the contact itself avoids the obstacle. SafeHarness attains 71.9% task success and 87.5% collision avoidance, surpassing the previous SOTA by 6.5% and 27.0%, respectively. These results are $2.3\times$ and $1.5\times$ those of the same agent without harnesses.

</details>


### [322] [GeoAAC: Geometry-Based Adaptive Action Chunking from Denoising Trajectories in VLA Policies](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20776)
*Xin Chen,Sen Chen,Yujuan Ding,Jian Liu,Guoqing Wang,Wei Ye,Heng Tao Shen,Yi Bin*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: GeoAAC introduces a geometry-based, training-free adaptive action chunking for flow-based Vision-Language-Action policies. By analyzing the prefix geometry of Flow Matching denoising trajectories, it estimates predictive reliability to adapt the action horizon during a single generation, improving performance over fixed horizons and existing adaptive methods.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Fixed action horizons fail to match varying task-stage requirements for action continuity, precision, and closed-loop control. There is a need for horizon adaptation based on reliability estimates derived from the policy’s own trajectory information.

Method: Use prefix-wise geometry of Flow Matching denoising trajectories to build a horizon-wise geometric profile. This profile guides an adaptive action horizon selection during a single generation without additional training, selecting the horizon based on predicted uncertainty.

Result: Empirical evaluation on GR00T N1.5 and π0.5 across LIBERO, LIBERO-Pro, RoboCasa365, and real-world manipulation tasks shows consistent improvements over fixed-horizon baselines and existing adaptive methods, with up to 8.7 percentage points gain in simulation and the real-world success rate increasing from 53.3% to 74.4%.

Conclusion: GeoAAC provides a simple, training-free mechanism to adapt action horizons in flow-based VLA policies by leveraging the geometry of denoising trajectories to assess reliability, yielding robust performance gains across simulated and real-world tasks.

Abstract: Action chunking is widely used for action generation and execution in Vision-Language-Action (VLA) policies, yet existing approaches commonly use a fixed action horizon. During a rollout, different task stages may require different levels of action continuity, control precision, and closed-loop feedback, making a fixed horizon unable to accommodate changing control requirements. We propose \textbf{GeoAAC}, a geometry-based adaptive action chunking method for flow-based VLA policies that adjusts the action horizon according to the reliability of the current action prediction. We show that the geometry of Flow Matching denoising trajectories provides process-level information for characterizing prediction reliability, with geometric variation across action prefixes remaining positively correlated with predictive uncertainty. GeoAAC uses this prefix-wise geometry to construct a horizon-wise geometric profile and adaptively determine the action horizon from a single generation without additional training. Experiments with GR00T N1.5 and π0.5 on LIBERO, LIBERO-Pro, RoboCasa365, and real-world manipulation tasks show consistent improvements over fixed-action-horizon baselines and existing adaptive methods, including up to 8.7 percentage points in simulation and an increase in average real-world success rate from 53.3\% to 74.4\%.

</details>


### [323] [StageGuard: Learning Stage Transitions for Long-Horizon Robot Tasks via Agentic Distillation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20791)
*Jinbang Huang,Yuanzhao Hu,Zhiyuan Li,Ran Qi,Yixin Xiao,Yangzheng Wu,Tengyue Ba,Zhanguang Zhang,Yingxue Zhang*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: StageGuard distills teacher reasoning into a lightweight vision-language model to improve stage-transition decisions in hierarchical robot control, enabling accurate predictions and efficient online monitoring.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Determining when to terminate a current skill and advance to the next subtask is difficult in real-world robotics. Pre-designed completion checkers are hard to obtain; while large vision-language models can reason, their decision boundaries do not align with task completion and they incur latency, hindering real-time monitoring.

Method: Leverage teacher-model reasoning and demonstration trajectories to generate structured explanations of subtask completion and policy switching. Train a lightweight student VLM to produce compact self-explanations, which are used for supervised fine-tuning.

Result: StageGuard achieves substantial improvements in stage-transition prediction on two benchmarks and enhances closed-loop task success when integrated into hierarchical control on BEHAVIOR-1K, with additional validation on real robots, while enabling efficient online monitoring.

Conclusion: StageGuard effectively distills task-relevant reasoning into a compact, explainable model to improve stage-transition decisions, balancing accuracy and latency for real-time robotic monitoring and control.

Abstract: Hierarchical planning frameworks combine skills from multiple robot control policies for long-horizon task execution, where determining when to terminate the current skill and advance to the next subtask is essential. Existing approaches often rely on pre-designed completion signal checkers that are hard to obtain in real-world execution. Large-scale vision-language models (VLMs) offer strong reasoning capabilities, but their decision boundaries are not inherently aligned with task completion criteria, while cloud deployment and lengthy reasoning introduce substantial latency, limiting real-time monitoring. We propose StageGuard, an agentic distillation framework for accurate and efficient stage-transition decisions. StageGuard combines teacher-model reasoning with demonstration trajectories to generate structured explanations of subtask completion and policy switching. A lightweight student VLM uses these explanations to generate compact self-explanations, which are used for supervised fine-tuning. We evaluate stage-transition prediction on trajectories from two benchmarks and assess closed-loop task success through integration into hierarchical robot control on BEHAVIOR-1K, with further validation on real robots. Results show substantial improvements in stage-transition prediction while supporting efficient online monitoring.

</details>


### [324] [Workspace Models: Lightweight Robotic Memory via Saliency-Driven Supervision](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20820)
*Nitish Dashora,Douglas Chen,Idan Shenfeld,John Marangola,Pulkit Agrawal,Max Simchowitz*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: A method to learn a compact latent memory (workspace token) via train-time VLM guidance, enabling deployment-time policy observations without in-loop VLM queries, improving memory-intensive manipulation tasks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Policies struggle with long-term histories and generic memory; in-the-loop VLM use is costly and can induce spurious correlations. A lightweight, train-time distilled memory can improve performance and efficiency.

Method: Use a vision-language model (VLM) at training to identify task-relevant current and historical information; distill this into a lightweight latent representation called the workspace token via a set-reconstruction decoder loss; during deployment, replace observations with the workspace token and avoid VLM querying.

Result: In both simulation and hardware, the workspace token matches or outperforms full-history or VLM-in-the-loop baselines, while being more lightweight; it enables memory-intensive tasks with no VLM reasoning in deployment.

Conclusion: Training-time distillation yields a compact, efficient, and effective memory representation (workspace token) that preserves task-relevant information for policy execution and improves performance over naive history compression.

Abstract: Complex robotic manipulation tasks frequently require a long-term memory of past events and actions. As conditioning on full histories renders policies prone to spurious correlations and degrades performance, many approaches to policy memory involve compressing historical information through expensive VLM queries in-the-loop to process only task-salient information. In this paper, we propose an alternative approach in which computationally intensive VLM queries are made during train-time to learn a lightweight latent memory that can be efficiently queried at deployment time. Our representation, which we call the \textbf{workspace token}, is trained by (1) using a VLM to identify current and historical information necessary for completing a task, then (2) distilling these into the workspace token using a set-reconstruction decoder loss. In both simulation and hardware, we show that the workspace token can be used as a drop-in replacement for observations during deployment, enabling policies to solve memory-intensive tasks without the need for VLM reasoning in-the-loop. Interestingly, we found that workspace tokens are not only more lightweight but also lead to better policy performance.

</details>


<div id='cs.AI'></div>

# cs.AI [[Back]](#toc)

### [325] [Regularized Emphatic Temporal-Difference Learning: Stability under Constant Stepsizes](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.19170)
*Xingguo Chen,Zhaohui Wu,Jinguo Ye,Chao Li,Shangdong Yang,Guang Yang,Skylar Liang,Wenhao Wang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: RETD offers a normalization-based post-shock repair for ETD that preserves the emphatic trace while stabilizing constant-stepsize off-policy dynamics and recovering ETD fixed points, with convergence guarantees and large-scale validation; it does not reduce follow-on-trace variance.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Address instability and unpredictable dynamics of constant-stepsize off-policy temporal-difference learning under ETD, and separate true contraction properties of the mean map from the sampled product dynamics.

Method: Construct an ergodic two-state counterexample to separate mean-map contraction from sampling dynamics; apply regenerative-cycle analysis; design RETD with a leaky scalar state storing the emphatic TD signal, a normalized post-shock repair, and delayed corrections; derive theoretical results (almost-sure convergence under diminishing steps; moment contraction under conditional constant steps) and analyze fixed-point relationships; perform large-scale experiments (10,000 runs) on canonical problems including Baird’s counterexample.

Result: ETD’s mean map contracts while the sampled product can have a positive top Lyapunov exponent; RETD yields negative exponents on the two-state construction and on a Baird point; RETD fixed point equals an affine shift of ETD’s, and ETD fixed point is recovered exactly by one- or two-regularization READOUTS; convergence results established; empirical validation confirms separation of effects, fixed-point recovery, nonmonotone stability, and task dependence; RETD alters post-shock dynamics but does not reduce the shared follow-on-trace variance.

Conclusion: RETD provides a theoretically grounded, normalization-based repair that stabilizes constant-stepsize off-policy TD without altering the fundamental trace structure, achieving fixed-point recovery and convergence guarantees; however, it does not mitigate follow-on-trace variance, indicating room for variance-reduction strategies or alternative regularizations.

Abstract: Emphatic temporal-difference learning (ETD) stabilizes the expected off-policy TD update and changes its projection geometry, but neither property determines constant-stepsize sampled dynamics. We construct an ergodic two-state counterexample in which the ETD mean map contracts while the sampled product has a positive top Lyapunov exponent. Regenerative-cycle analysis separates this sign from the infinite variance of the follow-on trace. We introduce regularized emphatic TD (RETD), a normalized first-order post-shock repair that leaves the trace and importance ratios unchanged, stores the emphatic TD signal in a leaky scalar state, and releases a delayed correction. RETD's raw equilibrium is an affine shift of the ETD equilibrium; single- and two-regularization readouts recover the ETD fixed point exactly. We prove almost-sure convergence for harmonic diminishing stepsizes and a conditional constant-stepsize moment-contraction result from a Markovian random-product bound. RETD has certified negative exponents on the two-state construction and one Baird point, whereas the positive Baird ETD sign remains numerical. Paired 10,000-run experiments validate both separations, fixed-point recovery, a nonmonotone stability region, and task dependence. RETD changes post-shock dynamics; it does not reduce the shared follow-on-trace variance.

</details>


### [326] [BioPhys-Bridge: A Benchmark for Interdisciplinary Scientific Reasoning in Physics-Grounded Biological Research](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.19180)
*Qingyang Xu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: BioPhys-Bridge is a new evidence-grounded benchmark for biophysics literature, featuring 500 cases with 1,517 tasks, strict quality gates, and multi-domain coverage; initial baselines show modest evidence-ID F1 scores (~0.36), and the dataset aims to evaluate attribution, faithfulness, and multi-step RAG/QA reasoning with open-source release.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Addresses the need for faithful, evidence-grounded reasoning in interdisciplinary biophysics, where answers hinge on source data, quantitative models, and mechanisms; creates a standardized evaluation platform for grounding, attribution, and mitigating hallucinations in LMs.

Method: Curated collection of cases with evidence blocks, stable evidence IDs, quantitative values and units, equations, assumptions, mechanisms, and next-step decisions; tasks for QA and retrieval-augmented generation; strict quality gates for schema, evidence-integrity, quantitative-grounding, licensing, duplicates, and unit normalization; domain expert review for 81 cases; 500 cases total, 1,517 agent-facing tasks across six biological domains and nine physical model families (three sparse for future expansion); initial release with GitHub and HuggingFace hosting.

Result: Baseline results show DeepSeek-V4-Flash achieves highest evidence-ID F1 of 0.360, followed by Qwen3.7-Max at 0.316 and GPT-4o-mini at 0.294; dataset usable for evaluating attribution, faithfulness, hallucination reduction, and biological experiment design in multi-step reasoning tasks; future expansions planned.

Conclusion: BioPhys-Bridge provides a rigorous, interdisciplinary benchmark for grounding scientific reasoning in biophysics, enabling evaluation of multi-step reasoning, attribution, and reduction of hallucinations. The authors plan to scale size/complexity and broaden evaluations, with code/data publicly available.

Abstract: Language models face unique challenges in analyzing interdisciplinary scientific research literature. In biophysics research, faithful answers require grounding observed data in source evidence, interpreting it through a quantitative physics model, and linking it to a biological mechanism. To address this challenge, we introduce BioPhys-Bridge, a novel benchmark dataset for evidence-grounded scientific reasoning over biophysical literature. Each case contains evidence blocks, stable evidence IDs, quantitative values, units, equations, assumptions, mechanisms, and next decisions as grounding targets for question answering (QA) and retrieval-augmented generation (RAG). The initial release contains 500 cases, 1,517 agent-facing tasks, and covers six biological domains and nine physical model families, including three sparse families reserved for future expansion. We enforce strict quality gates for all cases in schema, evidence-integrity, quantitative-grounding, source-license, duplicate, unit-normalization, with domain expert review and annotation for 81 cases. Preliminary evaluations show that DeepSeek-V4-Flash obtain the highest evidence-ID $F_1$ score (0.360), followed by Qwen3.7-Max (0.316) and GPT-4o-mini (0.294). BioPhys-Bridge is an interdisciplinary benchmark for evaluating attribution, faithfulness, hallucination reduction, and biological experiment design with complex, multi-step scientific reasoning. Future works will increase the size and complexity of the dataset and perform comprehensive evaluations. Code and data are available in the GitHub repository and on Hugging Face.

</details>


### [327] [What Do We Expect from LLMs? Mapping the Design of LLM Benchmarks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.19182)
*Chao Wang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Large-scale meta-analysis of 14,767 arXiv papers (2022–2026) on evaluation benchmarks for LLMs reveals a shift toward action, interaction, and professional use, with uneven model-participation in scoring and materials, raising concerns about whether expanding evaluation yields independent evidence or reifies model biases.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To understand how evaluation benchmarks reflect and shape capability expectations for LLMs, and whether expanding benchmarks improves objectivity or merely reproduces model preferences and blind spots.

Method: Staged screening of arXiv submissions followed by automated full-text coding to classify target systems and domains, evaluation materials and conditions, and scoring mechanisms; analysis of model participation in scoring and material generation.

Result: Benchmark design elements increasingly combine established and new features; emphasis on action/interaction/professional tasks; model participation in scoring (LLM-based) grows across agent and non-agent groups, while model-generated materials do not show sustained growth; uneven adoption across cohorts.

Conclusion: Expanding evaluation benchmarks illuminates capability expectations but risks embedding models’ preferences; highlights need for diverse, critical benchmarks and careful interpretation of evaluation as evidence of true capability.

Abstract: Benchmarks are central to how progress in large language models (LLMs) is assessed and communicated. Yet model rankings alone reveal little about how evaluation requirements themselves are changing. The expanding variety of benchmarks offers another perspective: what researchers expect LLMs to do, and what they count as successful performance. We systematically map 14,767 papers introducing or updating evaluation resources from arXiv submissions between January 2022 and August 2026. Using staged screening and automated full-text coding, we examine changes in target systems and domains, evaluation materials and conditions, and scoring mechanisms. The collection shows growing emphasis on action, interaction, and professional applications, while established and newer design elements frequently coexist. Model participation also develops unevenly: LLM-based scoring grows within both agent and non-agent groups, whereas model-generated materials show no comparable sustained increase in recent cohorts. These findings illuminate how public research translates capability expectations into concrete tests and criteria for success. As AI participates in constructing tests, performing tasks, and judging responses, they also raise a question: does expanding evaluation provide more independent evidence, or risk reproducing the preferences and blind spots of its participating models?

</details>


### [328] [Position: It is Time to Virtualize Foundation Models with a Self-evolving Operating System Layer](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.19203)
*Suparna Bhattacharya,Tarun Kumar,Cong Xu,Satish Kumar Mopur,Jiahao Li,Ashish Mishra,Aalap Tripathy,Annmary Justine Koomthanam,Martin Foltin,Ian Foster*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Proposes Foundation Model Operating System (FMOS): a system layer that virtualizes foundation model interactions to provide portable, governed, scalable FM usage, akin to an OS/VM abstraction.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Today's stacks for AI models are fragmented; even with protocols like MCP/A2A, runtime state, memory, budgets, and guardrails are embedded within each framework, making behavior non-portable and governance brittle. A unified FMOS would virtualize FM interactions, giving applications the illusion of dedicated, trustworthy FM instances with effectively unbounded capabilities.

Method: Conceptual design of FMOS: an orchestrator that manages memory across tiers, model selection and resource allocation, acceptance/verification, and policy enforcement. It employs adaptive intervention akin to fast (intuition) and slow (deliberation) thinking, updating policies based on operational experience to balance interference with inference.

Result: A conceptual architectural proposal (no empirical results). Defines components and interaction patterns for memory management, model selection, resource allocation, verification, and policy enforcement, arguing for portability, safety, and scalability of FM-enabled applications.

Conclusion: FMOS is a necessary system-layer abstraction to unify and scale foundation-model deployments, enabling effectively unbounded capabilities with governance. It lays out a roadmap for implementing and evaluating a working FMOS in future work.

Abstract: AI applications have shifted from single, monolithic foundation models (FM) to compound agentic systems. Yet today's stacks remain fragmented: even as protocols (e.g., MCP, A2A) ease tool/agent connectivity, each framework embeds an implicit runtime for state, memory, budgets, and guardrails, making behavior non-portable and governance brittle. It mirrors computing before operating systems, when every program re-implemented basic services. This position paper argues that the field now needs a Foundation Model Operating System (FMOS) -- a system layer that virtualizes FM interactions analogous to how virtual machines abstract physical hardware, giving applications the illusion of dedicated, trustworthy FM instances with effectively unbounded capabilities. Internally, the FMOS orchestrates knowledge across memory tiers, model selection and resource allocation, and verification and policy enforcement. Like the human brain switching between fast intuition and slow deliberation, the FMOS learns when to intervene and when to let inference proceed directly and continuously adapting its policies based on operational experience.

</details>


### [329] [What Do Current Systematic Generalization Tasks Miss? A Reasoning-Centered Analysis](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.19212)
*Chengwen Qi,Deheng Ye,Yatao Bian*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: TranSGrid is a reasoning-centric testbed for systematic generalization that combines deductive, inductive, and abductive reasoning; seven Transformers perform far worse on TranSGrid than on standard held-out tests, and simplifications that reduce inductive or abductive demands restore performance to typical test-set levels, indicating the need for tasks that require all three reasoning forms.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing evaluation setups rely on simplifications (near-linear action composition, productivity-based tests, action-explicit goals) that mask the full demands of systematic generalization. A task that jointly requires deduction, induction, and abduction is needed to rigorously assess this capability.

Method: Introduce TranSGrid, a unified testbed that integrates deductive, inductive, and abductive reasoning. Evaluate seven Transformer models on 4,800 TranSGrid instances. Create two variant conditions that isolate inductive and abductive demands by making actions nearly linear or goals explicit, respectively, and compare performance.

Result: On the full TranSGrid, the largest model achieves 79.6% on a held-out test set, but only 55.3% on TranSGrid and 15.8% on the hardest subset. The performance gap persists across training lengths, indicating productivity alone does not capture systematic generalization. When either inductive or abductive demands are reduced, solve rates climb back toward standard test-set levels, showing that each simplification alone can erode the three-way reasoning load.

Conclusion: Existing tasks tend to under- or over-smooth the necessary mix of inductive and abductive demands (and neglect deductive aspects). A comprehensive measure of systematic generalization requires a task that jointly engages deductive, inductive, and abductive reasoning, and benchmarks should avoid introducing simplifications that mask these demands.

Abstract: Systematic generalization, the ability to solve novel problems by recombining known atomic elements, is central to human intelligence but difficult to study rigorously under controlled settings. Existing studies therefore rely on simplifications such as approximately linear action composition, productivity-based tests, and action-explicit goals, which make systematic generalization easier to study but omit some essential aspects of this capability. To characterize what these simplifications miss, we adopt a reasoning-centered lens and introduce TranSGrid, a testbed that brings deductive, inductive, and abductive reasoning together within a unified task. Experiments with seven Transformers on 4,800 TranSGrid instances show that all models perform much worse on TranSGrid than on a held-out test set: the largest model solves 79.6% of the test set, but only 55.3% of TranSGrid and 15.8% of the hardest subset. The gap remains within the training length range, showing that productivity alone is not sufficient to evaluate systematic generalization. Additionally, we reintroduce the other two simplifications into TranSGrid: one variant makes actions compose almost linearly (reducing the inductive demand), the other makes goals action-explicit (reducing the abductive one). In both, solve rates return to roughly the test set level, showing that either simplification alone is enough to reduce TranSGrid to an ordinary held-out test set. Together, our results show that existing tasks reduce either or both of the inductive and abductive demands, and that comprehensively measuring systematic generalization requires a task that involves all three forms of reasoning.

</details>


### [330] [Characterizing Web Search by Conversational LLM Agents: From Search Decisions and Strategies to Results and Responses](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.19244)
*Mahsa Amani,Seungeon Lee,Abhisek Dash,Asmaa El Fraihi,Yunah Jang,Elisabeth Kirsten,Qinyuan Wu,Krishna P. Gummadi,Manish Gupta,Abhilasha Ravichander,Muhammad Bilal Zafar,Soumi Das*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This study analyzes how four major conversational platforms (ChatGPT, Claude, Grok, DeepSeek) use web search in agentic tasks, examining when to search, how queries are formed, domain biases in search results, and how results are transformed into grounded responses. Findings show substantial cross-platform variation, that more frequent searching does not always improve quality, diverse querying strategies, platform-specific domain biases, and reliance on generally grounded but sometimes uncited results. Implications point to design considerations for reliable, attributed conversational retrieval.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To understand the end-to-end lifecycle of agentic web search in conversational LLMs and how search decisions, query formulation, result selection, and attribution affect response quality and reliability.

Method: Mixed-methods study combining in-vivo real-user interactions with invitro controlled experiments across four platforms (ChatGPT, Claude, Grok, DeepSeek) to examine (i) when agents invoke web search, (ii) their query strategies, (iii) domain preferences in search results, and (iv) how results are transformed into grounded responses.

Result: Cross-platform variation in search invocation decisions; higher frequency of web search does not guarantee better response quality; agents employ complex querying strategies; platform-specific search engines favor certain domains; while most responses are grounded in search results, some claims rely on uncited sources, raising attribution and reliability concerns.

Conclusion: Platform-driven behaviors, domain biases, and attribution issues have important design implications for future conversational search tools and AI agents, underscoring the need for better grounding, provenance, and cross-platform consistency.

Abstract: Conversational LLM agents increasingly rely on Web search, yet the end-to-end lifecycle of agentic search remains poorly understood. We present the first study of Web search across four major conversational platforms (ChatGPT, Claude, Grok, and DeepSeek), combining real-world user interactions (invivo) with controlled experiments using the same platform's models by their APIs (invitro). We investigate the quality of agentic decisions to invoke Web search, their strategies to formulate queries, the potential domain preferences in the search results they receive, and the choices they make when transforming search results into grounded responses. We find that Web-search decisions vary substantially across platforms and models, while more frequent Web-search invocation does not necessarily yield better response quality. We further show that conversational agents employ different complex querying strategies and that platform specific search engines return search results from their preferred domains. Finally, although responses are largely grounded in search results, some claims rely on uncited search results, raising concerns about attribution and reliability. Our findings have important implications for the design of future AI agents and Web search tools optimized for conversational retrieval.

</details>


### [331] [Do AI Agents Understand Computer Architecture?](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.19387)
*Ambika Sharan,Grigory Chirkov,Soheil Abbasloo*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: AutoTuring separates whether agent improvements come from meaningful architectural reasoning or from generic optimization by providing the same accelerator space in two encodings. It finds that problem framing (meaningful knobs) yields gains and fewer simulations, while architectural knowledge and critique can substitute for each other.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To determine whether observed hardware-design improvements by agents arise from genuine understanding of the machine or from optimizing over uninterpretable knobs, which current evaluations conflate.

Method: Use a fixed 15-dimensional accelerator space presented in two forms: named architectural knobs with simulator counters (meaningful framing) and anonymous [0,1] variables (no meaning). Keep evaluator, space, and reachable optima identical. Compare performance and simulator calls on a nine-kernel FP16 GEMM basket against a modeled H200, with a critic loop.

Result: The architecture-aware agent outperforms the modeled H200 by 5.4% and outperforms the blind (opaque-knob) agent by 12.3% on average, using 70.1% fewer simulator calls. A critic loop recovers most of the blind-agent gap and offers no added benefit to the architect-enabled agent. Five to six runs per condition on a single accelerator were conducted; the contribution is the comparison itself, not the accelerator.

Conclusion: Meaningful architectural knowledge and structured critique act as substitutes rather than complements. The study presents preliminary findings and asserts that comparing problem framing is essential to attribute gains to genuine reasoning about the machine rather than to optimization over arbitrary knobs.

Abstract: Agents are increasingly asked to design hardware, and increasingly reported to succeed. Such reports establish that a design improved; they cannot establish why. An agent that improves an accelerator may be reasoning about the machine, or may be searching competently over knobs whose meaning it never recovers -- and only the first transfers to the next architecture. Existing evaluations cannot tell the two apart, because they vary the agent while holding the framing of the problem fixed. We do the opposite. AutoTuring hands the same agent the same 15-dimensional accelerator space twice: once as named architectural knobs with simulator counters, once as anonymous variables on [0,1], with the evaluator, the legal space and the reachable optima held identical, so that the only thing that varies is whether the problem means anything. The gap between the two is the measurement. On a nine-kernel FP16 GEMM basket, meaning pays: the architect beats a modeled H200 by 5.4% and its blind counterpart by 12.3% on average, with 70.1% fewer simulator calls. It does not pay uniquely: a critic loop recovers most of that gap for the blind agent and buys the architect nothing, so architectural knowledge and structured critique behave as substitutes rather than as complements. We report these as preliminary findings -- five to six runs per condition on a single modeled accelerator -- and take the comparison itself, not the accelerator, to be the contribution.

</details>


### [332] [MAGS: Multi-agent Auto-formalization Guarantees Safety for Agentic Outputs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.19391)
*Albert Wu,Nicholas Roberts,Tzu-Heng Huang,Haoran Lin,Gil Friedman,Sungjun Cho,Gabriel Orlanski,Frederic Sala*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: A unified multi-agent system (MAGS) generates executable programs with formal safety guarantees by using Dafny as a verification-aware intermediate representation, freezing APIs and safety requirements, and iteratively repairing code from verifier feedback. Evaluated on 220 tasks across CUDA, scripting, and robotics, it achieves 100% success in producing safety-guaranteed programs under frozen specs, with some failures when auto-formalization misses target semantics.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Growing scale of LLM-generated code increases risk of safety/security failures; traditional testing and static analysis miss edge cases and formal verification is too manual. A scalable pipeline that integrates LLM code generation with automatic formal verification can provide strong guarantees.

Method: MAGS coordinates multiple agents to generate code, translates produced code into Dafny (a verification-aware IR), freezes human-audited APIs and safety requirements, uses the Dafny verifier to detect violations, repairs violations via verifier feedback, and then compiles validated code back to executable form. This creates machine-checkable safety guarantees for the final programs.

Result: On 220 tasks (100 CUDA kernels, 100 terminal scripts, 20 robotic-arm tasks), MAGS achieved a 100% success rate in producing programs with non-trivial safety guarantees against the frozen specifications. Independent safety and functional evaluations show strong performance across domains, with identifiable failures when the auto-formalized semantics do not fully capture the intended behavior.

Conclusion: MAGS demonstrates feasibility of automated, formally verified code generation across diverse domains, leveraging a verification-aware IR (Dafny) and verifier-guided repair. While effective, the approach depends on the completeness of formalized semantics and frozen specifications; gaps can lead to failures, indicating areas for improving semantic capture and specification tooling.

Abstract: LLM coding agents now generate complex programs at a scale that makes thorough human review increasingly difficult, raising the risk of safety and security failures. Common approaches, including fuzz testing, static analysis, and LLM-as-a-Verifier, can detect many failures but struggle to cover all possible edge cases. Formal verification addresses this by providing machine-checkable guarantees over specified properties, but traditionally demands substantial manual specification and proof engineering. We introduce a unified multi-agent framework, MAGS, that generates executable programs with formal safety guarantees, using Dafny as a verification-aware intermediate representation where safety properties can be mechanically checked. MAGS formalizes and freezes human-audited APIs and safety requirements, translates generated code into Dafny, repairs violations using verifier feedback, and compiles verified programs back into executable code. We evaluate MAGS on 100 CUDA kernels, 100 terminal scripts, and 20 robotic-arm tasks. Across all 220 examples, it achieves a 100% success rate in producing programs with non-trivial safety guarantees against frozen specifications. Independent safety and functional evaluations further show strong performance across all three domains, while revealing failures when the auto-formalized semantics do not fully capture the target behavior.

</details>


### [333] [Closed-World Resolution Against Tool Hallucination in LLM Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.19425)
*Laxmipriya Ganesh Iyer*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: A measurement-focused study on tool hallucination in tool-augmented LLMs. Introduces a five-class taxonomy (H1-H5), a Resolution Rung baseline, and the Model Context Protocol (MCP). Proposes the Hallucinated-Tools Benchmark (HTB); reports substantial hallucinations across models/surfaces, arguing defenses must precede gating and revealing a fundamental, irreducible residue.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To address a blind spot where LLMs issue calls to non-existent tools or pass arguments outside any schema, which current tool-selection or gating defenses cannot catch because the calls aren’t tied to real tools or valid schemas.

Method: Define a five-class taxonomy of tool hallucination (H1-H5); develop the Resolution Rung baseline (registry membership + signature check); extend analysis to the Model Context Protocol (MCP) with merged multi-server namespaces; conduct large-scale measurement across ten hosted models and two invocation surfaces; compare raw JSON vs structured interfaces; release the HTB benchmark for cross-submission comparability.

Result: Found 322 genuine hallucinations across ten hosted models; fabricated-tool calls concentrated on the unconstrained raw-JSON surface (34 vs. 3); model scale did not improve performance (675B vs 7-8B similar). With MCP surface, 154 hallucinations observed, including frontier models clean on single-registry; collisions/shadowing are structural to merging. HTB released for benchmarking.

Conclusion: Defenses must act before any causal gate; there exists an irreducible residue where arguments resemble valid calls; tool hallucination is a structural blind spot. The study provides a taxonomy, a baseline resolver, and a benchmark to standardize evaluation and drive future defenses.

Abstract: Tool-augmented large language model (LLM) agents fail in a way no tool-selection or tool-security method addresses: they call tools that do not exist and pass arguments no schema declares. Existing defenses either pick the right tool (selection) or constrain what an agent may do with real tools (gating), both of which presuppose the emitted call refers to a real tool at all. We show this is a structural blind spot: a hallucinated call is by construction not a decision any gate made, so no gate can reject it. This paper is primarily a measurement and benchmark study. We give a five-class taxonomy of tool hallucination (H1-H5) and, as a reference point, the Resolution Rung: a training-free, closed-world resolver (registry membership plus a signature check) whose interest is where it must sit, not what it computes. We prove hallucination defense must precede any causal gate, and characterize the one irreducible residue (borrowed arguments schema-indistinguishable from a valid call). Across ten hosted models under two invocation surfaces we measure 322 genuine hallucinations; fabricated-tool calls concentrate on the unconstrained raw-JSON surface (34 vs. 3), and model scale does not help (a 675B model matches a 7-8B one). We then extend to the Model Context Protocol, where merging several servers into one namespace creates hallucination surfaces a single registry cannot express (a second taxonomy, M1-M5); on the live MCP surface we measure 154 hallucinations, including from frontier models that were clean on the single-registry surface, because collisions and shadowing are structural to the merge. We release the versioned Hallucinated-Tools Benchmark (HTB) so any resolver is comparable across submissions.

</details>


### [334] [The syntax and semantics of goals](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.19448)
*David M. Abel,Mark K. Ho*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The abstract argues that goals are compositional representations that couple with world knowledge to guide behavior, drawing parallels to the syntax–semantics interface in linguistics and logic. It advocates analyzing goal representations for expressivity, sufficiency, and equivalence, framing a design space of goal form and content, and exploring implications for cognition and motivation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To understand how different goal representations shape rational behavior, their expressivity and efficiency, and how beliefs about goals influence higher-level cognition and motivation. The aim is to synthesize cross-disciplinary work to identify design-space axes for goals beyond fixed constraints.

Method: Conceptual synthesis across cognitive science, computer science, linguistics, and logic. The authors examine properties of goal representations—expressivity, design choices, and their consequences—contrast different representations, and propose a framework for evaluating form and meaning of goals.

Result: A unified framework that characterizes goal representations as a design space with varying expressivity and content. It highlights criteria for evaluating representations (expressivity, sufficiency, equivalence) and connects goals to broader questions about cognition and motivation, but does not report empirical results.

Conclusion: Distinguishing the form and meaning of goals clarifies implicit assumptions, informs the study of higher-level cognition–motivation interactions, and identifies axes along which different goal-conception approaches may vary.

Abstract: In both cognitive science and computer science, goals are conceptualized as cognitive states that flexibly combine with world knowledge to organize and specify purposeful behavior. In this way, goals are compositional representations whose content relates to rational behavior. We here draw attention to goals as representations and their content because it highlights a parallel with other areas in cognitive science - in particular, the syntax-semantics interface in linguistics and logic - while also foregrounding foundational questions about the expressivity, design, and efficiency of different goal representations. For example, goals are typically taken as fixed and imposing constraints on desirable behaviors, but we can also identify constraints on goal representations themselves, such as whether a particular goal language is sufficiently expressive to capture behaviors of interest, or whether different goal representations capture the same behavior. Here, we synthesize work that aims to characterize the properties of different goal representations and suggest these are points of a broader design space. We close by discussing how distinguishing the form and meaning of goals can elucidate the implicit assumptions we make about goals, inform the study of interactions between higher-level cognition and motivation, and isolate axes of variation for different conceptions of goals.

</details>


### [335] [Compositional Reasoning in Language Models under Reinforcement Learning Post-Training](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.19465)
*Yu He,Yingxi Li,Yifei Wang,Ellen Vitercik*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Introduces a dependency-graph framework to formalize compositional reasoning with three increasing levels of complexity; uncovers a consistent decomposed-to-composed transfer asymmetry: training on decomposed skills does not reliably transfer to composed tasks, while training on composed tasks transfers more readily back to decomposed tasks; provides theory and broad evaluations, including a pilot on real-world tool-calling benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Understand robust compositional generalization under limited data and clarify how training regimes (decomposed vs composed tasks) influence transfer, beyond what RL alone achieves.

Method: Propose a dependency-graph framework and instantiate it on data-structure tasks with deterministic rewards to define three levels of compositionality; analyze decomposed vs composed training regimes, provide theoretical explanation for the observed asymmetry, and evaluate under length extrapolation, structural distribution shift, and transfer to unseen skills; conduct a pilot study on real-world tool-calling benchmarks.

Result: Empirically observe a decomposed-to-composed asymmetry: decomposed-skill training does not reliably transfer to composed tasks, whereas composed-task training transfers more readily to decomposed tasks; theory explains the asymmetry and the pattern holds under length extrapolation, distribution shift, and unseen skills; pilot real-world tool-calling benchmarks show the asymmetry extends to practical settings.

Conclusion: The dependency-graph framework clarifies levels of compositionality and reveals a robust asymmetry in transfer directions between decomposed and composed training. These findings have implications for curriculum design and RL fine-tuning to improve compositional generalization, and warrant further study on broader real-world tasks.

Abstract: Compositional reasoning is critical for real-world problem solving: since training data is necessarily limited, models must generalize by composing learned skills in new ways. While post-training methods such as reinforcement learning (RL) have substantially improved the reasoning abilities of language models (LMs), their effects on compositional reasoning remain less well understood. We propose a dependency-graph framework to formalize compositional reasoning, yielding three levels of compositionality with increasing complexity. Empirically, we instantiate this framework with data-structure tasks, which provide deterministic reward computation and clear compositional structure. We find a consistent decomposed-to-composed asymmetry: decomposed-skill training does not reliably transfer to composed tasks, whereas composed-task training transfers more readily back to decomposed tasks. We provide theoretical explanation for this asymmetry, and further evaluate compositional generalization under length extrapolation, structural distribution shift, and transfer to tasks requiring unseen skills. Finally, we present a pilot study on real-world tool-calling benchmarks, showing preliminary evidence that the decomposed-to-composed asymmetry can extend to practical settings.

</details>


### [336] [Safety Beyond the Interface: Detecting Harm via Latent States in Large Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.19472)
*Alizishaan Khatri,Chiquita Prabhu,Omkar Neogi*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Lightweight probes can detect harmful prompts using internal LLaMA-3.1-8B activations, achieving high F1 on multiple jailbreak datasets and offering latency/compute savings over large external guardrails.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Address latency and compute overhead of safety guardrails in resource-constrained, time-critical LLM deployments; fill the gap where external guardrails lack visibility into model internals.

Method: Extract activations from LLaMA-3.1-8B and train lightweight MLP probes (12.6M parameters) to classify prompts as harmful. Evaluate on WildJailbreak, Beavertails, and AEGIS 2.0; report precision/recall affected F1 scores.

Result: Probes achieve F1 scores of 99% (WildJailbreak), 83% (Beavertails), and 84% (AEGIS 2.0); performance competitive with 1000x larger guard models while reducing latency and compute.

Conclusion: Internal signal-based probes can close the assurance gap for LLM safety with substantial efficiency gains, though generalization, robustness, and potential adversarial evasion require further study.

Abstract: Autonomous systems increasingly rely on Large Language Models (LLMs) yet the safety infrastructure surrounding these models introduces latency and compute overhead. This limits utility in resource-constrained, time-critical deployments. Existing external guardrail models remain blind to the model's internal workings, creating a fundamental assurance gap. We ask: does the model already know when the content is harmful? We extract activations from LLaMA-3.1-8B and train lightweight MLP classifier probes (12.6M parameters) to detect harmful prompts. Evaluated on WildJailbreak, Beavertails, and AEGIS 2.0, our probes achieve F1 scores of 99%, 83%, and 84%, respectively competitive with 1000x larger guard models while cutting latency and compute costs.

</details>


### [337] [QVAC Genesis III: A Large-Scale, High-Quality Open Synthetic STEM Corpus for Efficient Language Model Pre-Training](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.19513)
*Davide Vitabile,N. Ranjan,Akshay Nambiar,Kamal K. Gupta,Amril Nazir*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: A large STEM-focused synthetic corpus (QVAC Genesis III) for edge-device models, using a dual generation strategy and LLM-based parsing to enable efficient training of small models with strong performance on STEM benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Fill the gap of open, STEM-focused synthetic data optimized for small, on-device models, delivering high per-token learning value despite tight token budgets.

Method: Dual generation: targeted teacher distillation from a weak edge-scale student; failures yield corrective explanations; successes yield contrastive option-level reasoning across all answer choices. Evaluation via an LLM-as-a-parser protocol that extracts final answers from free-form outputs and measures accuracy plus answer validity.

Result: With 1.7B-parameter models, QVAC Genesis III-trained models outperform Cosmopedia-v2 and Cosmo-1B baselines on ARC, GPQA Diamond, and MMLU STEM, achieving up to +28.57% on ARC-E, +21.35% on ARC-C, and a Valid Answer Rate up to 99.45%.

Conclusion: QVAC Genesis III provides high per-token learning value for small STEM models, advancing open-data ecosystems and offering a robust evaluation protocol for on-device educational LMs.

Abstract: High-quality pre-training data is a critical bottleneck for educational and STEM-specific language models targeting edge AI and on-device deployment where token budgets are tightly constrained. While major organizations train ever-larger models on private corpora, the open ecosystem lacks STEM-focused synthetic datasets that deliver high per-token learning value efficiently for small models. To address this gap, we introduce QVAC Genesis III, a 191.43B-token, STEM-focused multi-domain synthetic corpus covering 19 domains across several difficulty levels and different educational styles. QVAC Genesis III is built via a dual generation strategy that performs targeted teacher distillation using a weak edge-scale student model as signal: the student's failures are converted into corrective explanations, while its successes are expanded into contrastive option-level reasoning over all answer choices. We further introduce an LLM-as-a-parser evaluation protocol that extracts final answers from free-form outputs and tracks both accuracy and answer validity. To validate the effectiveness of our QVAC Genesis III data, we conduct controlled from-scratch ablations with 1.7B-parameter models, showing that models trained with QVAC Genesis III consistently outperform both models trained with the open-source synthetic corpus Cosmopedia-v2 and the publicly released Cosmo-1B model across ARC, GPQA Diamond, and MMLU STEM benchmarks, achieving up to +28.57% on ARC-E and +21.35% on ARC-C, while reaching a Valid Answer Rate of up to 99.45%.

</details>


### [338] [LLM-as-an-Improver: Turning Verification into Better Candidates](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.19515)
*Akiyoshi Tomihari,Yuma Ichikawa*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Verifier-based selection improves candidate generation: VRR uses verification feedback to repair and reselect candidates, not just rank them, boosting performance and enabling recovery when initial candidates are all incorrect.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Explore whether verification can actively improve the candidate set, not just select among it, by treating the verifier as an improver that edits and augments solutions.

Method: Propose Verify--Repair--Reselect (VRR) and LLM-as-an-Improver. VRR keeps the initial winner, then conditionally generates three complementary alternatives: repaired winner, repaired runner-up, and a new-approach solution. It filters invalid/duplicate candidates using inference-time signals and reselects the final answer under the original evaluation criteria.

Result: VRR improves over fixed-pool verifier-based selection across diverse models and benchmarks in code-generation and reasoning tasks. It can recover correct solutions even when all candidates in the initial pool are incorrect.

Conclusion: Verification feedback can actively construct stronger candidates beyond the initial pool, expanding the role of LLMs to serve as improvers that generate and refine solutions.

Abstract: Verifier-based selection improves LLM performance by generating multiple candidate solutions and using a verifier to select the most promising one. However, existing methods typically treat verification only as a ranking step and discard its feedback once a fixed candidate pool has been evaluated. In this paper, we ask whether verification can also improve the candidate set itself. To this end, we introduce LLM-as-an-Improver and propose Verify--Repair--Reselect (VRR), which uses verification feedback to generate and reselect improved candidates. VRR retains the initial winner while conditionally generating three complementary alternatives: repaired versions of the winner and runner-up, and a solution based on a new approach. It filters invalid and duplicate candidates using only inference-time information and then reselects the final answer under the original evaluation criteria. Across diverse models and code-generation and reasoning benchmarks, VRR improves over fixed-pool verifier-based selection in many settings and can recover correct solutions even when all candidates in the initial pool are incorrect. These results highlight a broader role for LLMs as improvers: verification feedback can not only select among existing solutions but also construct stronger candidates beyond the initial pool.

</details>


### [339] [An Architecture for Long-Horizon Agents: Levels, Ticks and Cascaded Intelligence](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.19519)
*Erik Nijkamp,Anurag Koul,Egor Pakhomov,Bo Pang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Long-horizon LLM agents require a persistent substrate and a hierarchical memory architecture to achieve continual learning. The authors propose a three-part system—time-scale hierarchical levels with bounded summaries, a clocked action tick, and cascaded intelligence with escalation after review—and validate it via a 10-day campaign showing persistence across resets, knowledge-driven behavior changes without updating model weights, and a pathway for incorporating learned components.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Address tasks that span days to weeks and exceed standard context windows, enabling continual learning and reliability when human attention cannot be maintained throughout.

Method: Propose a three-part architecture: (i) hierarchical levels indexed by time scale, each maintaining a bounded summary of the level below; (ii) a clocked tick as the unit of autonomous action; (iii) cascaded intelligence where work is escalated to a more capable model after failed review. Evaluate with a ten-day campaign where an agent reproduces a published RL result with daily human oversight; report that (1) thread persists across resets, (2) early-operating knowledge can alter later behavior without changing model weights, (3) identify where learned components would enter the system.

Result: Demonstrates that persistence and continual learning can be achieved by a substrate that outlives context windows and processes; the harness (checks) is where learning resides, and the architecture supports integrating learned components without constant retraining.

Conclusion: Continual learning for long-horizon agents requires a substrate that outlives every context and process. The proposed harness-based architecture delivers this by structuring memory and decision-making across time scales and leveraging escalation checks; future work should formalize bottlenecks and explore integration points for learned components.

Abstract: Language-model agents are increasingly asked to carry out work spanning days or weeks, such as an operations remediation or a research programme. Such a task outlives any context window, any process and any interval at which a person can attend. In this paper, we argue that a long-horizon agent must run continually without forgetting before it can learn continually. This ability lies in the harness around the model rather than in the model itself. We derive seven bottlenecks from the long-horizon setting and answer them with a hierarchical architecture of three parts: (i) levels indexed by time scale, each keeping a bounded file summarising the level below; (ii) a clocked tick as the unit of autonomous action; and (iii) cascaded intelligence, where work is escalated to a more capable model only after failing review. We report on a ten-day campaign in which an agent built on this architecture reproduced a published reinforcement-learning result with a human attending once a day, and show (1) the agent kept the thread across every context reset and session boundary of the campaign, (2) operating knowledge written early changed later behaviour with no change to model weights, and (3) where learned components would enter such a system. Overall, our experience suggests continual learning for these agents needs a substrate outliving every context and process, and the checks the harness already runs are where a learner belongs.

</details>


### [340] [EconSkills: Studying Skill Transfer and Retrieval for Web Agents on Live Economic Data](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.19523)
*Yinzhu Quan,Zefang Liu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: EconSkills distills verified EconWebArena trajectories into parameterized SOPs for economic data retrieval, enabling transfer of procedures and library-based selection. Abstraction over raw replay improves transfer; library-scale retrieval is competitive but benefits mostly from directly covered tasks; coverage gaps can offset gains. Provides a design target for coverage-aware context delivery.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Web agents repeatedly visit the same sites, but evaluations typically discard previously learned procedures. There is a need for reusable, transferable procedural knowledge with verification and recovery to improve live data retrieval.

Method: Distill verified EconWebArena trajectories into parameterized, source-agnostic SOPs with placeholders. Each skill records scope, navigation, site-specific guidance, verification checks, and recovery steps. Evaluate two questions: (1) transfer of known procedures to held-out tasks, (2) retention when selecting from a library. Conduct controlled transfer experiments comparing matched skills to no-skill prompting, and library-scale retrieval comparing against no-skill baselines. Analyze outcomes by direct coverage and coverage-stratified results; inspect browser trajectories to assess portal navigation impact and the role of semantic verification.

Result: In controlled transfer, matched skills improve success over no-skill prompts and reduce steps on successes; abstraction-based SOPs outperform raw trajectory replay. At library scale, retrieval is competitive with the no-skill baseline overall and excels on directly covered tasks; for uncovered tasks, approximate matches mitigate gains. Browser trajectories reveal when procedural guidance shortens portal-specific navigation and when semantic verification remains necessary.

Conclusion: Reusable economic web procedures can transfer across task instances and provide a concrete target for designing coverage-aware selection and context delivery mechanisms for web-agent data retrieval.

Abstract: Web agents often revisit the same sites, yet most evaluations discard the procedures learned in earlier successful interactions. We introduce EconSkills, a skill library and evaluation framework that distills verified EconWebArena trajectories into parameterized standard operating procedures for retrieving live economic data. Each skill records its scope, navigation procedure, site-specific guidance, verification checks, and recovery steps while replacing source-instance values with placeholders. EconSkills separates two questions: whether a known relevant procedure transfers to a held-out task, and whether an agent can retain that benefit when selecting from a library. In controlled transfer, matched skills improve success over no-skill prompting and require fewer steps on paired successes, while abstraction is substantially more effective than replaying raw trajectories. At library scale, retrieval is competitive with the no-skill baseline overall and performs best on directly covered tasks; coverage-stratified outcomes show that approximate matches on uncovered tasks offset these gains. Browser trajectories further identify when procedural guidance shortens portal-specific navigation and when semantic verification remains necessary. These results establish that reusable economic web procedures can transfer across task instances and provide a concrete design target for coverage-aware selection and context delivery.

</details>


### [341] [A Unified Evaluation Framework for Trustworthy Large Language Models, Agentic AI, and Multimodal Systems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.19524)
*Shaina Raza,Ahmed Y. Radwan,Imran Liaquat,Kathryn Hume*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: A unified 8-dimension trustworthiness framework for evaluating LLMs, agentic systems, and MLLMs across outputs, trajectories, and modalities, with uncertainty, traceability, and governance alignment; empirical validation needed.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Benchmark scores alone provide an incomplete basis for assessing trustworthiness; there is a need for interpretable, cross-domain evaluation evidence to support development and oversight across diverse AI systems.

Method: Proposes eight trustworthiness dimensions—capability, robustness, safety, fairness, transparency, governance, oversight, and efficiency—and connects output-level, trajectory-level, and cross-modal assessments. Preserves system-specific metrics while mapping native measurements to common performance bands with uncertainty estimates and traceable evidence. Includes a meta-evaluation layer for validity/reliability/reproducibility, multidimensional profiles, safety overrides, and mappings to governance frameworks and regulatory requirements (e.g., EU).

Result: Framework proposal with a structured evaluation basis; does not present empirical results yet. Emphasizes interpretability and evidence credibility; empirical validation across deployment contexts is identified as essential next step.

Conclusion: The proposed framework offers a comprehensive, governance-aligned approach to assess both model performance and the credibility of the supporting evidence, pending empirical validation in real-world deployments.

Abstract: Benchmark scores alone provide an incomplete basis for assessing the trustworthiness of modern artificial intelligence systems. Large language models (LLMs), agentic systems, and multimodal models (MLLMs) require different forms of assessment, yet their evaluation evidence must remain interpretable for development and oversight. We propose a unified framework that connects output-level, trajectory-level, and cross-modal assessment through eight trustworthiness dimensions: capability, robustness, safety, fairness, transparency, governance, oversight, and efficiency. The framework preserves system-specific metrics while mapping native measurements to common performance bands, accompanied by uncertainty estimates and traceable evidence. A meta-evaluation layer examines the validity, reliability, and reproducibility of the evaluation itself. Multidimensional profiles expose strengths and weaknesses, while safety-critical overrides prevent aggregate scores from masking critical failures. Mappings to governance frameworks, international standards, and European Union regulatory requirements connect technical assessment with oversight needs. The framework provides a structured basis for assessing both system performance and the credibility of the evidence supporting it, with empirical validation across deployment contexts remaining an essential next step.

</details>


### [342] [Self Improvement via Fast Tree-search](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.19526)
*Xinghong Fu,Aravinth Kulanthaivelu,Yutaro Yamada*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: SIFT provides a sample-efficient, tree-search-based self-improvement framework for coding agents by using an LLM as an evaluation judge to perform pairwise patch comparisons, aggregating results with a regularized Bradley–Terry model to guide a disaggregated tree search, and reserving costly downstream evaluations for the most promising patches, leading to better performance on Polyglot with lower compute.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The main bottleneck in self-improvement loops is the expensive evaluation of candidate self-modifications, since prior methods re-run numerous benchmark tasks with modified agents. A cheaper, more sample-efficient signaling and selection mechanism is needed to reduce compute while preserving or improving performance.

Method: Introduce SIFT: a disaggregated tree search where an LLM-based judge provides pairwise win/loss signals for candidate patches. These signals feed a regularized Bradley–Terry model to produce patch strength scores, which guide rank-based parent sampling in a lightweight tree search. Expensive downstream task evaluations are performed only for the most promising nodes. The pipeline decouples judging from expensive evaluation to reduce time and cost.

Result: SIFT outperforms existing tree-search self-evolution frameworks on the full Polyglot benchmark while using significantly less CPU hours, wall clock time, and API cost compared to baselines.

Conclusion: A resource-efficient self-improvement framework is feasible: LLM-driven pairwise judgments plus disaggregated tree search can steer patch exploration effectively, enabling cheaper yet competitive self-modification of coding agents.

Abstract: Coding agents can recursively modify their own implementations, forming a loop of self-improvement. While prior work shows this can boost performance on coding benchmarks, existing approaches are costly and compute-intensive. We introduce a simple, sample-efficient self-improvement framework that significantly improves coding performance under strict budget constraints. We identify evaluation of candidate self-modifications as the main runtime bottleneck since prior approaches estimate their effectiveness by re-running a subset of benchmark tasks with the modified agent, which is time-consuming. We introduce Recursive Self Improvement via Fast Tree-search (SIFT), which augments these downstream task evaluations with an LLM-as-a-judge signal that performs pairwise comparisons between candidate patches, where the win-loss record is aggregated with a regularized Bradley-Terry model, and the resulting strength scores drive rank-based parent sampling inside a lightweight disaggregated tree search. Expensive downstream task evaluations are reserved only for the most promising nodes. Using a fully disaggregated tree search pipeline, the judge scores provide intermediate signal to guide exploration on promising candidate patches without being bottlenecked by slow evaluation runs. SIFT outperforms existing tree-search based self-evolution frameworks on the full Polyglot benchmark with significantly lower resource requirements in terms of CPU hours, wall clock time, and API cost.

</details>


### [343] [When Hiring Becomes Agent-Mediated: Evaluating Access and Recurrence in Two-Agent Résumé Screening](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.19530)
*Jian Gao,Hang Jiang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Two-agent screening with employer- and candidate-side AI agents iteratively exchange evidence to decide who advances, altering outcomes compared with one-shot résumé screening. It increases pass-through rates, reshuffles selections, and reduces recurrency of discovery-selected cases, underscoring the screening protocol's shaping role in access to human review.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Address the limitations of static, single-pass résumé screening by introducing interactive, bilateral AI agents that simulate employer and candidate perspectives, to study effects on selection, stability, and fairness in hiring.

Method: Experiment with two AI agents (GPT-5.5 and Claude Opus 4.7) operating on 600 résumé–job pairs, including 191 borderline pairs, across three runs. Agents exchange evidence and update judgments before deciding advancement. Compare against traditional one-call screening and analyze pass rates, decision shifts, cross-system differences, and recurrence of discovery-selected cases.

Result: Two-agent screening increases applications advanced (GPT-5.5: 33.3%→39.3%; Opus 4.7: 34.0%→35.5%). On 191-pair borderline pool, pass rates rise (GPT-5.5: 4.5%→26.2%; Opus 4.7: 6.5%→16.1%). The approach changes decisions in both directions, not simply relaxing criteria. Different apps are advanced; no single one-call threshold recovers two-agent selections. Discovery-selected cases re-executed are less likely to recur under GPT-5.5 (and less certain under Opus 4.7). A separate one-call follow-up shows no comparable decline.

Conclusion: As hiring becomes agent-mediated on both sides, the screening protocol itself shapes who reaches human review and how reliably that access recurs, highlighting the screening procedure as a crucial determinant of selection dynamics beyond the model used.

Abstract: Hiring is bilateral: employers assess fit, while candidates present and defend evidence of their qualifications. Yet résumé screening, the first gate, is commonly automated as a static, one-call judgment over a résumé-job pair. We study a two-agent alternative in which employer-side and candidate-side agents represent these roles, exchange evidence, and update their judgments before deciding who advances. We compare procedures on 600 constructed résumé-job pairs using GPT-5.5 and Claude Opus 4.7. Two-agent screening advances more applications (33.3% to 39.3% for GPT-5.5; 34.0% to 35.5% for Opus 4.7). Across three runs on the common 191-pair borderline pool, pass-instance rates rise from 4.5% to 26.2% and from 6.5% to 16.1%, respectively. This is not a uniform relaxation: two-agent screening rejects applications one-call advances, changing decisions in both directions. At similar pass volumes, the procedures advance different applications, and no one-call threshold recovers applications consistently selected by two-agent screening. Among discovery-selected cases re-executed in fresh runs, two-agent-only selections recur less often than shared selections, clearly under GPT-5.5 and less certainly under Opus 4.7, while a separate one-call follow-up shows no comparable decline. As hiring becomes agent-mediated on both sides, the screening procedure, not only the model behind it, shapes who reaches human review and how reliably that access recurs.

</details>


### [344] [Agentic AI Networking for Heterogeneous Unmanned Aerial Systems in Low-Altitude Wireless Networks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.19538)
*Nguyen Duc Minh Quang,Chang Liu,Shuangyang Li,Derrick Wing Kwan Ng*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: A hierarchical dual-loop LLM-MARL framework for low-altitude wireless networks (LAWNs) enabling outer LLM-assisted orchestration of service requirements and inner MARL policies; demonstrates adaptation without MARL retraining; includes a logistics-monitoring case study; discusses challenges and future directions.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LAWNs entail dynamic, non-cooperative interactions among heterogeneous services with time-varying requirements, creating coupling among mobility, connectivity, and resources. Fixed objectives and traditional controllers struggle to adapt autonomously to changing service priorities and resource demands.
