Method: Proposes a dual-loop architecture: an outer adaptation loop uses LLM-assisted game orchestration to interpret service requirements and operator intent and reconfigure objectives/resource priorities; an inner loop executes decentralized, parameter-conditioned MARL policies under the configured game. Includes a logistics-monitoring case study illustrating adaptation without retraining the MARL policies.

Result: Demonstrates coordinated coexistence among heterogeneous services and adaptation to evolving operating conditions without retraining the underlying MARL policies; shows feasibility of the proposed architecture in a practical scenario.

Conclusion: Identifies key challenges and research directions toward scalable, trustworthy, and adaptive agentic LAWNs.

Abstract: Low-altitude wireless networks (LAWNs) are emerging as a key infrastructure for heterogeneous unmanned aerial systems that support concurrent services within a shared three-dimensional airspace. Their coexistence creates strong coupling among mobility, connectivity, and shared network resources, while heterogeneous services impose distinct and time-varying requirements. These interactions naturally form a dynamic non-cooperative game in which both operating conditions and coordination objectives evolve over time. Conventional optimization and learning-based controllers typically rely on predefined objectives, limiting their ability to adapt autonomously to changing service requirements and resource priorities. To address this challenge, we propose a hierarchical hybrid large language model (LLM)- multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) architecture organized as a dual-loop structure. Specifically, an outer adaptation loop employs LLM-assisted game orchestration to interpret service requirements and operator intent, and reconfigure objectives and resource priorities, while an inner loop executes decentralized, parameter-conditioned MARL policies under the configured game. A logistics-monitoring case study illustrates how the proposed framework facilitates coordinated coexistence among heterogeneous services, adapting to evolving operating conditions without retraining the underlying MARL policies. Finally, we discuss key challenges and research directions toward scalable, trustworthy, and adaptive agentic LAWNs.

</details>


### [345] [Continual Enterprise World Model Discovery in Dynamic Systems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.19551)
*Shambhavi Mishra,David Vazquez,Perouz Taslakian,Marco Pedersoli,Jose Dolz,Issam H. Laradji*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Continual world-model discovery for enterprise systems using a Continual Discovery Agent (CDA) evaluated on a live ServiceNow setup (EnterpriseWorldShift). CDA learns hidden business rules, transfers models across rule evolutions (discover, revise, extend, retire), and outperforms rule-lookup by up to 8.98 IoU points in predicting rule effects.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: In real enterprises, business rules controlling field interactions are not intrinsic to the platform and evolve over time. Agents must infer and revise these rules from interactions to predict outcomes and act reliably.

Method: Train and evaluate a Continual Discovery Agent (CDA) on EnterpriseWorldShift built on a live ServiceNow environment with 9 tables, 25 hidden rules, and 600 evaluation actions. Four world versions simulate rule changes (modification, addition, retirement). CDA carries its world model across versions and predicts effects of hidden rules, without querying the live system.

Result: CDA achieves higher predictive accuracy than rule-lookup approaches (up to 8.98 IoU points), and can answer from its own model rather than querying the running system.

Conclusion: Demonstrates effective continual discovery and adaptation of enterprise world models across rule shifts, with transferable models that improve offline reasoning about rule effects in live environments.

Abstract: In an enterprise system, updating one field can set another, create a record, or start an approval. These effects are produced by business rules that are not built into the platform but written by each organization and revised over time. An agent working in such a system cannot predict the result of its own actions without knowing these rules. We study continual enterprise world model discovery, where an agent starts without knowledge of these business rules and discovers them by interacting with records and observing the outcomes. From those observations it builds a world model, which it revises as the rules change. To evaluate this, we introduce EnterpriseWorldShift, built on a live ServiceNow environment with nine tables, 25 hidden rules and 600 evaluation actions. It presents four versions of the same enterprise world, with the tables and records held fixed while a rule is modified, then added, then removed, so that discovery, revision, extension and retirement are each tested in turn. Our Continual Discovery Agent (CDA) builds such a model and carries it from one world to the next. It predicts the effects of the hidden rules more accurately than looking them up for each question, the approach taken by prior work, by up to 8.98 IoU points, and it answers from its own model without querying the running system.

</details>


### [346] [SIMLIFE: Pattern Understanding for Long-Horizon Human-Agent Partnership](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.19610)
*Run Peng,Zinnia Nie,Jing Ding,Yinpei Dai,Yichi Zhang,Zengqing Wu,Yao Fu,Ziqiao Ma,Jiayuan Mao,Joyce Chai*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: A scalable long-horizon household life simulation (SimLife) and a long-context reasoning benchmark (SimLife-BP) evaluate models on inferring latent behavioral rules from weeks/months of observations; findings show current models are surface-level and rely on heuristics, highlighting the need for stronger long-context understanding for embedded agents.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Address the challenge of understanding and predicting long-term human routines, rule formation, and adaptation, which is critical for long-horizon planning in embodied AI.

Method: Develop SimLife platform with rich visual observations, ground-truth action logs, and synthetic dialogues with audio; create SimLife-BP benchmark with 106 episodes (~15.49 hours, 38.57 in-game days) and 1,439 QA pairs; tasks cover direct, counterfactual, noisy, and inverse reasoning with varying rule hints; evaluate frontier models and architectures.

Result: Current models show surface-level predictive ability, rely on frequency-based heuristics rather than robust if-then rule reasoning, and fail to adapt when behavioral patterns change; long-context pattern understanding remains a major bottleneck for future embodied agents.

Conclusion: SimLife enables study of memory, personalization, adaptation, and long-horizon planning in everyday human-AI interaction and offers a broader research space for understanding long-context behavioral rules; improvements in long-context reasoning are needed for robust agents.

Abstract: Understanding humans over long horizons requires agents to infer not only what people need in the moment, but also how routines form, why they repeat, and when they change. We introduce SimLife, a scalable platform for simulating long-term household life with rich visual observations, ground-truth action logs, and synthetic dialogues with audio. Built on SimLife, SimLife-BP evaluates long-context pattern understanding: the ability to infer latent behavioral rules from weeks or months of everyday observations. The benchmark contains 106 episodes averaging 15.49 hours and 38.57 in-game days, and 1,439 question-answer pairs. Each task probes direct, counterfactual, noisy, and inverse reasoning under different levels of rule hints. Evaluating frontier models and architectures, we find that current models often achieve surface-level prediction without comprehensive rule understanding, rely on frequency-based heuristics rather than if-then reasoning over evidence, and struggle to adapt when behavioral patterns change. These findings suggest that long-context pattern understanding remains a major bottleneck for future embodied agents, while SimLife opens a broader space for studying memory, personalization, adaptation, and long-horizon planning in everyday human-AI interaction.

</details>


### [347] [From Intent to Action: Benchmarking LLM Safety in Vehicle Voice Command Authorization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.19630)
*Diba Afroze,Xingli Zhang,Yazhou Tu,Xiali Hei*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: A 202-scenario benchmark evaluates pre-action safety decisions for vehicle LLMs; results show API LLMs achieve high alignment but still produce false executes; structured policy improves alignment but not eliminate safety risk; independent enforcement needed.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Safety-critical pre-action authorization in vehicle assistants: the decision to execute/refuse/clarify/confirm/defer/trigger emergency/no-call must be isolated from downstream tool calls and evaluated across speaker role, authentication, vehicle state, and tool availability.

Method: A 202-scenario benchmark with Reference Decisions across a seven-class taxonomy; evaluate two local open-weight models and three API-based LLMs using Decision Alignment and safety-specific error metrics; perform ablations with structured authorization policy and baselines (schema-only, generic safety); analyze errors in confirmation and manual-control decisions.

Result: Decision Alignment ranges from 40.1% (Llama 3.2 3B) to 89.1% (Gemini 3.1 Pro Preview); API LLMs score 83.2–89.1% with no significant differences; 2–3 False Executes among 161 non-execution scenarios across models; Llama 3.2 3B ablation under structured policy yields 40.1% alignment vs 28.2–29.2% for baselines but does not remove False Executes; persistent errors in confirmation/manual-control decisions; structured decisions are not a standalone safety mechanism.

Conclusion: Structured LLM decisions are insufficient on their own to guarantee safety; deployment requires an independent enforcement layer to verify tool permissions and vehicle-state constraints before invoking any vehicle function.

Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly integrated into vehicle voice assistants. But linking natural-language requests to vehicle functions creates a safety-critical authorization problem. Before executing a command, the system must choose whether to execute, refuse, clarify, require confirmation, defer to manual control, trigger an emergency response, or make no tool call. To our knowledge, prior evaluations do not isolate this pre-action decision across speaker role, authentication status, vehicle state, and tool availability. We introduce a 202-scenario benchmark with Reference Decisions under a seven-class taxonomy. We evaluate two local open-weight models and three API-based LLMs using Decision Alignment and safety-specific error metrics. Alignment ranges from 40.1% for Llama 3.2 3B to 89.1% for Gemini 3.1 Pro Preview. The API-based models score between 83.2% and 89.1%, with no statistically significant differences among them. Even these models produce two to three False Executes among 161 non-execution scenarios, and persistent errors remain in confirmation and manual-control decisions. A controlled Llama 3.2 3B ablation increases alignment to 40.1% under the structured authorization policy, versus 28.2-29.2% under schema-only and generic-safety baselines, but it does not eliminate False Executes. Structured LLM decisions are therefore insufficient as a standalone safety mechanism, and deployment requires an independent enforcement layer that verifies tool permissions and vehicle-state constraints before invoking any vehicle function.

</details>


### [348] [Reach or Solve? Attributing Agentic RL Gains with Checkpoint Handoffs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.19636)
*Xuan Liu,Jingbin Qian*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Introduces checkpoint handoff to decompose long-horizon RL evaluation into REACH (arrival at a promising state) and SOLVE (complete from that state) by cloning states between checkpoints without retraining; across benchmarks, RL history helps RL solvers more than SFT solvers, and RL improves both arrival and solving terms.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Endpoint success in long-horizon RL confounds two distinct factors: where the agent arrives and what it does from there. A fair assessment requires separating arrival (REACH) from completion (SOLVE) to understand contributions of policy history and training regime (SFT vs RL).

Method: Propose checkpoint handoff: clone a state reached by one checkpoint to another checkpoint without retraining; evaluate across roles (reacher vs solver) and policy types (SFT vs RL) to decompose endpoint gains into REACH and SOLVE. Test across two benchmarks and two pipelines; analyze interactions between reach and solve.

Result: Across five conditions (two benchmarks, two pipelines, plus role combinations), REACH x SOLVE interaction is positive; RL history is more beneficial to RL solvers than to SFT solvers; on ALFWorld, RL improves both REACH and SOLVE, and SFT solvers fail where RL solvers succeed; independent REACH and SOLVE gaps predict the aggregate interaction.

Conclusion: Checkpoint handoff enables long-horizon evaluation by reporting arrival and completion alongside endpoint success, revealing that RL improves both reaching of viable states and solving from them, whereas SFT lags particularly in the solving stage.

Abstract: Reinforcement learning now trains language-model agents that act over dozens of steps in live environments. The gains are large, and they are read as better decision-making. An agent in a closed loop writes its own inputs. Each observation follows from its own earlier actions, so the states it meets late in an episode are partly of its own making. An SFT checkpoint and an RL checkpoint are then scored from different states, even on identical tasks. Endpoint success mixes two changes: where the agent arrives, and what it does once it is there. Restricting the comparison to states both policies reach does not separate them. That restriction selects on an outcome, and in our data it flips the sign of the effect. We introduce checkpoint handoff, an evaluation protocol that clones a state one released checkpoint reached and hands it to another, with no retraining. Crossing a reacher role and a solver role over SFT and RL splits an endpoint gain into REACH and SOLVE. REACH is how often a policy arrives at a state the environment confirms is a fixed number of actions from success. SOLVE is how often it finishes from an identical cloned state. Across two benchmarks and two independently released pipelines, the reacher by solver interaction is positive in all five conditions. An RL history is worth more to an RL solver than the same history is to an SFT solver. On ALFWorld, RL improves both terms, and the SFT solver never succeeds where the RL solver fails. Independent REACH and SOLVE gaps predict the aggregate interaction. Handoff asks only that one checkpoint's history can be replayed under another, so long-horizon evaluation can report arrival and completion beside endpoint success.

</details>


### [349] [ScientistTwo: Pioneering the Human Knowledge Frontier with Autonomous AI](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.19644)
*Jaehyun Nam,Jinsung Yoon,Yanzhou Pan,Yubo Wang,Rui Meng,Parthasarathy Ranganathan,Tomas Pfister*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: An autonomous multi-agent framework, ScientistTwo, conducts end-to-end scientific discovery with minimal human input, producing publishable papers and executable code, and outperforming human baselines in automated reviews and SOTA benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To enable problem-driven, autonomous scientific research that expands the frontier with reduced human intervention, accelerating discovery and addressing bottlenecks in science.

Method: A fully autonomous multi-agent system that takes an initial problem, establishes state-of-the-art baselines, formulates novel hypotheses, coordinates specialized agents for the discovery cycle, runs automated experiments (with diverse datasets/metrics and ablation studies), and uses a closed-loop simulated peer-review rebuttal engine, benchmarking against top conference papers (ICLR, ICML, NeurIPS).

Result: ScientistTwo autonomously generates expert-level, publishable papers and executable codebases; it outperforms human SOTA models and achieves higher average review ratings than human-authored papers under automated AI review agents.

Conclusion: The work demonstrates that autonomous AI can act as a genuine scientific pioneer, not just an assistive tool, capable of pushing the frontiers of human discovery; it validates a path toward fully autonomous scientific workflows.

Abstract: Scientific discovery is defined by the ability to identify the boundaries of existing knowledge and venture into unexplored territory. The ultimate vision for AI in science is problem-driven autonomous research: given a fundamental challenge by a human expert, the AI independently navigates the scientific landscape, uncovers theoretical and empirical bottlenecks, and systematically expands the frontier of knowledge. In this paper, we introduce ScientistTwo, a fully autonomous multi-agent framework designed to realize this vision. Specifically, ScientistTwo takes an initial problem as input, establishes state-of-the-art baselines, formulates novel hypotheses, and coordinates specialized agents to orchestrate an end-to-end discovery cycle without human intervention. Moreover, the framework rigorously conducts experiments using diverse datasets and metrics, refines methodologies through automated ablation studies, and validates research findings via a closed-loop simulated peer-review rebuttal engine. To evaluate ScientistTwo's capabilities against the highest standards of human scientific achievement, we benchmark it across papers accepted at top-tier conferences such as ICLR, ICML, and NeurIPS. As a result, ScientistTwo autonomously generates expert-level, publishable papers and fully verified, executable codebases. Its solutions consistently outperform human state-of-the-art models, and achieve higher average review ratings than human-authored papers under automated AI review agents. These results show that ScientistTwo is not merely an assistive tool but an autonomous scientific pioneer capable of pushing the frontiers of human discovery. Project website: https://scientist-two.github.io/

</details>


### [350] [Replan, Repair, or Edit? A Unified Empirical Evaluation of Travel Agents for Itinerary Revision under Resource Disruptions](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.19654)
*Xiaofei Yuan,Yan Zhang,Shaobo Qiao,Huangleshuai He,Leyan Ni,Mingchen Ju,Lujia Yang,Sijia Xu,Yifu Tang,Zhengyi Yang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: A comparative study of three disruption-recovery approaches (LLM-Z3 full replanning, IPyHOPPER hierarchical repair, iTIMO local revision) on TREK benchmarks finds LLM-Z3+Gemini best for compound disruptions, IPyHOPPER preserves commitments with competitive single-disruption performance and lower cost, while hierarchical/local repairs edit less; offers practical trade-off guidelines.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To enable apples-to-apples evaluation of disruption-recovery strategies in travel planning by standardizing task formulations and benchmarks, given fragmentation in existing methods and protocols.

Method: Two TREK-derived benchmarks: 500 single-disruption cases (feasible and infeasible) and 200 feasible compound-disruption cases. Compare LLM-Z3 full replanning, IPyHOPPER hierarchical repair, iTIMO local-revision adapter on effectiveness, plan stability, and computational cost. Note each method's LLM usage/cost and token consumption.

Result: LLM-Z3 with Gemini achieved the highest observed compound-disruption success; IPyHOPPER nearly matched LLM-Z3 in single-disruption success and preserved more of accepted itineraries on repairs; hierarchical and local repairs required fewer edits and preserved more commitments than full replanning; IPyHOPPER used no LLM inference; LLM-Z3 adapter used compact one-call inference; iTIMO used substantially more tokens.

Conclusion: The study provides practical guidelines for balancing feasibility recovery, commitment preservation, and computational cost in travel-planning revision under disruptions, suggesting strategy choice depends on disruption type and resource constraints.

Abstract: Travel-planning agents generate itineraries that may become infeasible after acceptance because of flight cancellations, hotel unavailability, or attraction closures. Revising these itineraries involves full replanning, classical plan repair, and LLM-based travel-agent revision, whose differing task formulations and evaluation protocols hinder comparison. We conduct a systematic empirical study using two TREK-derived benchmark sets: 500 single-disruption cases, including feasible and infeasible instances, and 200 feasible simultaneous compound-disruption cases. We compare LLM-Z3 full replanning, IPyHOPPER hierarchical repair, and an iTIMO local-revision adapter across effectiveness, plan stability, and computational cost. LLM-Z3 with Gemini achieved the highest observed compound-disruption success. IPyHOPPER nearly matched that configuration's single-disruption overall success, while preserving substantially more of the accepted itinerary on successful repairs. Successful hierarchical and local repairs made fewer edits and retained more accepted commitments than full replanning. Computational profiles differed: IPyHOPPER used no LLM inference, the evaluated LLM-Z3 adapter used compact one-call inference, and the iTIMO adapter consumed substantially more tokens. The study provides practical guidelines for balancing feasibility recovery, commitment preservation, and computational cost within evaluated settings.

</details>


### [351] [When2Think: Learning Difficulty-Aware Length Control for Efficient Hybrid Reasoning Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.19671)
*Jaejun Shim,HyunJin Kim,Young Jin Kim,JinYeong Bak*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: When2Think is a post-training framework that enables instance-adaptive reasoning depth in Large Reasoning Models by using IDAC reward shaping to control computation based on problem difficulty, achieving better accuracy-efficiency on math benchmarks (AIME24/AIME25).


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LRMs waste computation due to uniform reasoning depth; need adaptive allocation to improve efficiency without sacrificing accuracy.

Method: Introduce IDAC (Instance-level Difficulty-Aware Control) with reward shaping based on precomputed reference stats (accuracy, token usage); verifier-based rewards; batch-wise standardized advantages; critic-free optimization; post-training; dynamic switching between System 1 (NoThink) and System 2 (Think).

Result: On AIME24, Pass@3 up by 10.0% with 27.9% fewer tokens; on AIME25, Pass@3 40.0% outperforming compression and routing baselines.

Conclusion: Instance-adaptive computation allocation via When2Think can improve efficiency-accuracy trade-offs in LRMs without online reward models or reference-model queries; promising for tasks requiring chained reasoning.

Abstract: Large Reasoning Models (LRMs) achieve strong performance on complex tasks but exhibit systematic inefficiency: they often overthink easy problems and underthink hard ones. Existing approaches based on uniform length penalties or rigid routing incur an efficiency tax, trading reduced computation on easy instances for accuracy loss on hard instances. We formulate efficient reasoning as an instance-adaptive computation allocation problem and propose When2Think, a post-training framework for hybrid reasoning that dynamically allocates computation based on problem difficulty. Our method introduces Instance-level Difficulty-Aware Control (IDAC), a reward-shaping mechanism that leverages pre-computed reference statistics (accuracy and token usage) to regulate reasoning depth. Combined with verifier-based rewards and batch-wise standardized advantages, IDAC enables stable critic-free optimization without learned reward models or online reference-model queries. When2Think encourages direct answering on easy instances while preserving extended reasoning on hard instances, thereby learning when to use System 1 (NoThink) versus System 2 (Think). Experiments on mathematical benchmarks demonstrate improved accuracy-efficiency trade-offs: on AIME24, Pass@3 increases by 10.0% while token usage is reduced by 27.9% relative to the base model, and on AIME25, When2Think achieves 40.0% Pass@3, outperforming compression and routing-only baselines.

</details>


### [352] [FINSKILLOPS: A Self-Evolving Multi-Agent System for SEC Filing QA](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.19680)
*Yanzhang Ma,Zhenghan Tai,Hanwei Wu,Sizhe Guan,Jianliang Lei,Hailin He,Chaolong Jiang,Jijun Chi,Tung Sum Thomas Kwok,Bohuai Xiao,Jingrui Tian,Xinlu Wu,Xingao Zhan,Peng Lu,Muzhi Li,Yihong Wu,Liheng Ma,Sicheng Lyu,Tianshuo Yan,Junhao Zhu,Yaqian Xu,Lei Ding,Yufei Cui,Ziquan Liu,Boyu Han,Hengli Liu,Ling Zhou,Xinyu Wang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Controlled behavioral maintenance for financial QA via FINSKILLOPS: a single frozen skill registry with evidence-grounded failure diagnoses, targeted validation, regression controls, and versioned skill lifecycle; achieves higher correctness and lower non-correct rate.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Post-deployment reliability gaps in financial QA; existing self-improvement can improve or break behavior; need scoped, validated fixes to avoid regressions while improving correctness.

Method: FINSKILLOPS is a multi-agent system that derives reusable skills from typed failure diagnoses grounded in evidence, governs them through targeted validation, protected-case regression checks, negative controls, and versioned replacement/retirement; employs a frozen skill registry and evaluates on six financial QA benchmarks and a 12-round operational study.

Result: Highest verdict-weighted correctness and reference consistency among evaluated systems; correctness increased from 3.70 to 4.55 on an enhanced benchmark; in the operational study, only six of 33 proposed skills are promoted, and the monitoring non-correct rate drops from 20.0% to 12.5%.

Conclusion: Controlled skill scope, admission, and lifecycle management enable reliable self-improvement for financial QA, demonstrating that patch-like updates with regression safeguards can improve performance without destabilizing existing capabilities.

Abstract: Financial QA systems are typically improved before deployment through better retrieval, prompting, or agent coordination, leaving their reliability behavior fixed thereafter. In practice, new SEC-filing questions repeatedly expose heterogeneous errors in period, entity, evidence use, and calculation. Existing self-improvement methods can turn failures into new behaviors, but offer limited control over where a correction should apply or which previously correct answers it may break. We therefore frame post-deployment improvement as controlled behavioral maintenance: recurring failures should become scoped skill patches, and each patch should earn deployment with- out introducing regressions. We instantiate this view in FINSKILLOPS, a multi-agent system for SEC filing QA. FINSKILLOPS derives reusable skills from evidence-grounded, typed failure diagnoses and governs them through targeted validation, protected-case regression checks, negative controls, and versioned replacement or retirement. Across six financial QA benchmarks, a single frozen skill registry achieves the highest verdict-weighted correctness and reference consistency among the evaluated systems. Evolved skills raise correctness from 3.70 to 4.55 on our enhanced benchmark. In a separate 12-round operational study, only six of 33 proposed skills are promoted, while the monitoring non-correct rate falls from 20.0% to 12.5%. These results establish controlled skill scope, admission, and lifecycle management as the foundation for reliable self-improvement.

</details>


### [353] [LearnActCoder: Role-Aware Error Memory for Adaptive Clinical Coding Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.19721)
*Meysam Ghaffari,Bhaskar Sen,Nasim Sabetpour,Nina Fatehi,Animesh Agarwal,Carlos Morato*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Structured MistakeKDB memory improves CPT F1 on MIMIC-III with LearnActCoder; mixed ICD-9/10 results; demonstrates stability and scalability of error-memory without model retraining, but overall low CPT/HCPCS performance and retrospective evaluation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To address recurring failure modes in clinical coding (unsupported codes, missed conditions, specificity, and procedure-coding mismatches) by deriving a structured, inference-time memory of mistakes that informs subsequent coding decisions without updating the model weights.

Method: Introduce Learn-Then-Act framework that builds a Mistake Knowledge Database (MistakeKDB) from a small labeled LEARN batch. Route false negatives to a recall-oriented Coder and false positives to a precision-oriented Judge. Instantiate as LearnActCoder with lookup-table grounding. Evaluate on matched MIMIC-III and MIMIC-IV data, and test memory behavior on 1,000 held-out MIMIC-III notes.

Result: On 150 MIMIC-III notes, MistakeKDB improves CPT F1 by 5.9 percentage points; ICD-9 gains are not significant. On MIMIC-IV, memory increases ICD-10 precision at the cost of recall, leaving F1 unchanged. On 1,000 held-out MIMIC-III notes, the ICD operating point remains stable, indicating scale/stability. Overall, memory improves adaptation without weight updates, but CPT/HCPCS performance remains relatively low and the study is retrospective rather than deployment.

Conclusion: Structured, feedback-derived error memory can adapt clinical coding behavior across cases without retraining, showing stability and scalability, though with limited absolute performance and without prospective deployment.

Abstract: Clinical coding agents repeatedly encounter the same failure modes, including unsupported codes, missed documented conditions, specificity errors, and procedure-coding convention mismatches. We introduce Learn-Then-Act, an inference-time adaptation framework that converts errors from a small labeled LEARN batch into a structured Mistake Knowledge Database (MistakeKDB). False-negative lessons are routed to a recall-oriented Coder, while false-positive lessons are routed to a precision-oriented Judge. We instantiate the framework in LearnActCoder, a Coder-Judge clinical coding pipeline with lookup-table grounding where available. On 150 matched MIMIC-III notes, structured MistakeKDB improves CPT F1 by 5.9 percentage points, while raw-example and reflection-style memories remain near the no-memory baseline; the ICD-9 improvement is not significant. On a matched MIMIC-IV cohort, memory shifts ICD-10 coding toward higher precision at a recall cost, leaving F1 statistically unchanged. Applying the same memory to 1,000 held-out MIMIC-III notes maintains a stable ICD operating point, providing scale/stability evidence. Overall, the results are consistent with structured, feedback-derived error memory being useful for adapting clinical coding behavior across cases without weight updates or changes to the underlying workflow. Absolute CPT/HCPCS performance remains low, and the system is evaluated retrospectively rather than in clinical deployment.

</details>


### [354] [AutoData: Agentic Search for Pre-training Data Selection](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.19754)
*Yan Meng,Dhruv Srikanth,Bingchen Zhao,Zhengyao Jiang,Yuxiang Wu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: AutoData reframes pre-training data selection as an agentable optimization over executable data-selection algorithms, using per-document features and proxy-feedback to automatically discover scoring, stratification, and sampling rules that improve downstream performance (CORE) and transfer to larger scales.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Data curation is a bottleneck in ML pipelines; current methods rely on fixed, human-designed pipelines and weight-based mixtures. The work proposes automating data engineering as an agentic ML problem to close the loop on data selection.

Method: AutoData searches a rich program space of data-selection algorithms (scoring, stratification, stochastic selection). It uses per-document features (lexical stats, labels, perplexity) and validates candidate recipes against a proxy model, refining them via overnight search until performance improves on CORE.

Result: An automatically discovered data-selection algorithm outperforms existing human-designed curation pipelines on the proxy, and transfers to larger scales, improving the downstream CORE metric.

Conclusion: Data engineering can be treated as an agentic ML problem, extending autonomous research from model and training-code optimization to data selection, with potential gains in data efficiency and performance.

Abstract: LLM agents have recently shown promise in automating machine learning engineering by editing model and training code under execution feedback. Data, however, remains largely outside this agentic optimisation loop. We frame pre-training data selection as heuristic engineering over per-document features, i.e., lexical statistics, categorical labels, and perplexity. We introduce AutoData, an agent that searches directly over executable selection algorithms. Unlike prior data mixture methods that optimise weights over a fixed set of domains, AutoData searches a richer program space of scoring, stratification, and stochastic selection rules, discovering feature interactions automatically by iteratively refining algorithms with validation feedback from a proxy model. Within an overnight search, AutoData discovers a selection algorithm that outperforms existing human-designed curation pipelines. Despite being searched only on this small proxy, the discovered recipe transfers to larger scales and improves the downstream metric CORE. These results suggest that data engineering can be treated as an agentic machine learning problem, extending autonomous research from model and training-code optimization to the data.

</details>


### [355] [Rethinking Multi-Agent Collaboration: When More Is Less](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.19759)
*Yishuo Yuan,Yibo Wu,Yihan Zhang,Minyuan Sun,Shenliang Li,Xinkai Ma,Yifan Li,Jiaheng Liu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Multi-agent collaboration yields systematic benefits mainly for long-horizon tasks with sparse dependencies; in tightly coupled or sequential workflows, single-agent harnesses are superior. SAIGE provides a semantic-aware, incremental graph-based collaboration mechanism; experiments show context-efficient performance and that more agents do not guarantee gains.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: As LLMs and single-agent systems advance, it is unclear when collaboration across multiple agents adds value; context overhead grows and returns diminish. The paper aims to delineate capability boundaries and determine when multi-agent coordination is advantageous.

Method: Introducing SAIGE: a lightweight multi-agent system modeling collaboration as a dynamically evolving graph; nodes are agent instances spawned on demand; edges encode semantic dependencies via content-based retrieval. Evaluation on long-horizon benchmarks.

Result: SAIGE achieves a favorable trade-off between context efficiency and task performance; scaling the agent pool or recursion depth does not consistently improve outcomes.

Conclusion: The superiority of multi-agent systems is task-structure dependent; more agents do not automatically yield higher intelligence; guidance on when to use multi-agent collaboration.

Abstract: The rapid advancement of large language models and single-agent harnesses has reshaped the landscape of autonomous systems, raising a critical question of when multi-agent collaboration offers genuine value. As individual agent capabilities continue to scale, multi-agent collaboration faces diminishing returns while incurring growing context overhead. Through systematic analysis, we delineate the capability boundaries of multi-agent collaboration relative to single-agent alternatives, showing that it confers systematic benefits specifically in long-horizon tasks with sparse dependencies, while single-agent harnesses remain superior in tightly coupled, sequential workflows. Building on these insights, we propose SAIGE, a lightweight multi-agent collaboration mechanism based on Semantic-Aware Incremental Graph Evolution. SAIGE models collaboration as a dynamically evolving graph, where nodes are agent instances spawned on demand and edges encode semantic dependencies established through content-based information retrieval. Experiments on long-horizon, complex task benchmarks show that SAIGE achieves a favorable trade-off between context efficiency and task performance, and that scaling the agent pool or deepening the recursion level does not consistently improve outcomes. Our findings suggest that multi-agent superiority is bounded by task structure rather than universal, and that more agents do not necessarily make a system more intelligent.

</details>


### [356] [TorchCraft: Unified binder design by inverting an all-atom structure predictor](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.19770)
*TorchCraft Team,Yu Liu,Zhouhanyu Shen,Zhengyi Li,Xikun Huang,Jiaqi Liu,Shuxian Gao,Qilin Yu,Xiayan Qin,Yucheng Zhang,Mingchen Chen*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Unified all-atom predictor-based binder design framework (TorchCraft) that optimizes sequence logits against a frozen predictor, enabling minibinders, VHHs, cyclic peptides, and ligand-binding proteins using pretrained AlphaFold 3. Achieves experimentally validated binding across targets without post hoc redesign; extends predictor inversion across multiple binder formats and contexts.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Reuse learned structural priors from all-atom structure predictors for binder design, addressing challenges in applying these priors across diverse binder formats and molecular contexts.

Method: TorchCraft, implemented in TorchFold, optimizes sequence logits by freezing an all-atom predictor. It combines confidence, contact, geometric, and sequence-prior objectives within a shared optimization loop. Uses pretrained AlphaFold 3 weights to generate representative minibinders and VHHs, and extends to cyclic peptides and ligand-conditioned pockets.

Result: Generated representative minibinders and VHHs with experimentally measured binding across four targets per format, without post hoc sequence redesign. Computational benchmarks show applicability to cyclic peptides and ligand-conditioned pocket design.

Conclusion: TorchCraft extends predictor inversion to multiple binder formats and molecular contexts, providing a common framework for reusing all-atom structural priors in binder design.

Abstract: All-atom structure predictors model diverse molecular interactions, but using their learned structural priors for binder design remains challenging. Here we present TorchCraft, a unified binder-design framework that optimizes sequence logits through a frozen all-atom predictor. Implemented in TorchFold, TorchCraft combines confidence, contact, geometric, and sequence-prior objectives within a shared optimization procedure for minibinders, framework-conditioned VHHs, cyclic peptides, and ligand-binding proteins. Using pretrained AlphaFold 3 weights, TorchCraft generated representative minibinders and VHHs with experimentally measured binding across four targets in each format, without post hoc sequence redesign. Computational benchmarks further demonstrated the framework's applicability to cyclic peptides and ligand-conditioned pocket design. TorchCraft extends predictor inversion to multiple binder formats and molecular contexts, providing a common framework for reusing all-atom structural priors in design.

</details>


### [357] [Integrating knowledge from case reports: a medical ontology based multimodal information system with structured summary](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.19775)
*Shuyu Guo,Lan Huang,Yichen Liu,Hanbin Ma,Tian Bai*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Multimodal information system for case reports linking structured clinical summaries, medical images, and biomedical entities into a medical ontology to improve retrieval for rare diseases.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Keyword-based retrieval on unstructured case reports is inefficient for locating relevant cases, especially for rare diseases; need integrated multimodal data and a structured ontology to aid clinicians.

Method: Assemble 52,949 open-access case reports (2000–2021); extract structured clinical summaries, images, and biomedical named entities; organize into a medical ontology; develop a search/browse interface for clinicians.

Result: Introduction of a multimodal case-report information system with a structured ontology and a user interface intended to enhance retrieval and support diagnosis and identification of rare diseases.

Conclusion: The approach addresses limitations of traditional keyword search in unstructured case reports and provides a scalable framework for multimodal case information to aid clinicians.

Abstract: Published medical case reports serve as a crucial medical information carrier, documenting discoveries in rare diseases, diagnostic methods, and innovative treatments. Despite the wealth of clinical knowledge in millions of case reports in the public medicine literature database (PubMed), accessing relevant information efficiently is hindered by the limitations of traditional keyword-based retrieval tools on unstructured and diverse case reports. To address the above issues, we introduce a comprehensive multimodal information system for case reports integrating structured clinical summaries of patients including medical images and biomedical named entities from 52949 open-access case reports published from 2000 to 2021. The multimodal essential information is organized in a well-structured medical ontology. Also, a powerful interface for searching and browsing case reports is designed to assist junior clinicians in retrieving cases effectively and improving the identification and diagnosis of rare diseases.

</details>


### [358] [Contagion on the Trading Floor: How Adversarial Signals Spread in Multi-Agent Trading Systems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.19789)
*Qi Rong Sua,Junhao Dong,Nguyen Duc Thai,Yuqing Wen,Cheston Tan,Yew-Soon Ong*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Proposes GMATS framework for multi-agent LLM-based trading, analyzes black-box poisoning via social-media feeds, introduces contagion metrics, and demonstrates both vulnerability (degraded Sharpe) and mitigations through topology/prompts.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Assess robustness of LLM-driven multi-agent trading stacks to adversarial, input-only perturbations delivered via admissible social-media feeds.

Method: Introduce Generic Multi-Agent Trading System (GMATS). Instantiate a class of black-box poisoning attackers who use the LLM as a post-generator to inject budget-constrained, plausible social-media content into the analyst's evidence stream. Define contagion metrics (belief-shift at analyst/coordinator layers, attack-clean deltas on backtest metrics). Run offline experiments with historical market and social data to evaluate impact; explore how multi-agent topologies and coordinator prompts affect robustness.

Result: Adversarial inputs materially degrade risk-adjusted performance (e.g., Sharpe ratios) under poisoning; however, certain multi-agent topologies and curator/prompts can dampen shocks and improve average robustness at equal attack budgets.

Conclusion: LLM-based trading stacks are vulnerable to input-only adversarial perturbations, but architectural and prompting designs can mitigate impact, highlighting the need for security-aware system design in such frameworks.

Abstract: Multi-agent trading systems built on large language models (LLMs) are beginning to appear in quantitative finance, yet their robustness to adversarial inputs is largely unknown. We study the vulnerability of LLM trading stacks to black-box, input-only attacks that enter solely via admissible social-media feeds. We introduce the Generic Multi-Agent Trading System (GMATS), a framework that captures modern multiagent trading architectures and instantiate a class of black-box poisoning attackers that treat an LLM as a post generator and inject budget-constrained, plausibly benign social-media content into the analyst's evidence stream. We define contagion metrics that trace how adversarial content propagates through the stack, including belief-shift scores at analyst and coordinator layers and attack-clean deltas on standard backtest metrics. Experiments on a safe offline benchmark with historical market and social data show that even simple input-only attackers can materially degrade risk-return profiles, sharply reducing Sharpe ratios. At the same time, we find that suitably designed multi-agent topologies and coordinator prompts can dampen adversarial shocks and improve average robustness under identical poisoning budgets.

</details>


### [359] [Steering Equilibrium Selection in Regularized Self-Play via the Reference Policy](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.19820)
*Luis Leal*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Anchoring a reference policy during regularized self-play can steer a two-player zero-sum game toward a chosen Nash equilibrium within a polytope, by projecting the reference onto the equilibrium set (I-projection). Refinement maintains targeting even as the reference changes; results show precise steering and predictable sensitivity to anchor type and curvature, with practical implications for KL anchors in RLHF-like RL.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To address how, in self-play with entropy regularization, a reference policy can be used to select among a polytope of value-equivalent Nash equilibria, enabling controlled steering to a target equilibrium.

Method: Entropy-regularized self-play where a slowly moving reference policy ρ is best-responded to; anchoring the reference at a target equilibrium member and applying refinement (mirror steps) to steer toward that member. Experiments on five exactly solvable games plus a 2-D polytope with exact BRs and seed-level equivalence tests; metrics include mean coordinate error, exploitability, TOST, and slope of the I-projection (reach-weighted) across targets.

Result: Anchoring and refinement steer self-play to the target equilibrium with median exploitability ~5e-5 and mean coordinate error ~0.007; selection follows reach-weighted I-projection with slope ~0.969 (CI [0.950, 0.987]). Fixed off-manifold references raise exploitability; boundary targets underperform; interior precision is curvature-independent; table and MLP steering match within ±0.03 across 30 seeds. Against BRs, steering is significant mainly against fixed non-equilibrium opponents. The approach reinterprets the KL anchor in RLHF-style RL as a controllable selection knob.

Conclusion: Anchoring the reference at the desired equilibrium member and refining provides a practical mechanism for targeted equilibrium selection in self-play, with predictable sensitivity to anchor type and game curvature. The KL anchor serves as a selection knob, not just a stability constraint, enabling deliberate steering toward a chosen Nash equilibrium.

Abstract: Regularized self-play -- the family behind DeepNash's Stratego play -- drives a two-player zero-sum policy to a Nash equilibrium by best-responding to a slowly moving, entropy-regularized reference policy $ρ$. When the game has a polytope of value-equivalent equilibria, the regularizer silently breaks the tie: with a uniform reference it selects the maximum-entropy member, the I-projection of $ρ$ onto the Nash set. Can the reference be used to choose the equilibrium on purpose? On five exactly solvable games plus a 2-D polytope, with exact best responses and equivalence tests over independent seeds, anchoring the reference at a target member and refining steers self-play to that member with mean coordinate error 0.007 at median exploitability $5\times10^{-5}$, TOST-equivalent to the request within $\pm0.05$; the anchoring persists through refinement and follows the reference, not the initialization. Selection follows the reach-weighted I-projection (slope 0.969 [0.950, 0.987]). We report with equal emphasis where the story breaks: fixed off-manifold references cost 0.08-0.25 exploitability; stiff or flat families require a smaller mirror step, set by a pre-registered rule; boundary targets undershoot; curvature predicts where boundary saturation bites (rank correlation 0.90, p=0.037) while interior precision is curvature-independent. Table and MLP steering maps are equivalent within $\pm0.03$ at every target (30 seeds); matched control arms show attention's robust signature is excess seed variance, any systematic shift bounded at 0.018 and not significant. Against a best response the selection-robustness trade-off is degenerate: steering matters only against fixed, non-equilibrium opponents. The recipe -- anchor the reference at the desired member and refine -- reinterprets the KL anchor of RLHF-style RL as a selection knob, not only a stability leash.

</details>


### [360] [Dual-Axis Policy Optimization for LLM Agents: Bayesian Feedback Attribution and Trajectory Mass Normalization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.19830)
*Yingxuan Zhuang,Binhe Yu,Jingxiao Yang,Ruopei Sun,Ziting Li,Cheng Tan,Xuhong Zhang,Jianwei Yin,Jintao Chen*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: BATON is a dual-axis RL framework for LLM agents that separately optimizes intra-trajectory feedback (Bayesian Feedback Attribution) and inter-trajectory objective aggregation (Trajectory Mass Normalization), yielding additive gains and strongest performance across scales.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To address two distinct optimization dimensions in RL for LLM agents: (1) exploiting environment feedback within a trajectory (how actions are attributed to feedback) and (2) aggregating information across complete trajectories (batch-level objective normalization).

Method: Introduce BATON with two components: Bayesian Feedback Attribution — a feedback-conditioned posterior over actions to capture attribution of feedback to actions, and Trajectory Mass Normalization — equalizes optimization mass across complete trajectories in a batch. Validate via experiments with GRPO and GiGPO on ALFWorld, WebShop, and SearchQA.

Result: Both axes provide independent performance gains; their combination yields the strongest overall performance across different model scales; effectiveness demonstrated on multiple environments and policy baselines (GRPO, GiGPO).

Conclusion: A dual-axis policy optimization framework (BATON) with Bayesian attribution and trajectory normalization improves RL-based LLM agents, with complementary gains from each axis and robust gains across model scales and tasks.

Abstract: Reinforcement learning for LLM agents involves two distinct optimization di- mensions: how environment feedback is exploited within a trajectory, and how complete trajectories are aggregated across a batch. We formulate these dimen- sions as Intra-Trajectory Feedback Attribution and Inter-Trajectory Objec- tive Aggregation, and introduce BATON (Bayesian Attribution and Trajectory Objective Normalization), a dual-axis policy optimization framework. BATON instantiates the first axis with Bayesian Feedback Attribution, which constructs a feedback-conditioned posterior over sampled actions, and the second with Trajec- tory Mass Normalization (TMN), which assigns equal optimization mass to com- plete trajectories. Experiments with GRPO and GiGPO on ALFWorld, WebShop, and SearchQA show that both axes provide independent gains and that their combi- nation consistently achieves the strongest overall performance across model scales.

</details>


### [361] [MetaRTL: Meta-path Attention Enhanced Relational Table Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.19832)
*Ken Zhong,Weichen Li,Zheng Wang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: MetaRTL is a two-stage scalable relational table learning framework that replaces deep GNN/HGNN stacks with lightweight pre-training plus non-parametric meta-path feature learning, then uses MetaAttn to aggregate features.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Relational table learning on large databases is computationally expensive with deep message passing; a scalable approach that preserves relational semantics is needed.

Method: Stage 1: lightweight pre-training to obtain initial table embeddings. Stage 2: non-parametric message passing to derive meta-path features; aggregation via attention module MetaAttn. The approach shifts heavy computation from deep message passing to efficient meta-path aggregation.

Result: Evaluated on 10 real-world datasets across 24 tasks, demonstrating effectiveness and scalability of MetaRTL.

Conclusion: Decoupling representation learning from deep relational reasoning and using meta-path-based aggregation with attention yields rich relational semantics with high efficiency.

Abstract: Relational table learning has gained increasing attention with the widespread use of relational databases. Existing methods typically rely on deep GNN or HGNN stacks, leading to high computational costs and limited performance on large real-world databases. We propose MetaRTL, a two-stage framework for scalable and expressive relational table learning. In the first stage, MetaRTL obtains initial table embeddings via lightweight pre-training. In the second stage, it performs non-parametric message passing to derive meta-path features, which are then aggregated by an attention module, MetaAttn. By shifting computation from deep message passing to efficient meta-path aggregation, MetaRTL captures rich relational semantics while maintaining high efficiency. Experiments on 10 real-world datasets across 24 tasks demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method.

</details>


### [362] [A Dual-Process Perspective on Nudge Susceptibility in LLM-Based GUI Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.19843)
*Haya Halimeh,Sascha Kaltenpoth,Kevin Bösch,Oliver Müller*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: LLM-based GUI agents exhibit susceptibility to both automatic (Type 1) and reflective (Type 2) nudges; their reasoning configuration redirects how nudges influence decisions, reducing default nudges but increasing social-influence nudges, with model scale shaping this effect. Implications point to interface design as a governance concern for autonomous agents.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To examine how cognitive dual-process mechanisms apply to agents acting on interfaces and whether increasing internal reasoning reduces susceptibility to nudges.

Method: A randomized online shopping experiment with 3,600 agents and 21,600 simulations across six frontier models from three providers, assessing automatic default nudges (Type 1) and reflective social-influence nudges (Type 2). Reasoning configuration varied to test moderation effects.

Result: Agents were vulnerable to both nudge types. Increased reasoning reduced susceptibility to automatic default nudges but heightened susceptibility to reflective social-influence nudges. Model scale systematically structured this redirection. Interface design emerged as a governance concern for organizations delegating decisions to autonomous agents.

Conclusion: Nudge susceptibility is a behavioral property of agentic AI. Greater reasoning does not necessarily confer robustness; instead, it alters the pathways of influence. Governance considerations should account for interface design and model scale when deploying autonomous agents.

Abstract: LLM-based GUI agents increasingly act on behalf of users in digital environments that were designed with human users in mind. These graphical user interfaces were designed to support, but also deliberately steer, the behaviour and decisions of users. While behavioural biases in the textual outputs of LLMs are well-documented, far less is known about how such influence operates when models act as agents that perceive interfaces and execute decisions---and, in particular, whether the reasoning capabilities increasingly built into these agents make them more robust to it. Drawing on Dual-Process Theory, we empirically investigate whether LLM-based GUI agents are susceptible to automatic (Type 1) and reflective (Type 2) digital nudges, and how their reasoning configuration moderates this susceptibility. In a randomized online shopping experiment with 3,600 agents and a total of 21,600 simulations across six frontier models from three providers, we found that agents were vulnerable to both nudge types. Crucially, the reasoning configuration moderated these effects in opposing directions, reducing susceptibility to automatic default nudges while heightening it to reflective social influence nudges. Extensive reasoning therefore did not make agents more robust but redirected the route through which choice architecture takes effect. Exploratory analysis further showed this redirection to be systematically structured by model scale. Beyond establishing nudge susceptibility as a behavioural property of agentic AI, the study positions interface design as a governance concern for organizations that delegate decisions to autonomous agents.

</details>


### [363] [Constraint-Safe Graph-Context Scoring for Stable Point-Feature Labels Under Text-Width and Accessibility-Inspired Profiles](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.19848)
*Taimoor Ahmad*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: LABELSENSE-Pilot: a reproducible prototype for point-feature label placement that uses eight compass candidates, an MLP over graph-context, and a prior-placement bonus, optimized via mixed-integer programming; enforces viewport containment, per-feature uniqueness, and pairwise clearance.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To reconcile geometric validity, display yield, local utility, and stability under camera motion in map label placement while accommodating accessibility and multilingual dimensions, which are often reduced to overlap counts in evaluations.

Method: Generate eight compass candidates per feature; score candidates with a multilayer perceptron over graph-context summaries; include a previous-placement bonus; select a layout via mixed-integer optimization; explicit checks for viewport containment, per-feature uniqueness, and pairwise clearance; note that the scorer is not described as a graph transformer.

Result: In experiments with 2,500 airport coordinates across 155 countries, across five seeds, LABELSENSE-Pilot achieved 85.62% label display, 2.09% flicker, and zero collisions. Compared to a handcrafted-utility integer program, it sacrificed 1.43 percentage points of display but reduced flicker by 12.04 points. Enlarged-box-aware layouts yielded zero proxy violations; standard geometry reevaluation at 1.5x violated 52.57% of selected placements.

Conclusion: Demonstrates an auditable engineering trade-off in label placement decisions. The abstract notes that official baselines and participant evidence remain required before submission, and does not claim improvements in accessibility, multilingual usability, or user preference.

Abstract: Point-feature label placement on interactive maps must reconcile geometric validity, display yield, local placement utility, and stability across camera motion. Accessibility and multilingual requirements further change label dimensions, yet algorithmic evaluations often collapse these concerns into overlap counts. We present LABELSENSE-Pilot, a reproducible prototype that generates eight compass candidates per feature, scores candidates with a multilayer perceptron over graph-context summaries, adds a previous-placement bonus, and selects a layout through mixed-integer optimization. The executed scorer is deliberately not described as a graph transformer. Every returned layout is checked for viewport containment, per-feature uniqueness, and pairwise clearance. Experiments use 2,500 airport coordinates and names spanning 155 countries, with country-grouped splits and generated density, camera, text-suffix, preference, and enlarged-font stressors. Across five seeds, LABELSENSE-Pilot displayed 85.62 percent of labels with 2.09 percent flicker and zero collisions. Versus a handcrafted-utility integer program, LABELSENSE-Pilot sacrificed 1.43 percentage points of display while reducing flicker by 12.04 points. Enlarged-box-aware layouts produced zero proxy violations, whereas standard geometry reevaluated at 1.5x violated 52.57 percent of selected placements. These results establish an auditable engineering trade-off, not human accessibility, multilingual usability, or preference. Official recent baselines and participant evidence remain required before submission.

</details>


### [364] [Reproducibility is not construct validity: LLM measurement of institutionally situated communication](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.19866)
*Veronika Batzdorfer,Carlo Romano Marcello Alessandro Santagiustina*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: LLM-inferred annotations are highly reproducible but can diverge from the intended construct; reproducibility does not imply validity. Divergence varies by stakeholder group and shows spatial patterns; survey measures still predict explainability across divergence levels. Calls for validation distinguishing reproducibility, construct validity, and context effects when using LLMs as measurement tools.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Address whether high annotation reproducibility of LLM-derived labels translates to valid measurement of a targeted construct in policy-relevant data, using a linked survey and free-text dataset from the EC AI Act consultation.

Method: Link structured survey responses with free-text consultation submissions from the same stakeholders; annotate free text with LLMs; assess reproducibility (intraclass correlations >0.99); compare LLM annotations with survey-reported measures of the nominal construct; analyze divergence across stakeholder groups; test for spatial autocorrelation (Moran's I); evaluate association with support for explainability across divergence levels.

Result: LLM annotations show ICC > 0.99 indicating high reproducibility, but limited convergence with nominal construct measured by surveys; divergence across stakeholder groups (e.g., business associations show greater text-based concern than survey; public authorities show smaller/negative divergence); positive spatial autocorrelation across neighboring countries (Moran's I = 0.347, p = 0.036); despite divergence, survey-reported concerns remain strongly linked to support for explainability across divergence levels.

Conclusion: Reproducibility of LLM annotations can coexist with poor construct correspondence; validation procedures are needed to distinguish reproducibility, construct validity, and communication-context variation when using LLMs as measurement instruments.

Abstract: High annotation reproducibility does not necessarily imply that an LLM-inferred measure captures the construct it is intended to measure. We test this distinction using a dataset from the European Commission's AI Act consultation, linking structured survey responses to free-text consultation submissions from the same stakeholders. LLM annotations of consultation submissions are highly reproducible (intraclass correlations > 0.99), yet show limited convergence with survey-reported measures of the nominal construct they were intended to approximate. Divergence between survey-and LLM-inferred text-based measures varies systematically across stakeholder groups: business associations express greater concern about AI risks in text-based consultations than in survey responses ({g} = +1.0), whereas public authorities and several nonbusiness groups show smaller or negative divergences. Divergences between scores suggest positive spatial autocorrelation across European countries (Moran's I = 0.347, p = 0.036), indicating that stakeholders from neighboring countries tend toward more similar text-based stances towards AI safety concerns. Despite divergence, survey-reported concerns remain strongly associated with support for explainability across all divergence levels. These results demonstrate that LLM annotation reproducibility can coexist with poor construct correspondence and motivate validation procedures that distinguish reproducibility, construct validity, and communication context variation when LLMs are used as measurement instruments.

</details>


### [365] [Physical knowledge on historical data matters more than enforcing physical constraints on the forecast](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.19871)
*Etienne Lehembre,Pascal Audigane,Vincent Nguyen,Christel Vrain,Thi-Bich-Hanh Dao*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: A Physics-Informed Recurrent Neural Network (PIRNN) predicts unobservable intermediate physical variables along with targets, guided by physical equations. Demonstrated on groundwater level forecasting with the Gardenia model; achieves top performance on 5 of 12 real datasets; ablation highlights the value of physics-informed components; domain expert validates the physical coherence of predicted variables.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Address forecasting in physical processes where intermediate, unobservable variables are important for interpretation. Existing PINNs often estimate outputs but not intermediate states, limiting interpretability and trust.

Method: Introduce PIRNN, which jointly predicts target variables and unobservable intermediate variables using historic data and forecast targets. The model is modular and can incorporate multiple physical equations, each with its own set of unobservable variables. Case study uses Gardenia groundwater models with transfer equations and data assimilation. Evaluation includes comparisons with several neural network baselines across 12 real-world datasets, plus an ablation study to assess component contributions.

Result: PIRNN outperforms competing models on five of the twelve datasets. Ablation studies confirm the importance of incorporating physical knowledge. The coherence of the predicted physical variables is evaluated by a domain expert and found satisfactory.

Conclusion: Integrating physics into recurrent forecasting that estimates unobservable states enhances robustness and interpretability, and the framework is adaptable to different physical models and equations.

Abstract: Time series forecasting has seen signicant advancements with the emergence of new deep learning models. However, forecasting time series in applications involving physical processes remains a major challenge. Despite the apparition of Physics Informed Neural Networks (PINN), recent models do not estimate unobservable intermediate physical variables, which are important for domain experts to understand the target behavior. To this end, we propose a Physics Informed Recurrent Neural Network (PIRNN) which predicts, along the target, unobservable variables on both historic data and forecast target. This approach enhances the model robustness and results interpretation using domain knowledge. Our method is easily adaptable to any physical model using several equations, each having its own set of unobservable variables, to describe it-self. As a case study, we incorporate physical equations used for groundwater levels predictions by the physical model called Gardenia. This model uses transfers equations between reservoirs, optimized with data assimilation, to simulate the evolution of groundwater levels. Evaluation includes several well known neural network models and the Gardenia model compared on twelve real world datasets. In addition, we study the impact of each component through an ablation study. Our model outperforms other models on ve out of the twelve datasets and our ablation study underlines the importance of having a physical background in our time series forecasting task. Finally, the coherence of the physical variables predicted by our neural network is assessed by a domain expert.

</details>


### [366] [TRACE: Accountable Agentic Retrieval for Source Discovery in Digital Archives](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.19897)
*Donghan Bian,Marie Puren,Florian Cafiero*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: TRACE is a training-free, corpus-aware, agentic retrieval framework for historical archives that delivers accountable source discovery; it outperforms several baselines on HistoriQA-ThirdRepublic with low cost, enabling scalable scholarly retrieval.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Historical archives are OCR-degraded, heterogeneous, and require strong source traceability. Training-heavy or graph-based RAG approaches are costly or insufficient for accountability in scholarly use.

Method: TRACE is a training-free agentic retrieval framework designed for accountable source discovery over historical corpora. It was developed in the DECIDON project and evaluated on HistoriQA-ThirdRepublic (1,752 questions) using BnF digitized collections; deployed internally for 24 researchers across six institutions.

Result: TRACE achieves R@10 = 0.856 and MRR = 0.653, outperforming sparse, dense, graph-based, and agentic RAG baselines, with the largest gains on multi-hop and cross-corpus questions. Cost is approximately $0.02 per question under the default hosted inference configuration.

Conclusion: For large digital libraries and archives, retrieval accountability and corpus-aware agent design offer a practical alternative to heavier training-based or graph-construction approaches; TRACE demonstrates feasibility and economic viability for heritage institutions.

Abstract: Historical archives pose a difficult retrieval problem for retrievalaugmented generation systems: documents are OCR-degraded, heterogeneous across genres and sources, and require strong source traceability for scholarly and institutional use. We introduce TRACE, a training-free agentic retrieval framework designed for accountable source discovery over historical corpora. The system was developed in the context of DECIDON, an interdisciplinary project on the circulation of political discourse between parliamentary debates and the press during the French Third Republic, involving digitised historical collections and institutional use cases. The prototype is currently deployed internally within the project and accessible to 24 researchers across six partner institutions. We evaluate TRACE on HistoriQA-ThirdRepublic, a benchmark of 1,752 French historical questions over parliamentary debates and newspapers from 1887, with documents derived from Biblioth{è}que nationale de France digitised collections. TRACE achieves R@10 = 0.856 and MRR = 0.653, outperforming sparse, dense, graph-based, and agentic RAG baselines, with the largest gains on multi-hop and cross-corpus questions. At approximately $0.02 per question under the default hosted inference configuration, TRACE also remains economically feasible for heritage institutions, laboratories or companies that cannot rely on costly local GPU infrastructure. These results suggest that, for large digital libraries and archives, retrieval accountability and corpus-aware agent design can provide a practical alternative to heavier training-based or graph-construction approaches.

</details>


### [367] [From "Who Is This User?" to "What Does This Purchase Mean?": A Deployed Pipeline for Semantic User Profiling at Bank Scale](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.19928)
*Ryota Mitsuhashi,Tetsuro Morimura,Hirotake Ito*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: A pattern-based inference approach reduces LLM calls from per-user to per-pattern, maintaining similar predictive power while scaling to tens of millions of users; deployment yields ~1000x fewer inferences than per-user methods.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To overcome the linear growth of inference cost with the number of users by aggregating inference over transaction-patterns rather than individuals, enabling scalable attribute profiling.

Method: A three-phase pipeline: (1) Resolve abstract item names with optional web grounding; (2) Profile infers attributes for each frequent pattern via one LLM call per pattern, emitting predefined categorical labels, free-text attributes, and per-attribute prevalence estimates; (3) Tag clusters free-text attributes into a queryable database. Inference budget then grows with pattern count instead of user count.

Result: On Open e-commerce data, the produced attribute database is statistically indistinguishable from an LLM that reads each user’s raw history (AUC-equivalent across evaluated attributes); prevalence estimates preserve discriminative signal for positive vs negative users. Deployed at a major Japanese bank for tens of millions of users, achieving roughly a 3-order-of-magnitude reduction in LLM inference targets versus a per-user pipeline.

Conclusion: Pattern-based profiling is a scalable alternative to per-user LLM inference, preserving predictive utility while substantially reducing inference burdens; code is publicly available.

Abstract: Per-user LLM inference on transaction histories binds the inference budget linearly to user count, which becomes prohibitive at applied scale. We re-cast attribute inference from per-user to per-transaction-pattern. The pipeline runs in three phases: Resolve abstracts item names with optional web grounding, Profile infers attributes for each frequent pattern, and Tag clusters free-text attributes into a queryable database. In Profile, a single LLM call per pattern emits predefined categorical labels, free-text attributes, and per-attribute prevalence estimates. Because inference runs over patterns rather than users, the budget grows with the pattern count rather than the user count. On the public Open e-commerce corpus, the database is statistically indistinguishable from an LLM that reads each user's raw history directly in AUC across the evaluated attributes, and the prevalence estimates carry discriminative signal between positive and negative users. The pipeline is deployed at a major Japanese bank profiling on the order of tens of millions of users, with close to a three-order-of-magnitude reduction in LLM inference targets versus a per-user pipeline. The code is publicly available on https://github.com/CyberAgentAILab/profiling-agent-open-ecommerce.

</details>


### [368] [Beyond Depth Truncation: Controlled Evaluation of Depth Utilization in Recursive Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.19934)
*Ha Van Dau,Thanh Tung Khuat,Nguyen Thanh Dung*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Introduces the Depth Control Protocol (DCP) to disentangle depth effects in depth-recurrent LMs by isolating block count, compute/operations, and residual readout; includes positive controls, negative control on dense transformers, and a training intervention; a linchpin control requires depth-wise weight sharing.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current depth-truncation evaluation conflates multiple factors (fewer blocks, reduced computation, and shifted readout) into a single slope, risking misinterpretation of depth’s true effect.

Method: DCP provides three positive controls that isolate each factor while varying the others, a negative control applying the same interventions to dense transformers to rule out protocol artifacts, and a controlled training intervention to test causality. The linchpin control—maintaining full block budget while executing only one distinct iteration—is realizable only with depth-wise weight sharing.

Result: A diagnostic suite to separately measure the impact of (i) number of blocks, (ii) computation/operations, and (iii) residual stream readout on model performance; includes a negative control and a training-based causality check, clarifying the interpretation of depth-based performance changes.

Conclusion: DCP enables causal disentanglement of depth-related effects in depth-recurrent architectures and provides a principled framework for evaluating depth beyond a single slope metric, with feasibility specifically tied to depth-wise weight-sharing designs.

Abstract: Depth-recurrent language models iteratively apply a small layer stack, decoupling per-token compute from distinct parameter count. To determine whether such a model genuinely utilizes its depth, both recurrence and layer-pruning literatures rely on a shared evaluation: truncating depth at inference time, plotting quality against retained depth fraction, and reading off the slope. While cheap and training-free, this metric suffers from an unexamined flaw: it extracts a single scalar from an intervention that alters multiple model properties simultaneously. Depth truncation concurrently reduces the number of block applications, decreases the volume of distinct computation performed, and pushes the readout head onto an out-of-distribution residual stream. The observed slope conflates all three factors, yet is conventionally interpreted as reflecting solely the second.
  We propose the Depth Control Protocol (DCP), a diagnostic suite that disentangles these three quantities. DCP comprises three positive controls that isolate each factor while varying the others, a negative control applying the identical interventions to dense transformers to ensure the effect is not an artifact of the measurement protocol, and a controlled training intervention to verify causality. The linchpin control, running the full budget of block applications while executing only a single distinct iteration, is strictly realizable only in depth-wise weight-sharing architectures, since in a dense network repeating a layer yields an entirely different model rather than the same model in an alternative configuration.

</details>


### [369] [MaSCoD: A Multi-Agent Framework for Structural-Context-Guided Candidate Causal Graph Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.19944)
*Yudai Nakada,Yuichiro Nishiura,Jin Michael Splichal*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: MaSCoD is a multi-agent causal-discovery framework that pre-structures candidate variables and local patterns before edge judgment. Across Auto-MPG, DWD, and Sachs, with GPT-5.4 and GPT-4o, it increases recall and F1 when using structural pre-organization (Full) versus constructing edges during judgment (No Phase 1) but at the cost of more false positives; gains are dataset- and backbone-dependent, with partial ablations showing mixed benefits.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To address premature omission of potentially relevant causal relations by treating omission control as an explicit design objective in causal discovery.

Method: MaSCoD organizes candidate third variables and local structural patterns as a pre-judgment stage (Phase 1) before direct-edge evaluation.
