The framework is evaluated on three datasets (Auto-MPG, DWD, Sachs) using GPT-5.4 as the primary backbone and GPT-4o for replication, comparing configurations that include structural hypotheses before judgment (Full) versus constructing them within the judgment (No Phase 1).

Result: Full generally yields higher mean Recall and F1 across six dataset–backbone settings but also increases false positives. Additional reference-edge retention is observed on DWD with GPT-5.4 and Sachs with GPT-4o. Partial ablations show that supplying both information components does not always outperform supplying only one. Stage-wise analysis indicates retention gaps arise after direct-edge judgment, and reconciliation may cause further reference-edge loss in some settings. The findings support evaluating structural pre-organization as a design target for omission control and for joint evaluation of context construction and its use in judgment.

Conclusion: Structural pre-organization is a viable design and evaluation target to manage omission in causal discovery, advocating joint evaluation of how context is constructed and later used in edge judgments.

Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have been applied to causal discovery, but candidate-graph generation rarely treats premature omission of potentially relevant causal relations as an explicit design objective. We propose MaSCoD, a multi-agent framework that organizes candidate third variables and local structural patterns before direct-edge judgment. We evaluate MaSCoD on Auto-MPG, DWD, and Sachs using GPT-5.4 as the primary backbone and GPT-4o for replication. MaSCoD exhibits a dataset- and backbone-dependent retention-selectivity profile rather than uniform superiority. Across all six dataset-backbone settings, Full, which supplies structural hypotheses before direct-edge judgment, achieved higher mean Recall and F1 than No Phase 1, which instead constructs them within the judgment procedure, while also increasing false-positive rates. Additional reference-edge retention over all evaluated baselines was observed on DWD with GPT-5.4 and on Sachs with GPT-4o, rather than uniformly across settings. Partial ablations showed that supplying both information components did not always outperform supplying only one. For GPT-5.4, stage-wise analysis showed that the Full-No Phase 1 retention gap was already present after direct-edge judgment, while reconciliation introduced additional reference-edge loss for Full on Sachs. These findings support structural pre-organization as an explicit design and evaluation target for omission control and motivate evaluating context construction jointly with its utilization in judgment.

</details>


### [370] [Not All AI Agents Are Equal: Characterizing Resource and Performance Dynamics](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.19947)
*Wonmi Choi,Minuk Park,Zhixiong Niu,Yongqiang Xiong,Chuck Yoo,Gyeongsik Yang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Study of resource dynamics in LLM-based AI agents across retrieval-augmented QA, web search, and coding. Finds task-dependent latency and bottlenecks when handling concurrent requests; shows faster LLMs or more CPU cores don't always help. Proposes CPU-aware tool admission and task-aware CPU allocation, achieving ~5.4x improvement for CPU-sensitive tasks and ~32% lower average latency vs native agents.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Agents performing iterative reasoning with remote LLM APIs and local containers suffer from resource contention and bottlenecks that vary by task and concurrency. Optimizing resource management is crucial to reduce latency and resource waste.

Method: Empirical measurements across three representative tasks (retrieval-augmented QA, web search, software coding). Analyze latency as a function of resource dynamics under concurrent requests. Observe task-dependent behavior and bottlenecks. Evaluate the impact of CPU cores and faster LLM responses. Propose and demonstrate CPU-aware tool admission and task-aware CPU allocation.

Result: Finds wide variability in resource dynamics across tasks and tools; concurrent requests reveal task-dependent bottlenecks in CPU, disk I/O, and memory; increasing CPU speed or cores does not always accelerate agents. Demonstrates performance gains with CPU-aware admission and task-aware allocation: CPU-sensitive tasks see ~5.4x latency improvement; average latency across tasks reduced by ~32%.

Conclusion: Resource dynamics-aware management can substantially improve latency for AI agents. Tailoring admission and allocation to task characteristics yields meaningful gains and should be integrated into agent serving systems.

Abstract: LLM-based AI agents process user requests through iterative reasoning and tool execution, often involving the invocation of remote LLM APIs with local tool containers. This execution model can make the optimization of agent serving difficult because latency, local resource demand, and container bottlenecks inter-mix across requests. However, the current agent ecosystem runs without much consideration of resource dynamics, which results in significant waste of the precious resources. This paper analyzes the resource inter-mix of AI agents for three representative tasks: retrieval-augmented question answering, web search, and software coding. To this end, we characterize the latency with respect to the resource dynamics of processing multiple requests and tasks concurrently. Our measurements show that agents have a wide range of behaviors depending on tasks, so that even the same tool can differ substantially in resource dynamics. We also find that running multiple requests concurrently exposes task-dependent bottlenecks in resource dynamics such as CPU, disk I/O, and memory. Furthermore, we uncover that faster LLM responses or more CPU cores do not always accelerate agents. Based on these observations, we demonstrate new optimization opportunities that exploit the resource dynamics of tasks: CPU-aware tool admission and task-aware CPU allocation. Our results show that the latency of CPU-sensitive agent tasks improves $\sim$5.4$\times$, and the average latency across multiple tasks is reduced $\sim$32% compared to native agents.

</details>


### [371] [Neuro-Symbolic Agentic AI for Networked Low-Altitude UAVs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.19961)
*Yuqi Ping,Tianhao Liang,Nanchi Su,Guangyu Lei,Junwei Wu,Qinyu Zhang,Tingting Zhang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Proposes neuro-symbolic agentic AI (NSAAI) for networked UAVs, fusing neural grounding with symbolic planning/verification to enable reliable, data-efficient, adaptive autonomy under intermittent connectivity; includes a reference architecture and a fire-inspection case study.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Tackle hallucination, data dependence, and weak generalization in autonomous UAVs by integrating neural grounding with symbolic reasoning and closed-loop agentic control to improve reliability under uncertain observations and intermittent connectivity.

Method: (1) Establish capability foundations: data efficiency, compositional generalization, continual learning, zero-shot transfer. (2) Propose a reference architecture with modules for task/goal management, neuro-symbolic planning, verification/metacognition, skill execution/network interaction, and shared knowledge/memory. (3) Demonstrate with an urban fire-inspection scenario in LAESim showing sensing/cloud coordination under intermittent connectivity, reuse of a verified image-delivery skill, and evidence-based condition satisfaction before mission completion. (4) Discuss research directions for uncertainty-aware reasoning, knowledge/skill expansion, adaptive self-monitoring, and standardized evaluation.

Result: NSAAI yields reusable skills, evidence-grounded decision-making, and adaptive mission execution in networked UAVs, as illustrated by the LAESim case study.

Conclusion: The NSAAI framework shows promise for reliable, adaptable UAV autonomy under uncertainty and intermittent connectivity; future work should emphasize uncertainty reasoning, expanding knowledge/skills, self-monitoring, and rigorous, standardized evaluation.

Abstract: Networked low-altitude unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) need reliable and adaptive decision-making capabilities to operate under uncertain observations, dynamic environments, and intermittent connectivity, while many existing agentic systems remain limited by hallucination risks, data dependence, and weak generalization. This article investigates neuro-symbolic agentic AI (NSAAI) as a framework for combining neural grounding, symbolic reasoning, and closed-loop agentic interaction to support more reliable and adaptive UAV autonomy. We first examine its capability foundations in data efficiency, compositional generalization, continual learning, and zero-shot transfer, and then develop a reference architecture integrating task and goal management, neuro-symbolic planning, verification and metacognition, skill execution and network interaction, and shared knowledge and memory. An urban fire-inspection case implemented in LAESim illustrates how a UAV can coordinate sensing and cloud access under intermittent connectivity, reuse a verified image-delivery skill, and satisfy explicit evidence conditions before completing the mission. The results illustrate the potential of NSAAI to support reusable skills, evidence-grounded decision-making, and adaptive mission execution in networked UAV systems. We further discuss key research directions in uncertainty-aware reasoning, knowledge and skill expansion, adaptive self-monitoring, and standardized evaluation.

</details>


### [372] [Customizable and Jointly Optimized Route Planning: A Deep Architecture Enabling Differentiable Shortest-Path Search](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.19996)
*Rui Zhao,Chao Chen,Longfei Xu,Chenguang Ji,Hengbin Cui,Kaikui Liu,Xiaolong Li*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Differentiable, data-efficient route optimization leveraging offline Pareto-optimal routes and constrained objective loss to jointly optimize cost and ranking for user preferences.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Overcome lack of optimality guarantees in heuristic routing and avoid feedback loops from using user trajectories by standard navigation apps; enable customizable route preferences.

Method: 1) Offline multi-objective Dijkstra to collect Pareto-optimal routes; 2) neural architecture that emulates shortest-path search and route ranking in differentiable end-to-end fashion; 3) novel loss aligning a single objective under other attributes constrained; 4) evaluation on real-world datasets.

Result: Outperforms state-of-the-art in route quality and customizability; achieves better alignment with diverse user preferences while maintaining completeness via Pareto frontier.

Conclusion: The proposed architecture provides a principled approach to jointly optimize cost functions and ranking, leveraging complete candidate set and constrained optimization to deliver flexible, high-quality routing.

Abstract: With the widespread use of online navigation and ride-hailing services, achieving optimal route planning for diverse user preferences has recently attracted increasing attention. Classic graph algorithms for pathfinding use heuristic cost functions to define edge weight, thus providing no optimality guarantee of route quality. Prior data-driven approaches equating ground truth of the optimal route with user trajectory, which is however moderately influenced by the navigation service, suffers from the feedback loop problem. To address these issues, we propose a deep architecture that is able to jointly optimize cost functions and route-ranking model towards any route preference. First, we run a multi-objective Dijkstra algorithm offline to collect the set of Pareto optimal routes, deeming it as the complete candidate set. Exploiting the property of such a set, we design a neural network structure that emulates shortest-path search and route ranking in an end-to-end differentiable manner. Second, we define route preference as a task of constrained optimization of route attributes, and propose a novel loss function that optimizes a single-objective variable, with other variables strictly under constraints. We conduct extensive experiments on real-world datasets. The results show that our architecture significantly outperforms state-of-the-art methods in route quality and customizability.

</details>


### [373] [E-AVI: Evidence-Grounded Multimodal Assessment for Automated Video Interviews](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20001)
*Haoshen Wang,Dongbo Che,Zeyi Xie,Yuanjie Du,Shicheng Hua,Xingyu Wang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: E-AVI is an evidence-grounded, multimodal video interview assessment framework that extracts timestamped evidence, uses dimension-conditioned evidence attention with source embeddings, and supports NL feedback and QA; it outperforms baselines and provides inspectable grounding for feedback and interactive analysis.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Address the need for interpretable, evidence-backed predictions in automated video interview assessment beyond mere numerical scores.

Method: Extracts timestamped multimodal evidence; applies dimension-conditioned evidence attention; uses source-level embeddings; maintains a shared evidence pool for NL feedback and QA; evaluation on RecruitView and hospitality dataset; extensive ablations and analyses.

Result: E-AVI consistently outperforms fine-tuned multimodal baselines in rank correlation; evidence pathway is predictive and grounded; various analyses (ablation, deletion, bootstrap, human-audit, QA) quantify contributions and utility.

Conclusion: The framework improves predictive performance while providing inspectable, actionable evidence for assessment, feedback, and interactive analysis.

Abstract: Automated video interview assessment integrates verbal content, acoustic delivery, and visual behavior, yet numerical predictions alone provide limited inspectable support. We present E-AVI, an evidence-grounded framework that extracts timestamped multimodal evidence and integrates dimension-conditioned evidence attention with source-level embeddings for scoring. A shared evidence pool further supports natural-language feedback and follow-up question answering. On RecruitView and a private hospitality dataset, E-AVI consistently outperforms fine-tuned multimodal baselines in rank correlation. Ablation, evidence-deletion, bootstrap, human-audit, and QA analyses characterize the predictive contribution, grounding, and practical utility of the evidence pathway. Together, these results demonstrate that our proposed E-AVI framework improves predictive performance while providing inspectable support for assessment, feedback, and interactive analysis.

</details>


### [374] [Geopolitical Divisions Across Languages in Large Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20005)
*Maxim Chupilkin*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Language of a question shifts AI systems' political assessments of the Ukraine war; across 112 languages, Russia-leaning vs Ukraine-leaning responses vary and correlate with official-language groups and public opinion, repeating across three models.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Assess whether multilingual prompts influence AI political outputs, with implications for information warfare, bias in AI training data, and geopolitical influence via chatbots.

Method: Prompt three large-language models (GPT, Claude, Gemini) with 20 statements about the Ukraine war in 112 languages, collecting 67,200 responses. Classify responses as Russia-leaning or Ukraine-leaning. Analyze by language group (by official language) and compare to external proxies (UN votes, aid). Test robustness by removing statement pairs.

Result: Language-driven bias observed: more Russia-leaning answers cluster in languages corresponding to Russia-friendly public views; pattern replicates across all three models and persists when statement pairs are removed. The distribution aligns with worldwide political divisions at the language level.

Conclusion: Multilingual prompts may propagate geopolitical biases through AI training data; information warfare could shape conversational outputs and, in turn, real-world opinions and policy attitudes. Calls for monitoring, auditing, and mitigating cross-language bias in AI systems.

Abstract: People increasingly turn to AI chatbots for news and explanations of world events. But do they receive the same political answers when they ask in different languages? Here we show that the language of a question can change how the same AI systems assess the war in Ukraine. We ask GPT, Claude and Gemini to evaluate twenty statements about the war in 112 languages, collecting 67,200 responses. The balance between Russia-leaning and Ukraine-leaning responses differs across languages. When we group responses by countries' official languages, they follow a pattern resembling worldwide political divisions: relatively more Russia-leaning answers correspond to more favourable public views of Russia, less support for Ukraine in United Nations votes, and less aid to Ukraine. The broad pattern recurs across all three models and remains when individual statement pairs are removed. Our findings suggest a possible route through which information warfare may shape the text used to train AI models, which may in turn spread geopolitical biases.

</details>


### [375] [FedeRICo: Federated Region-Influenced Coupling for Traffic Flow Prediction](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20026)
*Fermin Orozco,Man Luo,Johan Wahlström*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: FedeRICo introduces a federated traffic forecasting framework with gradient-level collaboration and boundary-aware residual communication to address heterogeneity and cross-client propagation, using a dual-branch architecture and boundary messages via trend-residual decomposition; it outperforms federated ST baselines on four real-world benchmarks with competitive runtime.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Federated spatio-temporal forecasting faces heterogeneity across client graphs and loss of cross-boundary spatial dependencies due to parameter aggregation; there is a need to recover cross-client spatial dependencies while preserving data privacy.

Method: Dual-branch forecasting: a globally guided branch captures transferable forecasting structure coordinated by gradient alignment across clients, and a private residual branch preserves client-specific corrections. Boundary signals are extracted via a trend-residual decomposition to isolate transient spatial-temporal effects and communicated between physically adjacent clients.

Result: Empirical evaluation on four real-world traffic benchmarks shows FedeRICo consistently outperforms state-of-the-art federated spatial-temporal baselines while maintaining competitive training runtime.

Conclusion: FedeRICo effectively mitigates heterogeneity across client graphs and enables recovery of cross-client spatial dependencies through boundary-aware communication, advancing federated spatial-temporal traffic forecasting.

Abstract: Urban traffic forecasting often relies on information distributed across stakeholders who may be unable to share raw data due to privacy or commercial constraints, motivating federated spatial-temporal approaches. In such federated settings, each client observes traffic over a distinct sensor subgraph with its own spatial topology and temporal dynamics, leading to significant heterogeneity across clients. Existing federated spatial-temporal methods typically rely on model parameter aggregation and provide limited mechanisms for recovering spatial dependencies across client boundaries. This introduces two key limitations. Specifically, parameter aggregation across heterogeneous graph domains tends to dilute client-specific representations, while road network partitioning breaks the propagation of traffic dynamics across client boundaries. To address these challenges, we propose FedeRICo, a federated traffic forecasting framework that combines gradient-level collaboration with boundary-aware residual communication. FedeRICo employs a dual-branch forecasting architecture in which a globally guided branch captures transferable forecasting structure, while a private residual branch preserves client-specific corrections and incorporates boundary residual signals. The global branch is coordinated through gradient alignment across all clients, enabling collaborative optimisation without destructive parameter interference. To recover cross-client spatial dependencies, boundary messages are extracted through a trend-residual decomposition that suppresses periodic structure and communicates only transient spatial-temporal residual signals between physically adjacent clients. Experiments across four real-world traffic forecasting benchmarks demonstrate that FedeRICo consistently outperforms state-of-the-art federated spatial-temporal baselines while maintaining competitive training runtime.

</details>


### [376] [Can Data Attribution Filter Out Subliminal Learning? Not Reliably](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20027)
*Moritz Weckbecker,Sweta Jena,Jonas Müller,Ponnurangam Kumaraguru,Sebastian Lapuschkin,Wojciech Samek,Louis Jaburi,Gonçalo Paulo*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Gradient-based data attribution partially detects training data responsible for subliminal learning; EK-FAC at token level is most effective among tested methods, but overall results are inconsistent and divergence tokens remain stronger baseline.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Subliminal learning enables transmission of behavioral traits via training data despite lack of semantic relation, challenging content-based data filtering; seeks content-agnostic attribution methods to identify responsible data for safety interventions.

Method: Evaluate three gradient-based attribution methods (GradCos, a contrastive GradCos variant, EK-FAC) across three models; compare to divergence tokens; perform token-level and sample-level filtering; assess effectiveness and consistency across model-setup pairs.

Result: EK-FAC reduces the subliminal-learning signal at token level; other gradient-based methods offer little benefit and largely underperform divergence tokens; sample-level filtering is less effective for all methods, though EK-FAC can outperform divergence tokens in some cases; results are inconsistent across model/setting combos with no single explanatory pattern.

Conclusion: Gradient-based attribution can identify data contributing to subliminal learning in some settings but reliability varies by method and configuration; EK-FAC shows relatively stronger signal among tested approaches; divergence tokens remain a strong baseline; further work needed to understand inconsistencies and improve robustness.

Abstract: Subliminal learning allows language models to transmit behavioral traits through training data with no obvious semantic relationship to those traits, undermining content-based data filtering as a safety intervention. Training data attribution offers an alternative: it identifies the training examples responsible for a given model behavior, independent of their semantic content, and so may apply in exactly the cases where semantic inspection fails. We evaluate three gradient-based attribution methods (GradCos, a contrastive GradCos variant, and EK-FAC) across three models, comparing them against divergence tokens, a strong baseline previously shown to localize subliminal learning (albeit one that requires access to counterfactual teacher models). Filtering at the token level, EK-FAC mitigates a significant part of the effect, the other methods provide little benefit, and all mostly fall short of divergence tokens. Filtering entire samples is less effective for every method, though EK-FAC often gives a stronger signal than divergence tokens in this setting. Success is inconsistent across methods and settings: variants that work well for some model-preference combinations fail for others, and we do not identify a consistent explanation for these differences. Our results suggest that gradient-based attribution can identify data responsible for subliminal learning in some settings, but that some approximations are more reliable than others.

</details>


### [377] [DART: Distillation-Aware Reparameterization for Training-Free LoRA Reuse in Few-Step Video Diffusion Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20051)
*Shihong Li,Juntao Xu,JinCao,Maowen Tang,Jun Huang,Jintao Li*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: DART improves distilled-model LoRA reuse under shortened schedules via training-free calibration plus low-rank coordinate transport, boosting joint video-quality and preserving functional behavior without source training.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Address negative transfer and functional drift when reusing LoRA trained on longer trajectories with step distillation, without requiring new training data.

Method: Training-free approach: combine low-rank coordinate transport with target-schedule response calibration using forward evaluations and no source training videos (DART).

Result: On Wan2.2 four-step target, DART-F raises joint quality from 0.9029 to 0.9227 and macro functional retention from -0.4644 to +0.1349; calibration accounts for most improvement; coordinate transport provides complementary gains; adapter-level effects vary (some positive, some attenuated); results replicate on two additional targets showing the same trend.

Conclusion: Evaluating distilled-model LoRA reuse should consider functional preservation and negative-transfer avoidance rather than assuming universal recovery across adapters; calibration is the primary driver with coordinate transport as a complementary boost.

Abstract: Step distillation reduces the cost of video generation, but reusing a LoRA trained for a longer trajectory can alter its functional effect or degrade target quality. Static parameter compatibility offers one perspective on this problem; our observations show that similar measured geometry can coexist with different adapter behavior under a shortened denoising schedule. We propose DART, a training-free method that combines low-rank coordinate transport with target-schedule response calibration using forward evaluations and no source training videos. On a four-step Wan2.2 target, DART-F improves the joint quality score from 0.9029 to 0.9227 and changes macro functional retention from -0.4644 to +0.1349. Component analysis shows that calibration accounts for most of the quality improvement, while coordinate transport provides complementary gains when combined with calibration. Adapter-level results reveal positive functional effects for some adapters and strong attenuation with reduced negative functional effects for others. Evaluations on two additional targets show the same aggregate trend. These results motivate evaluating distilled-model LoRA reuse jointly through functional preservation and negative-transfer avoidance, without assuming recovery for every adapter.

</details>


### [378] [MAGMA-GEN: Validated Recovery Supervision from Ambiguous Failures via Counterfactual Re-Execution](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20056)
*Loan Bernat,Matthieu Grard,Ariane Herbulot,Florent Lamiraux*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: MAGMA-GEN converts ambiguous failed long-horizon rollouts into validated recovery data via an on-policy coach-guided diagnosis and re-execution check, improving success and recovery.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Hierarchical robotic systems must make high-level decisions for long-horizon tasks, but failures are ambiguous. Traditional supervised learning lacks recovery data; reinforcement learning struggles with sparse rewards and non-local credit assignment.

Method: An on-policy data-generation pipeline where a privileged coach hypothesizes an early decision-level error and proposes localized corrections or recovery actions. Since diagnosis may be fallible, candidates are retained only if re-execution from the same state under matched conditions improves downstream progress. This yields supervised examples from the agent’s own failure distribution without per-step human demonstrations.

Result: MAGMA-GEN improves task success and recovery capabilities compared with distillation and trajectory-repair baselines under evolving task constraints, in both simulation and real-robot execution.

Conclusion: The approach provides scalable recovery supervision by leveraging the agent’s failure distribution, enabling better handling of ambiguous rollouts and adapting to changing task constraints without requiring step-by-step human demonstrations.

Abstract: Hierarchical robotic systems executing long-horizon manipulation tasks must make high-level semantic decisions that orchestrate stochastic low-level skills. In this setting, failed rollouts are ambiguous: a poor downstream state may reflect an invalid high-level decision, partial observation, or a valid decision whose physical execution failed. Traditional supervised learning lacks data for such recovery states, while reinforcement learning struggles with sparse rewards and non-local credit assignment. We propose MAGMA-GEN, an on-policy data-generation pipeline that converts ambiguous failed rollouts into validated recovery supervision. MAGMA-GEN first uses a privileged coach to hypothesize an early decision-level error and propose localized correction or recovery actions. Because this diagnosis is fallible, candidates are retained only if re-execution from the same state under matched conditions improves downstream progress. This produces supervised examples from the agent's own failure distribution without per-step human demonstrations. Evaluated on interactive long-horizon manipulation tasks, MAGMA-GEN improves task success and recovery capabilities, against distillation and trajectory-repair baselines under evolving task constraints in both simulation and real-robot execution.

</details>


### [379] [WiCleanData: Guaranteeing the Type Consistency of Wikidata by Taxonomy Refinement and Constraint Enforcement](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20057)
*Yiwen Peng,Marc Jeanmougin,Thomas Bonald*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: WiCleanData is an automated pipeline that cleans Wikidata taxonomy and type constraints, producing a publicly accessible, consistent knowledge graph free from type violations.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Wikidata’s collaborative nature introduces errors, inconsistencies, redundancy, ambiguity between instances and classes, incorrect taxonomic paths, and type constraint violations, making manual curation infeasible at scale.

Method: An automated pipeline: (1) taxonomy cleaning with language-model assistance; (2) hierarchical aggregation to simplify type constraints; (3) filtering of facts to enforce consistency; (4) publication of the resulting clean knowledge graph via a Web interface.

Result: A refined knowledge graph with a consistent taxonomy and no type constraint violations, made publicly available through a Web interface for easy exploration and downstream applications.

Conclusion: Demonstrates the feasibility of automated knowledge graph cleaning and provides a publicly accessible, clean Wikidata-derived resource for downstream tasks.

Abstract: Because of its collaborative nature, Wikidata suffers from errors, in- consistencies, and excessive complexity, such as redundant classes, ambiguity between instances and classes, wrong taxonomic paths, and type constraint violations. The manual curation of these issues is infeasible at scale. To address these challenges, we introduce WiCleanData, a refined version of Wikidata with a consistent tax- onomy and free from type constraint violations. Specifically, we have designed an automated pipeline that first cleans the taxonomy with language model assistance, then simplifies type constraints by hierarchical aggregation, and finally filters facts accordingly. The resulting knowledge graph, free from any type violation, is made publicly available via a Web interface, enabling easy exploration and downstream applications.

</details>


### [380] [FCA-Guided Counterfactual Explanations for Multi-Modal Breast Cancer Diagnosis: A Framework Achieving Perfect Validity with Emergent Sparsity](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20067)
*Abdullahi Isa,Souley Boukari,Muhammad Aliyu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: FCA-CF uses an FCA concept lattice as a hard structural constraint to guide counterfactual generation for a multi-modal breast cancer classifier, achieving perfect validity, sparsest changes, and competitive proximity, with lattice-driven sparsity highlighted by ablation as a key novelty.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Address the lack of actionable, counterfactual explanations for deep learning in clinical diagnosis; improve counterfactual quality via structural constraints to ensure valid, sparse, proximal changes.

Method: Build FCA-guided counterfactual generation framework; apply to TCGA-BRCA multi-modal data; compare with Wachter, DiCE, FACE, NICE; evaluate 60 benign-predicted cases; analyze ablations on lattice constraint and Phase C refinement.

Result: Validity 1.000, Sparsity 2.37 (best), Proximity 0.900; classifier metrics: Acc 0.980, F1 0.976, ROC-AUC 0.9947; ablations show lattice constraint reduces sparsity by ~40%, Phase C adds significant sparsity gain when disabled; claims Pareto-dominant, structurally novel contribution.

Conclusion: Formal concept lattice as a structural prior yields a novel, sparsity-driven approach to counterfactual explanations with perfect validity and strong proximity; advances the counterfactual literature by introducing topology-induced sparsity.

Abstract: Deep learning models for multi-modal breast cancer diagnosis achieve high predictive accuracy but remain clinically unacceptable without actionable, counterfactual explanations. Attribution-based methods (LIME, SHAP) are categorically inapplicable to this purpose, as they generate no alternative instances and thus cannot be evaluated on counterfactual quality metrics. This investigation provides empirical evidence that FCA-Guided Counterfactual (FCA-CF) framework that uses a Formal Concept Analysis (FCA) concept lattice as a hard structural constraint on counterfactual search, operating over a multi-modal TCGA-BRCA dataset. We benchmark against four genuine counterfactual methods: Wachter-style CF, DiCE, FACE, and NICE, evaluated on 60 benign-predicted TCGA-BRCA instances. The FCA-CF framework achieves Validity = 1.0000 (100% of counterfactuals successfully flip the prediction), Sparsity = 2.37 features changed (best among all valid methods), and Proximity = 0.900 (normalised L2-based, matching NICE as joint best). The classifier achieves Accuracy = 0.980, F1 = 0.976, ROC-AUC = 0.9947. Ablation analysis confirms that the FCA lattice constraint is the primary sparsity driver (removing it increases sparsity by +40%, p < 0.001, Cohen's d = 0.78), while Phase C greedy refinement accounts for the largest individual contribution (+113% sparsity increase when disabled, p < 0.001, d = 5.01). FCA-guided counterfactual generation achieves a clinically important Pareto-dominant outcome; it is simultaneously the sparsest and among the most proximate of all valid methods, with perfect validity. The emergent sparsity property arising from lattice topology rather than numerical penalty terms constitutes a structurally novel contribution to the counterfactual explanation literature.

</details>


### [381] [Marginal utility, matrix factorization, and the Key-Value (KV) cache: a unified information-economic framework for sovereign geo-mining inference](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20068)
*Caroline Gans Combe*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: A theoretical framework links marginal utility from economics to ML concepts (matrix factorization, transformer caches) via a unified dimension-retention rule under memory constraints, and applies it to geo-mining information extraction with notable but mixed empirical results.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To unify resource-allocation principles across latent factors and model caches by mapping spectral properties to marginal utility, enabling a single decision rule under a binding memory constraint and guiding multi-pass inference and model merging in structured document extraction.

Method: 1) The singular value/eigenvalue spectra are interpreted as marginal utility schedules for latent factors and learned representations; 2) cache eviction and low-rank compression are cast as constrained utility maximization; 3) derive a single rule: retain dimensions whose eigenvalues exceed the shadow price of the memory constraint; 4) apply to geo-mining extraction with a multi-pass inference protocol, TIES model merging, and a CVaR-regularized selection policy; 5) implement a hierarchical classifier (LoRA-tuned) and analyze TIES merging behavior.

Result: Two empirical contributions: (a) an 11.2M-parameter hierarchical classifier achieves 90.0% level-1 accuracy on a 973-document uranium-exploration test set (latency 2.62 ms per card) vs 92.0% on a 50-document audit of the same corpus by a proprietary model (latency ~2000 ms); (b) a diagnostic of uniform-density TIES merging reveals a degenerate mode with token-identical outputs across districts, removable by layer-wise calibrated densities; full-scale extraction benchmarks with LoRA tuning are reported as projected, not measured.

Conclusion: The framework collapses dimension/serialization decisions under a single allocation rule based on the shadow price of memory, supporting efficient, multi-pass structured extraction and model merging, while highlighting potential degeneracies in TIES merging that require calibrated density controls. The work remains primarily empirical and projection-based for full-scale benchmarks.

Abstract: This paper builds a theoretical bridge between the economic notion of marginal utility and two machine-learning constructs, matrix factorization and the Key--Value cache of transformer language models. The singular value spectrum of a rating matrix is shown to be a diminishing marginal utility schedule for latent factors, the eigenvalue spectrum of the projected covariance operator to be the marginal utility schedule of a model's learned representation, and cache eviction and low-rank cache compression to be instances of constrained utility maximization under a memory budget. The three collapse into a single allocation rule: retain the top dimensions whose eigenvalue exceeds the shadow price of the binding constraint. The framework is applied to the automated extraction of structured information from geo-mining documents, where it motivates a multi-pass inference protocol, a layer-wise TIES model merging procedure, and a selection policy combining extraction quality, localization drift and energy, scalarized with a Conditional Value-at-Risk term on drift. Two empirical contributions are reported. An 11.2-million-parameter hierarchical classifier, trained in about five minutes on a single GPU, reaches 90.0 per cent level-1 accuracy on a held-out test set from a 973-document uranium-exploration corpus, against 92.0 per cent for a proprietary model on a fifty-document human audit of the same corpus, at a latency of 2.62 ms per card against approximately 2,000 ms for the API and at negligible cost. A diagnostic of uniform-density TIES merging exposes a reproducible degenerate mode in which the merged model returns token-identical outputs across five geographically distinct districts while declaring high confidence; re-executing the merge under layer-wise calibrated densities removes that signature on the diagnostic sample. The full-scale extraction benchmark, including LoRA fine-tuning, is reported as projected rather than measured and remains an empirical extension of this work.

</details>


### [382] [Tailored to you: longitudinal effects of personalising language models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20077)
*Canfer Akbulut,Justine Breuch,Arianna Manzini,Lujain Ibrahim,Matija Franklin,Roma Patel,Iason Gabriel,Kristian Lum,Laura Weidinger*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Longitudinal study comparing baseline, memory-based, and survey-based personalization of language models over 5 days shows repetition effects dominate some outcomes, while personalization shapes self-disclosure and perceived creepiness/regret differently across methods.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To understand how sustained exposure to personalised LMs influences user perception, behaviour, and downstream social consequences, and how different personalization signals (memory vs survey data) compare.

Method: Experiment with 992 participants over 5 days of daily advice-seeking interactions with LMs; three conditions: non-personalised baseline, memory-based personalization (using prior chat history), and survey-based personalization (using pre-study intake data); measured outcomes include self-disclosure, perceived creepiness, regret about sharing, information-sharing attitudes, and general interaction dynamics.

Result: Repeated exposure, not personalization per se, drives many changes in human-AI interaction. Memory-based personalization increased self-disclosure and reduced perceived creepiness; survey-based personalization increased regret about sharing personal information. Overall, personalization effects are nuanced and depend on implementation; outcomes vary across measures.

Conclusion: Personalisation of LMs yields nuanced behavioral and attitudinal effects over time. Memory-based signals may foster openness and comfort, while survey-based signals may raise privacy concerns. Designers should weigh long-term user experience, privacy, and trust implications when deploying personalised AI, and consider tailoring personalization signals to user goals and risk tolerance.

Abstract: Interest in developing personalised language models is rapidly growing. While personalisation is often viewed as a mechanism to better serve diverse user needs, the effects of sustained interactions with personalised models on people's perception of and behaviour toward AI remain poorly understood. Most critically, downstream consequences outside the immediate human--AI interaction loop, such as effects on users' self-perceptions and interpersonal relationships, remain largely unexamined. In this study, we recruited 992 participants to complete daily advice-seeking interactions with language models over the course of five days, comparing outcomes from a non-personalised baseline against two personalisation approaches: memory-based (conditioned on prior conversational history) and survey-based (conditioned on information collected through a pre-study intake survey). We find that several changes in human-AI interaction over time are driven primarily by repeated exposure rather than personalisation itself. However, participants interacting with personalised models experienced differences in advice-seeking and information-sharing attitudes and behaviours: participants in the memory-based condition engaged in greater self-disclosure and rated the model as less creepy, while participants in the survey-based condition reported higher regret about having shared personal information with the AI. We conclude by highlighting the nuanced effects of different personalisation approaches on interaction outcomes, and discussing the implications of these findings for the responsible design and deployment of personalised AI systems.

</details>


### [383] [A Proposal for an Agentic AI Architecture to Support Multi-Domain Decision-Making in the Brazilian Armed Forces](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20080)
*Gioliano de Oliveira Braga,Sidnei Barbieri,Ágney Lopes Roth Ferraz,Wagner Comin Sonaglio,Henrique Curi de Miranda e Lourenço Alves Pereira*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Agentic AI architecture enabling autonomous planning, data access, tool execution, and audible action to support decision-making across Brazil's Navy, Army, and Air Force. Addresses multi-domain data volume and OODA-cycle strain with four application fronts: decision support, situational analysis, feasibility studies, and countermeasure suggestion; emphasizes data access requirements and security/governance across admin, strategic, operational, and tactical levels.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Reduce the observe-orient-decide-act (OODA) loop burden in complex, multi-domain military environments by enabling proactive, autonomous AI-assisted decision-making while maintaining control via safeguards.

Method: Conceptual architecture proposal for an Agentic AI system with capabilities to plan, access data sources, execute tools, and act autonomously/audibly. Defines four application fronts and outlines required data/sensor access and governance safeguards across organizational levels.

Result: Conceptual framework and architecture proposal; no empirical results provided.

Conclusion: Feasibility and potential benefits are discussed, but practical implementation requires detailed architectural design, safety and governance mechanisms, interoperability standards, and rigorous evaluation.

Abstract: The growing complexity of multi-domain operational environments (land, aerospace, naval, cyber, and electromagnetic spectrum) has increased the volume and velocity of data reaching command-and-control (C2) centers, straining the observe-orient-decide-act (OODA) decision cycle. Artificial Intelligence (AI) systems currently employed in defense are, in general, reactive and isolated tools that still rely heavily on human operators to integrate information, assess scenarios, and formulate courses of action. This paper proposes a conceptual Agentic AI architecture for AI systems that can plan, access data sources, execute tools, and act autonomously and audibly, aimed at supporting decision-making across the three Brazilian Armed Forces (Navy, Army, and Air Force). Four application fronts are discussed (decision support, situational analysis, feasibility studies, and countermeasure suggestion), as well as the data and sensor access requirements and the security and permission safeguards necessary for responsible employment across administrative, strategic, operational, and tactical contexts.

</details>


### [384] [UnifiedPlayers: Enhance Tool-Integrated Reasoning in Agentic Reinforcement Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20089)
*Wenjie Liao,Liangjie Zhao,Zehong Cao*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: UnifiedPlayers is a cooperative, three-agent framework that jointly learns planning, execution, and evaluation for self-evolving, tool-using agents; it surpasses strong baselines on reasoning benchmarks and yields a high-accuracy verifier with discriminative feedback under GRPO.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Decoupled data generation and static verification limit adaptability to emergent failure modes in self-evolving agents; a coordinated, three-player system can align data, actions, and evaluations to improve learning.

Method: Introduce Planning Player, Execution Player, and Evaluation Player that operate under GRPO with role-specific rewards. Planning generates tasks, Execution produces multi-turn tool-augmented trajectories, Evaluation builds executable verifiers. The three players co-evolve, with feedback signals aligning toward a shared learning objective.

Result: Across two model backbones and twelve benchmarks, UnifiedPlayers improves strongest prior baseline by ≥3.5% on mathematical reasoning and ≥3.9% on general reasoning. The learned verifier attains 84.2% adversarial detection accuracy, and the verifier's reward signal has 2.03× higher per-question variance than a self-consistency baseline, indicating more discriminative feedback.

Conclusion: Cooperation among specialized players enables self-enhanced tool-integrated agents and offers a promising path to robust, adaptable self-evolving systems.

Abstract: Self-evolving methods reduce the need for human-annotated trajectories by allowing tool-using agents to generate their own training data. Yet existing methods typically separate trajectory generation from evaluation, relying on static verifiers that cannot adapt to emerging failure modes or self-consistency signals that may reinforce errors shared across trajectories. Jointly adapting planning, execution, and evaluation offers a promising alternative, but introduces a fundamental coordination challenge: each component continuously changes the data or feedback used to train the others. We address this challenge with \textbf{UnifiedPlayers}, a cooperative framework comprising a Planning Player that generates tasks, an Execution Player that produces multi-turn trajectories with Python tool calls, and an Evaluation Player that constructs executable verifiers. We design role-specific rewards that coordinate the three players toward a shared learning objective under GRPO. Across two model backbones and twelve reasoning benchmarks, UnifiedPlayers outperforms the strongest prior baseline by at least 3.5\% on mathematical reasoning and 3.9\% on general reasoning tasks. Moreover, the learned verifier achieves 84.2\% adversarial detection accuracy, while its reward signal exhibits 2.03$\times$ higher per-question variance than a self-consistency baseline, providing more discriminative verifications. These results highlight cooperation among specialized players as a promising path toward self-enhanced tool-integrated agents.

</details>


### [385] [Solving Minimum Span Antibandwidth and Cyclic Antibandwidth Labeling Problems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20091)
*Hieu Truong Xuan,Khanh To Van*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Introduces MSABL/MSCABL as minimum-span variants of antibandwidth problems and proposes a SAT-based unified exact framework; demonstrates competitive performance against MILP/CP solvers, especially with no-hole constraints.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current research emphasizes maximizing minimum distances in antibandwidth problems; the complementary minimum-span perspective has received less attention, motivating an exact method.

Method: Unified SAT-based framework that formulates MSABL/MSCABL as a sequence of decision problems using monotonicity. Two SAT strategies are explored: parallel SAT solving (searches multiple candidate spans concurrently) and incremental SAT solving (reuses a single SAT instance while progressively restricting the label domain). Benchmarking against CPLEX CP/MIP and Gurobi, with and without the no-hole constraint.

Result: SAT-based approaches are highly competitive in solution quality. Parallel approach best for MSCABL; incremental approach best for MSABL. Under no-hole constraint, approaches are competitive with CPLEX CP and significantly outperform CPLEX MIP and Gurobi, particularly for MSCABL.

Conclusion: A SAT-based exact approach is effective for MSABL/MSCABL. The unified framework and the two solving strategies offer competitive, practical solutions against established MILP/CP methods.

Abstract: The Antibandwidth and Cyclic Antibandwidth problems are NP-hard graph labeling problems that aim to maximize the minimum (cyclic) distance between labels assigned to adjacent vertices. Extensive research on these problems has resulted in a variety of mathematical formulations and computational approaches. However, their minimum span perspective, in which a prescribed minimum (cyclic) distance is fixed and the objective is to minimize the label span, has received comparatively little attention. In this paper, we consider this complementary perspective by introducing the Minimum Span Antibandwidth/Cyclic Antibandwidth Labeling (MSABL/MSCABL) problems and developing a unified Boolean Satisfiability (SAT)-based framework for solving them. The SAT-based framework formulates MSABL/MSCABL as a sequence of decision problems and exploits their monotonicity to accelerate the search process. We also consider two SAT solving strategies, parallel and incremental SAT solving: the former examines multiple candidate spans concurrently, while the latter reuses a single SAT instance while progressively restricting the label domain. The proposed approaches are evaluated on benchmark instances from the Harwell-Boeing Sparse Matrix Collection and compared with CPLEXCP, CPLEXMIP, and Gurobi. The results show that SAT-based approaches are highly competitive in solution quality, with the parallel approach performing best overall for MSCABL and the incremental approach for MSABL. With the no-hole constraint, they remain competitive with CPLEXCP and significantly outperform CPLEXMIP and Gurobi, particularly for MSCABL. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of SAT solving as an exact approach for MSABL and MSCABL.

</details>


### [386] [Perception, Layout, and Validation: Calibrated Confidence for Reliable Straight-Through Processing of Financial Documents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20110)
*Yichao Jin,Yushuo Wang,Yuxuan Han,Kwan Ching Yee Sonia,Weiyang Song,Chiu Jin-Chun Kent,Wong Chong Hwee,Wong Tiong Kiat,Kenneth Zhu Ke,Jingyuan Zhao*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Introduces a three-channel decomposed confidence layer plus conformal risk control to enable reliable straight-through processing for VLM-extracted key-value fields from financial documents; achieves large AUROC gains and higher auto-approval rates while meeting error targets.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: VLMs provide out-of-the-box key-value extraction but their verbalized confidence scores poorly reflect correctness, hindering safe automatic approval in financial document processing.

Method: Decomposed confidence score across perception, layout, and validation channels, combined with conformal risk control; evaluated on real/synthetic invoices and ad-buy forms using Qwen3.6-27B and Gemini-3.1-Flash-Lite; measures include AUROC for correct vs incorrect extraction separation.

Result: AUROC improved from 0.54-0.74 (verbalized signals) to 0.90-0.99 with the three channels; native VLM confidence clears 0.1%-7.0% under risk control at target <10%; proposed method auto-approves 49-72% of fields while empirical error stays at or below target.

Conclusion: The three-channel decomposed confidence layer with conformal risk control enables reliable STP in financial document extraction, significantly improving automatic acceptances without compromising error bounds, across multiple datasets and VLM families.

Abstract: Straight-through processing (STP) on extracted key-value fields from financial documents without human review requires a calibrated probability together with a bounded guarantee on the residual error of the auto-approved tier. The emergence of modern Vision Language Models (VLMs) provides an out-of-the-box capability for extracting the key-values, but their verbalized confidence signals are unreliable and weakly track field correctness. This paper introduces a decomposed confidence layer along three interpretable channels, including perception, layout, and validation. Together with a final conformal risk control, the score can be used for reliable STP of financial documents. The method is validated on three public datasets covering real invoices, synthetic invoices, and ad-buy forms, using two different VLM families (Qwen3.6-27B and Gemini-3.1-Flash-Lite). Our decomposed score consistently improves the separation of correct from incorrect extractions, substantially raising the AUROC from 0.54-0.74 for VLM verbalized signals to 0.90-0.99 with contributions from all three designed channels. Crucially for industrial deployment, this enables usable STP. The native VLM confidence signals could clear only 0.1%-7.0% of fields under risk control at a target error of <10%. In contrast, the proposed method auto-approves 49-72% of fields while holding the empirical error of the accepted tier at or below the target.

</details>


### [387] [MTVA-Bench: Evaluating the Language Model Inside Cascaded Voice Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20152)
*Pritish Mishra,Ishaan Kumar,Akshat Mandoli,Sudarshan Kamath*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: MTVA-Bench proposes a multi-turn voice agent benchmark to evaluate LMs within cascaded ASR-LM-TTS systems under realistic constraints, using 490 scenarios across 7 languages and dual-judge scoring to diagnose tool-use behavior.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To better isolate language-model decision quality in conversational voice systems, bridging shortcomings of end-to-end and isolated LM benchmarks, and to surface error modes related to tool use, script compliance, and multi-turn discourse.

Method: Create a benchmark with 49 agents, 490 scenarios, 7 languages. The caller is simulated by an LLM following rubrics; a mock backend responds to the model's tool-call arguments. Scoring combines deterministic tool-call checks and two LLM judges, who cite transcript messages, for scenario-level rules and conversation quality. Task and conversation scores are equally weighted. Evaluations across six models assess tool selection and overall performance.

Result: Across a seven-model study, six models chose the correct tool within 6.4 points of each other, yet overall scores span 24.4 points, indicating large variance in governance of arguments, action ordering, rule adherence, and phrasing around tool calls.

Conclusion: MTVA-Bench highlights that LM behavior around tool invocation and script compliance largely drives performance in multi-turn voice tasks. It provides a scalable, multilingual framework to diagnose and improve conversational tool-use in cascaded speech systems, with potential improvements in rubric design, realism, and evaluation reliability.

Abstract: Generally, most voice agents are cascaded systems, i.e., an ASR model transcribes the caller's audio, a language model reads the transcript and decides what to say and which backend tools to call, and a TTS model speaks the reply. Nearly all of the decision making happens in the language model, but existing evaluations measure it either too broadly or too narrowly. End-to-end voice benchmarks score the full pipeline, so recognition errors and model errors mix into a single number. LLM benchmarks isolate the model but they do not evaluate what makes real phone calls hard, such as transcription issues, caller's voice being split across messages and the requirement that replies follow the language and script specified. We introduce the Multi-Turn Voice Agent Benchmark (MTVA-Bench), which evaluates the language model on the same conditions it faces inside a cascaded system. The caller is played by an LLM following a set of rubrics and tool calls are answered by a mock backend which responds to the arguments the model actually sent. The benchmark contains 49 agents working across 490 reviewed scenarios and supports 7 languages. Scoring is a combination of deterministic checks on tool calls with two LLM judges, one that scores scenario specific rules and one that grades conversation quality without access to the task. Both judges must cite specific messages from the transcript. Task and conversation scores are weighted equally, since a call can complete its task and still go badly for the caller. In a seven-model study, six of the models select the correct tool within 6.4 points of one another, but their overall scores span 24.4 points. Most of the gap comes from argument values, action ordering, rule compliance, and what the model says around its tool calls.

</details>


### [388] [PaGNet: A Panel-Aware GBDT--Neural Network for Multi-Target Corporate Tax Avoidance Proxy Forecasting](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20177)
*Wonho Song,Hyungjoon Kim*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: PaGNet combines a panel-temporal LightGBM branch with an attention-based Panel-MLP branch, fused via per-target, trainable-free blending to forecast corporate tax-avoidance proxies with explicit branch-reliance diagnostics; it yields modest but robust gains in explained variance on a Korean firm-panel dataset, and provides interpretable insights into which branch drives which targets.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Forecasting tax-avoidance proxies from firm-year data is challenging due to dispersed predictive signals across short histories and targets, while screening needs transparent, interpretable model behavior. The authors seek a hybrid, panel-aware approach that preserves predictive power and offers per-target interpretability without trainable fusion.

Method: A two-branch hybrid: (1) LightGBM branch using panel-temporal summaries; (2) Panel-MLP branch using attention-pooled temporal aggregation with a shared trunk for multi-task learning. A per-target, validation-optimal blender combines branches without trainable fusion parameters, yielding final predictions and a compact branch-reliance diagnostic. Evaluation on KoTaP (1,754 Korean firms, 2011–2024) under leakage-free, shared-hyperparameter protocol across four feature regimes.

Result: In FS1 (lag-excluded) and FS2 (tax-history-augmented), accrual targets (TSTA, TSDA) predominantly route to the LightGBM branch, with PaGNet increasing explained variance by ~0.08–0.11 on the primary split over the strongest baselines. GETR tends toward the neural branch, CETR reveals a validation–test branch-selection mismatch. A panel-flatten control indicates gains mainly come from multi-year base-panel values, with the panel-aware representation providing a smaller but directionally consistent refinement. Rolling-origin analysis confirms stable accrual routing, bounds ETR diagnostics to split-specific behavior, and shows a far-horizon split where supervised models underperform persistence.

Conclusion: PaGNet should be viewed as a proxy-aware panel model that blends competitive forecasting with explicit per-target branch-reliance reporting, rather than a universally superior tabular learner. It offers interpretable, per-target insights and robust performance in panel forecasting contexts where signals are distributed across histories and targets.

Abstract: Forecasting corporate tax avoidance proxies from firm--year panel data is challenging because predictive signals are distributed across short firm histories and related targets, while screening-oriented use requires transparent model behavior. We propose PaGNet (Panel-Aware GBDT--Neural Network), a two-branch hybrid that combines a LightGBM branch using panel-temporal summaries with a Panel-MLP branch using attention-pooled temporal aggregation and shared-trunk multi-task learning. A per-target validation-optimal blender produces both the final prediction and a compact branch-reliance diagnostic without trainable fusion parameters. On the KoTaP panel of 1{,}754 Korean listed firms from 2011--2024, PaGNet is evaluated under a leakage-free, shared-hyperparameter protocol across four feature regimes. In the direct-proxy-lag-excluded FS1 regime and the tax-history-augmented FS2 regime, accrual targets (TSTA, TSDA) route stably to the LightGBM branch, where PaGNet raises explained variance over the strongest of six baselines by roughly $0.08$--$0.11$ on the primary split. GETR often leans toward the neural branch, while CETR exposes a validation--test branch-selection mismatch rather than a stable branch assignment. A panel-flatten control shows that most accrual gains come from observed multi-year base-panel values, with PaGNet's panel-aware representation adding a smaller but directionally consistent refinement. Rolling-origin analysis confirms stable accrual routing, bounds ETR diagnostics to split-specific behavior, and identifies a far-horizon split where supervised models underperform naive persistence. PaGNet is therefore best viewed not as a universally superior tabular learner, but as a proxy-aware panel model that combines competitive forecasting with explicit per-target branch-reliance reporting.

</details>


### [389] [Sequential Contextual Fit Predicts Human Behavioural and Neural Dynamics Across Domains](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20179)
*Kun Sun,Rong Wang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: A universal embedding-based metric (SCF) quantifies contextual fit between current information state and recent context, using a recency-weighted similarity kernel; demonstrated across language, music emotion, audiovisual EEG, gambling decisions, activity recognition, and decision-related EEG. Lower SCF predicts longer processing times, larger affective/behavioral transitions, and stronger neural-state changes, beyond traditional predictors.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To develop a domain-general predictor of contextual compatibility in sequential processing, unifying perceptual, cognitive, and neural state dynamics across modalities.

Method: Compute sequential contextual fit (SCF) via a simple recency-weighted similarity kernel applied to embeddings of the current state and recent context. Evaluate SCF across multiple domains: language processing, music-evoked emotion, audiovisual emotion EEG, gambling decisions, human activity recognition, and decision-related EEG, while controlling for established predictors (surprisal, RL prediction error, acoustic/visual/sensor change).

Result: Lower SCF associated with longer processing times, larger transitions in affective/behavioral measures, and larger neural-state changes. Effects persist after controlling for known predictors, indicating SCF captures a distinct contextual compatibility signal.

Conclusion: SCF provides a general computational measurement layer linking contextual compatibility to behavioral processing and cognitive/neural state-transition dynamics, with broad applicability across modalities and tasks.

Abstract: Human perception, action and decision making unfold in sequences, but computational predictors are often domain-specific. This study computes and tests sequential contextual fit (SCF), an embedding-based measure of how well a current information state matches its recent context. The metric uses a simple recency-weighted similarity kernel and can be applied to words, sounds, visual scenes, affective states, choices, actions and neural representations. Across language processing, music-evoked emotion, a subset of audiovisual emotion EEG data, gambling decisions, human activity recognition and decision-related EEG, lower contextual fit predicted longer processing times, larger affective or behavioural transitions and stronger neural-state changes. These effects remained after controlling for established predictors including surprisal, reinforcement-learning prediction error, acoustic change, visual change and sensor change. SCF therefore provides a computational measurement layer for relating contextual compatibility to behavioural processing and cognitive/neural state-transition dynamics.

</details>


### [390] [JointMatch: A Unified Heterogeneous Graph Neural Solver for Large-Scale Ride-Sharing Matching](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20200)
*Kun Zhao,Xu Chen*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: JointMatch jointly optimizes request pairing and vehicle assignment for ride-sharing using a graph neural network on a sparsified proximity graph, achieving faster and more revenue-aligned dispatching than two-stage methods and heuristics.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Traditional two-stage formulations for ride-sharing dispatch (pairing then assignment) commit to bundles before vehicle availability is known, causing revenue loss and poor scalability. A joint, end-to-end approach can better leverage information about both requests and vehicles.

Method: Construct a sparse interaction graph based on spatial proximity. Use a graph neural network to score all candidate decisions (pairings and assignments) in a single forward pass, enabling end-to-end learning. Train in two stages: supervised pretraining to recover revenue; policy-gradient fine-tuning to align with realized revenue.

Result: On NYC Yellow Taxi data, JointMatch outperforms Blossom heuristic and a faithfully-trained two-stage GNN baseline, often by a wide margin. At fleet size 10,000, it runs >20x faster per dispatch epoch than both baselines. Supervised training recovers most revenue; policy-gradient fine-tuning further aligns outcomes with revenue.

Conclusion: End-to-end, graph-based joint decision-making for ride-sharing dispatches with sparsified graphs yields substantial revenue gains and scalability advantages over traditional two-stage methods and heuristic baselines, with a practical training regime.

Abstract: Ride-sharing platforms must continuously decide which open requests to bundle into shared trips and which idle vehicles should serve them. The dominant academic approach decomposes this into two sequential matching problems -- request pairing first, then vehicle assignment -- and applies a separate solver to each. This decomposition is convenient computationally but loses revenue and scales poorly because the first stage commits to ride bundles before the available vehicles are known. We propose JointMatch, a learning-based framework that handles request pairing and vehicle assignment together on a single graph. The graph is sparsified by spatial proximity so that its size grows linearly rather than quadratically with the number of vehicles and requests, and a graph neural network scores all candidate decisions in one forward pass. On the New York City Yellow Taxi data, the framework already exceeds both the classical Blossom heuristic and a faithfully-trained two-stage GNN baseline -- often by a wide margin -- and at city scale (fleet 10000) it runs more than $20\times$ faster per dispatch epoch than either. A supervised training stage closes most of the remaining revenue gap, and a policy-gradient fine-tune aligns the trained model with realised revenue.

</details>


### [391] [When AI Agents Commit: Cognitive Serializability Across Data, Evidence, Policy, and Authority](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20261)
*Jun He,Deying Yu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Proposes Cognitive Transaction Theory (TCT) for secure, serializable reasoning in autonomous agents, combining immutable definitions, sealed provenance, and guard-first commits; validated by a falsification suite showing zero injected anomalies and ~3.22 ms commit overhead.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Ensure input integrity and deterministic reasoning in agentic workflows where reads, evidence, policies, beliefs, and delegated authority may change during reasoning, by establishing formal, verifiable transaction semantics and serializability guarantees.

Method: Defines cognitive serializability and an effect-compatible admission, and then builds TCT: immutable versioned executable definitions, registry-based authority plans, sealed envelopes, guard-first commit transactions, post-seal envelope and witness-bound grants, co-committed receipts, idempotent grant finalization, and receipt-driven epistemic reconciliation; enforces a complete registered footprint and a single growing phase to yield an acyclic lock-point order over guards and external reservations.

Result: Derives serializability conditions and an observational-equivalence boundary for zero-error soundness with positive progress. A falsification suite shows the prototype prevents all injected anomalies and incurs a mean commit overhead of 3.22 ms.

Conclusion: The framework furnishes a rigorous, implementable basis for reliable, provenance-rich autonomous reasoning with strong correctness and performance guarantees, demonstrated by formal conditions and a practical prototype.

Abstract: Autonomous agents derive concrete mutations from database reads, retrieved evidence, policy, beliefs, and delegated authority. Those inputs may change while reasoning is in progress. Database isolation orders the submitted transaction; agentic transaction processing determines whether a proposal satisfies an executable contract. Neither guarantee establishes a common valid point for the mutation and its derivation inputs unless the contract represents the relevant predicates. Typed dependency tokens distinguish content integrity from applicability, and trusted mediation captures the values exposed to reasoning. Under strict Cognitive Serializability, committed effects admit a serial order and a logical event at which every value exposed to derivation is unchanged. The fences last until the runtime event that realizes the sealed durability domain. The weaker Effect-Compatible Cognitive Admission recertifies an effect against a simultaneously held current dependency vector and current policy without claiming to serialize the original stochastic derivation. TCT combines immutable versioned executable definitions, registry-derived authority plans, sealed envelopes, guard-first commit transactions, post-seal envelope- and witness-bound grants, co-committed receipts, idempotent grant finalization, and receipt-driven epistemic reconciliation. Complete registered footprints and a single growing phase induce an acyclic lock-point order over local guards and incompatible external reservations. The corresponding results give serializability conditions and an observational-equivalence boundary for zero-error soundness and positive progress. A falsification suite tests the implementation obligations: the prototype prevented all injected anomalies and added 3.22 ms mean commit overhead.

</details>


### [392] [AI-Driven Real-Time Relay Optimisation in Smart Urban NR-V2X Networks via Learning-to-Optimise Graph Neural Networks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20271)
*Giambattista Amati,Federica Mangiatordi,Emiliano Pallotti,Simone Angelini*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: An AI-driven L2O framework using graph neural networks (GNNs) with edge features is trained via offline MILP supervision to perform real-time multi-hop relay selection in NR-V2X. It models the network as a graph of CAVs/RSUs, yielding near-optimal connectivity with substantial runtime speed-ups (up to 100x) for scalable smart city/Industry 4.0 deployment.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Address limited RSU deployment and complex urban propagation that hinder stable connectivity for CAVs in NR-V2X, requiring reliable, low-latency, scalable relay decisions.

Method: Model vehicular network as a graph with nodes (CAVs/RSUs) and edge features representing radio links. Use an offline MILP to compute optimal relaying, then train an edge-aware Graph Isomorphism Network with Edge Features (GINE) to imitate these decisions (supervised learning). Evaluate on realistic urban datasets for real-time performance.

Result: The approach achieves near-optimal connectivity, gaining up to 11.3% connectivity improvement, while delivering up to 100x speed-up in execution time compared to MILP, demonstrating scalability and real-time applicability.

Conclusion: An effective L2O framework that combines MILP supervision with edge-aware GINE enables scalable, real-time multi-hop relay decisions in NR-V2X, suitable for smart city and Industry 4.0 deployments.

Abstract: Reliable and low-latency communication is a fundamental requirement for smart city services and Industry 4.0 applications enabled by NR-V2X networks. However, limited Road-Side Unit (RSU) deployment and complex urban propagation conditions often prevent Connected and Automated Vehicles (CAVs) from maintaining stable connectivity. This paper proposes an AI-driven Learning-to-Optimise (L2O) framework based on Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) for real-time multi-hop relay selection in NR-V2X systems. The vehicular network is modelled as a graph, where nodes represent CAVs and RSUs, and edges encode radio-link characteristics. An offline Mixed-Integer Linear Programming (MILP) formulation provides optimal relay decisions used as supervision for training an edge-aware Graph Isomorphism Network with Edge Features (GINE). Extensive experiments on realistic urban datasets demonstrate that the proposed approach achieves near-optimal connectivity performance, recovering up to 11.3% connectivity gain, while reducing execution time by orders of magnitude (up to 100 x speed-up) compared to MILP. The framework enables scalable and real-time network control, making it suitable for smart city and Industry 4.0 deployments.

</details>


### [393] [JEPA-WAM: Connecting Generated Visual Instructions to World Action Models through JEPA Latent Representations](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20277)
*Tianbin Liu,Jian Zhu,Taiyi Su,Jianjun Zhang,Chong Ma,Zitai Huang,Yi Xu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: JEPA-WAM improves instruction-following in World Action Models by augmenting text instructions with diverse, semantically aligned visual references generated from a text-to-image model, encoded by a frozen V-JEPA 2.1 encoder, and integrated via cross-attention; achieves strong real-robot performance across ID and OOD settings.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Address the data imbalance in robot learning where rich visual-action trajectories are paired with sparse language annotations, causing policies to rely on visual cues rather than the instruction itself. Provide diverse visual goal references to ground instructions.

Method: For each text instruction, sample multiple task-completion images using a pre-trained text-to-image generator without training. Encode these references with a frozen V-JEPA 2.1 encoder and compress into dense goal tokens. Condition both video and action experts via cross-attention. Evaluate on a real-robot benchmark across in-distribution, out-of-distribution scene, and out-of-distribution instruction settings.

Result: Real-robot benchmark: success rates 87.3% (ID), 74.5% (OOD scene), 80.9% (OOD instruction). JEPA-WAM outperforms π0 and Fast-WAM by at least 10.0, 27.3, and 14.5 percentage points respectively.

Conclusion: Augmenting text with semantically aligned, diverse visual cues significantly improves instruction grounding in WAMs, enabling better generalization to unseen scenes and instructions.

Abstract: World Action Models (WAMs) have demonstrated strong robotic manipulation capabilities by augmenting pretrained video generative models with action experts. However, current WAMs still show limited instruction-following ability when conditioned solely on text instructions. We argue that this limitation stems in part from a structural imbalance in robot-learning data: rich visual-action trajectories are often paired with sparse and repetitive language annotations, allowing policies to identify tasks from visual context and motion regularities rather than grounding the instruction itself. To address this limitation, we introduce JEPA-WAM, which augments each text instruction with a bank of stochastically generated visual instructions, providing diverse visual cues for instruction following. Specifically, JEPA-WAM uses an off-the-shelf text-to-image generator to sample multiple task-completion images conditioned on the text instruction, without training the generator. Although these generated images may differ from the current visual scene in appearance and layout, they remain semantically aligned with the instruction and serve as visual goal references. To focus on task-level semantics beyond appearance, we encode these references with a frozen V-JEPA 2.1 encoder.
