The resulting dense goal representations are compressed into compact goal tokens that condition both the video and action experts through cross-attention. We further construct a real-robot instruction-following benchmark covering in-distribution, out-of-distribution scene, and out-of-distribution instruction settings. On this benchmark, JEPA-WAM achieves success rates of 87.3%, 74.5%, and 80.9% in these three settings, outperforming π0 and Fast-WAM by at least 10.0, 27.3, and 14.5 percentage points, respectively.

</details>


### [394] [AgentPProf: Semantic Profiler for Long Horizon AI Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20301)
*Yusheng Zheng,Chaokun Chang,Yu Mao,Tianyuan Wu,Yuxi Huang,Tao Ma,Wenan Mao,Shuyi Cheng,Andi Quinn,Wei Wang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: AgentPProf profiles long-running AI agent trajectories using a semantic operation stack and recursive segmentation to attribute resources across tasks, enabling flame-graph-style profiling and cross-run analysis for cost and safety optimization.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing agent observability focuses on per-run debugging; there is a need for cross-run, long-term profiling to locate hotspots, trigger points for unsafe effects, and budget-heavy tasks, despite lack of stable task identifiers.

Method: Propose a semantic operation stack model with uniform operations and operation stacks as at-runtime abstractions. Use hierarchical attribution and recursive operation segmentation to split trajectories at task boundaries, and aggregate trajectories into pprof-compatible profiles for flame-graph visualization.

Result: AgentPProf achieves 0.764 B^3 F1 against human annotations on CodeTraceBench. On three problem-localization benchmarks, profile-based metrics improve MAP by up to 56%. Open-source at https://github.com/eunomia-bpf/agentsight.

Conclusion: The approach effectively attributes resources, localizes problems, and supports cost optimization for agent systems, providing a scalable profiling solution with practical profiling cost.

Abstract: AI agents increasingly orchestrate long-running activities with users, tools, and system resources for days and weeks. To improve agent quality, safety, and cost efficiency, developers need to determine where failures happen, what triggers unsafe effects, and which tasks consume the most budget, then optimize those tasks. In systems software, profiling answers similar questions by aggregating resource consumption and attributing it to responsible code paths to identify hotspots. Yet existing agent observability tools focus on per-execution debugging and tracing rather than cross-run, long term profiling, making these questions difficult to answer at scale. Agent observability needs profiling, not only debugging, but profiling agents is challenging: the responsible entities are task intent like diagnose authentication, compare branches rather than code paths, and lack stable identifiers for aggregation. We propose a semantic operation stack model that adapts profiling to agent trajectories. Uniform operations represent all activities, and operation stacks replace the runtime call stack, enabling hierarchical attribution at different granularities. We observe that an agent's task occupies a contiguous span and decomposes into subtasks, so we introduce recursive operation segmentation, which recursively splits trajectories at task boundaries. AgentPProf is a profiler that aggregates agent trajectories into pprof-compatible profiles, enabling flame graph visualization and analysis. AgentPProf reaches 0.764 $B^3$ F1 against human annotations on CodeTraceBench. On three problem-localization benchmarks, the profile raises MAP by up to 56%, demonstrating that it effectively attributes resources, locates problems, and helps optimize token cost at practical profiling cost. AgentPProf is available at https://github.com/eunomia-bpf/agentsight.

</details>


### [395] [Diagnose, Recover, Certify: Task Readiness under Hidden Dynamics Changes](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20304)
*Nguyen Viet Tuan Kiet,Huynh Thi Thanh Binh*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: A decision framework for dormant actuator drift that unifies diagnosis and post-change recovery under a limited interaction budget, via Evidence-Gated Matched-Pulse Transport (EGMPT), enabling task-conditioned policy selection with readiness certification and selective fallback. Evaluated on dormant-actuator benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Deployed policies may hide consequential dynamics changes; current task unaffected but future tasks require localization of changes and recovery; need a task-agnostic interaction budget to diagnose and recover before task identity is revealed.

Method: Intervention-based Bayesian procedure coupling fault localization with actuator effectiveness estimation using a shared matched-response representation; Evidence-Gated Matched-Pulse Transport propagates diagnostic uncertainty to task-conditioned policy selection and readiness certification; supports deployment decisions that trade off expected performance, confidence, and fallback use.

Result: Benchmarks across multiple simulators show the framework effectively separates diagnosis from recovery, achieving readiness coverage and accounting for interaction cost and return; identifies regimes where transported evidence is decisive.

Conclusion: The framework provides a principled, task-agnostic approach to diagnose and recover from dormant-dynamics changes under limited interactions, enabling informed deployment decisions with quantified risk and fallback strategies.

Abstract: A deployed control policy can conceal consequential dynamics changes: an actuator may lose effectiveness without affecting the current task when the policy rarely excites it, despite being critical for a future task that has not yet been specified. We introduce task readiness under dormant dynamics drift, a decision problem that unifies active change diagnosis and post-change control recovery under a limited, task-agnostic interaction budget. An agent must identify whether and where local dynamics have changed, use a small number of informative interactions to characterize the change before downstream task identity is revealed, and subsequently provide each candidate task with either a recovered policy and a calibrated lower bound on its achievable return or an abstention decision to a safe fallback. We propose Evidence-Gated Matched-Pulse Transport, an intervention-based Bayesian procedure that couples fault localization with estimation of actuator effectiveness through a shared matched-response representation, thereby preserving diagnostic reliability while converting localized evidence into recovery-relevant uncertainty. This uncertainty is propagated to task-conditioned policy selection and readiness certification, enabling deployment decisions that explicitly trade off expected performance, confidence, and fallback use. We evaluate the resulting framework on a diverse suite of dormant-actuator benchmarks spanning multiple simulators, under a protocol that separates diagnosis from capability recovery, scores deployment by readiness coverage, selective risk, and interaction cost as well as return, and identifies the fault regimes in which transported evidence is decisive.

</details>


### [396] [NeuSOGA3D: A Neuro-Symbolic Framework for Explainable 3D Geometric Reconstruction](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20323)
*Qingde Li,Qingqi Hong,Zihan Li,Jie Tian*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Hybrid neuro-symbolic 3D reconstruction combining learned priors with explicit symbolic geometry to yield CAD-friendly representations from unorganized point clouds.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Neural implicit methods offer high reconstruction accuracy but rely on latent representations, reducing interpretability and hindering reuse in engineering workflows; a symbolic, CAD-friendly alternative is desirable.

Method: NeuSOGA3D projects point clouds onto principal orthographic planes, builds symbolic implicit spline representations from the observations, and fuses them via shape-preserving constructive solid geometry (CSG) operations to produce a coarse visual hull. It adds geometric detail through cross-sectional decomposition and volumetric reconstruction using Partial Shape-Preserving Splines. The pipeline progressively transforms observations into explicit symbolic entities (control polygons, implicit spline fields, cross-sections, volumetric lofts).

Result: Experiments on ModelNet40 across 40 categories show the framework can recover structurally meaningful and CAD-compatible geometric representations from diverse point-cloud data, illustrating the viability of combining learned perception with symbolic geometric reasoning for explainable geometric intelligence.

Conclusion: NeuSOGA3D demonstrates the potential of a neuro-symbolic approach for 3D reconstruction that yields interpretable, CAD-friendly geometry and integrates well with engineering workflows.

Abstract: Three-dimensional reconstruction from unorganized point clouds remains a challenging problem in computer vision, geometric modeling, and computer-aided design. While neural implicit methods achieve impressive reconstruction accuracy, geometry is typically encoded in latent representations that limit interpretability and reuse within engineering workflows.
  We present NeuSOGA3D (Neuro-Symbolic Geometric Abstraction in 3D), a hybrid framework that combines learned perceptual priors inherited from NeuSOGA with explicit symbolic geometric reasoning. The method projects point clouds onto principal orthographic planes, constructs symbolic implicit spline representations from the resulting observations, and fuses them through shape-preserving constructive solid geometry operations to generate a coarse visual hull. Additional geometric detail is recovered through cross-sectional decomposition and volumetric reconstruction using Partial Shape-Preserving Splines.
  Unlike conventional neural implicit approaches, NeuSOGA3D progressively transforms observations into explicit symbolic entities, including control polygons, implicit spline fields, cross-sections, and volumetric lofts. Experiments on all forty categories of the ModelNet40 benchmark demonstrate the ability of the framework to recover structurally meaningful and CAD-compatible geometric representations from diverse point-cloud observations. The results highlight the potential of combining learned perception with symbolic geometric reasoning for explainable geometric intelligence.

</details>


### [397] [Structured Four-Stage Legal Translation: From Natural-Language Traffic Rules to PROLOG](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20334)
*May Myo Zin,Wachara Fungwacharakorn,Ken Satoh,Katsumi Nitta*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: A Structured Four-Stage Legal Translation (S4L→Prolog) framework markedly improves translating traffic rules into executable Prolog over two baselines, achieving 75% accuracy on 20 rules, and better capturing implicit relations and modalities; demonstrates benefits of structured prompts for legal/safety-critical NL-to-logic translation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To address ambiguity and underspecification in natural-language traffic regulations and provide executable, precise logic for reasoning engines in safety-critical domains.

Method: Introduce S4L→Prolog, a four-stage guided-prompt pipeline: semantic role extraction, scene completion, logical mapping, and Prolog rule generation. Compare against NL→Prolog and LE→Prolog baselines using 20 real-world traffic rules, evaluated on syntactic validity, semantic correctness, and logical completeness.

Result: S4L→Prolog achieves 75% correctness; NL→Prolog 60%; LE→Prolog 55%. Qualitative analysis shows S4L more reliably captures implicit causal relations, deontic modality, and exception structures.

Conclusion: Structured reasoning prompts substantially improve NL-to-logic translation for legal/safety-critical applications, enabling more reliable, executable representations of natural-language rules without human intervention.

Abstract: Traffic regulations are written for human interpretation and therefore rely on shared background knowledge and flexible phrasing, which inherently introduce ambiguity, context dependence, and semantic underspecification. These linguistic characteristics conflict with the precision required by computational reasoning engines such as Prolog, which demand explicit logical structure. This study evaluates two baseline translation approaches, Natural Language to Prolog ($NL\rightarrow Prolog$) and Logical English to Prolog ($LE\rightarrow Prolog$), and introduces a new reasoning-guided translation framework called Structured Four-Stage Legal Translation ($S4L\rightarrow Prolog$). The proposed S4L framework performs semantic role extraction, scene completion, logical mapping, and Prolog rule generation within a single guided prompt, enabling direct translation of raw traffic rules into executable logic without human intervention. A benchmark consisting of twenty real-world traffic rules was used to evaluate each approach in terms of syntactic validity, semantic correctness, and logical completeness. $S4L\rightarrow Prolog$ achieves the highest accuracy, correctly formalizing 75 percent of the rules, while $NL\rightarrow Prolog$ reaches 60 percent and $LE\rightarrow Prolog$ reaches 55 percent. Qualitative analysis further shows that S4L captures implicit causal relations, deontic modality, and exception structure more reliably than the baselines. These results demonstrate that structured reasoning prompts can substantially improve the reliability of natural-language-to-logic translation for legal and safety-critical applications.

</details>


### [398] [A Qualitative Model for Reasoning about Path and Support](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20349)
*Abhishek Jaiswal,Zoe Falomir*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Hybrid qualitative reasoning model integrates symbolic QR with center-of-mass stability logic to guide a Camelot Jr. solver, enabling interpretable feedback for spatial skill training.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Spatial reasoning skills strongly relate to STEM performance; games can train these skills, but require AI that can make commonsense, interpretable inferences from spatial events; qualitative reasoning provides symbolic, explainable representations for human-like tutoring.

Method: Develop a hybrid QR framework that translates Camelot Jr. states into qualitative representations and augments them with a mathematical center-of-mass stability check to resolve actions; a qualitative solver guides platform stability, path planning, and block usage to construct multi-level bridges.

Result: The work introduces the model and demonstrates its applicability to Camelot Jr., outlining an explainable solver for spatial tasks; the abstract emphasizes feasibility and potential for training and human-centric guidance, with no reported empirical evaluation in this abstract.

Conclusion: The hybrid QR-COM approach enables explainable, human-centric game-playing agents for spatial skill development and could generalize to other physics-based, symbolic-reasoning domains.

Abstract: Spatial reasoning abilities correlate strongly with performance in STEM fields. Games offer a compelling medium for training these critical skills in developing children who have a natural proclivity for play. However, to facilitate human-like tutoring and player guidance, these games require an AI agent capable of making commonsense inferences from spatial events. Qualitative reasoning (QR) models appear to be a suitable framework for these application domains. As these models reason in symbolic representations, they can seamlessly translate game states into interpretable feedback for human-like player guidance. This paper introduces a hybrid qualitative model designed for Camelot Jr., a block-puzzle game that requires constructing multi-level bridges to connect two avatars stationed on separate towers. The game poses a challenge for the player, who must make platforms stable, plan their path, and ensure they use all the provided blocks. To handle the precise physics required by the domain, we integrate a mathematical center-of-mass stability logic to guide our qualitative solver. Our work facilitates spatial skill training in Camelot Jr. and contributes to the development of human-centric, explainable game-playing agents.

</details>


### [399] [Generating Heterogeneous 3D Geological Microstructures from 2D Images via a Stable Diffusion-Adversarial Model](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20358)
*Ali Aouf,Eric Laloy,Bart Rogiers,Christophe De Vleeschouwer*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: A diffusion-model–based 3D microstructure generator uses an adversarial loss to train without 3D ground truth, improving on SliceGAN for complex heterogeneous materials by yielding artefact-minimal 3D volumes that match phase fractions and structural descriptors.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: 3D property simulations require expensive 3D imaging; 2D images are more accessible. GAN-based 3D generation from 2D data shows promise, but SliceGAN struggles with complex heterogeneous microstructures. A stable, high-fidelity generative framework for 3D microstructures from 2D data is needed.

Method: Introduce a hybrid approach that combines denoising diffusion models with an adversarial loss, circumventing the need for 3D ground truth. Train for 3D microstructure generation from 2D slices, achieving stable training and generating volumes with varying complexity and minimal slice artefacts.

Result: The proposed model produces 3D microstructures across a range of complexities, with minimal slice artefacts and close agreement to ground-truth phase fractions and structural descriptors.

Conclusion: A diffusion-adversarial hybrid effectively overcomes SliceGAN limitations, enabling stable, high-fidelity 3D microstructure generation from 2D data for heterogeneous materials.

Abstract: Characterizing the physical properties of clay and cementitious materials matters across many fields, from materials science to geological waste disposal. Property simulation typically calls for 3D imaging, which is expensive, not always accessible, and technically limited for certain materials. Recent progress in deep generative models offers a way around this, reconstructing 3D volumes from the more easily acquired 2D images.
  Among GAN-based methods for 3D microstructure generation, SliceGAN has shown strong results for homogeneous isotropic and anisotropic systems. It struggles, however, to capture the finer detail of more complex heterogeneous microstructures, which motivates alternative generative frameworks.
  We introduce a hybrid approach that draws on the stability and generation quality of denoising diffusion models. Since no 3D ground truth is available, we replace the standard denoising loss with an adversarial loss, which yields a stable training process in our experiments. We show that the resulting model generates microstructures of varying complexity with minimal slice artefacts and close agreement with ground-truth phase fractions and structural descriptors.

</details>


### [400] [The Organization of Inference: Information, Resource Constraints, and AI Production](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20449)
*Yukun Zhang,Kemu Xu,Yishen Chen*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Resource distribution across AI production stages determines economic value; information-constrained planning under limited capacity reduces performance relative to direct execution, but the gap narrows with scale and task-informed planning becomes advantageous at higher token ceilings.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Understand how capacity allocation and task information distribution across stages affect productive value in AI systems, by isolating planning versus direct execution and assessing how information access (e.g., task issue visibility) and token ceilings influence outcomes.

Method: Controlled workflow experiments on externally verified software-engineering tasks with two matched resource panels. Comparisons between direct execution and information-constrained planning across token ceilings of 12,000 and 24,000. Manipulations include issue access to the planner and measurement of success rates, binding rates, and downstream execution contributions.

Result: Direct execution achieves 59.6% success at both token ceilings. Information-constrained planning improves from 36.2% to 51.2%, narrowing the planning disadvantage by 15.0 percentage points (CI 4.2–25.8). Issue access raises success by ~16 percentage points at 12k tokens. At 12k tokens, task-informed planning lags direct execution by ~10 points; at 24k tokens, it gains a ~29.6-point advantage. Binding rate in planning drops from 46.2% to 0.8%; downstream execution accounts for 89.9% of total use increase. Scale determines capacity; workflow and information structure shape productive value.

Conclusion: Scale governs available capacity while workflow and information architecture govern how that capacity is used. Task-informed planning can outperform direct execution at higher capacities, and access to task information can materially affect outcomes under constrained planning. Overall, efficient distribution of resources and information across stages is crucial for maximizing the productive value of AI systems.

Abstract: The economic value of inference depends on how capacity and task information are distributed across stages of AI production. We study these organizational margins using controlled workflow experiments on externally verified software-engineering tasks. In two matched resource panels, direct execution records the same success rate of 59.6 percent at logical-token ceilings of 12,000 and 24,000, while success under information-constrained planning rises from 36.2 to 51.2 percent. The planning disadvantage narrows by 15.0 percentage points (95 percent task-cluster bootstrap interval: 4.2 to 25.8). A strict read-only planning campaign varies whether the planner sees the task issue. At 12,000 tokens, issue access raises success by about 16 percentage points over issue-hidden planning. Compared with direct execution, task-informed planning is about 10 points lower at 12,000 tokens; at 24,000 tokens, it shows a 29.6-point advantage. In the resource panels, direct execution uses substantially less than either ceiling, while the planning workflow's binding rate falls from 46.2 to 0.8 percent and downstream execution accounts for 89.9 percent of the increase in total use. Scale determines the capacity available to a system; workflow and information structure shape the productive value

</details>


### [401] [SkillAA: Attribution-Guided Skill-Graph Updating with Targeted Validation and Rollback](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20455)
*Ziqiao Shang,Ling-Yue Ge,Lan-Zhe Guo*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: SkillAA introduces a graph-based abductive attribution framework for frozen LMs, enabling targeted, topology-aware skill updates and validation via attribution-guided repair and graph-scoped checks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To address unstructured, ad hoc skill updates and underutilization of semantic boundaries and graph topology in skill retrieval, update routing, and validation.

Method: SkillAA represents skill applicability, execution, and composition in a unified graph, supporting skill selection, attribution-guided repair, and update validation. It contrasts successful and failed executions to route repairs to specific graph objects and updates only the selected local structure, with Local and Big Gates screening candidate changes before commitment.

Result: On gpt-5.6-sol, achieves 81.5% on SearchQA, 66.7% on LiveMath, and 91.2% on DocVQA, attaining the highest observed mean in every main setting.

Conclusion: Attribution-guided graph editing and graph-scoped validation are effective for controlled skill updates in frozen language models.

Abstract: External skills provide domain procedures without parameter updates, but existing methods often edit skills directly from failed rollouts without structured routing from an observed failure to an editable location; existing skill graphs also underuse semantic boundaries, object addresses, and topological dependencies for skill retrieval, targeted updating, and scoped validation. We introduce SkillAA (Skill Abductive Attribution), a structured skill-optimization framework for frozen language models. It represents skill applicability, execution, and composition in a unified graph, allowing the same structure to support skill selection, attribution-guided repair, and update validation. SkillAA contrasts successful and failed executions to route candidate repairs to specific graph objects, updates only the selected local structure, and uses Local and Big Gates to screen candidate changes before commitment. With gpt-5.6-sol, SkillAA reaches 81.5%, 66.7%, and 91.2% on SearchQA, LiveMath, and DocVQA, respectively, and attains the highest observed mean in every main setting. These results support the utility of attribution-guided graph editing and graph-scoped validation.

</details>


### [402] [How Do Agent Harnesses Create Value? Planning Information and Release Control in Stateful LLM Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20474)
*Yukun Zhang,Kemu Xu,Yishen Chen*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Fixed task-specific plans outpace shuffled guidance in two Retail tasks and an airline pilot benchmark, improving oracle-verified success by 7.17 points (90% CI 1.15–13.36), especially in high-complexity tasks. A read-only verifier rejects 61% of oracle-invalid Retail episodes and withholds 17% of correct ones at under $0.01 per episode. The relative value of planning vs verification depends on liability: planning dominates at low liability, while verifier-driven false-pass avoidance dominates at high liability; a standalone verifier captures most false-pass benefits at a fraction of the cost.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Disentangle the contribution of guidance content from plan form by comparing fixed (prewritten task-specific plans) against sham (word-count-matched but content-different) guidance across tasks, and assess how planning and verification affect success, rejection of erroneous acceptance, and cost under varying liability.

Method: Two Retail experiments and one Airline pilot in a τ^2-bench setting. 265 matched cells compare Fixed (prewritten task-specific plans) with Sham (shuffled policy text matched in word count). Outcomes: success, erroneous acceptance, and cost. Oracle verification distinguishes oracle-verified success from oracle-invalid episodes. A read-only terminal verifier is used to evaluate false-positives/false-negatives. Inference uses task-clustered bootstrap (90% interval).

Result: Fixed improves oracle-verified success by 7.17 percentage points (90% CI 1.15–13.36), with larger gains in high-complexity tasks. Read-only verifier rejects 61% of Retail oracle-invalid episodes and withholds 17% of correct episodes, at <1¢ cost per episode. The effect of guidance content vs verification depends on loss attributed to erroneous acceptance: low liability favors planning gains; high liability favors verifier-driven false-pass avoidance. A standalone verifier recovers nearly all false-pass benefit of the full planning-plus-verification stack at a fraction of the cost.

Conclusion: Guidance content (the actual plans) contributes nontrivially to performance, especially in complex tasks, but a lightweight verifier can capture most benefits of verification, and its value scales with liability. In risk-sensitive settings, a modular approach—planning with optional verification—can achieve similar false-acceptance reductions at lower cost compared to full planning+verification stacks.

Abstract: Agent harnesses supply planning guidance, organize execution, and check completion. We study how these components affect success, erroneous acceptance, and cost in two Retail experiments and an Airline pilot in $τ^2$-bench. The primary comparison pairs prewritten task-specific plans (Fixed) with shuffled policy text matched in word count (Sham), isolating the contribution of guidance content. Across 265 matched cells, Fixed improves oracle-verified success by 7.17 percentage points (90\% task-clustered bootstrap interval, 1.15--13.36 points), with gains concentrated in higher-complexity tasks. A read-only terminal verifier rejects 61\% of Retail oracle-invalid episodes while withholding 17\% of correct ones, at less than one cent of additional cost per episode. Which component matters more depends on the loss assigned to erroneous acceptance: at low liability the planning gain dominates; at high liability the verifier's avoided false passes dominate---and a standalone verifier captures nearly all the false-pass benefit of the full planning-plus-verification stack at a fraction of its cost.

</details>


### [403] [SoL-Pi: Recursively Scaling Auto-Research Loops for Efficient Agent Harness](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20519)
*Haozhe Liu,Tian Ye,Sensen Gao,Qihang Cao,Yitong Li,Mingchen Zhuge,Duomin Wang,Ruihua Zhang,Ping Luo,Jiawang Bian,Lei Zhu,Ligeng Zhu,Enze Xie,Song Han*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: SoL-Pi is a scalable harness framework that reduces token traffic and API costs while matching Pi's performance on EdgeBench tasks, enabling production-like auto-research with reusable improvements.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To improve token efficiency and scalability of auto-research loops in coding agents, by developing a robust harness layer that supports long-horizon reasoning, tool use, and feedback across diverse environments.

Method: RSI-inspired harness layer (SoL) that scales auto-research loops via four surviving mechanisms (action execution, context compaction, observation handling, delegated reading) across 51 tasks on EdgeBench, comparing against Pi on GPT-5.6 Sol and Opus 5.

Result: SoL-Pi achieves performance comparable to Pi on EdgeBench while cutting recorded token traffic by 44.7–49.0% and reducing API cost by ~33%; estimated hourly savings range from $8.75–$13.50 versus native Codex/Claude Code harnesses and $4.36–$5.71 versus Pi.

Conclusion: SoL-Pi demonstrates producible, transferable improvements in automated harness discovery at scale, enabling cost-efficient, production-grade auto-research across diverse environments.

Abstract: As coding agents move from supervised code completion to unattended, around-the-clock exploration, their work expands from isolated predictions into long trajectories of reasoning, tool use, and feedback. Token efficiency therefore becomes important for scaling recursive self-improvement. We take an RSI-inspired approach at the harness layer, scaling auto-research loops across increasingly numerous and diverse environments for harness rollouts. At this scale, the process yields reusable improvements that transfer beyond their development setting, moving automated harness discovery toward production-level outcomes. Four mechanisms survive selection and form SoL-Pi, spanning action execution, context compaction, observation handling, and delegated reading. On the 51-task EdgeBench evaluation, SoL-Pi achieves performance comparable to Pi across GPT-5.6 Sol and Opus 5 while reducing recorded token traffic by 44.7-49.0% and API cost by about one third. In other words, estimated hourly savings are \$8.75-\$13.50 relative to native Codex and Claude Code harnesses, and \$4.36-\$5.71 relative to Pi.

</details>


### [404] [FreqCondNorm: Towards Cross-domain Predictive Maintenance through a Frequency-Conditioned Transformer Foundation Model](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20535)
*Zaynab Raounak,Camille LHermine,Zhiguo Zeng*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: A frequency-conditioned FiLM normalization for Transformers unifies heterogeneous time-series in predictive maintenance, enabling strong fault-diagnosis transfer across sampling frequencies but not improving remaining useful life (RUL) prediction.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Address poor transferability of deep learning predictive maintenance across machines and sampling frequencies, especially with scarce labels and signals spanning large frequency ranges.

Method: Transformer with FiLM-style frequency-conditioned normalization (FreqCondNorm); pretraining on five datasets (CWRU, MFPT, UOC18, PRONOSTIA, CMAPSS) using masked auto-encoding and contrastive learning with balanced domain sampling.

Result: Fault diagnosis: 99.2% accuracy on CWRU (+6.4 percentage points vs. CNN); zero-shot MFPT accuracy 82.1%; strong cross-frequency transfer. No observed improvement in remaining useful life (RUL) prediction, suggesting pretraining objectives mismatch.

Conclusion: FreqCondNorm improves classification/detection transferability across frequencies but may require objective alignment or architectural tweaks to enhance RUL prediction; future work should investigate aligning pretraining tasks with RUL goals and domain generalization across equipment and operating conditions.

Abstract: Deep learning predictive maintenance models suffer from poor transferability across machines and operating conditions, especially when labelled data are scarce and signals span five orders of magnitude in sampling frequency (1 Hz to ~100 kHz). We propose FreqCondNorm, a Transformer-based architecture that introduces a FiLM-style frequency-conditioned normalization layer to unify heterogeneous time-series within a single model. The architecture is pretrained on five public predictive maintenance datasets (CWRU, MFPT, UOC18, PRONOSTIA, CMAPSS) using masked auto-encoding and contrastive learning with balanced domain sampling. On fault diagnosis, the model achieves 99.2% accuracy on CWRU (+6.4 pp over CNN) and 82.1% zero-shot accuracy on MFPT, demonstrating strong transfer across sampling frequencies. However, the approach does not improve remaining useful life prediction, suggesting a mismatch between pretraining and RUL objectives that warrants future investigation.

</details>


### [405] [Refuse, Decompose, Refresh: A Claim-Safe Protocol for Closed-Loop AI Evaluation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20538)
*Peiying Zhu,Sidi Chang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: A protocol to ensure claim safety in AI evaluation for closed-loop systems, featuring three actions (Refuse, Decompose, Refresh). Implemented in a simulational setting with 24 policy components and 3 demand regimes; results emphasize abstention, limited false admissions, and a move away from universal PASS/FAIL labels toward an executable contract linking support, calibration, and justified claims.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Reproducible AI evaluations can still make wrong claims in closed-loop systems where policy, observable states, and traceability affect conclusions. The work seeks a claim-safe framework that prevents overconfident conclusions when evaluation artifacts are insufficient or misaligned with the reference

Method: Aggregate-only simulator with 24 policy components, 3 demand regimes, 2 fault-mask families, and independent development/heldout seeds. Preregistered heldout: 1,440 cases, 21,600 partition rows. Protocol actions: Refuse, Decompose, Refresh. Treat distribution-shift alarms as requests to invalidate/recompute the reference map. Report results per regime-component; report protocol execution and structural hypotheses separately rather than a single PASS/FAIL. Key metrics: reference-admitted counts, runtime-admitted counts, abstention incorporation, stable false admission, NLL differences, drift logs.

Result: 55/72 regime-component units reference-admitted; 54/55 remained runtime-admitted; abstention part of result. Stable false admission 0/20 under a one-sided 95% upper bound of 0.1391 (frozen 0.20 rule). Across 540 unit-arm rows in 20 component clusters, cell-minus-traffic negative-log-likelihood difference = 0.1264 nats/row; 95% component-cluster CI [0.0593, 0.1918]. Drift log shows null streams trigger alarms differently across regimes; only middle regime matched the frozen detector reference. Proposes executable contract linking observable support, statistical calibration, and justified claims instead of a universal threshold.

Conclusion: The claim-safe protocol (Refuse/Decompose/Refresh) demonstrates a practical approach to credible evaluation in closed-loop AI, balancing abstention with admitted evidence and emphasizing reference-relative calibration. It advocates moving away from universal thresholds toward an executable contract that ties observable support, calibration, and justified claims.

Abstract: An AI evaluation can be perfectly reproducible and still support the wrong claim. This risk is acute in closed-loop systems: policy determines visited states, observable components, and which failures leave a measurable trace. We propose a claim-safe protocol with three actions. Refuse: abstain when a clean reference stream or matched runtime comparison lacks support. Decompose: report protocol execution, operational false admission, and structural hypotheses separately rather than as one PASS/FAIL label. Refresh: treat distribution-shift alarms as requests to invalidate and recompute a reference map, not as fault evidence. We instantiate the protocol in an aggregate-only simulator with 24 policy components, three demand regimes, two fault-mask families, and independent development and heldout seeds. The preregistered heldout contains 1,440 cases and 21,600 partition rows. Only 55/72 regime-component units were reference-admitted and 54/55 remained runtime-admitted, making abstention part of the result. Stable false admission was 0/20 represented components, with a one-sided exact 95% upper bound of 0.1391 under a frozen 0.20 rule. Within admitted units, affected clean traffic outpredicted nominal fault-cell fraction: across 540 unit-arm rows nested in 20 component clusters, the cell-minus-traffic negative-log-likelihood difference was 0.1264 nats per row, with a 95% component-cluster interval of [0.0593, 0.1918]. A drift log shows why "null" must be reference-relative: clean fault-null streams triggered 15/15, 0/15, and 14/15 alarms across three regimes, while only the middle regime matched the frozen detector reference. Rather than a universal threshold, we contribute an executable contract linking observable support, statistical calibration, and justified claims.

</details>


### [406] [Language-model groups overstate consensus when replaying human deliberation on a reasoning task](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20543)
*Tengfei Shao*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: LLM-agent groups show higher apparent consensus than humans on Wason tasks, with measurement choices (participation rate, final-state definition) drastically shaping full-consensus estimates; sensitivity analyses reveal persistent gaps between human and agent consensus that converge only under specific reparameterizations, while memorizable answers distort results. Simulated consensus fails to track actual accuracy and can bias estimates of human deliberation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To understand how participation and outcome definitions affect measured consensus in human-versus-LLM-deliberation studies and to assess whether simulated groups can validly approximate human collective cognition.

Method: 100 held-out human Wason groups were matched with LLM agent groups seeded with one belief-anchored agent per participant’s pre-discussion answer. The same scoring code was used for humans and agents. Across multiple human scoring definitions, and under two post-unblinding sensitivity analyses (submit-based and participation-matched), comparisons were made between humans and agents in chat and reasoning modes. A reparameterization removing the memorizable answer was also tested to assess robustness. 

Result: Human consensus estimates ranged from 24.0% to 57.0% depending on scoring; about 20% of participants never posted, while agents almost always posted. In post-unblinding analyses, gaps between agent and human consensus were 34.0–43.9 percentage points (submit-based) and 34.1–44.4 points (participation-matched). Both routes reduced different measurement asymmetries but converged within 0.5 percentage points. Without early stopping and after removing memorizable answers, reasoning-mode groups approached near-unanimous agreement, predominantly on incorrect answers. Simulated consensus failed to track actual collective accuracy, and belief-anchored agent groups biased human-outcome estimates in this setting.

Conclusion: The study highlights that scoring definitions and participation dynamics substantially shape measured consensus; even with matched procedures, simulated agent groups do not reliably mirror human deliberation and can bias estimates of collective cognition. A scoring-explicit framework is needed when using simulated groups to approximate human deliberative outcomes.

Abstract: Full-consensus rates are often treated as indicators of collective cognition, yet depend on how participation and final states are operationalized. We replayed 100 held-out human Wason groups with matched large language model (LLM) agent groups, seeding one belief-anchored agent per participant's pre-discussion answer and scoring agents and people with the same code. Across human scoring definitions, estimates ranged from 24.0% to 57.0%; about one fifth of participants never posted, whereas agents almost always did. Agent groups remained more consensual in two post-unblinding sensitivity analyses: the submit-based comparison (n = 98) yielded gaps of 34.0 and 43.9 percentage points for chat and reasoning modes, and the participation-matched comparison (n = 45) yielded gaps of 34.1 and 44.4 points. These complementary routes reduced different measurement asymmetries yet converged within 0.5 percentage points. The gap persisted without early stopping and under a reparameterization removing the memorizable answer; reasoning-mode groups then agreed nearly unanimously, mostly on incorrect answers. Simulated consensus did not track collective accuracy, and belief-anchored agent groups were biased estimators of the human group-outcome distribution in this setting. These analyses provide a scoring-explicit basis for assessing simulated-group estimates of human deliberative outcomes.

</details>


### [407] [Limits of Confidence in Diffusion](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20581)
*Russ Webb,Amitis Shidani,Alice Bizeul,Dan Busbridge*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Discrete diffusion with remasking reveals that matching training distributions requires conditional independence across written positions; per-position marginals can misrepresent dependencies; empirical test on ScanAndAdd confirms strong dependencies and significant distribution mismatch despite perfect per-sample metrics.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To understand how per-position factorization in discrete diffusion aligns with the training distribution and whether per-position marginals capture joint dependencies, given token interdependencies in domains like pixels, phonemes, and words.

Method: Provide theoretical arguments: a step matches the training distribution only if the written positions are conditionally independent given fixed tokens; show that no product of per-position distributions can match a dependent group; show that identical per-position marginals can correspond to different joint distributions; empirical verification on a synthetic task ScanAndAdd with a closed-form joint distribution; assess which groups of positions a confidence ranking writes are dependent; quantify distribution mismatch via total variation distance, compare to per-sample metrics.

Result: The analysis shows every group of two or more undetermined positions a confidence ranking writes is dependent; the generated distribution is 29× the sampling-noise floor in total variation, while per-sample metrics are 1.0.

Conclusion: Per-position marginals are insufficient to capture joint dependencies in discrete diffusion with remasking; to faithfully reflect training distributions, modeling joint dependencies is necessary; observed joint-distribution mismatch is substantial even when per-sample scores appear perfect.

Abstract: Discrete diffusion, including remasking and uniform-state samplers, generate a sequence by writing multiple token positions per step, drawing each from a per-position distribution and choosing which positions to write from those same distributions. For domains of general interest (pixels, phonemes, or words) there are inherent dependencies between tokens. We show that a step matches the training distribution only when the positions it writes are conditionally independent given the tokens already fixed, that no product of per-position distributions can match a dependent group, and that per-position distributions do not determine whether a group is dependent: two joint distributions can have identical per-position marginals while differing in which combinations of values occur. On ScanAndAdd, a synthetic task whose joint distribution is available in closed form, we verify that every group of two or more undetermined positions a confidence ranking writes is dependent, and measure the generated distribution to be $29\times$ the sampling-noise floor total variation while per-sample metrics are $1.0$.

</details>


### [408] [PAA: The Probabilistic Allen Algebra: A Generative and Complete Probabilistic Extension of Allen's Interval Relations](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20634)
*Julian Eggert*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Introduces Probabilistic Allen Algebra (PAA): a generative, probabilistic extension of Allen's interval algebra that models temporal relations via distributions over interval boundaries, yielding a scale-invariant, uncertainty-aware taxonomy that recovers the crisp algebra as tolerance vanishes; Monte-Carlo validated and released as an open Python package.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Crisp Allen relations fail to capture uncertainty in temporal information from language, perception, databases, and histories. A probabilistic, boundary-based framework is needed to express graded temporal relations and to preserve taxonomy under interval collapse.

Method: Time points are modeled as Gaussians; intervals have Gaussian midpoints and truncated-Gaussian durations. All relations are boundary-ordering predicates represented in a single probability space. Point-point relations use error functions; point-interval and interval-interval relations use multivariate Gaussian orthant probabilities from linear inequalities. A tolerance band gives positive measure to contact relations; with a single tolerance, the 13 relations form a partition and recover crisp Allen as tolerance → 0. Coarse predicates are unions of leaf relations; hierarchy persists as intervals collapse to points, reducing 13 relations to 5 and then 3. Each relation decomposes into correlation-aware temporal primitives (CIDOC CRM style). The framework is scale-invariant and separates graded expressions like "shortly before" from contact relations.

Result: Monte-Carlo validation across the probabilistic model. The authors provide an open, tested Python package implementing PAA.

Conclusion: The approach derives Allen's taxonomy from probabilistic foundations, enabling graded, uncertainty-aware temporal reasoning. It supports expressions such as "shortly before" and preserves hierarchy under interval reduction, with results validated by Monte Carlo and available as software.

Abstract: Allen's interval algebra is a qualitative calculus for temporal relations, but its thirteen base relations are crisp predicates over exact interval boundaries. This is inadequate for temporal information from language, perception, databases, or uncertain histories, where times, durations, and boundaries are uncertain and expressions such as "just before" or "roughly during" have graded meaning. We develop the probabilistic Allen algebra (PAA): a generative and complete extension in which relation probabilities are derived from distributions over interval boundaries rather than assigned as scores. Time points are Gaussian; intervals have Gaussian midpoints and truncated-Gaussian durations. Every relation is a boundary-ordering predicate in one common probability space: point-point relations reduce to error functions, and point-interval and interval-interval relations to multivariate Gaussian orthant probabilities induced by linear inequalities. Contact relations (meets, starts, finishes, equals) receive positive measure through a tolerance band, and under a single tolerance the thirteen relations form a true partition that recovers crisp Allen as the tolerance vanishes. The construction derives Allen's taxonomy rather than positing it: coarse predicates such as precedence, overlap, and containment are unions of leaves whose probabilities are leaf sums, and this hierarchy is preserved as intervals collapse to points and thirteen relations reduce to five and then three. Each relation further decomposes into correlation-aware temporal primitives in the spirit of CIDOC CRM. The algebra is scale-invariant and separates graded expressions such as "shortly before" from contact relations. All results are Monte-Carlo validated and shipped as an open, tested Python package.

</details>


### [409] [Ownership in AI-Assisted Everyday Tasks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20658)
*Megan Wei,Melanie Subbiah,Audrey Lee,Annya Dahmani,Dave Edwards,Helen Edwards,Ellie Pavlick*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Qualitative study on how AI affects perceived ownership of co-created work; ownership hinges on collaboration process and leadership in the task; disowning when simply approving AI input, retain ownership when leading/iterating; ownership can extend when one provides the vision but AI handles execution; high ownership when AI enables otherwise impossible tasks; loss of voice and lack of comprehension erode ownership; willingness to disclose AI use is shaped by norms and fear of credit erasure; proposes research directions to foster authorship alongside AI.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To understand how integrating AI into daily task work influences individuals' sense of authorship and ownership, addressing a gap in empirical knowledge about human-AI collaboration and ownership.

Method: Exploratory qualitative survey in which participants described two self-selected tasks completed with AI: one that felt like their own and one that did not; analysis of ownership perceptions across collaborative modes.

Result: Ownership depends on the collaboration process: disown when merely approving AI suggestions; retain ownership when leading, iterating, or rewriting; ownership can extend to scenarios where the user owns the project vision but AI handles execution; high ownership when AI enables tasks users could not complete without AI; loss of personal voice and lack of output comprehension erode ownership; willingness to disclose AI use is shaped by community norms and fear of credit erasure.

Conclusion: Recommend several research directions to develop AI tools and practices that sustain or enhance people's sense of authorship and control over their work and lives as AI becomes more integrated.

Abstract: When does work done with AI still feel like ours? As AI becomes woven into everyday tasks, we must examine what happens to our sense of ownership and contribution when a machine shares in producing what we make. We report an exploratory qualitative survey in which participants were asked to describe two recent, self-selected tasks completed with AI: one that felt like their own and one that did not. We find that felt ownership depends on the process of collaboration: people disown work when they merely approve AI's suggestions, but retain ownership when they lead, iterate, or rewrite. Ownership can also extend to settings where people own the vision for a project but not the execution; respondents reported high ownership on tasks they could not have completed without AI. Loss of personal voice and a lack of comprehension of the output both erode ownership. Finally, willingness to disclose AI use is often decoupled from actual pride or ownership, and instead shaped by community norms and fear of credit erasure. We propose several research directions as a result of these findings to promote AI development that supports people's sense of authorship over their own lives.

</details>


### [410] [Deep Noir: Autonomous Steering Discovery via Architectural Chronometry in Transformer Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20722)
*Frank E. Bobe,Gregory D. Vetaw,Darshan W. Bryner,Matthew G. Cook,Jose L. Salas-Vernis*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Deep Noir autonomously discovers steering parameters for LLMs using Logit Lens convergence and causal head attribution, yielding large performance gains on spam and SST-2 across multiple model scales, with generalization across tasks/architectures and a growing prompt-injection surface tied to steering magnitude.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Manual, ad-hoc steering at inference is brittle and difficult to optimize across models and tasks. An automated, mechanistic method is needed to locate and tune steering interventions that generalize.

Method: Introduce Deep Noir framework leveraging Logit Lens convergence and causal head-level attribution to autonomously identify optimal steering parameters. Evaluated across model scales 1B×3, 2–3B×2, and 7–9B×4, comparing against RepE innovations, and analyzing intervention points and attack surface.

Result: Spam: 16.7 percentage-point gain at 1B (sd 4.7; 39 runs); 21–42-point gains at 7–9B across four architectures. SST-2: 13.1-point improvement with zero code changes. RepE without head masking underperforms baseline on sentiment; Deep Noir improves all models (p<0.01). Mechanistic grounding enables generalization of intervention points across tasks/architectures. Steering increases a predictable prompt-injection attack surface, with vulnerability rising with steering magnitude.

Conclusion: Mechanistic grounding supports automated discovery of transferable intervention points for steering, improving performance across tasks and architectures, while also revealing security implications (attack surface) that escalate with steering magnitude in agent systems.

Abstract: Activation steering modifies LLM behavior at inference time, but identifying where and how strongly to steer remains manual. We introduce Deep Noir, a framework that uses Logit Lens convergence and causal head-level attribution to autonomously discover optimal steering parameters. Across three scales (1B x 3, 2-3B x 2, and 7-9B x 4), our engine achieves 16.7 percentage-point improvement on spam at 1B (standard deviation 4.7; 39 runs), with gains increasing to 21 to 42 percentage points at 7-9B across four architectures. On SST-2 sentiment, it achieves a 13.1 percentage-point improvement with zero code changes. Mechanistic grounding enables automated discovery of intervention points that generalize across tasks and architectures. On sentiment, RepE without head masking fails to improve over baseline, while Deep Noir improves all models (p less than 0.01). We further show that steering creates a predictable prompt-injection attack surface whose vulnerability increases monotonically with steering magnitude. This finding is relevant to agent systems deploying steered classifiers.

</details>


### [411] [Q&A on Any Spreadsheet Requires Interpreting Its Grid Structure](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20732)
*Zofia Smoleń*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Semantic cell annotation enables chunking spreadsheets into interpretable units for LLM-RAG, beating state-of-the-art but limited by intrinsic 2D structure; advocates dimensionality reduction to flatten spreadsheets into 1D text for easier retrieval and generation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Spreadsheets are 2D, unstructured data with continuous relationships; finite predefined cell classes cannot capture the full structural nuance, hindering interpretability and downstream LLM performance.

Method: Introduce a framework that splits a spreadsheet into interpretable chunks by annotating cell roles (cell-type classification) to guide chunk creation; uses discrete, pre-defined classes for cells.

Result: The framework achieves state-of-the-art performance in chunking interpretability but hits a hard ceiling due to the inherent limitation of discretizing 2D data into finite categories.

Conclusion: To overcome the bottleneck, move beyond discrete cell classification and pursue dimensionality-reduction methods to flatten 2D spreadsheets into 1D text, yielding text chunks that downstream RAG can interpret and generate from.

Abstract: Semantic cell annotation improves chunking interpretability for spreadsheets in LLM-driven RAG systems, aiding answer generation through enriched context rather than improved retrieval accuracy. We propose a novel framework of splitting any spreadsheet into interpretable chunks using cell role annotation. Our framework beats the state of the art, yet it faces a hard ceiling. Spreadsheets are fundamentally two-dimensional unstructured data with continuous relationships and infinite potential cell roles. Because classification models are restricted to finite, pre-defined classes, they cannot perfectly capture this structural nuance, even with human-level annotation. We show that addressing the spreadsheet-to-LLM bottleneck requires moving beyond discrete cell classification. Instead, the field must develop dimensionality-reduction techniques to directly flatten 2D unstructured spreadsheets into 1D unstructured text. Text chunks would be easier for downstream RAG to interpret and generate from.

</details>


### [412] [RAFT: A Stateful Retrieval-Augmented Framework for Troubleshooting Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20754)
*Mingxuan Zhang,Xiaowen Wang,Anupma Sharan,Zhengyi Chen,Chenyu Diana Zhang,Shanshan Yang,Chittibabu Pacharu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: RAFT: a stateful retrieval-augmented framework for troubleshooting that operates at the timeline-entry level within historical cases, optionally linking cases via a similarity graph; shows improved case-hit performance over vanilla RAG and GraphRAG on synthetic and real datasets; released benchmark and datasets.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current RAG systems treat support cases as static documents, neglecting multi-stage, stateful nature of troubleshooting, which impedes retrieval relevance for progressive case handling.

Method: Represent each historical case as a directed chain of timeline entries; retrieve at the entry level to surface intermediate-state matches and return the parent case trajectory anchored at the matched state; optionally connect cases with a case-level similarity graph.

Result: RAFT achieves higher Case Hit rates than vanilla RAG and GraphRAG at all stages of case progress with statistically significant gains; Jira data suggest transfer of advantage to real case histories; benchmark and datasets released.

Conclusion: RAFT provides an effective, reusable retrieval layer for stateful troubleshooting that improves retrieval quality without requiring full production deployment; the released benchmark and datasets support reproducibility and broader evaluation.

Abstract: Effective troubleshooting agents in enterprise customer support depend on retrieving actionable guidance from similar historical cases, yet existing retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) systems treat support cases as static documents and overlook their multi-stage, stateful nature. We introduce RAFT (Retrieval-Augmented Framework for Troubleshooting Agents), a stateful RAG framework that abstracts each closed historical case into a directed chain of timeline entries and retrieves at the entry level, surfacing cases whose intermediate states match the active case and returning the parent-case trajectory anchored at the matched state; an optional case-level graph links cases through a configurable similarity representation. We evaluate this retrieval layer directly, which, unlike evaluating a full agent system, requires no production deployment. Because public multi-stage troubleshooting data is extremely rare, we pair a synthetic benchmark built from Microsoft Learn Windows Server documentation with real Apache Jira issues carrying human-created duplicate labels. RAFT improves Case Hit over vanilla RAG and GraphRAG baselines at every stage of case progress, with statistically significant gains over the strongest baseline; the Jira results provide directional evidence that the advantage transfers to real case histories. We release our benchmark, implementation, and the Apache Jira evaluation set.

</details>


### [413] [An Empirical Study of Harness Design for Coding Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20804)
*Run-Ze Fan,Zihao Zhang,Simin Ma,Yebowen Hu,Shouju Wang,Kaiqiang Song,Fei Liu,Hamed Zamani,Xiaoyang Wang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: A modular coding-harness study shows context management, planning, and action-space choices affect long-horizon autonomous coding performance, with effects depending on model strength and context-window budgets; provides a framework for component-level evaluation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To enable component-level comparison of harnesses for LLM-driven software tasks and understand how each component contributes to performance and cost.

Method: Fixed-loop lightweight harness; vary planning, action space, and context-management strategies; 4 models; 176 settings; 5 context-management strategies; 4 context-window budgets; targeted ablations; trajectory-level analysis; tasks SWE-Bench Verified and Terminal-Bench 2.1.

Result: Context-management gains grow as context window tightens, mainly by preventing context-overflow; staging elision before LLM summarization is most efficient; elided content recoverability adds little; planning shifts from accuracy to cost-saving with model strength; predefined tools help weaker models; bash-capable models can use bash-only interface at lower cost; trajectory analysis indicates these components influence where trajectories stop and granularity of code-writing.

Conclusion: Findings inform budget- and model-aware harness design and provide a modular framework for evaluating future harness components.

Abstract: Coding harnesses shape how autonomous coding agents translate model capabilities into long-horizon software-engineering performance, yet existing work typically evaluates harnesses as monolithic systems, leaving the effectiveness of individual components unclear. To enable component-level comparisons, we study this question with a lightweight coding harness whose execution loop is fixed while three components are varied: planning, action space, and context management. Across four models evaluated on SWE-Bench Verified and Terminal-Bench 2.1, we evaluate 176 matched settings spanning five context-management strategies, four context-window budgets, and targeted ablations of planning and action space. We find that: (1) Context management becomes increasingly valuable as the context-window budget tightens, with most of its benefit coming from preventing context-overflow failures. (2) Staging rule-based elision before LLM-based summarization provides the strongest overall efficiency among the context-management strategies, whereas making elided content recoverable adds machinery that models rarely use and yields no accuracy gain. (3) Planning shifts from an accuracy scaffold for weaker models to a cost saver for stronger models, with little change in accuracy. (4) Predefined tools improve performance for models with weaker bash proficiency, whereas bash-capable models can operate effectively with a bash-only interface and achieve substantially lower cost, especially on command-line-centric tasks. Trajectory-level analysis explains these effects: context management extends execution trajectories without substantially altering agent behavior, planning changes where trajectories stop, and the action space changes the granularity at which code is written. These findings inform model- and budget-aware harness design and provide a modular framework for evaluating future harness components.

</details>
